->THEY ARE OCCUPIED IN THESE THREE<- <note>original: "VERSANTUR HIS TRIBUS." This cryptic motto likely refers to the three kingdoms of nature—animal, vegetable, and mineral—from which early modern pharmacists sourced their ingredients, or perhaps the three primary actions of the apothecary: selecting, preparing, and dispensing.</note>

# LIST OF AUTHORS
## AND TREATISES OF THE SECOND PART.

Gaston Claveus. <note>Also known as Gaston Le Doux (c. 1530–1595), a French lawyer and alchemist who defended the possibility of transmutation against contemporary critics.</note> *An Apology for Gold-making and Silver-making* <note>original: "Chrysopœiæ & Argyropœiæ." These are Greek-derived terms for the alchemical creation of gold and silver respectively.</note> *against Thomas Erastus: in which it is debated and taught whether it is, what it is, and how it is done.* <note>Thomas Erastus was a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his fierce intellectual attacks on Paracelsus and alchemical theory.</note>

Giles de Vadis. <note>original: "Ægidii de Vadis." A 14th-century alchemist whose works were highly regarded for their philosophical depth.</note> *A Dialogue between Nature and a Son of Philosophy.*

*A Table explaining the names of various metals which the ancients used to conceal the art.* <note>Alchemists used "decknamen" (cover-names) to hide their recipes from the uninitiated; this table acts as a decoder.</note>

George Ripley. <note>original: "Georgii Riplæi." One of the most famous English alchemists (c. 1415–1490), known for his "Twelve Gates."</note> *A Summary of the Twelve Gates, arranged in two ways.*

Albertus Magnus. <note>original: "Alberti Magni." A 13th-century Dominican friar and Bishop, though many alchemical works were later attributed to him to lend them his immense authority as a scholar.</note> *A Brief Compendium on Minerals.*

Isaac Hollandus. <note>The "Hollandus" names (Isaac and John Isaac) are associated with highly practical, laboratory-focused Dutch alchemical writings from the 15th or 16th century.</note> *A Fragment on the Work of the Philosophers.*

Bernard Gilles Penot. <note>original: "Bernardi G. Penoti." A French doctor and alchemist (c. 1519–1617) who traveled widely in Europe and corresponded with many major scholars of his day.</note> *Three questions concerning bodily Mercury: whether, if extracted by art from perfect bodies* <note>original: "corporibus perfectis," referring to gold and silver.</note> *and mixed with its own body, it contributes to the generation of the Physical Stone,* <note>original: "lapidis Physici." This refers to the Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its role in the physical transformation of matter.</note> *as is the firm opinion of some.*

> *A response to various questions.*
> 
> *Fifty-seven Rules concerning the Physical Work, by which the art is made clearer.*
> 
> *The true extraction of Mercury from gold, with its history.*
> 
> *Chrysorrhoas,* <note>original: "Chrysorrhoas." A Greek name meaning "Streaming with Gold," often used as a title for works claiming to reveal the true path to wealth or enlightenment.</note> *or a Dialogue on the Chemical Art, which demonstrates that the most excellent actions of this art are consistent with reason and natural principles: and exposes the dreams and trifles of impostors and sycophants.*

# LIST OF CONTENTS <note>original: "ELENCHVS"</note>

Joseph Quercetanus of Armenia. <note>Also known as Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), he was a French physician to King Henry IV and a major proponent of Paracelsian medicine, which emphasized chemical remedies over traditional herbal ones.</note> *A response to the abusive letter of Jacques Aubert of Vendôme concerning the origin and causes of metals.* <note>Jacques Aubert was a vocal critic of the chemical philosophy; this response is a spirited defense of the "new" chemistry of the 16th century.</note>

John Dee of London. <note>A world-renowned Elizabethan polymath, mathematician, and advisor to Queen Elizabeth I.</note> *The Hieroglyphic Monad.* <note>original: "Monas Hieroglyphica." First published in 1564, this is one of the most famous works of Western esotericism. It uses a single complex symbol to represent the unity of the cosmos, combining the signs for the sun, moon, elements, and the zodiac sign Aries.</note>

Lorenzo Ventura. <note>A 16th-century Venetian physician and alchemist.</note> *A book on the method of preparing the Philosophers' Stone.*

Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola. <note>The nephew of the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He wrote this treatise in 1515 to argue that the transmutation of metals was possible and consistent with Catholic doctrine.</note> *On Gold.*

Roger Bacon. <note>A 13th-century English Franciscan friar and philosopher (c. 1214–1292) known as "Doctor Mirabilis." He is celebrated for his early emphasis on the experimental method.</note> *The Mirror of Alchemy.*

Richard the Englishman. <note>Often identified with Richard of Wendover, a 13th-century physician. This text was highly influential in the late Middle Ages.</note> *The Correctorium.* <note>original: "Correctorium." A title implying a "correction" or a guidebook to the proper path of the alchemical work.</note>

*The Lesser Rosary, on the knowledge of metallic things.* <note>original: "Rosarius Minor." An anonymous medieval alchemical text, part of a genre of "Rosaries" (rose gardens) that collected the "flowers" of alchemical wisdom.</note>

Albert the Great. <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican bishop and teacher of Thomas Aquinas. He was one of the most prolific scholars of the Middle Ages, though many alchemical texts were attributed to him by later writers to gain authority.</note> *On Alchemy.*

Giovanni Agostino Pantheo. <note>A 16th-century Venetian priest and alchemist.</note> *The Art and Theory of metallic transmutation, together with the Voarchadumia, illustrated with numbers and images suited to the subject.* <note>"Voarchadumia" is a term Pantheo invented, likely from Hebrew and Chaldean roots, to describe a "holy" alchemy or a "liberal art" of metal-working that he distinguished from common, fraudulent alchemy.</note>

## TO THE READER

# PREFACE OF BERNARD G. PENO-
# TUS OF PORT-SAINTE-MARIE IN AQUI-
# TAINE, IN WHICH HE SHOWS

### *that the entire power and efficacy of the whole art consists in two words.* <note>These "two words" likely refer to the famous alchemical maxim *Ora et Labora* (Pray and Work), which appears at the end of this passage, or perhaps *Solve et Coagula* (Dissolve and Congeal), the fundamental process of the Work.</note>

*THERE is no reason (friend Reader) for me to rub open those long-debated questions in which it is asked: Whether the Art of transmutations* <note>original: "Ars transmutationum," referring to the alchemical transformation of base metals into gold.</note> *is true; since in the year just passed, I have proven it sufficiently and more than enough by the testimonies and authorities of the most serious men, and since many books have been published on this subject. Therefore, I refer my readers to that preface which I not long ago prefixed to that "Dialogue which is between Nature and the Son of Philosophy."* <note>Penot refers here to his own earlier work, typically an introduction to a text by the 14th-century alchemist Bernard of Trevisan.</note> *It would indeed be ridiculous if I used repetitions at present; since the Author of this book,* CLAVEUS, <note>Gaston Le Doux de Claves (c. 1530–1595), a French lawyer and alchemist who wrote vigorous defenses of the craft.</note> *disputing against* THOMAS *Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his fierce intellectual attacks on Paracelsus and the validity of alchemy.</note> *and solidly refuting all his arguments with the strongest reasons as well as demonstrations (add also certain experiments), shows and confirms that the Art is true, certain, and easy. For this reason, you who wish the truth of the Art to be proved to you by authorities and examples (Reader), run through this book of* CLAVEUS. *But before you begin to work, weigh the causes of natural things with prudent counsel, or do not approach the task at all. The incautious, looking at this book at first glance, will become entangled. You (friend Reader) read with great judgment, reread, pray, and work,* <note>original: "ora, labora." This is the foundational spiritual and physical command of alchemy: success requires both divine grace through prayer and physical effort in the laboratory.</note> *and the God of mysteries*

<summary>This preface by Bernard G. Penot introduces a defense of alchemy by Gaston Claveus, arguing against critics like Thomas Erastus and emphasizing that the "Art" is both a physical and spiritual pursuit.</summary>
<keywords>Bernard G. Penot, Gaston Claveus, Thomas Erastus, alchemy, transmutation, Ora et Labora, Aquitaine, Paracelsianism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface by Bernard Georges Penot. In the previous page, Penot addressed the reader regarding the validity of the alchemical art and introduced the author of the current work, Gaston Le Doux de Claves (Claveus), noting Claves’s defense of alchemy against critics like Thomas Erastus.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

...the author will have mercy on you. One thing I do not wish to remain hidden from you: all power and the efficacy of the entire art consists in two words, namely, **DISSOLVE & CONGEAL** <note>original: "SOLVE & COAGVLA," the central axiom of alchemy describing the process of breaking down a substance to its essence and then rebuilding it into a perfected form.</note>.

<margin>The solution is twofold. Solution through Mercurial water relates to the universal work.</margin>
The solution is twofold. The first dissolves bodies into Mercury, which is done through Mercury itself. This was discovered for "particulars" <note>Lesser alchemical works aiming at specific transmutations rather than the universal Stone or Elixir.</note>, a path which the Author of this book follows. The second solution, however, is into Mercurial water. This belongs to the universal work. It is a certain transmutation of metallic bodies into their own first matter <note>original: "primā materiam," the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made.</note>. The learned Author of this work denies that this can be done, and claims that the spirits of minerals cannot be fixed <note>rendered solid and non-volatile</note> with perfected bodies; he contradicts Raymond Lully <note>A legendary 13th-century philosopher and alchemist, though the alchemical works attributed to him are now considered to be by later authors.</note> and calls that impossible. I do not follow his opinion. Indeed, I prove the contrary by the authorities of many men of this Art. For **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note> says concerning gold in the third part of the *Perfect Magistery*, chapter 32:

<margin>GEBER’S opinion is worthy of note.</margin>
> Gold is also the most precious of Metals, and it is the tincture of redness, because it tints and transmutes every body; it is calcined and dissolved with benefit and without benefit, and it is a medicine that brings joy and preserves the body in youth. It is easily broken with Mercury, and is worn down by the scent of Saturn <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note>. **Jupiter** <note>tin</note> and **Luna** <note>silver</note> agree with it in substance. <margin>Take great note of this.</margin> In weight and putrefaction, **SATURN** <note>lead</note> agrees, and finally **Mars** <note>iron</note>. And it is one of the greatest secrets of nature. Spirits are likewise mixed with it and are fixed through it with the greatest ingenuity—something that does not reach the craftsman of a stiff neck and heart. Thus says **GEBER**.

From the **LADDER** of the Philosophers <note>original: "SCALA philosoph.," referring to the *Scala Philosophorum*, a well-known alchemical treatise.</note>: Spirits are congealed by the benefit of the dissolution of the fixed nature and of the body, and of its mixing with quicksilver. And another says: Fix therefore earth and water, so that air can be fixed in water; for if you have "killed" the water well, you have killed all the elements, and they are dead.

<margin>The little book called the *Seven Keys of the Art* should be sought out.</margin>
Thus far. Read more about these things in the book titled *The Seven Keys of the Art*, which I shall one day publish, along with a treatise on Mercurial waters, by which any metals are reduced into running Mercury—if eternal **GOD** the Greatest should wish us to remain among the living. In the meantime, [friendly reader] enjoy these things and farewell; look with favor upon our late-night labors.

<summary>This page concludes the preface, emphasizing the core alchemical principle of "Solve et Coagula" and debating the possibility of returning metals to their "first matter." Penot cites authorities like Geber and the "Ladder of the Philosophers" to argue for the universal work against the more limited approach of the author Claveus.</summary>
<keywords>Solve et Coagula, Geber, Raymond Lully, first matter, transmutation, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Scala Philosophorum, alchemical solvent</keywords>

# A DEFENSE OF
# SILVER-MAKING AND
# GOLD-MAKING.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
Upon hearing the title of this Apology <note>A formal defense or justification of a position.</note> or defense, many will immediately condemn this new subject of discussion as an Introduction <note>original: "Exordiū"</note> that is foreign to our profession. But even more will charge me with recklessness because I dare to clash with so powerful an adversary as **Thomas Erastus** <note>A Swiss-German physician and theologian (1524–1583) famous for his fierce intellectual opposition to Paracelsian medicine and alchemy.</note>, a German Physician and most excellent Philosopher, in a matter that has been judged against so many times before. Furthermore, I contend to pronounce something certain and true in a matter so hidden <note>original: "abstrusa"</note>, and hitherto unknown to many most distinguished men across many centuries. Many, as human temperaments vary, will judge this our Apology or defense of **Silver-making** <note>original: "Argyropœiæ"</note> and **Gold-making** <note>original: "Chrysopœiæ"</note> in various ways. To all of them, I wish it to be answered that I cannot be called away from this my undertaking by any of their judgments, as long as I believe it benefits the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipubl."</note>, to which we all owe the greater part of our fortunes. Indeed, as human inclinations vary by nature, whenever I have had leisure, I have diligently read through the volumes of the ancients who have treated this subject. I have explored the nature of metals through my own examinations, and I have heard and consulted those who were thought to excel others in knowing the secrets of this art. I have attempted many things for many years now; and the same labor that great men have spent during their spare hours in unfolding books foreign to their own profession, I have at times spent in the study of this art during those same hours. Nor was there any other goal than the desire to acknowledge the truth, which every honorable man ought to embrace with all his strength.

<margin>The writings of the ancients are obscure.</margin>
I have found the writings of the ancients to be truly all enigmatic, and like the oracles of Apollo, handed down without any system of art, so that I have departed from reading them more uncertain than when I first approached them. 

<margin>Geber.</margin>
Only **Geber the Arab** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), an influential polymath considered a founder of early chemistry; his works were the "gold standard" for medieval alchemists.</note> seems to have handed down this art with some order and method; but, as he himself confesses in the final chapter of his *Summ of Perfection* <note>original: "summæ perfectionis," one of the most famous alchemical textbooks in the Latin West.</note>, where he spoke most openly, there he most concealed his art. He also mixed many sophistical and useless things with the true and useful, and more than...

<summary>In this opening of the treatise, Gaston Le Doux de Claves introduces his defense of alchemy (specifically the making of silver and gold) and acknowledges the controversy of opposing the famous critic Thomas Erastus. He justifies his study as a search for truth and notes that while ancient alchemical texts are confusingly symbolic, only Geber offers a systematic, albeit intentionally obscured, method.</summary>
<keywords>Argyropoeia, Chrysopoeia, Thomas Erastus, Geber, alchemy, metals, Summa Perfectionis, scientific method, defense of alchemy</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s introductory defense. He moves from his initial justification for writing to his specific goal: protecting the public from the financial ruin and deception often associated with poorly understood alchemy. He draws on his background as a lawyer to justify why a man of the law is writing about a "secret" art.</meta>

->### DEFENSE<-

...many expected a metamorphosis <note>original: "metamorphofin," referring here to the physical transformation of base metals into gold</note> from his books, yet they experienced it only in themselves: so much so that they turned from rich men into paupers, and from honorable men they came to be held as shameful. I see that this same thing has happened to those who follow the writings of others that are supported by no reason, but merely passed down from hand to hand; through such experience, these men are seen to become miserable and beggars. When I weighed all these things in my mind, I thought I would bring some fruit to the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reip." or "Res publica," meaning the state or the common good</note> 

<margin>*The Author’s purpose.*</margin>

if I were to bring to light how truly this Art could subsist, doing so openly and with a certain method, having exploded all ambiguities, as far as the powers of the mind allow. For in this way, it will happen that those who are held in so hidden a matter more by a zeal for acknowledging the truth than a desire for acquiring wealth will perhaps not regret having read these pages. Indeed, those who have wasted oil and labor <note>A classical idiom for wasting time and effort on a fruitless task</note> until now might finally amend their own errors and those of their authors, and begin to be wise. Furthermore, those who have not yet tasted anything of these matters, if they should happen to apply themselves to study, might enter the right path and never be able to wander thereafter. All, moreover, who read and understand these things, shall be safe from the tricks and frauds of impostors and sophists <note>original: "sophistarum," used here to mean deceptive charlatans or people who use clever but false arguments</note>. What, I ask, is more useful or more human than to show the right way to those traveling a path they do not know, and to call them back to the same if they should happen to wander? Nor can anyone, except by injury, condemn this my project as if it were alien to that art which I profess <note>i.e., the law</note>. For questions often arise in forensic judgments which seem alien to the responses of legal experts <note>original: "Iureconfultorum"</note>, such as about the medical art, and about very many other arts, which nevertheless those who plead cases should be ashamed to be ignorant of; for this reason, they are often compelled to consult experts of the art before they can defend their clients.

<margin>*An Example.*</margin>

I remember a few years ago in our court at Nevers <note>original: "Niuernenfi," a city in central France where the author practiced law</note>, while I was still pleading cases, that this very question was handled. A certain citizen of this city, intending to buy a chain from someone whom he did not then know was an impostor, and which the seller asserted was gold, had commanded the same to be proven by the test of a touchstone <note>original: "lapis lydij," the Lydian stone used to test the purity of precious metals</note> by a goldsmith <note>original: "fabro aurario"</note>. That test having been immediately performed in the presence of the buyer, the metalworker reported that the chain was golden and consisted of pure gold. Relying on this confidence, the citizen bought the chain as if it consisted of pure gold. A short time later, when one link <note>original: "fibula," a clasp or buckle</note> of the same chain was broken, it was discovered to be only silver inside, but golden on the outside and on the surface. The buyer, the fraud having been immediately recognized, contended against the goldsmith for damages and interest <note>original: "damnis & intereffe," a legal term for compensation</note>, because he had been deceived by the goldsmith's affirmation...

<meta>catchword: buying-</meta>

<summary>The author explains his intent to provide a clear, honest method for alchemy to protect seekers from the ruinous deceptions of charlatans. He justifies his legal perspective on the subject by recounting a court case from Nevers involving a fraudulent "gold" chain that was merely silver-plated.</summary>

<keywords>alchemy, metamorphosis, Commonwealth, legal ethics, Nevers, goldsmith, fraud, touchstone, damages and interest, professional expertise</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s introductory defense, specifically recounting a legal case he adjudicated to illustrate the practical need for metallurgical knowledge, before transitioning into a critique of Thomas Erastus and the "ancients" who obscured the art of alchemy.</meta>

-># SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING<-

...had bought [it], as if he were held at fault for the ignorance of his own craft. On the other hand, the goldsmith <note>original: "faber aurarius"</note> argued that he had only been asked for a test by the Lydian stone <note>The "lapis lydius" or touchstone, used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave behind</note>, which he had reported truly, but that he had not attempted a test with a chisel <note>original: "scalprum," a tool used to scrape or cut into the metal to see what lies beneath the surface</note>, and had received no payment for that specific task. Being consulted by a most wise and noble man, who is now my colleague, as to what I thought should be judged, I replied: if the necklace were only gilded <note>original: "deauratus," meaning surface-level gold plating</note>, the judgment ought to be given against the goldsmith, because the gilding alone could have been detected by repeated testing with the Lydian stone. But if, in truth, the gold had been attached to the surface while the body of the necklace remained a distinct substance underneath, the goldsmith would be protected by the legal exception and should be acquitted, because such a thing could by no means be judged by the Lydian stone, but only by the chisel. Immediately after this interlocutory decree <note>A provisional court order</note> was issued, a test by nitric acid <note>original: "aqua acri," literally "sharp water," a common term for nitric acid used to separate gold from silver</note> was performed on one of the filaments; we saw the body of gold remain at the bottom of the glass vessel, while the silver was poured out and dissolved in the nitric acid. If it had been mere gilding, it would have settled at the bottom of the same glass vessel as an impalpable and very thin powder. When the buyer learned this, he withdrew from the lawsuit, for he foresaw a prejudicial judgment. But the case could not have been so judged unless goldsmiths had been consulted on this matter and their advice obtained.

Indeed, Erastus was a man of the highest authority, but he was a man, and he was ignorant of many arts, even easy ones, which men of weaker intellect did not ignore. He brought forward many universal propositions, but he was ignorant of those which are proper and peculiar to this art. As for others, let them value this undertaking of mine as they will. I write only for those who judge rightly—not with an unheard cause, but after all things have been examined and weighed from both sides—and who look upon and venerate the secrets of God. Nor let anyone impute it to me as a vice or a crime if I bring to light things that have been hidden until now.

For if they were allowed to hide the method of operation, they at least ought to have opened up the reasons and causes from which, by which, through which, and for which the art can exist; which I see has been performed by none of them.

# APOLOGIA

...[silver-making] can be discovered, however clearly and truly it is committed to writing, unless it is handled by the hands of one most skilled and highly experienced in the principles of the art. <margin>The sum of this treatise.</margin> Yet speculation alone is most pleasant, and refreshes minds weighed down by more serious studies. Now therefore, all you who are the keenest searchers of secrets and the greatest lovers of truth, come hither; for I shall lay open for you things worthy of admiration, which have never been clearly and truly committed to writing by anyone, and I shall illustrate them with physical definitions, divisions, and demonstrations, as much as can be done. <margin>The age of the author.</margin> In a single moment you will grasp whatever I—now an old man of sixty years—have been able to understand through many meditations and experiments since nearly thirty-five years ago, when leisure allowed, so that I might investigate whether this art truly exists. <margin>The method of procedure is not treated here.</margin> However, I shall remain silent regarding the method of procedure <note>The author refers to the "Praxis" or the specific laboratory steps of the "Great Work," which alchemists often kept secret</note>, nor shall I touch upon it except generally, as far as the necessity of the question to be proved—whether the art exists—incumbents upon me.

<margin>The Proposition.</margin> Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss-German physician and theologian famous for his fierce opposition to Paracelsus and alchemy</note>, a German by nation and a Professor in the school of Heidelberg, published a book to which he gave the title, *On the New Medicine of Paracelsus, Part One* <note>original: "De medicina nova Paracelsi, Pars prima"</note>. That book was printed in Basel by Peter Perna in the year of our Lord 1572. When I had read through this book in my successive spare hours, I saw toward the end this question treated by Erastus: *Whether from quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note> or more ignoble metals transmuted, true, legitimate, natural, and pure gold or silver can be made by art.* At length, with many and most powerful arguments, and from the authority of those who excel in judgment and erudition, he constantly denies that it can be done. I, however, constantly affirm that from silver, lead, tin, copper, iron, and also from quicksilver, gold can be made; and from these latter five, true, legitimate, natural, and pure silver can be made, by natural causes with art acting as the minister. These are the two opinions, diametrically opposed. I undertake the defense of the latter opinion; and that is exactly what I shall endeavor to provide in this Apology. Indeed, if anyone has ever attacked this art with the most powerful arguments, Erastus alone is the greatest philosopher of them all and possessed of consummate erudition. But the victory will be all the more distinguished if I prevail in this part of philosophy, which I am confident I can achieve. And although for the proof of the proposed question—namely, that Silver-making <note>original: "Argyropœiam"</note> and Gold-making <note>original: "Chryſopœiam"</note> are a true art—experience alone would suffice, which holds the place of a demonstration, nevertheless, so that the matter may be clearer and more manifest, I have deemed it necessary to dig deeper.

### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING

<margin>The definition of Silver-making & Gold-making.</margin>
<term>Silver-making</term> <note>original: "Argyropœia"</note> and <term>Gold-making</term> <note>original: "Chrysopœia"</note> is the art which teaches how to advance matter that is naturally very close to gold and silver, by means of natural efficient causes, into the form of silver or gold. And so that the definition may be explained, I said it is an "art" that moves natural causes; this is to distinguish it from "nature" itself, which, by its own power alone and without the help of any other, produces silver and gold from its own principles and causes. I also said that the matter is moved by *natural causes*, so that, insofar as the matter and the efficient causes are considered, the method of making silver and gold depends on nature. However, insofar as the artist submits nature’s own proper matter to it so that it may act, this management is proper to the art. This is how many arts are defined, such as Agriculture and Medicine; their effects are natural, but because they provide specific instructions that are proper and peculiar to the art, they are said to "produce" these effects.

<margin>By an analogy.</margin>
Thus, one who provides eggs to a hen so that she may sit on them until they are hatched, or who fosters them by mimicking the heat of the hen so that chicks are generated, is said to "produce" the chicks—even though this birth depends on the natural power implanted in the eggs. In the same way, the practitioners of Silver-making and Gold-making are said to "produce" silver and gold, while they, like servants, submit the proximate matter <note>The "proximate matter" refers to the starting substance that is chemically closest to the desired metal</note> and provide the instructions by which the same are made by a natural efficient cause.

<margin>What Art is.</margin>
Thus <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The author refers to the Aristotelian idea of the "four causes," specifically the efficient cause as the source of change</note> established that "art" is certainly that from which all movement ultimately proceeds. I added in the definition that it is necessary for the "proximate matter" to be submitted to the gold and silver, because everything cannot be made from any matter indiscriminately. Rather, it must be made
<margin>What the matter is.</margin>
from that matter alone which is ready to take on a certain form from an efficient cause without any intermediate step; this will become more manifest in the progress of this work. Finally, and in the last place, it was added that this proximate matter must be "advanced into the form of silver and gold," so it may be understood that the very same silver and the very same gold are made by nature—with Art as its servant—as are produced by nature alone.

<margin>The division of Silver-making and Gold-making.</margin>
From this definition, it seems to me that this art of Silver-making and Gold-making should be divided into three parts.
<margin>Part I: Knowledge of the nature of metals.</margin>
The first of these will be the knowledge of the nature of metals, just as nature itself has brought them forth into the light of its own accord. For since art, serving nature, strives to produce the very same silver and gold that nature produces, it could in no way achieve this if the nature of metals were unknown—especially that of silver and gold—so that it might produce exactly the same things.
<margin>Part II: Knowledge of the proximate matter and the efficient cause.</margin>
The second part will be the knowledge of the proximate matter of silver and gold, and of the efficient cause that moves it toward the form of silver and gold

# APOLOGIA

...and of gold, with the art clearly serving as a minister to nature. <margin>Part III. The method of operation.</margin>
The second part <note>The author likely means the latter part of his division mentioned on the previous page.</note> will be the method, or way of acting. This belongs to art alone and does not mimic nature indiscriminately, except insofar as it leads to the same goal and end toward which nature leads.

<margin>The order of topics to be discussed.</margin>
We will therefore treat these three parts of <term>Silver-making</term> <note>original: "Argyropœia"</note> and <term>Gold-making</term> <note>original: "Chrysopœia"</note> in order, through which we will defend our position. Next, we will confirm it with certain experiments. Finally, we will respond to the arguments of Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his fierce opposition to alchemy and Paracelsian medicine.</note>: thus the end of this *Apologia* [Defense] will be reached. But before we investigate the nature of metals, we think it is appropriate to explore nature in all composite bodies—briefly and generally—as this subject is otherwise to be drawn more fully from the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicis"</note>.

<margin>The nature of all things is recognized by their causes.</margin>
Thus it happens that, once the nature of all things is known in general, there is an easier path to penetrating the nature of metals. The nature of all composite bodies is recognized from their causes. For to know something, as Aristotle says in the first book of the *Physics*, is to know it through its causes.

<margin>The causes of things are four.</margin>
The causes are the **material**, the **formal**, the **efficient**, and the **final**. The material cause is that out of which something is made; for in nature, nothing is made except from pre-existing matter or a "subject." The formal cause is that which gives "being" to a thing, and by which the thing receives its name. The efficient cause is the cause that moves matter toward some end. The final cause is that for the sake of which the efficient cause moves the matter.

<margin>The division of matter. Remote matter.</margin>
There is a division of **Matter**: one kind is **remote**, another **intermediate**, and another **proximate**. "Remote matter" is said to be that which will undergo many changes and take on many forms before it takes on the form of any of the four types of natural bodies.

<margin>The four types of bodies.</margin>
These four types of bodies are the **composite** <note>mineral/mixed</note>, the **vegetable**, the **sensible** <note>animal</note>, and the **rational** or intelligent <note>human</note>. This remote matter is at a great distance from each of these. This is <term>Primary Matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima"</note>, which is understood only by the imagination and the intellect, not by the senses. Likewise, the four first principles of things are **earth, water, air, and fire**. For before those, no other matter can be imagined.

<margin>Intermediate matter.</margin>
**Intermediate matter** <note>original: "materia media"</note> is between the remote and the proximate; it is indeed closer to the forms of these four types of bodies...

...than <term>remote matter</term> <note>original: "materia remota"; refers to the basic elements (earth, air, fire, water) before they are shaped into a specific substance</note>, but it differs more from those same forms than <term>proximate matter</term> <note>original: "materia proxima"; matter that has been prepared and is ready to take on a specific final form</note>. For example, food is closer to the body of an animal than the basic Elements are, yet it is further away than the blood, which is produced from that food.

<margin>Proximate matter.</margin>
Proximate matter is that which most closely approaches the form; it is, as it were, something imperfect when compared to the more perfect form of another body. This proximate matter is like the seed of each kind in <term>univocal generations</term> <note>reproduction where the offspring is the same species as the parent</note>, or that which takes the place of the seed in <term>equivocal generations</term> <note>reproduction from different or inorganic sources, such as the historical belief that insects could spring from decaying matter</note>. <margin>The four kinds of forms.</margin>
Moreover, there are four natural kinds of forms which have been mentioned: namely, the form of simple mixtures, the vegetable form, the sensible [animal] form, and the rational and intelligent [human] form. These possess the character of "form" more than of "matter," because it is from them that every effect is produced; matter, however, exists only in potentiality—it does not act, but properly speaking, it is acted upon.

<margin>Division of the efficient cause.</margin>
The <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the agent or force that brings something into being</note> can be divided in various ways, but let this one suffice for now: that one is universal, and the other is particular.

<margin>The universal efficient cause.</margin>
The universal cause is God—the highest, best, and greatest—who in the beginning, acting alone from Himself by His infinite power without any other causes, created all things from nothing. But when, after the world was created by Him, He willed that the same things be reproduced naturally and without miracles from those things already created, He entrusted these duties to the heavens and the stars as universal causes. He did this in such a way, however, that God Himself always concurs with these and with the particular causes. Therefore, these universal causes produce all these things of different kinds or different species that are seen in this totality of the world. <margin>Equivocal.</margin> They are called "equivocal" because they impart themselves equally to all things and are the causes of diverse effects.

<margin>The particular efficient cause. Univocal.</margin>
The particular efficient cause, however, is that which acts only upon proximate matter—or upon a subject disposed toward it—and produces an effect of a single species or quality. It is called "univocal," such as the force and faculty in every seed which moves it until it reaches its intended end.

<margin>The final cause.</margin>
The "end" or <term>final cause</term> <note>the purpose or goal for which a thing exists</note> in these same bodies, which are formed from the mixing of the Elements, is that the "form" may be achieved. In the study of Nature <note>original: "Physicis"</note>, the end is the same as the form.

### DEFENSE

...is distinguished by the causes of metals—namely, its matter, its form, and its <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the force or agent that brings a thing into being</note>—more so than the other <term>composite bodies</term> <note>original: "mista corpora"; things made of a mixture of the four elements</note> of the world.

<margin>The remote matter of metals.</margin>
Therefore, the <term>remote matter</term> <note>original: "materia remota"; the most basic, underlying ingredients of a substance</note> of metals, just like that of all other bodies, is (as has been stated) earth, water, air, and fire. It is the unanimous opinion of all philosophers that metals draw their origin from these. For the matter of a single element could not have been sufficient for the generation of composite bodies; rather, it was necessary for those four elements to have been blended and poured together to provide a suitable foundation and substrate for things. Although these first principles of things are the remote matter of metals, they are nevertheless more closely related to metals than they are to plants or sentient beings. This is because these four elements are perceived by the senses as if they were the primary and natural offspring of metals, and indeed of all inanimate things.

<margin>The intermediate matter of metals.</margin>
The <term>intermediate matter</term> <note>original: "materia media"</note> of metals within the bowels of the earth is that which, by the power of the efficient cause, passes from the first mixing of the elements into a sort of middle state, which is not yet the <term>proximate matter</term>. This intermediate stage is something like an unformed thing and does not have a certain "species" in nature; the ancient authors have not handed down a specific description of what this state is.

<margin>The proximate matter of metals.</margin>
But the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>original: "materia proxima"; the final stage of matter before it becomes a specific substance like gold or iron</note> of metals is that which is perfected by the efficient cause without the intervention of any other changes, and most closely takes on the metallic form. It is not yet a metal, but it possesses a form different from a metal, and the metallic form arises from it through a single final transformation.

<margin>Aristotle’s opinion on the proximate matter of metals.</margin>
However, regarding what that proximate matter actually is within the mines of the earth, there have been various opinions among those who have written on this subject. <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose theories on the four elements and "exhalations" dominated medieval science</note> says that the matter of both the "sublime" things above the earth and the "inferior" things generated in the bowels of the earth is a twofold exhalation. One is an exhalation from the earth, which is dry and hot; the other is a vapor from the water, which is cold and moist. It is not, however, that the dry exhalation is entirely without moisture, nor the moist vapor entirely without dryness; rather, dryness prevails in the former and moisture in the latter. He says, therefore, that the dry exhalation is the source of "fossils" <note>in this period, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the ground</note>, such as types of stones that cannot be melted, <term>sandarac</term> <note>original: "sandaracha"; a reddish arsenic ore</note>, sulfur, <term>ochre</term> <note>original: "achra"</note>, <term>red chalk</term> <note>original: "rubrica"</note>, and others of that kind. But he says that metals belong to the vaporous exhalation. He claims that this vapor, before it is turned into water, is coagulated by the dry exhalation and becomes metal. For this reason, all metals contain dry exhalation and can be set on fire and consumed by heat—with the exception of gold alone.

The Alchemists, however, say that the proximate matter of metals is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note> and sulfur; they argue this because quicksilver...

# SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING

...d <note>Completing the word "had" from the previous page</note> seen as fused, and from them <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> is drawn out by art, as well as because they breathe a sulfurous odor. Many authoritative men have followed their opinion.

<margin>The opinion of Gilgil.</margin>
Gilgil the Moor <note>A medieval Arabic alchemical authority often cited in Western texts</note>, however, declared that a certain ash of very fortified earth, when infused with water, was the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>the immediate substance from which a specific thing is made</note> of metals, just as all ash is the matter closest to glass.

<margin>The opinion of Albert.</margin>
Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on minerals</note>, however, holds it to be a moist, viscous, and tenacious substance.

<margin>The opinion of Georgius Agricola.</margin>
Georgius Agricola <note>1494–1555; known as the "father of mineralogy," he favored empirical observation over alchemical theory</note> refutes all these opinions regarding the proximate matter of metals in the earth's mines, and he contends with many arguments that a <term>juice</term> <note>original: "succum"; Agricola's term for mineral-rich waters or solutions found underground</note> arising in those same mines is the proximate matter for metals.

<margin>The opinion of Scaliger.</margin>
Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned Renaissance scholar</note> calls metals "watery earth," but calls quicksilver "earthy water." Which of these opinions is truer, I think I must not dwell upon, since nature exhibits to us another matter proximate to silver and gold, as will be clear from what follows. If, however, I must say what I feel, I would judge that Aristotle’s opinion and authority should be more relied upon and trusted.

---

<margin>The forms of metals.</margin>
After the knowledge of the matter of metals, their <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is</note> must also be investigated, which is the nobler part of their substance, as it is in all natural bodies. For the form of all things is marked more by the name of "nature" than by their matter, and from it alone is the name given to each natural body. For Aristotle usually calls it the <term>reason of the essence</term> <note>original: "rationem essentiae"; the defining characteristic that explains why a thing exists as it does</note>. The knowledge of the forms of metals looks to this: that by the aid of art, the same silver and gold as the natural kind must be formed; this cannot be achieved unless their form and nature—and what and of what kind it is—be understood, and in what ways they differ from the forms of other metals.

<margin>The forms of metals are not easily judged.</margin>
However, the forms of metals are not as easily distinguished as those of other types of bodies—namely plants, sentient beings, and humans. For the knowledge of forms depends on their actions, inasmuch as form is <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the full realization or activity of a thing</note>, while matter is <term>potency</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the potential to become something</note>. Moreover, actions are distinguished by their works.

<margin>Knowledge of forms depends on actions; actions depend on works.</margin>
Therefore, whatever the senses perceive to act more based on their effects, those the senses will judge to be composed of more conspicuous forms; those that act less, it will judge to be of more obscure and less manifest forms. Hence the form of plants is better known to the senses, because they grow, take in nourishment, and produce things like themselves. But the nature of sentient beasts is even better known, because besides these functions, they both move and feel.

<margin>The form of man is most manifest.</margin>
Indeed, the form of man is the most manifest of all, because in addition to all these, through the faculty of understanding, he becomes a human.

# APOLOGY

...that a human is endowed <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: "nature exhibits to us another thing... [such as that] a human is endowed."</note>. Since metals are deprived and bereft of all these faculties (for they neither grow, nor are they nourished, nor do they move, nor do they feel), their forms are less distinguishable by their actions. Nevertheless, all metals have forms by which they consist, and they take their names from these, and by them, they are distinguished from each other and from other bodies. They consist of and are composed solely from the mixing of elements; therefore, they have no other name than **mixed bodies** <note>original: "mista corpora"</note>. Nor do they possess other faculties besides those that cause them to exist and to have the single form of mixed elements, which is uniform throughout. These faculties are the qualities of the elements: **heat** and **cold** as active causes, and **moist** and **dry** as passive ones. And because metals possess more of these passive qualities, they are judged more by the endurance <note>original: "perpessione"; in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to how matter "suffers" or is "acted upon" by qualities rather than being the source of action itself</note> of their matter than by the action of their form.

<margin>
Metals are only mixed bodies.
</margin>

<margin>
The forms of metals are recognized more by the endurance of matter than by action. Metals are simply mixed.
</margin>

For it is the property of form to act, and of matter to endure. If they do act, they act only by the power of the qualities from which they grew together, such as by heating, cooling, moistening, and drying. Other types of bodies—namely plants, irrational animals, and humans—are indeed mixed bodies, but because they possess something else more excellent beyond and above this mixture, they are not properly called "mixed," but take their name and specific form from those faculties through which they act. Metals, however, because they possess nothing besides this mixture, are simply and absolutely called **mixed**, because those primary qualities produced nothing else in the elements except a mixture. Indeed, the <term>accidents</term> <note>properties like color, weight, or hardness that belong to a thing but do not define its essential nature</note>, both common and specific, follow the forms of all inanimate mixtures. And because these accidents are more suited to matter than to form, the nature of the forms of these mixtures is understood to some extent from them.

<margin>
Accidents common to all metals. The definition of a metal.
</margin>

Therefore, the accidents common to all metals are **ductility** and **fusibility**. Thus, a metal is defined by <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a famous alchemist whose writings formed the foundation of medieval European alchemy</note> as:

> A metal is a mineral body, fusible, and capable of being extended in every dimension under the hammer.

For "mineral body" is the genus, while "fusible" and "ductile in every dimension" is the specific difference which distinguishes metals from other mineral bodies. For silver and gold have their own specific accidents by which they are distinguished from other metals: namely, that they are perfectly mixed and are not consumed by fire—especially gold.

<margin>
Definition of gold.
</margin>

Gold, therefore, is rightly defined by Geber as follows:

> Gold is a yellow metallic body, the heaviest of all metals. <note>original: "omniũ metallorum grauis"; literally "heavy of all metals," though it implies the superlative "heaviest" in this context</note>

# SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING
<note>original: "ARGYR. ET CHRYSOP." refers to Argyropoeia and Chrysopoeia, the alchemical arts of making silver and gold.</note>

...very heavy, mute, shining, equally matured <note>original: "digestum"; in alchemy, the "digestion" of metals refers to their slow perfection or ripening within the earth</note> in the belly of the earth, washed for a very long time by mineral water, and enduring the trial of the ash-cup <note>original: "cineritij"; the process of cupellation, where metal is heated in a cup made of bone ash to remove impurities</note> and the cement <note>original: "cementi"; a refining process using "cement" (a mixture of salts and bricks) to purify gold</note>. This endurance of the cement is the specific difference, because in this trial all other metals are burnt up and turned to ash, but gold alone remains unharmed within it.

<margin>
Definition of silver.
</margin>
Silver is also defined by the same Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note> as follows: **Silver** is a metallic body, white with a pure whiteness, clean, hard, sounding, and lasting through the ash-test. This last part is its own specific property, since tin, lead, copper, and iron perish and are corrupted in the trial of the ash-cup, while silver persists in it. Other metals also have their own specific properties by which they differ from silver and gold and from each other, but discussing these and the solutions to the proposed question is of little relevance here, since their definitions have been sufficiently treated by the same Geber, Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on minerals.</note>, Georgius Agricola <note>A 16th-century German scholar known as the "father of mineralogy."</note>, and others. We only need to investigate the nature and form of silver and gold, which is recognized from the aforementioned specific properties and their definition, so that by art we may lead a matter closely related to them to those same properties through the efficient cause.

<margin>
A metallic body sustaining the tests proper to gold, is gold.
</margin>
For even if the forms of silver and gold are not as clearly known to us as the forms of other plant and animal bodies—which are perceived by their actions and effects—nevertheless, whatever metallic body we see enduring and persisting in the trials proper to silver and gold, we shall rightly say it is silver and gold. For the first knowledge of things comes from the senses. And just as we judge plants and animals by their action, so we judge silver and gold by the endurance <note>original: "perpessione"; as established on the previous page, this refers to how the matter is "acted upon" by external forces like fire.</note> of their matter.

<margin>
Causes of the properties specific to gold and silver.
</margin>
The causes of these properties specific to silver and gold are these: that all metals are fusible is caused by moisture. Likewise, they are ductile because of the viscosity <note>original: "lentorem"; a quality of being sticky, tenacious, or able to be stretched without breaking.</note> of the moisture from which they consist. For things that are viscous preserve their continuity longest; for the viscosity of this moisture has a firm balance with the dry parts. Therefore, both viscosity and dryness, with a certain balance, ensure that they are not shattered when struck by hammers, but are ductile. And according to how much more or less of this is in the metals, some are drawn out more or less than others.

<margin>
Why gold is the most ductile.
</margin>
Hence gold, which has the most viscosity tempered by dryness, is the most ductile of all metals; silver follows it, then copper, then iron; then lead and tin.

# DEFENSE
<note>original: "APOLOGIA"; in this context, it refers to a formal justification or systematic explanation of a doctrine.</note>

<margin>Gold ☉ retains its moisture in fire.</margin>
For almost these same specific reasons, metals retain their internal moisture when placed in the fire; for their natural viscosity <note>original: "lentor"; a stickiness or thickness of the substance</note> prevents the moisture from evaporating. Furthermore, this watery moisture prevents the metals from being consumed by the heat. Because watery qualities are diametrically opposed to fire, they are not overcome by it: Fire is hot, dry, and thin, while water is cold, moist, and dense. Therefore, the more that metals participate in this watery nature, the less power fire has over them. For this reason, **gold** is not consumed by the heat of any fire, and **silver** is only slightly less resistant for the same reasons. Other metals possess an airy, sulfurous, and flammable moisture, which is why they eventually waste away <note>original: "distabescant"; to melt away or be consumed</note> in the fire. More must be said regarding these specific properties a little later.

<margin>On the efficient cause of metals.</margin>
Now we must also speak of the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> of metals. An efficient cause is the source from which the principle of motion begins. It acts upon matter so that metals may take their origin. However, since all matter is either remote, intermediate, or proximate, it is certain that the efficient cause acting upon the remote and intermediate matter to create a metal is <term>universal and equivocal</term> <note>A "universal cause" is a broad force (like the sun) that affects many things, while "equivocal" means the cause is of a different nature than the effect.</note>, rather than particular or innate.

<margin>God and the Heavens are the remote and universal cause of metals.</margin>
Indeed, metals acknowledge no parent of their birth other than God and the Heavens, because they do not spring from a seed as living bodies do. In the seeds of living things, a power instilled by the parents lies hidden, which always produces offspring similar to those from whom the seeds flowed. This is not the case with the remote and intermediate matter of metals. Those who have recorded the history of metals do not focus on this, but rather on the efficient cause acting upon the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>The "proximate matter" is the immediate physical substance (like sulfur and mercury) that is ready to be turned into a specific metal.</note>—that is, the matter which has transitioned from remote and intermediate states into a form ready to become metal. This efficient cause within the proximate matter is particular and innate, as it belongs to that substance alone, just as there is a particular cause within every specific type of metal.

<margin>Aristotle’s opinion on the efficient cause of metals.</margin>
There are also various opinions regarding this proximate efficient cause. **Aristotle** says that this efficient cause is coldness and dryness. These qualities, found in stones, compress and thicken the <term>vapor</term> <note>Aristotle's "moist exhalation," which he believed was the raw material of metals trapped underground.</note> (which he judged to be the proximate matter of metals) that is trapped and enclosed within them. This should not be understood as a denial of the role of heat in their birth. For those exhalations are mixed together, brought to a certain thickness, and <term>concocted</term> <note>original: "concoquuntur"; the alchemical "ripening" or "cooking" of substances by internal heat.</note> by the work of heat; but 

<margin>The opinion of the Alchemists.</margin>
that mixture is afterwards thickened by cold and turns into a metal. The **Alchemists**, however, [think] that **sulfur**, which [is] part of the matter of metals...

...they think, and they profess that it obtains the force of the efficient cause, following the example of artificial cinnabar, which solidifies from a mixture of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur. <margin>The opinion of Gilgil.</margin> **Gilgil the Moor** <note>original: "Gilgil Maurus"; an Arabic author often cited in medieval mineralogical and alchemical texts</note> is of the opinion that the most intense heat is the efficient cause, as is seen in glass, which is forged from ashes. <margin>The opinion of Albertus Magnus.</margin> **Albertus Magnus** <note>a 13th-century philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on the "secrets of nature"</note>, however, says this efficient cause is the greater power of the celestial sphere, which unfolds natural forms through the motion of the heavens and the qualities of the elements, just as a craftsman unfolds artistic forms with an axe or a hammer. But this opinion of Albertus concerning the efficient cause should be considered and understood as referring to a universal cause rather than a specific one. For this universal cause acts first upon the elements, which after many changes it eventually transforms into the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>the immediate substance from which something is directly formed</note>.

<margin>The opinion of Georgius Agricola.</margin>
**Georgius Agricola** <note>a 16th-century German scholar known as the "father of mineralogy"</note>, however, follows Aristotle regarding the specific proximate efficient cause, which seems to me to be the truer opinion; for proximate causes are recognized by their effects. Now, metals are natural bodies that are only simply mixed, and they possess nothing beyond that mixture; and the effect of a simple mixture proceeds from the primary powers of the elements alone. <margin>How the elements are moved and mixed to produce metals.</margin> For the elements are moved and mixed by their own specific qualities. Therefore, heat first mixes them and leads them to the proximate matter of metals, which cold afterward constricts and solidifies.

Furthermore, this opinion is proven by induction. For if it is true, as they say, that iron is born in the clouds from that "double exhalation" <note>In Aristotelian science, metals were thought to form from two types of underground vapors: one moist and one dry</note> thickened by cold and falls to the earth, how much more likely is it that metals are born beneath the earth from that same exhalation thickened by cold?

These are the things I thought should be said concerning the knowledge of the nature of metals, which have solidified by the force of nature alone. Nor is there need for more discussion, either because these things have been explained by many highly respected authors, or because for the [alchemical] art there is a different proximate matter and other efficient causes—though still natural ones—which tend toward the same goal with art as the servant.

# DEFENSE
<meta>catchword: proxi- (continued from "proxima" on the previous page's ending text)</meta>

...having examined and understood everything belonging to this art, anyone will be able to reason and dismantle all the arguments brought against it. Without these principles, all efforts are vain and useless, and one must necessarily grope in the dark. Therefore, one must strive with all their strength to explain and uncover, as exactly as possible, this most excellent part of this art—hidden until now and never handed down by the ancients.

<margin>Concerning the matter closest to gold and silver according to the art.</margin>
But first, we must define the matter closest to silver and gold according to the art—that which is immediately perfected into silver or gold by the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the force or agent that triggers a change</note> without any other intervening transformation. This substance is the <term>individual</term> <note>a specific instance of a substance</note> of the silver or gold species that is "about to be." It is not yet silver or gold in <term>act</term> <note>actualized, physical form</note>, but only in <term>proximate potential</term> <note>ready and able to become the thing immediately</note>, which will take on the form of one or the other as soon as it is moved by the efficient cause.

<margin>What an individual is.</margin>
For an "individual" is that which possesses properties that, taken together, can never be attributed to many different things. These properties do not constitute the <term>specific difference</term> <note>the core characteristic that defines a species</note> but only provide the aptitude and readiness to take on the next form. For example, consider "dog seed" <note>original: "semen caninum"; in historical biology, "seed" referred to the reproductive essence of a living thing</note>, which has the property of producing a dog in the very next stage of its development. This property will never exist in "horse seed" unless it first undergoes many stages of decay and transformation into dog seed—if such a thing were even possible. 

In the same way, the matter closest to silver and gold has this property within the art: that with only a little assistance, it can be changed into them. This property will never exist in any other matter. For this is an inviolable law of nature: no individual of one species can ever pass into an individual of another species unless it first possesses the property and potential closest to that second state. That is, it must first be an individual with the <term>proximate potential</term> to become the species that is about to arise.

<margin>The material cause in mines is not the proximate matter of the art.</margin>
<margin>The proximate matter in nature is unknown.</margin>
To investigate this matter as it exists in natural mines, and to subject it to the efficient cause so that it may act upon it and complete its work, is impossible. Indeed, it is a rule that nothing can reach the power of the intellect that was not first perceived by the senses. But the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>the immediate "raw material"</note> deep beneath the earth, from which nature alone produces silver and gold, is unknown to our senses. Even the serious authors who have written on this subject do not agree on what that proximate matter is in nature; indeed, they disagree, and each defends his own opinion with probable reasons, though not with absolute proofs. Even if it were granted that the matter...

# THE MAKING OF SILVER AND GOLD
<meta>catchword: proxi- (continued from "proxima" on the previous page's ending text)</meta>

...can be understood by the senses and by demonstration. Nevertheless, the art <note>the practice of alchemy</note> should be able to bring the potential of matter into <term>act</term> <note>actual physical existence or form</note> or form outside of the natural location of the mines. Therefore, in **Argyropoia** <note>original: "Argyropœia"; the art of making silver</note> and **Chrysopoia** <note>original: "Chrysopœia"; the art of making gold</note>, we must seek the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>the raw material in the state closest to the final product</note> and the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the agent or force that triggers the change</note> from another source, so that by the power of the cause, the matter may break forth into act, and from its potential, the form of silver and gold may arise and emerge.

<margin>Where the proximate matter of metals must be sought.</margin>
It must be sought, I say, in a thing where the judgment of the eyes and senses tells us this property is inherent—that is, a certain natural ability and disposition to receive the silver and gold form. The investigation of this matter depends on a twofold demonstration. The first is based on the similarity of the whole substance of silver and gold with this proximate matter we are seeking. This similarity is perceived by the senses through the easy mixing and "embrace" of these substances.

<margin>We must investigate the proximate matter through a twofold demonstration.</margin>
For these substances relate to one another so well that they join together without effort and without art, but of their own accord. We shall explain later which substance it is that joins so easily with silver and gold.

<margin>The second demonstration.</margin>
The second demonstration will concern the property, ability, and disposition of the matter that is to take on the form of both silver and gold. This ability or disposition will be made manifest to the senses by the similarity of the <term>accidents</term> <note>in Aristotelian philosophy, these are qualities like color or weight that describe a thing but aren't its core essence</note> of that same matter we seek, compared to those we observe in silver and gold—qualities resulting from the "suffering" <note>how the material is shaped or affected by external forces</note> of their matter, and which most distinguish them from other metals.

<margin>Four accidents common to gold and silver with the proximate matter.</margin>
These accidents are four in number. **First**, that silver and gold are not consumed by fire or set aflame. **Second**, that the parts they consist of—namely, the "moist" and the "dry"—are not dissipated or pulled apart by fire, which normally dissolves everything. **Third**, that they are of a very fine essence. **Last**, that they are dense and very heavy. To be precise—lest anyone complain—these belong most properly to gold, and to silver less so. Let those craftsmen who work with silver and gold judge these specific accidents, as I will soon demonstrate more clearly. Based on the authority of **Aristotle**, these accidents are physical states judged by the senses.

<margin>The matter which is proximate to gold and silver.</margin>
Therefore, the matter which we see with our own eyes joining easily with silver and gold, and which is endowed with these same specific accidents, will be the "proximate matter" for silver and gold within the art. It is this, and no other, which will be transformed into silver and gold by the efficient cause. We shall describe this matter by its proper name once we have demonstrated that these four accidents exist in silver and gold, explained their causes, and showed that...

# APOLOGIA

...[qualities that] are not present in the other metals, and why. Therefore, the fact that silver and gold are not burned or consumed by fire becomes clear because, when melted by fire, they breathe out no sulfurous or flammable vapor.

<margin>
1.
Gold and
silver are not
burned out.
</margin>
The cause is that they are devoid of all sulfurous, flammable, and oily substance. For almost every natural body consists of a <term>double moisture</term> <note>original: "duplici humore"; a reference to the Aristotelian theory that matter is composed of various 'fluids' or principles</note>: one is greasy, oily, and flammable—such as <term>sulfur</term> <note>here meaning the "principle of combustibility" rather than just the mineral</note>, oil, or fat; the other is watery, which acts like a "glue" to hold the earthy parts of bodies together, and which is common to all things created from the mixing of the Elements. Therefore, whatever body is subject to burning possesses a moisture similar to oil, and it is by this kind alone that a thing catches fire. Indeed, because this oily moisture arises from the Air, it retains the hot quality of the Air. But the watery moisture, which is the glue of the earthy parts, cannot be conquered by fire. For that moisture is cold and wet, while fire is hot and dry. And since they fight against each other with contrary qualities (as has already been said), neither yields to the other. Therefore, the watery moisture alone **protects** <note>original: "tuetur"; this is the catchword for the page continuity</note> silver and gold so they are not consumed by fire. For they partake in no oily or sulfurous moisture that might assist the fire in gaining a victory over the watery moisture within them. However, the remaining metals—because they partake in a certain sulfurous moisture that can even be detected by its smell—are burned and contract a blackness from the fire.

<margin>
The essential
parts of gold
and silver
are not
dissolved
by fire.
An experiment.
</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that the essential parts of silver and gold—namely, the **Moist** and the **Dry** from which they are composed—are not dissolved or separated by fire is proven by their repeated melting [colliquatio] in the fire. For nothing of their weight is lost. Indeed, I remember that in former years I took one ounce of the purest gold enclosed in a small earthenware vessel, and another ounce of pure silver likewise enclosed in a separate vessel. I placed them in that spot where glass is kept perpetually melted in a glassmaker’s furnace. There, both remained fused and liquefied for two continuous months. When those months had passed and I removed them from both the vessels and the furnace, I weighed them on scales. I observed that the gold had not lost even the smallest amount of weight, while the silver had lost only a twelfth part. This is certainly worthy of admiration, yet I have learned through experience itself that it is most true.

<margin>
The cause and
reason.
</margin>
The cause of this is the perfect mixing and union of the **Dry** and the **Moist**, which are joined in such a tight bond that they are indissoluble even by the most violent fires. For the Moist is tempered by the Dry, and the Dry by the Moist; in both silver and gold, they become one equal substance, <term>homeomerous</term> <note>original: "homeomera"; a philosophical term meaning that every part of the substance is identical in nature to the whole</note> and uniform in its similar parts. Hence, when the fire strives to rarefy and dissolve them, and to carry off the watery Moist into vapor...

### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING

[The watery moisture] protects and holds [the metal] back from the earthy part so it does not fly away. Conversely, when the same fire strives to separate the earthy from the moist and turn it into ash, it is restrained by the moisture, so that both persist safe, unharmed, and unconquered in the battle of fire. This indissoluble <margin>A solid mixture of the moist and the dry.</margin> solid mixture and union is properly understood regarding gold, which Sacred Scripture mentions: *God tested us,* it says, *like gold in a furnace.* And Augurellius in his *Chrysopoeia* <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524) was an Italian humanist who wrote a famous Latin poem on the "art of making gold."</note> sang thus:

> Since nothing of gold is lost 
> By fire, just as no old age consumes the sun, 
> And neither rust nor verdigris destroys it, 
> So much do all things cling there in wondrous joints.
<note>original Latin: "Vni quoniam nihil deperit auro / Igne, Velut solum consumit nulla vetustas, / Ac neque rubigo aut ærugo conficit illa, / Cuncta adeo miris illic compagibus hærent."</note>

Closest to this solid mixture is the mixture of pure silver, which the Royal Psalmist also mentions: *The words of the Lord,* he says, *are pure words, silver tested by fire, proven for the earth, purified seven times.* <margin>Silver is lost in the fire.</margin> Nevertheless, a small amount of it is lost and burned away by fire. For as I said earlier, I saw that silver melted for two months in the fire had lost a twelfth part of its original weight; I saw it clearly on the surface as a very bright yellow glass, which, when struck with a hammer on the anvil, was separated from the silver, while the inside remained pure. This twelfth part of the silver, lost and burned away, passed into that very bright yellow glass.

But all other metals, when continuous fire acts for a short time, exhale, and as the metallic matter and form vanish and perish, what remains is transmuted into glass. For every metal, as <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of alchemy; his works were fundamental to European chemistry.</note> rightly perceives, when deprived of its own moisture, gives no fusion except that which turns to glass. <margin>Vitrification of metals.</margin> The cause of this dissolution and corruption is the opposite of what we said regarding silver and gold: namely, that a certain sulfurous and flammable moisture is mixed with their watery moisture, and also because their mixture is imperfect compared to the mixture of silver and gold.

<margin>That gold and silver are very thin, and why.</margin>
Furthermore, the thinness <note>Here referring to ductility or malleability—the ability to be drawn into wire or beaten into leaf.</note> of silver and gold can be expanded in a wonderful way, but that of gold is found to be incredible from the fact that a single ounce of it will gild the surface of a body which ten ounces of silver could scarcely plate; gilders and silver-platers know this. Indeed, the other metals do not approach the thinness of gold at all.

<margin>The purity of the refined moisture.</margin>
The cause of such great thinness is the purity of the refined moisture in silver, and specifically in gold. But the cause of thickness <note>Meaning coarseness or lack of ductility.</note> is terrestrial impurity. <margin>Density and weight of gold and silver.</margin> Finally, the last proper quality of gold and silver—especially gold above all others—is density and weight. And so that it may be known with certainty how much one differs from the other in weight, I will bring forward what I have experienced.
