->### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING<-

<margin>It resembles gold and silver by the similarity of its entire substance.</margin>
...namely, by the similarity of the entire substance of <term>quicksilver</term><note>The common historical name for mercury; the Latin text uses 'argentum vivum' (living silver).</note> with silver and gold, and by the agreement of their specific <term>accidents</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, 'accidents' are the observable qualities or characteristics of a substance (like color or weight) that are not essential to its nature.</note> with those of both metals. First, <term>gilders</term><note>Artisans who apply a thin layer of gold to other surfaces.</note> know that quicksilver joins more willingly with no other metal than with pure gold, and after that with silver. From these they make an <term>amalgam</term><note>A mixture of mercury with another metal; the original text uses the term 'malagma'.</note>, especially from gold and quicksilver, when they wish to gild vessels; and the purer each ingredient is, the more quickly they mix together. This occurs for no other reason than the similarity of their entire substance. Other metals do not embrace quicksilver so willingly; or, if it does join with them, such as with tin and lead, it is not because of a similarity of substance, but because of their undefined moisture, or because quicksilver is already naturally present within them.

<margin>That it shares specific and common properties with gold and silver.</margin>
Furthermore, it is proven by demonstration that the same properties we have described in silver, and specifically in gold, are present in quicksilver. For it is free of all oily, greasy, and <term>sulfurous</term><note>In alchemy, 'sulfur' often refers to the principle of combustibility and impurity.</note> moisture. Hence, it cannot be scorched and is less liable to be set on fire. Because of this, fire has no mastery over it, nor does sulfur, which scorches all metals except gold—this fact is manifest to the senses.

<margin>The experiment of Cinnabar. It is not consumed by fire.</margin>
For manufactured <term>Cinnabar</term><note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide.</note> is refined from quicksilver and sulfur; when ground and mixed with <term>oil of tartar</term><note>A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used here as a chemical agent.</note> and subjected to a strong fire in a glass vessel blocked with clay, it rises up into a vapor and returns to its state as quicksilver, and nothing of it is lost. The same happens in what craftsmen call "sublimated" quicksilver. These things are known to the artisans. If a certain portion of sulfurous exhalation had been mixed by nature with the quicksilver, there would be no doubt that it could be inflamed and scorched, as usually happens with the other metals, gold excepted.

<margin>It is not dissolved by fire.</margin>
As for the perfect union and mixture of its parts—namely, the dry and the moist—it can no more be dissolved by fire than gold can. It is indeed carried off into its own vapor, but its constituent parts are not thereby dissolved by the fire. For if that vapor, driven by the action of the fire's heat, falls into a receiving vessel, it will unite and return into its previous form of quicksilver, with no part of its original weight removed. Nor will any of its substance remain behind in the vessel from which the vapor emigrated. For it is of an entirely uniform substance and composed of similar parts, yet it is not equally mixed in regards to its <term>temperament</term><note>The balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) within a substance.</note>.

<margin>Why it turns into vapor.</margin>
For moisture prevails in the mixture; hence, it turns into vapor when fire acts upon it. For that same reason, it is not <term>ductile</term><note>Capable of being hammered out thin or drawn into wire.</note>. That it is extremely thin and fine is apparent from the fact that when wrapped in leather and squeezed...

<margin>The Author concludes that no material in the art is closer than quicksilver.</margin>
Let it therefore be established and fixed that no other material is closer to silver and gold in the <term>art</term><note>Alchemy.</note> than quicksilver, both the common kind and that which is present in imperfectly mixed metals. Upon that, as the material, let all those who expect the fruits of <term>Argyropoeia</term><note>The art of making silver.</note> and <term>Chrysopoeia</term><note>The art of making gold.</note> bestow all their efforts; let every other sulfurous, oily, inflaming, burning, flammable, and combustible matter be driven away. Only the substance of quicksilver—watery, most subtle, viscous, indissoluble, yielding to the heat of no fire—is the material closest to silver and gold. For it is that which conquers fire and is not conquered by fire. 

<margin>On the efficient cause.</margin>
Enough concerning the material closest to silver and gold. These things being thus established, we must proceed to the knowledge of the <term>efficient cause</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the agent or force that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair.</note>: which is as much nobler and more excellent as the craftsman is to his work. 

<margin>What the efficient cause is.</margin>
For it is, as I said, that from which the principle of motion comes, which moves all natural bodies so that they are such as we perceive them to be. I said also that this cause is either universal or particular. And both are defined by their kind. Both are also natural, but sometimes it is moved by its own impulse, driven by nothing other than nature alone to act. Such is the case in the generation of metals in the bowels of the earth, which come forth by the power of nature alone. Such also it is in common quicksilver, and in that which is enveloped in metallic bodies, which nature alone has brought into the light. 

<margin>Natural efficient causes are unknown to us.</margin>
But what and of what sort these natural causes may be, the human mind cannot know or attain for certain, nor is it sufficiently agreed upon among the experts who have treated them. Let the generosity of nature suffice for us, which from its hidden efficient causes has freely offered us common quicksilver, and that which is inherent in metallic bodies as the nearest potential, which we have called our "closest matter." 

<margin>The particular efficient cause in this art.</margin>
We only need to investigate the particular efficient cause which moves this matter so that silver or gold may congeal from it. The nature of this efficient cause will be understood from its definition, just as in all other things. We have deemed it necessary to define this cause both from the powers through which it acts, and from the silver-making or gold-making matter in which these powers reside. # APOLOGIA

<margin>...is of the proximate matter.</margin>
...the gold-making power is within. For in an egg, there is an inherent efficient force which, with the help of external heat, produces a chick. So too in plants and the seeds of other animals, there is an inherent prolific force that does not need to be sought elsewhere. But in our <term>proximate matter</term><note>The substance physically closest to the desired result; in this context, quicksilver.</note>, the silver-making or gold-making force is not naturally implanted in such a way that it can advance into silver or gold on its own; rather, it exists in another matter of the same kind, but of a nobler form, the reason for which difference will be explained as we proceed.

<margin>Definition of the efficient cause in the art.</margin>
Therefore, the <term>efficient cause</term><note>The active agent or force that triggers a change.</note> is the silver-making power and faculty which—through its fiery qualities and with the help of external heat—draws apart and resolves the proximate matter, or <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, which is potentially present in tin, lead, copper, and iron. It cooks this, as well as common quicksilver, and perfects its incomplete mixture, shaping it from the roots so that once the mixture is perfected and finished, a new form of silver or gold may flow into it.

<margin>What is Argyrogonia? What is Chrysogonia?</margin>
<term>Argyrogonia</term><note>The generation or "birth" of silver.</note>, moreover, is the silver-making seed, perfectly cooked from silver or gold previously dissolved, or a silver-making tincture of white color. Just as <term>Chrysogonia</term><note>The generation or "birth" of gold.</note> is the gold-making seed, most perfectly cooked from gold previously dissolved, or a gold-making tincture of red color, endowed with an admirable thinness of substance; in these, the silver-making and gold-making power is naturally present.

<margin>Efficient causes are twofold.</margin>
Those fiery qualities through which they act are acquired through the <term>art</term><note>The practice of alchemy.</note> and through cooking. From these definitions, it is well understood that the active forces are divided into two parts. Some are the primary agents, and others are the helpers.

<margin>Helping causes.</margin>
The primary agents are the silver-making and gold-making force, and the fiery qualities inherent in the silver-making and gold-making seed. The helpers, however, are fire and external heat. Furthermore, that seed is divided in two, so that one is silver-making and the other gold-making. All these things require a clearer explanation, so that the truth of the proposed question—*Whether the Art exists*—may shine forth more clearly.

<margin>Explanation of the definition.</margin>
In the definition, therefore, the efficient force is the <term>genus</term><note>The general category or class.</note>. For in all natural bodies that have undergone birth—whether from a seed, or from some place of seeds, or in those things that have passed into decay—there was first a force and a certain faculty that acted upon them and moved them, which otherwise would have remained without motion.

<margin>All efficient forces and faculties proceed from three things.</margin>
This efficient force flows from a triple source. Indeed, since these three things—Matter, Form, and <term>Temperament</term><note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance.</note>—are present in every natural body, it is certain that all forces proceed from them and from no others. These are so interconnected among themselves that they require mutual labor, and none can stand apart. But of all...

# THE BIRTH OF SILVER AND GOLD
BB 5
<meta>catchword: simi-</meta>

<margin>The property of things arises from form.</margin>
The most excellent and effective power of all things is that which proceeds from the **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is, as opposed to "matter," which is the physical substance.</note>. Because the form is more noble than both the matter and the temperament <note>The specific mixture or "complexion" of qualities.</note>, it must produce more excellent effects. This force, which has its origin in the form, is called a "property" <note>original: "proprietas"; also known as a specific virtue or innate characteristic.</note>; it is native to each form and cannot be acquired through any art, but only through nature. Therefore, it is first stated in the definition that the silver-making and gold-making power and faculty of *Argyrogonia* and *Chrysogonia* is implanted by nature. For just as there is an inherent power in the seed of a dog which moves the matter of the seed so that a dog is generated—a power and faculty which exists in no other seed—so too in the silver-making or gold-making seed there is its own power, so that it may become silver or gold. But since this power and property is an **accident** <note>A philosophical term for a quality that does not exist by itself but must belong to a "substance."</note> which cannot exist on its own but always clings to a substance, the definition of *Argyrogonia* and *Chrysogonia* was added as a seed, and from what matter they take their origin.

<margin>The seed of silver draws its origin from silver, and the seed of gold from gold.</margin>
Specifically, the seed of silver takes its origin from silver, and the seed of gold from gold. For although these bodies are inanimate and do not reproduce things similar to themselves in the mines of the earth, nevertheless, through the impulse of the **art** <note>Meaning the art of Alchemy.</note> by means of a "transfer," they are said to produce things similar to themselves when they have leaped over into a "seed," or into that which holds the place of a seed. And just as we say a dog is the **efficient cause** of a dog, so too silver is the cause of silver, and gold of gold.

<margin>Gold is the efficient cause of gold.</margin>
On this point, Augurellius <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), an Italian humanist and alchemist who wrote the famous poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note> wrote beautifully:

> *He who has a heart for barley, sows barley; do not then*
> *seek the beginnings of gold from elsewhere; in gold*
> *are the seeds of gold, though they lie hidden and withdrawn*
> *far off, and are to be sought by us with much toil.*

<margin>Form is ineffective for acting without the primary qualities.</margin>
However, although all effects we perceive proceed primarily and mostly from the form and its powers, nonetheless, without the **primary qualities** of the Elements <note>The four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> which are in the mixed body, the form would be ineffective—not unlike a craftsman without tools. It is not that the tools act on their own, but that the work is better performed through them. And so, in the definition, I said that the silver-making or gold-making faculties act through **fiery qualities**.

<margin>The powers of the primary qualities.</margin>
For the ancient philosophers and physicians, especially **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, attributed such great power to the primary qualities that they believed everything we see in this entire universe arose from them.

<margin>Heat and cold act.</margin>
I have called them "fiery qualities" because they act more than the others; indeed, unless their force were blunted by the other qualities in which they are soaked, they would ruin everything. These active qualities—namely **heat and cold**—are the only efficient causes of bodies...

-># DEFENSE<-

<margin>Form organizes the primary qualities.</margin>
Regarding uniform substances <note>In Aristotelian physics, "similar" or "homogeneous" substances (similarium) are materials like stone or metal where every part is the same as the whole.</note>, Aristotle established this while considering only their matter. But when he arrives at the **form**—as to why this is silver and that is gold—he says there is another, more constant cause: the **formative faculty** <note>original: "facultas formatrix," the internal power that gives a thing its specific shape and nature.</note>. For this formative power directs the primary qualities <note>The four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> so that they act and move the matter toward a specific form, just as it exists in the mover either in act or in power. In this way, the silver-making or gold-making power, through fiery qualities, will move our "proximate matter" <note>The immediate raw material ready to be transformed.</note> to take on the form of silver or gold.

<margin>The powers of secondary qualities.</margin>
The secondary qualities will also be of assistance; these take their origin from the matter, such as the thinness and subtleness of the substance. It is not that they act on their own, but rather, just as the form acts through the primary and principal qualities, it also acts through these secondary ones, either more powerfully or more weakly. For this reason, it was added to the definition that this "seed" is endowed with an admirable thinness, so that it might most swiftly enter and penetrate all parts of our proximate matter.

<margin>These qualities can be intensified by art.</margin>
Moreover, we have said that both types of qualities, both the primary and secondary, can be intensified by **art** <note>In this context, "art" refers to the skilled practice of alchemy or chemistry to enhance natural processes.</note> since they are "accidents" <note>Qualities that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing.</note>. Because of this intensification alone, the form acts more sharply, even though the form itself (as the Physicists say) does not admit of "more or less." That they can be intensified is also clear from the testimony of Aristotle, who affirms that all things that are **concocted** <note>original: "concocta"; a process of ripening or perfecting through heat, like digestion or ripening fruit.</note> are hot, even if they were previously cold; and the more they are "cooked," the hotter they become.

<margin>Form is the principal efficient cause.</margin>
These, therefore, are the principal **efficient causes** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note>. In every creation of natural things, the "species" is the first and principal efficient cause. Therefore, *Argyrogoma* <note>Likely a variation of "Argyrogonia," meaning the "birth of silver."</note> generates silver, and *Chrysogonia* <note>"Gold-birth."</note> generates gold in our proximate matter.

<margin>Temperament aids the form.</margin>
Indeed, the fiery temperament <note>The specific balance of qualities dominated by heat.</note> and the thinness of the matter come to the aid of the formative faculty as its instruments. However, the reasoning regarding how both seeds must be dissolved and concocted, and in what manner, must be referred to another question. Meanwhile, let it not be misunderstood from what was said in passing in the definition regarding dissolution and concoction: from silver, only the white silver-making **tincture** <note>A concentrated essence or "dye" capable of transforming matter.</note> can be drawn; and from gold, the same, as well as the red gold-making tincture. Perhaps more will need to be said about both seeds later.

<margin>The helping efficient force.</margin>
The helping force is also proposed in the definition; it does not act first or principally, but as an external force that helps the internal one to act. That helping cause is **external heat**. This is so necessary in the birth of all natural bodies that, without the help of this cause, those principal efficient causes would lie as if asleep, destitute and bereaved, and would produce no effect at all. ### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING

<margin>
The powers and effects of external heat.
</margin>
If a hen, or another bird, did not warm them with her heat, the chicks would never hatch. Likewise, the offspring of animals would perish in the womb without the heat of the mother. The power of external heat must be esteemed no less in the completion of this entire "work" <note>The "Great Work" or *Magnum Opus* of alchemy.</note>. Indeed, Aristotle attributed the primary "efficient cause" <note>The agent that brings a change about.</note> in the minerals of metals to external qualities—namely, to heat for "concocting" <note>original: "concoquendi," a process of ripening or maturing through heat, similar to digestion.</note> and to cold for "constraining" <note>Solidifying or thickening.</note>. This external heat, therefore, separates, draws out, and burns away whatever is foreign to the nature of quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note> within imperfectly mixed metals. At the same time, as the "seed" is ripened and brought forth, the heat intensifies and immensely increases the fiery qualities implanted within it. This same heat assists those qualities when the seed is cast into metals, or into common quicksilver; thus, with doubled and multiplied strength, they may mix and "decoct" the materials. By either overturning or perfecting the previous imperfect mixture, they summon the state of silver or gold to those same materials.

<margin>
The actions and works of the efficient cause.
</margin>
Finally, it was added to the definition that the efficient cause moves, dissolves, and perfects the mixture, so that I might demonstrate the works that belong to its "hands."

<margin>
What is motion?
What is the goal?
</margin>
First, every efficient cause moves the subject, or the matter, toward some "end" <note>The final goal or purpose (Greek: *telos*).</note>. Motion, however, is the path and the flow between the matter and that end. This end is either a form, a quantity, a quality, or a place. The efficient cause, therefore, moves toward various ends. Since the end of <term>Argyropoeia</term> <note>The art of making silver.</note> or <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>The art of making gold.</note> is that silver or gold be produced, that motion strives toward a "new form." For the form of lead, tin, bronze, iron, and quicksilver is not the form of silver or gold; rather, those base metals are the subject and the matter for them. <margin>When one form perishes, another is introduced.</margin> As these forms perish—since matter cannot exist without a form—one of these must be introduced: namely, the form of silver or gold. We must see, then, by what kind of motion the forms of tin, lead, bronze, iron, and quicksilver depart (as they cannot remain forever if they are moved) and another form—namely silver or gold—succeeds them. <margin>Movement toward a form is not always through "generation and corruption."</margin> It is commonly thought that all movement toward a form happens through "birth and passing away," or <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>The Aristotelian term for the creation of a new substance and the destruction of an old one.</note>, where one always succeeds the other. They say that "generation" is movement (or rather, change) from non-being to being, while "corruption" is from being to non-being. We grant that this is true in the birth and death of plants and animals. <margin>In "simply mixed" bodies, form is introduced through mixing.</margin> But in the case of "simply mixed" bodies <note>Inorganic substances like minerals or salts.</note> alone, we shall show that the form is introduced to the subject not through generation and corruption, but through "dissolution" and simple mixing. ### APOLOGIA

<margin>Motion in silver-making and gold-making is simple mixture and dissolution.</margin>
...is corrupted or generated in plants and animals, or is dissolved and mixed in simple mixtures only, whether distant or near. For that which belongs to the "hands" <note>Referring to the practical alchemical operations or the "efficient cause" mentioned on the previous page.</note>, that is, the seed, is neither corrupted nor dissolved, but its origin comes through perfection alone. I have decided to explain all these things more clearly, lest I seem to put forward a paradox, and because this explanation will hereafter satisfy both the proposed question and almost all the arguments of Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who was a famous critic of Paracelsus and alchemical transmutation.</note>. All motion in <term>Argyropœia</term> <note>Silver-making</note> and <term>Chrysopœia</term> <note>Gold-making</note> consists of simple mixture and dissolution. What mixture and dissolution are, how they are divided, how they differ from birth and death <note>original: "ortu & interitu," referring to the Aristotelian concepts of generation and corruption.</note>, and what they have in common, I shall say, since these questions are of very great importance.

<margin>What Mixture is according to Aristotle.</margin>
There are various opinions concerning mixture. Aristotle, near the end of his treatise on mixture, defines it thus: "Mixture is the union of altered mixables." <note>original: "Mistio est miscibilium alteratorum vnio." A standard Aristotelian definition where the ingredients are changed but persist in the final product.</note> Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned scholar whose *Exercitationes* was a standard text on natural philosophy.</note>, in his book of *Exercises*, criticizes this definition, considering it unworthy of a philosopher, and defines it thus: <margin>Another definition of Mixture.</margin> "Mixture is the movement of the smallest bodies toward mutual contact." <note>Scaliger’s definition is more "atomistic" or corpuscular than Aristotle's, focusing on tiny particles touching.</note> This variety of definitions, and what most have felt about it, have produced difficulty because the word "mixture" is equivocal <note>Having multiple meanings.</note>. Since all the types of natural bodies we have mentioned—namely, inanimate things like stones and metals, and animate things like plants and animals—have grown together from a thorough mixing of the elements, they can all be called "mixtures." <margin>Inanimate bodies arise through mixture alone.</margin> But the name "mixture" properly suits bodies of the first kind [inanimate], and they have their origin through the motion of mixture alone; whereas other kinds of bodies [animate] have something else besides mixture, and their perfection does not proceed from the motion of mixture alone. Hence, Aristotle, before his definition of mixture, set down the distinction between it and other moving changes, though obscurely enough and in fewer words than would have been necessary; he also passed over the division of mixture in silence, nor did he add a single word about "simple dissolution," which is the opposite of mixture.

<margin>Mixture and dissolution are opposites.</margin>
However, since, as I said, the terms "mixture" and "dissolution" are equivocal, and in equivocal things one must distinguish <note>original: "partiendum," to divide into categories.</note> before defining, some divisions of both must be offered—namely, of that which is mixture generally and confusedly, and that which is called mixture properly. <margin>The first division of mixture.</margin> The word "mixture" indicates that those things being mixed are several in number. One type of mixture is "prior," another "posterior": the prior is that which [comes] from the first four elements...

<margin>The second division.</margin>
The division can be made in another way: one being from nature alone, as is the case in all natural bodies which have grown together by the force of nature alone. The other is from art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human skill or technology, particularly alchemy or chemistry.</note>, such as exists in bodies already born from nature, which are mixed again by art—as seen in bodies of different species, whether they be meltable, liquid, dry, or ground into the smallest possible particles. 

<margin>The third division.</margin>
There is yet another division of this same "mixture": one is for the purpose of establishing a single form <note>original: "formam unicam." In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential identity of a thing.</note> for those things being mixed; such is the case in all natural bodies, each of which has attained its own unique form. The other type is for the union and contact of the smallest bodies while their native forms remain, such as in liquid bodies—for example, water and wine mixed together—or in meltable things like metals, or dry things which are ground into very fine parts and mixed together. For in this kind of mixture, these various bodies each retain their own forms. 

<margin>The fourth division.</margin>
There is also another division of the same mixture: one is simply perfect, the other is comparatively perfect. A "simply perfect" mixture <note>original: "Mistio perfecta simpliciter"</note> consists of things which, although they were previously of different species, have attained a single substantial form after they have combined, as is the case with all natural bodies. 

<margin>Comparatively perfect mixture is judged in various ways.</margin>
A "comparatively perfect" mixture is one which, although it may be called perfect when looked at simply in its being, is nonetheless more or less perfect when compared to others—both among those of different genera and those of different species categorized under a single near genus. Furthermore, this comparative perfection of a mixture is judged in various ways: either by the actions of the mixed bodies (whether they are more noble or more ignoble); or by the connection of the parts of the mixed bodies (whether solid or weak); or by both the powers and actions of the mixed bodies as well as their structural assembly. 

<margin>Because of their power of action, plants and animals are more perfect than simple mixtures.</margin>
For if we consider only mixed bodies like stones and metals, and look at their powers and actions, they will be judged more ignoble than the other kinds of bodies because they consist only of the mixture of elements. But plants have a certain movement; animals have a more manifest movement; and humans, truly, beyond movement, are participants in reason and intelligence and produce the most excellent works. Therefore, by the faculty of acting...

-># APOLOGY <note>original: "APOLOGIA"; here meaning a formal defense or explanation of the author's alchemical theories.</note> <-

<margin>
Resolution into prime matter.
In simple mixture and dissolution, the resolution of all accidents does not occur.
</margin>
...of the matter of the wood, nor are its <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color, texture, or smell that can change without the object becoming a different type of thing.</note> perceived. This corruption they call "resolution into prime matter" <note>Prime matter is the most basic, formless substance from which all physical things were thought to be composed.</note>. But in these, namely mixture and simple dissolution—by which different bodies are mixed, or mixed things are dissolved—the sensible accidents that existed before do not vanish entirely. Instead, some part of their prior sensible matter perishes, while some remains. For when elements are mixed for the birth of a stone or a metal—which is a true mixture—those qualities that were sensible in them before are still seen even after the mixture. For stones reflect the sensible quality of earth, and metals reflect that of water. Indeed, even when these same stones are dissolved into lime, they reflect earth. When metals are dissolved into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum", the common name for mercury.</note>, they reflect water. In other types of mixture or resolution, where bodies of different forms are separated, there is no doubt. For metals that are melted by heat are thought to be mixed and are again dissolved by art; they preserve their own proper forms and their own proper accidents, like the grains of different bodies.

<margin>
In simple mixture, qualities meet with equal strength.
</margin>
There is also this difference between generation and corruption, and dissolution and simple mixture: in a true mixture, the contrary qualities of those things being mixed meet with somewhat equal forces and are brought back to a middle ground and moderation. This motion tends toward a simple mixture.

<margin>
In generation, the forces of contraries are unequal.
</margin>
But in the generation of contraries, the forces (beyond the motion) are unequal; therefore, that which is smaller and weaker is overcome and destroyed by the larger. For this reason, we do not say that wood is "mixed" with fire, nor food with the body, but rather that those things are corrupted and new things arise. For this motion tends toward the death of one thing and the birth of another.

<margin>
Commonalities between birth and death, mixture and dissolution.
</margin>
However, these things are common to both birth and death, and to true and simple mixture and dissolution: the prior form of the moved body perishes, and a new one arises and succeeds it. But this is also common to them: just as death is the opposite of birth, so dissolution is the opposite of mixture.

<margin>
Properties of true mixture.
</margin>
For a true and perfect mixture—the subject of this inquiry—these properties are required: that there be a common matter among those things being mixed; that they be extremely thin and easily divided, such as liquids or substances that can be melted; that they fight with opposing qualities; and that they struggle with somewhat equal forces.

<margin>
Definition of True, Perfect, and Simple Mixture.
</margin>
Therefore, with these laws observed, there shall be mixture, which can be defined thus: A true, perfect, and simple mixture is the motion of various tiny bodies within a common matter, occurring through opposing qualities with equal forces, so that a union of matter and future form is achieved, and a single [thing] out of...

<margin>
The difference in definition and perfection depends on the nature of the subject.
</margin>
What was said previously—that when one thing is <term>corrupted</term> <note>meaning destroyed or broken down</note> another is born, and when one is born another is corrupted, and when a simple mixture is dissolved another mixture arises, and one follows the other—requires a distinction based on the nature of the subject. For these successive changes only take place in **remote**, **medial**, or **near** matter, but not in **proximate** matter. For example, if a dog is to be born, the 

<margin>
Remote, medial, and near matter is corrupted and dissolved.
</margin>
elements are the **remote matter**; the bread, meat, and nutrients are the **medial matter**; and that which immediately precedes the seed is called the **near matter**. Likewise, in metals, the elements are the remote matter of silver and gold; that which follows them before the birth of the metal is the medial matter; and the metals themselves are the 

<margin>
Proximate matter is not corrupted, but perfected.
</margin>
**near matter**. In this varied and manifold matter, before reaching the **proximate** stage, many changes must occur through birth and death in plants and animals, and through dissolution and mixing in simple mixtures. But when one reaches the **proximate matter**—that is, the seed, or what takes the place of the seed—the subject does not die so that something else may arise; rather, the same subject is simply **perfected**.

<margin>
Scaliger.
</margin>
This is what **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous Italian scholar and physician whose "Exotericarum Exercitationum" was a standard textbook on natural philosophy.</note> seems to me to have observed more clearly and stated more subtly than anyone else in his sixth exercise, second distinction. For an **egg**, which is the proximate matter for a chick, is changed while being warmed by the hen until it reaches the form of a chick; it is not corrupted (destroyed), but perfected. That it is perfected is evident from this: if the shell of the egg is broken, nothing "corrupt" or rotten is found inside. And because, he says, the egg and the seed cease to be egg and seed after the animal is born, the common people say they are "corrupted." 

<margin>
In perfection, matter does not perish, but another form succeeds the one that passes.
</margin>
But among the wise, because nothing of the subject perishes, they are not corrupted but **perfected**. For in "perfection," nothing of the matter is lost, but the whole persists; only the prior form is lost as another succeeds it. Thus, **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>—whether the common kind or that extracted from other metals—is not destroyed when mixed for **Silver-making** <note>Argyrogonia</note> or **Gold-making** <note>Chrysogonia</note>, but is merely perfected. I have said that the efficient cause draws out quicksilver from tin, lead, copper, and iron. For these metals themselves are not the **proximate matter** <note>The substance immediately ready to be transformed.</note> of silver or gold, but only **near matter**; therefore, by a simple dissolution, the proximate matter must be separated from their bulk matter, which is quicksilver. Nor does it matter whether that quicksilver was fluid or not, provided it has been purged of all filth and substance foreign to the nature of quicksilver. Indeed, the more perfectly it is <term>decocted</term> <note>A term for "cooking" or maturing matter through heat, similar to how fruit ripens.</note>, the more ready a subject it will be. For if we were to define silver and gold by their matter, surely both would be nothing other than **pure quicksilver**, cleansed of all foreign substance, refined and cooked according to the degree of each. For gold is far purer and much more thoroughly cooked, even to the very limit of metallic nature, while silver is less so. That this is the case is manifest from the mutual embrace of quicksilver with gold and silver, as well as from the similarity of certain specific qualities between them discussed previously, and also because by art, gold is almost always dissolved into fluid quicksilver.

<margin>Fire releases quicksilver from metals.</margin>
Fire, which I called the aiding efficient cause, performs this dissolution most effectively. For it separates **heterogeneous** things <note>Things of a different nature or "impurities."</note> and gathers **homogeneous** things <note>Things of the same nature.</note>. And it achieves this either alone, or repeatedly and often, by purging these bodies in turns, or in an instant by the addition of the **silver-making or gold-making seed**, which retains the quicksilver of those four bodies while the external fire dissolves and drives out what is foreign and impure.

<margin>The effect of the seed and fire acting upon the proximate matter.</margin>
After the substance foreign to the nature of quicksilver has been dissolved from those four bodies, what remains is invincible against the fires: namely, **pure quicksilver**. However, its mixture is not yet perfect when compared to the mixture of silver and gold. For this reason, I added that it, as well as common quicksilver, must be perfected.

<margin>Perfect mixture in a natural body in the definition of the efficient cause.</margin>
I call the **mixture of the elements** in every natural body "perfect" when their equal powers have united into one, so that the portions of the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry are equal, achieving a state of **justice** <note>original: "iustitia"; refers to a perfect medical or physical equilibrium.</note>, as physicians are accustomed to say. Therefore, among the metals of different species, only gold is temperate and balanced.

<margin>Definition of Temperament.</margin>
For **temperament** <note>The "complexion" or specific ratio of the four primary qualities.</note> is the equal proportion of the primary qualities which are in the mixtures. However, this equality is not to be measured by the magnitude of its mass or by weight—since in metals or quicksilver there is a more abundant supply of earth and water than in all other natural bodies—but rather by the force and efficacy of its power...

It explains that alchemy uses fire and a "seed" to strip away impurities, leaving behind a balanced temperament of the four elements.</summary>

# SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING <note>original: "ARGYR. ET CHRYSOP." referring to Argyropoeia and Chrysopoeia</note>

<margin>
Why gold does not yield to fire.
</margin>
<margin>
In gold, all things are balanced.
</margin>
<margin>
Mercury flees from fire, but is not destroyed.
</margin>
<margin>
The moisture in mercury is undefined.
</margin>
<margin>
Mixing occurs through concoction.
</margin>
...efficiency, to which all things are clearly credited. Because the powers and qualities of the elements from which gold is composed are equal, it does not allow itself to be pulled apart into pieces or to be raised up as smoke. For the dry element holds onto the moist to prevent it from flying away, and the moist element binds the dry so it does not turn into ash. The cold element restrains the ferocity of the hot, and the hot awakens the sluggishness of the cold. In short, in gold, all things—acting and being acted upon with equal forces—bring themselves to a state of moderation. 

But common <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury, referred to here as *argentum vivum*.</note>, because of its abundance of cold and moisture, is carried upward into vapor by the violence of external fire. However, the dry parts are not separated from the moist ones because of the extremely tight mixing of both, which causes the moisture to drag the earthy part along with it. This is as if to say that the substances of the elements in quicksilver are indeed so united that they can in no way be torn from each other; yet their powers or qualities are uneven and unequal. Furthermore, the powers or qualities of the other metals that exist within the elements of quicksilver are not so unequal, and they approach closer to a balanced temperament. Yet in all of them, the moisture is "undefined" <note>In Aristotelian physics, "undefined" moisture refers to a liquid that has no shape of its own and is not yet "fixed" into a solid state.</note>, and it must be defined so that it may reach the temperament of silver or gold. 

Then the mixture is called perfect. This perfection is achieved through **concoction**. For Aristotle says that <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; a natural ripening or "cooking" process by which heat brings matter to its final, perfect form.</note> is a certain kind of perfection. For whatever things have been concocted are also perfect and fully generated. That concoction is perfection is proven by observation: for all things commonly admitted to be concocted are seen to be imperfect before they are cooked, and finally become perfect through that very process. I have said that this concoction and perfection are brought about by the **efficient cause** which I have defined. How and why this happens must be explained even more fully.

<margin>
How and why the efficient cause prepares the proximate matter.
</margin>
The matter from which—by the service of the art—the **seed** of silver or gold has come forth, was quicksilver, but "cooked"—that is to say, silver and gold. This seed is hot and dry; for it acquired these powers and qualities through concoction, since all things that are concocted are hot. But our **proximate matter**—that is, common quicksilver and that which exists as a "proximate potential" within other metals—is cold and moist, some more or less than others. Therefore, when the seed and the quicksilver are mixed, they unite easily because of the same proximate origin of both, and the fiery heat of fusion mixes them even more thoroughly. The hot and dry qualities of the seed then act upon the cold and moist qualities of the quicksilver, and while those qualities act, they also experience a reciprocal effect...

# DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGIA"</note>

...and these, by being acted upon, react in turn. But if the contrary forces of both are equal—for example, if the <term>seed</term> <note>The active principle or "soul" of a metal that directs its growth.</note> is hot and dry by eight degrees, and the quicksilver is cold and moist by the same number of degrees—the quicksilver will be brought to a balanced temperament. This is very much like what happens when hot, boiling water is mixed with cold water; because of the struggle between contrary qualities, it becomes lukewarm and tempered. However, the heat in water is accidental and comes from the outside, whereas in the seed of silver or gold, it is innate. 

If the forces of the seed and the quicksilver are unequal, a balanced temperament will not follow. For instance, if the heat and dryness of the seed are eight degrees, but the coldness and moisture of the quicksilver are only one degree, the latter will be subjected to the mastery of the former. The quicksilver will then be turned into the seed, though it will have less power because the degrees of heat and dryness in the seed have been somewhat defeated. I have said before that "birth" and "destruction" occur when the powers of the agents greatly overwhelm those of the things being acted upon, while "mixing" occurs when they contend with equal contrary forces.

<margin>Why gold and silver in their own nature do not act upon quicksilver.</margin>
For this reason, gold and silver, when mixed in their natural state with quicksilver, do not act upon it; they do not fight amongst themselves with contrary qualities, but are of almost the same balanced temperament. Therefore, when the temperament of gold or silver is added to common quicksilver—or to that which is mixed into other bodies—the thorough mixing will be completed by the power of the qualities of either seed, fighting equally with the help of external fire. Immediately, the silver or golden form will leap forth, and the metal will be found <term>tinctured</term> <note>Meaning "transformed" or "dyed" throughout its entire substance, not just on the surface.</note> to its very roots. 

The earthy part of quicksilver is white in its current state but red in its potential; when it is "cooked" by the mixing of the gold-making seed, it turns red and shapes its moisture into a lemon-yellow color. Indeed, all color comes from "cooked iron" <note>original: "ferro decocto"; likely referring to a specific metallic state or the "sulfur" principle associated with color.</note>; this is demonstrated in the appearance of the lemon-color, which becomes red through further cooking. But the silver-making seed, since it is only half-cooked, does not change the color of the earthy part as much; instead, the transformed quicksilver retains its own color, though it is more thoroughly cooked. More should have been said about the <term>proximate matter</term> <note>The immediate substance used in the work, usually mercury.</note> and the <term>efficient cause</term>, but those belong to other questions. Let it be enough to have demonstrated these things truly, openly, and without deception for the matter at hand.

<margin>III. The third part of Silver-making and Gold-making is Method.</margin>
The third part of Silver-making and Gold-making <note>original: "Argyropœiæ & Chrysopœiæ"</note> follows in order to be treated: namely, the **Method** of acting. This provides the instructions on the art by which common quicksilver is to be prepared so that it approaches more closely the nature of silver or gold, and how metals that are imperfectly mixed are turned into the matter proximate to silver or gold...

# SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING <note>original: "ARGYR. ET CHRYSOP."</note>

...must be resolved: Then truly, by what way the silver-making or gold-making <term>seed</term> <note>The "seed" is the active alchemical principle believed to contain the "form" or "soul" of the metal, capable of transforming base matter.</note> is produced from silver or gold. Finally, how the same <term>proximate material</term> <note>materia proxima: The immediate substance, usually mercury, that is ready to be transformed by the seed.</note> is mixed with either seed, so that from the mixture of both, the body of a silver or golden form arises. Regarding this part, I have decided to discuss it more briefly.

<margin>The author knows the art of preparing quicksilver, of resolving metals into the same, and how the seed arises from gold.</margin>
Indeed, I know by what art quicksilver is prepared, or how tin, lead, and copper are resolved into the same, and I touched upon this earlier. But I have also caught the scent of how each seed arises from silver and gold. However, I thought it better to pass over in silence those great secrets which the Ancients skilled in this art concealed—lest the art become cheapened—rather than rashly profaning such great mysteries to the common people.

<margin>The method of mixing the proximate material with the seed.</margin>
It will be enough, indeed more than is proper, if I indicate the method of mixing the proximate material with each seed. The method of this mixture is divided into two paths. One is the rival and imitator of nature. The other is violent.

<margin>Definition of the former method.</margin>
The former is that which teaches one to <term>concoct</term> <note>An alchemical term for "ripening" or "digesting" a substance through steady heat, mimicking natural processes.</note> the proximate material together with its silver-making or gold-making seed, first with a weak external heat, then gradually and increased by degrees, until they arrive at a perfect mixture and union, so that from this, silver or gold grows together.

<margin>Definition of the latter method.</margin>
The latter method of mixture is indeed "violent"; it demonstrates how, by throwing either seed into tin, lead, copper, iron, or quicksilver of any kind, it produces silver or gold immediately in a moment, with the help of fire.

<margin>The reason for the difference between the two methods.</margin>
The reason for this difference is that in the former method of acting, the powers and fiery qualities of the seed are too weak to be able to "ripen" and define the moisture of the quicksilver—whether it be common or drawn from other metals—in a single moment; therefore, it is necessary for the material to be moved gradually. But in the latter mode, these fiery powers of the seed are so strong that, at the very first meeting and contact with the help of external heat, they decoct and transmute every kind of quicksilver into silver or gold. This is not unlike a most violent fire which consumes and burns up both dry and green wood immediately without distinction; the watery moisture does not hinder it, since it cannot resist such great heat. However, if that fire were weak, it would not burn green wood with such great speed.

<margin>Many and diverse ways of each method.</margin>
The way of putting each method into practice is not one and the same for everyone, even though the end and goal are the same for all. However, I will briefly touch upon the method which approaches closer to nature and will more greatly provide proof to the senses.

This, then, is the preparation. I speak to the craftsmen who are experienced in these things, and I am forced to use the terms of the art so that all things may be understood more clearly. ¶ Let the quicksilver be sublimated <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid; used here to remove impurities.</note> four times or more, until it surpasses snow in whiteness and appears transparent like glass cooked out in sublimation. Thus you will have quicksilver most pure and splendid, and to some extent freed from its natural excessive coldness and moisture. For the dregs, which are mixed with it in sublimation, retain whatever is impure; however, the thinner moisture—which is also less "cooked"—rises to the upper part of the vessel in the likeness of a powder. But the purer part, more thoroughly cooked, heavier, and solid, remains and sticks in the middle part of the vessel, which is passable; and from this, the resolved and fluid quicksilver is in some way tempered. From this clarified quicksilver, and from silver or gold reduced to a lime <term>calx</term> <note>A powder produced by heating a metal until it loses its metallic properties; an oxide.</note>, let an amalgam <term>malagma</term> be made. Let it be ground for a very long time upon marble, then let it be squeezed out wrapped in a thicker linen cloth, until some thinner part of the silver or gold flows out together with the quicksilver. Let new purified quicksilver be added to the amalgam which could not pass through because of its thickness, and let it be squeezed out again. And let these works be repeated again and again just as many times, until the entire amalgam has filtered through. But if it is too stubborn, it must be softened and thinned by being buried for several days in warm horse dung <term>fimus equinus</term> <note>Used by alchemists as a steady, gentle heat source, similar to a modern laboratory incubator.</note>, and this must be repeated until either **seed** has flowed through entirely with the quicksilver.

# APOLOGIA
<note>original: "Apologia" – A formal defense or justification of a position or belief.</note>

<margin>
The second method of operation through projection.
</margin>
...require the diligence and hand of a craftsman, and can only be accomplished over the course of time. We shall be excused from these [labors] by the *a posteriori* method of operation <note>A method based on results or effects rather than theoretical principles.</note>—namely, if we obtain the desired perfected "seed" for making silver or gold. For when this is projected <note>The act of "projection" involves throwing a small amount of the transmuting "Stone" or powder onto a mass of molten base metal.</note> onto any metals melted in a fire, a small portion of it is immediately mixed with the parts of "living silver" <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note> within them; it retains them, ripens them, and, being perfectly united, tints them into silver or gold. Meanwhile, the external fire burns away whatever is impure and separates it into a dross that floats on the surface.

<margin>
Confirmation of Gold-making and Silver-making.
</margin>
To follow our proposed order, we must now confirm that the arts of **Silver-making** <term>Argyropoeia</term> and **Gold-making** <term>Chrysopoeia</term> are true. Since authority, reason, and experience carry great weight in confirming the question "Does it exist?", I could first confirm the truth of this art by the testimonies and authority of many highly respected men. However, a book has already been published on this subject titled *On the Truth and Antiquity of the Chemical Art and Powder* <note>original: "De veritate & antiquitate artis chemicæ & pulveris"</note> by the author **Robertus Vallensis** <note>Robert Duval (c. 1490–1567), a French alchemist and scholar.</note>, published in Paris by Fridericus Morellus in 1561. Therefore, those who wish to have the truth of the art proven to them by authorities, we refer to the reading of that booklet. But we have decided that we must lean more upon reasons and demonstrate the art through certain experiments.

<margin>
Arguments drawn from probable reasons confirming the art.
</margin>
We must, therefore, defend these arts of Silver-making and Gold-making with no more probable reasons and arguments than those which have been said, and those which are to be said hereafter in refuting the arguments of **Erastus** <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who was a famous opponent of Paracelsus and alchemical transmutation.</note>. Specifically, this defense arises from the knowledge of the "proximate matter" <note>The raw material that is closest in nature to the desired result.</note> of silver and gold, and the **efficient cause** <note>The primary agent that produces an effect.</note>. I believe no one should doubt that since both of these can be drawn out by art from things that nature has brought to light of her own accord, the matter can be perfected by art and take on the form of silver or gold according to both prescribed methods.

<margin>
Matter and efficient cause are the foundation of all effects.
</margin>
For the foundations of all works and effects, whether natural or artificial, are **matter** and the **efficient cause**. This should be considered all the more achievable because it is most true that it lies within the power of art to provide what is necessary

<margin>
It is in the power of art to provide what is necessary to drive natural causes to act.
</margin>
to drive natural causes to act. Indeed, that which seems necessary in art is only this: that it mixes the elements of the proximate matter and completes the imperfect mixture. For the subject of the acting cause is an inanimate body, and the duty of that same agent is nothing other than to mix—not to give life, to nourish, or to perform the other duties that are necessary in the birth of plants and animals. Furthermore, external heat [completes] the qualities of the metals and the elements of the matter...

by the benefit of fire, can mix those things which are miscible <note>Substances capable of being mixed together.</note>, having observed those laws which I mentioned a little earlier when I was discussing mixture. That this mixture can be effected by fire, although
<margin>Scaliger proves against Cardanus that one can mix with fire.</margin>
Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who often criticized alchemical claims.</note> had denied it in his book *On the Subtlety of Things* <note>original: "libro de subtilitate rerum"</note>, he was rightly rebuked by Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar known for his "Exotericae Exercitationes" which critiqued Cardano.</note> in his hundred-and-first exercise, twelfth distinction. For in an alembic <note>An early chemical still used for distillation.</note>, Scaliger says, many diverse and contrary things are accumulated, and the fire mixes them in that vessel which is called the receiver, in such a way that they can be separated by no force thereafter. And this is surely from nature: nor, he says, should the nature of fire be rashly torn away from nature itself. But lest examples of the art be sought from too far away, by which it can be demonstrated that things are truly 
<margin>That one can truly mix through art is demonstrated by the example of glass.</margin>
mixed: Is not glass a natural body consisting of matter and form? For it is not earth, nor water, much less air or fire, but a concrete mass from the mixture of these by the power of qualities. And yet, that which becomes glass has no other craftsman than the glassmaker, nor any other active cause than fire. The art, indeed, cannot produce the matter from which glass is made, but it subjects wood to the fire, by which it is consumed and turned into ash. Then the ash is mixed with pure sand or with transparent pebbles ground very finely; hence both materials are reduced to lime by the fire, and finally, the same is melted by violent fire and turned into glass. In the same way, art does not produce the metals, nor the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>, nor the matter of the silver or gold seed, but it subjects them to the fire, which subdues and alters their qualities, mixes them, and effects the works proper to the art, the effect of which is mixture, or
<margin>In the matter of vegetables or animals, innate powers are present.</margin>
the opposite of this: a resolution into another simple mixture. Certainly, if it were necessary to introduce growth, sensation, or the transformation of one individual into an individual plant or animal, fire or fiery heat would by no means provide this; rather, it would be the power and efficient heat innate to the matter and the seed. This is not of the genus of fiery heat, but is celestial and corresponds in proportion to the element of the stars, as Aristotle rightly says.
<margin>The matter of inanimate bodies is moved by an external impulse, not an innate force.</margin>
But the question is not about growth or sensation, but about the mixture of inanimate bodies, which are not moved by an innate power, but by an external impulse. But if it should be objected that even in the matter of simply mixed bodies their own powers are present, by which [they move] toward a form...

<margin>The first experiment.</margin>
into pure silver. From five pounds of tin, one pound or thereabouts of quicksilver is drawn out. Once removed, it is purified in a bath of salt and vinegar until it is shining; with four ounces of this quicksilver is mixed one [ounce] of a certain silvery "gum," both fusible and <term>fixed</term> <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that remains stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to fire.</note>. It becomes fusible and fixed by the mixture of one ounce of pure silver with four ounces of arsenic, previously sublimated, purified, and through repeated sublimation, fixed with the same silver. From here it is dissolved by hot water vapor until it appears like a thick oil. Therefore, one portion of this oil, mixed with four portions of the quicksilver drawn out of tin by art, is enclosed in a glass vessel, and by the power of heat—at first weak, then increased until the tenth day—it is cooked until it remains as a fixed ashen powder.

### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING
### 43

...[it] will have, which when melted with lead and proven by the cupellation test <note>original: "examini cineritij" — a refining process where ores are heated in a "cupel" made of bone ash; the lead and impurities are absorbed, leaving pure silver or gold</note>, is turned into the truest silver. The cause of this effect was handed down in the previous sections.

<margin>Second experiment.</margin> The other experiment is the mutation of silver into gold by this method. Let there be distilled a very sharp and staining water <note>original: "aqua acerrima & tingens" — likely nitric acid or aqua fortis, used for dissolving metals</note>, which most people know; once distilled, it must be distilled again and more often, until no dregs remain at the bottom of the vessel after distillation. For it is of great importance that all things be purged of impure dregs and thickness. Common quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> must also be purged by several repeated sublimations <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify chemicals</note>, until it becomes clear, and then let it be revived. Let two ounces of the purest silver be dissolved separately in the distilled sharp water. In the same water, let four ounces of the purest quicksilver be dissolved separately; let the dissolved liquids be mixed. First, let the water be distilled with a weak fire until it has all dripped through. Then let the degree of heat be increased, so that even the quicksilver "breathes out" <note>vaporizes</note> through distillation; then let the glass vessel be broken. At the bottom of the vessel, you will see a silvery mass tinted partly with an ashen color, and partly with a dark reddish color. Finally, reduce it into a body <note>melt the powder back into a solid metallic form</note>. Even if this silver has not yet changed its color, nor is it yet gold, it is nevertheless purer and more solid than natural silver, and its "moisture" <note>An alchemical term for the internal fluid quality of a metal that gives it malleability</note> is more defined. Therefore, in the examination of gold—namely, the cement <note>original: "cementi" — a purification process where gold is heated with corrosive salts to remove silver</note>—it is separated with great difficulty and only after frequent repetitions. Indeed, even when it has been dissolved by the sharp water of separation <note>Nitric acid, used to part silver from gold</note>, you will see certain filings of pure gold settle at the bottom. By this sign, you will judge that the entire mass of silver can be changed into gold, since the same principle applies to the whole as to a part. This work 
<margin>A probable example.</margin> bears a certain resemblance to the ripening of fruits. For when grapes first ripen, you will see certain grains steeped in a black color, while the rest are without any change of color; yet, when the ripening is completed through the preceding and continued heat, they all become black. Thus, if the same silver is dissolved more often by the same sharp water, and quicksilver dissolved in it is mixed with it, and the water is distilled, and the quicksilver has evaporated and the mass settling at the bottom is reduced into a body, the whole will be changed into gold. 
<margin>Different heats are a sign of ripening.</margin> By repeating the concoctions <note>original: "coctiones" — literally "cookings" or heat-treatments</note>, it will periodically take on various colors, until finally a red, splendid, fixed, and unchangeable color will appear, which is the sign of perfect concoction. 
<margin>Silver vanishes with strong water unless it is held back by a skilled artisan.</margin> But great diligence must be used in the reduction into a body, lest it fall too much in weight; otherwise, almost all the silver will vanish into the vapor of the spirits of the sharp waters during the repetition of the work. ### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING ###

...it dissolves the gold, and once the dissolution is complete, a "germ" or sprout is generated. This is the material closest to the future silver-making and gold-making seed, which gradually increases in strength through <term>concoction</term> <note>From the Latin 'concoctio,' referring to a process of ripening or "digesting" through steady, controlled heat, similar to how fruit ripens or food is digested.</note> until it finally hardens into a red mass, as hard as glass. I believe it was for this reason that the name of "the Stone" was given to it.

<margin>
From where the name of the Stone comes.
</margin>

Once the vessel is broken, this Stone is ground into very fine pieces. It is then enclosed in a glass vessel sealed with <term>lute</term> <note>A specialized clay or cement used to airtightly seal alchemical vessels.</note> and must be digested by an excellent fire for three days, until it turns into a fixed and fiery red or purple powder, having achieved the highest perfection.

<margin>
The damned and reviled earth. 
The work of three days.
</margin>

On the surface of this powder, an impure earth will float, which they call "damned and reviled" <note>original: "damnata & vituperata"; refers to the 'caput mortuum' or the useless chemical dregs left after a process.</note>, and this must be cast away. They usually call this final stage "the work of three days." During the entire period of its transformation, the matter of our seed takes on no fewer colors than a plant does.

<margin>
Three colors in the gold-making seed while it is in motion.
</margin>

Among these colors, experts in the art have noted three principal ones: black, white, and red. However, once the whiteness has been reached, it is called the silver-making seed or <term>Argyrogonia</term> <note>From Greek, meaning "the birth or generation of silver."</note>. In this state, it has the power and ability to change quicksilver <note>mercury</note> of any kind into pure silver. But practitioners have preferred to proceed further, continuing the digestion alone with increased heat to produce the gold-making seed.

Just as a farmer, once the seeds are cast into the fields, commits the rest to Nature until the time of harvest arrives, so too the practitioner of <term>Argyropœia</term> <note>The art of making silver.</note> acts. As soon as he has enclosed the material in the vessel and applied and continuously nurtured the appropriate heat, no further labor will be required of him. Instead, the rest must be committed to the heat until the seed first takes on its whiteness—and thus its silver-making power—and then finally, through continued digestion, it emerges as a red, gold-making powder.

<margin>
Few things suffice for this art.
</margin>

To complete this work, there is very little need for many furnaces, vessels, waters, or oils; a single suitable furnace, gold, and its own quicksilver are enough. A single ounce of gold at most is sufficient, nor must anything else be added thereafter. No dangers can occur, either. For once the seed is enclosed and the heat applied around it, it is neither touched nor moved from its place until it reaches maturity. Nor is there a need for constant labor, but only the fire must be tended. One's own professional duties need not be neglected; rather, while working on great and admirable things, the common people will think nothing is being done. In this way, a favorable reputation will be maintained among everyone, and nothing will be taken away from it. Furthermore, if profit is to be sought more than...

# APOLOGIA #

<margin>
The wonderful power of God in this art.
</margin>
...how wonderful is the power of God in the works of nature, which have flowed from His omnipotence; no treasure can be compared to this gold-making powder. Indeed, a single <term>drachma</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 3.9 grams.</note> of it, even if it has undergone the process of "birth" only once, will immediately—with the help of external fire—constrain and transform 200 or more times its own weight of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; also known as mercury.</note> into the purest gold, depending on the strength of its power.

<margin>
Riches. From where this so wonderful effect arises.
</margin>
The cause of this most wonderful effect is a fiery force within the gold, sought out through a long and temperate <term>concoction</term> <note>The process of "ripening" or "digesting" through steady heat.</note> after it has been dissolved from its own "moisture" or quicksilver. While this force was at first dormant in the gold and existed only as a potential, it breaks forth into action through that same dissolution and concoction. It is not unlike the power lying hidden in an egg, which is awakened by the heat of a hen so that a chick eventually emerges from it—a creature consisting of a far more noble and excellent form than the egg itself. In this same way, the gold-making seed is far nobler than the gold from which it took its origin. This gold-making power, through the fiery qualities acquired by the seed during its long ripening, restrains and tempers the overflowing moisture of common quicksilver (or that which is within metals). From this tempering, the imperfect mixture of the quicksilver is perfected, and the golden form is immediately bestowed upon it.

<margin>
The augmentation of powers into infinity.
</margin>
But what is even more worthy of admiration is that its powers are increased into infinity by repeating the work. For if that gold-making seed, once produced from gold, is mixed again with its own moisture in a certain proportion, dissolved, and ripened with temperate heat, it will eventually emerge as a red powder in an even shorter amount of time. Its previous powers will be multiplied, and the more often the work is repeated, the more quickly it is completed, and the work will be increased with more effective power. For just as grains of wheat, sown again and again, increase in number and quantity into infinity, so the gold-making seed, dissolved and ripened again and again, will increase its own powers into infinity. And as it is the specific duty in the seeds of plants and animals to propagate their offspring through generation, so it is specific to the gold-making seed that, once it has been frequently dissolved from its quicksilver and ripened, it increases in strength. By these powers, through mixture with common quicksilver or the quicksilver of metals, it propagates its own golden species. <term>Augurellius</term> <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), an Italian poet and alchemist famous for his poem "Chrysopoeia" (Gold-making).</note> mentions this increase near the end of his *Chrysopoeia* in these verses:

> Therefore, let the wise man not yield here to the final labor,
> For the use is brief and of very little skill, but rich.

# DEFENSE #

[it] can [not], nor is it so easy, nor does it yield an exit with such great profit. Let us follow the footsteps of the fathers, who most truly declared that we can never go astray if we follow nature as our guide.

<margin>The path of the ancients is easier and safer than that of the moderns.</margin>
However, from what has been said, one should not think the art so easy that anyone may attain it immediately. For gold must be prepared so that it is not at all resistant to dissolution, and that is indeed quite arduous.

<margin>The art is difficult.</margin>
Nor truly should it be thought that the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note> which possesses the faculty of dissolving gold is that common kind which is sold openly by pharmacists or merchants. For since it is necessary that the dissolution of that gold be performed by a body which resembles gold in the likeness of its entire substance, and is of a hot and moist temperament, it cannot be denied that quicksilver possesses that likeness; however, it is certain that it is of a very cold and most indefinite temperament.

<margin>The quicksilver of the Philosophers is not the common kind.</margin>
But we must, by an ingenious art, draw out and lead forth a quicksilver from another source—from a body known to very few, which nature has cooked, which even more closely resembles gold in the likeness of its entire substance than common quicksilver, and which, by no human art, but by its first contact and rubbing with gold, joins and mixes with it no less than water does with water.

<margin>Philosophical furnace.</margin>
Now contemplate more deeply what that body might be. Furthermore, few know the furnace which can supply a continuous and equal heat. <margin>The tripod of secrets.</margin> But fewer still know the tripod of secrets, and very few know the fuel <note>original: "pabulum"; literally 'fodder' or 'food', referring to the fuel source that maintains the flame.</note> for the heat, through which one can provide uniformity.

<margin>The secret consists in the degree of heat.</margin>
Almost the entire secret consists in the degree of heat. For just as the formative power of a chick implanted in an egg must not be overcome by external heat—otherwise the egg would harden and never afterward produce a chick—so the power of the future seed, that is, of gold mixed with its quicksilver, must not be exhausted; otherwise the gold would not be dissolved, nor will it germinate, nor will it become a matter closest to gold, but it would congeal into gold by the action of excessive heat. On the other hand, if the heat should fail, it will frustrate the labor of the craftsman.

<margin>The powder is placed in the power of God.</margin>
Finally, truly, this gold-making powder is placed in the power of God, who grants it to whom He wills and withdraws it, and it is sought in vain by those to whom it is denied.

<margin>Palingenius.</margin>
Hence Palingenius <note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus (c. 1500–1543), an Italian poet whose didactic work "Zodiacus Vitae" (The Zodiac of Life) blended science, philosophy, and alchemy.</note> says in his *Zodiac*, when Apollo had answered pious men seeking this gold-making powder under an enigma and a certain obscure oracle, and had summoned them from here to the vaults of heaven, he adds this:

->*Then men, turning over the hidden oracles of the divine mind*<-
->*In their wavering souls, [could] scarcely [do so] for a long time.*<-

However, so that all things may become clearer, I have thought it appropriate to change the style I previously maintained in the continuous narrative of the Defense's confirmation, and to use a different method hereafter in refuting the arguments brought by Erastus against the same.

<margin>On the nature of metals in the bowels of the earth.</margin>

What the opinions of Aristotle and the others were, I have touched upon above. Out of these, I would not dare to pronounce anything as certain regarding which might be truer. But let it be as you wish, and let it be granted that Aristotle’s opinion should be favored. Yet this pertains nothing to the proposed question of whether Argyropoeia or Chrysopoeia is a true art. This art does not inquire into the primary matter from which metals first arise in the mines; rather, the generosity of nature has offered another matter very close to silver and gold, whose imperfect mixture an "efficient cause" <note>In Aristotelian terms, the agent or force that brings something into being; here, the alchemist or his catalyst.</note> can perfect, as is manifest from what has been said previously. 

You continue your discussion on the nature of metals, stating that they differ in species and that they are ductile <note>Capable of being hammered thin or drawn into wire.</note>, and you declare that quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> is not a metal. I also agree with you on this. But whereas you assign its "specific difference" <note>The essential characteristic that defines a species.</note> as being ductile, I assert that this property is common to all metals, used to discern them from quicksilver and other bodies. However, I deny that being ductile is the *specific* difference. For the specific differences of things are unknown to us, and we use their unique properties in place of those differences. Metals do not differ from one another because they are ductile, but because they are more or less perfectly mixed, and because some are burned up by fire or pulled apart into their essential parts, while others—like silver and gold—are not at all.
