## THE FIRST ARGUMENT OF ERASTUS
### *against Silver-making and Gold-making.*

Whatever art relies upon ruinous foundations is soon to collapse.
But the foundations of Silver-making <note>original: "Argyropœiæ"</note> and Gold-making <note>original: "Chrysopœiæ"</note> are that some metals are perfect and others are imperfect, and that these can be changed into perfect ones: which are false foundations.
Therefore, Silver-making and Gold-making are soon to collapse.

No one doubts the first premise <note>original: "propositione"</note>. However, you wish to prove the second premise <note>original: "assumtionem"</note> by this argument: Whatever things have a natural form and consist by that form are perfect. Every metal, however, is perfect and consists by its own form and has its name from it, and it is false that the remaining metals are some sort of "rough drafts" of gold. Therefore, every single metal is perfect. Furthermore, you strive to prove by this argument that the remaining metals cannot attain any greater perfection: As soon as the natural efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; in this context, the force of nature acting upon matter.</note> has completed the movement in the matter, it ceases, and no longer contemplates anything further within it. Nor has nature anywhere changed any metal in the mines of the earth into another; it is a fiction what the Chemists <note>original: "Chemici"</note> have said concerning the imperfect mixture of these metals in the mines. For as soon as the matter has been thickened into metal by cold, any further "ripening" <note>original: "coctionem"; literally 'cooking' or 'decoction,' the alchemical process of maturation in the earth</note> is expected in vain. Since, therefore, nature has never transmuted the cheaper metals into the nobler ones, art will be even less able to provide this.

### *Response to the first argument.*

<margin>Metals are called perfect because of their mixture, not because of their form.</margin>
I respond to the second premise: Metals are not said to be either perfect or imperfect because of their "form," but because of their mixture <note>original: "mistionem"; the specific ratio and quality of the elemental components</note>. For each metal is indeed perfect if we look at its "form," because each exists as a distinct thing through it; but if we look at the mixture, one is perfect and another is imperfect. For that which is imperfectly mixed can be called imperfect, such as the less noble metals which, because they are less [thoroughly] mixed, are dissolved by fire. Silver...

<meta>This page continues the author's rebuttal of Thomas Erastus’s arguments against alchemy. ->APOLOGY<-

Silver and gold are called perfect because they are indestructible by fire—especially gold. Thus, Aristotle called "rawness" <note>original: "cruditatem"</note> imperfection and "concoction" <term>concoction: the process of "ripening" or refining matter through heat, an Aristotelian concept</term> perfection in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*. And yet, even things that have not yet reached maturity possess a **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the internal essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "grape-ness" of a grape)</term> by which they are consistent and "perfect" in their own right, such as unripe grapes. For this reason, I would not wish to agree with those who think the remaining metals are merely "rough drafts" of gold, as might be said of unripe grapes. In the case of grapes, the innate efficient force has not yet finished its movement; however, in those metals, once the matter has been thickened by cold into the appearance of a metal, nature has completed its movement. Therefore, the foundation of **Silver-making** and **Gold-making** <note>original: "Argyropœia & Chrysopœia"</note> is not false when it calls one metal perfect and another imperfect, provided we are comparing their mixtures <note>original: "mistionem"</note> to one another—noting that one is imperfect, another perfect, and another even more perfect.

<margin>
Perfection and imperfection cannot be spoken of in plants and animals as they are in metals alone.
</margin>
This distinction of perfection and imperfection cannot be applied to plants and animals, which possess a substantial form. They do not consist through a simple mixture alone, like these inanimate and mute bodies which differ from one another only by the law of their composition; rather, they possess something more excellent that moves them to achieve their form, as I have said previously. Regarding your later point—that a thing already perfected by its form cannot be further perfected by nature, and that nature does not transform ignoble metals into noble ones within the bowels of the earth—we concede this. Nor do we agree with those who say nature was "hindered" because it did not transmute everything into gold. But we do not, therefore, grant you the conclusion of your argument: namely, that the same nature, with art as its helper, cannot produce noble metals from ignoble ones outside the mines of the earth. For some things are solely in the power of nature, such as metals solidified from their own principles; these arise spontaneously from nature alone and require no art or outside help. In these matters, we cannot imitate nature at all, since

<margin>
Nature alone cannot achieve certain things.
</margin>
we are ignorant of what their "proximate matter" and efficient cause may be. Yet some things nature cannot produce alone without the help of art, such as wheat. For unless the earth is first tilled and the wheat then sown, it will not propagate. Some things are even more within the power of art—things which nature alone never produces, nor will ever produce on its own, such as things mixed or dissolved by art. For although every physical body emerges from the womb of nature, nature alone has never produced, nor will ever produce, **glass**.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of alchemy against the criticisms of Thomas Erastus. Having previously argued that metals are "mixtures" rather than biological entities, the author now explains how the alchemist (Art) acts as a specialized assistant to Nature by controlling heat and refining matter in ways that do not occur spontaneously in the earth.</meta>

->SILVER AND GOLD-MAKING<-

But Art <note>Here, "Art" refers to the skill of the alchemist.</note> subjects every natural body to fire, which burns it and turns it into ash, and from this ash, glass is produced. Likewise, Nature has never distilled "water of life" <note>original: "aquam vitæ"; likely referring to concentrated alcohol or medicinal spirits</note> from wine, yet Art draws it out. Art also truly mixes "waters" <note>Refers to various chemical solutions or acids.</note> of different kinds and species which Nature never mixed. Therefore, it is no wonder if Nature, after producing the base metals <note>original: "ignobiliora metalla"</note> in the bowels of the earth, could not or cannot produce silver and gold from them on its own. Indeed, Nature itself, without Art, cannot dissolve these base metals into the **proximate matter** <term>proximate matter: the immediate substance or "building blocks" from which a specific thing is formed</term> of silver and gold; it has not even contemplated doing so, nor can it refine <note>original: "concoquere"; literally "cook" or "ripen"</note> that same matter in its own mines. For Nature has one kind of matter and one kind of **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the external force or agent that brings something into being</term>. Art, however, knows how to achieve this dissolution of base metals into their proximate matter, how to refine both that matter and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>, and how to bring an imperfect mixture to perfection. Yet Art is only the helper of Nature. This is because every body is natural, whether it is an "agent"—like the fire Art uses—or "passive," like the metals. Art cannot perform these works in plants and animals because the movement in them is not within the power of Art, but is a force innate to the matter itself.

<margin>Natural causes in a mixture are within the power of Art.</margin>
But for those things which consist of a simple mixture or dissolution, the causes that provide them are within the power of Art—such as fire and things of a fiery nature. Art can begin and "half-cook" this mixture, or complete the refining process, just as one sees in bricks that are either half-fired or perfectly fired. I have been rather wordy in solving this argument, both because you, Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who famously attacked the theories of Paracelsus and alchemy.</note>, thought that by this logic (as if by some insurmountable engine) the whole of **Gold-making** <note>original: "Chrysopœiam"</note> would collapse, and because it will serve to dismantle many other objections. But another argument follows, which is no less able to pierce through the whole Art than this one.

<margin>II.</margin>
### The Second Argument.

Among things perfect in their species, there is no change into another species contained under the same immediate genus; for example, a donkey cannot be transmuted into a dog, because both are contained under the same genus: "animal."

But lead, tin, copper, iron, silver, and gold are perfect in their species, and are all contained under the same genus: "metal."

Therefore, there can be no change between them.

### APOLOGY

->*Those things cannot be transmuted into these.*<-

->*Response.*<-

You repeat this second argument quite often, *Erastus*. But I will demonstrate that your prior proposition is not universally or always true. I will grant that your point should be conceded regarding plants and animals of different species within the same genus, because they are produced through the cycles of birth and death—that is, the movement of **generation and corruption** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "generation" is the coming-into-being of a thing, while "corruption" is its passing away or decay.</note>—and in the things corrupted or born, no prior **sensible quality** <note>original: "accidens sensile"; a physical property perceivable by the senses, such as color, weight, or smell.</note> remains. But in **mixed bodies** <note>Referring to inorganic substances like minerals and metals.</note>, I simply deny that your proposition applies. <margin>The change of iron into copper without the destruction of its metallic species.</margin> For the change of iron into the purest copper, which I explained above, proves the opposite; and one must trust a demonstration more than your opinion. Moreover, iron and copper are both under the same genus of "metal," and there is no total dissolution of sensible qualities in that change; instead, both remain under the "form" of metal. <margin>The change of silver into gold.</margin> I also added an experiment proven by me regarding silver changed into gold without the destruction of the metallic **form** <term>form: the essential nature or "soul" of a substance that makes it what it is, as opposed to its raw matter</term>, though that is indeed more difficult. Therefore, in changing iron into copper, anyone can easily experiment with little or no expense, and judge for themselves that your proposition is not always true. <margin>An egg is perfected, not destroyed.</margin> What if I say, along with *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned scholar and physician.</note>, that when an egg changes into a chick, it is not "corrupted" but perfected? It does not pass into a different genus of species, but its form is already present in it? But let it be; suppose your proposition and your assumption were granted: do you think your conclusion must therefore be granted to you? <margin>A donkey is changed into a dog.</margin> If a donkey were eaten by a dog and, after long transformations, was transmuted into the dog's seed, would you not believe that the seed could be transmuted into a dog? I do not think you would deny this. What if I also said that **tin**, **lead**, **copper**, and **iron** can be changed into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>? If I prove through Art that this is the matter closest to silver and gold, will you not concede that the one can be changed into the other? For the reasoning is no different. But perhaps you will say those metals cannot be dissolved into quicksilver. From your perspective, since you are ignorant of such a dissolution, I do not think you believe it possible. <margin>Mercury changed into gold through refining alone.</margin> You will also deny that quicksilver is the **proximate matter** <term>proximate matter: the immediate substance from which a thing is directly made; the "raw material" stage just before the final product</term> of silver and gold. I, however, have experienced this with quicksilver extracted <note>original: "prolicito"; drawn forth or enticed out</note> from tin, which through **refining** <note>original: "coctione"; literally "cooking" or "digestion," referring to the alchemical application of heat over time</note> alone was changed into the purest gold by an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the agent or force that brings a change about; in this case, the alchemist or the fire</term>. And I have demonstrated with many arguments above that it is the proximate matter of silver and gold, and I shall declare it even more clearly in what follows. Therefore, this [argument] of yours...

# SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING

...your argument will by no means be able to weaken **silver-making** <note>original: "Argyropœiam"; the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into silver.</note> or **gold-making** <note>original: "Chryſopœiam"; the art of making gold.</note>. For, as I have said, the logic of **birth and death** <note>original: "ortus & interitus"; referring to the Aristotelian cycle of generation and corruption.</note> is not the same in all things as the logic of simple mixing and dissolution.

<margin>III.</margin>
### *The Third Argument.*

What Nature effects, Art cannot effect.
But Nature alone can generate silver and gold. Therefore,
Gold-making cannot generate gold, nor can silver-making generate silver.
You prove this proposition by this reasoning: if Art were the producer of **generation** <note>The process by which a new substance comes into being.</note> just like Nature, there would be no distinction between the one and the other.

<margin>Art is not a prolific efficient cause, but a helping one.</margin>
### *Response.*

The answer was given above in the first argument: Art is only a helper and a driver, but all things happen through natural causes as the primary **efficient causes** <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; the "agent" that brings something about</term>. Nature sometimes, by itself alone in the bowels of the earth, produces metals from its own matter; and that same Nature generates silver and gold from the matter it has already produced. However, Nature cannot achieve this alone <insert>in the laboratory</insert> without Art as a helper and driver. By means of fire and substances possessing a fiery power, Art dissolves the remaining metals into a **matter** <term>materia: the underlying "stuff" of the universe that receives different forms</term> very close to silver and gold, afterwards **ripens** <note>original: "concoquit"; an alchemical term for maturing or perfecting a substance through heat, similar to digestion or ripening fruit.</note> them, and perfects them via an efficient cause, provided they are promoted from **potentiality to actuality** <note>A classic Aristotelian concept: "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, while "actuality" is the fulfillment of that capacity.</note>. I also brought forward the example of **glass** <note>original: "vitro"</note>, which is a natural body consisting of matter and form, fused by the power of fire from any matter turned to ash; Nature alone could never have produced this unless Art had prepared the material from those same natural causes. Therefore, regarding your claim that Nature alone effects what Art cannot: if you mean this in terms of the *primary* efficient cause, I will easily grant it to you; but if you mean it as the *helping* cause, I do not agree at all. This is especially true in those things which hold the logic and name of simple "mixture" alone, such as fusible and liquid things which are mixed by fire.

<margin>IV.</margin>
### *The Fourth Argument.*

That which is imperfect and incomplete is found in no species.
But every single metal is perfect in its own species.
Therefore,
The remaining <note>i.e., "base"</note> metals cannot be called "imperfect" or "incomplete" such that they might be changed into silver or gold.

DD 5
<meta>catchword: Respon-</meta>

# DEFENSE

->*Response to the Fourth Argument.*<-

<margin>
The mixture of metals is imperfect, not the form.
</margin>
To this argument, based on what was said above, we respond that the name "perfection" is ambiguous <note>original: "aequivocum"; having multiple meanings depending on the context.</note>. If the form and species of each metal are considered, each one is perfect in itself. But if the mixture of elements is considered, only the mixture of gold is perfect, while that of the others is imperfect. In natural bodies, those things whose moisture is undefined and capable of being defined are called "imperfect." For **concoction** <term>concoction: a process of ripening or maturing through heat, similar to how fruit ripens or how the earth "cooks" minerals into metals over time</term>, as Aristotle says, is a type of perfection; and immature fruits, before they ripen, are considered imperfect in regards to maturity, which is a species of perfection. Erastus, the fact that an unripe grape is classified as a natural species actually overturns your proposition. No one doubts that a sour and unripe grape is very close and related to a ripe grape. However, common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver," known to us as mercury.</note>, when slightly freed from its moisture and coldness, or that which has been extracted from metals by Art, remains more firmly within the natural species of things—and is a matter closer to silver and gold—than a sour grape is to a ripe one. This is because the grape, if the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that brings about a change; here, the natural heat of the sun</term> is absent, immediately rots; and even if that cause is present, it cannot ripen except over a long interval of time.

<margin>
Mercury is not corrupted. Eternal liquid.
</margin>
But quicksilver is never corrupted <note>original: "corrumpitur"; in this context, it refers to natural decay or decomposition.</note>, even if the prior cause that gave it its origin is absent. For this reason, Pliny called it the "eternal liquid." Yet, by the efficient power implanted in the silver-making or gold-making "seed," and with the help of external heat from fire, silver or gold immediately solidifies from that same quicksilver.

->*The Fifth Argument.*<-

<margin>V.</margin>
> Nature produced all species for certain ends and uses that are necessary to mankind.
> But iron is just as necessary for human use as gold. Therefore:
> Nature did not produce iron or the other metals so that she might make gold out of them, but so that they might be of use to humans.

->*Response.*<-

Even if this argument were true, it nonetheless has nothing to do with the question proposed: "Whether the Art exists." Nor does it follow that if Nature produced each metal for various uses, one cannot be generated from another. For the conclusions are different, and the means of reaching those conclusions are different.

->*The Sixth Argument.*<-

<margin>VI.</margin>
Those who say that the cheaper metals differ from silver only by the same reasoning...

ARGYROPOEIA AND CHRYSOPOEIA
H iij
<meta>catchword: Response.</meta>

...to say that [silver or gold] differ from [other metals] as a sick man differs from a healthy man is said ignorantly. But the Alchemists <note>original: "Carbonarij"; literally "charcoal-burners," a common derogatory or trade name for alchemists due to their constant use of furnaces.</note> believe this to be so. **Erastus:** They speak ignorantly.

You confirm this proposition by the fact that each metal differs from another by its own proper species. You remain silent on the proof of the assumption, but you say it should be gathered from the fact that some have called the "seed" of silver or gold a **medicine of metals** <term>medicine of metals: a term for the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, which was thought to "heal" the imperfections of base metals to turn them into gold</term>.

<margin>
Three orders of the medicine of metals according to Geber.
</margin>
Regarding this medicine, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath; however, the "Summa" referenced here is likely the 13th-century Latin work by Pseudo-Geber.</note> established three orders in his *Summa*: the first, which would only alter; the second, which would perfect only by "palliation" <note>original: "palliando"; meaning to mask or cover the surface, like a medicinal coating</note>; and the third and final one, which would separate all extraneous substance from the nature of **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> and truly perfect it.

### Response.

I have already granted the first proposition to you, and I acknowledge that Geber is the author of that assumption in his *Sum of Perfection*. But he established these three orders of medicine **metaphorically**. 

<margin>
What has been said concerning the medicines of metals is said metaphorically.
</margin>
For just as one who is healthy casts off the color of the sick and performs all the duties of a healthy man, so also the lower metals, when changed into silver or gold, acquire a splendid color and endure the same **trials** <note>original: "examina"; technical tests like cupellation or the touchstone used to verify purity</note> as silver and gold. For I have said that their forms are judged by their endurance of these same trials. However, Geber never even dreamed that all metals have only one single form, as he divided the types of metals into six distinct species. I agree with you, Erastus, that it is said improperly that lower metals differ from noble ones as a sick man from a healthy one, if their forms are to be judged by their own **accidents** <term>accidents: in philosophy, the non-essential qualities of a thing (like color or smell) that can change without changing the thing's essential nature</term>. But if only their common accidents are to be inspected, I will not consider it entirely ignorant of them to have said so.

### Seventh Argument.

The matter of one form cannot become the matter of another form unless the matter is first changed into the **proximate matter** <term>proximate matter: the stage of matter immediately preceding a final form, like dough is the proximate matter of bread</term> of the future form. But the Chemists <note>alchemists</note> do not strive for this, but say instead that the matter of all metals is common. Therefore:

They will not be able to produce silver or gold from the matter of the remaining metals.

You prove the proposition in this way: the flesh or blood of a pig, or any other creature, will never be a suitable nourishment for our soul <note>meaning our life-force or body</note> until it is first changed into white **chyle** <term>chyle: a milky fluid produced in the intestines during digestion, seen here as an intermediate stage between food and blood</term>, and then into new and different blood. You prove the assumption from this: that the Chemists do not labor so that the matter of lead or other metals is transmuted in such a way that it becomes a suitable and proximate matter for silver or gold.

### Response.

### *Response.*

I grant your first proposition. For in the previous sections, I stated that it is an inviolable law of nature that an individual of one species can never be suited to another species unless the former is changed into the latter. However, I deny your assumption; on the contrary, those skilled in **Silver-making** <term>Argyropœia: the alchemical art of making silver</term> or **Gold-making** <term>Chrysopœia: the alchemical art of making gold</term> strive for nothing else than to make the matter of the remaining base metals incline toward a matter most similar to silver and gold, so that it may be moved and perfected by that "efficient cause" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the efficient cause is the agent or force that brings something into being—in this case, the alchemist or their "medicine."</note>.

<margin>VIII.</margin>
### *Eighth Argument.*

If the matter of one species must be changed into a matter close to another species, then all of that matter must be changed.

Yet, when Chemists change the matter of metals into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, or others change it into a different metal, the whole of it is not changed.

Matter of metals that has been changed into the matter of another metal or into quicksilver will not be the matter most similar to silver or gold. It will never obtain the form of silver or gold. You confirm your first proposition by bringing forward the argument of pig flesh or blood, which will never be matter close to the human body unless it is first changed into **chyle** <note>a milky fluid produced during digestion</note> and human blood. You prove your assumption by the testimony of the senses. For when metals are changed into other metals or into quicksilver, they seem to be the same matter; for their metals appear to be quicksilver, yet this is a liquid even without the use of fire.

### *Response.*

<margin>The change of metals does not happen through corruption, but through simple dissolution.</margin>
You are greatly mistaken, Erastus, in your comparison between pig flesh and blood being changed into human blood, and metals being changed into quicksilver. For the change of that blood occurs through "corruption" <note>original: "corruptionem"; in this context, the philosophical term for the total destruction or "death" of a substance's current form</note> or its destruction, followed by the "generation" or birth of human chyle and blood. In that change, all previous accidental qualities perish, and there occurs, as they say, a **resolution** <term>resolution: the breaking down of a substance into its most basic components</term> all the way back to the **prime matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless, fundamental base of all physical reality in Aristotelian thought</note> before it becomes human blood. No part of the sensible matter of the previous state is perceived, just as when wood is changed into ash, which is the matter closest to glass. However, the transformation of metals is not through corruption, but through a simple **dissolution** and the separation of that matter which is foreign to the nature of quicksilver. The quicksilver that is seen after this dissolution does not arise through a new birth or generation, but through a simple mixing under a new proportion of the mixed body. In this change, there is no resolution of the metallic matter...

If the matter of metals were the matter most similar to silver and gold within the mines of the earth, it would be changed into silver or gold by the presence of the efficient cause itself.

You should not labor too much, Erastus, in the proof of this argument, for we concede to you that it is entirely true within the mines of the earth. But that quicksilver cannot be drawn out from those same metals outside the location of the mines by natural causes with the help of **art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy or human skill.</note>, and perfected into silver or gold, is indeed impossible to you, Erastus, because you are ignorant of it and have not seen it. But to those who know and have experienced it, it is possible and easy. These things, however, have been demonstrated above, so that there is no need for a longer response to this argument.

What nature does not effect in its mines, art also does not effect outside the mines.
But from a mixture of vapors of different species in the mines, one and the same species of metal does not arise, but rather different ones. Therefore:
From a mixture of metals of different species with silver or gold outside the mines, a single species of metal will not arise. Therefore, Silver-making and Gold-making are in vain.

->Response.<-

<margin>A natural efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary force or agent that brings a change about; in this context, the alchemist’s heat acting on the matter.</note> can, with the help of art, achieve something that it cannot achieve alone.</margin>
The same answer must be given to the first proposition as to the other arguments: that nature is the primary acting cause, while art is truly the helper and the provider of the materials, so that the efficient cause may act upon them. Furthermore, that same natural efficient cause, with the help of art, can achieve something outside the location of the mines which it cannot achieve alone in that same place: namely, to resolve <note>To "resolve" here means to break a substance down into its more basic components.</note> metals into the matter most similar to silver and gold, which nature alone cannot provide within the mines. It is no wonder, then, if different types of metals arise from different vapors in the same veins, nor if one is not changed into another in those same veins. It is no less surprising if metals retain their own forms and species when subjected to a common and imperfect mixing through melting; for they do not combine under those laws by which we have said a "perfect mixture" <term>mixtio perfecta: a philosophical term for a union so complete that the individual components can no longer be separated by simple means</term> is achieved. After these things written by you, Erastus, which seemed to press the point more urgently and which we have reduced to the rules of logic and answered, you describe in many words the various opinions of the "Chemists" <note>At this time, "Chemists" (Chemicorum) referred to alchemists following the traditions of Paracelsus or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> regarding the matter closest to metals in the mines of the earth. But whether these opinions are true or false matters little as far as the resolution of the proposed question is concerned: whether the Art exists.

<margin>The proximate matter <note>The material in its final state before it becomes the finished product.</note> of metals is one thing in the mines, and another in the hands of the Art.</margin>
For we who are about to work gold do not need that proximate matter that was in the mines before they solidified; for we have already said that this is impossible, especially since there are so many and such great opinions regarding that proximate matter, not only among the Chemists, but among others as well. Instead, we seek the matter most similar to silver and gold, which is common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, which nature has offered to us of her own accord, and that which is extracted from metals by art.

<margin>A thing truly and perfectly mixed is not resolved again into that from which it was most recently mixed.</margin>
<margin>Whether metals congealed from quicksilver in the mines.</margin>
Therefore, I pass over in silence those arguments you brought against the opinions of the Chemists concerning the matter most similar to metals in the mines of the earth, lest I "waste my work and oil" <note>A Latin idiom (operam et oleum perdere) meaning to labor in vain, like a student burning midnight oil for no result.</note> in refuting them. For these do not attack **Silver-making** <term>Argyropœia</term> and **Gold-making** <term>Chrysopœia</term>, which rely on other principles. I have only proposed to respond to those arguments with which you strive to attack this Art. However, I will not deny many things learnedly written by you in refuting the opinions of the Chemists: namely, that no thing truly and perfectly mixed or born can be resolved back into that from which it was most recently mixed or born. For if blood is made from bread and wine, the blood cannot be resolved back into bread and wine. In the same way, a metal cannot be resolved into that from which it was most recently mixed. For even if we say that metals are resolved into quicksilver, we do not therefore concede that they congealed <note>original: "creuiſſe"</note> directly from that quicksilver in the mines of the earth.

### Eleventh Argument.

<margin>XI.</margin>

From such a great conflict of differing opinions, Erastus, you found some occasion to criticize the art, pronouncing the same thing that Davus says to Pamphilus in the works of Terence: *A matter that possesses in itself neither logic nor moderation—if you demand to govern it by certain reason, you would achieve nothing more than if you were to make an effort to be insane with reason.* <note>The author quotes Terence’s comedy *Andria* to show that Erastus views alchemy as an inherently irrational pursuit because its practitioners disagree with one another.</note>

<margin>
Many ways of producing the stone.
</margin>
As for the method of operation, it does not bother me so much, provided there is agreement on the material or subject. For there are many paths that converge toward one and the same effect.

<margin>
External heat is an external helping efficient cause.
</margin>
Yet, both objections can be answered: the matter closest to producing silver or gold—which is indefinite, namely quicksilver, whether the common kind or that which resides within other metallic bodies—requires only concoction <term>concoctio: a process of ripening or "cooking" a substance through heat to bring it to perfection</term> so that it may be defined and perfected. The efficient cause of this process is external heat, which assists the innate qualities of the proximate matter. For if someone has learned through some method, and confirmed by experience, how to summon the fiery powers and faculties to produce what they call the "stone" from whichever matter they have chosen, and uses those same faculties to cook and perfect our proximate matter, there is no reason for anyone to be deterred by the variety of the subject.

<margin>
Variety of matter is not an obstacle.
</margin>
For all things tend toward that goal, and finally return to one point and produce the same effect. For whether a chick is produced from an egg by the brooding heat of a hen, or by some other similar heat, it matters not. What if I were to say that silver can even be changed into gold without "gold-making seed," an experiment of which I have revealed in earlier writings?

<margin>
Silver can be changed into gold without gold-making seed.
</margin>
For the cause of this effect is the fiery power of "sharp waters" <note>original: "aquarum acrium," referring to strong acids like aqua fortis (nitric acid)</note> and other causes which we have reported. But if a diversity of opinions—and often a diametrical opposition—were a sufficient argument for condemning an art, what is more contradictory than the clashing opinions of the Physicists, Doctors, and Lawyers in the schools on most matters under dispute? In the Pandects <note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* is a massive compendium of Roman law writings.</note> of our Lawyers, is it not common for one to condemn the opinion of another while defending his own? Do we not experience daily in courtroom judgments that both judges and counselors are drawn into different sentiments, especially in those questions that rest upon the law? Even among the Doctors who are called into consultation to consider the diseases of the sick and bring a remedy, you will rarely see several—

<margin>

</margin>
No counsel is truer or more useful than that which is sought, taken, or hoped for from nature. From her oracle, the truest answers are returned in ambiguous and doubtful matters. Hence you may see all who know this art send those eager to produce the birth of silver or gold to this same nature and her works. I, therefore, subscribe only to the opinion of those who, imitating nature, take gold and their own quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> as the material or subject of the silver-making or gold-making seed; they dissolve and concoct <term>concoct: to "cook" or ripen a substance through steady heat</term> it until it comes together into a hard stone, and finally comes forth as a calx <term>calx: a fine powder produced by heating or "calcining" a metal</term> or a red powder. We must now proceed to dissolve the remaining arguments.

### *The Twelfth Argument.*
<margin>XII.</margin>

Erastus thinks—and rightly so, if there is any truth in the whole matter—that those who have studied how to prepare the Philosopher's Stone from gold seem to have come closer to the truth. However, he uses this argument to claim it cannot be produced from gold:

In order for the Philosopher's Stone to be made from gold, the gold must be rendered more perfect than it is in its own nature.

<header>A D E F E N S E</header>
<note>original: "APOLOGIA"</note>

And yet, it cannot be rendered more perfect. **E.** <note>This likely refers to Erastus, the opponent being addressed.</note> It cannot be created from gold; therefore, even less so from any other material. Therefore, all the efforts of the chemists are vain and useless.

The first proposition requires no proof, as it is manifest to the senses; nor do we see gold in its own nature, when mixed with other metals or with quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>, completing their mixture and changing them into gold. But you prove this assumption, Erastus, by the authority of Bracesco <note>Giovanni Bracesco, an Italian alchemist known for his dialogues on the art.</note> and Roger Bacon <note>The famous 13th-century English friar and philosopher associated with early experimental science and alchemy.</note>, and you confirm it by both reason and experience, which demonstrates that the mixture of gold is so solid and perfect that it cannot be dissolved or destroyed by fire.

### *Response to the Twelfth Argument.*

<margin>The opinion of Bracesco and Roger Bacon.</margin>
Bracesco and Roger Bacon, as well as others of that sort, handed down the art enigmatically, metaphorically, and in no particular order. They did not give gold the name of the "matter" of the Philosopher's Stone, but rather called it the "efficient and informing cause" <term>efficient cause: the agent that brings something into being, like a sculptor to a statue</term> of the unformed, raw, and imperfect matter; they held that the Stone took its origin from the mixture of both.

<margin>Gold as the efficient cause, its own quicksilver as the matter.</margin>
But because the matter exceeds in quantity—just as the "menstruum" <term>menstruum: here referring to the nourishing fluid in the womb</term> does in a fetus—while the gold exceeds in power like the seed and efficient cause, they did not want gold alone to be the "matter" of the Stone. In truth, however, both gold and its own quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> are the matter of that same Stone to those who have knowledge and understanding; the one is useless without the other, for the former is the agent, like the male, and the latter is the passive, like the female.

<margin>Gold cannot be destroyed by fire alone.</margin>
Moreover, as to the point that gold cannot be rendered more perfect by fire, or cannot be dissolved and pulled apart into its components: I concede this occurs in its own metallic nature by the heat of fire alone. For gold seems to have reached the ultimate degree of perfect mixture of all metals by nature.

<margin>The water of common salt dissolves only the tincture of gold from the gold.</margin>
However, it can be dissolved and pulled apart into its components by certain "waters" <note>likely referring to mineral acids</note>, and indeed easily by those who have often practiced it. For a "water" is distilled from common salt <note>likely spirit of salt or hydrochloric acid</note> which, when a slow fire is applied, dissolves only the **tincture** <term>tincture: the essential color or "soul" of a substance in alchemy</term> of the gold. For the water is dyed with a lemon-yellow color, whereas previously it was white like water from a well or spring. And when all the tincture has been drawn out, the white body of the gold settles at the bottom; when this is reduced back into a body by the action of fire, it is seen to be silver. Furthermore, the tincture of gold is never again to return into a metallic body; but because it is of a most subtle essence and is carried upward into a vapor by distillation when certain things are added, and is distilled into a liquid, they have called it a "spiritual body" or a "corporeal spirit." This tincture must be delivered from the sharpness <note>acidity</note> it received from the dissolving water, and then it serves many and wonderful uses and effects.

<header>ON THE MAKING OF SILVER AND GOLD</header>

<margin>The power of the tincture of gold.</margin>
<margin>Tauladanus <note>Robertus Tauladanus, a 16th-century commentator who defended alchemy against critics.</note></margin>
But because you are ignorant of these things, Erastus, and have not witnessed them with your own eyes, you will not grant them any faith—nor will those who are like you. However, that which I have seen with these very eyes and felt with my own hands, and which was even performed by an untrained youth at my command, provides a greater proof than your ignorance or that of your peers, and your false and empty presumption of knowing everything. When you read the works of Tauladanus disputing against Bracesco <note>Giovanni Bracesco, an Italian alchemist.</note>, you learned that gold, in its natural state, cannot be changed by fire alone, but can be broken down into its parts if other substances are added. You then employ the following argument and dilemma to prove that gold—whether it retains its metallic nature or casts it off—has no relevance to the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin>XIII.</margin>
### *The Thirteenth Argument.*

Gold, which the chemists use as the material for the Stone, either dissolves into a liquid and spirit, thereby changing the substance and power of the gold, or it remains as gold under the appearance of a liquid and form.

If the former is true, it will not create a metal, because it has exceeded the nature of the metallic genus. If the latter is true—since it is not being changed, nor can it be rendered more perfect in its own nature, nor does it possess an "exuberant perfection"—it will not communicate that perfection to other metals, nor will it perfect them. **E.** <note>The letter "E" stands for Erastus, marking the conclusion of his syllogism.</note>

In whatever way gold is used or prepared as the material for the Stone, it will not change other metals or quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; "argentum vivum"</term> into gold. Therefore, the chemists attempt to fashion the Philosopher's Stone from gold in vain.

### *The Response.*

<margin>Altered gold can change Mercury into the Sun <note>The "Sun" (Sol) is the alchemical symbol and name for gold.</note>.</margin>
<margin>The powder of altered gold changes the Mercury of metals.</margin>
I respond that whether the gold has retained its metallic nature (provided it has been altered) or has cast it off, it is capable of perfecting our material that is most similar to it—that is, quicksilver. For gold reduced to a calx <term>calx: a fine powder produced by heating a substance to remove its moisture or volatile parts (calcination)</term> does not cast off its metallic nature, no more than a stone reduced to powder loses its stony form. Indeed, one can speak more truly of the metallic nature remaining unharmed in calcined gold than of the stony nature in a calcined stone; for the stone loses much of its weight in the heat, while the gold loses nothing. But in both cases, a "fiery power" is summoned by the calcination. Therefore, when that powder of gold is mixed in a certain proportion with quicksilver extracted from metallic bodies (especially from silver that has been skillfully layered), and both are cooked together through specific degrees of fire, a battle of contrary qualities occurs within the shared material. For the qualities of the gold powder are hot and dry, while those of the Mercury of metals are cold and moist. From this comes a tempering and a new mixture, and from this, the form of gold emerges. I said "altered gold"...

...to obtain this power and capability. <margin>Common mercury and metallic mercury differ from one another.</margin>

<margin>When it has cast off its metallic nature, it is endowed with more excellent powers.</margin>
But if, to take the other part of the dilemma, gold has cast off its metallic nature, it will not be equipped with lesser powers, but rather with far more effective and excellent ones. These are sought through the solution from its own quicksilver and by the long, daily concoction of both. This is what occurs in the silver-making <note>original: "argentifico"</note> and gold-making <note>original: "aurifico"</note> seed, which cannot be reduced back into a metal; rather, by its mixture with common quicksilver or that which is innate in metals, a true new mixture is made. From this emerges a body of a new form, which is neither the gold-making powder, nor quicksilver, nor the metal it was before, but gold—as I have often said, and am forced to repeat in a matter so serious and of such weight. But in these things, Erastus, which you are ignorant of, you judge like a blind man about colors. You do not know what that quicksilver is that dissolves gold, nor the manner of concoction, nor by what reasoning that gold-making powder becomes the cause of this transformation. Therefore, your argument and dilemma are invalid.

### *The Fourteenth Argument.*

<margin>XIV.</margin>
> The Philosopher’s Stone necessarily consists of matter which is more perfectly concocted than gold itself.
> And yet gold cannot be more perfectly concocted, nor is there any metal as perfect as it. Therefore:
> All the labor of the Chemists is in vain.

### *The Response.*

<margin>Erastus is ignorant of concoction.</margin>
Your assumption is false, Erastus. But because this concoction—occurring after a true solution—is unique to this art (of which you are ignorant), it seems impossible to you. However, your ignorance neither adds to nor subtracts from the truth, which rests upon the authority of the most excellent men, on reason, on experiment, and on demonstration.

### *The Fifteenth Argument.*

<margin>XV.</margin>
Forms are produced from the "bosom of matter" <note>A phrase referring to the potentiality within matter to take on a new shape or essence.</note> by an efficient cause implanted in that same matter; they do not fly in from elsewhere.

<sig>EE 3</sig>

But the Chemists say that form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that gives matter its identity.</note> is established in an external matter, and is truly separated from the matter to be perfected, and that through projection <term>projection: the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast onto a base metal to transform it</term>, the form is infused into the matter to be shaped. ->Response.<-

<margin>Whether forms migrate from the depths of matter or into matter from the outside.</margin>
<margin>That forms enter into matter from the heavens.</margin>
There is a great controversy among the more learned as to whether the forms of things migrate from the "bosom of matter" (implanted there by an efficient cause) and do not come from elsewhere or from the outside. Jean Fernel of Amiens <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a highly influential French physician who attempted to reconcile Galenic medicine with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, easily the prince of physicians and philosophers of this century, disputes nothing else through the character of Eudoxus against Brutus in the entire first book of his work *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "de abditis rerum causis"</note>. And finally, he concludes that not even the smallest part of the form existed before it migrated into the matter. Instead, he argues that once the preparation is perfect and complete, the form immediately enters that matter from the heavens. He confirms this with many reasons and by the authority of Aristotle, not only regarding the human soul—which is most certain to exist by itself outside the body, enter the human body from the outside, and again exist by itself after exiting its body, a point no one doubts—but also in animals, plants, and inanimate bodies. You, however, Erastus, feel the opposite regarding all these things, except for the human soul. But which opinion in this question is truer, Fernel’s or yours, is not the place for debate here. Even if we grant that your view prevails and the first part of your argument is true, the conclusion of that same argument will not necessarily be true. This is because it is taken from a false hypothesis: when you say the Chemists claim the form of gold is separated in an external matter and infused into the matter to be shaped. Even if some among them have thought so, I cannot agree with them; rather, the matter stands thus:

<margin>The Philosopher’s Stone is not the "form" of gold.</margin>
The Philosopher’s Stone, as you call it, is not the "form" of gold, but something far more noble, even if it has not cast off its gold-making power and faculty. For it is not always necessary that the thing which provides the shape must already possess the exact same form as the body that is to be shaped. For example, those animals that arise from putrefaction <note>The author refers to the ancient theory of "spontaneous generation," where living creatures like maggots were thought to emerge from decaying matter purely through the action of heat.</note> have only heat as their "maker." Furthermore, our "proximate matter" <term>proximate matter: the immediate physical substance used at the start of an alchemical work</term> is not the form of gold. However, both the Philosopher’s Stone and its proximate matter consist of their own form; nonetheless, they flow from the same source and resemble each other in their entire substance. Yet they fight with contrary qualities: the Stone is hot, dry, fiery, and "concocted" <term>concoction: a process of "ripening" through steady heat</term>; the matter is cold, moist, watery, raw, and unrefined—

<meta>catchword: defi- (likely "definite" or "definitely")</meta>

<summary>The author rebuts Thomas Erastus by citing Jean Fernel's theories on how "forms" enter matter from the heavens. He argues that the Philosopher's Stone is not merely the "form" of gold, but a more noble substance that acts upon matter through its unique qualities.</summary>

<page-num>70</page-num>
<header>APOLOGIA</header>
<meta>catchword: Response.</meta>

<margin>
That a true mixture is made from contrary qualities fighting in a common matter.
</margin>
...defined. In the mixture <term>mistio: a true chemical union where the individual components are transformed into a new substance, as opposed to a simple mechanical mix</term> of both, with external heat acting as the agent, a battle of these contrary qualities occurs in a common matter; the prior forms of both are abolished, and a new, golden, and unique form succeeds in the body mixed from both substances. For from the battle of these contrary qualities, a balance <term>temperamentum: the proportional balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature</term> suitable for the golden form is produced, provided the qualities fight with equal strength. Otherwise, if the qualities and powers of the stone or the "gold-making powder" <note>original: "pulueris aurifici"; a term for the Philosopher's Stone in its powdered state</note> were too overpowering, a true mixture would not occur (in which it is necessary for one quality not to exceed another, but for the whole to be reduced to a balance); instead, the destruction of the mercury <note>original: "argenti viui," literally "living silver"</note> would result. It would simply pass away into the nature of the stone, though the stone's own powers would be weakened in the process.

<margin>
He teaches the powers and faculties of the gold-making powder from experience.
</margin>
How great the powers and faculties of the gold-making powder may be, however, cannot be known for certain except by experience. For if it is cast <note>original: "Proiectus," referring to projection, the final alchemical step</note> in too great a quantity into mercury, it will change the mercury itself into more gold-making powder—though diminished in strength—until finally the last powder changes the mercury not into more powder, but into a ductile <note>Malleable or able to be hammered thin; a defining characteristic of true metals.</note> body. For then the victory of both will be equal, from which a new form of gold will proceed. Nature teaches us that this is how things stand in mixed bodies that she has produced of her own accord. For from the mixing of earth and water, with the forces of the other elements concurring, stone is made, and metal is made, but by a different law of proportion. In this mixing, the forms that were previously active in the elements are now present in the stone and metal only potentially, and a new and unique form of stone or metal arises from their mixture. The same thing happens in those things that are distilled by the power of fire: if they fight equally with contrary qualities and are truly mixed, then once the former forms of the substances being mixed are exhausted, a single unique form comes forth in the distilled water.

<margin>
The forms of the gold-making powder and of the proximate matter are infused by their own powers.
</margin>
Thus, the form is not infused into the mercury or the "proximate matter" <term>materia proxima: the immediate raw material ready to receive a specific form</term> from elsewhere or externally—as you falsely think the Chemists say—but from the proper powers implanted in that same mercury and gold-making powder.

<margin>
XVI.
</margin>
->*The Sixteenth Argument.*<-

That which truly transforms bestows the "form" <note>the essential nature</note> upon the matter to be shaped. But the Philosopher’s Stone, when melted with metals, does not give them form in any other way than wormwood water <note>original: "aqua absinthij"; wormwood was known for its extreme bitterness and strong scent</note> infused into wine; the water does not bestow the essential nature of wormwood upon the wine, but only its odor and flavor. Therefore:

**The Philosopher’s Stone, mixed and melted with metals, does not impart a golden form to them.**

<summary>The author explains that alchemical transmutation occurs through a "battle" of qualities that results in a new, balanced "form" emerging from within the matter itself. He refutes the critic Erastus by arguing that the Philosopher's Stone acts as a transformative agent that changes a metal's essence, not just its outward appearance or "flavor."</summary>

<page-num>71</page-num>
<header>SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING <note>original: "ARGYR. ET CHRYSOP."; abbreviations for Argyropoeia and Chrysopoeia, the Greek-derived terms for the arts of making silver and gold.</note></header>

->*Response.*<-

The assumption is derived from a false hypothesis; neither do those skilled in the art say this, nor is it true that a "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the internal principle that makes a thing what it is (e.g., what makes gold "gold" rather than "lead").</note> is bestowed upon metals by the stone in any way other than how wine is affected by wormwood water <note>original: "aqua absinthij"; Erastus likely argued that the Stone only "flavors" or stains the metal like wormwood bitters flavor wine, rather than changing its essence.</note>. Rather, through the mixture <term>mistio: a true chemical union where the components are transformed into a new substance</term> of the stone with common quicksilver <note>original: "argēto viuo," literally "living silver."</note> or by the power of metals, a single form is imparted by the force of contrary qualities fighting equally within a common matter, as was stated above.

<margin>XVII.</margin>
### *The Seventeenth Argument.*

The forms of things do not act except upon their own appropriate subject matter; they act not at all upon foreign matter. This must be said especially of the primary qualities <note>The four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, which constantly change all substances.
But the matter of the stone is different from the matter of metals. Therefore:
The stone will act only upon its own matter, and not likewise upon the matter of other metals. Therefore, it will not transform them.

->*Response*<-

<margin>The forms of things do not act upon foreign matter by themselves alone.</margin>
I respond that the forms of things do not act upon foreign matter by themselves alone, but by summoning the power of the primary qualities. For the soul does not act upon food, nor make the food its own, except through the natural heat implanted within it, as you even admit in this argument. Therefore your proposition, Erastus, is not true without distinction, but only if forms are considered in isolation by themselves. Thus, the form of the Philosopher’s Stone does not act upon metals or quicksilver alone, but by the power of contrary and fiery qualities.

<margin>The form of the stone does not act through corruption, but through mixture.</margin>
Furthermore, it does not act like the soul acts upon food (which involves "corruption" and "generation" <note>Biological digestion where the food is destroyed to create new tissue.</note>), but through the mixture of both substances. In this union, there is not a total dissolving of all specific accidental properties back into "prime matter" <note>The formless "stuff" that underlies all physical things.</note>—as happens in birth and death—but rather, the previous forms having been cast off, a new golden form arises, provided the qualities of both (namely the stone and whichever metal or quicksilver) fight with equal strength. Nor do we grant you your proposition, Erastus, without distinction. Because the Philosopher's Stone, quicksilver, and metals all flowed proximately from the same source, they are not "foreign matter" to one another; rather, they are of the same genus and in a certain way share a common matter, though they are considered "different" matter insofar as they possess different forms.

<margin>XVIII.</margin>
### *The Eighteenth Argument.*

**Only living things can "inform" <note>To give "form" or essential nature to something.</note> the matter upon which they act.**
**But the Philosopher’s Stone lacks a soul. Therefore:**
**It will not be able to "inform" common quicksilver, or that which is within metals.**

<header>DEFENSE</header>

### *Response.*

<margin>Stones and metals do not receive their form from any soul. Glass did not receive its form from art. The Philosopher's Stone lacks life and a soul.</margin>
The proposition is false. For stones and metals, arising directly from the Elements, possess a form <note>In this context, "form" refers to the essential nature or "blueprint" of a substance that defines its properties.</note> by which they exist; no soul bestowed this form upon them. Rather, they grew together by the power of their own specific quantities, aided by external heat and cold. Furthermore, glass has a natural, substantial form by which it exists, and art did not grant it that form; instead, art subjected the material to fire—which must not be excluded or separated from the number of natural efficient causes—and mixed the material from which the glass was formed. In the same way, the gold-making powers in the Philosopher's Stone, having summoned its own fiery qualities and with the help of external heat, impart the golden form to metals and to quicksilver <note>original: "argētovivo," literally "living silver," the common term for mercury.</note>, even though the stone itself lacks life or a soul. For I cannot agree with those who have said that metals, or our gold-making or silver-making seed, or the Philosopher's Stone, are "alive"—though perhaps they understood this metaphorically, due to the excellence of its fiery powers and qualities.

### *The Nineteenth Argument.*

<margin>XIX.</margin>
Every natural agent makes the thing it acts upon <note>The "patient," or the substance being transformed.</note> like itself in substance or quality. Therefore, if the Philosopher’s Stone acts upon other metals or quicksilver, it will make them like itself in substance or quality. Therefore,

<margin>The Philosopher's Stone does not act through generation or corruption.</margin>
The Philosopher’s Stone, by acting upon those metals, will not produce silver or gold from them—which is the goal of silver-making <term>argyropœia: the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into silver</term> and gold-making <term>chrysopœia: the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into gold</term>—but will instead produce a stone, which is not of the genus of metallic bodies; or, it will only induce a quality or alteration, and not a new form.

### *Response.*

<margin>The difference between generation and corruption, and dissolution and simple mixture.</margin>
<margin>The Philosopher's Stone does not corrupt metals, but through mixture it awakens a new form in them.</margin>
It is easy to respond to this proposition from what has been said above: the Philosopher's Stone does not change metals or quicksilver through generation or corruption <note>In Aristotelian physics, "generation" is the birth of a new substance and "corruption" is the total destruction of the old one.</note>, but through simple resolution <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> and mixture. There is a difference between these: in generation and corruption, that which acts and overcomes transforms the thing it acts upon into itself, and the latter is destroyed along with the dissolution of all its accidental traits—just as fire acting on wood destroys it and converts whatever is subjected to its power into itself. But in this dissolution and mixture, the things that are mixed do not perish, but remain; the previous forms pass away, and a single new form succeeds them. And if anything does perish—as in the mutation of metals—it is not from the matter of the quicksilver, but is overcome and destroyed by the external fire, passing into dross, ash, and glass. Thus the Philosopher's Stone, acting upon metals and quicksilver, does not destroy them, nor does it transform them into itself...

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "transform" on the following page.</meta>

<summary>The author argues that the Philosopher's Stone does not need a "soul" to transform metals, comparing the process to glass-making. He distinguishes alchemical transformation from "generation and corruption," defining it instead as a "mixture" where a new, noble form (gold) emerges from the combination of ingredients.</summary>

<header>SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING</header>

<margin>The property of a true mixture.</margin>
...transforms it, nor does it bestow its own form upon them; instead, from the mixture of those things with it, another form succeeds—namely, that of silver or gold—provided the fiery qualities of the Philosopher’s Stone and the contrary cold and moist qualities of common quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui vulgaris," or mercury</note> or of the metals fight each other in balance. For I have said that this is the characteristic of a true mixture: that from two mixed bodies of different forms, a third body of a new form results. Indeed, if the powers of that same stone or gold-making seed were to act upon a smaller quantity of quicksilver than would be required for its powers to resist the stone’s powers, the mercury would pass into the nature of the stone, but the mixture would become less effective, as I said in the response to the fifteenth argument, and repetition would be superfluous. 

<margin>All effort of the art is to intensify the fiery qualities of the gold-making seed.</margin>
Furthermore, what was said concerning "alteration" <note>In the science of the time, "alteration" usually meant a change in outward qualities like color or heat, rather than a change in the substance's essential nature.</note> must be understood in this way: unless the gold-making stone, or the metals, or the quicksilver fought with contrary primary qualities, a true mixture would not occur, but only a certain alteration according to secondary qualities, such as hardness and softness. But all <term>Argyropoeia</term> <note>silver-making</note> and <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>gold-making</note> tends toward this goal: that when the gold-making or silver-making power in the seed is impaired, the fiery qualities are intensified; and the more effective these qualities are, the more numerous and abundant the resulting effect becomes.

<margin>20.</margin>
### The Twentieth Argument.

> It is impious to believe that Art can produce anything more excellent than what God and nature produce.
>
> However, the Chemists say they can produce a stone that is more excellent, more perfect, and more effective than gold. Therefore:
>
> It is impious to believe that the Chemists can provide what they claim by means of the Philosopher's Stone.

### Response.

<margin>Art does not act, but God and...</margin>
It is slanderous to suggest that the Chemists either attempt, desire, or are able to produce anything more excellent than what God and nature produce. For they acknowledge God as the first and universal cause, the author and omnipotent creator of all things. When He wishes to accomplish anything miraculously, He does so without the intervention of natural causes; but when He acts naturally, He works in concert with those same natural causes which He commanded. Thus, when the first beginnings of all things—namely, the four Elements—have come together according to certain laws and proportion, a natural body consisting of matter and form comes into the light of day, just as you yourself, Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who was a famous critic of alchemy and Paracelsus.</note>, admit in another place when speaking of mixture. We confess, therefore, that the Chemists are able to produce nothing at all by themselves, but that all effects of all things must be referred back to God and to natural causes...

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of alchemy, specifically addressing the role of the alchemist as a facilitator of natural processes rather than a creator of them. <header>DEFENSE</header>

<margin>
Universal causes, while art provides the material.
</margin>
...those [universal causes] from which they are received. It cannot be denied that alchemists <note>original: "Chemicos"</note> can provide the material to nature so that nature itself may act. When a farmer <note>original: "Agricola"</note> tills the earth and casts seeds into it, he does not perform the act of growth himself, but is a servant of nature. He who places wood, coal, oil, or flammable things under a fire does not do the burning himself; the fire does. A glassmaker does not "make" the glass that comes from ashes and sand, but rather the fire does, to which he has provided the material. Nevertheless, all these people are said to "make" these things—not as the primary causes, but as those who impel and assist the process.

<margin>
A more perfect mixture can be produced by natural causes with the help of art.
</margin>
In this way, alchemists do not "make" gold; rather, they provide the material to natural causes so that those causes may act upon it. Furthermore, it is not a sacrilegious belief to think that some mixture more perfect than what nature produces alone can be created by those same natural causes when art provides the material—at least in those things that hold the nature and name of "mixtures." For example, glass is a more perfect mixed body than any natural body. Fire, which corrupts, burns away, and dissolves all natural bodies (except gold), can nowhere corrupt glass.

<margin>
Why and how the Stone is more perfect than gold.
</margin>
Similarly, the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is far more perfect than gold, and this for two reasons. The first is that, if one considers the ratio of an invincible and indissoluble mixture, the Stone has acquired such a firm, solid, and united composition through long solution and "cooking" <term>coctio</term> <note>A standard alchemical process of sustained heating to mature a substance.</note> that the power of fire will have no mastery over it in the future, no matter how long-lasting or violent the heat. The second reason is that if one looks at the "primary qualities" <note>In Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note> to which the Philosophers attributed all powers, the Stone has acquired fiery qualities through that same solution and cooking—qualities which both gold and glass lack, even though they are otherwise perfectly mixed. Hence, gold does not act upon other metals, whereas the Philosopher’s Stone does. As for why the Philosopher’s Stone consists of a more perfect and noble "form" than gold, I have already explained this above.

<margin>
Natural mixed bodies, if mixed again, are more perfect.
</margin>
In general, whatever natural bodies are already mixed and then mixed again become more perfect. A chick is more noble than the egg, and a living animal more noble than the seed from which they had their origin. Thus, the gold-making stone is more noble than the gold and its own quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo," or mercury</note> from which it most recently took its origin. Furthermore, when people say that gold formed from mercury by the power of the "gold-making powder" <note>original: "pulueris aurifici," another name for the Stone</note> is more perfect than natural gold, that is also not impossible. For mercury is entirely free of the flammable substance <note>likely referring to "sulfur" in the alchemical sense of impurity</note> from which the matter of gold, hardened in the bowels of the earth, is perhaps not entirely purified.

<margin>21.</margin>
### *The Twenty-First Argument.*

The infusion of forms into matter is an act of creation. But creation belongs only to Almighty God. Therefore, Alchemists <note>original: "Chemici"</note> cannot infuse the form <term>Form: In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the internal principle or "essence" that makes matter a specific thing, like gold or a tree.</term> of gold into matter.

#### *Response.*

To this argument, the same answer must be given as to the previous ones: namely, that Alchemists neither wish nor are able to bestow form upon things themselves. They see that in plants and animals, a formative power <note>original: "vim formatricem"</note> is implanted in the seeds; however, in mixed bodies <note>In this context, "mixed bodies" refers to chemical compounds or inorganic substances.</note>, they recognize that the command and will of God is the efficient force, occurring whenever elements come together according to a certain law and proportion. They come together when art supplies the matter, which the forces and qualities implanted within it—aided by external heat—subdue and mix; and from this, the form "leaps" into the matter.

<margin>22.</margin>
### *The Twenty-Second Argument.*

That which nature produces as the most perfect in any genus <note>Genus: a general category or class of related things.</note>, and which it either could not or would not make more perfect, art will not be able to achieve. But nature has produced gold as the most perfect within the genus of metals, and it either could not or would not make it more perfect. Therefore, Art will not be able to make gold more perfect. Consequently, it cannot produce the Philosopher's Stone <note>original: "lapidem Philosophicum"</note> from it, which ought to be more perfect than gold.

#### *Response.*

I respond, as I did to the twentieth argument, that in mixed bodies alone, when art serves as a minister and supplies the material to natural causes, the mixture can become more perfect than in those bodies mixed by nature alone.

<margin>23.</margin>
### *The Twenty-Third Argument.*

That which nature does not attempt, nor is able to achieve, art can by no means provide. But nature neither attempts nor is able to change one species of a close genus into another, more noble species of that same genus. Therefore, art will not be able to perform the same.

<margin>In the birth of plants and animals, corruption occurs.</margin>
#### *Response.*

The same answer must be given here as to the previous arguments. In the birth of plants and animals, there is a corruption <term>Corruption: The philosophical term for the breakdown or "death" of a substance's current state so that a new form can emerge.</term> of the prior matter and a dissolution of all its accidents. For this reason, one species of a close genus cannot be transmuted into a more noble or less noble species of that same genus—just as a dead dog does not...

<header>APOLOGIA</header>

...[be] transmuted into a goat or another animal; or a plant of one species into a plant of another species under the same genus of plant (although some have said that wheat changes into darnel <note>original: "lolium"; a weed that looks like wheat often used as an example of botanical "mutation" in early modern science</note> and vice-versa); but rather a resolution of accidents <term>Accidents: In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential properties of a thing—like its color, weight, or shape—that can change while the underlying substance remains the same.</term> occurs down to the first elements, unless from the same matter, after many changes, the seed of another species under the same genus is produced.

<margin>
In the origin of mixed bodies, corruption does not occur in a simple sense.
</margin>
In the origin of mixed bodies <note>Inorganic substances like minerals or chemical compounds.</note>, however, there is not simply a corruption of matter, nor a resolution of all prior accidents. Instead, there is a certain simple dissolution, while those accidents common to both the prior and subsequent species are left behind; and when the "proximate matter" <note>The underlying material that is most ready to take on a specific new form.</note> is reached, it is perfected, and neither dissolved nor corrupted. Therefore, it is not necessary for metals—which are merely mixed bodies—to be changed into a species of a different genus than the metallic, since gold is produced from them. These points are most manifest from what has been said, and I think they do not need to be repeated.

<margin>
Nature alone cannot accomplish what it does with Art as its servant, and this applies only to mixed bodies. Erastus's error.
</margin>
Furthermore, as to why nature does not change the remaining metals into gold within the mines themselves, it has already been answered: in mixed bodies, nature alone cannot accomplish what it can do when Art is its servant <note>This is a central alchemical tenet: that the Alchemist (the artist) accelerates and perfects natural processes that nature, left alone, might never complete.</note>. All your arguments, Erastus—both those above and those following—rest on the same foundation: you wish to measure the mixing of mixed and inanimate bodies by the same laws as the birth of plants and animals. However, it has been sufficiently demonstrated above, in my opinion, that these two categories are separated by a vast distance in many respects. And from this follows your next argument.

For in the former [plants], propagation only happens at a fixed interval of time; in the latter [gold], it happens through projection <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process where a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone is "thrown" onto a molten base metal to transmute it instantly into gold or silver.</term> in an instant. This propagation of gold, however, mostly occurs through the progress of time, as we said above in the first method.

<margin>XXV.</margin>
### Twenty-fifth argument.

For art to transmute the remaining metals into silver or gold, they must be reduced to their "proximate matter" <term>Proximate Matter: In Aristotelian physics, this is the material in its state most ready to receive a specific form (e.g., dough is the proximate matter of bread).</term>, and the same form must be inscribed upon it which nature inscribes.

But nowhere is a body changed by nature or art into its proximate matter; for the body of an animal does not return to blood, nor blood into chyle <note>original: "chylum"; the milky fluid of digested food in the intestines before it turns into blood.</note>, nor chyle into food; but even if art could go backward, it could not inscribe the form as nature does. Therefore, Art cannot fashion silver or gold from metals.

### Response.

<margin>One matter and efficient cause is necessary for art, and another for nature alone, in the making of gold.</margin>
We maintain that nature or art cannot resolve metals or any other natural body into that [original] proximate matter from which they immediately and with no intermediary arose, nor is that necessary for the art. For we have proved by the most solid reasons and experiments that the proximate matter from which nature alone produces silver or gold in the bowels of the earth is not the same as that which art subjects to nature outside of the mining sites. Instead, that matter which is proximate to silver and gold is also natural—namely, "living silver" <note>original: "argentum viuum"; quicksilver or mercury</note>, both the common kind and that which exists as a "proximate potentiality" within the other metals. It is extracted from them not through corruption <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the total destruction of a substance's essence, as when a body decomposes.</note>, but through simple resolution; nor in the same ways [is] the form of silver or gold [applied] to our proxi-

...to be brought in next, which nature uses in the mines. For concerning all these things, nothing is yet certain among the authors who have written the history of metals.
