### *The Twenty-sixth Argument.*

Chemists <note>original: "Chemici"; in this context, alchemists</note> say that they make natural gold by assisting matter, no differently than farmers do for wheat, or doctors for health. Yet farmers and doctors can neither provide the matter nor the efficient cause, nor can they confer the form, nor give birth to the wheat, nor bring about health. Therefore,

Neither will chemists be able to produce silver or gold by their art.

### *Response.*

<margin>Art is the silent servant of nature: however, nature produces the result. 27.</margin>

Since farmers, doctors, and chemists only assist matter, they do not properly and truly produce the result, but only subject it to nature, of which they are the servants. Natural causes, however, act and are the primary acting and efficient causes. Therefore, it is wrongly objected to the chemists, based on the premise and assumption, that art cannot generate silver or gold. For they do not say that they do this themselves, nor can they; rather, only nature and natural causes do so.

### *The Twenty-seventh Argument.*

Nature makes gold from its own proper matter, and from its same natural efficient causes, it bestows the golden substantial form <note>The "substantial form" is the internal essence that gives a substance its specific properties and identity.</note>.

But art creates both the beginning and the end, and acts entirely from the outside. Therefore, art cannot give a substantial and indwelling form.

### *Response.*

<margin>Art, as the servant of nature, acts through natural causes. 28.</margin>

The same must be answered as in the previous argument: that art does not produce silver or gold, but nature alone, of which this same art is the servant; and it does so through the same natural causes, though not necessarily from the same matter and efficient cause that are found in mines.

### *The Twenty-eighth Argument.*

In the matter of the remaining metals, in order for silver or gold to be made from them, silver-making or gold-making powers must be indwelling.

But in the matter of the other metals, these powers are not indwelling. Therefore, silver or gold can never be made from the matter of the other metals, neither by nature nor by art.

<summary>This page addresses objections to alchemy by arguing that the alchemist (the "artist") does not personally create gold, but rather acts as a servant to nature, providing the conditions for natural causes to work. <header>SILVER AND GOLD MAKING</header>

### *Response.*

<margin>Certain powers reside in the matter, others in the efficient cause.</margin>
Powers are assessed in two ways: some reside in well-disposed matter, and others in the efficient cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of change; for example, a baker is the efficient cause of bread.</note>. The former are found in quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, both the common variety and that which exists within metallic bodies. This is what we call <term>proximate potential<note>A philosophical term meaning the material is in a state where it is ready to be transformed immediately once the right agent is applied.</note></term>, or the material closest to silver and gold. This quicksilver, I say, is prepared to be acted upon and to be given form by an efficient cause.

<margin>Mercury is disposed to be acted upon, so that it may be shaped by the efficient cause.</margin>
However, we admit that the efficient powers for making silver or gold do not reside in the quicksilver itself, but in the powder or "seed" of silver or gold. From the mixing of this seed with the same mercury (whether common or from metals), and with the help of external fire, gold emerges, as has been frequently stated. Certain substances can even take the place and role of the Stone or the gold-making seed, as we have discovered by experience when silver is changed into gold. Yet, that process is achieved with great labor and little profit or return when compared to our silver-making or gold-making seed.

### *The Twenty-ninth Argument.*

<margin>The efficient gold-making powers are not in Mercury but in the Stone.</margin>
Natural forms inherent in things do not give shape to another material outside themselves until they have made that material their own. But neither the Philosopher's Stone nor anything else can make the material of other metals its own—that is, make it the material closest to silver or gold. Therefore,

->The Philosopher's Stone will not be able to transform other metals into silver or gold.<-

<margin>Some things can also be changed into gold without the Stone. 29.</margin>

### *Response.*

<margin>The Philosopher's Stone and Mercury flow from the same origin.</margin>
This argument is almost the same as the fifteenth. Therefore, one must respond to it as one did to that one, so that the repetition is not tedious. Regarding the claim in the premise that the Philosopher's Stone cannot make the material of other metals its own—that is, reduce it to the material closest to silver and gold—this must be granted if one is speaking of "proximate matter" as it exists in the bowels and mines of the earth, for that is impossible. But if one speaks of "proximate matter" according to the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of alchemy.</note>, which is quicksilver, then the premise is false.

<margin>How the Philosopher's Stone transmutes metals into gold.</margin>
For the Stone and quicksilver flow from the same origin, and both are indestructible by fire. Therefore, because of the similarity of their entire substance, they mix easily. The gold-making Stone retains, ripens, fixes, and tints the quicksilver by the power of its fiery qualities. Since neither yields to fire nor is destroyed, a stable and lasting mixture is created. Meanwhile, the external fire acts upon the material that is foreign to the nature of the quicksilver...

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence as it transitions to the next page; the catchword is "it".</meta>

<summary>This page explains that while mercury is the "passive" material ready for change, the "seed" or Philosopher's Stone provides the active "form" to create gold. The author argues that the Stone and mercury are naturally compatible because they share a common origin and a resistance to fire.</summary>

<margin>30.</margin>

### *The Thirtieth Argument.*

Alchemists <note>original: "Chemici"</note> assertively write that it is impossible for silver or metal to be established unless one has a thoroughly certain knowledge of the materials from which, and the manner in which, nature generates metals.
But they themselves are ignorant of all these things. Therefore,
They will not be able to create gold from metals.

### *Response.*

It is false for critics to say that Alchemists must understand the nature of metals exactly as they grew together by nature alone in the bowels of the earth. For this cannot be known for certain, nor can we know what their proximate matter <note>The material in its state immediately before becoming metal</note> was before they underwent their birth. Instead, their nature must be investigated based on their matter and form as they exist *after* their natural birth, and as we see them now.

<margin>
The nature of metals is judged by the reaction of their matter.
</margin>

This is judged by the "passion" <note>original: "perpeſſione"; in this context, it refers to the way the matter reacts to or is acted upon by external forces</note> of the matter, and by how gold and silver differ from the remaining metals derived from that same matter. These reactions and differences are seen with our own eyes during proper tests <note>original: "examinibus"; assays or chemical trials</note> and by fire. Thus, whether things are perfectly or imperfectly mixed is demonstrated by the judgment of the senses. Once these things are perceived, the investigator of this work immediately inquires how it might be possible for the remaining metals to undergo the same tests as silver and gold. This can by no means be achieved unless one knows the matter inherent in them—which is closest to silver and gold—and the efficient cause <note>The active force or agent that triggers the change, such as the Philosopher's Stone or "seed"</note>. 

<margin>
The things necessary to be known in the Art.
</margin>

These, then, are the things necessary for our Art, and they can be easily demonstrated since the judgment of the senses confirms them. The same cannot be said for the proximate matter as it exists in the mines of the earth.

<margin>31.</margin>

### *The Thirty-first Argument.*

Even if the Alchemists knew the proximate matter and the cause that produces gold, they still could not make gold in any place other than in natural mines.
But they have no other place than furnaces. Therefore,
In those furnaces, they cannot create silver or gold.

### *Response.*

The proposition is false. For Art relies on different principles than those which nature employs in the mines. Furthermore, it is clear enough from the preceding arguments that silver and gold can be formed in another place; no further refutation is needed.

### *The Thirty-second Argument.*

<margin>32.</margin>
Alchemists <note>original: "Chemici"</note> admit: If nature does not transmute baser metals into silver and gold within natural mines, the Chemical Art will likewise be unable to transmute them.

But nature never transmutes them into silver or gold. For the "proximate matter" <note>The immediate material substance from which a specific thing is formed.</note> of each individual metal is unique, and the matter of one cannot be the matter of another. Therefore,

The Art also will not transmute them into gold.

->*Response.*<-

<margin>The opinion of Pietro Bono of Ferrara <note>A famous 14th-century Italian alchemist, author of the *Precious New Pearl*.</note> regarding the efficient cause that produces gold.</margin>
This proposition finds its author in Pietro Bono of Ferrara. For he says that the "efficient cause" <note>The active agent or force that brings something into being.</note> in the mines of metals is sulfur, or something of the nature of common sulfur. He claims that if nature, through a process of "cooking" <note>original: "coctione"; the alchemical idea that heat matures metals in the earth like fruit on a tree.</note>, separates this sulfur from the substance of any metal, gold is produced; if not, the metal remains imperfect. Therefore, over the course of time, that sulfur is secreted within the mines until at last the metal, entirely purged of it, is found to be gold. However, he notes there are many impediments in the mines of the earth by which that purification is halted and restrained.

<margin>The opinion of Pietro Bono is rejected.</margin>
In truth, I cannot subscribe to this opinion. Instead, I feel that a different matter and a different efficient cause are necessary for the Art, and a different mode of operation must be employed, from which the same effect follows, as we have proven. Therefore, whether nature has transmuted baser metals into silver or gold in the mines of the earth or has not, it is a poor logical leap to say that they cannot be changed into silver or gold through those other natural causes we have mentioned, with the assistance of the Art.

### *The Thirty-third Argument.*

<margin>33.</margin>
If the species of metals are not to be exchanged into another species of the same immediate genus, it is necessary that they be resolved back into the "common matter" shared by all species of that same genus.

But metals, having been solidified by the most intense cold within the mines <note>Refers to the Aristotelian theory that metals are formed by the condensation of "moist vapors" due to cold.</note>, cannot be resolved back into the common matter of that same genus. Therefore, they cannot be further perfected within the mines.

->*Response.*<-

It matters little to know whether metals solidified by cold in the mines are resolved into common matter or not. For the answer was given in the previous argument: the Art cannot be defeated by such reasoning.

### The Thirty-Sixth Argument.

<margin>XXXVI</margin> The forms <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of an object that makes it what it is.</note> of things are not separable, but they act only upon their own proper matter, not upon another.
But the forms of the Philosophers' Stone and of metals are separable. Therefore,
The form of the Stone will not act upon the matter of metals.

->*Response.*<-

<margin>From the struggle of contrary qualities, a new mixture is made and a new form arises.</margin> This is the same argument as the fifteenth and twenty-ninth. Therefore, the same must be answered to this as was answered to those. For the qualities which exist in mixed bodies of different species, if they are contraries, they fight; they act and are acted upon in turn, and they reduce themselves to a moderation, and one body of one form is made, the former forms having been emptied out.

### The Thirty-Seventh Argument.

<margin>XXXVII</margin> An individual of one species cannot be transmuted into an individual of another species within the same proximate genus <note>"Genus" and "species" are categories of classification; for example, "metal" is a genus, while "lead" and "gold" are species within that genus.</note>.
But tin, lead, copper, and iron are under the same genus—namely, metal. Therefore,
One cannot pass into an individual of another.

->*Response.*<-

This argument is a repetition. For it is the second in the order established above. Therefore, it must be answered in the same way as that one.

### The Thirty-Eighth Argument.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin> Alchemists say that metals must be resolved into their first matter <note>original: "materia prima"; the most basic, formless substance from which all things are made.</note> if they are to be changed into silver or gold. But this cannot be done. Therefore,
They cannot be transmuted into silver or gold.

->*Response.*<-

When those skilled in Silver-making and Gold-making discuss the resolution into "first matter," they understand it as the matter closest to silver and gold, which is "living silver" <note>original: "argentum viuum"; quicksilver or mercury.</note>, as has already been said often, and not the raw matter from which they are mixed in the mines of the earth.

The Art is not true, but false.

#### *Response.*

The assumption is false. For if, Erastus, you have never seen any true experiment anywhere, it does not follow that everyone has found nothing true through experience. Your assumption is a universal negative <note>In formal logic, a "universal negative" is a statement like "No experiments are true."</note>, which a particular affirmative <note>A statement like "Some experiments are true."</note> overthrows.

## The Fortieth Argument.

It is impious to affirm that art can do what nature effects. But the Chemical Art affirms this. Therefore, what it affirms is impious.

#### *Response.*

The assumption is false. For the Chemical Art does not affirm that it effects anything properly by itself, but it is said to "effect" by supplying and subjecting matter to nature and to the <term>natural efficient cause<note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, it means the alchemist provides the materials, but nature does the actual work of transformation.</note></term>. Response has been made in this way to similar arguments above.

## The Forty-first Argument.

If this Art were true, it would enrich everyone who practiced it. But almost all who practice it have been reduced nearly to poverty. Therefore, this art is false.

#### *Response.*

This argument is commonly raised, nor is any other considered more valid for overthrowing <term>Argyropoeia<note>The chemical art of making silver.</note></term> or <term>Chrysopoeia<note>The chemical art of making gold.</note></term>.

<margin>That the ends of the sciences and arts are various.</margin>
But this argument can be answered in various ways. The final goals <note>original: "fines"; refers to the purpose or objective of a study.</note> of all sciences and arts are diverse. In the first rank of these is contemplation alone, especially in those arts in which the wonderful works of God Almighty—the Best and Greatest—and of nature obeying Him (which are not commonly known) shine forth; in the contemplation of these, the human mind is satisfied and finds peace. In the second rank, the goal is the Action of these same sciences or arts, so that whatever art one has learned, by exercising it, he might not lack the necessities for passing through this most miserable life, and might benefit the Commonwealth.

<margin>Praiseworthy ends of the sciences and arts.</margin>
And indeed, whoever is wise will profess these ends to be praiseworthy: for the sake of which even Silver-making and Gold-making are rightly to be sought. For there, one may contemplate the wonderful secrets of nature, nor will she ever permit those who rightly know her to be starving.

<margin>Which end of the arts and sciences is to be blamed.</margin>
But there is another end of the arts to be blamed and condemned, namely the "cursed hunger for gold" <note>original: "auri sacra fames"; a reference to Virgil's Aeneid regarding greed.</note> and an insatiable desire for possession. You, Erastus, have mistakenly thought this last goal to be the true goal of Silver-making and Gold-making. For if Medicine, which for—

-> SILVER AND GOLD MAKING <-

<margin>The truth or falsehood of an art is not to be judged by the abundance or lack of results, but by a lack of knowledge regarding the art itself.</margin>
...you profess, if your only goal is to become richer and not to bring some benefit to the state, you are by no means to be praised. Therefore, it is certain that from a false premise, both the assumption and the conclusion will be false and flawed. But suppose it is granted that the goal of <term>Argyropoeia<note>From the Greek *argyros* (silver) and *poiein* (to make): the alchemical art of making silver.</note></term> and <term>Chrysopoeia<note>From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make): the alchemical art of making gold.</note></term> is wealth and riches; even so, whether the art is true or false cannot be judged by the abundance or scarcity of those things. For your argument is based on what is *possible*, which does not create a logical necessity. If, through ignorance of this or any other art, a person who practices it becomes poorer, it should be blamed not on the art, but on the practitioner's ignorance. Nor should the art be accused of falsehood or impossibility on that account. However, if it is practiced by a clever and skilled person, nothing will be lacking from their works; and whether they are content with a little, requiring only what household necessity demands (which is the true goal of the wise), or whether they demonstrate in reality that they overflow with and take pride in riches (which is the goal of the foolish), the truth of the art will be discovered.

<margin>The unskilled usually cause poverty. The difficulty of the art.</margin>
But since this art is mostly handled by the unskilled, it is no wonder if it is said to cause poverty. Indeed, unless it is taught by experts and demonstrated in practice, one can hardly master it except over a very long time. In short, if those practicing the making of silver or gold are reduced to want, the cause of that poverty is not the falsehood of the art, but their own shameful ignorance.

# APOLOGY #

<margin>
Certain new arts are superior to those of the ancients
</margin>
...therefore, it should not, as you think, be denied the name of "art." For the arts of the nautical compass, of cannons, and of printing books with type were unknown to antiquity; yet antiquity has nothing equal to these arts. Nevertheless, they are true arts. No less true and admirable than all these is <term>Argyropoeia<note>From the Greek *argyros* (silver) and *poiein* (to make): the alchemical art of making silver.</note></term> and <term>Chrysopoeia<note>From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make): the alchemical art of making gold.</note></term>, which are also known to the most esteemed men and those most skilled in the precepts of natural philosophy—though they are few. 

<margin>
Geber proved this art to be most true.
</margin>
Among them, the leading role is held by <term>Geber<note>original: "Geber"; An influential 8th-century figure, often identified with Jabir ibn Hayyan, whose writings were the cornerstone of medieval European alchemy.</note></term>, whom you, Erastus, call the "idol of the Chemists." But he proved the art to be most true through definitions, divisions, causes and effects, and certain precepts drawn from physics. You, however, invent many things said by him and then refute things he never even dreamed of.

<margin>
Erastus attacked Chemistry in the year 1566.
</margin>
These are your arguments, Erastus, with which you fought against the chemists—not without insults, injuries, and anger—in the year (as you write) 1566, in the month of August. But when your anger had cooled, and after certain arguments opposing your opinion were proposed by a "distinguished and learned man," as you write, you responded to them at the end of this disputation, and indeed more modestly than in your earlier arguments.

<margin>
Mercury extracted from gold.
</margin>
That man showed you, as you say, <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note></term> extracted from gold, and argued that it can be extracted from other metals; he professes this, and you do not strongly disagree. But you deny that quicksilver—whether the common kind or that reduced from "imperfectly mixed" metals—is the <term>proximate matter<note>The immediate, raw substance required to create a specific result, in this case, silver or gold.</note></term> for silver and gold. And even if this were the case, you still deny that it can be 

<margin>
Erastus concedes some things, but denies others.
</margin>
changed into silver or gold by art. Yet you admit that quicksilver extracted from gold can easily and quickly return to gold through <term>concoction<note>A process of heating or "ripening" a substance to bring it to its most perfect state.</note></term>. However, you argue that quicksilver, whatever it may be, is not the proximate matter for silver and gold because each instance of quicksilver is merely an individual of its own specific kind, and an individual of another species can never exist. For example, if quicksilver is extracted from lead by art, it is an "individual" of lead; if from another metal, it is an individual of that same metal. To make this point, you add an analogy concerning the blood that flows from different species of animals; they all look the same in color and hold the same name of "blood," but they do not possess the same essence, nature, or species. You also bring examples from flesh and many other things of the same name. From this you conclude: common quicksilver, or that which is extracted from metals, is not the proximate matter for silver and gold, or of those same...

### ON THE MAKING OF SILVER AND GOLD ###

...individual substance, that all efforts of all Chemists are in vain, since no matter can, by the motion of an efficient cause, take on a specific form unless it is <term>proximate matter<note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "proximate matter" is material that is in the immediate state required to receive a specific form. For example, flour is the "remote matter" of bread, but dough is the "proximate matter."</note></term> to that form.

<margin>Nearly all of Erastus's arguments for establishing proof are neither helpful nor do they imply necessity, because they are drawn from analogy.</margin>
Indeed, of the many arguments you have brought against this art, Erastus, none is more plausible or seems to press harder—and yet, it is easily answered. For your argument relies on a similarity of name, not of thing or substance. All these arguments based on <term>analogy<note>original: "a simili"; reasoning by comparing two similar things.</note></term> serve more to illustrate a proof than to actually establish it. For almost all weak arguments are drawn from similarity, since no similarity is so great that it extends through every detail. They do not introduce any logical necessity, but are most suited for making listeners or readers compliant with what is said or written; therefore, it happens that the unwary are more easily deceived and misled by no arguments other than those drawn from the similarity of things.

<margin>Response to the final arguments sought from analogy.</margin>
To this argument of yours sought from analogy, Erastus, I shall respond thus. <term>Remote matter<note>Materials that are far removed from the final product and require several stages of transformation.</note></term> and proximate matter can be called by the same name, but they are not judged by the same reasoning: for instance, pig’s blood is the remote matter of human flesh, while human blood is the proximate matter, and yet both have the name "blood." But that pig’s blood will never be the proximate matter for human flesh unless it has been changed into human blood through many transformations. This distinction between proximate and remote matter, although true for pig and human blood, does not mean it follows that common <term>mercury<note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note></term>, or that which is extracted from metals by art, is one thing as remote matter and another as proximate matter for silver and gold. For we have proven from the preceding sections that all mercury is proximate matter for silver and gold and differs only by <term>coction<note>original: "coctione"; the alchemical process of "cooking" or "ripening" a substance with heat to bring it to perfection.</note></term>: and the more it has been "cooked," the closer it is to being their specific substance. For just as the ashes from any herbs or wood or other burnt things are the proximate matter for glass, even though they came from bodies of different kinds or different species: so too, from whatever bodies the matter of mercury has been dissolved, it will be the proximate matter for silver and gold.

Although we have proven these things with the strongest arguments, both from the similarity of the whole substance and from the specific qualities common to both, it must be considered all the more true because it is certain that gold and silver are the end 
<margin>Gold and silver are the end-point of nature.</margin>
and the completion of the metallic nature; not unlike how glass is the end...

## APOLOGY ##

<margin>...metallic [strengths]: glass is the end of all natural bodies.</margin>
...[the end] of all natural bodies. By "end," I mean that which fire can neither dissolve nor corrupt, but which withstands every force of art and always remains the same. This is properly said of gold and glass; however, the former is born of nature, while the latter is crafted by art. This cannot be said of other bodies, which are not proximate and unchangeable matter, but are subject to constant mutations. Quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, however, by its efficient cause, can become nothing other than silver or gold, just as ash becomes glass through the action of violent fire.

<margin>A distinction between the natures of bodies with the same name but different essence.</margin>
Therefore, Erastus, all your arguments—which you brought from the distinction of bodies with the same name but different essence—are overturned by this distinction: among bodies with the same name, some are of a different essence (as in the blood of a pig versus that of a human), and some are <term>remote matter<note>Material that is many steps away from its final form, like soil is to a tree.</note></term> while others are <term>proximate matter<note>Material that is in the final state of readiness to become a specific substance.</note></term>. Yet others share not only the same name but also the same form and essence, differing only by certain accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or location that don't change what a thing is.</note>—such as quicksilver, whether it be the common kind, or that which is found within metallic bodies or other things.

Furthermore, certain bodies are proximate matter capable of being changed into many other proximate matters, such as the elements and the many bodies that have grown from them. Yet others are proximate matter directed toward a certain unchangeable and fixed extreme, such as quicksilver, from which gold is made, and all ash, from which glass is smelted.

But I see an objection raised against me: if quicksilver can become nothing other than silver or gold, and gold is an unchangeable body, then <term>Argyrogonia<note>original: "Argyrogonia"; from the Greek words for "silver" and "birth," meaning the generation of silver.</note></term> or <term>Chrysogonia<note>original: "Chrysogonia"; from the Greek words for "gold" and "birth," meaning the generation of gold.</note></term> cannot be produced from them, even though we have called them the proximate matter for these things. We respond that what we said concerning proximate and unchangeable matter must be understood as referring to a body produced by nature alone and known to all, such as silver and gold; but the silver-making or gold-making "seed" is not produced by nature alone, but by art acting as a servant and driving force, though working through natural efficient causes.

<margin>Closing argument.</margin>
These things, Erastus, are what I think suffice to overturn your arguments—perhaps even more than what I first proposed—and they even go beyond the limits of the question at hand.

This one thing I ask of you, whom I appoint as judges of this whole disputation: that you recall these <term>axioms<note>Self-evident truths or established principles used as the foundation for an argument.</note></term> to memory—namely, that we are not dealing here with the death of plants or living animals, but of bod-

### SILVER-MAKING AND GOLD-MAKING ###

...between the simple mixture and dissolution of animate and inanimate <note>original: "animorum & mutorum"</note> beings: both are bounded by different laws. The origin of the former [living beings] proceeds from an internal <term>efficient cause<note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the 'efficient cause' is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note></term> which is neither in the power of art nor requires its help. The mixture of the latter [inanimate things], however, proceeds from an efficient cause—namely, heat and cold acting upon the moist and the dry—if we believe Aristotle. Since these are inanimate, they must be moved by an external impulse; this external cause is within the power of art. To infuse the inherent and prolific power into the seed of plants and animals is not the task of art, but the duty of nature alone. 

However, to resolve the matter of imperfectly mixed metals, and to reduce it to a <term>proximate matter<note>Matter that is in its final state of readiness to be transformed into a specific substance; the immediate precursor.</note></term> close to silver and gold, and to perfect both that and common quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, is a work not only of nature within the mines of the earth, but also a work of art outside of them. Art impels natural causes so that they act upon the subject matter. The "forms" <note>The essential nature or identity of a substance.</note> of these same metals are judged more by the enduring state of the matter and its bodily qualities than by its actions. These same qualities and the proportion of silver and gold are brought about in that proximate matter by mixture alone. Once these are sought out and prepared in that same proximate matter, the silver or gold form immediately leaps forth from the efficient cause. 

Silver and gold—but especially gold—are the "end" or goal of nature’s metallic mixture. Glass, however, is the end of all natural bodies that can be corrupted; the matter of all such things is eventually mixed into glass. Indeed, the mixture of both glass and gold is indissoluble by fire. All metals and quicksilver may be reduced by art to this golden mixture through natural causes, and thus the natural and substantial form of gold arises in the matter. The proximate matter for each body is not destroyed by this process, but perfected. Bodies that are already mixed, if they are mixed again, are more perfect and noble than those which first grew from the four beginnings of things—namely, the Elements.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
When you have weighed all these things in an even balance against Erastus’s arguments, I know that you—who are skilled in natural things and are not disturbed by any passions of the mind—will judge that I have not without reason undertaken the defense of <term>Argyropœia</term> <note>Silver-making</note> and <term>Chrysopœia</term> <note>Gold-making</note>. You will see that he [Erastus] has wrongly and incorrectly condemned this same art as false, and that I have rightly appealed his opinion to your Tribunal. It was necessary to judge this dispute by overturning his opinion and [the contrary]...

### BERNARD G. PENOTUS OF PORT-SAINTE-MARIE, ETC., WISHES HEALTH TO THE FAVORABLE READER AND PRAYS FOR A SPIRIT OF SINCERITY, UNDERSTANDING, AND SKILLFUL LABOR.

**N**ot a few will there be (favorable reader), I know well, to whom the publication of this little book may seem a novelty, and who will condemn the publication of the Mysteries of nature and the treasury of secrets. They will sing that verse of the Gospel: *Do not cast pearls before swine.* Likewise, they will cite that phrase of the Author: *Yet we do not write this for everyone, but for ourselves alone and our own; we seclude it from the common rabble with a strong wall and a firm lock.* Others will not indeed argue against it entirely, but will assert that the time has not yet come in which such things ought to be made public. Without a doubt, some are also found (just as today there is an infinite <term>malignant itch<note>original: "cacoethes"; a Greek-derived term used to describe an incurable habit or an urge to do something harmful, often used by Roman satirists to describe the "itch" for writing or slandering.</note></term> for slandering) who will object to me: by what right do I reveal these Mysteries, since I am not their author? Others, finally, will demand signs by which I might prove the art is true, so that I may be believed. I know, I say, I know and have experienced myself, while these things were being published, that there were some so <note>original: "nasutos"; literally "big-nosed," a Latin idiom for people who are overly critical, mocking, or censorious.</note> critical, so crafty, and so stripped of all humanity—like Cynics—that whatsoev[er]...

->### PREFACE###<-

...who sought by whatever means they could to hinder the edition; and even now, speaking against it at length, they do not cease to bark. Truly, since I see their barking is mad beyond reason, I judge they should be held of no account. 

<margin>To reveal secrets is not against God or neighbor.</margin>

It is certainly great praise to be led by such piety toward God and neighbor that nothing is taken away from the majesty of God in His great works while they are being published; nor is any part of the neighbor’s benefit envied—benefits which could have been suppressed by hiding them, hindered by sinister interpretation, or certainly thrown into confusion by negligent editing. But lest I seem lengthy in writing, I respond first to the "barking." For what they bring forth from the Gospel they twist into such a sense as if they alone were men, and they alone were worthy to have these most precious gifts of God and true pearls, while all others are swine and unworthy of these goods. 

<margin>Objection. Response.</margin>

Are we then, who publish these things, thieves and squanderers of honors? But hear, I pray, what I say: surely all those who, kindled by the love of God and charity for their neighbor, rejoice and desire to attain knowledge of the <term>mysteries and secrets<note>original: "mysteriorum arcanorumque"</note></term>—among whose number we place you also, (reader)—are men. We, however, who communicate these things to such men, are faithful <term>stewards of the mysteries of God<note>original: "dispensatores mysteriorum Dei," an allusion to 1 Corinthians 4:1</note></term>. But those very people who envy their neighbors these things and trample them into the mud of their own envy are the swine: because, in the manner of swine, they greedily and spitefully mix and devour even the better fruits with filth. 

As for what they cite from authors—that these works should not have been published because the authors of these treatises wrote not for the common good but for themselves and their own? Did not <term>Aristotle<note>The famous Greek philosopher, whose "secret" teachings to Alexander the Great were a common medieval trope</note></term> respond to Alexander, King of the Macedonians, that he had published his <term>physics<note>original: "physica," referring to Aristotle's works on nature</note></term> in such a way as if they had not been published? Shall Aristotelian books therefore not be printed? Far be it. 

<margin>Geber, king and philosopher.</margin>

What of that Arab philosopher and most skillful King, <term>Geber<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary figure in alchemy whose works were central to the field</note></term>? Has he not left it written: "We have published for ourselves alone the art investigated by ourselves alone, and not by others," etc. Should Geber’s writings therefore not have been submitted to the press...

<margin>The Chemical Art is acquired not by writings but by hands.</margin>
<margin>Gold is not easily dissolved.</margin>
<margin>The philosophers' quicksilver is drawn out by ingenious art.</margin>
...indeed, it is for this very reason that these and similar things ought to be sent out into the public: so that, because they were written obscurely for the benefit of all, they might attain a greater light of truth while being sought out with greater diligence by the wits of everyone, and thus bring even greater utility to mankind. For words can be published and printed, but the industry of manual operation is situated in the experience of each individual; it cannot be printed with type; indeed, it can hardly be handed down by word of mouth except through the hands. For gold must be prepared so that it is not at all stubborn toward solution, and that is indeed quite an arduous task. Nor should it be thought that the <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note></term> which possesses the faculty of dissolving gold is that common sort which is openly sold. For since it is necessary that such a solution be provided by a body which reflects gold in the likeness of its entire substance and is of a hot and moist temperament, it cannot be denied that quicksilver does possess that likeness; however, it is certain that its temperament is extremely cold and mostly undefined. But we must, by ingenious art, entice and draw out a quicksilver from elsewhere—from a body known to very few which nature has concocted. This body reflects the likeness of the entire substance of gold more than common quicksilver does, and by no [special] art, but by the very first contact and friction, it joins and mixes with gold no less willingly than water with water. Now contemplate more deeply what that body might be.

<margin>The Athanor of the philosophers.</margin>
Furthermore, few men know of the furnace which can supply a continuous and equal heat. But those who desire practical knowledge of it should read the work of that great philosopher, <term>Rouilliasco of Piedmont<note>Referring to a Piedmontese author whose work Penotus edited in 1582; possibly related to the works of Guglielmo Gratarolo or a contemporary alchemist.</note></term>, which I published in the year 1582. This furnace is properly called an <term>Athanor<note>original: "Athanor," a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature for the long process of "digestion" or ripening of the chemical stone.</note></term>—that is, a furnace for digestion—not of the kind the ignorant imagine for themselves. But fewer still know the "tripod of secrets," and very few know the "fuel of heat" to which the furnace can provide uniformity. Almost the entire secret [lies] in the degree...

<margin>Example.</margin>
...consists in heat. For just as the formative power of the chick, implanted within the egg, must not be overwhelmed by external heat—otherwise the egg would harden and never bring forth a chick—so too the power of the future seed (that is, of gold mixed with its own <term>quicksilver<note>Latin: "argento vivo."</note></term>) must not be exhausted. Otherwise, the gold would not be dissolved, nor would it germinate, nor would it become the "proximate matter" of gold; instead, it would congeal into gold prematurely due to the excessive action of the heat. <margin>Error destroys the work.</margin> Conversely, if the heat is lacking, the labor of the craftsman will be frustrated. Ultimately, however, this <term>gold-making powder<note>Latin: "pulvis aurificus," the Philosopher's Stone in its powdered form.</note></term> is situated in the power of God, who grants it to whom He wills and withdraws it from others. It is sought in vain by those to whom it has been denied. Hence <term>Palingenius<note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus (c. 1500–1543), an Italian poet whose "Zodiacus Vitae" blended science, philosophy, and alchemy.</note></term> says in his *Zodiac*:

> Then men, revolving the dark oracles of the divine mind
> Within their wavering souls for a long time,
> Having experienced much, and at no small expense,
> Found that art, than which no art is more worthy:
> Of fashioning the ethereal stone, which the profane
> Are by no means permitted to know, and the wicked commoners seek in vain.
> He who possesses it can live decently wherever he wishes;
> He fears neither the wrath of fortune nor the arms of thieves,
> But the gods deign few with so great a gift. etc.

Now, concerning the confirmation of the question: *Whether the art exists, authority, reason, and experience carry much weight.*
<margin>Those who wish the art to be true by authority.</margin>
I could first confirm by the testimonies and authority of many most serious men that the art is true, were it not for the fact that many books have been published about them. Among these are: a booklet on the truth and antiquity of the chemical art and powder, authored by <term>Robertus Valensis<note>Robert Duval (c. 1490–1567), a French alchemist and the first historian of alchemy.</note></term> and published in Paris by Maurellus Fredericus in the year 1561; another by <term>Chrysippus Phanianus<note>Giovanni Crisippo Faniano, an Italian lawyer who wrote "On the Right of Alchemy" (De jure artis alchemiae) in 1576.</note></term> on the right of Alchemy; and recently another, titled *An Apology for Chrysopoeia and Argyropoeia* <note>Chrysopoeia means "gold-making"; Argyropoeia means "silver-making."</note>, in which it is disputed and <margin>Apology against Erastus<note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian famous for his fierce attacks on Paracelsus and alchemy.</note>.</margin> taught whether, what, and how <term>Chrysopoeia</term> (the art of transmuting and perfecting metals) exists. It [was proved] by the firmest reasons, demonstrations, and certain experiments that the art is true, certain, and easy...

...is proven and demonstrated; on the other hand, the arguments brought forth by <term>Erastus<note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who famously attacked the medical and alchemical theories of Paracelsus.</note></term> against this art and doctrine are solidly refuted. It is truly ridiculous what is objected regarding the timing by those "pseudo-timers" <note>Latin: "pseudotemporistis," likely referring to critics who argued that the time for such "miraculous" knowledge had passed or was not yet right.</note>, to whom it has not been granted to know the times and moments; nor has the hour of publishing come for them, so they do not know that ours has arrived. One of these indeed is the very purpose for which 
<margin>The works of Christ through theology; those of nature through philosophy.</margin> 
we were created by God: so that we may know both the works of Christ through Theology and the works of nature through philosophy. This one thing I do not wish to be hidden from you (kind reader): all the books of the philosophers, whoever speaks of that abstruse Hermetic medicine, are nothing but <term>spagyric<note>From the Greek words for "to tear apart" and "to bind together," referring to the alchemical process of separation and purification.</note></term> labyrinths, in which most disciples of the art fall into various obscurities and deceptions of the pathways. So much so that, until this very day, either none or very few have found the true exit. For if some easy path opens itself to those wandering in this labyrinth, which seems to lead straight to the final doors, soon there occur inescapable corners which shut in the straying ones in perpetual prisons. Thus, if in the writings of the philosophers there sometimes offer themselves easy and manifest ways, which at first glance seem plain to those looking at the literal sense: soon the incautious operators, deceived by the plain words of the philosophers, are entangled in innumerable snares. Added to this is the fact that many pseudo-chemists deceive many with their frauds and sophistries, selling and spreading lying chemical operations and papers; to those who are too gullible, they promise mountains of gold and, while sowing <term>weeds<note>Latin: "lolium," often translated as darnel or cockle; a common biblical metaphor for something worthless or deceptive.</note></term>, bid them expect wheat.

<margin>The books of the philosophers must be read with keen judgment.</margin>
*Therefore, moved by compassion, I offer you these treatises full of truth and natural reasons, in which you will have the complete art clearly depicted as if on a painted panel. Examine these, weigh them, and fortify the convictions of your mind with firm arguments; in this way, you cannot go astray. For he who believes all sophistries without judgment is willingly deceived; the true art is hidden under many veils <note>original: "involucris," referring to allegorical or obscure language used to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, in which the cautious are easily entangled. Therefore, before you begin to work, weigh the causes of natural things with prudent counsel, or do not attempt the matter at all: it is better to devote time to skillful judgment and meditation than to pay the penalty for rashness and foolish thoughtlessness. You, friend reader, look upon what has been published with a kind mind, and with a kinder one, take it up; read faithfully and with great judgment, reread, pray, work, operate, and repeat <note>original: "ora, labora, operare, reitera," a famous alchemical maxim emphasizing both spiritual and physical effort.</note>. And without a doubt, you will be made a participant in such great secrets to the honor of God, the author of mysteries, and for the benefit of your neighbor, through the experience of considering nature. Farewell.*

# DIALOGUE BETWEEN NATURE AND THE SON OF PHILOSOPHY.

->*Egidius de Vadis <note>Giles de Vadis, a 16th-century writer on alchemy.</note> sends many greetings to his friend N.*<-

Do not be surprised at me (excellent sir), who, being ignorant of all the sciences, attempt so great a work beyond my strength; for virtue is of such vigor that it not only unites strangers through burning love and desire, but even goads the ignorant, the lazy, and the sluggish so that they long for the very marrow <note>The "medulla" or essential core of knowledge.</note> of all the sciences. I call God to witness, I am in doubt: for I see many indeed who, because of their ornate style of speaking or writing, claim great honors for themselves; yet they teach nothing other than mere fables and trifles with the allurements of words and "trappings of speech" <note>original: "phaleratis dictis," referring to decorative but empty rhetoric.</note>. These people have not yet left behind their childhood toys <note>original: "nuces" (literally "nuts"), which Roman children played with; hence, a metaphor for being immature.</note>, nor do they possess the wisdom of elders <note>original: "sapere patruos," a Latin idiom meaning to have the stern or mature judgment of an uncle.</note>. Rather, like children or youths, if someone offers them a piece of fruit and gold at the same time, they think nothing of the gold—which is of the highest price and value—and prefer the fruit or the nut, which is worth very little. This is indeed the "exchange of Achilles and Glaucus" <note>A reference to the lopsided trade in Homer’s Iliad (usually between Glaucus and Diomedes) where gold armor was exchanged for bronze; it denotes a foolish or unequal bargain.</note>. For if anyone were to discourse on the secrets of Nature, they would surely answer like babblers, with polished and ornate words that have little or nothing to do with the matter—just like those who lick the shell of a nut but never taste the sweetness of the marrow within. Therefore, the words of the man who said "Enough talk, but too little wisdom" <note>original: "loquentiæ satis, ſapientiæ parum," a famous quote from the Roman historian Sallust describing the character of Catiline.</note> apply perfectly to them. 

But in truth, even if I am much worse than they are—chiefly because of my ignorance, and also because of my unrefined speech, which they call "stammering" or "solecism" <note>A "solecism" is a grammatical error or an unidiomatic use of language.</note>—I take as much delight in diligently searching for the innermost sweetness of that nut (however unpolished my style) as they do in arguing over the shell with their refined words. They see only the outside; I clearly perceive both the exterior and the interior. Therefore, my confidence in you is so great that I have addressed these works of ours to you, hoping you will receive my gift (however small) with a joyful countenance. And you shall love me in return (as is your custom). Farewell, from the royal library at Richmond <note>original: "Richemetum," referring to Richmond Palace in Surrey, England.</note>. July 17th, in the year 1521.

->E. D. V. <note>The initials of the author, Egidius de Vadis.</note><-

### AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

*When for many years I had exhausted myself in the investigation of nature’s secrets, with no few late-night studies <note>original: "lucubrationibus," referring to work done by candlelight or late at night.</note>, a focused mind, and tireless labor; and finally, when I had weighed all the paths and tracks of such an investigation—the irregularities, the diversions, and the surrounding paths—I found they were occupied not only by difficulties, but by crags, riddles, tropes, and various enigmas and maxims (not to mention "masks") <note>The author is describing the intentionally obscure and symbolic language used by alchemists to hide their secrets.</note>. But she, wishing to console me, spoke with a very sweet and gentle voice, saying: "Do not be afraid, O son, for I am Nature, whom you have sought with such great effort, and I have been sent to you by the command of God. Well done then; exult and be glad, because I shall make you happy in two ways. First, in that you see how much the mercy of God has deigned to do for you, a most vile sinner, in that you see me with your physical eyes, though you are unlearned and very meagerly qualified in the sciences. Second, you will be comforted in this: that I will answer you concerning all things you doubt. Ask, therefore, as you please, and I will reveal what has been granted to you." 

To which I replied: "O good Lady, spare me, I beseech you, for my stammering <note>original: "balbuties," a term often used by medieval authors to humbly describe their lack of polished rhetoric or formal education.</note> does not allow me to return worthy thanks to you. For as you have already said, I am poorly qualified in letters; I shall proceed, therefore, and return thanks to my God, who by His bounty and immensity has destined me [for this]. Returning then to the doubts in which I am submerged, I will question you." 

But she said: "Go on, son, and do not delay in rendering what you have known; I, meanwhile, will wait for the end of your prayer."

# CHAPTER I.

->*In which Nature teaches the son of art what the matter of the stone is, saying that the beginning of the work results from the end of the intention.*<-

->*The Son.*<-

Now therefore, Lady, after I have given thanks to my God for all his benefits, I will question you; if it truly pleases you, you shall answer.

*Nature.* Propose your question, my son, and with God’s help I will satisfy your doubts.

*The Son.* O lady, since I have found such grace in your eyes, tell me, I beseech you: why do the Philosophers not name the matter in their books from which their stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> is produced? Indeed, I remember reading many treatises, yet I have understood none of them to name it in any way.

*Nature.* Son, you should know that all the Philosophers name it openly in their books; but because they speak only to Philosophers and their sons, those who are not qualified and steeped <note>original: "imbibiti," literally "soaked" or "saturated."</note> in Philosophy do not notice how they name it. Indeed, what is subtlety among them is folly and boorishness among the ignorant.

<margin>Form acts according to the disposition of matter</margin>
Listen then, and heed my words, because I will show you how they name [it] with a living voice: Have you heard the authority of Aristotle saying, "the actions of active things are in a disposed patient" <note>original: "actus actiuorum sunt in patiente disposito." In Scholastic philosophy, the "patient" is the passive recipient that receives the action of an "agent."</note>? Therefore, form does not act except according to the disposition of matter. Do you understand this?

*Son.* Yes, indeed, Lady.

*Nature.* See now how they name it. Since if you say what you intend to do, you will see and clearly understand and weigh what you seek: because from the end of any intention results its beginning.

*Son.* I indeed intend to produce the sun and the moon <note>In alchemical texts, "sun" (Sol) and "moon" (Luna) are standard terms for gold and silver.</note>.

<margin>From the end of the intention results the beginning of the sun and the moon. Understand this concerning univocal and not equivocal generation.</margin>
*Nature.* Take note now of how you have named the principles of your operation by stating the end of your intention: which is that you wish to produce gold and silver. These will certainly be the beginning of your work, just as if you had said you wanted to produce a human, you would have named your agent <term>agent: the active force or "father" of a process</term> there. Once that is obtained, nothing would be lacking to you except a recipient <term>patient: the passive matter or "mother" that receives the form</term> suitable for such generation. For just as it is not possible to generate a human without a human, so neither can one generate gold and silver without gold and silver: because every like thing produces its like <note>This refers to "univocal generation," the biological rule that species only produce their own kind.</note>.

->CHAPTER II.<-

*In this second chapter, Nature says that minerals are of a hermaphroditic nature because they have both sexes—namely sulfur and quicksilver. And that the increase of any thing depends upon its beginning.*

*Son.* How, Lady? I see a human being generated from the coupling of male and female; in the production of silver or gold, I do not perceive any coupling.

*Nature.* Know, son, that every growing thing—whether among vegetables, minerals, or animals—is not led out from potentiality into act <note>A phrase from Aristotelian physics referring to a thing becoming what it has the potential to be, like an acorn becoming an oak.</note> except through the conjunction of form and matter, which are taken in the place of male and female. If, therefore, in minerals and vegetables, physical sexual intercourse does not occur, there is nevertheless an attraction between them, through which a person recognizes the form suitable to the matter. Because, as Plato says, forms are given according to the merit of the matter; there is no suitable generation except from things consistent in nature. Nevertheless, minerals and vegetables are of a hermaphroditic nature, because they have both sexes. Nonetheless, a conjunction of form and matter occurs from within themselves, just as it happens with animals.

*Son.* Oh Lady, I most earnestly entreat you that I may hear of that coupling from your own mouth.

<margin>Plato.
The growth of any thing depends on its beginning.
Milk is blood twice-cooked.</margin>
*Nature.* Hear what Plato said, that upon which the beginning of any thing depends, in that same thing will its growth be. Do you not see that the generation of man and his production is made from menstrual blood, and his nourishment or upbringing comes from milk, which is blood twice-cooked <note>original: "sanguis bis coctus." In medieval physiology, it was believed that breast milk was actually menstrual blood that had been further "cooked" or refined by the heat of the mother's body.</note>? For it does not differ from the menstrual flow except through the repetition of the cooking [decoction]. In a similar way, a plant is made from a subtle earthy and watery substance. Therefore, when you have its seed, commit it to the earth, so that through its subtle parts combined with a similar moisture, you may lead it from potentiality into act. Consider the nature of the mineral body in the same way: that is to say, find where it took its origin, and reduce it back to its own matter, just as was said regarding the plant, and you shall fulfill your desire.

# CHAPTER III.

*Nature teaches what that matter necessary for the physical work may be; she proves it by example, and it may be seen by reading this third chapter.*

<margin>First matter is neither dry, cold, nor humid.</margin>
*Son.* Truly, Lady, it seems to me that if I wished to reduce the mineral body itself to its first matter—that which it was before—it will be impossible. For according to the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle, often called simply "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note>, first matter is neither hot, nor dry, cold, nor humid. Therefore, that reduction will be very far removed from the nature of metals.

<margin>Commit to memory 1st, 2nd, and 3rd matter; the fourth is "proximate."
Confused matter is necessary for the Art.
Proximate matter of metals is necessary for the Art.
An example.</margin>
*Nature.* How do you understand "first matter"? For I am not speaking of that most remote matter which is called <term>hyle: the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe</term>, nor of that which is called <term>Chaos</term>, although you do have need of a "confused" matter <note>Matter that has been stripped of its specific metallic form but is not yet reduced to total formlessness.</note> because you will strive to introduce a new form. Nor do I mean the natures from which the elements come, nor the qualities arising from those elements, but only the **proximate first matter**. In animals, these are called sperm; in vegetables, seeds; and in minerals, they are called **sulfur and quicksilver**—the Philosophers' kind, I should add. For that most remote first matter (the second, third, or fourth degree) is no more fit or disposed to create a metal than it is to create a donkey. I want you to reduce [the metal] to its first matter while *preserving the species*, and indeed while preserving the individual itself; for species are not subject to the actions of the senses. Now, note well the example I will give you regarding this "reduction": when men and women mate, they are then reduced to their first matter, because from their bodies the raw sperm is generated from which they themselves first came forth. Yet their bodies are not destroyed, as they would be if they were reduced to that remote first matter...

<summary>Nature explains that alchemical creation follows the laws of biology, requiring a "proximate" starting material (sulfur and mercury) rather than a return to the formless "hyle" of the universe. She uses the analogy of human reproduction, where parents produce sperm (their own origin) without being destroyed in the process.</summary>

that the most remote matter is called <term>Hyle</term> <note>Hyle (from the Greek word for "wood" or "stuff") was used by ancient philosophers and alchemists to describe pure, formless matter—the most basic substance of the universe before it has been given any specific shape or characteristics.</note>, and it is the primordial principle of all things. Regarding this, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). This refers to his discussion of formless matter in the "Confessions," where he struggles to imagine a "nothingness" that is still "something."</note> says: "When I conceive of something formless, I first understand nothing where I once understood something; for just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard." It follows, therefore, that *Hyle* is that which is perceived between "something" and "nothing."

Another matter, however, which is not quite so remote, is called <term>Chaos</term> <note>While Hyle is a philosophical abstraction, Chaos represents the actual physical mixture of the four elements before they were organized into the world. Alchemists sought this "Chaos" as the starting point for their Great Work.</note>; this Chaos is a raw and undigested mass in which all things were confused and mixed together. Some call it the "confused matter" or "confused mass," gaping from the beginning; others call it the formless matter of heaven and earth, which was first made out of nothing, and from which all things afterwards came forth individually through various species and their own proper forms. Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero." His descriptions of the creation were popular in alchemical and philosophical texts.</note> defines it thus: "Chaos is a raw and disordered matter, a confused heap."

And so that you may better understand this "first matter"—which is more necessary to you than all others, because without it you will not complete your work at all—I will tell you more clearly what it is like. Although in the beginning the Most High God prepared the four elements which were confused within it, the Earth and Water (which are heavier than the others) reached all the way to the orb of the Moon, and Fire and Air (lighter than the other elements) descended all the way to the center of the Earth. <note>Nature describes a state of total elemental inversion: the "heavy" elements are in the heavens, while the "light" elements are at the core. This "confusion" is the definition of Chaos.</note> Because of this, such matter was rightly called "confused."

There remains in this world a certain part of that confused matter which is known by everyone and is sold openly <note>This is a recurring theme in alchemy: the secret "First Matter" is not a rare substance, but something common and cheap that the ignorant overlook or despise.</note>. Yet, there are few who believe this thing to be Chaos or "confused matter." Therefore, my son, it will be necessary for you to know it, since without it (as I said above) you will labor in vain. For since it exists without form and is fit for all forms, it most easily [receives] such a form—

<margin>
Note.
</margin>
From that third part, which was divided into five parts, God first created the <term>fifth substance</term>; from the remaining parts, He created the four elements. Read, therefore, the chapters cited above, and you will have all these things at length.

<margin>
Two natures. Heat is generated by motion.
</margin>
Now, son, it remains to look at the "natures" <note>In this context, "natures" refers to the fundamental qualities or forces that precede physical matter.</note>, which are simpler than the elements. Know then that there are two natures: the first is heat, and the other is cold. The nature of heat is active, while that of cold is passive. Heat is generated by motion, and cold—or the nature of cold—comes from the stillness of the earth. Read Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works formed the backbone of medieval science.</note> in his *Key of Wisdom* <note>original: "claui sapientiæ"</note>, and you will find all these things discussed at length and in a delightful manner, distinguishing what is a "simple" made from a "simple," and a "composite" made from a "composite." These first two natures are called simple, and their work is called "simple from simple," which consists of the natures of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Regarding the generation of these natures, he says that in the beginning the Creator, without uttering a word, said, "Let such a creature be made." Afterward, a creature was created that could be called neither large nor small, neither subtle nor coarse, neither moving nor resting, nor could it be defined by any other description or compared to any known thing. In this creature, all things existed potentially. To bring these into actuality, He created a second creature, which He decreed should be called Light. This is Avicenna’s view regarding the four elements. I have already told you that reducing things all the way back to the elements themselves is too remote a path; however, once you have the "first matter" near at hand, you may make a reduction to the qualities that come from them. You necessarily have to divide the elements, and for that reason, you do not need other materials—except for that "confused matter" <note>Chaos, or the unrefined starting material of the Alchemical work.</note> already mentioned, for the reasons touched upon above.

*Son.* May you be blessed, My Lady. I have noted all your words...

Wherefore it is concluded, just as was said of animals and vegetables, that the thing from which metals are [made] is not to be taken, but rather that which is *from* the metals themselves. ### CHAPTER VI.

*Nature teaches the Son of Art that he cannot himself make the matter from which the Mercury of the Philosophers is made, and why it is called the Mercury of the Philosophers.*

*Nature.* Son, the Philosophers say, "take *our* Mercury." In this, they give you to understand that they are not speaking of the common kind, because they say "ours." For Mercury is said to be "theirs" just as a son is said to be the father's who begot him. For it is not given to me (says Nature) to produce their Mercury from <term>potentiality into act</term> <note>original: "de potentia ad actum"; an Aristotelian concept meaning moving from a state of possibility to a state of physical reality.</note> without the help of the Philosopher; wherefore it is deservedly called "theirs," because they bring it through to its completion.

For a man looking upon a woman draws and is drawn by her, more than by other animals existing outside his own genus and his own species. ### CHAPTER IX.

*That in this art two things are necessarily required, namely the agent and the patient: Because a single and simple thing does not act upon itself.*

*Nature:* Son, you speak the truth, because the whole power of your mastery consists in this; but to understand this, you must not be ignorant that this science is the science of the four elements, <margin>This science is of the four Elements.</margin> which treats more abundantly and better than all others of their correspondence <note>original: "symbolizatione"; the shared qualities (like heat or moisture) that allow elements to interact.</note> and discordance: and which of them are noble, which ignoble; which active, which passive—although all things in turn act and are acted upon—what is concordant and what is discordant, which we understand as correspondence; by these precepts of the art, you will know by what reasoning the agent acts and the matter is acted upon, because <margin>The agent is always more noble than its patient. An equal has no command over an equal.</margin> (according to Aristotle) every agent is more noble than the thing it acts upon. ### CHAPTER XII.

*In this art, the roots of metals must be understood. Once this science is known, other sciences will be easily understood. Therefore, God, the giver of all sciences, must be prayed to.*

*Nature.* My son, use the counsel of Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational to medieval science.</note>, who says that the knowledge of metals and their roots makes this mastery easy. Do not, therefore, inquire further into this matter, because it does not please my master that such things be publicized; instead, study diligently and implora the help of your Creator, so that by His mercy He may deign to illuminate your intellect—not only in this species but in all others—so that 
<margin>God, the giver of secrets, must be prayed to.</margin>
together with this mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy; the process of transformation.</note> you may recognize all things at once. Because whoever 
<margin>Once this science is known, the rest are known.</margin>
understands this science through cause and reason, almost all my secrets will be revealed to them; because this science is uniquely suited for understanding all others. Furthermore, my son, I want you to know that the Mathematicians establish their matter in the "Dyad" or binary, but their form in the "Monad" or unity <note>In Pythagorean thought, the Monad represents the One or the Divine, while the Dyad represents duality or matter.</note>. For Averroes 
<margin>Matter is in the binary and form in the unity.</margin>
the commentator on Aristotle (says): *The lowest things are bound to the highest by a double proportion.* Therefore, my son, you have asked prudently; indeed, there are few who question such things. Indeed, I do not see one in a thousand who considers what the matter or form will be in the work, and thus they are deservedly deceived. For their inquiry is only about Mercury—and if they once understand it to be quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, they ask no further. Whether it be divided in two, or single, it suffices

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*All things are situated in numbers. Indeed, the elements are bound by certain numbers.*<-

<margin>Boethius on the Consolation of Philosophy. The elements are bound by numbers.</margin>
*Son.* Indeed, My Lady, I remember reading at the beginning of Boethius, in the *Consolation of Philosophy*, "You who bind the elements with numbers" <note>original: "Tu qui numeris elementa ligas," from Book III, Meter 9 of Boethius's famous work</note>; I do not think he said this recklessly. I have seen by certain experiment that the elements are combined with one another by a specific number, which cannot be done by any other number at all. Furthermore, the Philosophers say wondrous things about numbers. For Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a Renaissance philosopher known for his "900 Theses," in which he argued that mathematics and numbers were the key to understanding all things.</note> extols them so much that he is not afraid to say that through them, an answer can be given to everything knowable, which I certainly think is most true. Therefore, I would have gladly asked about them, except that you refuse to teach such things.

<margin>All things are situated in numbers.</margin>
*Nature.* Many secrets are situated in numbers; nevertheless, if you indicate to me what you wish to be taught, I might perhaps comply with your prayers.

*Son.* For I desire to be informed about the balanced body <term>balanced body (corpus aequatum): a state of perfect physical equilibrium where the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—are perfectly proportioned, making the substance incorruptible and medicinal.</term>, or rather the body that is to be balanced; for the Philosophers affirm that by means of our medicine, every body—whether human, mineral, or vegetable—can be rectified. If, therefore, it was not balanced, how will it give what it does not have?

## CHAPTER XV.

->*This science is the investigator of natural things, through which one arrives at the knowledge of hidden things.*<-

<margin>The nature of one into the nature of another.</margin>
*Nature.* Indeed, son, what you ask is difficult enough; however, because I first promised to respond to your doubts, I will manifest everything to you, on the condition that you reveal it to no unworthy person. Therefore, you must first know that this science investigates my secrets more deeply than others, because it alone imitates me, both in generations and in transmutations through the digestions <term>digestions: the process of slow, steady heating used in alchemy to mature or refine a substance, mimicking natural biological processes.</term> declared above. These indeed show by what reasoning vegetables are converted into animals and animals into humans—that is to say, into human flesh and blood. Finally, it explores all kinds of combinations of elements that are in the universe, and (as it pleases Avicenna <note>A Latinized reference to Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and natural philosophy were standard texts in Europe.</note>) one hundred and forty-five

...are numbered. By these [numbers], all things propagated through me are generated, varied, and diversified; and knowledge of these will be absolutely necessary for you to find what you are seeking. These 145 aforementioned ways can be reduced to 24 modes, which I will explain in order. Once you have heard them, you will perceive how some qualities act and others suffer <note>In the Aristotelian physics used by alchemists, "action" and "passion" refer to the way one quality (like heat) acts upon another (like coldness), which "suffers" or receives that change.</note>; and this happens according to "the more and the less," through which you will finally find the way of balancing the elements in one body, which is exactly what you seek. 

Do not think, however, that such an equalization can be achieved according to the quantity of "light" and "heavy" <note>This refers to physical weight. Nature is arguing that alchemy is not about mixing equal pounds of dirt and water, but about balancing their internal powers.</note>, because a body mixed in such a way would neither move nor rest. It must, therefore, happen according to the substances and qualities of the elements. As for the equality of the power and virtue <term>virtue: the inherent strength or specific natural power of a substance</term> in operation: it is possible to use a large amount of Earth and a smaller amount of Fire, so that the portion of Earth has as much power for acting as the portion of Fire; and so it is for the rest. 

When elements have been gathered in a mixture in this way, the Philosophers say the mixture has equality, in which I truly take great delight. This is because in such a body there is neither action nor passion <note>Because the forces are perfectly balanced, they no longer fight to change one another.</note>, as you can see in gold, which can be corrupted the least, by reason of this aforementioned equality. 

Let us therefore proceed to these combinations. The first is such: either there will be two elements that are "major" and two "minor," or three major and one minor, or three minor and one major; or all will be equal. And this combination cannot be based on weight, nor on the physical quantities of the qualities; it must instead be according to the virtues and active powers of the qualities themselves, because complexions <term>complexion: the specific "temperament" or balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature</term> are considered according to the powers and virtues of the qualities, and not according to weight and quantity. 

Understand, therefore, that I am speaking here of complexions, as I told you above. 

If two elements are major: 
*   **First mode:** Fire and Air are major; Water and Earth are minor. 
*   **Second mode:** Fire and Air are minor; Water and Earth are major. 
*   **Third mode:** Fire and Water are major; Air and Earth are minor. 
*   **Fourth mode:** Fire and Water are minor; Air and Earth are major. 
*   **Fifth mode:** Fire and Earth are major; Air and Water are minor. 
*   **Sixth mode:** Fire and Earth are minor; Air and Water are major. 

If indeed Air is combined with Water and Earth (as was said before regarding Fire), or with Earth, six [more] combinations are made. Although these will not be different modes in reality, but only according to the logic of the combination...
