as is clear: Because if it is said that air and water are greater, and earth and fire are lesser, it becomes the sixth mode; but if it is said that air and water are lesser, and fire and earth are greater, it becomes the fifth mode; but if it is said that air and water are greater, and earth and fire lesser, then it is the fourth mode; and so conversely it is then the third mode; but if it is said that water and earth are greater, and fire and air lesser, then it is the second mode; if conversely, then it is the first mode. Therefore you should understand that Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were central to medieval European alchemy.</note>, by obscuring these divisions, posits twelve modes, which are in truth only six. If these are divided into twenty-four, each will have 4 modes. For when it is said that air and fire are greater, it can be that fire is the greatest, air minor, water minor, and earth the least. And so all other modes can be varied by four, according to the form just described. For in the second mode, when it is said that fire and air are lesser, and water and earth greater, it can be that fire is the least, air major, water major, and earth greatest; and thus the first mode: or fire least, air major, earth major, and water greatest; and thus the second: or air is the least, fire major, water major, and earth greatest; and thus it is the fourth mode. Understand the other modes by the example of these. Therefore, my son, if you wish to know all these things, read Avicenna himself in his *Greater Alchemy* <note>original: "maiori Alchemia," likely referring to the pseudo-Avicennian work *De Anima in arte alchimiae*.</note>.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## He still pursues the knowledge of the degrees, and how one degree surpasses another.

<margin>One degree surpasses another.</margin>
<margin>Everything manifest is contrary to its hidden nature.</margin>
*Nature:* My son, know that the first degree with respect to the human temperament is that in which there is equality; the second truly exceeds it equally; the third in some way declines toward injury; but the fourth, because of its excess, hurts the senses. For example: Water that is very lukewarm yields to the sense, nor does the sense take pleasure in it: and thus it is the first degree. When it is well tempered, hot with cold, so that the sense takes pleasure in it, then it is the second degree. When it is hot and hurts the sense, then it is the third degree; but if it is boiling, then it is the fourth degree. And so these degrees can go to infinity as far as we are concerned, according to the increase of these qualities, yet they stay in the fourth state with respect to the human temperament. This is especially true when the temperament <note>original: "complexio"</note> mentioned above is called "equal" and "tempered" to the human temperament, because it is most suitable to human nature. Yet one should not feel or know the degree sought here in things only according to touch and sense; I have seen it according to virtue <note>internal power or essence</note> and power. For ginger, according to touch, nature, sense, and substance is cold and dry; but according to the virtue of its temperament, it is hot and moist. And wine is cold and moist according to external touch, and according to substance and sense; but according to the virtue of its temperament, it is hot and dry. And thus you can understand that one mastery <note>original: "magisterium," referring to the alchemical process or the "Great Work."</note> is contrary to its hidden nature.

*The Son:* O Lady, how sweet are your words! Explain to me a little more about that equation which I desire so much, because you have involved me in these combinations to such an extent that I do not know which part to follow.

*Nature:* If you desire to know more about that body which has been or is to be equalized, hear what the Philosophers think about this.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

*Here he teaches what the squaring of the circle is—which many experts seek in vain and do not understand Aristotle—and various matters are treated in this chapter.*

**Nature.** Euclid in the *Rosary* <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical florilegium or collection of authoritative quotes.</note> says this: you will be able to know the proportion of this water if you multiply the weight of the bodies by twelve. 
<margin>Note.</margin>
Likewise another says: if the container holds two pounds, add twelve grains of prepared Mercury. Likewise, let the "eagle stone" <note>original: "lapis aquilæ." Historically, this refers to aetites, a stone believed to be found in eagles' nests, but here it likely refers to a specific alchemical stage or substance.</note> be 9. The ferment is a part of the earth, because a little bit of ferment corrupts <note>In the sense of "transforms" or "leavens," like yeast in dough.</note> the whole mass. Socrates in the *Crowd* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says: if you place a little gold, a powerful and white tincture will come out. Parmenides says: one overcomes ten. Hali says: regarding the quantity itself, know its weight, and add to it as much moisture as can be; its quantity does not have a determined weight. Likewise, another says in verse: let the tenth part of things be full of sprouts. In the treatise that begins "The earth stands": The earth must drink as much as there is of the wine itself. Likewise in the same treatise: put in as much of the wine as of the other. Also, Bacon <note>Likely Roger Bacon, the 13th-century philosopher and scientist associated with alchemy.</note> on the temperaments of bodies: The proportion of the Spirit should be a tenth part of the body. Likewise in another treatise: Let the proportion of the body be according to your reason; but the proportion of the metal is the fifth and sixth part of the medicine. Likewise in the treatise that begins, "Venerable father," understand by the square the four elements, and by the twelve: the tertiary soakings <note>original: "imbibitiones," the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated.</note>. Take the weights, then turn the square into a circle <note>original: "quadrangulum in rotundum," the "squaring of the circle," an alchemical metaphor for creating the perfect, unified Philosopher's Stone from the four square elements.</note>, and you will have the whole. Likewise, in the same it must be noted clearly that the weights in this place are taken as equal without an angle, and that is because we use an equal line; therefore take an equal weight of each. Again, another says in verse: Let as much of the sulfur be taken as of the river. Likewise, the treatise *Because the speech is too long*: see that the quantity of the mother belongs to the son, so that the number three remains, led into itself four times. Listen similarly to what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> defines regarding this. O son of wisdom (he says), know that the water is wisely weighed, the proportion of which I will teach consequently. Take therefore 2 thirds of the moisture, and of the "southern redness" a 4th part, of *sebit*—that is, yellow earth—likewise, and of orpiment <term>auri pigmento; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used in alchemy</term> likewise a half, which makes eight. These indeed are mystical words full of mysteries, and related in an obscure sense. Likewise John Dastin, who was an excellent Philosopher.

### CHAPTER XX.

*Teaching what is the first mover in natural things. How Nature multiplies infinitely from one sown grain. So also Art acts by the imitation of nature; and once the Stone is completed, you will be able to lead it to whatever form you wish.*

<margin>
The first thing born is the vegetable Spirit, the Fire of nature, neither hot and dry, but hot and moist.
</margin>
**Nature.** Now, my son, I see that you are beginning to be wise, wherefore I shall instruct you more willingly from now on. Know then that the first mover in me, Nature, is the vegetative spirit, which in plants is called the "airy moisture" <note>original: "humus aereus"</note>, but in animals is called the "radical moisture" <term>radical moisture: the vital fluid or life-force believed to sustain living beings</term> or the "innate heat." And it is of the nature of fire itself. Do not understand it, however, to be a hot and dry fire. On the contrary, as I said before, it is natural: which is properly called hot and moist. And for this reason, the Philosophers say that their Stone is "vegetable" <note>original: "lapidem esse vegetabilem." In alchemy, the "Vegetable Stone" refers to the life-force or growth principle within matter, allowing the alchemist's work to "grow" or multiply like a plant.</note>.

...because without such a spirit, it would neither grow nor sprout.

**Son.** How do you say it grows and sprouts, O Lady? For I do not understand how it grows or multiplies, except in the same way bread grows by adding more flour and the other things required to make it.

<margin>Note.</margin>
**Nature.** Son, you understand poorly: because the stone—that is, the medicine you seek—sprouts and multiplies just like a grain of wheat falling into good earth; when it has died, it brings forth much fruit. Because (as Saint Paul testifies) that which is sown does not bear fruit unless it first decays and dies <note>original: "Divo Paulo testante... nisi prius corrumpatur, & moriatur." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:36.</note>. When it is decayed, you can then produce many other grains from it. You must understand it in a similar way here, because from one <term>calcus: the smallest unit of weight, roughly the weight of a seed</term>, a single grain excepted, you can produce a hundred thousand <term>talents: an ancient unit of weight representing a very large sum or mass</term>; indeed, a thousand times a thousand million talents, even into infinity, without end or any fixed number, as much as you yourself wish to bring from potentiality into reality. Therefore, you took a quite weak example from bread, because bread has no likeness to it (except for fermentation alone), which is indeed very necessary in this 
<margin>Example of human generation.</margin>
work, and for several reasons. For example, in the creation or rather the generation of a human, if the woman's womb did not have some of the menses after their generation (which are taken there as ferments), the generation of a human would be impossible. Similarly, the bread you brought as an example: if it were not fermented, it would be quite difficult to bring it to the 
<margin>Note. After the stone is perfected, you can lead it to whatever form you wish.</margin>
taste of bread. Therefore, son, many secrets lie hidden in fermentation, which would be long to narrate. For in truth, almost the whole secret lies there. Because after the stone is completed and perfected, you can lead it to whatever form you wish, by means of this fermentation. Look at what the Philosophers say on this subject: *Everything fixed in the fixed is turned into the nature of the fixed.* Do you not see that the 
<margin>Sperm is twice-cooked blood. Here.</margin>
sperm in all animals is one? Because it is generated from <term>twice-cooked blood: a traditional biological theory that sperm was blood refined and concentrated by the body's heat</term>, and yet, depending on the diversity of the place where it is cast, it produces different forms? Observe, then, what I said above: that the place generates that which is placed. For sperm is in all animals just as Mercury is in minerals;

indeed, it is called Mercury because of its wonderful adherence to changeability: for it is so <term>versipellis: literally "skin-changer," a shape-shifter or chameleon</term> that it always assimilates—

## CHAPTER XXI.

*The medicines of the pharmacists are corruptible, but the Medicine of the physicians is incorruptible; the Stone is multiplied by the multitude of spirits.*

<margin>
Raymond Lully and Jean de Roquetaillade on quintessences.
</margin>
**Nature.** Hear, Son, what Raymond Lully and his colleague Jean de Roquetaillade <note>two of the most influential medieval alchemical authors</note> think about this in their works on the <term>quintessences: the "fifth essence," a pure, indestructible spiritual substance extracted from matter</term>. To wish to preserve a thing by means of something rotten and quickly corruptible, or to seek reformation through something subject to deformity, or to make something incorruptible through a failing thing, or to cure the sick through a sick thing, or to make something beautiful through a foul thing—this is fantastic and vain. For with this Medicine, you will be able to heal every infirmity, even those despaired of: you can produce gold, silver, and precious stones.

<margin>
The medicines of the pharmacists are changed, but they do not change others.
</margin>
If this Medicine were made from a corruptible thing—like the medicines prepared by the apothecaries, whose momentary power vanishes after the first action is performed—it would fail. This is because such medicines do not change the body, but are themselves changed: although they act upon various things, the body's digestion eventually overcomes them and turns their substance into the same medicated state. This happens because they are composed of quickly corruptible things, as I said before. Hear also what Roger Bacon <note>a famous 13th-century English philosopher and scientist</note> thinks about this; for he says in his *Letter on the Retardation of Old Age*:

<margin>
The matter of the Stone must be incorruptible.
</margin>
"Most things show their powers and strengths through their form, their matter, essence, color, durability, preservation, and corruption." For as he says: that thing preserves as long as it is itself preserved; and that thing corrupts which is itself quickly corrupted. See therefore what kind of temperament and power it must

<margin>When the vegetative power is weakened, the other powers are likewise weakened.</margin>
which I explained to you above, and they are called the appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive <note>These were the four "natural virtues" in Galenic medicine that managed how the body took in food, kept it, processed it, and expelled waste.</note>; when these are well-proportioned without any alteration, just as I have ordered them, the whole human body will be healthy; and the other power, which is called the sensory, is completed. You judge all their objects perfectly through its five external senses, and then follows the third, which is called the imaginative: and finally the fourth, which is called the rational. For see, if anything in the vegetative power is weakened, the sensory power is made foolish; because it thinks it sees what it does not see, and hears what it does not hear: its taste is not good, nor does it discern rightly through smell. Therefore, when the vegetative power itself is altered, the other powers are altered and destroyed. Thus, it follows most excellently that the vegetative power, or its particular spirit, is necessary for generating or producing your medicine.

<margin>Note. This spirit is to be sought both in bodies and in the mediums.</margin>
But if you (as you said before) are ignorant that such a spirit exists in minerals, inquire diligently concerning it, both in bodies and in spirits or "mediums" <term>mediums: intermediate substances used by alchemists to bridge the gap between solid "bodies" (metals) and volatile "spirits" (like mercury or sulfur)</term>, because without it you will never achieve perfection.

### CHAPTER XXII.

->*Digestion occurs by the benefit of moist heat, and it is not sufficient in the work to have external heat, but rather that heat which lies hidden within the matter.*<-

<margin>
Digestion occurs by the benefit of the mover.
</margin>
Nature: Understand, my son, that wherever the vegetative power serves as the instrument, the sensitive power <term>sensitive power: in medieval psychology, the level of the soul responsible for perception and movement, higher than the "vegetative" level</term> serves as the mover: therefore, it appears that digestion occurs by the power of the mover, and not the instrument: Because, given that an animal takes some vegetable as food for itself, that food is not converted into a vegetable, but into a sensitive being; it is necessary, therefore, that this conversion occurs by the power of the natural heat of that which digests the food; since we perceive no other cause why this happens. However, it is not likely that this happens merely by the mediation of heat; for if it were so, digestion would occur more quickly by a fire than by natural heat. Which, being done thus [by fire], would not be converted into blood and flesh and bones (as experience teaches); it is necessary, therefore, that some other hidden cause...

### CHAPTER XXIII.

> *Nature teaches that every thing possesses a soul—that is, a **vegetable spirit**—and it is this spirit that moves things into being. Likewise, she teaches that this art does not depend on our own will, but on Almighty God; therefore, He must be invoked and prayed to.*

*The Son.* My Lady, you speak profoundly here and I seem to see your point; those things you have just brought forward hit the mark. <note>original: "tangunt rem cum acu" — literally "touch the thing with a needle," a Latin idiom meaning to hit the nail on the head or speak with precision.</note> Yet I do not see clearly how I can direct my work according to the pattern of that hidden cause, except for what you say about the **mover** of that effect being the cause. For though they may cause those bodies to move, speak, and eat, they nonetheless do not digest through natural heat (which they lack entirely) nor, consequently, through that other hidden cause of which you have spoken. <note>The student is using the example of a "reanimated" corpse to show that while a spirit can move a body, it cannot give it true biological life or "internal heat" unless it is properly united with the soul.</note>

*Nature.* My son, you have answered excellently, for such is the truth of the matter. Therefore, **join the soul with its body** (by means of its spirit), <margin>Join the soul with its body.</margin> because the soul will take up its body in no other way except through its own spirit. This is because, in its nature, the soul is too far removed from its physical body; but if a spirit is placed between them which shares the qualities of both—even though the body is by itself ineffective, unfit, and far removed from the soul’s nature—nevertheless, by being <margin>Note.</margin> compatible with both, it will easily be drawn to each, and each to it. Receive me as your own and willing professor <note>original: "professorem" — in this context, one who "professes" or practices the sacred Art of alchemy</note>, since all our trust depends on you alone: we can go no further: we must submit ourselves to you; deign to reveal your hidden treasures to us. Show us your hidden things, and be kind to us. Among others who have professed you, I offer myself praying with humble submission, that I may be your servant, with an upright life, not foreign to my profession: I pray, Lord, that you would deign to forgive me—and your faithful servants—if I should open your secrets. Amen.

# THE PHILOSOPHICAL AXIOMS OF THE TWELVE GATES BY GEORGE RIPLEY.

The eternal God in the beginning created all things from nothing, a spherical and obscure work out of a confused chaos.

From one confused mass were created all things that now exist.

This one principle can serve to declare the matter of our blessed stone.

Our stone is called the Microcosm <note>Meaning "little world"; the idea that the stone contains the essence of the entire universe.</note>, one and three, Magnesia and Sulfur, and Mercury proportioned by Nature.

Philosophers call it quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, and not the common kind, without which no existing thing can be.

It is found more closely in certain things than in others.

Understand that there are three Mercuries, which are the keys of the entire science; Raymond <note>Referring to Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval philosophy and alchemy.</note> calls them his solvents <note>original: "menstrua" — a term for transformative liquids used to dissolve materials in the alchemical vessel.</note>, without which nothing happens in the art.

The essential Mercury of other bodies is the primary material of our stone.

The stone is the soul and substance through which the earth receives its splendor.

What else are Gold and Silver than clean earth—white and red?

We call the whole compound our lead; the quality of its splendor proceeds from the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold/the masculine principle, and the Moon represents Silver/the feminine principle.</note>.

<note>Vocabulary: George Ripley, alchemy, the blessed stone, Microcosm, Magnesia, Sulfur, Mercury, Raymond Lull, gold, silver</note>

<summary>This page concludes a prayer for divine permission to reveal alchemical secrets before beginning a series of foundational philosophical axioms by the famed English alchemist George Ripley. These axioms define the "Stone" as a microcosm of creation, composed of specialized Mercury, Sulfur, and Magnesia.</summary>

## PHILOSOPHICAL MATTERS.

Take away from them the aforementioned splendor, and then the earth will be of little importance.

No unclean body enters into our mastery (except for one) which is commonly called the <term>Green Lion</term> <note>A symbolic name for a potent raw material or solvent, often associated with vitriol or antimony, used to "devour" and transform metals.</note> by Philosophers; this is the medium for joining the tinctures between the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> with perfection.

Both material and formal principles must be dissolved; otherwise, they would be of little importance.

I tell you that you must know these <term>solvents</term> <note>original: "menstrua" — the transformative liquids used to break down substances.</note>, without which neither true calcination nor natural dissolution can take place.

This stone is the potential vapor of metal; you must be cautious in how you acquire it.

This Solvent is truly invisible, although with the second philosophical water, through the separation of the elements, it <margin>appears</margin> in the form of clear water, it appears <unclear>apparent</unclear> <note>Ink blot obscures the end of the word; marginal note suggests "apparet" or appears.</note>. And from this Solvent, with labor brought to fruition, the "sulfur of nature" can be made with it, if it is circulated into a pure spirit. Then with it, you will be able to dissolve your base or mass in various ways.

An oil is extracted from there of a golden color, or similar to it, from our subtle **red lead**. For Raymond <note>Raymond Lull, a famous medieval philosopher and alchemist.</note>, when he was close to death, made <term>potable gold</term> <note>A medicinal elixir made of dissolved gold, believed to grant longevity.</note> from it, which revived him.

This potable gold, or oil, very quickly "kills" <note>In alchemy, to "kill" Mercury usually means to "fix" it, changing it from a liquid, volatile state to a solid, stable one.</note> crude Mercury when it is cast upon it, and that Mercury tints all bodies into the perfect **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note> with a stable tincture. In this way, govern both bases, the red and the white.

<margin>1.</margin> **Calcination** is the purging of our stone, restoring it by its own natural heat, and bringing about the dissolution that is first necessary for our stone.

For our stone is not calcined by corrosives, nor by fire alone, nor by "burning waters" <note>Strong acids like nitric acid.</note>, nor by the vapor of lead; for by this kind of calcination, the bodies are destroyed, and they diminish the moisture of our stone.

In our calcination, we multiply the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential, life-giving fluid or "sap" found within all matter.</note>; for like has a desirable inclination for its own kind; he who does not know this is blind in the science.

Join like with like, and species with species, as is right; for every seed responds to its own seed.

Every Spirit is fixed with the "ashes" <note>original: "calcibus" — the powder resulting from calcination.</note> of its own kind.

Philosophers make an oily "lime," both white and red.

### AXIOMS

...red, of three degrees, before our base is perfected, liquid as wax; otherwise, it is of no use.

For we allow a year for our expectation; for in a shorter space of time, our <term>calx</term> <note>The fine powder or ash resulting from the calcination (intense heating) of a substance.</note> cannot be prepared.

If your water is equal in proportion with the earth, under measured heat, from these emerges a new sprout, at once white and red, which will endure in the fire forever.

Make a trinity of unity without discord; this is the most certain and best proportion.

The smaller the spiritual part, the easier the dissolution will be, rather than if you were to submerge the earth in too much water, which destroys the whole work.

Always carry this in your heart: that your earth must never be suffocated by the water.

Do not seek the thing in a substance where it does not exist—such as in eggs, blood, wine, <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfate minerals; the author warns here against "vulgar" alchemy that uses common chemicals instead of metallic "seeds."</note>, or in intermediate minerals.

There is no profit in non-metallic things.

In metals, from metals, and through metals, perfect metals are made.

First of all, perform a rotation of your elements, and turn the earth into water before everything else. Then from the water make air, and lead the air back into fire. Once this is finished, lead your earth back again; otherwise, you labor in vain.

Our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> has almost infinite names: for it is named after every thing that is black in appearance. When it is bright, it has names of delight, following white things as well as red, and yet in the end, it is but one thing.

<margin>a. 2.</margin> By the power of our first <term>Solvent</term> <note>original: "Menstruum" — a transformative liquid catalyst.</note>, clear and bright, in which our bodies suffer an <term>eclipse</term> <note>original: "Ecclipsin" — a symbolic term for the 'nigredo' or blackening stage where the metal's form is destroyed.</note>, and from their hard and dry compositions, they are made subtle and return to their first matter.

Nothing is here except for Sister and Brother—that is, the active and the passive—where <term>Sulfur</term> and <term>Mercury</term> <note>The two primary principles of alchemy: Sulfur (the hot, dry, masculine seed) and Mercury (the cold, moist, feminine solvent).</note> are generated as co-essential parts.

The dissolution of one corporeal part causes the congealing of the other spiritual part.

When the earth is reduced entirely to ash, then it is congealed water; understand this. When the body is altered from its first form, a new form is immediately introduced.

Nothing in the nature of things is stripped of all form.

Every metal was once a mineral water. For this reason, all things are reduced into water by means of water, in which water...

# PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS.

...delight. There are naturally four qualities resisting each other with diversity <note>Referring to the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>.

In one glass vessel all things must be done, similar in shape to an egg and well closed.

Never allow your glass to be hotter than you can bear with a bare hand for as long as you like, during the time of dissolution.

Beware that you neither open nor move this glass ever, from the beginning until the end; if you do otherwise, you will never complete your work.

<margin>3</margin>
Dry out the earth until it is thirsty by <term>calcining</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or achieve oxidation.</note>; otherwise, you labor in vain.

Divide the matter into two parts, so that you separate the subtle from the gross, until the earth remains at the bottom with a leaden color.

The other part is spiritual and volatile, but all those things must be converted into one single thing.

<margin>Lead</margin>
**THE WATER**, with which you must revive the stone: see that you distill it by itself many times before you work with it. You will be able to recognize by sight alone when it is purged of dreggy dross, which some are able to multiply with <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturno" — the alchemical name for lead.</note> and other substances which we reject.

Distill it until it is clean and thin as water, with a shining, leaden-blue color, retaining at once its form and weightiness. With this, <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note> moistened his tree within his glass, and made flowers grow upward on high.

For then it is a true <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "theriaca" — historically a "universal" medicinal paste or antidote against poison.</note>, most effective for expelling poisons, and it shows certain wonders in its work, snatching many from death and preserving them for life. Wherefore, do not mix it with corrosives.

<margin>Wind 4</margin>
Hermes called it his "wind," because of its swift flight from the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles.</note>, the husband and wife, soon making our stone volatile with it, returning the dead to life, and imparting life to the Sun and Moon, the husband and wife.

Therefore, first divide what nature had previously bound, converting the essential Mercury into wind; without which natural and subtle separation, the generation will never be profitably completed.

The water must be <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process where a solid turns into gas and back to solid, used here to describe purifying the liquid essence.</note> seven times, otherwise no dissolution will naturally occur, nor will you see any <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage where the matter turns black and "dies" before being reborn.</note> like liquid pitch, nor will the colors appear, due to a lack of the fire working in your glass.

<margin>4 types of fire</margin>
There are four kinds of fires which you must know: Natural, Unnatural, Contrary to Nature, and Elemental (which ignites wood). We use these fires and no others.

-># AXIOMS<-

<margin><image-desc>A hand-drawn curly bracket spans the first three paragraphs of the text.</image-desc></margin>
The fire of Nature is present in all things, and it is the third solvent <note>original: "menstruum" — in alchemy, a solvent or liquid medium used to dissolve solids.</note>. The unnatural fire is called "circumstantial," and it is the fire of ashes and baths used for the purpose of putrefying; without these, you will bring nothing to the stage of decay.

Fire against Nature must torture the bodies; it is the dragon that burns violently, like the fire of hell.

Therefore, create a fire inside your glass which burns the bodies more effectively than elemental fire.

### On Conjunction.

Conjunction is the joining of separated qualities, or the balancing of principles.

He who cannot separate the Elements and divide them wanders from the path.

Divide the Soul from the Body; the soul will cause a perpetual union.

<margin><image-desc>A small curly bracket marks the beginning of this paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
The Male—that is, our Sun—must have three parts, and his wife nine; then like will always rejoice with like <note>This refers to the specific proportions of the "male" (Solar/Sulphur) and "female" (Lunar/Mercury) principles required for a successful reaction.</note>.

One hundred and fifty days are required in putrefaction until the stage of whiteness <note>original: "albedinem" — the Albedo, the second major stage of the Great Work signifying purification.</note>, which looks like the eyes of fish.

Without doubt, solution and connection are the two principles of this arduous science, although there are many other principles.

### On Putrefaction.

This is the destruction of the bodies; keep the matter for such a time in a bath or in our "dung" <note>A "dung bath" (fimus equinus) provided a gentle, steady heat via composting organic matter.</note> until ninety nights have passed; preserve this diligently in moist heat. Soon after, blackness will be your indicator that the matter is hastening toward putrefaction.

For at that time, it will swell and bubble like liquid pitch; colors will appear like those of a rainbow, most beautiful to behold, and then the Water begins to turn entirely white.

In moist bodies, the action of tempered heat produces blackness; once you have achieved this, you have nothing to fear. For in this way, the germination of our stone follows, and as soon as thirty days have passed, you will have the "Grapes." This is our <term>Adrop</term> <note>A term for the philosophical lead or the raw body of the stone.</note>, <term>Uzifur</term> <note>Likely a variation of cinnabar or a prepared red mercury.</note>, and red lead.

Defend your glass from violent heat and sudden cold; use only moderate fire, and beware of <term>vitrification</term> <note>The process where the matter turns into useless glass or slag due to excessive heat.</note>.

Pay attention to what material you choose for yourself; do not mix in salts, sulphurs, nor intermediate minerals. For whatever the <term>sophist</term> <note>A derogatory term for fraudulent alchemists who used false materials or logic.</note> may chatter about, our Sulphur and Mercury are found in Metals only.

->PHILOSOPHICAL MATTERS.<-

If God should grant you this knowledge through any medium, do not reveal it to anyone who asks, neither for favor nor for any price. Do not be an oppressor, a fornicator, or impudent, but serve God, and let the poor be your concern.

### ON COAGULATION.

Congelation <note>original: "congelatio" — here used interchangeably with coagulation, the process of turning a liquid or "spirituous" substance into a stable solid.</note> is the hardening of soft things in white heat and the fixing <note>original: "confixatio" — the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> of volatile spirits.

The elements are immediately transformed, but our coagulation is not so: that which is coagulated does not melt into water in the air; otherwise, our work would be destroyed.

When the Matter has been made white <note>Referring to the Albedo, the stage of purification.</note>, then the Spirit will be coagulated with the bodies. You must still wait for a long period before such a coagulation appears to you in the likeness of pearls.

The cause of all these things is a most temperate heat, operating and moving the matter continually.

Believe me, all your labor is lost unless your earth is revived by water; you will never see true Coagulation.

Water is the secret from the life of all things existing in the whole world; individual things have their beginning from water, as can be seen in women giving birth, from whom water first flows before the birth, not without great pains.

The substance is nourished by its own proper solvent <note>original: "menstruo" — in alchemy, a 'menstruum' is a solvent or nutritive liquid medium, not biological menstruation.</note> which Water and Earth alone have produced, the color of which is green in its natural appearance.

Understand now that our fiery Water, thus sharpened, is called the Menstrual water, in which our earth is dissolved and naturally calcined <note>original: "calcinata" — reduced to a powder through heat or chemical action.</note> through coagulation: so that they can never be divided.

When you have performed seven imbibitions <note>original: "imbibitiones" — the process of repeatedly adding liquid to a dry substance and letting it soak in to "nourish" it.</note>, then you must again revolve and putrefy all that matter without any addition, first watching for the blackness <note>original: "nigredinem" — the Nigredo stage, representing death and decay.</note>, then coagulate the whole into whiteness: then you have brought the base to its end; and afterward, through the middle, ascend into redness <note>original: "rubedinem" — the Rubedo, the final stage of the Great Work representing perfection and the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

Thus your water is divided into two parts; with the first part, the bodies are purified. The second part is destined for the imbibitions, with which the matter is afterward blackened and immediately whitened over a light fire; then reduce it to Redness.

### ON FEEDING.

Feeding <note>original: "Cibatio" — the metaphorical "feeding" of the alchemical substance to give it strength and volume.</note> is the name for the nutrition of our dry matter, with milk and food given moderately to both, until it is reduced to the third order. Never give it so much that you suffocate it, lest the watery humors...

...surpass the blood: for if it drinks too much, vomiting must be provoked, otherwise it will be sick for a long time. <note>In alchemical "cibation," the matter is "fed" with liquid; "vomiting" refers to the removal of excess moisture to prevent the work from becoming waterlogged or "sick."</note>
You shall turn your wheel <note>original: "rotam" — likely referring to the "Wheel of the Philosophers," a metaphorical representation of the repeating cycles of distillation and condensation.</note> three times, observing the rule of the aforementioned nourishment, and then, as soon as it feels the fire, it will melt as quickly as wax.

### ON SUBLIMATION.

Do not sublime <note>original: "sublimes" — the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again at the top of the vessel.</note> to the very top of the vessel: for without force, you will not be able to drive it back down to the bottom.
Maintain a temperate heat from below for the space of forty days, until the matter is black and dark. <note>This refers to the "Nigredo" or blackening stage, associated with putrefaction and the death of the old form.</note>
While the bodies are putrefying, they are sublimed more and more, until they have all been raised into water.
We perform sublimation for three reasons: the first is so that the body might become spiritual; second, so that the spirit might become corporeal, and be fixed with the body, and become of the same substance. The third reason is so that it may be purged of its original impurity, and its sulfurous saltiness <note>original: "salcedo sulphurea" — a technical term for the impurities or "burning" qualities of sulfur that must be cleansed.</note> in which it is infected might be diminished; then they are sublimed on high, whiter than snow.

### ON FERMENTATION.

Fermentations are performed in various ways, through which our medicine is made perpetual.
Into clear water, some dissolve the Sun <note>original: "Solem" — Alchemical code for Gold.</note> and the Moon <note>original: "lunam" — Alchemical code for Silver.</note>, and with their medicine, they cause them to coagulate; such fermentation is not our purpose.
Our entire intention is this: that you first grind the matter down before you ferment it.
Fix <note>To "fix" a substance is to make it resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates.</note> your water and earth together immediately, and when your medicine flows like wax, then see to it (as mentioned above) that you cast it upon amalgams. And when all that is mixed together within your well-closed glass, apply the fire until the whole is fixed; then perform the projection <note>original: "proiectionem" — the final stage of the Great Work where the philosopher's stone is thrown onto a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note> as you please, because it is then a completely perfect medicine; in this way you shall make your ferment, both red and white.
True fermentation is the incorporation of the soul with the body, restoring to it its natural and proper odor and color through the natural thickening of the separated things.

<image-desc>A large decorative curly bracket on the left margin encompasses the next paragraph starting with "For just as the magnet".</image-desc>
For just as the magnet draws iron to itself, so our earth by Nature draws its soul down to itself, which had been raised up with the wind.
For the earth is undoubtedly the ferment of the water: and in turn, the water is the ferment of the earth.

PHILOSOPHICA.
II 2
<meta>catchword: Cooperi</meta>

We make a most fragrant water, with which we reduce all bodies into oil, and with this we make our medicine flowing. We call this water the **Quintessence** <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence," a pure, spiritualized substance extracted from matter through distillation</term>, and it heals all the ailments of men: therefore, make Oil from the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: "Sole & Luna" — Alchemical code for gold and silver</note>, which is a most fragrant fermentation.

### ON EXALTATION.

**Exaltation** <term>Exaltation: An alchemical process that increases the power or "dignity" of a substance, often through repeated refinement</term> differs little from sublimation, if you understand the words of the Philosophers.

If, therefore, you wish to **exalt** your bodies, first sublime them with the **Spirit of life**, until the earth is well refined through the natural rectification of all the Elements. Then they will be much more precious than gold, because of the quintessence which they retain.

When cold overcomes heat, then air is converted into water, and thus two contraries meet together until each agrees rightly with the other.

In this way, therefore, cause each thing to be circulated into the other, quickly **exalting** them; let all these things be performed in a single, well-sealed glass vessel, and **not by hands** <note>This implies the process happens naturally through the action of heat within the sealed vessel, rather than by manual manipulation</note>.

Convert water into earth, which is immediately the nest of the other Elements: for earth is in fire, which rests in air. You must begin this circulation in the west, then toward the south, until they are exalted.

### ON MULTIPLICATION.

**Multiplication** is the thing that causes the increase of the medicine in color, odor, power, and quantity: for it is a fire which, once kindled, never dies but always lives with you, one spark of which can kindle more fire in multiplied power.

Rich is he who possesses a small piece of our **Elixir**, because it can be increased infinitely in one way: if you dissolve our dry powder and perform frequent coagulations of these, you will achieve an increase. Thus you can multiply it so that it grows in the glass in the manner of a tree, which **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many alchemical foundational texts were attributed</note> calls a tree most beautiful to behold. One grain of this is multiplied into a thousand, if you wisely know how to perform your **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of the Great Work, where the perfected alchemical medicine is cast upon base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term>.

Just as powdered **Saffron** <note>original: "Crocus"</note> is gradually tempered with liquid, and afterwards a greater quantity of liquid is added, it tints much more liquid in quantity than if it were whole in its gross substance. So our **Elixir**, the thinner it is made, the more widely it will spread its **tincture** <term>Tincture: The soul or coloring power of the alchemical stone that allows it to transform other substances</term>.

Cover your fire in the evening as well as the morning, so that you do not need to search door-to-door among your neighbors to borrow it from them; the longer you retain it, the more you will gain. ## ON PROJECTION.

If the **tincture** <term>Tincture: A potent substance, often the final form of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transforming base metals</term> is true and stable, you will test it with a small quantity of the medicine on metal or **Mercury**; like pitch, it will adhere and tinge in the **projection** <term>Projection: The final step of the alchemical process where the Stone is cast upon base metals to achieve transmutation</term> so that it sustains all fire. But many have destroyed their work through ignorance when they perform the projection upon an impure metal.
   See that you cast your Medicine upon your **ferment** <term>Ferment: A substance, usually pure gold or silver, added to the "Stone" to determine its final direction toward becoming gold or silver</term>; then that ferment will be breakable like glass. Cast that brittleness upon cleansed bodies; then you will have Metal proven by every judgment.

->BLESSED BE THE ETERNAL GOD, AMEN.<-

## RECAPITULATION.

Pay close attention to the breadth of our **stone** <note>original: "lapidis" — the Philosopher's Stone</note>, and begin in the West, where the **red male** and the **white spouse** <note>original: "mas rubens & coniux alba" — symbolic representations of Sulfur and Mercury, or the active and passive principles of the work</note> shall become one, wedded by the **spirit of life**, so that they may live in love and peace.
   Earth and water should be equally proportioned: one part of earth for three of spirit is also a good proportion, which is twelve parts of spirit for four parts of earth or body. You should take three parts of the female and one of the male.
   And the less there is of the spirit in this wedding, the more quickly you will complete your **calcination** <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter and reduce it to a fine powder</term>.
   By which means you will dissolve, divide, and rot <note>original: "putrefacies" — referring to the stage of Putrefaction, often called the "crow's head," where the matter turns black</note> the perfectly calcined bodies. All the secrets of our other, **lower Astronomy** <note>original: "infimæ Astronomiæ" — a common metaphor for alchemy, suggesting the laboratory work mirrors the celestial movements of the stars</note>, with perfect understanding of all the poles shining in our sky with inexplicable colors—finer than have ever been seen—will appear before the **perfect white**.
   And after the perfect white, there will appear the **Citrine** <note>A yellow or golden-yellow color</note> and the **false citrine**, and afterward the unchangeable **red blood** will appear. Then you have a medicine of the third order, capable of being multiplied in its own kind.
   But you must not be ignorant of this secret: our **red male** does not tinge, nor does his **spouse**, until they are themselves tinged.

II 3

If you wish to prepare the matter for yourself through this art, hide the *height* of your bodies and reveal their *depth* <note>original: "altitudinem... abſconde, & patefac eorū profunditatem." This is a fundamental alchemical maxim: to internalize the external qualities and externalize the internal ones</note>; destroy the first quality of all your materials, and separate the second, more excellent qualities from them as quickly as possible. In a single glass vessel, under a single regimen, convert the four natures into one.

You must divide your **red Elixir** into parts before you complete the reddening process; place these portions into two separate glasses.

If you desire to possess the double Elixir of the **Sun** <term>Sol/Sun: Alchemy's name for Gold</term> and **Moon** <term>Luna/Moon: Alchemy's name for Silver</term>, proceed thus: multiply it immediately with **Mercury** into a great quantity. Even if you only have a spoonful at the start, you can multiply it into both the white and the red forms simultaneously, even if you were to live a thousand years. Convert this into a perfect oil through the process of circulation, as is our intent. These oils will then *fix* <note>Fixation: The process of turning a volatile, liquid, or "spiritual" substance into a stable solid that can withstand the heat of a furnace</note> crude Mercury into perfect Gold and Silver.

**Raymond Lull** <note>Raymundus Lullus (c. 1232–1316), a major philosopher and purported alchemist whose works emphasize the use of "alphabets" and "circles" of elements</note> called this fixed and pure oily substance his **Basilisk** <term>Basilisk: Usually a deadly mythical serpent; here, Lull uses it to describe a substance so potent and penetrating that it "slays" the base nature of metals to transform them</term>. He never provided a clearer explanation of it than this.

Remember that man is the noblest creature in all of earthly composition that God ever created. Within him, a neutral **mercurial essence**—composed of the four Elements proportioned by nature—is produced by Art from its own "mine" <note>In alchemical philosophy, the "mine" or "mineral" of man refers to the human body or soul as the source of the ultimate spiritual Stone</note>, and it costs absolutely nothing.

For our **Metals** are nothing other than our two minerals—namely, the Gold and Silver—as Raymond wisely notes: the splendor of the Moon and the light of the Sun. Secrets descend into these two minerals, even though their splendor is hidden from your sight. Through Art, you can cause this splendor to appear clearly.

Purify this **hidden stone**, this "One Thing." Wash it in its own liquor until it becomes white; then, ferment it wisely, and you shall possess the sum of the entire Work.

### OTHER AXIOMS OF PHILOSOPHY FOLLOW.

**Albertus Magnus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, renowned for his vast knowledge of natural philosophy and minerals</note> says in his *Book of Minerals* that Gold is found everywhere. This is because there is no elemental thing—composed of the four Elements—in which Gold is not naturally found in its final refinement. Therefore, he says that the matter of the **Stone** is found everywhere.

<header>AXIOMS</header>

Likewise, he states and proves that the greatest **mineral virtue** <term>mineral virtue: the innate power or essence within a substance that allows it to grow or transform into a mineral state</term> exists in every human being, and especially in the head among the teeth; just as in his time, gold was found in small, oblong grains <note>This likely refers to historical accounts of "golden teeth" or dental anomalies interpreted as alchemical proof that the human body can generate minerals</note>. This could not happen unless that mineral virtue was present in man. This mineral virtue is found in our elixir, and for this reason, it is said that the **Stone** is in every person.

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note> possessed three parts of the philosophy of the whole world, which he revealed as the **mineral**, **vegetable**, and **animal** parts. These three parts are contained in one stone—namely, in **Mercury**—that is, under the name of "Mercury." This is because everything from which the Stone is made, whether it be mineral, vegetable, or animal, is called by the name of "Mercury" <note>In this context, "Mercury" refers to the universal "First Matter" rather than the common liquid metal</note>.

If the Stone could not be made from all things, then what **Alfidius** <note>An Arabic alchemical authority, often cited in medieval Latin texts</note> says would not be true; for he says that there are many things which dissolve and congeal. And **Ortulanus** <note>A 14th-century commentator on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes</note> says that the Philosophers call "the Stone" anything from which the four elements can be separated by our alchemical art. Since the elements can be separated from any vegetable or animal substance by our alchemical art, it follows that a **physical Stone** <gloss>the Stone of the Philosophers</gloss> can be made from any vegetable or animal source.

<margin>Example.</margin>
We see, for instance, that if we extract water from **Wormwood** <note>original: "Absynthio"</note>, and if a fiery heat extracts it suddenly, the watery moisture is pulled out and the burnt parts of the earth remain. However, if we proceed with a moderate heat—which is similar to natural heat—only the **vital moisture** <gloss>the life-force or essential oil</gloss> is extracted, and thus the remaining parts will be perfectly cooked, with no rawness remaining.

Metals are made of earth and water; whatever things melt in a fire through a strong mixture, the water is converted into a certain kind of burnt earth which contains within itself some substance of **salt** or **alum**. For this reason, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy</note> says at the beginning of his *Testament*: "A salt can be made from every burnt thing." This salt, which is hidden in such burnt earth, is the most remote principle of all metals; it is commonly called **vitriol** <term>vitriol: a sulfate mineral, often seen as a key "green" starting material for alchemical work</term>, and that is the mineral medium and the proper seed for generating all metals.

Metals can be transmuted into one another because they are natural things and their matter is the same. Hermes proposed a "circulation" in metals, just as there is in the Elements. For one metal is converted into another through its own decay or breakdown.

<margin>Note.</margin>
**Rhazes** <note>Rafis: Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist</note> says in the *Book of Divinity*: "Know that the things of Nature are so bound together by subtle craftsmanship that in any one thing, every other thing exists in **potentiality**, even if it is not seen in **act**." <note>original: "in qualibet re, est res quælibet in potentia, quamuis actu non videatur." This is the core alchemical doctrine of "all is in all," suggesting any substance can be transformed into any other because they share a hidden essence</note>

<meta>This page continues the practical instructions for the creation of the Elixir, shifting from the theoretical definitions of "Mercury" on the previous page to specific laboratory procedures involving distillation and putrefaction. # PHILOSOPHICA. 135

Take the honored stone <note>original: "lapidem honoratum"</note> and place it into a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a distillation apparatus</term>, and cover it with an **alembic** <term>alembic: the cooling cap or "still-head" that sits atop the cucurbit to condense vapors</term> and seal it perfectly. Afterwards, place it in very hot manure; then you shall distill it, placing a receiver beneath it into which the water may be distilled. Leave it thus until all the water is distilled and the moisture is dried up, so that dryness prevails over it. Then, extract the dry substance and save the water that distilled from it until you need it. Take the dry body that remained in the bottom of the cucurbit and grind it; place it in a suitable vessel, according to the quantity of the material, into horse manure. Bury the well-closed vessel there for forty days, renewing the manure so it does not grow cold <note>In the pre-modern laboratory, fermenting horse manure provided a gentle, steady, and "natural" heat source for long-term chemical reactions</note>. The medicine will dissolve within itself and become a thick white water. When you see it thus, determine its weight and add half that weight of the water you reserved. Close the vessel well. Then the medicine will be congealed in the same number of days in which it was previously dissolved.

In the Elixir, the water is the soul of the stone, and the power of the water is the spirit of the stone, because sometimes the water itself is called the Stone.

We see in nature that one thing generates many others like itself; in the same way, through art, the **sun** <note>original: "sol." In alchemical texts, "Sun" almost always refers to gold</note> generates the sun.

Composition in this mastery <term>mastery: the "Magisterium" or the Great Work of alchemy</term> is the union or marriage of the congealed spirit with the dissolved body; their union and their passion <note>original: "passio," referring to the undergoing of a process or transformation</note> occurs over the fire.

For heat is its nourishment, and the soul will not leave the body, nor is it joined with it in a total union, except through the mutation of both from their own power and property, and after the mutation of their natures. And this is **solution** and **congelation** <term>solution and congelation: the fundamental alchemical cycle of "solve et coagula," or dissolving a solid and then re-solidifying it to achieve a higher state of purity</term>.

And know that the sages have long hidden this solution and congelation.

Were it not for composition, no thing would be produced into being; and division is the separating of the parts of the compound, and thus separation was its union.

And I say that the spirit will not dwell in the body, nor will it be within it, nor will it remain with it in any way, until the body itself attains the same subtlety and thinness that the spirit possesses.

And when it has been thinned and made subtle, and has moved from its density and thickness to thinness—from grossness and bodiliness to spirituality—it will then mix with the subtle spirits and be soaked into them. Thus, both will turn out to be one and the same, and they shall not be separated, just as water mixed with water cannot be parted.

# AXIOMS
<page-num>136</page-num>

->**A X I O M A T A**<-

It is well-established that the matter for the procreation of both perfect and imperfect [metals] is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and **sulfur**, and without these two, no new transmutation can occur.

Therefore, it is a wonder that any wise man would fix his intentions upon animals or vegetables, which are very far removed [from the nature of metals], since nearby minerals are found in plenty. Nor should it be believed that any of the philosophers placed the Art in the aforementioned remote things except metaphorically <note>original: "similitudinarie"</note>; and thus, by right, we must accept quicksilver and sulfur as the material of the Stone. Neither **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> nor sulfur alone generates any metal; rather, from the mixing of both, various metals and many minerals are procreated in different ways.

Therefore, our chosen matter consists of the mixture of both. However, our final secret is most deeply hidden: from which mineral substance it ought to be most nearly and closely made. We are bound to seek out and choose this very thing with great care.

Suppose, then, that our material was chosen first from **vegetables**, such as herbs, trees, or everything that rises from the earth. Then it would first be necessary to produce quicksilver and sulfur from them by **decoction** <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance in liquid to extract its essence or chemical components</term>, a labor from which we are excused, since Nature already offers us quicksilver and sulfur [directly].

And if we were to choose from **animals**, such as human blood, hair, urine, excrement, chicken eggs, and all things that proceed from animals, it would [likewise] be necessary to produce quicksilver from them.

I do not deny that metals can be purified or dissolved with **semi-minerals** <term>semi-minerals: substances like arsenic or antimony that possess some, but not all, properties of metals</term>, and a **sophisticated** <note>In alchemy, "sophisticated" usually means a deceptive or artificial appearance rather than a true essential change</note> form introduced through them, so that men might be led into error.

The blackness or impurity of **lead** can also be wiped away; nevertheless, lead will always be lead, even if other qualities are introduced so that it might appear to be silver.

Every metallic body is known to clearly contain sulfur and Mercury within itself. When it melts by means of heat, the substance of Mercury appears, and the sulfur appears especially in the color and the red "skin" floating on top. But the property of one nature is the adherence of the other, since one cannot generate a metal without the other. And the more **simple** <note>In this context, "simple" means pure, refined, or stripped of external impurities</note> the sulfur becomes, the more it rejoices and clings to simple and clean Mercury, so that one is more strongly joined with the other.

The works of nature and art are the same in essence: they differ only in form: because the works of nature are invisible and hidden.

## CHEMICAL PHYSICS

->according to Trithemius.<- <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German Benedictine abbot, polymath, and occultist whose writings deeply influenced later alchemical thought.</note>

It is certain that in all things produced by nature, both superior and inferior virtues are present.

Artificial corruption <note>original: "corruptio"; in alchemy, this refers to the necessary breakdown or "death" of a substance—often through heat or fermentation—before it can be purified and reborn.</note> is necessary for the separation of the spirits, so that they may live more splendidly once reunited, and communicate a better life to others.

The goal of the Hermetic doctrine <note>The tradition of alchemy and philosophy attributed to the mythical figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note> is a certain universal medicine, which takes away without distinction not only the [impurities] of inanimate bodies, but also all corruptions and diseases of men.

Our bodies are able to die voluntarily while the natural life remains, and our spirits or souls are drawn away from their bodies intellectually and above nature, without the physical bond being dissolved; and this is done by thinking deeply, meditating, looking down upon earthly things, and contemplating heavenly things.

Most prophetic, natural, spagyric <term>spagyric: the alchemical process of separating a substance into its components and then recombining them in a purified state</term>, and poetic secrets are almost all hidden.

We see everywhere in nature that God has willed to do this in all things: namely, to cover the precious beneath the vile, so that it might not be snatched away by the unworthy.

How much gold do cheap sand and despised stones veil from the eyes looking at them—[stones] which the hand of the ignorant casts away, and the unknowing foot tramples.

How secretly He has enriched barren regions with unknown wealth on the surface, which He denied to fertile lands.

Within physical bodies there is a certain hidden, incorruptible truth or virtue; that will be the true medicine, if only it is freed from its shackles and from the foul prison in which it is held.

It is certain and most certain that any compound <term>elementatum: a physical object or body composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water)</term> contains something else within itself than the Elements [alone], which is indeed known to very few, but certain to the fewest.

Every soul is a participant in a certain more sublime essence.

The heaven and these inferior Elements are of one and the same substance, and do not differ except by accident <note>original: "per accidens"; in philosophy, an 'accident' is a quality like color or weight that is not essential to the core nature of a substance.</note>, such as corruptible and incorruptible, pure and impure, active and passive, heavy and light, clear and opaque; from which [it follows] all these things are accidents and not substances.

# AXIOMS

For it is the nature of substances to generate, and not of accidents. <note>In traditional philosophy, a "substance" is the essential nature of a thing, while "accidents" are its non-essential properties like color or weight. This axiom suggests that true transformation must occur at the essential level.</note>

It is impossible for any mortal to understand this art unless they are first illuminated by divine light.

The more a medicine tends toward unity, the more it approaches life, departing far from death. <note>This refers to the "Universal Medicine" or Elixir, which seeks to harmonize all conflicting elements into a single, perfect state.</note>

There is one God and not many: he willed to first create one world through the One out of nothing in his mind, and thereafter to bring it into effect: so that all things he created would be contained within it: so that God might be one in all things.

Every thing has its being from God, and is born from nature, which itself received its being from nothing by the Word of God.

He teaches that there is a single most general genus of created things, from which the remaining genera, species, and individuals are born, and are propagated day by day until the end of the age; this thing is the Primitive Nature created by God.

The natural bodies of inanimate things, once divided and purified from their own spirits, can be joined to them again for their resurrection—that is, their perfection—in the hope of our own future resurrection. <note>The alchemical process of purifying and reuniting substances was often seen as a physical ritual mirroring the Christian hope for the resurrection of the body.</note>

There are, therefore, these three things for natural life: the spirit as the mover, the soul as the motion itself, and the body as the thing moved; when joined together, they produce a single natural entity.

The three primary principles of all things are Form, Light (or the life of nature), and Matter.

The Chemical Chaos <note>original: "Chaos Chemicum"; this is the *Prima Materia* or First Matter, the raw, undifferentiated "womb" of the universe containing all potentiality.</note> is a universal thing, enclosing within itself everything we work upon; from its belly the ingenious craftsman must draw out his matter, form, Heaven, and the Elements, so that he may compose medicines from them.

Spagyric matter <term>spagyric: the alchemical art of separating a substance into its components and then recombining the purest parts.</term> is called the first and universal matter, or Mercury moving toward growth, extracting the first particular matter of form from the creator. <note>original: "Mercurius"; in alchemy, "Mercury" is not just the liquid metal, but the philosophical principle of fluidity, spirit, and the medium of transformation.</note>

The form of things is the generative power by which each thing can produce something like itself; just as the form of a man lies hidden in a man and not in another, the form of a tree in a tree, and likewise the form of a metal in a metal.

Raw things must not enter the work, but must be emptied through sublimation <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then recollected as a purified solid on the sides of a vessel.</note> toward the sides of the sublimatory vessel, so that it may be free from its own empty and superfluous earth. Only then is it the form of the Stone, and not before, and it is called the Sulfur of Nature. <note>original: "sulphur Naturae"; "Sulfur" here represents the active, fiery, and stabilizing "soul" of the substance being refined.</note>

Heaven is our Mercury, of a heavenly color on account of its incorruptibili- <meta>catchword: ptibili- (continuing to "incorruptibilitatem" or "incorruptibility" on the next page)</meta>

### COMPENDIUM OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and scholar. In the later Middle Ages and Renaissance, many alchemical texts were attributed to him, focusing on how nature "ripens" metals in the earth.</note>, regarding the *origin and matter of metals, upon which the <term>Spagyric</term> <note>term: Spagyric (from the Greek words for "to separate" and "to combine"); it refers to alchemical pharmacy where plants or minerals are broken down to their purest elements and then reunited.</note> founds his radical principles.*

The principal matter of all metals in their mines, from which they are caused, is "dry water," which we call living water or **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum* (mercury)</note>, and a "stinking spirit" which we otherwise call **sulfur**: yet not in their nature as they are created in their mines, for in the places where they are generated, no metal is found; rather, this matter is a certain substance created by nature, having within itself the nature and substance of those two. 

And from such matter or substance procreated from these aforementioned things, a certain subtle, smoky substance is generated and created in the bowels of the earth and the mineral veins, where they are gathered and held.

And thereafter, a natural power coming upon that smoky matter congeals it, and unites itself with it in an inseparable and firm union through natural **decoction** <note>original: *decoctio*; the process of "cooking" or ripening through steady heat, which alchemists believed happened naturally inside the earth over centuries.</note>.

From these things it is clear that the four elements are naturally within metals, and that they are homogeneous, because they are nothing other than the most subtle smokes, congealed and fixed in their mines by natural decoction, and converted into the nature of metal.

<header>AXIOMS</header>

Likewise, it is clear that the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humidum radicale*; the essential, life-sustaining fluid thought to exist within all matter</note> of metals is consumed within them during their **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to ash or powder</note> because of the homogeneity and strong union of the elements with one another; it is not separated out as the moisture of a stone is separated, because in metals, the moisture is unified with the dry principle in the greater part of both.

->**A wonderful way of nature in the generation of metals.**<-

There is a certain uniform matter in the mines—namely, **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> and **sulfur**—contained in a single body. From this matter, nature causes that smoky substance or subtle matter to emerge, which, by the benefit of nature, is converted into metal. That smoky matter is a certain body. And that smoky substance generated from it is a certain spirit. Thus, nature makes a **spirit** out of a **body**; and so it causes it to ascend from the earth into the heaven—that is, it makes a bodily thing spiritual—and afterwards, by circulating, it makes the spiritual thing bodily, and thus it descends from the heaven into the earth.

Likewise, it is clear: that all metals, as far as the root of nature is concerned, are of the same substance or matter; and yet they are not of the same form. This is due to the weakness or health, the cleanliness or uncleanness, and the scarcity or quantity of the substance of quicksilver and sulfur in their natural union and conjunction; it is also due to the nature of different mines and the long or short **decoction** <note>A "cooking" or ripening process in the earth's heat</note> of nature itself.

<margin>Note.</margin>
There is a certain smoky and most subtle matter or proper substance of quicksilver and sulfur, generated by our craftsmanship <note>meaning the alchemical art</note> from the nature of the two aforementioned things; it is most limpid and clear, like a tear, and within it lies and dwells the spirit of the **fifth essence** <note>original: *quinta essentia* or quintessence; the purest, most refined element that transcends the four physical elements</note>, as we shall say below. Yet, this substance is not sulfur itself, nor is it quicksilver itself as they exist in their own nature in the mines; rather, it is a certain part of those two which is neither quicksilver nor sulfur.

Certain Philosophers say that this matter is generated from quicksilver alone without the admixture of sulfur; but this amounts to the same thing, because quicksilver naturally contains red sulfur mixed within it. We have separated this red sulfur from its whiteness with our own hands, and we have seen it.

In no way can the aforementioned smoky substance be naturally drawn out except from the substances of the two aforementioned things—quicksilver and sulfur—joined together. Earth and air are the **passive elements** <note>original: *patientia*; those that receive action</note>; Water and fire are the **active elements** <note>original: *agentia*; those that exert force</note>. **Water** is the male, and **earth** is the female.

Likewise, note that by causing the aforementioned smoky [matter] to be generated...

...matter from the substances of the aforementioned two, **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurij viui*; quicksilver</note> and **sulfur**, and their adjuncts: because the said substance is joined in a certain way to the body from which that smoky substance exits. For the artisan causes a certain material or bodily substance to ascend from the earth into the heaven, turning it into a spiritual matter or substance. And when that material has afterwards become a spiritual substance, it is congealed and fixed, and is converted into a **stone** <note>original: *lapidem*; the Philosopher's Stone</note>: then he causes it to descend from heaven to earth, and makes the spiritual matter or substance bodily once again. 

And a certain Philosopher says: that from the substance of Mercury alone, without the addition of the substance of sulfurs, the stone is drawn out or generated. He does not mean this concerning the aforementioned smoky substance—in which lies hidden the **spirit of the quintessence** <term>quintessence|The "fifth essence," a pure, celestial substance thought to be the latent soul of matter</term> which we seek, and with which we may perform the **tincture** <note>The process of "dyeing" or transforming a base metal into gold</note>—but rather concerning the fixed and firm substance of the stone, which is its "earth." In this earth, that same spirit is fixed; and by this earth, the spiritual stone itself is impregnated in the "belly of the wind" <note>original: *ventre venti*; an allegorical phrase from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the air or vapor carrying the alchemical seed</note>, through the mastery of this art.

The Philosophers, observing their matter which is in its vessel and feels the heat, see it evaporate into the appearance of smoke and ascend to the top of the vessel: and they call this **sublimation**.

And seeing that it descended to the bottom of the vessel, they called it **descension**. Furthermore, seeing the matter thicken and turn black, and give off a foul stench, they called it **putrefaction** and the **raven’s head** <note>original: *caput corui*; the alchemical symbol for the *Nigredo* or black stage, representing death and the breaking down of matter</note>.

Seeing the black, dark, and foul color pass away after a long time, and a certain whiteness—after the fashion of an ash color—emerge, they called this **incineration** or **whitening** <note>original: *dealbationem*; the *Albedo* stage, signifying purification</note>.

Therefore, the sum of the entire art is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the returning of the water onto the earth until it rots. And when this earth rots with the water and has been cleansed by the help of Him who rules all things, the whole **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the completion of the Great Work</note> is perfected.

See, the **sperm of the philosophers** <note>original: *sperma philosophorum*; the initial "seed" or life-force of the work</note> is living water. The Earth, however, is the imperfect body: which Earth is called the mother of all elements.

The **dissolution** of the body and **coagulation** are two things, but they have a single operation; for the body is not dissolved unless the spirit is coagulated. When water is joined to the earth, the water—by its moisture and power—strives to dissolve the earth, for it makes the earth more subtle than it was before: and it renders the earth like unto itself, because water is more subtle than earth.
