### *concerning the Philosopher’s Stone.*

When you have decided to perform a **projection** <term>projection|The final step of the alchemical process where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transmute them into gold or silver</term> upon **Venus** <note>original: *Venerem*; copper</note> to reach the red state, remember always to **sublime** <term>sublime|To heat a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, a process used to purify and "spiritualize" matter</term> and also to fix the matter of the stone with a slow fire; for although this takes a longer time, its moisture is better preserved by that method.

->*Sublimation of the Stone.*<-

Therefore, to make your earth, or body, or **ferment** <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance that "leavens" the alchemical matter to trigger transformation</note>, or fixed thing volatile, three parts of the volatile substance must be mixed with one part of the fixed substance, and they must be sublimed with a moderate fire, as I showed before. When the volatile parts overcome the fixed ones, they carry them up with themselves into the heights <note>original: *in sublime*</note>, and all the more easily; for then they embrace each other more greedily. Others place the whole matter in glass to be fixed as before, and as many colors as there are in the world appear; then they begin gradually to diminish, and finally they will all end in one white color. Rejoice in this, because then the stone is fixed.

Here again, there were others slightly sharper than the former ones, who, thinking their stone (brought to this point) was complete in every respect, performed a projection upon **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> and **Jupiter** <note>original: *Iouem*; tin</note> with no result, because it could neither melt nor enter the metal; wherefore, despairing of the matter, they ceased from the work. They would undoubtedly have thought otherwise if they had understood the writings of the ancients, in which they say everywhere that the lower world must be moistened with **May dew** <term>May dew|Dew collected in the spring, believed to be rich in celestial life-force and "astral" energy</term> for so long until it bears white and red flowers.

Likewise, they say that the King must be nourished with his own milk until he has grown up; and furthermore, that the earth must be irrigated with the clear **water of paradise** <note>original: *aqua paradisi*; a poetic term for the pure, distilled alchemical solvent</note>, which frequently ascends into heaven and descends to earth.

And so, that we may arrive at the completion of the work, that stone—

# OF THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE

...and <note>original: *que*; likely the end of the word *atque* (and) from the previous page</note> of your fixed substance, as was stated above, mix a fourth part of the spirit, so that there are three parts of the stone and one part of the spirit; place these in a fixing vessel <note>original: *vitro fixatorio*; a glass vessel designed to withstand heat while sealing the contents</note>, and that single part of spirit will be fixed with the stone in a short time. For just as three parts of the spirit easily draw one part of the body upward with them into a sublime state, so conversely, three fixed parts make one volatile part fixed without difficulty, and of the same nature and temperament as themselves. Now, once that part has been fixed—always preserving the same proportion of fixed and volatile—mix another part with it to be fixed, and repeat this until your stone melts upon a glowing plate of **Venus** <note>original: *Veneris*; copper</note>, and penetrates it just as oil penetrates dry leather; then you have the Philosopher's Stone, perfect in every respect.

From this it now appears how much material must be taken at the beginning so that the entire work may be completed, and how great a supply of spirits is necessary. For at the start, a large quantity of them must be fixed with the earth, and that spirit fixed with the earth must always be drawn upward by a triple portion of new spirit. And again, the whole matter, fixed with its **ferment** <term>ferment|In alchemy, a substance added to a base material to catalyze its transformation into a higher state, similar to how yeast transforms dough</term>, must always be sublimated with a triple amount of spirits until the whole is made volatile, and having been fixed a third and final time, it must be introduced to new spirit again until it melts like butter. Thus, all these things must be perfected by the benefit of the spirit.

Indeed, when more spirits are fixed with it, it is rendered so much more meltable, to the point that it could finally be reduced to a viscous powder which would melt in the sun more easily than butter. This is not at all recommended, but you must guard against it and render it of a metallic nature, either more or less meltable; so that if you wish to **project** <term>projection|The final step where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transmute them into gold or silver</term> it upon **Venus** <note>original: *Venerem*; copper</note>, it should be less meltable than upon **Jupiter** <note>original: *Iouem*; tin</note>, and if upon **Jupiter**, less than upon **Saturn** <note>original: *Saturnum*; lead</note>, and if upon **Saturn**, less than upon **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*; quicksilver</note>.

Know that all metals must first be purified and cleansed of filth; concerning this, see **Isaac** <note>Isaac Hollandus, a 15th-century Dutch alchemist known for his practical laboratory instructions</note> in the first part concerning the medicine upon the white.

Pulverize the <term>caput mortuum</term> again, dissolve, filter, congeal, and distill as before, and do this as many times as necessary until the whole salt ascends together with the **aqua fortis**; you will have—

...and <note>original: *que*; the end of the word *atque* (and) continuing from the previous page</note> that precious red water which shines by night like the fire of hell; rectify this by distilling and **cohobating** <note>original: *cohobando*; the alchemical process of repeatedly distilling a liquid off its own solid residue to increase its purity or "virtue"</note> it in a **water-bath** <term>balneum Mariae|Literally "Mary's Bath," a double-boiler or water bath used by alchemists to provide gentle, consistent heat</term> until the whole of it rises from the bath. It will then be prepared for the multiplication of your stone within it through the process of solution in this manner:

Dissolve your blessed stone in your water, which will happen immediately. Place it in a warm water-bath in a vessel sealed with a distilling head <note>original: *alembibico*; an alembic</note> and a receiver; draw the water off from it. Once the water is drawn off, take some of the powder out of the gourd-vessel <note>original: *cucurbita*; a glass vessel shaped like a gourd</note> and test upon a red-hot metal plate whether it is **volatile**, as I have said elsewhere. Then pour the water back on, and draw it off as before, until nothing more rises. Test it again to see if it is somewhat more volatile than before. If it is not, pour the **strong water** <term>aquam fortem|Historically referring to nitric acid, but in this context, it refers to the specialized alchemical solvent previously prepared</term> on it again, and distill as above, until the entire powder flies away from the red-hot plate. This is the sign that it is sufficiently dissolved.

Then, three or four times—without adding any further dregs—**sublime** <note>original: *sublima*; to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, purifying it</note> it as described above. Then place it in a **fixing furnace**, using at first a slow fire, and then increasing it by degrees until it becomes **fixed** <note>original: *fixus*; a substance is "fixed" when it can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating</note>. Then weigh it, and to three parts of the fixed substance add one part of the spirit. Fix it again as before, and repeat this work until that which was sublimated becomes fixed. This will happen quickly because it was already fixed once in all its parts, and thus the fixed part fixes the other. Know that our stone is neither fixed nor volatile, but contains both, and the spirit is equally strong.

Furthermore, what we call **fixation** here is not truly fixation in the common sense, but merely the gathering of the subtle parts back into one, so that it may endure the fire once more and become fit for **projection** <term>proiectio|The final stage of the Great Work, where a small amount of the Stone is "projected" or thrown onto a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</term>.

In this way, therefore, you will be able to multiply your stone twice or thrice, but not more often; for because of its excessive subtleness, when it is dissolved into water, it would fly away and escape invisibly. But enough on this for now.

The **Ancient Philosophers** were ignorant of "strong waters" in the making of the stone. Instead, they were forced to gradually open their stone through **calcinations** <note>original: *calcinationibus*; reducing a metal to powder through heat</note>, **reverberations** <note>original: *reuerberationibus*; heating in a furnace where the flame is "reverberated" or reflected back onto the material</note>, solutions in the air, vinegar, and congelations, until it was rendered spiritual. However, when it was entirely perfected, they did not know the true art of multiplying it. Instead, they would turn it into something like a clear oil using distilled vinegar. When they wished to compress this again into a hard mass, they would mix it with **decorporated gold** <note>original: *solem decorporatum*; gold that has been stripped of its metallic form and reduced to its essential "mercury" or "sulfur"</note>, red like blood, through a single solution and congelation; and thus they would cook it down into a red mass in a secret furnace with a light fire.

It must be known that under all **greenness** lies **blackness**, and under blackness lies **whiteness**, and indeed in everything created by God...

# ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

...it is <note>original: *est*; the end of a sentence from the previous page</note>, that it contains perfect redness either in its interior or its exterior. For whatever is red on the outside is white on the inside, and vice versa, with infinite colors always cast between these two.

The Stone, such as it is on the outside, so it is in its interior and in its center; upon whatever thing it is projected <note>The act of "projection" involves casting a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note>, it performs a perfect work within it, and changes its interior to its exterior and vice versa. Moreover, **Luna** <term>Luna|The alchemical name for Silver</term> is, in its interior, a good **Sol** <term>Sol|The alchemical name for Gold</term>, bright and red. And the stone, when projected upon **Venus** <term>Venus|The alchemical name for Copper</term>, calls forth its interior, which is white, and it becomes white and bright **Luna** <note>silver</note>, with its redness having been driven inward. Thus every metal contains its own **tincture** <note>original: *tincturam*; in alchemy, the "tincture" is the essential soul or coloring principle of a metal</note> within itself, whether toward red or toward white; so that if the stone gave no tincture from itself (which it nevertheless does), the metals would not have need of it.

The stone elicits the hidden tinctures of metals, just as the Sun makes all things grow, and yet if it fixed its rays upon a seed for 1,000 years, it would never infuse into it either odor, color, or taste from itself; for those qualities lie enclosed and hidden within the seed, never to come forth into the light or into action, nor would any fruits emerge from the seed, unless they were warmed and penetrated by the rays of the sun. And yet the sun does not impart anything from its own body to them. For God has enclosed in all created things that which they have need of, and enough tincture exists in each, nor does it require the help of another. Each thing has its own medicine within it; nor does it have need of external things for its own perfection and the driving away of all diseases, whether in **vegetable** <note>plant-based</note>, **animal**, or **mineral** work.

If this were not so, the works of God would not be perfect (which heaven forbid). For God created all things for perfection, so that they should lack nothing.

Furthermore, the more properly anything approaches its own perfection, the simpler it is; it is closer to its supreme end and limit, and thus has fewer colors. But when it reaches that extreme and supreme end toward which it was ordained by God, then as it has only one tincture both inside and out, so it encompasses within itself all the virtues and powers of all the colors that appeared in it before.

## PHILOSOPHICAL QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS 
## *by [the author] from the Port of St. Mary of Aquitaine.*

The philosophical preparation of Mercury <term>Mercury|Commonly known as quicksilver, Mercury represents the fluid, transformative principle in alchemy</term> is: 1. That its leaden darkness is entirely removed, and it is rendered translucent, bright, and transparent. 2. That its excessive earthly weight is subtracted; for excessive earthiness and wateriness hinder its powers. 3. That its volatility <note>its tendency to evaporate or escape</note> when exposed to fire is also removed. These are the superfluous things in Mercury that hinder its perfections. And thus, through purification by art, the **Salt of the Philosophers** is made; it is washed with the salt and vinegar of the philosophers. For superfluities are to be removed by nature, and what is absent must be supplied.

### *Question.*

Whether Mercury extracted by art from perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver are considered "perfect" because they do not rust or decay</note>, when mixed with its own body or with common Mercury, provides a true and philosophical conjunction sufficient for the physical generation of our Stone, as is the firm opinion of some?

### *Answer to the Question*

The Mercury of bodies will achieve no less with its own bodies, just as the sperm of a man generates nothing outside his body, because it is not sown in the place prepared for it by nature—especially since the "place" <note>the womb or vessel</note> preserves and generates that which is placed within it. Likewise, "like" does not act upon "like," just as fire does not act upon fire, nor water upon water. The Mercury of **Sol** <term>Sol|The alchemical name for Gold</term> is hot and dry. **Sol** is likewise; therefore, where there is no passion <note>original: *passio*; here meaning "receptivity" or the capacity to be acted upon by an opposite force</note>, there will be no action. If a man desires to procreate, he must necessarily sow his seed in a land other than his own body. Therefore, every elemental thing has its own proper **womb** <note>original: *matrix*; in alchemy, this refers to the vessel or the substance that receives and nurtures the "seed" of the metal</note>, in which its species is generated and multiplied. But the Sun <note>original: *Sol*; the alchemical name for Gold</note> is not the proper earth of its own Mercury in which it can be multiplied and generated through **breakdown** <note>original: *corruptionem*; in alchemy, "corruption" is the necessary first stage of change where a substance "dies" or decomposes to be reborn in a higher form</note>. But the Mercury of gold is not the form of gold, and therefore the Mercury of gold and the body of gold relate to each other as two males, and two males do not procreate.

->Another question.<-

If, therefore, the Mercury of gold were joined to common Mercury so that it might be mixed with it, could it produce anything toward the generation of the Stone?

->Response.<-

It was sufficiently shown above that two males can by no means generate anything; likewise, neither can two females. Those two Mercuries relate to each other like two waters or two females. Therefore, an equal has no power over an equal. In natural things, it is necessary for perfect generation that two things concur: namely, the **active** and the **passive** <note>original: *agens & patiens*; the active "male" principle and the passive "female" principle required for any creation</note>, in a well-disposed subject. Yet the Mercury of the Sun and common Mercury joined together do nothing, but remain like two dead bodies—just as earth to earth or water to water.

Philosophers seek with the greatest diligence the purest substance of Mercury, which is held as the earth and the matter. Within this, the <term>Sulfur of Nature|A metaphorical term for the active, fiery, and organizing principle within a substance, contrasted with the fluid Mercury</term> is sown so that it may **putrefy** <note>original: *putrefcat*; the stage of decay (often signaled by a black color) that alchemists believed must precede new life</note> within it. This earth is held in the place of a womb, in which the seed of the woman is preserved, awaiting the seed of her husband. By this, they are joined and mixed inseparably—one hot and dry, the other cold and moist—so that by the moisture and coldness of one, the heat and dryness of the other may be balanced. And at a certain time, that which was sown will break forth from the potential of the matter into a specific form and into action. For no quality can act primarily and by itself; for all action belongs to the form as to the substance. Indeed, it is a certain efficient principle.

->Another response or reason.<-

<margin>Nature works in a circle.</margin>
For nature always works **circularly** <note>original: *circulariter*; referring to the alchemical cycle of distillation and condensation, or the natural cycle of life, death, and rebirth</note>; it never goes backward, it always goes forward, and it always returns to the same, though not always in the same way. You sow one grain, nature proceeds, and it multiplies one into a thousand, but not in the same way.

<header>QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS</header>

<margin>
Art violently breaks the bond of nature.
</margin>
Nature dissolves its own body while its **seminal power** <note>original: *virtute seminaria*; the innate life-force or "seed" within a substance that allows it to grow or change</note> is not only kept from destruction but is actually multiplied and increased. This is something that Art <note>meaning the artificial techniques of the alchemist</note> can by no means achieve, because Art violently breaks the bond of nature in any thing. Once that bond is broken, the seminal power of that thing necessarily vanishes.

<margin>
Nature gently dissolves the bond of its own nature.
</margin>
But Nature dissolves the bond of its own similar nature gently. When this bond is dissolved, the seminal power grows even more because it receives air and thus begins to move and become active.

<margin>
The Mercury of gold is not alive.
</margin>
When Art creates the **Mercury of bodies** <note>a liquid state of metals produced through chemical means</note>, it breaks the bond of nature. By breaking it, the seminal power—that is, that bond consisting of the vegetative spirit and the natural fire that binds the body to the spirit—vanishes. Therefore, the **Mercury of the Sun** <note>original: *Mercurius solis*; Mercury derived from Gold</note>, when mixed back into its own body, will generate nothing. Although it may appear "running" <note>liquid and mobile like quicksilver</note>, the body is nonetheless without soul and spirit, and consequently remains dead. No matter what the craftsman attempts, he will never **sublimate** <note>original: *sublimabit*; here meaning to refine or elevate it to a higher state</note> it, because it is not alive; rather, it will simply return to its original metallic body. The same must be understood regarding the **Moon** <note>original: *luna*; the alchemical name for Silver</note>.

The **Elixir** <note>the perfected Stone or medicine</note> is multiplied with the same Mercury from which it was first created. By placing it upon the work that is already finished, according to the weights prescribed by the wise, it will be multiplied in both power and quantity.

*This is not my opinion alone, but is an invincible and proven judgment.*

->B. Penotus from Port-Sainte-Marie of<-
->Aquitaine. Doctor of Medicine.<-

---

->*Again concerning Mercury.*<-

Just as there are three things that hinder the earth from germinating—namely, extreme cold, extreme heat, and extreme humidity—sterile women are made so in the same way. By too much humidity, the **womb** <note>original: *matrix*</note> is loosened and the seed flows out and is not retained; likewise, by too much dryness, the seed withers and has no means to sprout. Our Mercury behaves in the same way regarding these factors. If we desire fertile earth, it is necessary to cultivate it by purging, plowing, and tending it, as well as by cleansing it of all excesses. Then, being liberated from excessive humidity, cold, and dryness, it may bring forth a hundredfold the seed we wish to sow in it. It is the same with a sterile woman: if we wish to make her fertile, let us first strive to restore her womb to a balanced temperament. Otherwise, no matter what a man attempts in order to produce offspring, he labors in vain.

## 57 PHILOSOPHICAL RULES OR CANONS.

<margin>Why metals differ from one another.</margin>
Metallic bodies differ in their composition from **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuo*; in alchemy, Mercury is the fluid, feminine principle of all metals</note>, by which they are generated, according to whether that mercury was pure or impure, or whether it came from clean or unclean **sulfur** <note>the fiery, masculine principle that provides form, color, and hardness to the metal</note>.

If quicksilver is thickened by pure sulfur, in which the power of fieriness is simple, it will become gold.

If the sulfur is weak, but the Mercury is of good substance, it converts it into **copper** <note>original: *æs*</note>.

If, however, the quicksilver is heavy, earthy, and unclean, and the sulfur is likewise unclean, foul-smelling, earthy, and of a fixed substance, iron is made from it.

Thus metallic bodies differ from quicksilver according to how much foreign or "burning" sulfur is within them.

<margin>The source of the perfection and imperfection of metals.</margin>
A great quantity of sulfur is the cause of their imperfection, and a great quantity of Mercury is the cause of their perfection.

Sulfur burns and is burned, and it hinders perfection in every alchemical work.

<margin>Gold and silver are caused by simple, "living" sulfur.</margin>
Sulfur is of two kinds: namely "living" <note>original: *viuum*; refers to the pure, philosophical principle of heat</note> and "burning" <note>original: *vrens*; refers to common, destructive sulfur</note>.

Simple "living" sulfur causes gold and silver; it is nothing other than a hot and dry vapor, generated from the purest terrestrial dryness, in which fire is the dominant element.

<margin>Simple sulfur.</margin>
The more "simple" a sulfur is, the more it delights in and clings to simple and clean Mercury.

Common sulfur always infects and blackens; it corrupts in whatever way it is prepared by art, and for this reason, it is not the **sulfur of the philosophers**.

<margin>The nature of the sulfur of the philosophers.</margin>
The sulfur of the philosophers is a simple, "living" fire that brings life to other bodies and ripens them. For it possesses an abundance of maturity and is further purified by the chemist's art.

The intention of all philosophers is to perfect the worse by means of the better.

<header>ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.</header>

<margin>What bodily Mercury performs</margin>
Raw Mercury, made from clear water from the beginning, always desires to corrode—namely gold and silver, which are near to its own nature—an act that Mercury solidified from bodies can never perform.

Every composite thing must be separated, and this separation is death. <note>In alchemy, "death" refers to the breakdown of a substance into its base components so it can be reborn in a more perfect form.</note>

Whatever is created from simple and most subtle fire alone neither drinks, nor sleeps, nor eats; but that which is created from thick fire is otherwise.

Why are various creatures seen? Because the four elements are enemies to one another; for if all elements were created from the same thing, they would be of one nature and would agree. But by the power of God, they are united and joined, and they shall observe perpetual peace.

Composition is of a double complexion: for one is moist, while the other is dry.

There are many ways to investigate this art, which philosophers have ultimately reduced to two paths: the **universal** and the **particular**.

<margin>Philosophical mineral.</margin>
The particular path is achieved by means of "dry water" and is called a **mineral** <note>original: *minera*</note>: it is multiplied by the addition of common Mercury; yet no "projection" <note>the final stage of transmutation where the Stone turns base metal into gold</note> occurs.

<margin>Wetting water.</margin>
The universal path, which is multiplied by a multitude of spirits, is a "water that wets the hands," known to only a few.

**Copper** <note>original: *æs*; while this usually means copper or bronze, in alchemy it often refers to the "body" or base matter of the work</note> falling into that water is called the **leaven of gold** <note>original: *fermentum auri*; an additive that triggers the transformation of the substance</note>; it melts like water, which is then solidified by cooking. And then the redness appears.

<margin>Why it is called the Philosopher's Stone.</margin>
This copper, while it is first cooked, becomes water: and the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened until it becomes a stone, excelling every metal; hence it received the name of the **Philosopher's Stone**.

If you call it water, you speak the truth. If you deny it is water, you do not deny falsely: do not, therefore, be deceived by the plurality of names. <note>Alchemists often used many names for the same substance to confuse the uninitiated.</note>

<margin>He notes the weights.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, to take one part of our copper, and three parts of the "permanent water," which is also called copper.

<margin>The above and the below.</margin>
The whole **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the complete alchemical process</note>, however, is that the "above" becomes the "below," and the "below" becomes the "above," and it is cooked until the "lead of copper" flows with the leaven added at the beginning, middle, or end; and then it stains and will flow like wax.

Nothing else is as useful as **subliming** <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</note> the water and vapor; this will be achieved when you see those two purified natures become water, and the whole body of **magnesia** <note>original: *magnesiæ*; a term for the raw, dark primordial matter used in the work</note> melted into water; then

<header>CANONS 57.</header>

Certainly all things have been made into vapor, and rightly so, for then the vapor contains its mate <note>original: *compar*; in alchemy, this refers to a complementary substance that "matches" another to allow for union</note>.

Philosophers have called both substances "vapor" because both are joined during the decoction <note>the process of heating a substance in a liquid</note> and one contains the other, not allowing it to flee; therefore, they become permanent.

The ancients said the "work" consists of two things, and some have called these two joined together a "composite," because those two are actually four: for within them are dryness and moisture, spirit and vapor.

<margin>
Water turned into powder.
</margin>
If you doubt how water may become powder, it is necessary that the "body"—which was not water before it fell into the water—becomes water at the same time as the water, so that water is mixed with water and they become one.

The ignorant, however, when they hear the name "water," think it is the water of the clouds. If they understood the books of the philosophers, they would surely know that it is "permanent water" <note>original: *aqua permanens*; a metaphorical term for a stabilized alchemical solvent that does not evaporate</note>: which cannot be permanent without its mate, with which it has been made one.

<margin>
This water belongs to Johannes Pontanus, the fire of the work. <note>Johannes Pontanus was a famous alchemist known for his "Epistle" regarding the "Secret Fire" of the philosophers.</note>
</margin>
This water is called the water of golden fire, the "good poison," sand, and blackness; for this reason, cast aside all plurality. For Nature is content with one single thing.

<margin>
Earth is in water, water is in earth.
</margin>
Cook, cook with a gentle fire until it liquefies and is turned into water; for by the heat of the water, the whole will easily become water. And unless you turn both into water, you will not arrive at the precious work: the body must become weak with the water, in the water, until the whole becomes water.

Do you not see that the composition of a human being is from soul and body? Thus it is necessary for us to join two things together, a mixture which the philosophers have compared to spouses, from whose embrace the "golden water" results.

Bronze <note>original: *Æs*; often used to represent the "base" metal or the "body" of the stone</note>, conceiving the quicksilver <note>term: <term>Quicksilver</term> (Latin: *argentum vivum*), the common name for Mercury.</note>, coagulates it; the quicksilver itself, conceiving the bronze, is congealed into earth, and this is done with a very gentle fire.

<margin>
Note: here is understood the Mercury that wets the hands.
</margin>
Know that quicksilver is fire, consuming every body more than fire, and "mortifying" <note>to "mortify" in alchemy means to kill or strip a metal of its external properties to reach its inner essence</note> the bodies.

Therefore, join the quicksilver to the quicksilver of its own kind, and you shall have the secret.

They call bronze "the coin." The "blackness" of the philosophers, however, they have called "lead."

<margin>
The composition of the stone is twofold.
</margin>
The composition is twofold: one in the moist, the other in the dry; and when they are prudently cooked, they become one. They are called by many names: when it becomes red, it is called the flower of gold, the leaven of gold, the glue of gold, red sulfur, and orpiment <note>original: *auri pigmentum*; a gold-colored mineral</note>. # CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

...[silver?] <note>original: *tem*; likely the end of *argentum* (silver) from the previous page</note> remains crude; it is called the lead of copper, the rod of metal, and the plate.

Things are not made except according to their own natures, just as a human comes from a human, and a lion from a lion.

If you seek the medicine that cures metals, its origin will be in the metals, since a species is colored <note>original: *tingatur*; to be "tinged" or "tinctured" refers to the alchemical transformation of a metal's color and property</note> by its own kind: however, that metals are reduced to simple elemental water is not to be understood in that way, because nothing is made from a simple substance, but from a composite.

Nature is a certain power implanted in things, which procreates like from like, and increases and nourishes all things. God is nature, and nature is God; from God originates something closest to Him.

It is the Mercurial nature by which we are fed and nourished; without it, there is no power in animals or plants, for if it is removed from any thing, corruption and death immediately follow, as it is the ferment of life and of the existence of the whole universe.

The fire of the philosophers is their water; if you know how to join fire to fire, and Mercury to Mercury by fire, it is enough for you.

Quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*</note> is the spirit, and it is called permanent water, vinegar, or the menstruum <note>original: *menstruum*; a solvent, often associated with a monthly cycle or period of digestion in alchemy</note>, and by other names.

<margin>The spirit is the tincture <note>a substance capable of dyeing or transforming metal</note> that colors the body.</margin>
The spirit or water is the elixir of whiteness and redness <note>original: *albedinis & rubedinis*; referring to the two major stages of the alchemical work</note> of the tincture, as well as the tinging spirit and metallic water, pouring itself into the body and vivifying it. And the body is the recipient of the tincture from that very spirit, and not from another. And that which fixes the spirit is fixed and non-combustible <note>original: *incremabile*</note>, and it is named the sulfur of the philosophers.

Care must be taken lest the spirit, which dries the body and is dried by the body, becomes volatile; for if it flies away from the body, the body cannot be made perfect.

Join the moist to the dry, and it shall rejoice: because the moist is the spirit and soul; the dry is called earth, or the dead body.

<margin>The difference between the unctuous <note>oily</note> and the viscous <note>sticky</note>.</margin>
It must be noted that the unctuous is one thing, and the viscous another; for the stone is generated from the viscous moist: but metals are generated from the unctuous.

<margin>Most worthy of note.</margin>
Whatever truth consists in the art of Alchemy, it is to join the moist to the dry: by "moist" understand the liquid spirit, cleansed of all filth; and by "dry" understand the perfect body, pure and calcined <note>original: *calcinatum*; reduced to powder through high heat</note>. And indeed, the operation of these two parts consists of this: making the fixed volatile and the volatile fixed—that is, to fix the spirit.

# EXTRACTION

<margin>A certain sign of perfect operation.</margin>
When, during the thickening <note>original: *congelatione*; the process of a liquid becoming solid or viscous</note>, you see things like fish eyes and peppery grains, know that you have walked the right path; if you do not, your labors are in vain.

Every general action has a single span of time in which it is perfected and finished. For there is no act without motion, and no operation without a limit.

<margin>Middle minerals are to be chosen for the work.</margin>
If you wish to take up mineral elements to create the Stone, do not take from the first nor from the last, but from the middle.

When you wish to eat, take the bread and leave the flour; and when you wish to make bread, take the flour and leave the wheat. <note>This metaphor suggests using substances that have already been partially refined by nature or art, rather than raw materials or final products.</note>

To separate the elements is to set aside heterogeneous things, which are merely accidental. To join the elements is to gather homogeneous things together. That is, those things which belong to the nature of the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: *humidi radicalis*; the fundamental life-fluid or "essential oil" believed to sustain all things</note>.

<margin>It is necessary to close the vessel firmly.</margin>
Great care must be taken lest the spirit, which dries out the body, becomes volatile. If the vessel in this Art were not closed, its entire power would exhale—just as in the generation of a metal, if the smoke from which the metal is born were to escape, no metal would be produced.

<margin>God created that essence which they call the Soul of the World from the beginning.</margin>
God, remaining within Himself before the constitution of the world, willed by His kindness that things known from eternity should come into being. In the beginning, He created a certain essence of these things, as yet unformed in crude outlines, which Moses calls the "earth without form and void," <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2.</note> sometimes calling it the "abyss" and "water," while Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher</note> calls it "chaos," in which resides that spirit which we seek.

God therefore fills all things so that there is nothing where He is not; all nature is His image, and He is joined to His creatures in a manifold way. Therefore, all things are in God: to whom be praise, honor, and glory through Jesus Christ.

### *The true extraction of MERCURY, or QUICKSILVER, from gold, which I received from a certain famous and noble Bohemian Lord, and I offer to you freely.*

Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813), the most famous figure in Arabic alchemy.</note>, the most skillful King of the Arabs and investigator of natural things, says: "The treasure of the whole matter is <term>calcination</term>." <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note> And because the ancients lacked "strong waters" <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; nitric acid or other mineral acids</note>, they reduced all things to lime by the most violent fire. From this, the invention of glass arose. In these times, a shorter and more concise way has been found, by which metals are calcined by sharp waters, as can be seen in this recipe.

<sig>Cati.</sig>

## A most excellent calcination of gold.

<margin>An error if you do otherwise.</margin>
Take <note>original: *Rx*, the traditional symbol for a recipe or prescription</note> aqua regia <term>aqua regia</term> <note>literally "Royal Water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving the "king of metals," gold</note> in which you shall dissolve gold; then take pure common water and in it dissolve as much calcined tartar <note>potassium carbonate derived from wine sediment</note> as you wish—a small quantity suffices, just enough so that by adding it drop by drop we may make the gold fall to the bottom, which it would otherwise do only with great difficulty. And take note: it is necessary that the vessel for the dissolution be large, and that you pour in only a little of this water of tartar at a time; otherwise, the whole mass would fly away <note>the author warns of a violent chemical reaction or "boiling over"</note>, which must be diligently avoided.

Furthermore, when all the lime <note>original: *calx*; the powdery residue left after a metal is dissolved and precipitated or burnt</note> is already at the bottom, it is necessary to sweeten <term>dulcify</term> <note>to wash away the acids or salts with water until the substance is neutral</note> it well with warm water. Then, in a clean and polished wooden vessel, let it dry out gradually by itself, without any heat being applied. If it were done otherwise, it would vanish into the air with a massive sound and crash, like <margin>An unheard-of thing.</margin> gunpowder, so that not even a single atom could be found. This, indeed, happened to me three times. For when I was moving the dried powder with a small silver spoon upon a glass table (without any heat), it suddenly caught flame and produced a sound similar <margin>A story worthy of note.</margin> to a large gun <note>original: *sclopetum*; an early firearm or musket</note> being discharged; it was so powerful that it nearly took away my hearing. And so the whole thing was scattered, and everything it touched was ruptured and broken. Therefore, one must act cautiously, and for the sake of greater safety, it should be moved with a wooden spatula rather than any other kind.

Finally, when it is already well dried, one must add as much common sulfur as desired—that is, at your discretion—and grind them together. Place this in a crucible and seal it well with <term>lute</term> <note>original: *perlutare*; sealing a vessel with a paste of clay or dung to make it airtight</note>, placing a lid on top that has a small hole so that the flame of the sulfur may escape. These things having been performed, let it be given a circular fire <note>original: *ignis circuli*; a fire built in a ring around the crucible to provide even heat</note> and be burned thoroughly. Note well: afterwards, for greater perfection, I reverberated <note>original: *reverberaui*; to heat in a furnace where the flame is "turned back" or reflected onto the material</note> the gold thus burnt, and the resulting lime was so delicate, so beautiful, and of such a deep color that it tended toward brown; I have never seen its equal.

It is necessary, however, to first sublimate the sal ammoniac through fused common salt, so that it may attack and dissolve the gold more quickly. In this aqua regia, dissolve as much gold as you please, and afterwards draw off <note>distill</note> the water until only half remains. Let the vessel cool with the material inside, and in this way, crystals will form, and

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter P featuring a floral and landscape scene with a building in the background.</image-desc>
PERPETUAL and common is that misery of mankind which I cannot sufficiently bewail, when I see that all those things in which even the mere shadows of good reside are so difficult and intricate that hardly one in a thousand can obtain them; and once obtained, they flee from us with such a swift foot. But those things, on the other hand, which are joined with atrocity, dangers, and every heap of evils, so constantly loom over us that they might be judged to have conspired for human destruction. For in a moment we go to ruin, overwhelmed by misery, poverty, weakness, and pains; but to be happy, to be enriched, or to be healed, many years of work are required: and to never be in want is something that hardly happens to us in an entire lifetime. Indeed, as far as my own affairs are concerned, I find myself in plainly that condition. For since the very beginning of my life, I have held nothing higher in my desires (though I blush to confess it openly) than to become very rich; and though a thirst for gold itself has entirely seized me, I have not yet achieved a perfect method for obtaining it. Although I am despairing of realizing my vow, I am pleased to try every extreme, and I shall again take up that art which the common people call Alchemy <term>Alchemistica</term>, which I had set aside for a time, with Mercury <note>original: *fauente Mercurio*; referring to the Roman god of gain and the patron of alchemists</note> favoring me. But I see Theophrastus von Hohenheim walking there, a man who—if Germany ever bore such a one—is the absolute master of this art. If I could lead him to the opinion of being a help to me in this endeavor, I would undoubtedly be the happiest of men. I will approach him first with magnificent promises, and later even with threats. *Theo.* That this was done by almost everyone, as you say, I do not deny; however, they seem to me to have been led to commit this for four reasons in particular. **First**, to exercise the minds of idle men. **Second**, to provide an opportunity for the ingenious to investigate many famous and useful things that flow from those studies. **Third**, so that they might wretchedly (as was fitting) vex curious and greedy men who thirst for gold, and abuse their work and labors—not without great delight and laughter on the part of the authors. Do you not understand that this has been done by them so many times? They have given many names to the same thing everywhere, just as many epithets were once given to **Jove** <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note> himself by the worshippers of idols. **Finally**, they wrote to leave a testimony for posterity that they understood the secrets of nature and the physical actions themselves.

*Chr.* Why then did they not remain silent, rather than writing such wordy commentar-

...ries, they preferred to write down things that no one ever understands. I confess there is a great heap of books; as far as has come to my knowledge, they are all hindered and confusing regarding this business. A great part of them are unworthy of being inspected by an ingenious man; and yet they are circulated under the names of *Hermes*, *Avicenna*, *Averroes*, and the like, though they are spurious and compiled by Europeans—and barbarians at that. To name a few, there are the works of *Richard the Englishman*, *Gilgilides*, *Christopher of Paris*, *Morienus*, *Rosinus*, and *Stephanus*, who all dare to call themselves "philosophers" (if it please the gods!). To this group belong those little books that falsely claim the title of *Mary, sister of Moses* <note>Known in alchemical tradition as "Mary the Jewess," a legendary figure credited with inventing the *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie.</note>. 

On the other hand, there exist commentaries by others which, if read with judgment, are indeed tolerable and not unworthy of reading; yet to extricate yourself from them, you need the **thread of Theseus** <note>A reference to the myth of the Labyrinth; it means a guide or clue to find one's way through a complex problem.</note>. Among the older authors, the writings of *Geber* and *Simplicius* should hold the first place. More recent ones include: *John of Roquetaillade*, *Roger Bacon*, and *Aloysius Marlianus*. Yet none is found to have been of a saner mind than *Giovanni Agostino Augurelli*.

*Chry.* Good God, why did I not understand this so many years ago? Truly, bring a remedy to these desperate matters.

*Theoph.* As if indeed you could use me as a counselor! I differ **diametrically** <note>original: "εκ διαμέτρου" (ek diametrou)</note> from the opinion of all those whom you have understood to have spoken on this matter—at least regarding what they claim. However, I do not disagree regarding those things discovered and made public by the benefit of this art. For methodical experience has proven those to be true. If you wish to be occupied with such things, you will be able to spend your life in an honest occupation, not without varied delight and at no great expense. 

For example, consider **metallic castings** <term>fusiones: the process of melting and pouring metal into molds</term>, by which not only small animals and solid objects, but even herbs, flowers, and indeed the most minute things can be most accurately expressed. Likewise **distillations** <term>destillationes: the process of purifying a liquid by heating and cooling</term>, as they call them; by their benefit, not only herbs and juices, but also the "tears" of trees, and even...

...stones and even flints themselves can be reduced into oils, into waters, and into spirits. In these and similar matters (if you so desire), I will not be reluctant to oblige you.

**Chr.** Why are you telling me about fusions and distillations? I promised myself far greater things from you. You understand what I want. To say it in one word: I primarily desire to know this: Can metals be transformed, and by what means? Can the baser metals be changed into the more noble, and into the purest gold? If you say this can be done, it remains for you to explain what those spirits or principles are by which this *transubstantiation* <note>The term *transubstantiation* is borrowed from theology (the changing of bread/wine into the body/blood of Christ) to describe the total conversion of one elemental substance into another.</note> (as they call it) occurs. For you cannot deny that these things are well-known to you.

**Theo.** It is absurd that you wish to learn things from me that I have never claimed to know, and of which I have never personally made an experiment. Indeed, your own ignorance of physical matters (which you reveal quite clearly) betrays that you have wasted your effort until now and will continue to do so hereafter. For these axioms are accepted by natural philosophers: *Nothing can be created from nothing.* <note>original: *Ex nihilo, nihil posse generari.*</note> Furthermore, the principles of any generation (to speak without ambiguity) ought not to be incompatible with the thing they are striving to create, but should share as much as possible with it (as I shall explain below). Thus, a metal is not made from an egg, nor is a crocodile born from a metal, even though you might think one or the other could happen. <note>Theophrastus is using "absurd" examples to show that things must be created from materials of the same "nature" or category.</note> And yet you have attempted to perform far more ridiculous things. 

To answer your questions more clearly: Metals cannot be transformed, especially those that differ in weight and density. Gold differs from all others in its heaviness and solidity. Therefore, I will not even speak of other metals which hardly differ in these qualities, nor does it pertain to your questions.

**Chr.** And yet, even the ancient Arab authors <note>Refers to foundational alchemists like Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) or Rhazes, whose works formed the basis of medieval European alchemy.</note> do not deny what you usually assert as false.

**Theo.** On the contrary, you have not grasped their sayings. Why did you not more diligently examine that saying which they hold as an oracle? When they say: *That which is created must be reduced to its own principles.* <note>original: *Generatum debere ad sua principia reduci.*</note> Go ahead now and bring forth your evasions and dreams—such as "transubstantiation," or the "artificial generation of things," or "creation from nothing through art"—all of which are absurd according to the laws of nature, in which there is no natural sympathy <note>In this context, "sympathy" refers to a natural, occult connection or compatibility between two substances that allows them to interact.</note> for such things. This includes those ideas repeated so often they are like songs chanted at every street corner—it is almost embarrassing to repeat them—when they say: *There is a certain "first matter" of all things, which they call Hyle; and from it comes perpetual generation.* <note>*Hyle* is a Greek term (ὕλη) meaning "wood" or "matter," used by philosophers to describe the formless "prime matter" that underlies all physical reality.</note> Now, that first matter, when prepared for creation, exists as a potential; in itself, however, it is an actual thing—and vice versa. Regarding those things for which it lacks the potential, it never...

...which it receives (as is clear in the previous example). However, once it is embraced by the form to which it is then subject, it attains its actualization. And, pertaining to this, **First Matter** <note>original: *materia prima*; the formless "stuff" of the universe that precedes specific identity</note> does not perform just anything at random, but retains within itself a certain quantity, which they have called "indefinite." Since these things are most manifest, you, along with your tricksters, have preferred to go mad. What natural reason has established as belonging to First Matter, you subject to fires and burnings; you cannot deny that you seek every belief in **generation** <note>The natural process of growth and creation</note> from fires, though fire should neither be considered an element nor can it generate anything. Instead, fire calls everything outward, whereas generating matter calls everything inward.

**Chr.** I can agree with you, even as you deny what is most accepted by the Arabs themselves: that they subject not only metals, but metallic substances themselves to fires in so many various ways.

**Theo.** You are always harping on the same string. I am no longer talking about metallic operations, but about the reduction of generated things to their principles. The Arabs, so they don't disagree with me, learned from **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often cited in alchemy as a source of wisdom regarding fire</note> that the nature of fire is to consume everything, and once everything is consumed, to perish along with them. It is the property of **celestial heat**—not fire’s heat—to generate.

**Chr.** But those same Arabs say that the generation of all metals consists of these principles: namely, **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyrio*</note> and **sulfur**. Therefore, gold can be made from mercury and sulfur.

**Theo.** If you had said **cinnabar** <note>The bright red ore from which mercury is extracted; technically mercury sulfide</note>, perhaps I would agree. But do you not see that it is one thing to *make* and another to *generate*? The matter will become clearer with an example, and I will propose it with "plain wit" <note>original: *crassa Minerva*; literally "with a coarse Minerva," a Latin idiom for a simple, common-sense explanation</note>. If someone offered you ten grains of wheat and said bread could be made from them in infinite proportion, you would easily believe it once you understood the process. You understand the generation required for this and the delay involved, since—as the proverb goes—it is not the field but **time** that produces the ears of grain. 

But if you wanted to teach this to a man from the furthest Indies or Iceland who had never seen sowing or harvest, and you didn't want to speak openly but gave him mere riddles—like saying the earth must first be **calcined**, ground, the grains **dissolved**, buried, **sublimated**, then **coagulated** (I think you recognize your own terms), and **cooked out**—he would understand (if I'm not mistaken) that the earth must be furrowed with a plow, the clods turned over again, and the seeds sown in a certain order...

For if I knew these things exactly, you already know that it is the inviolable law of the mysteries: the so-called secrets must not be made manifest. Furthermore, if I had attempted such a thing or wished to experiment, and confessed it openly, it would follow that either the business did not succeed—in which case I offer myself up to be laughed at by everyone, and must be considered similar to those vagabonds of yours—or if I said it had succeeded, and most people understood this, then you surely realize this could not be without manifest danger to me. 

To speak candidly, this is the sort of business whose actions have almost never occurred to a private man without loss, and have often been the ruin of kings themselves. Therefore, it is not to be desired even by a wise man, unless he is so perfect that he can even despise an abundance of all riches and stand in need of nothing. And now (unless I am mistaken) you understand how it happens that the secrets of this science have reached so few over so many centuries. 

**Chr.** I actually think that these secrets were never committed to any writings or books at all, but just as it is said of the Hebrew **Kabbalah** <note>The Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition, which alchemists believed held secret keys to the structure of the universe</note>, they consist solely of oral tradition passed to posterity. 

**Theo.** Although these things are plausible, it is nevertheless most true that this science was once even without any disguise or obscurity, but was most openly committed to books, and passed down from the Asians to the European Greeks. 

**Chr.** As if indeed it could have been passed by the Greeks...

...lulled by such mist for the vainest of men, that it could scarcely have been hidden in thicker darkness even among the Cimmerians <note>A mythical people described by Homer as living in a land of perpetual mist and darkness; here used to mean total obscurity</note>.

**Theophrastus:** You are right indeed about the Cimmerians; but it is difficult to guard what everyone seeks. This is proven true in the case of treasures, which are dug up at such great risk. **Chrysopoeus:** Indeed, I learned of their preparation and departure from Apollonius of Rhodes <note>Author of the *Argonautica*, an epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts</note>. 

**Theophrastus:** Did you notice that the entire history of the discoveries of the Chemical art lies hidden in that story? 

**Chrysopoeus:** Not at all.

**Theophrastus:** I believe Luigi Marliani <note>original: *Aloisium Marlianum*; a 16th-century Italian physician and scholar</note> suspected the same thing, as he calls his commentaries on this art *The Golden Fleece*. For one must believe it was something momentous for which the leaders of Greece, with Jason as their guide, would first brave the sea and endure such a long and troublesome journey. Therefore, one should believe the Ram of the Golden Fleece was nothing other than the skins and books—which they later called parchment—written in golden letters, containing all the secrets of this art. It was suspended in the inner chambers of Aeëtes, King of the Colchians, and in the temple itself, not without constant guarding by men. Once this ineffable treasure was shown to the guests by his daughter Medea, driven by the madness of love, one must believe she not only possessed infinite riches, but also performed other wonders. Especially since, with little effort—something that cannot be done with any other medicines—she restored her decrepit father-in-law Aeson to firmer health and a state of youth. Do not mock these things as entirely fabled; for old age is nothing other than the diminishing of natural heat. It is diminished when its movement is hindered: therefore, that which can preserve its strength can also restrain that diminishing. Consider whether Apollonius himself makes mention of metals throughout his poem. 

**Chrysopoeus:** Good gods, have you not cunningly revealed yourself to me? From these words of yours, I am now certain that you dwell in the very inner chambers of absolute knowledge. Have you not performed the same many times yourself? Now do you still deny it? Have you not brought aid to the most desperate diseases, though you never entered the schools of physicians? Instead, by your ethereal and abstract qualities alone, you surpass all the physicians of Europe in the faculty of healing, and they have long since yielded the palm <note>A symbol of victory or superiority</note> to you. Therefore, to hesitate...

**Theophilus:** Even if I acknowledged these things as true, you know that it has been said by the wise: *What you wish to remain hidden, tell to no one.* I confess indeed that from the power and efficacy of metals and minerals, I have discovered many things with the help of Natural Philosophy <note>original: *Physices*; in this period, "physics" referred to the broad study of nature and the physical world</note>, the practice of which contributes greatly to the public good and to the art of medicine itself. These miserable men have only one solace: to find partners in their punishment wherever they can, deceiving others and leading them into the most obvious dangers.

...to unravel the riddles of [the ancients]: he promises to show the pitfalls and errors, and to lead the seeker out of darkness into the light. For if you proceed to attempt anything with him, you will soon understand that you may exclaim with the Greeks: *the treasure has turned to coals* <note>original: ἄνθρακες ὁ θησαυρὸς πέφυκεν (*anthrakes ho thesauros pephyken*); a classical Greek proverb describing a great hope that ends in a worthless result</note>. <meta>This page concludes a philosophical discourse on the nature of knowledge—specifically comparing the teacher’s role to a physician’s—and begins a formal rebuttal by Joseph Du Chesne (Quercetanus) against Jacques Aubert’s attacks on the Paracelsian chemical arts.</meta>

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>RESPONSE</header>

...as far as it pertains to all the noble sciences, to dispel the shadows of the mind. Socrates himself confessed that he never "administered" knowledge to anyone; rather, just as a physician does not provide sight itself, but clears away the fog so the eye may direct its gaze toward the object, so it happens regarding the sciences. The wise have observed that this is especially true in the absolute understanding of our Chemistry <note>original: *Chemicæ nostræ*; Du Chesne often uses "Chemistry" to refer to the "Spagyric" or Paracelsian art of medicine and transmutation</note>. For them, growing rich is quite easy (if they should so desire it), whereas for the foolish—who desire nothing more than wealth—it is most difficult. 

No one of sound mind will ever claim that the rewards of wisdom are merely riches, which are joined with a wondrous variety of hardships and exposed to the whims of Fortune. Therefore, riches are not to be sought after. And yet, despite the truth of this, the intemperance of men and their lack of wisdom—combined with the stubbornness of their passions and those "raging horses of desire" (as Sophocles used to say)—drive many headlong into valuing this miserable and precarious life and its comforts more than all the reasons for true happiness. It is inevitable that before these men begin to grow wise, extreme misfortune and **Ate** <term>Ατη; the Greek goddess of ruin, folly, and delusion</term> herself will strike them down and destroy them in a wretched fall and foul ruin.

Hermes Trismegistus, Geber, Lullus, Arnaldus de Villanova, and even our own Avicenna—whose testimonies, confirmed by authority, argument, and finally by practical use itself, are surely too weighty to be so easily dismissed by the jests or trivial reasonings of such men. For it reveals to us so many of the works of God the Best and Greatest, opens so many of nature’s secrets, and brings forth so many previously unknown preparations of medicines—from herbs, animals, minerals, and the hidden uses of almost all things concealed in the very bosom of nature—that those who wish to see it buried are ungrateful toward the human race. 

As for what pertains to Paracelsus, I have certainly not set out to undertake a defense of his Theology, nor have I ever thought to agree with him in all things, as if I had sworn an oath to his words. But beyond the testimony with which Erasmus honored him in certain letters, I would dare to say and maintain that he teaches many things in the medical art that are almost divine, which a grateful posterity can never sufficiently admire or proclaim—about which, I hope, another opportunity for speaking will be given. 

But as for you, Aubert, so that all may know with what judgment you have undertaken your attack, come, let us deal with those two things which you took it upon yourself to harass in the preface of your little book—you who are clearly, as I see, a very sharp-witted man. One of these, namely *Ladanum*, you believe to be very dangerous; the other, namely [the treatment for] *cancer of burnt eyes*, you believe to be ridiculous.

Certainly, no learned physician doubts that it <note>Referring to the "thick humor" mentioned on the previous page</note> must be softened, digested, thinned out, thinned, and cut into; those remedies which have a lesser power for this purpose are called *chalastika* <note>Greek: χάλαςικὰ; relaxing or loosening</note> or emollients, or *malaktika* <note>Greek: μαλακτικὰ; softening</note> by the Greeks. The timely use of these medicines is especially required and greatly praised in **quartan fevers** <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day, historically attributed to thick "black bile."</note>. Thus, ash bark, caper, bryony root, wild cucumber, dwarf elder, and iris—all of which are hot and dry, some even to the third degree—soften all hardnesses and dispel them when taken internally or even applied externally; they liquefy and consume the hardened spleens themselves. I could say the same of ammoniacum, bdellium, opoponax, and galbanum <note>These are various aromatic resins or gum-resins used in ancient and Renaissance pharmacy.</note>: although these are all hot and dry, it is known even to barbers that they have great power to soften and digest.

Therefore, since emollients and rarefying agents are suitable for the cure of quartan fever (as everyone admits) when taken at the right time, you will not think it so absurd and ridiculous, Jacques, if some people even use the ashes of the eyes, and sometimes the heads of crabs, or in their absence, even crayfish. For the ashes of those crustaceous animals—especially of the eyes—possess a great power, by drying, to thin and resolve those "dregs" of the melancholic humor which those whom you call **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> name "congealed **tartar**" <term>Tartar: In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony or solid metabolic waste that precipitates in the body (like wine-stone in a cask), leading to blockages and stones.</term>. <margin>
Chapter 11
</margin>
Eleven, where, speaking of salt, he reports the following: *Burnt salt digests more powerfully than that which has not been burnt, precisely because the body itself is rendered finer by the power received from the fire.* Furthermore, as he writes in the same book, since medicines composed of thin parts have more efficacy than those composed of thick parts (even if they possess equal strength) because they penetrate better, we use calcined crabs for that reason alone—especially for dissolving the dregs and the "tartarous" humor. For by calcination, the **salt** of things is extracted; and salt can only be resolved by salt, if you understand well. Thus you will learn that "like is cured by like" <note>original: *similia similibus curari*; a core principle of Du Chesne's chemistry, contrasting with the Galenic "contraries are cured by contraries."</note>, although for another reason not yet perceived by you. Otherwise, why would we use the stones of sponges, or burnt glass...

Why would you say that dried goat's blood, or the ashes of snails, or calcined **Jew's stone** <note>original: *Iudaicum lapidem*; a fossilized sea urchin spine used since antiquity to treat kidney stones</note>, or cuttlefish bone are so powerfully beneficial for a **calculus** <note>A stone or pebble formed in the body</note> or for **tartar of the kidneys**? What then would you say about the **wren** <note>original: *Troglodyte*; specifically the bird *Troglodytes troglodytes*</note>, that most praised medicine of the ancients for the same condition, mentioned by **Paulus Aegineta** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician whose medical encyclopedia was a standard textbook</note> in Book 3, Chapter 45, where he left these words written:

Furthermore, the effectiveness of **calcined crabs** for this same condition has been noted by **Hollerius** and **Mattioli** <note>Jacobus Hollerius and Pietro Andrea Mattioli, prominent 16th-century medical authorities</note> and proven a thousand times by certain experience.

When this salt is dissolved in moisture, it becomes a most excellent **oil** <note>In alchemy/early chemistry, an "oil" often refers to a concentrated liquid resulting from the dissolution of a salt</note>, highly useful for clearing away all obstructions of the internal organs. 

There is no reason, therefore, for you to think a remedy derived from calcined **crab's eyes** <note>original: *cancrorum oculis*; these are not literal eyes, but "gastroliths"—calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish, highly valued in early modern pharmacy</note> is so ridiculous, nor should you vomit the venom of your bitterness upon it in such a way. Physicians divide these into two types. Some can be eaten, while others are unfit for consumption: the former have a certain sweet, or at least obscure, mixed 
<margin>Galen, *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, Book 2, chapter 17.</margin> 
quality; the latter are deadly, if we believe **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note>, or at least they quickly produce an ulcer when applied to our skin. That this is not the case with **crab ashes** <note>original: *cancrorum cinere*; likely referring to "crab’s eyes" or gastroliths, which were calcined and used as a calcium-rich medicine</note> is shown by Galen’s own words when he discusses the differences between bitter and acrid flavors. 
<margin>Galen, *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, chapter 18.</margin> 
For he reports that the acrid flavor has a certain mixed humidity; but he admits that all bitter things possess not only a hot faculty, but also a dry one, and he says they are similar to **ash** <note>original: *cineri*; referring to the residue left after burning a substance, which was thought to have concentrated drying powers</note> (using those who compare them best). For this reason, he would have better said that the ash of crab’s eyes is bitter rather than acrid. When their moisture is consumed and flows away into vapor, released by the heat of the fire, dryness and "ashiness" are produced. From this, they acquire not an acrid but a bitter quality, and a substance which, though earthy, is nevertheless refined—insofar as the body itself is rendered more subtle by the faculty received from the fire, as we said above from Galen—and it is necessarily made hot and dry. 
<margin>Simple Medicines, 11, chapter 51.</margin> 
Therefore, there is no doubt that "bitter" also cleanses, grinds down, and cuts through thick and viscous humors, just like ash and **nitre** <note>original: *nitrum*; saltpeter or naturally occurring sodium carbonate, used as a cleaning agent and medicine</note>,

as Galen teaches. You could better consult him elsewhere, so that you do not appear entirely ignorant of the very first principles. But since I see that something must be conceded to you, come now, I willingly grant you that the **lime of crabs** <note>The powdered, calcined remains of crabs</note> is acrid; however, I utterly deny that it increases **quartan fever** <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day</note> by its acrimony. For I ask you, my dear man, are not mustard, pepper, and garlic so highly recommended for quartan fever by all the dogmatic physicians—both Greek and Arab, and by **Paulus Aegineta** himself—that they are even prescribed as part of the diet? It will not be out of place to bring forward

They preserve and vivify the body through the excellence of their **spirits** <note>the refined, active "breath" or essence of a substance</note>, and they purge impurities mostly through simple sweating. Finally, they are of no small benefit in their whole substance, as many learned men daily experience with happy success. But enough of these things. Now, therefore, we must proceed to those things which you write concerning metals.

<margin>Agricola, Book 8, *On the Nature of Minerals* <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy"; his works were the standard reference for mining and metallurgy in this period.</note></margin>
Some write that a **metal** <term>metallum: though the term originally referred to a mine or quarry, by the 16th century it referred to the materials extracted from them</term> is a mineral body that is naturally either liquid, such as **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum* (living silver)</note>, or hard and capable of being melted by the heat of fire, such as gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin—or capable of being softened, such as iron. Others, however, use the name "metal" in its literal sense for everything dug out from the bowels of the earth. Thus, **Onesicritus** <note>An officer under Alexander the Great who wrote about the natural history of India and Persia</note> wrote that in Carmania there is a "metal" of red ochre; and **Herodotus** <note>The 5th-century BCE Greek historian</note> wrote of a "metal" of salt in Libya near Mount Atlas. This is also testified by **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the massive 1st-century *Natural History*</note> in the 33rd book of his *Natural History*. But others have said that a "metal" is properly that which, when melted, returns to its original form, and which is **ductile** <note>capable of being hammered thin without breaking</note> and can be extended by a hammer, and is hard and capable of receiving an impression. For this reason, they divided them primarily into six: namely Gold, Silver, Copper, Tin, Lead, and Iron. Some have added Mercury, not because it is a metal in action <note>original: *actu*; meaning its current physical state</note> but because it may deservedly be called a metal in potential <note>original: *potentia*; an Aristotelian concept meaning it has the inherent capacity to become a solid metal</note>. The **Chemists** <note>Alchemists</note> have been accustomed to naming these by the names of the Planets—not because they link the material of the metals themselves to the planets (as Aubert foolishly imagines), but partly moved by a certain similarity to the greater and principal celestial bodies. For this reason, they called the two most perfect metals the **Sun** [Gold] and the **Moon** [Silver]. Because of the hardness of iron, they called it **Mars**, whom the poets devised as the God of war and arms; and they called quicksilver **Mercury** because of its very great and almost uncertain movement. Partly also, in the manner of the **Pythagoreans** <note>followers of Pythagoras, known for using numbers and symbols to hide sacred or scientific truths from the uninitiated</note>, they did this to cover their secrets with certain enigmatic veils. Furthermore, I see no reason why **antimony** <note>original: *stibium*; a brittle, silvery-white metalloid</note> should be properly numbered among the metals; therefore, it must be excluded from that class (if I may say so, with all due respect to Agricola, upon whose authority Aubert relies), since it completely contradicts the definition of a metal. ### TO AUBERT.

...they are all capable of being impressed <note>meaning they can take a physical impression from a stamp or die, a key characteristic of malleable metals</note>; for this reason, they are distinguished from many liquefiable stones in which moisture is not strongly mixed with dry earthiness, as well as from the infinite types of **marcasites** and **semi-metals**. Experts experience daily that **antimony** <term>Stibium: here referring to the mineral stibnite or the metallic element antimony</term>, once melted, completely loses its original form; and since it is established by practical use that it is neither **ductile** <note>capable of being hammered thin</note> nor capable of being impressed, it cannot properly be called a metal.

Nevertheless, our friend Aubert chose to assert this—he who is so "learned" in metallic matters that he still dreams that **tin-ice** <note>original: *glaciale stannum*; a historical name for bismuth</note> (which is actually **bismuth** <term>bisemutum: a brittle metal often confused with tin or lead in the 16th century</term> and that ash-colored type of lead about which Agricola says more in Book 8 of *On the Nature of Minerals*) is refined antimony and the **regulus** <term>regulus: the metallic heart or "button" that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</term> of the Chemists; which is plainly absurd. 

For "tin-ice," which is correctly called bismuth, is in no way a "prepared antimony"; nor can the Chemists' regulus, extracted with tartar and nitre, be called bismuth—a point I leave to be judged by the learned and all those of sound mind. But these points matter little, since, as we have said, many things are called by the name "metal" though not properly so. And indeed, this is to be forgiven in Aubert, who has never seen any mines anywhere to judge these things correctly, nor has he grasped the opinion of **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, the foremost mining authority of the age</note>.

Meanwhile, he complains that the Chemists divide the metals themselves into **perfect** and **imperfect**; he thinks this is ridiculous for many reasons. First, because a certain definition handed down by **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century scholar whose works were central to European alchemy</note> applies no less to one metal than to another; yet, he argues that so the perfect might be properly distinguished from the imperfect, one definition should have been established for the former and another for the latter. 

As if, indeed, the definition of a "man" does not apply to a "boy," even though he has not yet reached a man's age and appears different from him in other "accidental" qualities—just as metals differ among themselves. By this logic, there ought to be different definitions for white and red corals, although they differ only because the white ones have not reached the final degree of perfection by means of complete and finished **coction** <term>coctio: the alchemical "cooking" or ripening process by which nature matures base minerals into gold</term>; yet there is one and the same definition for all of them. 

But to better prove his opinion, Aubert writes that whatever things possess an "essential form"—which it is certain individual metals have—must necessarily be "perfect." He argues that kind Nature, the parent of all things, in no way ceases or rests in performing her duty until she has reached the goal she set for herself, unless she is hindered. He adds that the matter from which something natural is made, and with which nature occupies herself, is in motion for as long as it takes to achieve its essential form. From all these things...
