### RESPONSE

...finally, [Aubert] concludes that metals cannot rightly be divided into **perfect** and **imperfect**, and that **gold** should not be called more excellent or more perfect than the others in any way, even if it is more brilliant and better tempered. All of these arguments, which are weak and futile, must be refuted by us. And so that we may follow everything in the proper order, we must demonstrate that gold itself is deservedly called more perfect, more excellent, and purer than the other metals by true Philosophers, so that we may conclude from this that the division of metals into "perfect" and "imperfect" by the Chemists <note>meaning Alchemists</note> is not without reason. 

Therefore, let me rely on the authority of **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note>, from whom Aubert especially derived all these points of his. He certainly writes in Book 5 of *On the Origin and Causes of Subterranean Matters* that metals differ among themselves not only in luster, but also in color, taste, smell, weight, and power. Speaking especially of luster (which you, Aubert, admit is present in gold and silver), he says: <note>original: "Sed quo humor ipse fuerit subtilior, densior, & purior, eo metallum est nitidius & splendidius: qua de causa etiam hac parte cæteris præstat aurum."</note> *“But the more subtle, dense, and pure the moisture itself is, the more bright and shining the metal becomes; for which reason gold also excels the others in this regard.”* Agricola himself seeks this excellence of gold in the differences of smell, taste, and weight. 

For **imperfect metals**, when they are melted into a liquid state, are perceived as bitter to the taste, such as **copper** <note>original: *æs*</note> and **iron**. The cause of this bitterness is the "burnt earth" which those metals participate in, as Agricola himself testifies. But the others, because of their pure earth or more abundant water, do not affect the liquids with a very noticeable taste; rather, they are somewhat sweet, like **gold** and **silver**. Furthermore, since the purest earth is in gold itself, and is most perfectly tempered with its own water, it emits a very small and scarcely perceptible smoke when it is burned, and it is sweet rather than foul-smelling. 

Moreover, Georgius <note>Agricola</note> adds that because of its purity, gold has almost no "excrement" <note>impurities or dross</note> in it when it is purged by fire, while the others have much; but one has more than another according to how much more impure it might be. The excellence of gold is also to be investigated in its own force and power: for besides gold and the **Moon** <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term>, the others vanish into smoke during the process of **cupellation** <term>cineritio & copella: refining processes using a shallow porous cup (cupel) to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</term> and perish by the violence of the fire. This happens to them because less pure earth and a less perfect tempering is found in them—and it happens more quickly to one than another, as happens to iron, because of the impure earth of which much is inside it.

### TO AUBERT.

...moisture, it protects the earth so it is not set on fire, as **Agricola** says: this happens, as others believe, from the most subtle dry and moist parts, having no impurity mixed in. For this reason, according to the nature of things, **gold** is purer than the remaining metals, and surpasses them in value, because it is the simplest and purest metal, and most removed from the imperfection of the elements due to its form. <margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 33, chapter 3.</margin> Thus **Pliny** says, "To gold alone, of all things, nothing is lost by fire." This is also what the Poet sang, as can be seen from the previous pages. And from these points one may gather that among all metals, gold alone is not only the most splendid and well-tempered, but also the most perfect; in respect to which the other metals are rightly called "imperfect." 

For nature always tends toward perfection alone—namely, toward the making of gold—which alone among the metals is called "perfect." For no natural agent, as the **Philosophers** say, ceases its action upon its matter, nor is it separated from it, except with the introduction of the <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or identity that makes a thing what it is, as opposed to its raw "matter."</note> into that matter. Therefore, as long as the agent is joined to the matter, or acts upon the matter, that thing is called "imperfect," since the perfection of a thing does not exist except through the introduction of its form. 

When, therefore, in all metals a certain viscous water—which the **Chemical Philosophers** <note>Meaning Alchemists</note> call **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> because of its similarity—is placed in the position of "matter," and **sulfur** (which they call so by a similar likeness) acts as the "agent" that introduces the form into that matter, no metal can be called "perfect" except that from which the sulfur itself has been separated. But because the other metals have the aforementioned sulfur mixed into their matter, they are destroyed, blackened, <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to a powder or ash through heat</note>, and burned (which happens to them solely because of that dry exhalation—namely, the sulfur—which becomes a material suitable for ignition). For this reason, they are called entirely "imperfect." 

On the contrary, gold alone is entirely stripped of that sulfur, which is sufficiently indicated by the affinity between gold and quicksilver: <margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 33, chapter 6.</margin> (For all things, as Pliny writes, float upon it [quicksilver] except gold, which is the only thing it attracts to itself). By this reasoning, gold is immune to all those corruptions, both in the fire and out of it. It is rightly called the only "perfect" metal, formed according to the first and true intention of nature: complete, because it has reached the ultimate goal in which it is finished; and pure, because the "agent" is not mixed with the matter but is separated from it. On this opinion, **Aristotle** writes the following in the last chapter of *Metaphysics*, Book 3, when speaking of metals. "For this reason," he says, "they all contain earth within them and are burned, because [they contain] a dry exhalation..."

<meta>This page continues Joseph Du Chesne’s rebuttal to Jacques Aubert. The previous page established gold as the most refined metal because it resists fire. Here, Du Chesne addresses Aubert’s philosophical argument that all metals, having their own distinct "forms," should be considered "perfect" in their own right. Du Chesne uses the analogy of an egg and a bird to argue that while a metal might be a "perfect" version of itself, it is "imperfect" relative to the ultimate goal of nature: gold.</meta>

### RESPONSE

they possess. But gold alone of all things is by no means accustomed to being burned. But not content with these reasons, **Aubert** will respond: Whatever things have attained an essential <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the internal principle that gives a thing its identity and properties.</note> must necessarily be perfect; moreover, he will say that no one, except for some dull-witted bellows-blower <note>original: "ciniflonem" — a derogatory term for a low-level worker or a "puffer" who works the bellows without understanding the science.</note>, would deny that individual metals have their own **substantial form**, and by this reasoning he will conclude that all metals are also perfect. But it will be easy enough for us to respond to this objection: For those things which persist in their own nature are indeed called "perfect" within their own species through their substantial form; yet some things persist in nature in their own species which are nevertheless perfected in a certain way through their substantial form, toward which there is a certain limit of movement. But because they are carried toward another final substantial form which completely fills and perfects the thing itself, they are therefore said to be **imperfect** as long as they remain under that first form, when considered in relation to that final form which they strive to attain. If one does not consider that final form, but views them only in themselves, they are certainly perfect in that species of theirs, through that substantial form of theirs, just as that species requires. 

Everyone sees this in the **generation of eggs**, in which there is a certain limit of movement in the acquisition of its substantial form, which thus remains. But because the eggs themselves are destined by nature not to remain under that form, but to generate a **bird**, and thus the acquisition of the final substantial form takes place, the eggs are therefore said to be "imperfect" under the form of an egg; however, the thing is "perfect" after the generation of the bird, since that is the ultimate end of the eggs. This must also be judged regarding **metals**: although they have attained a certain essential form within their own species, they cannot be called "perfect" when gold is taken into account—which alone, as we have said, is perfect—until they have reached that final and absolute end, namely, the perfection of gold itself, and have turned into gold. 

And just as in the **generation of an embryo** a comparison is made of the <term>vegetative soul</term> to the <term>sensitive soul</term>, and the sensitive to the <term>rational soul</term> <note>In the biology of the time, life was thought to progress through stages: the vegetative (growth), the sensitive (feeling), and finally the rational (human reason).</note>, because the earlier ones are like preparations for the rational soul and not like final forms, so the other imperfect metals seem to relate to **gold**. Therefore, the **Chemical philosophers** <note>The alchemists.</note> rightly divided metals into "perfect" and "imperfect." For although the difference between metals lies in the form itself, it will not properly be a difference of species—like the difference between a horse and a man—but will be understood more properly in terms of the matter and its parts: namely, according to what is **digested** and **undigested**, **complete** and **incomplete**, since they are entirely of the same proper matter, but undigested and incom-

### TO AUBERT.

completed, and determined toward gold. However, because iron is more commodious for human use, **Aubert** judges it to be more noble than gold for that reason; a point which, I believe, he could not persuade any physicians to accept—no matter how unlearned—since they seek gold, not iron. But I think enough has been said by me concerning the excellence and perfection of gold. Yet, since we have said that all metals consist of the same proper matter (though not equally digested in all of them), which is the very hinge upon which this question turns, we must now proceed to investigate that matter of metals. 

Philosophers establish a twofold matter for metals, just as they do for all other **composite bodies** <term>mixtorum corporum: substances formed by the combination of the four elements</term>. One is general and most remote, which is taken from the elements as the primary components of all things; they consist of these as the simplest parts, and into these simplest parts they are eventually resolved. Regarding the qualities and virtues of these elements, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> contend against the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy that held that substances could occupy the same space simultaneously.</note> that they merely pass into one another and are mixed; the Stoics, on the contrary, attempt to assert that their entire substances are mixed throughout. But leaving behind those waves of slippery opinions, we retreat to a safe and tranquil port, and in this matter, we approve of **Aubert's** opinion, which holds that elements do not subsist in mixtures essentially or actually, but potentially. **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> testifies to this in the first book of *The Method of Healing*, where he writes that elements are mixed "whole with whole" only according to their qualities.

Concerning their second and "proper" matter, however, the opinion of many Philosophers is not one, but widely diverse. For some have called a **moist exhalation** <term>halitum humidum: a damp, smoky vapor rising from the earth</term> the proximate matter of metals, as **Aristotle** did; some say it is water affected by other elements, which was the view of **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, often called the "father of mineralogy."</note>, an opinion with which our **Aubert** agrees; others say it is ash moistened with water. But the **Chemists** <note>The Alchemists.</note>, whose opinion **Aubert** attempts to subvert, have said that **quicksilver** <term>argentum viuum: mercury</term> is their matter; some have added **sulfur**. All these opinions must be briefly and diligently examined by us so that the matter may become clearer, and so everyone may understand that **Aubert** and others have unjustly attacked so many distinguished Chemical Philosophers.

<margin>Aristotle, *Meteorology*, last chapter.</margin>
**Aristotle**, easily the prince of Philosophers, established a twofold matter for those things which are created within and above the earth by celestial power and force: namely, **exhalation** and **vapor**. He believes all things are born and created by the mixing of these in the depths of the earth. He distinguishes these into two categories according to the diverse nature of the matter: namely, into **fossils** <note>In this period, "fossils" referred to anything dug out of the earth (minerals, stones), not just organic remains.</note> and **metals**. They are called fossils because they are dug from the earth and are similar to the earth that is dug up, and they are not meltable, such as stones...

kinds of stones, which are produced from dry exhalation kindled by heat, and by the consumption and, in a way, scorching of moisture by their own heat. Others are metallic, some of which are **fusible** or **meltable**, because they lean more toward the nature of moisture than dryness—such as lead and tin—and they are so called because they melt more easily when they are worked. **Ductile** metals, on the other hand, are those which are melted with greater difficulty, such as iron. The immediate matter of these is a **vaporous breath** <note>original Latin: *halitus vaporosus*. In Aristotelian physics, this refers to a moist, gas-like substance trapped underground.</note>, which is condensed by cold and hardens into metal according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, whom our **Aubert** nonetheless believes is worthy of rebuke. For, **Aubert** says, it can in no way happen in the nature of things that a transition occurs from one extreme or contrary to another without some middle state. Now, it is clear that both metals and breaths are endowed with contrary qualities, because the latter are the thinnest while the former are the densest. From this he concludes that in the birth of metals, the breaths and vapors must necessarily condense into liquid before they harden into metals.

<margin>Book 5 of *On the Origins and Causes of Subterranean Things* <note>A reference to Georgius Agricola’s famous 1546 work on mineralogy, *De ortu et causis subterraneorum*.</note></margin>
These points he took from **Agricola**. But **Jacob Schegk**—a man by far most learned—defends the undeservedly rebuked **Aristotle** more than sufficiently in his commentaries on **Aristotle’s** *Meteorology*. There he teaches that the breath or vapor from which water condenses is one thing, and that from which metals condense is another; just as there is another still from which frost comes. For the metallic vapor is sometimes heavier and thicker than the vapor that produces water. For this reason, those who say that water is the "remote matter" of metals propose a more distant origin than those who say it is "breath"; since a great part of **meteorological phenomena** <term>μετεωρῶν (*meteōrōn*): phenomena occurring in the atmosphere or the earth's crust, including minerals and weather</term> are produced from these breaths and vaporous matters, stirred up from water and earth by the power of heat; since there is no fertility of earth and water without heat. 

For heat, as its first offspring and fruit, procreates these two vapors, in whose nature the vigor of their parents—namely the four elements—is represented. Their generative power conspires, so to speak, with two qualities acting with a masculine force <note>Heat and cold, the active qualities.</note>, and the other two being passive, like females <note>Moisture and dryness, the passive qualities.</note>; both, however, obeying the celestial tempering as if it were their father. Hence, these inanimate things are usually procreated by the instrument of these primary qualities. This can even be perceived by the senses: for such thick vapors sometimes present themselves in subterranean places that it is not possible for miners to breathe, and sometimes, as **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> testifies, they are even suffocated by the thickness. If they are so thick, who will believe that metals and breaths are endowed with such contrary qualities that they cannot transition into one another?

# TO AUBERT

...breath <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page, arguing that "breaths" or exhalations can turn directly into solids.</note>, so that they might be able to solidify into the solid matter of metals even without another intermediate state <note>Aubert had argued there must be a liquid state (like water) between vapor and solid metal.</note>, just as a heavy vapor turns into frost? Furthermore, if countless witnesses testify that it has rained bronze and iron, and that stones and such bodies solidify and are produced in the upper air, how then can these be generated from water and earth—which have no place to stay in the sky—rather than from breath and vapor, which can both penetrate and remain there due to their thinness and heat? Therefore, it is certain that metals arise from breath rather than from water; which breath, because it is thick, also solidifies easily.

But why say more on these matters? For it is established among all Philosophers that all things arise from those substances into which they are ultimately reduced <note>The principle that you can tell what a thing is made of by seeing what it turns into when destroyed.</note>. Now, all metals except the two "perfect" ones <note>Gold and silver, which were considered "perfect" because they do not lose weight or "vanish" when heated.</note>—which possess a more compact and fixed matter due to a greater **decoction** <term>decoction: a process of "cooking" or refining by natural heat within the earth</term>—are they not reduced into a breath or vapor? In the test of the ash-cup and the **cupel** <term>cupel: a shallow, porous ceramic bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</term>, do they not vanish entirely into the air? They turn indeed into smoke—not the kind that is converted into water or that makes things wet—but a thick smoke, on account of the earthy mixture, which solidifies and thickens by cold.

This can be seen daily through certain experience by **pyrotechnicians** <note>literally "fire-workers," referring to metallurgists and assayers</term> and can be perceived even more easily by Philosophers in their **sublimations** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, skipping the liquid phase</term>. This is proven by **Tutty**, **Cadmia**, **Pompholyx** <note>These are historical terms for various zinc oxides and furnace residues.</note>, and other substances of this sort, which are raised from the vapors of metals and cling to the walls of the furnaces. Even in the mines themselves, these substances indicate that those vapors are thick and do not represent water in any way.

Therefore, let **Aubert** be silent with his "leaden argument" <note>A pun meaning both a heavy/dull argument and one related to the metal lead.</note>, he who has attempted to tear apart the opinion of **Aristotle**. Let him realize that those vapors from which metals first solidify and harden without another medium are extremely thick.

Having defended **Aristotle**, let us see what opinion he holds concerning other most learned men and Philosophers. **Aubert** refutes the opinion of **Albertus Magnus**, **Geber**, and the rest of the **charcoal-burners** <note>original: *carbonariorum*. # TO AUBERT

...[most] heavy, so that even the most solid bodies of all metals float upon it, with the sole exception of gold because of the great affinity between the two. From this, it is clear that it is of a different substance than one that is simply "airy," like oil. 

Therefore, based on the likeness of this **quicksilver** <note>original: *argenti vivi*</note>, the Chemical Philosophers have said that the "proximate matter" <term>proximate matter: the immediate substance from which something is formed, as opposed to "prime matter" or basic elements</term> of metals is quicksilver itself. This is generated from a powerful mixing of the first matter of all metals—namely, from a viscous, incombustible moisture incorporated with a subtle earthiness, equally and strongly mixed through its smallest parts within the mineral caverns of the earth. 

To this, wise nature (since matter does not bring itself into being) has added a specific active agent, namely **sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur*</note>, which is nothing other than a certain fatness of the earth generated in its own mines and condensed through a temperate **decoction** <term>decoction: a process of heating or "cooking" substances in liquid to extract their essence or mature them</term>, so that by **digesting** <term>digestion: in alchemy, the slow maturation of a substance through steady heat, mimicking the Earth's natural processes</term> and cooking that quicksilver, nature converts it into the form of a metal. Thus, this sulfur relates to quicksilver as the male to the female, and as the specific active agent to its specific matter. 

This does not mean that this quicksilver and this sulfur are found in their own pure nature by themselves in the mines—as some foolishly think—but rather that they have already been mixed by nature and reduced into the nature of earth through a very long process of concoction. And this is indeed the "proximate matter" of metals, just as in the generation of a human being, food is a closer matter than the raw elements, blood is closer than the food itself, and the seed is closer still than the blood; until finally, through continuous digestion, the matter receives the form of a man. 

So, when metals are said to be made first from the four elements as if from a general and primary matter, it must happen in this arranged order: namely, that from those elements vapors are made; from the vapors, a viscous water is made (which is a matter closer than the vapors themselves—lest Aubert think we are contradicting ourselves while trying to defend Aristotle); and then a heavy water mixed with the finest sulfurous earth, which is called quicksilver. From this, as from a closer matter, through the mediation of the mixing and the action of extrinsic sulfur, gold is made, or another metal according to the greater or lesser "digestion" of nature itself. 

For as the **Philosopher** <note>A common title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> writes in the *Metaphysics*: "When something is said to be made from something else, it is made either as the extreme and perfect from the middle and imperfect—as a man from a boy—or as one extreme from another extreme—as air from water." 

But come, let us return to our Aubert. He also [claims] sulfur [is] the [matter of metals]...

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of Jacques Aubert. The previous page ended with a discussion of the properties of sulfur and its inability to dissolve in water, contradicting Aubert’s claims. This page continues the argument regarding the "proximate matter" of metals and transitions into a discussion of Aristotelian physics—specifically the active and passive qualities that govern the formation of all substances.</meta>

# TO AUBERT

...[pro]perties and virtues of these principles, so that from them each of the metals can be generated according to the diversity of its composition, its <term>digestion</term> <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturing or "cooking" a substance through gentle, continuous heat to bring it to perfection.</note>, and its location. This will suffice regarding the proximate matter of metals, which Aubert claims is water affected by other elements. However, he has remained silent on the reason why he thinks so, contenting himself with saying that this was handed down by others, or found by him in the writings of others. This is certainly the voice of a man who demonstrates his opinion by the faith of another, rather than by reason, as true philosophers are accustomed to do. 

But now the "active causes" call our attention, which philosophers establish as twofold, along with two corresponding passive causes. For heat and cold are called <term>active</term> <note>original Greek: ποιητικὰ (*poiētika*), meaning productive or creative qualities</note> by Aristotle, because they have the power to move or change things. On the other hand, the moist and the dry are called <term>passive</term> <note>original Greek: παθητικὰ (*pathētika*), meaning receptive or susceptible to being acted upon</note>. Because of these passive qualities, things are said to "suffer" change <note>The author uses "suffer" in the philosophical sense of *passio*, meaning to be acted upon by an external force.</note> rather than to act themselves. They are said to be affected by the former active qualities as if by more noble ones, which are eminent by nature, and through whose efficacy "form" is procreated in things. For matter is not known through itself, but through change, which does not occur without this "suffering" or being acted upon; just as matter itself cannot be understood without touch, which is abolished through <term>natural union</term> <note>original Greek: σύμφυσιν (*symphysis*), referring to the process of substances growing together or merging into one</note> and solidification, and through the introduction of actualized existence and form.

Furthermore, it must be observed that from the mixture of the dry and the moist, bodies are first called "solidified," and then either soft or hard. There is a triple difference among these solidified things: 
1. A watery moisture that solidifies.
2. Something dry and earthy.
3. A mixture of both. 

These substances are also sometimes melted, sometimes dried, sometimes moistened, or sometimes softened. However, those things are "uncoagulable" (cannot be solidified) which are dry and fiery, such as honey and <term>must</term> <note>Fresh, unfermented grape juice</note>, as well as those things that are predominantly moist and airy, such as oily substances. Therefore, these are not elements, nor are they the matter of these "sufferings" or physical transformations. 

Regarding bodies that solidify and harden, according to Aristotle, some are affected by heat and others by cold. Heat works by drying out the moisture, while cold works by squeezing out the heat. Therefore, those things that are coagulated by heat through the absence of moisture are dissolved by cold, which allows the moisture to enter again—as is the case with salt. But those things that solidify through the deprivation of heat are dissolved when heat enters them again—as is the case with metals. For whatever is dissolved by melting is liquefied either by fire or by water. It must be that what water liquefies was solidified by dry heat (that is, fiery heat); but what fire liquefies, or whose solidification it partially dissolves (such as horn), these coalesce from cold. This is because the causes of contrary effects are themselves contrary. And since by heat...

Regarding this, none of the **Chemical Philosophers** <note>The author uses "Chemici" to refer to alchemists or practitioners of the "chemical art."</note> doubt, although, as **Aristotle** sometimes says, experience demonstrates the opposite to us. For even salt solidified by heat can be dissolved and liquefied by fire itself, as I have quite often experienced, and that is called **fusible salt**. 

Nor should **Albertus Magnus**, that most eminent Philosopher, have been rebuked by our **Aubert**, because he attributes the power of forming metals to heat; for Albert by no means understood this to be caused by heat alone, as Aubert supposes. It must be understood, therefore, on the testimony of Aristotle, that things are said to "suffer" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, to "suffer" means to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> by the cause of cold rather than to "act": because clearly cold is the property of the passive elements—namely water and earth—both of which are cold by nature. For they do not receive cold from elsewhere as they do heat; rather, by the removal of heat, they grow cold by their own nature, nor are they cooled by an external cause in the way air and fire are.

Therefore, although cold may possess a power of acting in mixed bodies, it is nevertheless more effective for *corruption* <note>The breaking down or decay of a substance.</note> than for *generation*. For that reason, the Alchemists are not to be so rebuked, even if they say that nature requires **subterranean heat** for the procreation of metals, as a more effective "active cause" <note>original Latin: *causa effectrice*</note> which might mix, change, arrange, **digest**, and cook their matter, and finally, through a long stretch of time, shape it into gold as its ultimate end. 

Nor was it appropriate to accuse them for referring some power to the **influence of the celestial bodies**. For Aristotle confirms their opinion in his book *On the Heavens and the World*, and in the book *On the Causes of the Properties of the Elements*, with these words:

> Because the first moving principles for the generation and introduction of form in each thing are the stars and super-celestial bodies through their motion and light. For they are the ones which first move (being moved by the "intelligences") <note>In medieval cosmology, "intelligences" were spiritual beings or angels thought to guide the movement of the planetary spheres.</note> to complete the nature of generation and corruption for the preservation of species; and from them, form and perfection are given. And as he says in another place: "the sun and man together generate man." <note>original: *sol et homo hominem generant*. This was a common medieval philosophical shorthand for the idea that biological life requires both physical parents and the life-giving energy of the sun.</note>

Nor does Aubert rightly conclude from this reasoning that the art of **Chemistry** is vain simply because metals coalesce by the power of the stars, arguing that Alchemists are not permitted to make use of this celestial power. For the Alchemists believe, along with the Philosopher [Aristotle], that if forms are introduced into lower things by the motion and light of the celestial bodies—and by their positions and aspects—the same consequence must also occur in metals. But that happens as if from a general and very remote cause. For as we have said, they have another more **proximate active cause**, namely **heat**, by whose power the solidified metals in the bowels of the earth are arranged,

# TO AUBERT

...are digested and perfected. Having explained these things, we must see where Aubert is heading and what his ultimate goal is. He wishes to show that the labor of the **Chemists** <note>In this context, "Chemists" (Chemistarum) refers to alchemists.</note> is empty and useless when they undertake the perfecting of metals. He denies that copper, tin, iron, or lead (which they call "imperfect") can be perfected by any art or converted into gold and silver. First, he says, it is well-established that those four metals are perfect. On the contrary, we demonstrated a little while ago for many reasons that they are indeed imperfect; nor can it be denied that through art and a lighter preparation, they can be rendered more perfect and excellent within their own kind.

Rightly, therefore, **Aristotle** says in the *Meteorology*, Book 4, Chapter 6: "Even worked iron can be melted so that it becomes liquid, and then it thickens again. This is how they are accustomed to make **steel** <note>original: "chalybs"</note>. For the dross of the iron settles and is separated into the bottom; but when it has been frequently purified and emerges pure and clean, it becomes steel. Iron is more excellent the less **waste** <note>original: "excrementi"; referring to impurities or slag in the ore.</note> it contains." But let us set aside authority, since we have already sufficiently proved this very point by philosophical reasons, by which we have demonstrated more than enough that gold alone is perfect, while all others are imperfect.

Aubert adds further, in order to make the art of **transmutation** <note>The alchemical process of changing one metal into another.</note> seem impossible: "Those things which are perfected and formed by art are artificial; however, metals, by the very notion of their name and the definition of their essence, are natural." For he says they are minerals. Those things are derived from a natural principle alone; therefore they are natural, and this is according to Aristotle. For natural things have the principle of their own making within themselves; but those things made by art do not, but rather obtain it from the outside and from others. He adds, to finish his argument briefly, that no natural form can be given by art, from which he concludes that no metals can be considered artificial.

Come then, it is our duty to overthrow these arguments, so that we may finally demonstrate that the **Chemical Art** is true, which imitates nature itself to transmute metals. We said above that those things are called "imperfect" which are in motion toward that form for which they are ultimately intended; but they are "perfect" when they have reached the end of that motion. And since we have already shown that gold alone has reached the final limit of motion and is formed according to the true intention of nature, we have therefore concluded that gold alone is perfect, while the rest, which are in motion toward the form of gold, are imperfect. Nature always pursues the perfection of these in her own **womb** <note>The "womb of the earth," where minerals were thought to grow like embryos.</note>, so that they might finally reach that state, but only over a long stretch of time...

They advise that they be left alone for thirty years or more until a perfect **concoction** <term>concoction: the natural process of maturing or "ripening" metals through subterranean heat</term> is achieved by the heat beneath the earth.

For when the digestion is complete, then the gold is found as **pure gold** <term>pure gold: the author uses the term "obrizum," referring to gold refined to the highest standard</term>, most pure, and truly perfect. From these things, it is clear that although metals are at a certain stage of movement, they are not at the final stage; they are on a path and in transition toward gold, as if toward the only perfect state.

<margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 33, Chapter 6.</margin>
Furthermore, wherever any vein of metal is found, another is found not far away; for this reason, the Greeks (according to Pliny) seem to have named metals as if they were **one after another** <note>original Greek: "μετ' ἄλλα" (met' alla)</note>, because they are found one after the other.

But regarding this opinion, Aubert will say: "If imperfect things are reduced into gold by nature through further boiling, why do the miners not wait for that time? Especially since, if this were to happen, they would have a much more abundant profit from it." We respond that there are certain things that make the generation of metals different, not only in species but in properties and accidents, according to the regions and places in which they arise. In the same way, animals also vary, as **Aristotle** writes in Book 6 of *On Animals*. For in Egypt, scorpions are not venomous, whereas in other places they are the opposite; and over a span of time, depending on the locations themselves, **wheat** <note>original: "triticum"</note> degenerates into **rye** <note>original: "filigo" (usually "siligo"), referring to a lesser grain or winter wheat</note>, and conversely, rye into wheat. So it must be said of metals: although they are intended by nature for that end—namely, that they become gold—nevertheless, due to the diversity of regions and mines and their own corruption, some can be brought to their degree of perfection so that they become gold, while others remain on the path of imperfection, according to the diversity of their digestion and purification. ...coagulates those things that are undigested, such as lead and tin; others [it coagulates] by a scorching and superfluous heat, such as copper and iron; certain things, on the other hand, do not solidify due to a lack of that very heat and a defect in the acting force, such as quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver"</note>. Finally, nature produces the Moon <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for silver</note> with a sufficiently tempered heat, but the Sun <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical name for gold</note> with a heat far more tempered, needing no further operation by which it might be perfected, as it is that which has attained its ultimate end and completion. <margin>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, Book 2.</margin>
as Aristotle says in the second book of *On the Heavens*: That one thing is a good completion which needs no operation to become good; and all perfection of things is placed in this: that they receive their final completion. Since, therefore, imperfect metals have not reached that ultimate end of perfection and completion due to the aforementioned causes, they require the operation of art. By the help of art, through imitating nature herself, they may finally be perfected and attain the ultimate end for which they were ordained by nature: namely, that they become gold. For as the philosopher <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> writes in the second book of the 

<margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 2.</margin>
*Physics*: In every way, art completes those things which nature cannot perform, and in other matters, it imitates. Thus, with nature assisted by art, trees produce their flowers and fruits even in the winter time in cold regions—which nature on its own could never provide. This can be seen at Heidelberg in the **heated room** <term>heated room: the original "hypocaustum" refers to a room heated by an ancient Roman-style underfloor system, here likely a greenhouse or conservatory</term> of the Count Palatine, and in many other places. 

But in the whole work of Alchemy <term>Alchemy: the original term "Chemia" encompasses both what we now call chemistry and the traditional pursuit of transmutation</term>, where Aubert says that nature remains entirely at rest and that art alone moves the subject, he speaks most falsely. For by reason of the acting nature, Alchemy is a natural work; indeed, the matter is that very thing which, by boiling, seeks, retains, digests, expels, mixes, dissolves, generates, and forms—by the command of Almighty God—the **stone** <term>stone: likely the Philosopher's Stone, the substance believed to catalyze the transformation of base metals into gold</term> in its own time, with which nature forms metals through that very mixing. 

However, by reason of the service provided, I admit Alchemy is an artificial work; not because art itself dissolves, generates, and forms, but only insofar as it provides all these things to nature as it works—things which nature alone could not otherwise achieve by itself. For nature works in a twofold way to generate gold: one way, primarily and by itself, when it generates gold in its own mines from its own principles, in which way it is impossible for art to imitate nature. Second, it works by itself but not primarily: namely, because it first generates one of the imperfect [metals] from those same principles in its mine, and finally converts it into gold...

# RESPONSE

[philosophe]rs: in what way art follows nature itself, in that from imperfect metals—just as nature itself does—it finally procreates gold. From these points it is clear that one thing becomes another in two ways: namely, mediately and immediately. According to Aristotle in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, there can be multiple matters for the same thing—specifically, the mediate <note>a primary or intermediate stage of matter</note> and the immediate <note>the matter in its final state ready for transformation</note>—although it is necessary that mediate matter be ultimately reduced to the immediate. Otherwise, different things would be produced from different matters. 

Since, therefore, art assumes the same mediate and immediate matter as nature, and art reduces the mediate ultimately to the immediate (just as nature herself does), and it possesses one and the same agent <note>the active force or catalyst</note> which polishes the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> and finally transforms it; and if the end of art is the same as that of nature—namely, that from the union of that form with its matter it finally generates gold—there is no doubt that art, by imitating nature herself, is able to produce perfect metal from imperfect ones in all respects, just as nature herself produces it, as we have said above. Since the causes of these are all the same, it is necessarily the case that the thing itself is the same and must produce the same effects.

Nor do I think those are to be excused who seek the "subject" <note>the starting material</note> of the chemical philosophers in vegetables <note>plant matter</note>. For their operation is vain, since generation cannot occur except from the closest, suitable, and immediate materials. Others expend their operations on animal things, especially on the egg. Because of a certain similarity to the "movement" <note>the development or gestation</note> of eggs, the chemical philosophers called their own work the "philosophical egg." They said that the egg itself, just like the elixir, contains the four elements: the shell of which they call earth; the membrane, air; the white, water; and the yolk, fire. 

In the same way, these same philosophers enigmatically said that their stone is "one in three, and three in one," because it contains within itself the body that stands <note>the fixed, physical substance</note>, the soul that vivifies <note>the life-giving principle</note>, and the spirit that tints <note>original: "spiritum qui tingit"; the volatile principle that provides the color/quality of gold</note>. Those who did not understand these enigmas persuaded themselves that a literal egg is the philosophers' stone because it contains three things in one—namely, the shell, the yolk, and the "water" <note>the albumen</note>. Therefore, they finally concluded that the egg is that unique matter required by the chemists. They were no less deceived than the others, not noticing that this matter is entirely unsuited for drawing out metal. For man generates man, and beast generates beast <note>the principle of "like produces like"</note>. Because the good Aubertus <note>Jacques Aubert, a physician and critic of alchemy to whom this response is likely addressed.</note> experienced this to his own detriment (as I have heard), he who [used] the philosophical eggs...

->AD AVBERTVM.<-

...[philosophi]cally boiling, he boiled away several hundred gold coins, and now he mocks the art as if it had deceived him. This is indeed unjust, since he himself was the one who strayed, and the art should not be held responsible for his own fault. For genus ought to be joined with genus, and species with species, and every sprout must correspond to its own seed, as we have said above. There are others who seek the matter of their Elixir not in plants or animals, but in subterranean things that are more closely related <note>meaning other minerals or ores</note>. For they say that art imitates nature, and therefore they believe one must labor using the same principles by which nature operates; thus, they boil quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> and sulfur, having heard that these are the "nearest matter" of metals.

But the wretches lose both their oil and their labor <note>A Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort</note>, since the "quicksilver of the philosophers" is not the common variety, nor is the sulfur they use the same as common sulfur, as I have already stated. For who could follow nature's intention in the proper measure and proportion? Truly no one. Furthermore, if you apply quicksilver to even the smallest fire, it evaporates; even when mixed, it is easily separated—and sulfur is likewise easily removed—even though the conjunction of both is necessary until the very end of the "digestion" <note>the process of slow heating</note> in the generation of metals.

Thus are all those deceived who seek that Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> in marcasites <note>iron pyrites</note>, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, antimony, arsenic, or orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>. This is because it is either a sulfur that is entirely inseparable (and yet must be separated at the last stage, as we said), or because it is separated by a lesser fire, the writings of all philosophers denote that such a substance is not a sufficient "philosophical subject" <note>the starting material for the Great Work</note>.

They also err who think the male Sun <note>gold</note> and the female Moon <note>silver</note> should be taken and amalgamated—if I may use the technical terms of the art—with common Mercury, making one thing out of the three. They boil these chemically and sublime them <note>heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again</note>, and from them they finally try to draw out the "soul," which they then attempt to "fix" <note>make stable and resistant to fire</note>. For they depart from the writings of the philosophers, who all confess with one voice that the agent <note>the active force</note> is already joined and proportioned by nature within the minerals themselves, along with its own matter. They say there is a single thing in which the four elements are well-proportioned, so that within it are found the fixing and the fixed, the tinting and the tinted, the white and the red, and the male and the female composed together.

There is therefore, as we have also already said above, a certain "third nature" that is common and transformed by the various mixing and digestion of sulfur and quicksilver. Within this substance is the mineral power to generate the mixture; these two <note>sulfur and mercury</note> act upon each other perpetually, until they are led over from the form of imperfect bodies...

...of the things first generated (with the active agent not yet separated from its matter) into another form, until they finally reach—through continued digestions <note>The process of slow, constant heating</note> and purifications—that final and truly perfect form, which is the form of gold. This is the ultimate goal of the movement, where the active agent is entirely separated from its matter. Many seek to know what this is, but very few find it; or if they do find it, they are ignorant of the preparations and the intentions

<margin>Operations of the Philosopher’s Stone.</margin>
of the philosophers. Their medicine is drawn through art only from those things in which it lived potentially through nature, and in which the perfection of the "prime matter" <note>The fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made</note> and all metals are found.

<margin>I. Calcination.</margin>
Once they have found this matter, they believe it must first be calcined <note>Reduced to a powder by heat</note> and purged of all its filth by restoring the heat and preserving the innate moisture. For in chemical calcination, there should be no loss of the substance's body, but rather a multiplication of it.

<margin>II. Solution.</margin>
Next, they reduce the calcined matter—by thinning its density—into a certain liquid substance and back into its own "prime matter," which they call "mineral water that does not wet the hands" <note>original: "aquam mineralem, quæ manus non madefacit"; a classic alchemical term for a metallic liquid that represents the soul of the metal</note>. At that point, it becomes one in kind, though not one in number; they call the Sun its father, the Moon its mother, and Mercury the mediator. The "body" <note>the solid matter</note> is altered from its own form, and a new form is immediately introduced to it, since nothing in the nature of things can be found entirely stripped of all form.

<margin>III. Separation of the Elements.</margin>
This having been done, they separate the four elements from the now-dissolved matter and divide them into two parts: an ascending or spiritual part, and a lower or earthly part. These two parts are nevertheless of a single nature, for the lower part is the "ferment" that fixes the substance, and the upper part is the "soul" that brings life to the whole. However, this division is necessary so that all parts may eventually be transmuted into one another more easily: as the earthly part passes into water, it turns black; then as the water passes into air, it turns white; and finally, the air is converted into fire.

<margin>IV. Conjunction.</margin>
Once the separation of the elements is complete, they perform the "conjunction" <note>The joining of opposites</note> of the water of the air with the earth and fire, so that each of the elements is dispersed within the others while maintaining the proper proportion. In this way, they assign three parts of its water to the male <note>original: "mari"; likely a variation of 'mas' for the masculine principle</note> and nine to the female. Then like applauds its like, and equal rejoices in equal, due to the intense desire for material adherence and the sulfurous form.

It describes the transition of matter from a crude state into a spiritualized "mineral water" and finally into a unified, perfected form symbolized by gold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the alchemical "Great Work," moving from the initial stages of Calcination and Solution (described on the previous page) into the middle and final stages of the process: Putrefaction, Coagulation, Feeding, Sublimation, Fermentation, Exaltation, and the beginning of Augmentation.</meta>

->TO AUBERT.<-

<margin>V. Putrefaction.</margin>
These things, once joined, undergo putrefaction <note>The stage of "death" or decomposition of the matter, often associated with a black color (nigredo)</note>, yet through a moist heat—lest, if the fire be kindled too high, the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to the "spirit" or volatile principle of the metal, not necessarily common quicksilver</note> be separated or carried upward because of its spiritual nature. By this corruption, the matter is altered, the elements are naturally divided, and regeneration follows. For nothing is born or grows, not even inanimate things, unless putrefaction has first occurred.

<margin>VI. Coagulation.</margin>
After putrefaction, they proceed to coagulation. With the same very temperate and constant heat continually altering the matter, they work both internally and externally until the matter whitens and takes on the appearance of pearls. At this point, the "fixation" of volatile spirits with the solid bodies occurs, resulting in a true freezing or hardening. The chemical philosophers call this the "white thorn" <note>original: "Albam spinam"</note> and "white incombustible sulfur," which never retreats from the fire.

<margin>VII. Feeding.</margin>
Finally, they turn to feeding <note>original: "cibationem"; the process of "nourishing" the stone to increase its potency</note>, namely the thickening of the subtle and the thinning of the coarse. They do this by mixing their "water" with "ash," and their "milk" with "foliated earth" <note>Symbolic terms for the different liquid and solid states of the maturing matter</note>—doing so moderately, so that the whiteness and redness, the goodness, quantity, and power of the stone may grow and increase. By cooking and re-cooking, the matter is thus nourished.

<margin>VIII. Sublimation.</margin>
Then they sublime the matter, yet not through any common sublimation <note>Sublimation usually means turning a solid into vapor; here it refers to a spiritual refinement</note>. They purge it of all impurities, lifting the body up and rendering it spiritual, while making the spirit corporeal and "fixed." By diminishing the sulfurous saltiness, the whole is whitened and made so it can be liquefied very quickly.

<margin>IX. Fermentation.</margin>
When the sublimation is complete, they ferment the matter by joining the spirit with its whitened earth and "lime" as if with its own ferment <note>Like yeast in bread, the "ferment" (often gold or silver) imparts its nature to the rest of the matter</note>, or by incorporating the soul with the body. For spiritual qualities cannot show their permanent virtues unless they are joined with fixed bodies. The ferment reduces whatever is added to it to its own nature, color, and taste through this mutual impression of body and spirit. Without this, the work cannot be perfected, just as dough cannot rise without leaven.

<margin>X. Exaltation.</margin>
For the greater nobility of the matter, they judge it must be exalted by increasing the spirit and by refining the earth through a "natural rectification." This involves the circulation of all elements and their true "graduation" <note>Increasing the intensity of the qualities</note> until they are brought back into a perfect embrace.

<margin>XI. Augmentation.</margin>
Then they subject their Salamander <note>A symbol for the Philosopher's Stone, which, like the mythical lizard, thrives and matures in the heat of the fire</note> to solutions and coagulation—

It also shifts into a polemical defense against Jacques Aubert, a contemporary critic of alchemy.</meta>

-># RESPONSE<-

...by repeating [these steps], they increase the substance in power; and with a new ferment <note>A "leaven" or catalyst added to the alchemical matter to trigger a specific transformation</note>, they increase it in power and quantity, and this even unto infinity.

<margin>XII. Projection.</margin>
Finally, they perform the **projection** upon imperfect metals, using one part by weight upon many parts, according to the perfection of the medicine. For the more it is refined and colored, the more abundantly it works: and so, by imitating nature, they perfect the imperfect metals and convert them into the Moon and the Sun <note>Silver and gold</note>. This is done from its own material, purified by art and refined, then fixed by boiling and digestion, until it comes forth in a white color, and finally in a red color. Having been made volatile again, and once more fixed, until it has the power of ingress <note>The ability of the alchemical "medicine" to penetrate and permeate the molten base metal</note> and colors it perfectly, they prepare their medicine and their powder, which they call the **Philosopher’s Stone**.

And this [they do] through various operations, different substances, many vessels, and many furnaces, as those unskilled in the art might perhaps guess from the preceding; yet for the true philosopher, in all this "Great Work," there is but one operation, one way, one substance, one vessel, one fire, and one furnace, as they all confess with one voice. 

I wished to note all these things in passing so that I might overturn the opinion of Master Aubert <note>original: "Auberti"; referring to Jacques Aubert, a 16th-century physician who wrote against the chemical arts</note> concerning the stone of the philosophers (for it is lawful for anyone to play the fool by betraying their ignorance regarding unknown things) and to demonstrate that the naked form of both gold and silver, abstracted from its concrete body (which he himself believes), is not the matter of the philosophical medicine. 

But (he says), "I do not care from what thing the stone is composed; nevertheless, since it is not a natural being, it cannot take on a natural form, but only an artificial and deceptive one." 

I could here appeal to the testimony of many distinguished men, but I believe I must rely on reason instead. I say, therefore, that metals truly transmuted are known to be perfect, not through their pre-existing or introduced form (for this is impossible), but through the *accidents*, *properties*, and *passions* <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" and "passions" are the observable characteristics and behaviors of a substance</note> that follow those forms. Therefore, if in a transmuted metal all those things are found which are found in the true metal during any test, it must surely be judged that it possesses a form that is not deceptive, but that of mineral gold or silver. For that which performs the function of the eye is indeed an eye, and conversely, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the stone of the philosophers is natural, based on the method of its production: and this by means of a natural agent, namely fire, with its natural color, odor, and natural form—which are the forms of...

<summary>This page describes the final stage of alchemy, Projection, where the Stone transmutes base metals into gold or silver. It also refutes Jacques Aubert’s claim that alchemical gold is merely a "fake" imitation, arguing that if a substance shares all properties of gold, it is philosophically and physically gold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of alchemy against the criticisms of Jacques Aubert. The author is moving from a general description of the "Great Work" (the creation of the Philosopher's Stone) to a theoretical justification of how "Art" (human alchemy) can legitimately replicate the "Natural" processes of the earth to create metals and minerals.</meta>

->### TO AUBERT.<-

<page-num>291</page-num>

<header>TO AUBERT.</header>

<sig>NN 5</sig>

...<unclear>acc</unclear>idental properties, following their determined substantial form, as Art supplies the matter for itself. For art is connected with nature, since the principle of art is nature itself, as the Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle</note> writes in the second book of the *Physics*. For this reason, art can be called natural, and its works natural, and its forms likewise natural.

Forms are called "natural" in two ways: either when nature prepares the matter for itself and introduces the form, as in a human or a stone; or when art supplies and prepares the matter for itself (though not with the final preparation), which nature then disposes and prepares right to the end, introducing the form into it. This can be seen in the generation of ceruse <note>original: "cerussæ"; white lead, used as a pigment</note> and minium <note>original: "minij"; red lead</note>. Nor is it a new thing that art follows nature in many respects, and many natural things can be composed and perfected by art. Aristotle also suggests this in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "4. Metaphysic."; the author likely refers to the *Meteorology*, which contains Aristotle's primary discussion on minerals, often bound or cited with the *Metaphysics* in this period</note>, speaking of Colcothar <note>original: "Colchotare"; a reddish-brown iron oxide</note> and Chalcantum <note>original: "Calchante"; copperas or blue vitriol</note>. For nature, he says, generates vitriols <note>original: "atramenta"; literally "inks" or black substances, but in alchemy referring to metallic sulfates</note> in the mines of vitriols; he himself shows the mode of their generation. Yet he testifies a little later that those two vitriols can also be composed and perfected by art.

For since art is an imitator of nature, as he writes in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, by taking the substance of iron or copper (from which those things are naturally made) and administering it to nature through repeated solutions, distillations, and coagulations, it finally completes them skillfully—and so perfectly, indeed, that they possess the same properties and active and passive operations as those two mineral vitriols. The same is seen in the making of salt. For one kind is found as a mineral, as in Poland; another is artificial, as in France. Yet the latter has the same properties and qualities as the mineral, for which reason it can truly be called "natural," and its form can also be called natural and truly perfect.

The same must be thought regarding metals. For just as a defect in the proper material is the chief reason why one thing does not produce another similar to it, so too if suitable material is found, that is the primary reason why one thing is produced from another like it. Therefore, since it is possible for the transmuting art to find the same entirely natural matter of gold and silver—that is, that "third nature," namely quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> coagulated and mixed with its own sulfur—it becomes easy to follow and imitate nature herself in her operations. For she cooks <note>original: "decoquit"; a technical term for applying heat to mature a substance</note> and digests that matter with a most gentle heat until, at the final limit of the process, its active agent is separated from it; namely...

<meta>catchword: tra- (likely "transmutatio" or "transactio")</meta>

<summary>On this page, the author argues that alchemy is a "natural" art because it uses the same materials and processes (heat, digestion) as nature herself. He cites Aristotle to prove that substances like vitriol and salt can be produced both in the earth and by human skill without losing their essential natural properties.</summary>

->### RESPONSE TO AUBERT.<-

<page-num>202</page-num>

<header>RESPONSE TO AUBERT.</header>

<meta>catchword: IN.</meta>

...foreign sulfur <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemical theory, sulfur and mercury were the two primary principles of all metals; "foreign" sulfur refers to impurities that prevent a metal from becoming gold</note>: it follows, from the perspective of both the active agent and its own natural matter, that the art is called both possible and truly natural. But at last, Aubert will take refuge in this argument: "If that philosopher’s stone introduced the species of gold or silver, it would assimilate that thing to itself, and in this way form another philosopher’s stone." I respond that this conversion of metals is their reduction to a certain middle point—namely, to that temperament and highest equality (which is found in gold alone) in substance, color, digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow application of heat to mature a substance</note>, melting, resonance, and other properties. These things we have discussed so far shall suffice, not so that I might detract anything from Aubert’s reputation in other matters, but to show that he, and those who thought his book should be adorned with their insults, have attacked innocent people with so many bitter reproaches. Finally, I have written this that I might champion the truth, for which he himself ought to be a seeker, if he is a good man, as I judge him to be. For these things were not 
<margin>See Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 33, Chapter 4, who writes that perfect gold was made from orpiment <note>original: "auripigmento"; arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral named "gold-pigment" for its color</note>.</margin> devised by me, but handed down by the most learned men and confirmed by the most certain arguments: lest anyone think I use their authority alone—though even that authority should not have been despised by Aubert. For who would think that those men left those secrets to us—sanctified even by an oath—either rashly or in bad faith? Therefore, this very part of philosophy, which he so bitterly attacks, disapproves of, and mocks, I would dare to affirm on the contrary can never be praised enough or proclaimed according to its merits; whether it pleases us to contemplate the miracles of nature alone, which it draws out from her most hidden depths, or whether we look at its usefulness, which is almost innumerable, besides those infinite ways in which it illuminates many other arts. For to pass over the rest, the virtue and excellence of the philosopher’s stone alone is such that it suffices for healing most diseases, and demonstrates true and exquisite preparations of medicines; but it is no wonder these things seem base to those who are accustomed to more impure things, or to whom custom alone makes the law. But I warn such men either to learn better things, or not to envy those who are better instructed, or at least not to rebuke things unknown to them: if not, we shall not be delayed by their efforts, because we know the truth will eventually prevail, and finally dispelling those shadows with its brilliance, will reveal each thing as it truly is.

# TO THE EXCELLENT MAJESTY
# OF THE RENOWNED KING
## MAXIMILIAN, JOHN DEE
### OF LONDON,
->Wishes a Most Prosperous Reign.<-

The two reasons that can encourage a man of my station to present so great a King with so small a gift <note>Dee is referring to his book, the *Monas Hieroglyphica*, which he presents as small in size but immense in philosophical value</note>, both have now moved me to do so. These are, surely, my very great goodwill toward your Majesty, and the great rarity and not-to-be-despised quality of the gift itself, however small it may be. Your admirable virtues have stirred up and won for you an eternal goodwill; these virtues are so great that those who have not seen them with their own eyes <note>original: "oculata... fide"; literally "with the faith of the eye," meaning firsthand experience</note> would hardly believe others telling of them, even moderately—though they speak the absolute truth of these rarest qualities. But those who have carefully and accurately observed those same virtues in your presence will confess that they suffer from a great lack and poverty of speech and expression as soon as they desire to pour themselves out oratorically into the full breadth of those qualities. I myself, staying for some time in Pozsony <note>original: "Posonio"; the Latin name for modern-day Bratislava, then the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary where Maximilian was crowned</note> in your Hungarian Kingdom this past September, became an eyewitness to these causes, most clearly and through various experiences.

Concerning the rarity of the gift (small though it may be in physical size), I have something to say in as few words as possible. By the full effort of my mind's inquiry, it occurs to me that the course of human life is twofold, running in different directions (one of which almost everyone enters), and must be considered in this way: As soon as the race of Infancy is finished, and Youth <note>catchword: "ritiae", completing "Pueritiae"</note>...

# PREFACE TO THE KING

*...when youths reach maturity and the choice of which life they will henceforth enter begins to weigh upon their minds. Then, hesitating for a little while at the crossroads of a doubtful judgment, they finally decide: either (these, captured by the love of truth and virtue) to practice philosophy, straining every nerve through the whole remaining space of life; or (those, certainly ensnared by worldly allurements or burning with a greed for riches) to lead a luxurious or profitable life, laboring anxiously in all ways.*

*Of the latter sort, you might easily find a thousand; whereas of the former (those, namely, who sincerely devote their work to philosophy), you can hardly point to one who has tasted even the first and true foundations of Physics <note>original: "Physicæ"; in Dee's time, this referred to "Natural Philosophy," the study of the laws of the physical world</note>. But as for him who has more deeply and fully examined the causes of celestial forces and actions, and the origins, states, and deaths of all other things: the Republic of Letters <note>original: "Resp. litteraria"; the international community of scholars and intellectuals</note> cannot produce even a thousandth part of those who have turned themselves entirely to the study of wisdom.*

*What then of the man who, having overcome all these difficulties, aspires to the contemplation and understanding of super-celestial virtues and metaphysical influences? Where, in the entire world (in these most deplorable times of ours), can we find this great-souled man, this single* **HERO**; *when, according to the progression of our (not rashly accepted) thousandth proportion:* **FROM ONE MILLION SINCERE PHILOSOPHERS, OR RATHER, FROM ONE BILLION MEN OF THE COMMON SORT, WE OUGHT TO EXPECT THIS UNIQUE AND MOST BLESSED OFFSPRING.** *The* **HIEROGLYPHIC** *model of this demonstrated* **RARITY** *we shall attach to the (so-called) Pythagorean letter <note>The letter "Y", which Pythagoras used as a symbol for the "bivium" or crossroads where a young person must choose between the path of Virtue or the path of Vice</note>. There, to your Excellency looking more attentively, even greater mysteries will seem to offer themselves for consideration, described in this manner from our* **Cosmopolitical Theories.**

nor can any be applied from the outside to multiply it?
<margin>3.</margin>

The Geometer (my King) will begin to hesitate—being scarcely sure enough of the principles of his own art (which is very strange)—when he understands what is whispered and hinted here in secret:

And will the Astronomer not most greatly regret the cold, the vigils, and the labors he suffered under the open sky, when here, without having to endure any injury from the air—under a roof, with windows and doors closed everywhere—he is able to observe with his eyes most exactly the **revolutions** <note>original: "periphoras"; from the Greek *peripheria*, referring to the orbital paths or rotations of celestial bodies.</note> of the heavenly bodies at any given time? ### TO THE PRINTER.
# TO HIS SINGULAR FRIEND,
## WILLEM SILVIUS,
->*John Dee of London sends many greetings.*<-

You see, my friend, best Willem, how exceptionally dear I hold the most distinguished virtues of the most illustrious King Maximilian, to whom I communicate rare and most excellent **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcana"</note> from the storehouses of my heart. For that reason, I have taken care to communicate them to him so that even more people throughout the world might be able to enjoy these same things through your diligence and faithfulness. This is partly in his honor, on account of his extraordinary and Royal virtues, and partly so that others may take an example from him—for he is a man who is able both to attend most wisely to the Royal helms of governance and yet also to learn the stupendous Mysteries of the philosophers and the wise in abundance. 

Therefore, there are two things for which I must especially entreat you: one, that you imitate everywhere my accurate diligence (as much as you are able) in the variety of letters, points, lines, diagrams, schemes, numbers, and other things. This is so that the very thing which I (by God’s will) have brought forth as a body well-formed in every part, does not—through the negligence of the printing—come out into the light either mutilated or deformed: a thing unworthy...

*...since he is so great a King; it would be truly unworthy of the studies and greatest labors of Philosophers, who wish to bestow their efforts in examining this matter most deeply and most frequently. I seem to have guarded myself well enough against that misfortune, however, when I chose you as the typographical parent of this newly born work: you who, through your care, are able to send it forth polished in every way and well-composed in all its members.*

*The second thing I would wish you to perform is not light, indeed: namely, that you give these little books into the hands of the common sort of men in no way <note>original: "promiscuo... hominū generi". Dee is expressing the typical Renaissance "hermetic" concern that secret knowledge should not be shared with the uninitiated or the "vulgar," who might misunderstand it.</note>. Not that I would envy them these or even better things: but suspecting that evil would arise from it: not only because the wretches could never extricate themselves from this **Labyrinth** <note>Dee views his work as a complex intellectual maze that requires a specific "thread" of logic to navigate safely.</note> (meanwhile distressing their minds in incredible ways and looking out most poorly for their own family business) but also because they will persuade others to enter the path (which is impassable to them) or they will most wickedly lie about its certainty, as if they had explored it; such men are impostors and mere shadows of men. Or finally, they will dare to deny that these are the **Great Works of God** <note>original: "Magnalia"</note>, or most rabidly accuse my sincerity—being now at last driven to despair; just as, at first, these rash ones attacked these Mysteries with the greatest presumption.*

*But in this matter of such great weight, if I have known you well for many years (either on account of our friendship, or for the utility of the Christian Commonwealth, or at least on account of the Heroic virtues of the most wise Maximilian himself, which have nothing in common with the vulgar lot of men), you will take care, I hope, so that I might not seem to have sought your trust in vain. You indeed will take care: and through you, all most honest book merchants. Farewell.*

## BY JOHN DEE OF LONDON,
### *Explained Mathematically, Magically, Cabalistically, and*
### *Anagogically.* <note>Anagogical: A method of spiritual interpretation that seeks to find the "uplifting" or mystical meaning of a symbol, leading the mind toward divine realities.</note>

### THEOREM I.

It was by means of the straight line and the circle that the first and simplest production and representation of things was brought into the light—including both those things that do not yet exist, and those hidden within the veils of nature.

### THEOREM II.

But neither can the circle be skillfully produced without the straight line, nor the straight line without the point. It is by the logic of the point and the monad <term>Monad: From the Greek *monas* (unity). For Dee, this is the singular, indivisible point of origin for all creation, representing God, the individual, and the cosmos simultaneously.</term> that things first began to exist. And whatever things are defined by a periphery (no matter how large they may be), they can in no way lack the service of the central point.

<image-desc>A simple geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment to the left and a circle with a central point to the right.</image-desc>

### THEOREM III.

<margin>
THE HIEROGLYPHIC MONAD.
</margin>
Therefore, the conspicuous central point of the Hieroglyphic Monad represents the Earth; around which both the Sun and the Moon, and the rest of the planets, complete their courses. And in this office <note>original: "munere", meaning a duty or function.</note>, because the Sun holds the highest dignity, we signify it (by way of excellence) by a whole circle with a visible center.

<image-desc>The symbol of the Hieroglyphic Monad, composed from top to bottom of: a crescent (Moon), a circle with a central point (Sun), a rectilinear cross, and two intersecting semi-circles at the base (Aries).</image-desc>

### THEOREM IV.

Although the semi-circle of the Moon is here placed as if superior and prior to the solar circle, it nevertheless [regards] the Sun as its lord and king...

...observes its own [path]: it seems to rejoice so much in the form and proximity of the same [the Sun] that it emulates it in the magnitude of its semi-diameter (as it appears to common people), and always turns its light toward it.
