### THEOREMA V.

And indeed, once the lunar semicircle is brought to its solar completion, it is said: *The evening and the morning were the first day.* <note>original: "Factum est vespere & mane dies vnus." A reference to Genesis 1:5.</note> Let this, therefore, be the first [day], on which the light of the Philosophers was made.

### THEOREMA VI.

<image-desc>A mystical symbol consisting of a lunar crescent atop a circle with a central point (representing the sun), which in turn rests upon a cross.</image-desc>

We see here the Sun and the Moon resting upon a rectilinear cross. This cross can, through hieroglyphic reasoning, quite aptly signify both the **Ternary** <term>Ternary: A grouping of three. In Dee's system, this represents the union of two lines meeting at a central point.</term> and the **Quaternary** <term>Quaternary: A grouping of four, traditionally representing the four elements or the four directions of the physical world.</term>. The Ternary, indeed, is formed from two straight lines and a point common to both, acting as a sort of joining point. The Quaternary, however, is formed from four straight lines enclosing four right angles. Each of these being repeated twice for this purpose (and thus, in the same place, most secretly, the **Octonary** <term>Octonary: A grouping of eight.</term> also offers itself; I doubt if our predecessors, the magi, ever perceived it, and you should take great note of it). The magical Ternary of the first fathers and wise men consisted of body, spirit, and soul. From this, we clearly have here a primary **Septenary** <term>Septenary: A grouping of seven. Dee derives this by adding the 3 parts of the Ternary and the 4 parts of the Quaternary.</term>: namely, from two straight lines and a common point, and then from four straight lines separating themselves from a single point.

### THEOR. VII.

When the elements are moved out of their natural places, their displaced homogeneous parts will teach the experimenter that they naturally make their return to those same places along straight lines. Therefore, it will not be absurd to suggest the mystery of the four elements (into which all elemental things can be resolved) by means of four straight lines running out from a single, indivisible point in opposite directions. You will also note this diligently: geometers teach that a line is produced by the "flow" of a point; we advise that the same happens here in a similar way: while our elementary lines are produced in our **mechanical magic** <term>Mechanical Magic: The practical application of mathematical principles to create physical effects, often associated in the Renaissance with the construction of automata or the manipulation of the physical world through "natural" means.</term> from the continuous fall (as if a flow) of a **drop**, which acts as a physical point.

### THEOREM VIII.

Furthermore, the Cabalistic expansion <note>A method of calculation where a number is expanded by adding all the integers leading up to it.</note> of the **Quaternary** <term>Quaternary: The number four, representing the material world and the four elements.</term>, according to the phrasing of common counting (when we say: one, two, three, four), presents the **DENARY** <term>Denary: The number ten.</term> in total. As **Pythagoras** himself used to say: "For 1, 2, 3, and 4 make ten." It is not by chance, therefore, that the **Rectilinear CROSS**—which is the twenty-first letter of the Roman alphabet <note>In the 23-letter Latin alphabet of Dee's time (which lacked J, U, and W), X is the 21st letter.</note> and is judged to be formed of four straight lines—was adopted by the most ancient Latin philosophers to signify the **DENARY**. Its place is also defined in that same system where the **TERNARY** <term>Ternary: The number three.</term>, conducting its power through the **SEPTENARY** <term>Septenary: The number seven.</term>, establishes the Denary. <note>Dee is likely referring to the mathematical relationship 3 + 7 = 10, suggesting a mystical harmony between these numbers.</note>

### THEOREM IX.

Moreover, this will be seen to suit our **MONAD**, the **SUN**, and the **MOON** most perfectly; for when a most exact **SEPARATION** into their own lines has been made through the magic of the four **Elements**, a circular **CONJUNCTION** in **SOLAR** completion is then achieved through the circumferences of those same lines. (For by the laws of geometry, one is permitted to describe a circle from the magnitude of any given line). Then, indeed, it cannot remain hidden how much the proportion of the **Denary Cross** serves our Monad, the Sun, and the Moon.

## THEOREM XIV.

It is now clearly confirmed that this entire mastery <term>Mastery: referring to the "Magisterium," the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> depends upon the Sun and the Moon. Of this, the "Thrice-Greatest" Hermes <note>original: "Hermes Termaximus," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the Hermetic tradition.</note> once warned us, asserting that its father is the **Sun** and its mother the **Moon**; we know, truly, that it is nourished in the Lemnian earth <note>original: "terra lemnia"—traditionally a medicinal clay, but here referring to the "prepared earth" or prime matter of the alchemist</note> by the solar and lunar rays which exert a singular influence upon it.

## THEOR. XV.

We therefore propose that the "labors" of the Sun and Moon around the Earth should be considered by Philosophers. Specifically, how, while the solar radiance is dwelling in Aries, the Moon receives a new dignity of light in the very next sign (namely, Taurus) and is "exalted" <term>Exaltation: in astrology, a sign where a planet's influence is particularly strengthened, distinct from its "home" or rulership</term> above its innate powers. The ancients explained this proximity of the Luminaries—more notable than any other—through a certain mystical character bearing the name of Taurus. It is very well known that this has been handed down since the first age of man (among the accepted beliefs of Astronomers) as the Exaltation of the **Moon**. But only those understand the mystery who have become the absolute high priests of the mysteries. For a similar reason, they said that **Taurus** is the home of **Venus**: of chaste and prolific marital love, for **nature delights in nature** <note>original: "ἡ φύσις, τῇ φύσει τέρπεται" (*hē physis, tē physei terpetai*)—a core alchemical axiom meaning that substances of the same nature naturally combine and perfect one another.</note>, as the great **Ostanes** <note>A legendary ancient Persian magus and alchemist.</note> hid within his most secret mysteries.

<columns>2</columns>

Regarding the Sun, consider the reason why it receives the strength of Mars after certain eclipses of its light have been allowed; it is also said to triumph in its own **Exaltation** in his house (namely, our **Aries**). These most secret mysteries are demonstrated most clearly and perfectly by our Monad—

### *A N N O T A T I O N.*

*I believe two things are especially notable here: First, that this hieroglyphic figure of Taurus exactly represents the Greek Diphthong **ȣ** <note>The Greek ligature for "ou," which looks like a circle with horns, matching the astrological symbol for Taurus.</note>, which is always the genitive singular ending of the First Declension. Second, by a suitable local transposition <term>Metathesis: a rearrangement of parts or letters</term>, it demonstrates **ALPHA** to us in two ways: either by the Circle and Semicircle merely touching, or (as in this case) intersecting each other.*

### THEOR. XVI.

Now we must philosophize briefly for our purpose regarding the **CROSS**. Our **CROSS**, although composed of two straight lines (as we have said) and indeed equal ones, does not have them bisecting each other into equal lengths. Rather, we wished to have both equal and unequal parts in the mystical distribution of our Cross. We are suggesting that within the power of two lines divided in this way (since they are of equal magnitude), the virtue of the **Equilateral Cross** also lies hidden. For in the most general sense, when a Cross is ordered to be made from equal straight lines, a certain **Justice of Nature** requires that it be formed by an equal crossing <term>Decussation: the intersection of two lines in the form of an X</term> of those lines. 

According to the norm of this Justice, we propose the following things to be considered regarding the Equilateral Cross (which is like the twenty-first letter of the Latin Alphabet) <note>Dee refers to the letter 'X'. In the traditional Latin alphabet of his time, 'X' was often the 21st letter when including 'K' and 'Y'.</note>. If a straight line is conceived to pass anywhere through the common point of intersection and the opposite angles of a rectilinear, rectangular, and equilateral cross: the parts of the cross formed on either side of that passing line are altogether similar and equal. Their shapes are the same as that Latin letter which is accepted as the **Fifth of the Vowels** <note>The letter 'V', which in Roman numerals represents five.</note>, and was most commonly used among the most ancient Latin philosophers to denote the **Quinary** <term>Quinary: the number five or a set of five</term>. I believe this was done by them not without reason, since it is the conforming half of our **Denarius** <note>Original: "Denarii" — referring to the number ten, represented by the Roman numeral 'X'. If you split an 'X' horizontally, you get two 'V' shapes.</note>. From these figures, thus doubled (from this hypothetical division of the Cross...

That seems to me to be established first from this: because that too is a Sign of the **Quinary** <note>The number five</note>, essentially taken from our denary Cross <note>The "denary cross" refers to the Roman numeral X, which represents ten and is composed of two Vs</note>; but it is located in that position where the Cross itself is the most consummate **Hieroglyphic Sign** of the Greatest of all Mysteries. O, my God, how great are these mysteries! And its name is **EL** <note>The Hebrew name for God (אל), which is written here using the Roman letter L to link the numeral 50 with the Divine name</note>. And since we have shown that there are two such integral parts in the Cross (considering now only their numerical power), it is most clear that a **Centenary** <note>The number one hundred</note> grows from there. But if, by the law of Squares, they undergo mutual multiplication, they return two thousand five hundred to us: which square, compared to the square of the prior circular number <note>25, which is 5 squared</note> and applied to the same, will again restore the **Centenary** <note>2500 divided by 25 equals 100</note>: just as the cross itself, explaining itself according to the power of its ten, will be recognized as a **Centurio** <note>Dee puns on "Centurio," meaning both a Roman officer of a hundred and the number 100 itself</note>. And yet, since it is but a single character of the cross, it also represents **One**. Here, therefore (besides other most worthy things), from these Theories of the cross, we learn to count...

### THEOREM XVII.

As can be clear from the sixth Theorem, four right angles are to be considered in our cross. To each of these, the preceding Theorem taught us to attribute the significance of the **Quinary** <note>The number five, represented by the Roman numeral V</note>, when positioned in one way. But by assuming another position <note>The right-angle shape 'L' representing fifty</note>, the same Theorem allows those Hieroglyphic marks to become the **Quinquagenary** number <note>The number fifty</note>.

Thus, it is most evident that the cross commonly denotes the **Denary** <note>The number ten, written as the Roman numeral X</note>. Furthermore, in the order of the Latin Alphabet, it is the twenty-first letter <note>original: "vigesimam primam." In the Latin alphabet used by Dee, which did not distinguish between I/J or U/V in the same way we do, X was the 21st character</note>. From this it follows that the **Sophi** <note>The Wise</note>, called **Mecubales** <note>A Latinized term for Cabbalists, from the Hebrew 'Mequbbalim'</note>, signified the number twenty-one by this same letter. 

Finally, the cross can be considered in the simplest way: as it is seen to be one single mark, regardless of whatever and however great its other powers may be. From all of these observations, we see that it can be concluded by the best Cabbalistic demonstration that our cross, for the initiates, can signify **two hundred fifty-two** by a wonderful compendium. 

For four times five; four times fifty; ten; twenty-one; and one, make **two hundred fifty-two**. 

As we are able to elicit this number by two other reasons from the premises already given, we commend the same to be extracted by Cabbalistic beginners <note>original: "Tyronibus"</note>, being thus studious of brevity. Nevertheless, we judge the various skillful productions of this same magisterial number to be worthy of the consideration of Philosophers. 

Nor will I hide from you here another memorable **Mystagogia** <note>An initiation into mysteries</note>. Seeing that our Cross allows itself to be distributed into two other letters: if we previously weighed their numerical virtue in a certain way, let us now in turn compare their verbal force with the cross itself. From this, **Light** <note>original: "Lux"</note> shall arise. We shall understand with the highest admiration the final and magisterial **Word** (arising from that conspiracy and consent of the **Ternary** <note>The number three</note> within the unity of the word). <note>Dee is hinting that the components of the Cross—the numerals L (50), V (5), and X (10)—spell the Latin word LUX, meaning Light.</note>

### THEOREM XVIII.

From our twelfth and thirteenth Theorems, it can be gathered that celestial Astronomy is like the parent and teacher of the inferior Astronomy <note>Dee refers to Alchemy as "inferior" or "terrestrial" astronomy</note>. Therefore, with Cabbalistic eyes raised to the heavens (illuminated by the theory of the aforementioned mysteries), we shall behold exactly such an Anatomy of our **Monad**. It shows itself to us always in this way in the light of nature and of life, and by its own nod, it reveals the most secret things of this Physical **Analysis**...

# MONAD

We speak of those degrees which those skilled in Physics <note>original: "Physices periti"; refers to natural philosophers who studied the physical laws of the universe</note> are able to find among all created natures, which are four: namely, being, living, sensing, and understanding. Noting, therefore, that the first two of these degrees are present in this [part of the symbol], we shall say: the Moon, existing and alive. Indeed, some define life by motion. Moreover, there are six well-known species of motion. <note>In Aristotelian physics, the six types of motion are: generation (coming to be), corruption (passing away), increase, decrease, alteration, and change of place.</note> Certainly, the Cross that is attached here denotes that the craft of the Elements is required. Furthermore, in these theories of ours, we have very often taught that the semicircle is the <term>Hieroglyphic</term><note>A sacred or mystical symbol carrying hidden meaning</note> of the Moon. Likewise, the full circle signifies the Sun. Here, however, there are two semicircles; but they are separated (though joined at a common point), which, if they are joined fitly (as they certainly can be by art), can represent for us the solar and circular fullness. From these things considered together, it is clear that we can hieroglyphically offer this sentence as a summary:

<margin> { </margin> *The Moon, existing and alive, to be handled through the mastery of the Elements: having the power to represent solar fullness once its semicircles are joined together by art.* Let it therefore be completed; and let that circle (which we mentioned) be made: as we have noted here by the letter **E**. Let us therefore be mindful that this first solar degree was not met with by us through nature, but is now artificial and man-made. And indeed, it offered itself to us at first sight and by its own nature (namely in **B**) with its parts loose, fluid, and dissolved; not solidly compacted into a solar form. Furthermore, the <term>radius</term><note>original: "Semidiametrum"</note> of these semicircles is not equal to the radius of **D** and **G** (which are so born to us, and most well-known to all), but much smaller. Whence it is clear: that **B** itself is not of such great size as are **D** and **C** themselves. ->Our Rule of Permutation.<-
<note>original: *Metatheseos Canon*; "Metathesis" refers to the transposition or rearrangement of elements, here used in a mathematical sense similar to factorials.</note>

With the numbers written in their natural order starting from the first **Monad** <note>the number one, representing unity</note>: if a continuous multiplication is performed from the first to the last—for example, the first multiplied by the second, the result by the third, and that result by the fourth, and so on to the last—the final product determines every possible **Permutation** <note>original: *Metathesem*</note> in those many places. By the same logic, this applies to any number of diverse things. I highly recommend this operation to you (O King) both in the examination of all nature and in other most useful affairs of the State. I myself am accustomed to using this with the greatest pleasure in the **Tziruph** (or **Thmura**) of the Hebrews.

# MONAD

From these diagrams, many things can be drawn out (if they are considered more deeply) than is proper to set forth in open words. However, we advise this one singular thing above all others (which we have also been the first to publish along with this entire new art): that the **Reason** is placed here in the middle, because of which the **Quaternary** <note>the number four</note> or the **Denary** <note>the number ten; original: *Denarius*. In Pythagorean thought, 1+2+3+4=10, meaning the four elements contain the perfection of ten.</note> imposes a certain end to our counting. We assert that the cause which our ancestors brought forward was not absolute and exact, but rather it is this one which we shall now narrate.

Four most famous men, <note>Likely referring to the legendary four masters of alchemy or the four Evangelists as spiritual alchemists.</note> formerly philosophizing together, achieved this true effect in their **Work**. <meta>This page begins the treatise of Laurentius Ventura. It marks a transition from the symbolic and geometric mysticism of John Dee’s Monas Hieroglyphica on the preceding pages to a more traditional, medical, and philosophical defense of the alchemical art. Ventura, a Venetian physician, starts his work by addressing the common skepticism surrounding the transmutation of metals.</meta>

<page-num>244</page-num>
<header>ON THE STONE</header>

# LAURENTIUS VENTURA OF VENICE, DOCTOR OF ARTS AND MEDICINE, ON THE METHOD of making the Philosopher’s Stone, Book.

## THAT THE ART OF ALCHEMY is true.

### CHAPTER I.

Many are of the opinion that the art of Alchemy is not a true art. They are moved toward this view by two main arguments. First, because Aristotle says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*: “Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot be transmuted.” <note>original: "Sciant artifices Alchemiæ, species metallorum transmutari non posse." This famous quote was actually written by the Persian physician Avicenna in his *De Congelatione*, but in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, it was frequently misattributed to Aristotle's *Meteorologica*.</note> Second, because they see everyone laboring in this art performing nothing but fraudulent transmutations, and no one performing true ones. Therefore, they think and believe that since they see it done by no one, it can truly and really be done by no one at all. 

But neither of these foundations compels us to believe that this most precious and excellent art is not true. Indeed, the first foundation of the adversaries is not valid: for it is quite true, as the philosopher Alphidius <note>An early Arabic alchemical author often cited in Western manuscripts.</note> and the *Greater Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius maior*. This refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, one of the most famous alchemical texts, which uses the metaphor of a rose garden to describe the stages of the work.</note> state: that while the species of things are not transmuted, individuals of certain species can indeed be transmuted into one another. 

This is visible to the eye, especially in those things that have a shared connection <term>symbolum<gloss>A technical term in Aristotelian physics meaning a "shared quality" (like heat or moisture) that allows one element to change into another.</gloss></term> to one another in one or two qualities, as is evident in the elements. Thus, from earth a stone is made, from wood comes ash, and from ash and stones, glass is made, and so on. 

So it also happens in metals: for all metals share in one single matter, which is quicksilver <term>argentum vivum<gloss>Literally "living silver." The philosophical mercury believed to be the root of all metals.</gloss></term> with its sulfur. Metals differ only by a greater or lesser degree of digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation or "cooking" of substances through gentle heat, mimicking the natural processes within the earth.</note>, which occurs through the ripening of their sulfur by means of decoction. For sulfur is the "form" or defining principle of metals, and especially of gold—not indeed the common sulfur <term>sulphur vulgi<gloss>Common yellow brimstone, which alchemists distinguished from the "Philosophical Sulfur" needed for their work.</gloss></term>, but an "altered" sulfur, as the master philosopher Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century alchemist who wrote the *Precious Pearl*.</note> says. From these sayings it is gathered that if a medicine can be made by art which possesses within itself the power and property of the aforementioned altered mineral sulfur, such a medicine made by art will be able—

<meta>The catchword "rit" refers to the continuation of the word "poterit" (will be able) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Laurentius Ventura opens his treatise by defending alchemy against critics who cite Aristotle's alleged claim that species cannot change. He argues that while universal species are fixed, individual substances like metals can be transformed because they share the same fundamental matter (mercury and sulfur) at different stages of "ripening."</summary>

<keywords>Alchemy, Laurentius Ventura, Aristotle, Transmutation, Sulfur, Quicksilver, Digestion, Elements, Metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Laurentius Ventura’s defense of alchemy, moving from the debunking of skeptical arguments to the specific physical theories that make transmutation possible. He explains the "first matter" of metals and cites both medieval scholastics and legendary alchemical authorities like Geber to justify his claims.</meta>

<page-num>245</page-num>
->P H I L O S O P H Y.<-
<sig>QQ 3</sig>

...it [the art] is able to transform imperfect metals and quicksilver into the nature of perfect ones. Because of this, John Scotus <note>Likely referring to the medieval scholastic John Duns Scotus, who was frequently cited as an authority in alchemical texts to provide the art with academic legitimacy.</note> and many other philosophers say and grant it to be true that metals cannot be transmuted by any method or ingenuity unless they are first reduced to their **first matter**. Now, the **first matter** of all metals is quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury (Latin: *argentum vivum*)</term> and sulfur—not indeed in their raw nature, but altered, that is, converted into a vapor. And thus the first matter of metals is a moist, oily vapor, containing within itself the nature of both: namely, of sulfur and quicksilver.

From these things it necessarily follows that if this kind of oily vapor can be extracted by art from those things in which it is found—and if one is discovered similar to that which generates metals in the mines of the earth—then a **medicine** <note>The "medicine" is another term for the Philosopher's Stone, which was believed to "cure" base metals of their imperfections.</note> can be prepared which can lead simple, imperfect bodies, projected upon quicksilver, into a true and perfect metallic body, far more perfect than anything natural. But it must be known that this medicine is extracted more easily and abundantly from some things, but from others more with difficulty and imperfection, whether they be the metals themselves or any other things whatsoever. But this cannot happen unless such things are first destroyed through **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the chemical stage of breaking down a substance, often associated with the color black and the "death" of the old form</term> and, through proper boiling and long digestion, acquire another, more noble form.

The second foundation also, by which they argue against us, is not compelling. Our reasoning is as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of chemistry/alchemy. His *Summa perfectionis* was the most influential alchemical textbook in Europe.</note> says in his *Summary of Great Perfection*, Chapter XI, in which he treats the refutation of the arguments of those simply denying the art; and it is this: because for the adversary in his way of arguing, there is no necessity. A person who looks at only a few things is forced to believe this art is not true because he strengthens his own fantasy and error based on a similarity, or by moving from the greater to the lesser. In these things there is no necessity, but only contingency as in most cases.

Furthermore, it is certain in our times that very few philosophers are found who know the secrets of nature; indeed, they neglect to seek and know them. And therefore, they do not know how to improve and perfect imperfect things through proper operations: and for the most part, they are ignorant of how to discern the suitable from the unsuitable, the near from the remote. And because of this, many go astray and are foolish. But the ancient philosophers were of a higher intellect and more studious in their work. For, as Lodovico Lazzarelli <note>An Italian humanist, poet, and magician (1440–1500) known for his Hermetic writings.</note> says: The philosophers, for the sake of knowing the deep secrets of nature, sometimes dared [to enter] caves...

<meta>catchword: sub- [likely *subterranea*, meaning subterranean or underground]</meta>

<summary>Ventura explains that transmutation is possible because all metals share a "first matter" (a sulfur-mercury vapor); by reducing metals to this state through putrefaction, the alchemist can create a "medicine" to perfect them. He also critiques contemporary scholars for their lack of dedication compared to the ancient masters.</summary>
<keywords>first matter, quicksilver, sulfur, putrefaction, Geber, Lodovico Lazzarelli, John Scotus, metallic vapor, transmutation theory</keywords>

->ON THE STONE<-

...to withdraw, and to dwell in forests and mountains, so that with skillful wit they might investigate the stars—what powers they hold—and which places of the earth are suited for metals, what materials they are, and what distinction lies between them. And therefore for their own benefit, and that of their sons, this **divine mastery** <term>divine mastery: the *magisterium*, or the entire process of the alchemical Great Work</term> was discovered through their long investigation; for only the philosophers and their sons <note>In alchemical literature, "sons" or "sons of art" refers to initiated students and legitimate practitioners, rather than biological offspring.</note> understand the power of nature, and they are not ignorant of its disposition. Since, therefore, many great philosophers assert that this **transmutatory art** can be achieved, and have left many books in writing behind them, it is unjust and foolish to deny that the art itself is true, even if no immediate reason or experience provides testimony and proof. On this account, Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who allegedly taught the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> said well: that there is a great distance between the wise and the foolish, and between the blind and the seeing; and the same judgment applies between those who work poorly and those who are ignorant. It is concluded, therefore, from these points, that this art is true.

### THAT NOT ALL WHO BELIEVE THE ART IS TRUE KNOW HOW TO USE IT, AND WORK ACCORDING TO IT.

#### CHAPTER II.

There are truly those who firmly believe this most noble art to be true, but they have not attempted to discover through experience whether it is true, nor do they know how to prove it. Certain of them believe with a weak conviction, and though they probably agree with and adhere to the truth—either because of the multitude of sayings or the greatness of the authors—they yield when the battle of argument begins. There is, however, one thing that easily draws all men toward believing: namely, the desire for possession and the greed for pleasures. For pleasure alone makes men especially greedy. Indeed, the same philosopher Ludovico Lazzarelli <note>Ludovico Lazzarelli (1447–1500) was an Italian poet and hermeticist; his inclusion here highlights the Renaissance synthesis of humanism and alchemy.</note> says: Men devoted to earthly delights desire earthly delights above all else, and to acquire them they omit no work or labor, according to that saying of the eminent prophet Virgil:

> To what do you not drive mortal hearts,
> O accursed hunger for gold?
> <note>original: "Quid non mortalia pectora cogis / Auri sacra fames" from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 3.</note>

Because all men seek delights, and so that they might be able to live as well and blessedly as they can, almost all the delights of this world can be obtained chiefly through riches—according to that common proverb: "All things obey money." And the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the fifth book of the *Ethics*: "Money was invented for this purpose, so that it might be..."

<meta>catchword: qua-</meta>

<summary>Ventura defends the legitimacy of alchemy as a "divine mastery" discovered by ancient philosophers through the study of nature and the stars, while acknowledging that many seekers are driven by a greedy "hunger for gold." He cites authorities like Morienus, Virgil, and Aristotle to bridge the gap between alchemical practice and classical philosophy.</summary>

# PHILOSOPHY #

...held as if a guarantor <note>original: "fidei iussor," a legal term for one who stands surety for another’s debt</note> for whatever a man might wish. Moreover, the greatest riches are promised through the mastery of this art, such as true gold and true silver, and much of both without great labor, from which coins might be fashioned through which all things may be had; for this reason, men—both those who know and those who do not—readily believe, and by trying it, they desire and attempt to acquire it through testing. There are, however, few who reach the truth of the art by their labor, the primary cause of which has been set forth before: namely, ignorance of the secrets and negligence in study. There is also a specific twofold reason for this: the first is metaphorical speech. <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were central to medieval thought, though his views on alchemy were often debated.</note> says: I considered the books of those affirming the art, and I found them empty of the reasons or reasonings that exist in every other art, and I found most of what is contained in them to be like "alienation"—that is, metaphors or similitudes. But when I brought myself back to natural principles, I then knew the art to be true. The second reason is the mixing of falsehoods with truths; wherefore <term>Arnaldus</term> <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in his testament: the philosophers have placed a double mode in their books. One is true and the other false; the truth they placed behind obscure words, so that it could not be understood except by the <term>sons of doctrine</term> <note>Initiated students or "Sons of Art" who have proven their spiritual and intellectual worthiness.</note>, lest a profane way of acting be given to the impious; but the false they placed under words that seem easy to understand. And this is commonly followed by those working in <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulfur</term>, <term>Arsenic</term>, and even in the [metallic] bodies themselves, and they have found nothing. There are, therefore, very many who labor in this art in vain: because they can neither find the necessary things by their own wit, nor are they able to understand and extract the truth from the opinions of others. For they either err in the required material, or in an unsuitable operation. Therefore, such people should be advised either to stay their hands from working, or to read books more diligently and strive to understand what they have read more fully. Whence it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: the philosophers did not write their books except for their sons; and I call their "sons" those who perfectly understand their sayings, and not

->according to the letter. For operation according to the<-
->intention of the letter is the dissipation of riches,<-
->and the loss of time.<-

### THAT THE FIRST FOUNDATION OF
### *this art is to know the properties of the medicine.*

### CHAPTER III.

The goal of this art is to produce a medicine which converts all imperfect metals and **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the ancient term for mercury</term> into true gold and silver, as good in all its properties as that which nature produces. For gold is the ultimate goal of nature and art in the generation of metals. The **Elixir**, however, is the closest goal to gold, because it exists in the closest state of potentiality. For gold is the "form" of gold, converting all metals into gold, as <term>Master Bonus</term> <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara (c. 1330), author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella* (The New Pearl of Great Price), a major medieval alchemical text.</note> says in Chapter 4. Such a medicine must be most perfect, just as the form of gold is the most perfect among all metal forms; it is the final form toward which nature strives, and the boundary beyond which nature cannot pass in metals: for in gold, nature finds a state of rest.

The medicine will be most perfect if it not only transmutes imperfect bodies from one form to the best form by reducing those bodies into their **prime matter** <term>materia prima: the formless, fundamental substance from which all things are made</term>, but also suddenly coagulates the quicksilver itself before it can escape, preserving it in the fire and converting it in a moment into a true **Solific** <term>Solificum: a substance that makes or becomes "Sol" (Gold)</term> substance. This is as <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), known as Geber, the legendary father of alchemy. Ventura likely refers to the "Summa Perfectionis," a Latin work attributed to him.</note> says in the Chapter on Medicines of the second order.

Hence, the same medicine that perfects imperfect metals also coagulates and perfects quicksilver into the **Sun** or **Moon** <note>original: "in Solem vel Lunam," alchemical shorthand for Gold and Silver.</note>. This is because there is only one medicine that accomplishes all of this. Therefore, unless the medicine is such that it strips a molten body in a moment of its first form under which it existed, removes all imperfections, and likewise reduces it to the ultimate simplicity of prime matter—and in that same moment introduces another new form, namely that of Gold—it is not yet as perfect as the art requires. Similarly, if the mercury is not suddenly coagulated at its "rising," its form would fly off and escape along with it.

From this it is gathered that the components of metals, namely **sulfur** and **quicksilver**, do not remain under the form they had in their first mixture, but act and react upon each other continuously until the form of a metal is generated from them. And first, indeed, the form of an imperfect metal is generated, in which the sulfur, which is the active agent, has not yet been fully separated from its matter...

And these minerals are composed of their own elements. Or rather, of elements in determined quantities and measures, known indeed to nature, but entirely unknown to us, mixed together from the beginning in a single mineral place in which the **celestial power** <note>The "virtus cælestis" refers to the astrological and cosmic influences believed to penetrate the earth and direct the growth of metals.</note> is preserved. Therefore, nature thoroughly mixes the aforementioned two principles <note>The "two principles" are Sulphur (the active, masculine principle) and Mercury (the passive, feminine principle).</note> from the start in certain measures and weights, along with filth and contamination, within their ores. 

These principles then act upon one another and undergo change together through digestion, until, at the end of the digestion, the pure and digested part is separated from its contaminations and filth, and then it is perfected into a metal. And the more perfect the digestion is, the less impurity the metal possesses. 

Therefore, when the digestion is complete, the active form, which is **sulphur**, is totally separated from the matter of the quicksilver. This is because, from the beginning, sulphur is external to the quicksilver and contrary to its nature; thus, its substance does not pass into the metal as matter, but it only acts upon the quicksilver itself, as upon a thing fit to be acted upon. In this way, through digestion, it alters that which has been changed, separating the pure from the impure. Thus, after a long digestion, by its own power, it disposes the matter toward the most noble simplicity, and finally draws out from the potentiality of the matter a form which establishes it in a different species than it was before. 

For this reason, the form of the metal itself, and especially that of gold, can no longer be called sulphur. Although it is a substance insofar as it is the principal substantial part of the compound, it ought not to be called its matter; for it does not have the same "being" in the compound that it had outside of it, as its power demonstrates. For although it may be similar in part, etc., it is nonetheless of a far different nature, having an excellent, distinct, or separate power. 

Hence, that which is in a perfect body and is never [permanently] united to the body is called "sulphur" only **equivocally** <note>original: "equivoce"; meaning the term is used in a different or specialized sense rather than its common definition.</note>. Since sulphurs also differ in two imperfect bodies—which certainly differ in species, but only through their substantial forms—therefore, the body in which matter and form are so united is sometimes not inappropriately named after both. Nevertheless, they retain one proper and common name which encompasses both. Therefore, first matter is understood as matter stripped of every form. 

Consequently, a new form is not introduced unless the old one is first destroyed, and in the generation of things, there is a process from the first form to the last through many intermediate forms. This is also true in the process of corruption: because the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. And thus metals are reduced to first matter when they are brought back to that first simplicity which their elements had in the first composition: in which certainly they were spirits and vapors capable of being perfected by nature into the form of a composite. 

All these things must be considered in the perfection of the **medicine** <note>In this context, the "medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone used to "heal" base metals into gold.</note>. For the elixir is not only a quality, but also a substance; and therefore, when joined to metals, it suddenly changes them into another species and nature.

...ing, nor without long duration and persistent labor: by which all of its substance, and the most pure part, is perfected—becoming white indeed in the **Moon** <note>In alchemy, the Moon refers to Silver.</note>, but an intense yellow in the **Sun** <note>The Sun refers to Gold.</note>. And with this, the mystery of this work is completed into a **medicine**, which adheres most strongly to quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," or mercury.</note> and coagulates it, converting it into a **gold-making** <note>original: "solificum"</note> or **silver-making** <note>original: "lunificum"</note> substance. From this it clearly follows, as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry" whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says, that from whatever source this medicine is drawn, it must be: first, of a most subtle and pure substance that adheres to it by its very nature; second, it must have a very easy melting point, like wax; third, it must be **fixed** against the struggle of fire.

There are therefore five conditions which the medicine must possess, as gathered from the words of Geber.

**The first** is that it melts easily and reaches into the depths of the body to be altered—that is, it should be mixed instantly through the smallest particles, altering the metal perfectly and completely.

**The second** is that it illuminates with a shining brilliance into white or yellow. However, the medicine could not do these two things unless it were made extremely subtle through a certain and determined preparation, and unless the most radiant or shining substance were drawn from it by its method of separation. For in this way, during the melting, it separates all earthiness, sulfurousness, and impurity from the mixture.

**The third** is that it brings about a specific **lunar** or **solar** melting, which it could not do unless a **dyeing substance** <note>original: "res tingens," often referred to as a "tincture" in alchemical literature.</note> for perfect white or red were mixed into it.

**The fourth** is that it be **fixed**, so that a perpetual and immutable alteration follows; for its impression would not remain unless it were fixed <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy means to make it resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates or changes when placed in the fire.</note>.

**The fifth** is that it causes the proper weight for the metal, and consequently, all the natural properties which the best gold or the purest silver has from the nature of its ore, whether equally perfect or even more perfect.

The cause of great weight is **density**—namely, when the parts are dense with nothing else coming between them. For subtlety and uniformity in the substance and essence of bodies densifies and consolidates them, and increases weight; because of which, gold is more solid and heavier than all other metals. Moreover, the greater the weight of metals and the more subtle their substance, the greater their perfection; and therefore gold is more precious than all other metals. These are the things that one must know beforehand if they wish to rightly contemplate and practice this art.

# THAT IT IS GIVEN ONLY TO PHILOSOPHERS
## *to know and to make this medicine.*

### CHAPTER IV.

Since it was indicated above that the Philosophers possessed this art—because they all bring forth the **Philosopher's Stone** and sing of wonders concerning it in their writings—we must see whether they possessed it by their own natural wit or by divine assistance. Regarding this, it should be known that there are two things which are burdensome and difficult to discover: namely, the **material** from which the **Elixir** is generated, and its **regimen** <note>The 'regimen' refers to the precise sequence of operations—such as heating, cooling, or timing—required to complete the alchemical process.</note>. For among such a great multitude of things, it was difficult to recognize which substance is most fit for this work and closest to the nature of metals. However, it is much more difficult to know and understand which mode of operation is more effective; just as it was more difficult to know which metals and from what principles they are generated, than in what order and how they are perfected. And yet, they discovered both through their own industry and investigation.

Concerning the first point, the philosopher **Master Bonus** <note>Likely Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician from Ferrara known for his influential alchemical treatise, "The Precious New Pearl" (*Pretiosa Margarita Novella*).</note> says in Chapter 6: "The knowledge of the **material cause** is no small gift to those entering this art." For this is what the ancient philosophers sought first, so that they might arrive at the knowledge of the **formal cause** <note>In Aristotelian terms, used here by alchemists, the "material cause" is the physical substance used, while the "formal cause" is the essential nature or design that makes the Stone what it is.</note>. Because every form has its own proper material from which it is extracted; without the knowledge of which they would be devoid of understanding, and consequently, of the art and its operation.

Secondly, **Master Bonus** says in the same place: "The philosophers, through the most subtle wit and profound intellect, combined with wonderful, sublime, and hidden operations, devised a way to extract **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> from arsenic, which is essentially the same as the common quicksilver of the masses, so that it might be congealed with itself—just as melted gold is coagulated by itself alone through its own intrinsic **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle that gives form and solidity to the "feminine" and fluid mercury.</note>. For that quicksilver possesses the aforementioned sulfur from within itself as something substantial and proper to it." Furthermore, every sulfur, or anything possessing the nature of sulfur, has the property of congealing quicksilver.

From this, it is understood that the philosophers possessed both: namely, the certain and proper material, and the certain **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium," referring to the specific technical knowledge or the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> of it. From these and through these, they truly composed the **Philosopher’s Stone**, which is more precious than all other stones. Yet there is no doubt that many of them reached this secret through the greatest dangers, many errors, and very many labors, as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath; his Latinized works were the foundation of European alchemy.</note> reports concerning himself. Of others, it is also said by the same: "The philosophers wished..."

<meta>catchword: phi (Philosophers)</meta>

[Philosophers] seeking this division of sulfur, because they said that <term>arsenic</term><note>In alchemy, 'arsenic' often referred to various arsenic sulfides, prized for their ability to bleach or "whiten" copper.</note> is sulfur, or at least a companion to sulfur, rather than <term>quicksilver</term><note>Latin: *argentum vivum*; the metal mercury.</note>. Because sulfur is what is manifest (on the surface), but quicksilver is what is hidden—specifically when it is sublimated to the whiteness of snow—they had to exert themselves with great anxiety, laboring in investigation, reasoning, and frequent experimentation to gain knowledge of that occult material which exists within arsenic. Thus, the philosophers clearly established arsenic, or <term>orpiment</term><note>Latin: *auripigmentum*; a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and alchemical ingredient.</note>, as the material of the Stone.

That which is "occult" or hidden is said to be that which is in the thing in potential, and is first understood by the intellect. That which is "manifest" or apparent, however, is that which is first grasped by the senses and exists in the thing in actuality. For this reason, the philosophers—namely, **Hermes**, **Geber**, **Avicenna**, and **Rhazes**—said that it possesses the nature of sulfur rather than quicksilver (even though quicksilver greatly predominates in its composition), hiding as much as they could the greatest secret within it. Consequently, they said nothing clearly regarding the nature of the quicksilver existing within it, except from a distance or as if disparaging it. 

Hence **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist said to have taught the art to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "Orpiment turns bronze into whiteness, although it corrupts the bronze somewhat; it is the task of the wise man to heal this corruption." For arsenic has, in its manifest state, a sulfurous material that is volatile and combustible; but in its occult state, it has a silvery, white, and fixed material, beneath which is a fixed golden redness. Therefore, when this quicksilver has been stripped of its sulfur, it possesses its own hidden nature within itself. 

Because of this, the wise have strived to make manifest the nature of the hidden quicksilver in arsenic along with its hidden properties, and with the greatest ingenuity, to make their **Elixir** from its sulfur. Thus says **Rhazes** in his *Book of the Perfect Magistery*: "It is not enough for an inquirer and operator of this art to know only the manifest and apparent natures of things (for he would profit nothing in the art unless he recognized their interior and hidden natures without error)." But these words are not to be understood according to the surface, but according to the meanings conveyed through likeness. 

And therefore **Master Bonus** concludes: just as nature generated Orpiment in the mines of metals, from which it makes metals; so nature, joined to Art, generated Arsenic outside the mines of metals. This does not transmute from one nature into another, but rather Art receives it and alters it, transmuting it into the true substance of the Elixir. For if nature had not done this, the art of **Alchemy** would be entirely vain and useless. Although, therefore, the philosophers—

[Philoso]phers found it through their own genius, labor, materials, and operation, it must nevertheless be said that they possessed both through God revealing or inspiring it. For God—who is the first cause, creator, and governor of all things—through His wisdom and goodness, grants various graces to different men according to time and place, as He sees fit for those upon whom He bestows them. This is true not only of spiritual graces, which have as their end the salvation of the soul and the virtues, but also of temporal graces which pertain to the bodies themselves or even to external things, such as riches, honors, health, strength, and the mechanical arts. 

But among all other arts, this art is more excellent because of its philosophical utility: for it is closer to philosophy; likewise because of the ease of the work, since one does not have to labor long or heavily; and finally because of the immensity of the fruits, for innumerable benefits follow. Furthermore, this Stone is more noble and wonderful than all others, and for that reason it is not given to everyone: for better things are suited to fewer people. I do not say this to everyone, so that they may know what it is and how it is made; rather, it is given to the very few who know these things so that they might perform them. 

For God ordains all things, lest they harm themselves or others. If it were given to the wicked, they could do much harm; if it were given to all good people, not all would use such a great gift well. This was the case with those first and <gloss>venerable</gloss><note>original: "pre-pbi," likely an abbreviation for *presbyteri* (elders/priests), used here to denote the ancient fathers of philosophy.</note> philosophers, who contributed to the common good; therefore they worthily received this gift of God, so that they might be self-sufficient and do good to others. 

Therefore **Calid**<note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. c. 704), an Umayyad prince traditionally credited as the first Muslim patron of alchemy.</note> said (as is found in the translation by **Robert of Chester**<note>original: "Castrensis." Robert of Chester was a 12th-century scholar who translated the *Liber de compositione alchimiae* from Arabic to Latin in 1144.</note>): "The secret of glorious God is the greatest sister of philosophy." It was inspired by God to His prophets and to certain chosen ones who believe in Him. And **Hermes**<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> says near the beginning: "You possess the knowledge of this art only by the inspiration of the one God." 

And **Morienus**<note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to Prince Khalid.</note> says: "The intention of every man seeking this divine science ought to judge it as nothing other than the gift of God, the Highest and Great, who shows it to His servants; may His name be forever blessed." Likewise **Geber**<note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in early Islamic alchemy.</note> says: "Our art is reserved in the power of God, who bestows it upon whom He wills and withdraws it." And **Parmenides** in the *Turba*<note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among Greek philosophers.</note> says: "But this specifically belongs to him to whom God has granted the power." And **Balgus** in the *Turba* says: "Its <term>regimen</term><note>The specific management of heat or the sequence of operations in the alchemical process.</note> is greater than can be perceived by reason, unless it be given by divine inspiration." On account of this, all philosophers say that it is the gift of God: because to the one who knows it, perfects it, and receives it, God bestows and does not withdraw it. # THAT THE PHILOSOPHERS HAVE HIDDEN
### *this stone and its direction.*
## CHAPTER V.

The Philosophers have hidden this precious stone in two ways. First, by speaking of it through allegory: whence Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who reportedly taught the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in the *Castrensis*: The books concerning this science are composed under a figure <note>original: "sub figura"; meaning metaphorically or symbolically.</note>: the greater part of which are very obscure, and so entwined with various opinions that they can be understood by no one except their own authors. For this reason, they have called the Stone by many names; however, these names do not correspond to the items used by common people <note>original: "vulgares"; referring to those outside the specialized circle of alchemists.</note>. They have kept silent regarding its own proper name, by which it is called among the common folk. But if they ever do name it by its proper name, they always add something to it so that it might distract those trying to understand, lest it be recognized, as the *Lilium* <note>The *Lilium Alchimiae* or "Lily of Alchemy," a popular medieval alchemical text.</note> says. Second, they devise various operations and weights <note>Specific measurements or proportions of ingredients.</note>. Hence it is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: The Philosophers set down many things which they never actually do. They do this for two reasons. First, to make the practitioner intelligent, diligent, and cautious in their work. For it is necessary that the craftsman who reads their books does not merely attend to the literal text, but considers the natures of things. Indeed, everyone knows that if imperfect metals are to be perfected, they must be perfected by <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note> and <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver." In alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid, passive, and metallic principle.</note>: but not everyone knows what that mercury is, or of what kind. And for that reason, many work in ignorance. Therefore, whoever introduces himself to this work ought to be supported by authorities and by reason, and not work by chance, as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and author of the "Precious New Pearl."</note> says in chapter five. The craftsman must use the highest intellect so that through his understanding he may perceive the works which are hidden from sight according to nature, and perceive the various operation which is above nature. Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in Islamic alchemy, known in the West as Geber.</note> says: The craftsman must be assisted by the deepest investigation through doctrine. For no matter how much science he has acquired, unless he is assisted by natural ingenuity <note>original: "industria naturali"; an innate talent or sharp wit.</note>, he will not be invited to such precious banquets: and in that very...

# CONCERNING THE STONE

...by some it is called the **Earthly God**. <note>original: "Deus terrestris"; a term used to describe the Stone's perceived power to perfect material bodies, mimicking divine creative power on a terrestrial scale.</note> But far be it from us that through these names we should detract from divine honor, or attribute to a creature what properly belongs to God, except by way of analogy. Through these names, therefore, the nature of the stone, its composition, and its inestimable power are expressed. Thirdly, the stone contains four: because it is composed of the four elements, not only in the way all other things have the four elements mixed together, but even divided by locations and distinct in their own spheres. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy.</note> said in the works of **Morienus Castrensis**: <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist; "Castrensis" likely refers to his Roman or camp-dwelling origins.</note> all things proceed from four out of one; therefore the <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the technical term for the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is made from one substance and matter. And although the four elements are joined in one body, or united, and diffused through the whole body while yet being distinct: nevertheless, they have different colors and dominion.

And **Astanus** <note>A character or authority cited in early alchemical texts like the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says in the same work: The four elements, namely heat, moisture, dryness, and cold, are from one source and proceed from it. The roots are water and earth. Those things which are composed from these are fire and air. And **Mundus** in the *Turba*: <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), a foundational alchemical text structured as a debate.</note> Nature does not rejoice [unless] nature contains nature, nature overcomes and surpasses nature; <note>original: "Natura naturam vincit"; a famous alchemical axiom describing how the refined nature of the Stone transforms the "crude" nature of base metals.</note> and yet they are diverse natures and no more than four; truly one nature having within itself four natures, and its own things, with which it suffices for itself. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: Our stone is a triangle in essence, and a quadrangle in quality. And these four elements in the stone are in its hidden body, very well proportioned, and most suitable to the temperament of man. Whence in the *Universal Way* it is said: in this thing are the four elements, excellently proportioned by nature, and there the fixing agent and the fixed thing, the staining and the stained, white and red, male and female are composed together, and there must be no rest for the two seeds in this work until they are mixed together.

For this reason, this stone has the greatest similarity to an egg. For **Pandulphus** says in the *Turba*: An egg contains four elements, namely the shell, which is earth; the white, which is water; the membrane, which is air; and the yolk, which is fire: thus also the stone contains the four elements in the same order. And this is the reason why the philosophers named this art the **Egg**. Yet as the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilium"; likely referring to the alchemical treatise *Lilium Intelligentiae*.</note> says, they do not call it an egg simply, but with an addition. For they name the stone the **Egg of the Philosophers**, because of the similarity it has to an egg. Indeed, because of these things already mentioned, it is likened to the World. Whence **Morienus**: In this stone four elements are contained. For it is likened to the world and the composition of the world, nor is another stone found in this world that is likened to it in its ef[fect]...

## THAT THE STONE IS VILE AND PRECIOUS.

### CHAPTER VIII.

After having spoken of the stone and its composition, we must see to its vileness and its nobility. Concerning its vileness, **Morienus** <note>Morienus Castrensis, a legendary hermit who supposedly taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: Every thing that is bought at a high price is found to be false and useless in the artifice of this work. And **Haly** <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid (Haly), an early figure in alchemical literature.</note> says: This stone is found with the poor and the rich, and with the traveler and the sitter. And in the *Book of Saturn*: Anyone knows the stone, and even the blind know it and are able to possess it. And concerning its price, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a famous Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says in the *Book of Words*: Praised be He who created the most precious from the most vile. And the *Lily* <note>A reference to the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae*.</note>, as **Zinon** <note>A name often appearing in alchemical florilegia, possibly a corruption of Zosimos or another Greek authority.</note> says: But this stone is openly bought for the smallest price; if the sellers had known this, they would hold it in their hands and would in no way sell it. Concerning both, Rhazes says above: This art is far to be preferred to others, in which there is small expense, small labor, short time, great profit, desired security, and an abundance accompanying joy; and it is a **stone that is not a stone**, vile and precious, obscure and chosen, of one name and of many names. The same stone is also most precious because without it nature does not work.

But how can the same thing be both most vile and most precious? It must be answered: Because considered in itself it is vile, since it is even often thrown upon dunghills and bought for a vile price; but if it is considered according to its effect, then it is most precious, because from it is made the most noble <term>elixir</term> <note>original: "elixir"; in alchemy, the "medicine" or "tincture" that transforms base metal into gold.</note>. And thus in it are all metals in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the Aristotelian concept of the inherent capacity for a thing to transform into its perfected state.</note>, and especially gold, which is most precious. And this in two ways: first, in remote potentiality before its preparation; second, in the most proximate potentiality after its perfection. Whence, according to the intention of **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, the 14th-century author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella* (*The New Pearl of Great Price*).</note> in Chapter 5: Nature generates from a being in potentiality a being in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "ens in actu"; a thing that has fully realized its potential and achieved its final form.</note> in an instant, as **Aristotle** says in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*, provided all suitable dispositions precede, enabling the matter to receive the form; and according as the matter is variously disposed, one form or another is introduced into it. For all generation is from proximate and <term>univocal</term> <note>original: "vniuocis"; things of the same kind or nature; the principle that "like produces like."</note> principles, as is clear in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical justification for the composition of the Stone, building on the previous discussion that it is a "stone that is not a stone." It focuses on the relationship between Nature's processes and the Alchemical Art.</meta>

-># CONCERNING THE STONE<-

<meta>catchword: sub-</meta>

Just as therefore the two spirits of nature, namely **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphur & argentum vivum," the two primary principles of all metals in medieval alchemy.</note>, are bodies in potentiality—because they are the principles of metallic bodies, and conversely so in both material and form, as is clear by the evidence of one's own eyes in their mines. For from those spirits alone, nature actually makes bodies, and vice versa. And it does not do this by mixing bodies with spirits to convert spirits into bodies. So also the Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy, the human imitation of natural processes.</note> necessarily generates the **elixir** <note>The transformative substance or "Medicine" of the metals.</note> from those same proximate and like principles from which gold is generated: because the elixir is the closest form to gold; for the principles of gold are only these two spirits, namely sulfur and quicksilver.

Furthermore, nature makes fixed bodies—namely the Sun <note>original: "Sol," the alchemical name for Gold.</note>—out of these spirits alone, without the admixture of any other body. This occurs so that such spirits, through suitable **digestion** <note>term: digestion <gloss>The process of maturing a substance through gentle, continuous heat, mimicking the Earth's natural heat.</gloss></note>, receive the property, nature, and essence of a body, and are fixed by their own selves alone. Therefore, the Art also makes the fixed elixir from spirits alone upon its own fire. And just as the mineral spirits are not the common kind, but are altered, so also are the spirits of the Art. 

And just as nature makes actual bodies from spirits alone—that is, from these spirits which are bodies in potentiality—so also the Art ought to do. And just as nature mixes nothing else with its principles, because it would hinder generation, so also does the Art. And just as nature has two principles, one which holds the nature of the **agent** <note>The active, masculine principle (Sulfur).</note>, and the other which holds the nature of the **matter** or the **patient** <note>The passive, feminine principle (Mercury/Quicksilver) that receives the action.</note>, so also does the Art. And just as nature composes these principles together in certain measures and determined weights, so also the Art ought to compose them. 

But the Art cannot know the required weights; therefore it is necessary that, like a **handmaid** <note>A common medieval phrasing: "Ars imitatio naturae," Art as the servant or imitator of nature.</note>, it accepts such compositions from nature. There will therefore be one material weighted by nature, in which the Art must work, and that is sufficient. From which it is concluded that it is necessarily required that all the differences which are actually in mineral gold must also be potentially in the stone and in the elixir, and are manifested in the gold which is made through the elixir in actuality. Specifically, that it be the heaviest, the most yellow <note>original: "citrinissimum." The yellowing (citrinitas) was a key stage indicating the transition to gold.</note>, the most brilliant, impassible by those things which burn <note>meaning it is fire-proof or non-combustible.</note>, most tempered, and most medicinal.

From all these things it is further concluded: that those two spirits alone mixed by nature, namely sulfur and quicksilver, are the principles and matter of metals, and are metals in potentiality. Therefore, the Art also generates the elixir—which is gold in potentiality—from those same principles or from entirely subtle things mixed by nature, provided that suitable preparation precedes it. And indeed, those spirits by themselves alone with themselves alone are a body in potentiality. Thus, therefore, the mercurial spirit, existing...

It emphasizes that the Alchemist acts as nature's handmaid, using materials already balanced by natural processes.</summary>

the subject of nature, and a spirit entirely similar to itself, when it has become the subject of the Art, cleansed and purged of its filth through the ingenious art of **sublimation** <note>term: sublimation <gloss>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid as it cools.</gloss></note>, and through a suitable fire has come to its birth: then it is a simple spirit, fleeing in action <note>original: "fugiens in actu," referring to a volatile substance that evaporates when heated.</note>, which the philosophers foresaw, and it is a body in its most proximate potentiality. And this is the **philosophers' sulfur**, and their gold hidden in the **philosophers' quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally living silver.</note>. From this it is manifest that not only are the bodies of metals made only from their own spirits, but the generation of almost all other minerals is from their own vapors, whether simple or mixed. These vapors of all things are of the genre of spirits, because they flee from heat, and yet at the end of digestion they are fixed by a constricting cold: and they are fixed by themselves with their own hidden bodies existing in them in potentiality, without the mixing of any other external body whatsoever. From these things the preciousness of the stone is evident, yet more about this will be declared by us below.

### THAT THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE HAS ONE 
### proper name, and yet is called by many names.

### CHAPTER IX.

This blessed stone, just as it is one thing, so also it is named by one proper name: namely, *trifonis* <note>original: "trifonis"; a term possibly derived from "tri-phonos" (three voices/sounds) or "tri-physis" (triple nature), though its exact etymology in this context is obscure.</note>. Nonetheless, it is called by almost infinite names, and by the names of all things. And this multitude of names proceeded from two classes of men: first, from the Philosophers. Wherefore Bonellus says in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," a famous early alchemical text depicting a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>: "They present this thing by imposing various names upon it because of the different colors appearing during the operation." Hence the same Bonellus says: "The envious have multiplied the names so that they might lead posterity astray," as Hermogenes <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often conflated with Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says. Moreover, the Philosophers call this stone by different and diverse names. For now they call it by the name of a stone, now of animals; now of bronze, or tin, or iron, or lead; indeed, they have named it with the names of all bodies. Now they call it a spirit, now a body, now an egg, now by the name of whatever thing, as the *Lilium* <note>Likely the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical treatise.</note> says. And they did this for three causes or reasons. The first is because of the colors in its operation,

appearing, and signifying a variety and diversity of effects. For in its operation, all colors that can today be imagined in the world appear. And therefore, according to the different colors appearing in the operation itself, its names are diversified by the philosophers. Whence **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist, often portrayed as a hermit who taught the secrets of the Stone to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in the new translation made by **Castrensis** <note>Robert of Chester (Robertus Castrensis), an 12th-century scholar who translated the *Liber de compositione alchimiae* from Arabic to Latin.</note>: "The wise seek this **mastery** <note>term: mastery <gloss>original: "magisterium." The Great Work or the specific process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</gloss></note> much; and finding it, they love and adorn it, while the foolish truly mock it and consider it as nothing." For they are ignorant of what this is, and there are many names by which the wise call it in their books: one of which is **seed** <note>original: "sperma"</note>, which when it is turned into blood is changed, and finally is coagulated and becomes like a piece of eaten flesh. There are also many other names, of which there is one root for all; but according to the different effects, and different colors, and different natures, they name and impose many and diverse names. 

Secondly, the reason for these names is because of the containment of many things within itself. For this stone is composed of all four elements, as was said above; wherefore it is named by the name of any elemental thing. Also within it are all metals in potentiality, and many wonderful works, and the power of spirits and bodies, and the property of minerals, vegetables, and animals, as well as the nobility of all precious stones and herbs; and therefore it not undeservedly usurps the names of all. Whence **Pythagoras** says in the *Turba* <note>term: Turba <gloss>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient philosophers.</gloss></note>: "The stone itself is most precious, because without it nature does not work; its name is one, and yet we call it by many names because of the dignity or excellence of its nature." 

The third cause for these names is for its concealment. Whence the *Lilium* <note>Likely the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a common title for alchemical manuscripts symbolizing purity and wisdom.</note> says: "If the foolish knew this stone, they would not sell it for a cheap price as they do." Likewise, **Daucim** the philosopher says in *Morienus*: "The wise have multiplied the names, effects, and preparations of this mastery for no other reason than to instruct the wise in this mastery, but to utterly blind the foolish." Since just as this mastery has one proper name, and this is purified for itself: so also it has one preparation and one linear path. And therefore (as the *Lilium* says) if the common people knew what a great treasure they held in their hands, they would by no means despise this most cheap and most precious thing. But God has hidden this from the people, lest the world be devastated.
