# *Why many seeking the stone cannot find it, but wander in error.*

## CHAPTER 10.

Many who read the books of the philosophers and believe that the **philosophers' stone** <note>original: "lapidem philosophorum"</note> can be made, seek it but do not find it; they labor and wander in error, losing both their lives and their substance <note>meaning their wealth or worldly goods</note>. There is a double cause for this: the first is the concealment of its proper name, for they do not name it by its own name simply, but always with something added. Whence the *Lily* <note>Likely the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous medieval alchemical text</note> says: "Kings seeking this stone have not found it, except for a few; namely, those to whom God has revealed it." For if the philosophers ever do call this thing by its proper name, they always add something fictional to its name, which is done so that it does not become well-known.

The second cause is the multitude of different names. Whence in the book of **Morienus** <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist</note>, it is said to **Ernech**: "Nothing else has led the **mastery** <note>term: mastery <gloss>original: "magisterium." The Great Work or the specific process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</gloss></note> into error as much as the variety and multitude of names, and because in a single preparation they change the names just as the colors change." Therefore, those running through the books and finding various names conceive a false opinion regarding the matter of the stone—each person a different one, according to what their own fantasy, and not natural reason, suggests to them. From this it happens that some labor in one material and others in another; but all work in an unsuitable material, of which there are many kinds.

Among their number were many men of great authority and famous in philosophy, who considered the principles of nature universally and not in their **proximate** <note>term: proximate <gloss>The immediate or specific substances required, rather than general philosophical principles like "matter" or "elements."</gloss></note> state. And just as they descended to consider the generation of particular things, they judged falsely regarding the generation of metals; they did the same in the principles of the art and its various operations. Therefore they always produced **sophistic** <note>term: sophistic <gloss>original: "sophistica." In alchemy, this refers to "fake" gold or chemical imitations that look like the real thing but lack its essential properties.</gloss></note> works and always remained in sophistries, never arriving at that perfection of the stone which the philosophers intended. 

Others, however, worked in the true principles of the art and nature, but they were entirely ignorant of the true and direct **regimen** <note>term: regimen <gloss>The specific sequence of heating, cooling, and timing required to complete the alchemical process.</gloss></note> of the art, and therefore they erred no less. Since many recognized that the **elixir** <note>A substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note> is the form of gold and silver, informing and transforming imperfect metals, they estimated that the elixir ought to be made from the principles of metals. The principles of metals are **sulfur** and **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note>. From which they concluded that the philosophers' stone must be made from one of these, or from both together: because the philosophers name the stone by the names of these same things. Others truly by these...

...[ar]senic they added; others performed their operation using any kind of **marcasite** <note>term: marcasite <gloss>A term used by early chemists for various shiny minerals like pyrite or bismuth, often mistaken for metallic ores.</gloss></note>, or **tutia** <note>term: tutia <gloss>Zinc oxide, often collected from the chimneys of smelting furnaces.</gloss></note>, or **antimony**, or other minerals. Still others expended their labor on animal or vegetable substances, and all were deceived because of a defect in both: namely, the lack of appropriate matter and the lack of the required operation. This is because they did not know how to judge the proper and proximate principles, which are three: **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note> and **sulfur** altered and mixed in due measure by nature, and the digesting mineral heat, and the power of the place—which is the principle of generation—impressed by the celestial bodies. Each of these induces diversity in the bodies being generated on its own, but they do so much more when all are combined.

From the first principle follows the diversity of elements, or rather of *elementated* things <note>In medieval science, "elementated" refers to complex bodies composed of the four basic elements.</note>, from which metals are generated. From the second follows the diversity of perfections: because through different **digestion** <note>term: digestion <gloss>In alchemy, a process of slow, constant heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance, mimicking biological processes.</gloss></note>, the elements of metals are generated as either purer or more impure, and they are mixed, and once mixed, they take on their specific properties. From the third principle, the various species of minerals are procreated. 

Therefore, although metals and marcasites commonly have the same two primary principles—namely sulfur and mercury—nevertheless, because the quantity, measure, mixture, and digestion are so very different in different things (for the diversity of the mixture and digestion causes diversity in how the matter can be affected), the qualities of the elements will be different, whether in simple or composite forms. Thus, metals share in common "passions" <note>Properties or characteristics</note> because they tend toward one final form. 

However, neither marcasite, nor sulfur, nor mercury in their own nature are the principles that compose metals; rather, it is a certain **third nature**, blended and mixed in due measure, generated from them. Otherwise, nature could not heap them together in one place to complete their generation, because neither the nature of minerals nor even of vegetables possesses those local movements required for generation <note>The author argues that minerals cannot move themselves to "find" each other; nature must create a unified "third substance" to act as a seed.</note>. **Art** <note>meaning alchemy or human skill</note>, however, possesses the power of division and conjunction. It is necessary, therefore, that this third nature has a certain common nature, altered from the nature of its components, which arises from their diverse mixing and digestion; and in this third nature resides the mineral power for the generation of the compound. 

Now, there are two types of compounds. One is that whose components are entirely subjected as matter, and from their composition a new form is made, different from the forms of its simple parts; yet there does not remain within them the potential for a further metallic form, which

...could be made through the **digestion** <note>term: digestion <gloss>In alchemy, a process of slow, constant heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance, mimicking biological processes.</gloss></note> of nature, such as **marcasites** <note>term: marcasite <gloss>A term used by early chemists for various shiny minerals like pyrite or bismuth, often mistaken for metallic ores.</gloss></note>, **atraments** <note>term: atrament <gloss>A group of black, metallic substances, usually vitriols or copperas (sulfates).</gloss></note>, and **magnesia**. But there are certain things whose components are not entirely subjected as matter; rather, one acts as the **agent** and the other as the **matter**. And such things indeed do not remain under that form in which the components existed in their first composition. Beyond this, through mutual action and passion <note>original: "actionem & passionem"; in medieval philosophy, 'passion' refers to the capacity of a substance to be acted upon or changed.</note>, they can be digested and transmuted from form to form, until they reach the ultimate form and perfection, which is the form of gold. 

Then the agent is separated from the matter. Such digestion occurs in the generation of metals, whose matter is mixed from two principles in the mines—namely, from **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>. It does not remain in the form it held in its first composition, but they act and react upon one another continuously until a new form is generated, namely that of an imperfect body. At that stage, the agent is not yet separated from the matter, but if the digestion is continued to the very end—until the agent is totally separated from the matter—then a new form is generated: the form of a perfect metal, which is the form of gold. 

From these things it is clear that all minerals are composed of their elements in determined quantities and mixed measures, so that among the mixable parts, one is not prior or posterior to the other; rather, the generation of the simple and the composite happens simultaneously and at once, and vice versa. This is just as occurs in the generation of milk, which is composed of three substances: namely, cheese <note>original: "caseo," referring to the solid curds.</note>, butter, and whey; and their generation occurs simultaneously with the milk itself. 

From these points, it is concluded that since metals are composed only of two things—quicksilver and sulfur—and likewise their ores, and since art must imitate nature, it is absolutely necessary that the work proceeds from the very same principles from which nature does, or similar ones, for the generation of the **elixir** <note>term: elixir <gloss>The "philosopher's stone" or the medicinal substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</gloss></note>, and that it observes the same weights. From this it is clear that those who work with sulfur alone labor in vain. 

First, because however much sulfur is purified through **sublimation** <note>term: sublimation <gloss>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used for purification.</gloss></note>, it cannot belong to the composition and substance of gold, nor can it be subjected as matter, because no agent is subjected as matter. Second, because sulfur alone has no matter upon which it may act through continuous digestion to ultimately extract a form, as if from the potentiality of matter. For if this could happen, it seems it should happen most of all in the mine, where it would be reduced to the perfection of the medicine. And after it was suddenly mixed with quicksilver, it would suddenly coagulate into a metal, which does not happen. Third, indeed, because sulfur cannot be fixed unless it is **calcined** <note>term: calcination <gloss>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to oxidize it or make it brittle.</gloss></note>, and it is not calcined except through sublimation, both of which are difficult...

Others, however, who labor with **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note> alone, err even further, as Aldimarus <note>historical figure: Likely a reference to an alchemical authority cited in medieval texts, possibly associated with the school of Geber.</note> says:

Others have attempted to make the stone from quicksilver and sulfur mixed together: which is no less impossible. First, whether one digests each for itself, or both mixed together, he will not be able to follow the intention of nature. Second, because no one can know how great a measure of them is necessary, either in minerals or in metals. Third, since each by itself is difficult to prepare, both mixed together will be even more difficult.

Others, however, labor in gold alone, but neither do these act according to the intention of the philosophers. First, because although its sulfur is the dye for its quicksilver, from whose power it was extracted, it is nevertheless not sufficient to generate another gold, or to increase and multiply its tincture, since its tincture is the final degree in metals. Second, because the work of the philosophers is not expensive—at least for those who have correctly investigated the way of nature and the proper **regimen** <note>term: regimen <gloss>The specific method of governing the alchemical fire and the stages of the process.</gloss></note>. And of this Geber <note>historical figure: Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in Islamic and medieval Latin alchemy, known for emphasizing the sulfur-mercury theory.</note> says: 
> You ought not to consume your goods: because for a low price, if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art which we shall deliver to you, you will reach the complete **mastery** <note>term: magisterium <gloss>The "mastery" or the successful completion of the alchemical work.</gloss></note>. 

Gold, however, is expensive: and thus would the poor be forced to set aside this glorious work? And since it is necessary for the craftsman to err many times, a poor man could not repeatedly restart the work, as this art requires. And thus those who approach the operation and perfect understanding of this art would be unable to work because of extreme poverty. Of whom Geber says: 
> Yet these, oppressed by ultimate poverty, are forced by the lack of means to set aside this glorious work. 

Therefore, poverty does not prohibit the operation of the stone, except in the extreme. And so it is necessary that from the beginning of the operation, the matter of the art be one and cheap, in which there is the power of the body, spirit, and soul, similar to the matter...

mineral. Others truly labor with Mercury and brass <note>original: "ære," which refers to copper or its alloys like brass or bronze</note>, and the ferment of the sun <note>original: "solis," the alchemical name for gold</note> or the moon <note>original: "lunæ," the alchemical name for silver</note>, which they take from this: because philosophers frequently call the stone "brass," but they are deceived. First, because the philosophers speak of the "brass of the philosophers," which is also called "our gold," or "philosophical gold"—and similarly for iron or lead. Second, because common brass has many impure sulfurous qualities, infecting and corrupting the medicines, which can hardly or not at all be removed through purifications. Such sulfur is not of the essence of gold. Gold is also from the clearest and purest natures, and its parts are of a single substance and nature, and not diverse. Third, although the ferment of gold may be mixed in, gold cannot perfect brass by its own power as much as the gold itself is diminished in power by the brass. The same must be said of all who work with other metals, who labor uselessly, and after long effort find nothing or very little. Therefore, as is said by Arnaldus <note>historical figure: Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> in his book of the Testament: such operations are exceedingly long, tedious, and of great expense, and sometimes because of a single defect, the entire business is lost. And even if we begin well, we either give up or become negligent. Therefore, even if the stone could be made from metals, it is more advisable to leave the work aside than to begin or start it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;There are others who labor with salts, vitriols <note>original: "atramentis," literally "inks," but used here for metallic sulfates or vitriols</note>, and alums, dissolving gold or silver or other metals with them or with their "waters" <note>term: waters <gloss>In this context, strong mineral acids like nitric or sulfuric acid capable of dissolving metals.</gloss></note>, and afterward they distill and congeal the dissolved powders <note>term: calces <gloss>Metallic oxides or residues produced by heating a metal in air (calcination).</gloss></note>. And these err even more gravely: because these things are furthest removed from the intention of nature.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Some, however, approach closer to the truth: those namely who work with quicksilver and gold or silver. This is because gold is the most noble body and quicksilver is the most noble spirit, and through the mixing and digestion of both, the soul can be extracted. But not even these act according to the true intention of the philosophers, but are deceived by the names which the philosophers use. Know that this art is mystical: but they apply the names to the things exactly as they sound. For when philosophers speak of quicksilver or gold, they want their words to be understood as the "quicksilver of the philosophers," just as they mean the "gold of the philosophers." Because the gold of the philosophers is the sulfur of the philosophers, w<gloss>hich</gloss> is extracted from the quicksilver of the philosophers. Therefore, one who wishes not to err must consider the hidden names in the sayings of the philosophers, and not merely the literal meanings themselves.

# ON THE STONE

Others truly labor in arsenic or orpiment <note>original: "auripigmento," yellow arsenic sulfide</note>: because
both are composed by nature from two mineral prin-
ciples, namely quicksilver and sulfur, which is shown by
a shining sublimation that tints toward whiteness, as well
as by its metallic liquefaction. Now, that it might tint, quicksilver
has from sulfur a power that coagulates and digests it.
Hence, if arsenic is first boiled in sharp things, such as vinegar,
urine, and salt, and afterward sublimated with metallic
calces <note>powders or oxides produced by burning metals</note> and salts, it is made as white as snow and transparent
as crystal. Similarly, arsenic is very heavy and flammable,
but its weight can only come from quicksilver, while its
flammability comes from sulfur. Therefore, arsenic would be the subject
and the principle in the eyes of nature for the generation of Gold, and in the
eyes of art for the generation of the Elixir, as <term>Master Bonus</term> <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century alchemist who wrote 'The Precious New Pearl'</note> says in
chapter 6. But these people err most gravely. First, because the nature of arsenic is
volatile and caustic <note>original: "adustiua," burning or corrosive</note>. Second, because it is difficult to fix <note>to make a substance resistant to heat</note> or
to melt. Third, because it only whitens in the lesser work <note>original: "minori opere," the stage aimed at creating silver rather than gold</note>:
it is a heavy task to extract the citrinity <note>yellowness</note> from its hidden depths,
even though it has sulfur in its nature—by reason of which it could be fixed
and turned red—and which is also inseparably joined to its quicksilver
in the smallest parts, coagulating and somewhat digesting it.
Fourth, because although the philosophers seem to assert
that it is the matter of the stone, they nonetheless speak of it by
metaphor: which is shown by other words of the same philosophers,
which cannot be verified regarding common arsenic <note>original: "arsenico vulgi"</note>.
For the philosophers speak of another thing, which behaves in comparison
and properties in the manner of arsenic. And this is called "arsenic,"
and sometimes even "orpiment": Because just as arsenic
is first yellow, and afterward its hidden part is manifested (which
is hidden quicksilver with its hidden sulfur), so also that
thing from which the stone of the philosophers is made first turns yellow
and black in the operation, and afterward turns white, in which whiteness
the redness is hidden—about which matter we have spoken more clearly above.

Third, because in the mines of metals no marcasite is found, nor anything possessing its properties, but in every mine quicksilver and sulfur are found. Therefore, those [mercury and sulfur] are the principles of metals, not these [marcasites]; therefore, it is the same for the Art <note>the "Art" refers to alchemy</note>. And nearly the same reasons apply to tutty <note>original: "thucia," a zinc oxide residue collected from smelting furnaces</note>, magnesia, and antimony, except that their sulfur is in no way separable from them.

Others also labor to make the Stone from certain animals or from some of their parts, such as from oysters, the tortoise, the basilisk, the toad, the salamander, and the rest. Others from human blood, sperm, the skull, etc. Others from eggs and infinite similar things which would be vain to recount. And for all these, as <term>Master Arnaldus</term> <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says, there is one way of working: namely, that they are putrefied and the elements separated through an alembic <note>a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>, and rectified; afterward the earth is whitened, then they are joined and together congealed and fixed. But neither is this way agreeable to nature, nor according to the intention of the philosophers. From which it must be concluded that the philosophers used the words for all these things when they spoke of the Stone; they used many other names and did not lie according to their own intention, because they spoke the truth under an allegory. However, the unwise took the meanings of the things just as the words sound, and labored in them, and deceived themselves and others; they neither arrived at the knowledge of the philosophers' stone, nor even approached it perfectly, but always performed sophistries <note>meaning they produced deceptive or "fake" results</note>. Because work according to the literal meaning of the letters is the dissipation of riches, as is said in the *Book of Saturn*.

### *What qualities the Stone has, and by what signs it can be known.* CHAPTER IX.

Although the Stone of the philosophers cannot be easily known—because the philosophers name it by the names of other things, and obscure it with many [terms], and keep silent its proper name—nevertheless, if someone is faithful, and reads their books frequently, and if he sees the works of nature with intellect, he will find what he seeks by the inspiration of God. For there are two things that allow one to find this Stone with the mastery <note>original: "magisterio," referring to the successful completion of the Great Work</note>. The first thing is reading with diligent inquiry. # CONCERNING THE STONE #

If one remains idle regarding books, he will not be able to be ready in the preparation of things. Certainly, book explains and opens book, and unfolds the discourse: because what is incomplete in one is fulfilled in another. Therefore, he whose mind refuses to toil in theory cannot easily become accustomed to practice. And in the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilio," likely referring to the *Lilium Medicinae* or a related alchemical work such as the *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> it is written: He who desires to arrive more quickly at our Art should not [simply] look at our books: since they bring great trouble and injury to us before they are understood by readers, even after our volumes have been read through once, twice, or three times. 

The second requirement is honored faithfulness, along with devoted prayer to God. Wherefore the master in the *Lily* says: He who bends his back in reading our books and devotes himself to them, and is not entangled in vain thoughts, and prays to the Lord, shall reign in the kingdom without fail until he dies. And earlier the *Lily* says: if from what has been said or is to be said someone cannot reach the knowledge of our Stone because of the clouding of his own intellect, let him not blame the wise men, but himself. For if he seeks and remains ignorant, let him know that God has hidden the truth from him. For if God himself knew a faithful mind in him, He would certainly inspire the truth in him, as Diomedes <note>An authority frequently cited in medieval alchemical compendiums</note> says. 

From this, it follows that everyone ought to hide this Stone, and especially its regimen <term>regimen</term> <note>the specific "rule" or sequence of operations, such as heating and cooling, required to produce the Stone</note>, lest it fall into the hands of enemies, and we be the cause of them doing evil, for which we would deserve to be punished by God. For God alone can freely bestow it upon whom He wills, nor does He sin in bestowing it: because He cannot be unjust or imprudent, but perfectly knows what is profitable for men. From this blessed Art, therefore, are forbidden the soldiers of lust and feminine delights, the clients of crimes, the cruel, those greedy for revenge, the covetous, the avaricious, murderers, and the profane. But as a certain excellent Philosopher says:

> *Hither let Codrus <note>A legendary king of Athens who sacrificed himself for his people; used here as a symbol of piety and selflessness</note> come, the lover of piety:*
> *And whoever worships God and the holy stars.*

For this holy and golden virtue lies hidden from the impious. This Stone, therefore, so diligently hidden by the philosophers, is found with difficulty: because it transmutes many other metals, whether it is found truly or through sophistry <note>i.e., through deceptive or "apparent" chemical tricks rather than true transmutation</note>. Yet it is found by those whom God himself favors, and who pay attention to the meaning of the words and not the literal voices <note>original: "voces," meaning the outward names or sounds of the words used to confuse the uninitiated</note>. 

This Stone is called "copper" <note>original: "æs"</note> by the philosophers because of a certain similarity, and yet it is not copper: it is, however, the "copper of the philosophers." And this is to be understood according to the *Lily*, when our composition is perfected and converted into the elixir <term>elixir</term> <note>the final medicinal or transmuting powder</note>. And further down: "In all the bodies of alchemy, each planet in its place creates its own image until the completion of the work." Therefore, the Sun and Moon hold the beginning and the end. And just as the sun is hidden in the Moon at the beginning, so at the end, having been hidden, it is extracted from the Moon. 

The Stone, however, is more properly called sulphur and mercury, because it holds the power and nature of these. Whence says Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century physician and author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*</note> in his *Postilla* <note>A "postilla" is a marginal note or a short commentary on a specific passage</note> on the fifth chapter: "Just as an embryo is not generated from the menses without seed, nor is the generation of a bird made from wind-eggs <note>original: "ouis venti," unfertilized eggs which were thought by ancient naturalists to be produced by the wind</note> because the virtue of the soul is not in them except from the sperm of the male: so from quicksilver gold or silver is never made, nor even the elixir without the action of sulphur, because there is no generative power in it except through sulphur." 

Likewise, just as from sperm alone, or the seed of the male, without the menses and the matter of the female, no animal is generated (since the whole matter of generation and nourishment comes only from the female), so from sulphur alone without quicksilver, gold or the elixir will never be made. Therefore it is necessary that these two principles, mixed together by nature, concur for the generation of the elixir, just as for the generation of metals. Sulphur

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of the dual nature of the Philosopher's Stone. # PHILOSOPHY #

...therefore, by its own action, [sulphur] digests the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, giving it a metallic **tincture** <term>Tincture: In alchemy, a substance capable of infusing its color and properties into another body, often the final stage of transformation.</term>, first white and later red. However, quicksilver remaining in its own nature, no matter how white and pure it may be, does not dye anything by its own heat and dryness. Our Stone possesses these conditions. Because of this, under allegorical subject matter, the Stone is called **Arsenic** by **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century Italian alchemist and author of "The Precious New Pearl."</note>. And this is not without merit: for Arsenic contains both natures, namely that of sulphur and of quicksilver. Indeed, Arsenic possesses their natures, properties, and substances mixed together; Arsenic itself holds their place and serves as their deputy, being a principle of nature through their commingling, since it possesses their powers and virtues. Because of this, **Geber** <note>original: "Geber," the Latin name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the text likely refers to the "Pseudo-Geber," an anonymous 13th-century author whose works became the foundation of European alchemy.</note> says in the chapter on the principles of nature in the generation of metals:

> There are three principles of nature: namely quicksilver, sulphur, and the peer of sulphur, which is also Arsenic.

And again in the same chapter:

> The natural principles in the work of nature are the **stinking spirit** <note>original: "spiritus fœtens," a common alchemical term for sulphur due to its smell when burned.</note> and the **living water** <note>original: "aqua viua," referring to mercury/quicksilver.</note>: which we also allow to be called **dry water** <note>original: "aquam siccam." This is a paradox describing mercury that has been treated so it does not wet the hands.</note>. Because quicksilver coagulated into Arsenic is "dry water."

Thus, Master Bonus calls the stone Arsenic so that it may be understood that both natures are united in it within a third nature, which is neither the common sulphur nor the common quicksilver of the masses; rather, it is a single thing having the virtues and properties of both. It is also called this so that it might be understood that in the **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then becomes solid again, used here to purify the Stone.</term> of our Stone, one proceeds first toward whiteness, in the belly of which lies hidden the true and perfect redness. Regarding this, **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says:

> Know that sulphur and **Arzenech** <note>A transliteration of the Arabic "al-zirnikh" (arsenic).</note>—that is, **Orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>—are burned, and are quickly consumed by combustion; how then do you expect, or wish to expect anything from that which is quickly consumed by the fire’s burning and reduced to coal, etc.

Explaining this saying, Master Bonus says: that by considering Arsenic according to how it is produced by nature, it is entirely burned, because the combustible sulphur is never separated from the other parts, but all vanish together. Similarly, even in the **lesser work** <term>Lesser Work: Often refers to the creation of the White Elixir (for silver), as opposed to the "Great Work" for the Red Elixir (gold).</term>, if it is fixed in such a way, it never enters the composition. But by considering its hidden nature, which is of the nature of gold, in this way it is not burned: because its hidden parts are separated from the sulphurous ones through the deepest ingenuity. And therefore it seems that Morienus spoke in allegory, just as he and other philosophers were always accustomed to do.

The first tincture, therefore, is from the quicksilver, which it receives from the digesting sulphur; the sign of this is that every metal, when it has been purified, displays openly the nature of coagulated quicksilver rather than sulphur, because of its outward abundance. The second tincture is also from the quicksilver, because the final form is drawn out from its matter. And in this way, the Stone is called "quicksilver." And the contemplation of this is beautiful: because every thing that can be generated or corrupted has its own contrary within itself in potential, which can be brought into action without the presence or mixing of an external contrary. ## *On the governance of the stone in general.*

### CHAP. XII.

Having spoken of the matter of the stone, we must now speak of its **Governance** <term>Governance (Regimen): The precise management of heat and timing required to guide the alchemical matter through its stages.</term>. For many know the stone, but are ignorant of its governance. Whence it is necessary to know that although many working in this art—indeed, almost infinite numbers—err in knowing the proper and immediate matter of the stone, far more and much more greatly are they deceived and tricked in its governance, and therefore very few arrive at the perfection of the stone; from a thousand, scarcely one. Whence in *The Universal Way* it is said: "Scarcely anyone brings this most excellent work to the best end without impediment." And it is necessary for the craftsman of this mastery to arrive at its perfection with many labors and errors. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: Many have our stone and know it, but do not know its virtue; and if they knew its virtue, it would be worth nothing unless they also knew its operation. But the operation cannot be known except through the inspiration of God, or through the teaching and instruction of a master. **Rhodian** also says: In this work of Alchemy many

->*What sort of regimen is specifically necessary for the art.*<-

### CHAPTER XIII.

But what sort of regimen <term>regimen: the method of governing or managing the alchemical process, particularly the application of heat</term> is necessary for this art must be examined next. Indeed, it has seemed to some that the regimen of the stone is solely the work of nature, such that the artisan does nothing else but enclose it in a vessel and suspend it in shadowy air, quiet from whirlwinds, or bury it within the earth, while observing the proper times of the year, month, day, and hour, as well as the favorable paths of the planets and stars, so that nature performs all the rest until completion. And thus the regimen of the stone would be nothing other than its application to the due places and times. This seems to be proven by the fact that metals themselves in the bowels of the earth, as well as stones and other minerals and living things, are brought to their completion solely by the heat and power caused by the celestial bodies. And the *Rosarium* <note>original: "Rosar." refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a seminal 14th-century alchemical text</note> says: 

> Let it be sufficient for you to adequately arrange the matter externally, since it works sufficiently internally toward its own perfection. 

For it has a motion inherent to itself according to one way and one certain order—better and more certain than can be devised by man in the creation of anything generated. Therefore, such preparation alone should be the mastery of the philosophers. <margin>|</margin> Because nature, unless she be hindered by an opposing force, cannot pass by her certain motion before she has time for impregnating, for bringing forth, for nourishing, and for working. And similarly, an argument is drawn from this: that the philosophers say the digestion <term>decoctio: literally a "boiling down," referring to the long, slow heating process used to ripen the alchemical matter</term> of the stone is to be done in the heat of the Sun. Likewise also from this: that the philosophers divide the year into four seasons, and according to the variety of these, they say the Stone is to be governed. For **Zinon** <note>a recurring character/authority in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says in the *Turba*: The year is divided into four parts: the first is winter, cold and moist; the second is spring, hot and moist; the third is summer, hot and dry; the fourth is autumn, cold <note>original: "fridus," likely a scribal error for "frigidus"</note> and dry; according to this manner, it is necessary for us to govern the two natures. Whiten it, therefore, etc. And a certain poet says:

> *Tell me, what increases the number with doubled strengths:*
> *Nature does this, and the indwelling power of the species,*
> *And the stars walking in their right course under heat.*
> *Nay, it is art, arranging the powers of nature in order.*
> *Art and nature therefore perform it; if one fails,*
> *The power of the other, however marvelous, will be empty. etc.*

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the "regimen" or governance of the Stone. While the previous page considered whether nature alone completes the work, this page asserts the absolute necessity of artificial, controlled fire and the use of an alchemical furnace.</meta>

-># PHILOSOPHY<-

Many other things are written concerning this matter: but if anyone, by perusing the books of the philosophers, examines them diligently and rightly, he will find that the governance <term>regimen: the systematic management of the alchemical process, particularly the application of heat</term> of the stone cannot be perfected without the heat of fire administered through art. For all philosophers posit that the mastery <term>magisterium: the "Great Work" or the highest level of alchemical achievement</term> is performed with fire. Whence Morienus <note>original: "Morien." refers to Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have lived in the 7th century</note> says: 

> You should construct the furnace of the philosophers, in which you may kindle the physical fire. 

And the same author says: the greatest efficacy of this work is weighed in its fire; for with it minerals are prepared, and "bad souls" <note>This likely refers to volatile substances that are "fixed" or held within a stable form by the fire</note> are retained in their bodies, and with it souls are joined with the body, and fire is the whole true and perfect proof of this matter. And it is not to be understood from this that the heat of nature is sufficient, but it is necessary to exhibit or administer elemental fire, as is clear from other words of the same author, which are placed below. The same is said in the *Book of Saturn*: the whole governance of our work consists in the fire, in the vessel, and in the sealing. And certainly, without these, the mastery cannot be perfected. 

Likewise, Rhodianus <note>An alchemical authority often cited in medieval anthologies</note> says: 

> The work of Mercury, which is the seed, blood, and flesh, is created in the belly of the Athanor <term>athanor: a self-feeding alchemical furnace designed to maintain a constant heat</term> just as an infant is in the womb of a woman. 

And Bonedus says: Nothing useful is made from the elements without composition and governance, for the reason that seed is generated from blood and desire, etc. For if the moisture and heat of the womb were not present, the seed would not remain, nor would the fetus be perfected. Moreover, a fetus, once drawn out, is nourished only by milk, and by fire sparingly and gradually while it is a small child, and then more as it grows, etc. So also you must do in this operation: and you should know that without heat nothing is ever generated, etc. 

Likewise, it is certain that in the generation of metals, the heat must be continuous: because it would be preserved in its mineral vessels, but it would not be conserved unless the mountain were solid, and the surrounding cold compelled the heat to the lower parts and compressed it. Therefore, by a similar reasoning: the digestion <note>original: "decoctio" refers to the long, slow heating or "cooking" of the matter</note> of the Stone into an elixir is necessarily done with continuous heat conserved in a fit vessel, which could not happen in the open air; because the digestion would be varied now by excessive cold, now by excessive moisture, and now by other alterations. 

And for this reason, Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280): a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on "minerals" and was posthumously associated with alchemy</note> says in the third book of *Minerals*: 

> This is what the heat of fire does in Alchemical matters—provided it be temperate—which the heat of the sun does in the mines: because in both, the power of the planets and stars, having been received, is carried to the vessels and infused into the things themselves. 

Similarly, the fire in the generation of the elixir must be greater than in the generation of the elements: otherwise, if it were equal in both places, the time for both generations would also have to be equal; and thus it would take thousands of years.

The author cites various authorities like Morienus and Albertus Magnus to explain that fire acts as a catalyst, mimicking the sun's role in the earth but at an accelerated pace.</summary>

the elixir would not be perfected. Wherefore, as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century Italian physician and author of the influential alchemical text *The Precious New Pearl* (*Pretiosa Margarita Novella*).</note> says in the fifth chapter: The governance of the same thing with fire is one thing, even though heat is present in both cases. Because of this, the time required for the generation of gold <note>In nature, this was thought to take centuries underground.</note> is one thing, and the time for the generation of the elixir is another. From which it follows that it is necessary to apply another heat—both more intense and more continuous through art—than that which nature provides. For in this way, art is able to compensate for the long duration of nature’s operation. Whence the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note> says: You should diligently exercise the governances, and you will arrive at the virtue; which indeed is perfected neither by itself, nor miraculously, as you might perhaps think, but by the art and operation of the craftsman with a wise intellect.

Whence the philosophers similarly posit that this work is **women's work and children's play**. <term>ars mulierum ac puerorum ludus: A common alchemical aphorism suggesting that once the "Stone" is prepared, the remaining process is as simple as domestic cooking or a child's game.</term> And they said this because it is the work of women to cook; however, nothing is cooked without fire: therefore, neither is this work done, nor can it be done, without fire. Thus, with the fire administered from the outside, it is perfected by the craftsman. Truly, it is not concluded from this that nature does not also work. For nature perfects all things, and the craftsman only applies the necessary things, and among the rest, fire, as it is most necessary.

Since the matter itself is partly fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" substances resist fire and do not evaporate, while "volatile" substances fly away when heated.</note>, fire must be administered to it from the beginning and continued until the end—tempered, however, so that the matter gradually becomes accustomed to enduring the fire, until at last the whole is fixed, so that it fears no fire at all. For this is the end of the art: that a **sulfur**, or elixir, be generated that is entirely unburnable <note>original: "incremabile" - meaning it cannot be consumed or destroyed by fire</note>: just as the end of nature is that gold be generated, which is not diminished in the fire. This is achieved by nothing else so appropriately as by fire: because thus it is gradually strengthened by the power of fire and approaches incorruptibility.

The governance of this art, therefore, is fire and heat—and not only natural heat, or that of the stone, or of the celestial moons: nor is it necessary to observe the rising and courses of the celestial signs, or the aspects of the planets, or the seasons of the year, or the days or hours, except insofar as it pertains to the goodness of the root <term>radix: the base material or fundamental substance used to begin the Great Work</term>, about which will be spoken later. Because the generation of this Stone of ours is entirely natural, like other things which nature produces, and its effect is similar; although it should be called divine and celestial because of its excellence, being both corporal and spiritual: such as is the nature of images and rings. <note>This likely refers to astrological talismans or "constellated" rings thought to hold spiritual power within a physical object.</note> The sign of this is that any part of it has the same power as the whole, and it is worth as much crushed or melted as it is whole: nor in its generation is it right to ever observe characters <note>original: "characteres" - astrological symbols or magical sigils</note> by any philosopher...

<summary>This page argues that the alchemist's fire acts as a catalyst to accelerate nature's slow process of making gold. It emphasizes that the work is a natural physical process (likened to cooking) rather than one dependent on complex astrological timing.</summary>

## *WHAT PERTAINS TO THE GOVERNANCE,*
### *having a good root.*
### CHAPTER XIV.

Above all things, however, it is necessary for the root of the philosophers' stone to be the best; otherwise, nothing happens. For Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and purported teacher of Prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: The greatest root of this work is in the investigation of the species, which are better for the mastery <term>magisterium: the technical procedure or accomplishment of the Great Work in alchemy</term>. For every mineral is of many kinds. And in the *Book of Saturn* <note>An alchemical text often associated with the influence of the planet Saturn (lead).</note> it is said: Take our stone from the highest good, and do not receive it unless it is fresh with all its blood. Likewise, in the *Universal Way*: New species are better than old ones. And Mundus in the *Assembly* <note>Mundus is a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: Take care that you do not take the bronze <note>original: "æs"</note> unless it is pure and clean.

To ensure that the root is the best, one must specifically attend to three things regarding it. First, that it be extracted from the best bodies. For good fruits are gathered from good trees, and better gums flow from better trees; and better eggs are procreated from better hens; and good pasture makes good and fat meat. In the race of hens, black ones are better than white ones. Among temperaments <term>complexiones: the medical balance of humors in the body</term>, the sanguine and choleric are better; among ages, youth is better and more robust. Whence the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century collection of alchemical authorities.</note> says: You shall not eat of the son whose mother suffers her monthly period; but if you eat, eat of the fattest meat, and you shall have gold. 

And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: Do not eat of the son whose mother is a leper; because if we have a pure substance, we can create a pure body; and if the male is a leper and the female is a leper, it is inevitable that a leprous body will be generated. Hence, if we wish to create a pure body, it is necessary for us to have a pure male, clean from all filth; and a pure female, clean from all filth; and likewise a pure, clear seed, clean from all filth. And Raymond in his *Book of Terms* <note>Raymond Lully.</note> says: Take gum of India, if you can have it, which is a gum black and clear on the outside, and red on the inside, or from Spain, and join together the male with the female, etc.

# ON THE STONE
<meta>catchword: being born-</meta>

The second point you must consider is that the female is impregnated by her male seed. For the generation of the stone is almost exactly like the generation of man: because the seed of both must come together, namely of the male and the female. For every generative power of the soul comes from the seed of the male. Hence, just as a bird is not generated from "wind-eggs" <note>original: "ex ouis venti." An ancient belief, mentioned by Aristotle and Pliny, that some eggs were produced by the wind alone and were infertile.</note>, so the stone is not generated from the philosophers’ egg unless the female has been impregnated by her seed—that is, by her male. 

And this seed is a fiery power, penetrating and staining, and it is a coagulant that thickens the menstrual flow <note>In medieval physiology, the "menses" or menstrual blood was believed to provide the material substance for the fetus, while the male seed provided the form and spirit.</note>, and it is a subtle, life-giving soul or spirit. And because of this, a certain philosopher says: "Just as a man cannot be generated without the union of a man and a woman, so our medicine cannot be generated without the union of the male and the female." For the male is hot and dry, while the female is cold and moist. In the union of both, the heat is tempered with the coldness, and the dryness with the moisture; for an animal is not properly generated if heat exceeds coldness, or vice versa, or if dryness exceeds moisture, or vice versa. 

In the mixing of both, the extreme opposites are brought back to a middle disposition, namely to a tempered warmth. For the life of living things consists in heat and moisture—tempered heat and moisture, that is—as the doctrine of Aristotle <note>Referring to the Aristotelian theory of the four humors and qualities, where life is sustained by a balance of heat and moisture.</note> holds. So it is in all things concerning our one stone: which is not only composed of a twofold nature, namely male and female as was said above—by reason of which they act and suffer upon one another, and they perfect and are perfected, as will appear in what follows—but also from its first origin, it is conceived from the sperm of the male and the sperm of the female and the menstrual blood, and it arises by being born. 

On account of this, it is called an "animal," because it possesses life in potential, and it is always volatile for both <note>Likely referring to the spirit and soul being prone to evaporation unless fixed.</note>, unless it is cast into the dunghill <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the putrefaction stage (nigredo) or a literal source of steady, gentle heat.</note>. And because it is a "domestic animal," some have not undeservedly named it "man." Hence, in the *Book of Saturn* <note>A classic alchemical text focusing on the properties of lead and the foundational stages of the work.</note>, concerning the first and second procreation of this stone, it is said: "If the male is joined with the female through tempering, by means of the seed, it is necessary that the generation occurs from the menstrual blood." 

And another philosopher says: "That thing from which the stone is made is called <term>Rebis: from the Latin 'res bis', meaning 'a double thing' or 'a thing composed of two'</term>." And he spoke truly, because it is composed once or at one time in the belly of the earth (that is, of the mother) so that it might be born, and it is composed a second time in a glass vessel, so that it might be perfected into the <term>elixir: the final, perfected substance capable of transmutation</term>. It is composed of two things: from the sperm of the male and the menstrual flow of the female—that is, from the red and the white.

It introduces the concept of the Rebis, a substance "twice-composed" both in nature and in the chemist's glass vessel.</summary>

is born, even between two mountains, which are the father and mother. Others, however, say between two mountains, that is, **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum." In alchemy, sulfur and mercury are the two primary principles whose union creates all metals.</note>, or the **sun** and **moon**: but these consider the property of the stone in itself: while those demonstrate its origin: because it is born from male and female: and therefore it retains and preserves the properties of the male and female within itself.

The third point to be observed is that it be taken at the best time: for any thing comes to human use when it is in its own nature and at its most perfect state. Our Stone, however, just as it is found everywhere, so it is also found at all times: but it is not of equal power at all times, just as it is not in every place. Every living thing has its own proper time: any fruits and plants are better when they are ripe: thus our Stone is better because of two factors: first, because of the time, namely when it is born in the spring. Other things, such as <term>gum</term> <note>In alchemy, "gum" often refers to the viscous, semi-solid state of the matter during the early stages of the "Great Work."</note>, are ripened and flow out by the heat of summer. For at this time, as **Raymond of Marseilles** <note>An influential 12th-century astronomer and scientist.</note> says, heat and humidity increase more, as do blood and <term>choler</term> <note>original: "cholera." One of the four bodily humors, associated with fire and heat.</note> together. And therefore also this element of the stone abounds more in the spring, and in this way nature helps art, and the time helps the work, and the plants help the mastery. Second, [it is better] from the freshness of the fruit: recent things are better than aged ones, provided they are ripe: Because when a thing is born from individual things and plucked from its roots, its virtue is gradually drawn out more mildly until it is totally corrupted. Our stone, however, is most tender, and its virtue quickly exhales, unless it be nourished by our heat. And therefore some older material does not suit our work, as was said before. But the fresh is entirely uncorrupted, etc.

# CONCERNING THE STONE

To speak well of what comes first, it is necessary to know the **vessel**, which follows: in which, as in its own proper place, the stone is born. For every single thing is generated in a place suitable for itself. Therefore, the vessel of this stone, so admirable, is very necessary. Whence Morienus <note>Morienus is a legendary figure in alchemy, often identified as a hermit who taught the secrets of the Stone to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says:
> If the wise had not found their expositions regarding the quality of the vessel in which the creation of the stone is completed, they could never have reached the perfection of the mastery <note>original: "magisterij." In alchemy, the "Mastery" or "Magistery" refers to the successful completion of the Great Work.</note>.

For I have shown above that this mastery does not differ much from the creation of a human being: and the creation of a human is not perfected except in the maternal womb. For animals are nourished and perfected in the bellies of their mothers, in a tempered warm moisture, from the mixing of seeds, as Morienus says. Metals, for their part, are born in the "belly of the earth" through a boiling heat. The fetus is procreated in the uterus and the chick in the shell: it is therefore necessary to deduce the condition of the vessel from the nature of the stone. Indeed, the **Stone of the Philosophers** is not perfected unless its entire power is retained within its vessel. For this reason, the vessel in which this mastery is performed must first be very strong, so that it can withstand the fire. Whence says the *Lilium* <note>Referring to the "Lilium Alchimiae" or "Lily of Alchemy," a popular medieval alchemical treatise.</note>:
> This stone-like and circular vessel must be one that does not fear the fire, and it must not be porous but very solid.

Whence it is said in the *Book of Saturn*:
> Many have made vessels of earth, and of iron, and found themselves deceived in the end: because the **spirits** <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to volatile substances or gases that evaporate easily.</note> escape through the pores, and therefore they were unable to reach the perfection of the mastery.

Thirdly, it should be made of glass from one single material. For glass is created in the fire: and therefore it withstands fire more strongly than all other things. Glass is also solid and has no pores: therefore the spirits cannot exhale from it, as is said in the same book; indeed, no other material whatsoever would be effective. Fourthly, it must be good and thick. Whence the *Lilium* says:
> For few of these stone-like vessels which the glassmakers use last; rather, they are corroded in the work, or they are split.

Therefore Morienus says:
> And place the mixture in a thick vessel.

And in the "Universal Path" <note>original: "via vniuersali," likely referring to a specific alchemical methodology or text.</note> it is said:
> Let each part be placed separately in a double glass urinal <note>An "urinal" in alchemy refers to a specific shape of round-bottomed flask, named for its resemblance to the vessels used by physicians for uroscopy.</note>.

Fifthly, it should be round in the belly, and long and narrow in the neck. Whence Pandulphus and Horsoleus say:
> Let it be round or made in the fashion of the celestial moon.

And in the "Universal Path" it is said:
> Let the vessels be of glass, having a round bottom and a long neck to the measure of half a foot, or narrow around the mouth, yet thick enough that you could stick your thumb in; and let them be shaped like a phial, and be thick and strong: otherwise they could not hold this **water**, but would be broken by its excessive strength.

<meta>catchword: Sixthly</meta>

Sixth, only one vessel is sufficient. Whence the *Lilium* <note>The *Lilium Alchimiae* or "Lily of Alchemy," a popular medieval alchemical treatise.</note> says: It must be known that the philosophers attribute only one single vessel to this operation of ours; because all those speaking of the operation always speak of the vessel in the singular. Whence Bonellus says: "Place it in its own vessel." Xistus also says: "And place it in its own vessel with a narrow mouth." And in the *Book of Saturn*: "The whole is perfected in one vessel, and not in several." And Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note> says: "And all this is done in one furnace and in one vessel." This is, therefore, the miraculous vessel, which is called by various names. For it is first called the **Vessel of the Philosophers**, frequently found by the philosophers alone as the most suitable for the operation of the stone. It is also called the **Philosophers’ Egg**: because it is arranged in the shape of an egg. It is called a **sublimatory**, from the fact that the stone is sublimated within it. It is also called a **sieve**: because in it the stone descends drop by drop like water through a sieve. Whence Mireris says: "It must be sifted through its own sieve." It is furthermore called a **sphere**, because it is made in that likeness. And because in it the stone is rolled and rotated above and below, like in its own orb, in a circle. Whence Mireris says: "Sphere the sphere <note>original: "Sphęra sphęrate." This likely refers to the circular motion of the substances during distillation or the spherical shape of the vessel itself.</note> and you shall find." And Ascanus says: "The gold must be sifted seven times through the sieve of the sphere." It is also called a **sepulcher**, because in it the stone is buried, and by the operation of the fire it dies, as it is said in the *Symbolo*. It is called, moreover, a **prison**: because in it the male and female are violently detained. It is called both the **Old Lion** and the **Green Lion** <note>The "Green Lion" usually represents a strong mineral acid or the raw "Fixed" matter of the stone before it is purified.</note> by Morienus: because it is strong as a lion. It is also called a **urinal**, a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbita: a gourd-shaped chemical flask used for distillation</term>, a **flask**, a **phial**, an **egg**, and is named by many other names.

...joined the king’s son to his sister, and immediately the king’s son was dead: etc. <note>This refers to a common alchemical allegory where the "marriage" of substances results in their "death" or "putrefaction," a necessary stage of dissolution before rebirth.</note> The second error is of those who mix the entire stone together by grinding, and after it is mixed, they put it in the vessel. First, indeed, that the male and female, the Sun and the Moon, the sulfur and the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver," the technical term for mercury.</note>, the red and the white—which are the same—should be placed in the vessel at the same time: nor should one ever be separated from the other. Truly, the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) represents gold or sulfur, while the "Moon" (Luna) represents silver or mercury.</note> are joined for the generation of the **Elixir** <term>Elixir: derived from the Arabic 'al-iksir,' refers to the powder or potion that effects the transformation of base metals into gold.</term> in art, just as they are joined in nature. Wisely put these two into the vessel and pray to God, and you shall see this stone mixed in the work.*

From which it follows, that the mixing is not to be done by the craftsman before the imposition: but afterwards by nature and the operation. And thus the word of **Hermes** is understood: *Take the stone of Gold, and mix it with the moisture, namely the permanent water*, etc. And again, unless it were a ferment, the water would not be coagulated. Because of this, it is called by **Maria the Prophetess** <note>Also known as Mary the Jewess, a legendary foundational figure of alchemy to whom the invention of several laboratory apparatuses is attributed.</note> the **Coagulum** <term>Coagulum: Literally "rennet" or "curd," a substance that causes a liquid to solidify.</term> that coagulates. Thus what was said above is understood. And "place them mixed in the vessel" means mixed by nature. Whence a certain great philosopher says: *Shut the man and the woman in the same tomb.* And **Socrates** says: *The secret of the work is made from the male and the female; for the female rejoices when the strength of the male is received*, etc. And **Raymond Lull** <note>original: "Raymun. de terminis." And therefore, in the beginning, they reside at the bottom of the vessel like little stones <note>original: "lapilli"</note>: wherefore **Arnaldus** <note>Arnald of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says: 
> Take of the water of the pure sun, and of the water of the pure moon, mixed and united together, and place them in a glass vessel out of the sun: and then the sun and moon will be residing like small stones. 

From these things it is understood that the stones can be placed in the glass in any number at will. And therefore the vessel should be hollow and of good capacity. For according to the multitude of the material, one must establish the size or capacity of the vessel. However, it ought to be only half full: indeed it is safer that only the 3rd part be full and two parts empty, and even less. And therefore it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: Place the vessel with the material in a bowl containing ashes to a thickness of 2 fingers, and let it stand over the fire in the furnace <note>original: "furnello"</note>, and let only the 3rd part of the vessel be covered with compressed ashes, and fix the vessel well so it does not lean to one side, etc. Although the stone can be in an even or odd number: nevertheless, an odd number is more mystical and divine. Wherefore **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully, a Majorcan philosopher often associated with alchemical works.</note> says quite expressly in *On Terms*: Put 25 little sips <note>original: "sorbillia." This likely refers to small pellets, droplets, or measured doses of the substance.</note> into a closed vessel, and fit the vessel in the philosophers' bath, so that the heat of the sun may surround the vessel everywhere: and **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umayl), an influential Arabic alchemist whose symbolic visions were widely studied.</note> saw under a figure 9 eagles, and a statue in the middle upon a chair with a marble tablet in his hands, and two birds, one with wings and the other without wings: one held the tail of the other in its beak, and vice versa, and the sphere of the sun, the sphere of the moon, etc. Second, that the Sun or the male should be placed in whole. Therefore **Mundus** warns in the *Turba*: 
> Place these two into the vessel wisely. 

He says, moreover, "wisely," because care must be taken lest the sphere of the sun be broken by chance: but if it should be broken by chance, the sun must be extracted again: it is easily extracted if a stalk or a thin reed,

## THAT THE SEALING IS NECESSARY FOR THE 
### regimen.
### CHAPTER XVII.

It is not only necessary for the vessel to be extremely strong, but also for the sealing to be most heavily fortified: because, as has been said, unless the most subtle spirits are retained, the entire <term>magisterium: the Great Work or the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> is lost. Furthermore, as soon as the stone is placed in the vessel, it begins to sweat because of the narrowness of its prison, and the most subtle parts begin to exhale; the longer it is cooked, the more the spirits are multiplied, refined, and strengthened. And for this reason, it is necessary to close the vessel immediately from the beginning and obstruct it with a strong seal <note>original: "forti sigillo." This refers to the "Seal of Hermes," an airtight closure.</note>, lest the flowers <note>In alchemy, "flowers" refers to the volatile vapors or sublimates that rise to the top of the vessel.</note> flee and the entire mastery be lost. What would it help to have the strongest vessel if its closure were not firm and of the best quality? Nor is it even enough that it be firm, unless it is also perfectly solid: which is the case when it is in no way porous. Therefore, all philosophers urge a strong sealing. **Mundus** <note>A sage often cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says regarding this: "Close the mouth of the vessel firmly." **Theophilus** says: "Close the mouth of the vessel firmly, lest the flowers flee." **Artephius** <note>A famous 12th-century alchemist to whom many influential texts were attributed.</note> says: "Let it be placed in a glass house, and let it be covered most strongly with cement, lest air enter or the enclosed moisture escape." And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: "Place our stone with its whole substance into our vessel, and close it perfectly so that it cannot breathe." And **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit said to have taught the secrets of alchemy to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "Close the mouth of the vessel with bitumen <note>A natural mineral pitch or sealant.</note> lest the winds escape: for over time the winds are multiplied in the vessel and become extremely hot, so that there is a danger either that the vessel may be broken or the seal may be ruptured." Whence **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an Arabic astrologer and alchemist.</note> says figuratively of these winds: "Know that the roots of their minerals are in the air, and their summits in the earth: and when they are uprooted from their places, a terrible sound is heard, and there will be great fear. Go quickly, because they quickly vanish, etc." And for this reason it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: "Know that the whole <term>regimen: the governed process or sequence of the alchemical operation</term> consists in the fire and the vessel: because if the mouth of the vessel is not well closed, the fumes—which are most subtle—escape, and the entire mastery will be brought to nothing." There is therefore a double danger if the sealing is not strong: first, that the work and labor may be lost, as has been said; second, that it may kill or injure the craftsman: because from the beginning the stone is like a deadly poison <note>original: "toxicum mortificans." Alchemists often warned that the initial stages of the work produced toxic vapors, such as those from mercury or arsenic.</note>; in the middle...

PHILOSOPHY

### **THAT THE FURNACE WHICH IS CALLED THE A-**
### ***thanor, is necessary.***

### **CHAPTER XVIII.**

No less suitable is the furnace, in which the vessel with the matter is placed and cooked by fire. For it was said above that the whole regulation of the <term>mastery: the "magisterium," or the successful completion of the Great Work</term> and of our work consists in the fire, the vessel, and the seal: because without these, the mastery cannot be perfected, as is clearly stated in the *Book of Saturn*: "The required fire certainly cannot be administered except in a furnace suited for this purpose." It is necessary, therefore, according to the saying of **Morienus** <note>original: "Morienus." An 8th-century legendary alchemist associated with the transmission of the craft from the East to the West.</note> in the *New Translation*, that the craftsman knows the quality of the fire and of his furnace: and likewise the ascent of the fire: namely, in which part of the furnace, or in which place, the fire ought to be lit, etc. And concerning this, three things must be observed: first, the proper arrangement of the furnace and a suitable proportion of fire, so that it is neither too large nor too small, neither too high nor too low, and so that the walls are not too thick or dense, nor too thin: but rather so constructed that it receives, preserves, and provides sufficient and continuous heat. For a large furnace and a small one, or a thick and a thin one, are not heated equally and continuously with the same heat. Whence **Morienus** says: "Where above you build the furnace of the philosophers, in which you light the philosophical fire: for either its fuel will be composed of dung, or of olive leaves—which is nothing other than so that the fire may last with an even combustion." <note>Alchemists often used "lamp fire" or the steady biological heat from fermenting dung to maintain the low, constant temperatures required for the slow maturation of the Stone.</note>

He should seek, secondly, that the heat touches the vessel equally everywhere at the height of the material. Whence **Mireris** <note>An obscure alchemical authority often cited in medieval compilations.</note> says: "Bury the vessel in the fiery nature." The fiery nature <note>This refers to the medium used to distribute heat, such as a sand bath or ash bath.</note> being placed beneath and everywhere in a circuit, you must cover the vessel itself, placed in the middle, with two or three fingers' depth of the fiery nature, until it takes on the color of honey, or of red sulfur, or of vermilion. And **Raymundus de Terminis** <note>Likely referring to a follower of Raymond Lully.</note>: "Fit the vessel in the bath of the philosophers, so that the heat of the sun may surround the vessel everywhere." And in the same place where **Mireris** speaks above: "And let all this be done in the fire in a glass vessel, which a potter's vessel should contain." <note>This describes a "nesting" technique where a glass flask is protected inside a ceramic pot to prevent cracking and to ensure even heat.</note> And in the *Philosophical Soliloquy* it is said: "Place the glass vial among sifted ashes, upon a furnace suited to it." And in the *Book of Saturn* it says: "Place the vessel in the furnace, with ash beneath and at the sides, and let two parts of the vessel be uncovered from above, and the third part covered, and regulate the fire well in the furnace. And"

# THAT IN OUR GOVERNANCE THERE IS NO
## *other manual operation except fire.*

### CHAPTER XIX.

It has already been said before that fire is necessary in the mastery of the Stone, but it has not yet been declared whether another operation is required: such as **calcination** <term>Calcination: the reduction of a solid to powder by heat</term>, **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</term>, distillation, the separation of the elements, incineration, and many similar operations which are said to be done in the governance of the Stone, as well as many repetitions and distinct weights and times. But if anyone correctly perceives the sayings of the philosophers, they will find that in such great mastery, there is only one operation and one preparation: and all the other operations of which they speak are carried out and perfected by fire alone. For Master **Bonus** <note>original: "magister Bonus"; refers to Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemist from Ferrara, author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*</note> says in the second chapter: All posit that there is one determined and continuous time of cooking to perfect the white and red **elixir** <term>Elixir: the perfected substance of the Stone, capable of transmuting base metals into silver (white) or gold (red)</term>, although sometimes they vary and interrupt the times in their teaching to lead fools into error. And **Hamis** <note>An alchemist cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> in the *Turba Philosophorum* <note>The "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, originally translated from Arabic</note> says: The philosophers posit many things, none of which they do. Since there is one way and one thing: therefore, do not grind with your hands, nor cook, nor melt in any way like those which physicians prescribe: since the medicine is one, which they have called the pure tincture. Our **lead** <note>original: "Plumbum nostrum"; a symbolic name for the raw material or "First Matter" used at the start of the work</note> when it putrefies is called bronze; when the moisture of the exalted **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: mercury; regarded by alchemists as the "spirit" of metals</term> ends, they call it putrefaction; but after the transition from blackness to a yellow color, they call it gold: but when it shall be from the third tincture, it is called the flower of gold; when from the fourth, it is called ferment; but when the last, it is called the **poison of the tinctors** <note>original: "venenum tinctorum"; this refers to the ultimate potency of the medicine, so powerful it "attacks" and transforms everything it touches</note>. In the same place: The wise compose their books under figures <note>using metaphors and allegories</note>, so that they may completely blind the foolish. I say, however, that for the wise there is one preparation, one way, one thing, one governance: the preparation of which is the change of natures, namely the admirable mixing of hot with cold and moist with dry. Whence **Mireris** <note>Another figure from the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> and many others [say]...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous chapter, emphasizing that although alchemical texts use many different terms for chemical processes, they all describe a single, continuous operation governed by fire.
