# ON THE STONE

The authorities in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient philosophers</note> say: The whole mastery is finished by a single arrangement, from which, as if from a root, all things draw their strength and **tincture** <term>Tincture: in alchemy, a substance capable of infused color or transformative quality into other bodies</term>. The Philosopher, however, divided the work, saying: Cook, grind, repeat; and do not let it weary you, and see that you do not wander. For mixing, cooking, **sublimating** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance into vapor and then solidifying it again</term>, roasting, **calcining** <term>Calcination: reducing a solid to a powder through high heat</term>, whitening, grinding, watering, and dyeing are many names for these things; yet the governance is only one.

And some say that if the philosophers knew that one combustion—that is, one manner of cooking—was sufficient for them, they would not repeat their sayings so many times. However, they did this so that the compound might be ground and governed, and cooked continually; they urged us on so that we would not grow weary. Therefore, there is but one action, which is to cook, as Theophilus says, and also **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; usually referring to the 8th-century scholar Jabir ibn Hayyan, though here likely the "Pseudo-Geber" of Latin tradition</note> in the *Book of Roots*: "if you cook it down patiently and continuously," from which follows the whole governance with fire. For it is said in the *Assembly*: "you have no need for the grinding of hands," because the grinding is done with fire. Hence, when all things have been turned into water, they have been ground diligently.

And Alphidius <note>an alchemical authority, likely a Latinized version of an Arabic name like al-Kindi or similar</note> says: "When we dissolve, we calcine, sublimate, separate, and compose without an interval of time; and between the dissolution and composition of the body and the spirit, no space of time intervenes." Thus our physical dissolution is a true composition. And in the *Book of Saturn*: "I wish to teach you our fire, in which lies the whole perfection; because the work is perfected with fire, but cannot be perfected by hands. For with fire it is ground, with fire it **putrefies** <term>Putrefaction: a stage of decay or breakdown intended to release the 'spirit' from the 'body' of the material</term>, and with fire it is distilled; with fire it is purged and sublimated; with fire it is dissolved, coagulated, and calcined; with fire it becomes volatile and fixed."

Even in this sense, one must understand the separation, cleansing, repetition, and conjunction of the elements. Therefore, it is necessary for the pleasant, supreme, and already purified elements to be set aflame over a light fire, until they are joined and behold one another, and are burned little by little, until they are dried out in that light fire. And it is necessary for them to be washed again and purified, and whitened by fire, until the whole thing becomes one color. Likewise in the *Assembly*: "Our science is the conversion of the four elements and their qualities into one another." Therefore, convert the elements, and you will find what you seek.

Note also that there is no separation of the four elements as the ignorant and unskilled understand it, but in the nature of the elements there is a certain hidden secret—namely, of two elements whose work and power are felt, which are earth and water; but the other two elements, namely fire and air...

For air and water agree in wetness; earth and fire agree in dryness. And therefore these are easily converted into one another, and more slowly separated from each other. However, fire and water, or earth and air, are not converted into each other unless fire is first converted into air, and earth is first converted into water, or vice versa. When, therefore, you have converted the dry into the cold, and the cold into the wet, and the wet into the hot, then you will have the whole mastery of the elements. This is so that through his intellect, he may understand from what he sees the operations that are hidden according to nature, and perceive the divine operation which is above nature. Unless he is helped by natural ingenuity, no matter how much knowledge he gains through teaching, he will not be invited to such "precious feasts," as Geber says; nor could he correct his error at the moment it happens if he did not know how to apply the remedy.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the "governance" of fire, moving from the rejection of mechanical force (crushing) to the specific management of heat according to the metaphorical seasons of the alchemical work. ### ON THE STONE

We begin in winter in this operation—that is, from the moist and the cold—and we arrive at spring through **sprouting** <note>original: "pullulationem"; the stage where the matter begins to change and "grow" like a plant.</note>, which is the appearance of colors, occurring by a light boiling as if in springtime. Then we arrive at summer, namely at **yellowing** <note>original: "citrinationem"; the stage after whitening where the matter takes on a golden hue.</note>, through a greater intensity of fire, as in the heat of summer. Finally, we proceed to autumn; with a greater heat, we arrive at the **reddening** <note>original: "rubificationem"; the final stage of the Great Work, creating the Red Elixir.</note>. But nevertheless, whoever correctly examines the words of the philosophers will find that they all desire that the fire should always be equal and constant, especially until the **whitening** <note>original: "dealbationem"; the *albedo* stage, signifying purification.</note>. 

Wherefore it is said in the *Turba*: 
> "Know that the first moisture is cold; therefore, beware of the fire." 

Because of this, the philosophers ordered us to govern the heat gently until it becomes **incombustible sulfur** <term>Incombustible sulfur: A stable, fixed state of the matter that can no longer be destroyed or vaporized by fire.</term>. And Morienus says: 
> "Construct the furnace of the philosophers in which you light the natural fire; for the fuel shall be composed either of sheep dung or of olive leaves." 

<note>Sheep dung and olive leaves were traditional alchemical fuels used to maintain a very low, steady, and long-lasting heat, similar to a slow-cooker.</note> This, however, is for no other reason than that the fire may be able to endure in its burning until the "white" remains well-fixed within it, and you do not find it scorched because of the fire’s excessive burning. 

And Morienus says in the *Castrensi* <note>Likely referring to the *Liber de compositione alchimiae*, a foundational text attributed to Morienus Romanus.</note>: 
> "When you have directed the impure body, place within it afterward a fourth part of its own ferment, and set it in the sun and cook it. Let its fire be mild, and let it endure by burning equally through its days—that is, let its fire burn equal without ceasing, so that it neither grows stronger nor becomes weaker."

Because <gloss>quod</gloss> of this, Bonellus says in the *Turba*: 
> "Unless there is something in that matter which corrects itself, that which you seek will not happen. For truly, there is that within it which corrects it, provided it is not driven away by too much fire or too much haste." 

And therefore, patience and delay are necessary. Wherefore Zinon says: 
> "If anyone introduced to this art knew its nature, he would surely endure the long duration of the cooking until he drew out the intended purpose by the will of God." 

And Morienus says: 
> "Let the craftsman know the lighting of his fire, the number of its days, and the measure of their weights." 

From these things, therefore, it is clear that the fire ought to be continually equal until the end of the work. If, however, it is sometimes commanded to be made more intense or greater, this should not be understood as an increase in the heat itself, but rather in the duration of time. For the longer a thing lasts in an equal heat, the more it is altered and changed from one nature to another by the action of fire. And therefore, what was at first liquid will afterward be dry; and what was first black or white will afterward be yellow or red, and so on.

It cites several authorities to warn the practitioner against excessive heat and haste, arguing that time and steady warmth are the true agents of transformation.</summary>

PHILOSOPHER

### That the fire must always be slow and continuous.

#### CHAPTER XXI.

But since there are many degrees of fire, it must now be seen how great it should be—whether strong or weak. To this, however, it must be answered: that first, the fire must be slow. Wherefore *The Lily* <note>original: "Lilium"; likely referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous treatise often attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova.</note> says: "Know that without heat, nothing is ever generated; and that intense heat causes destruction, while a cold bath drives away the compound." But through a temperate fire, the body becomes smooth and suitable. For by a light fire, the corrupting moisture is drawn out. Indeed, all the philosophers testify that they have found no other fire for extracting corrupting moistures than a light one, praising endurance while simultaneously—and rightly—reproaching haste. For if the compound is governed more intensely than is proper, it is extinguished. And in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: "libro Saturni"; an alchemical text attributed to the planet/metal lead.</note> it is said: "The entire operation lies in the governance of the fire; for he who knows how to govern the fire will come to perfection."

He who governs his matter with a slow fire can arrive at the **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"; the hidden essence or the ultimate goal of the work.</note>, and thus the matter is not **vitrified** <note>original: "vitrificatur"; turned into glass. In alchemy, if the matter melts into a hard, glassy state, it becomes "fixed" too early and can no longer be transformed.</note> and always remains soluble; but with a violent fire, it is vitrified and hardened to such an extent that it cannot be dissolved except with the greatest labor, which is of no benefit. For it is necessary to separate the subtle parts from the coarse parts, and the volatile <note>original: "non fixas"; things that would normally evaporate.</note> from the fixed; but this does not happen except with a slow fire. For if it were done with a violent fire, either the matter would be burned, or the coarse parts would rise up together with the subtle parts and infect them.

And therefore, all the philosophers desire the fire to be gentle. Wherefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the coarse, gently and with great ingenuity." And Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: "What most fits these bodies together is their oily nature; for that enlivens and joins them, and from them all, one body is made." On this account, the softest fire must be prepared and applied, which throughout its days remains always equal. For when the heat of the fire creeps quickly into the body, the body itself is consumed by a hasty burning. For bodies are quickly burned after they no longer retain their souls <note>original: "animas"; the spirit or volatile principle that protects the physical matter from scorching.</note>. 

Moreover, **Endica** <term>Endica: A term found in translations of Arabic alchemy, often referring to a dross, sediment, or a protective "buffer" substance that regulates heat and prevents the matter from burning.</term> is well-suited for all bodies. For it enlivens and adapts them, defends them from all burning, and protects certain things joined in others and mixed together from excessive heat; and its strength is very great, etc. Because of this, Morienus said before these words: **Azoth** <term>Azoth: The universal solvent, often identified with mercury or the "First Matter."</term> and the fire wash the **latten** <note>original: "latonem"; an impure base metal (resembling brass) that must be purified into gold. The text cuts off as it begins to describe the process of cleaning the latten.</note>—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the precise "governance of fire," emphasizing that the heat must be constant and gentle, rather than fluctuating or intense. # PHILOSOPHY.

[...the] evils which have occurred to them; and therefore, just as decoctions <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence or mature it</term> are not to be increased, so they are not to be interrupted. Whence it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: "In this, many laborers are deceived: because once dissolution is achieved, they coagulate the matter, and then they calcine <term>calcine: to reduce a substance to powder by heat, often to remove impurities</term> it with a stronger heat of fire. Thus they act in every decoction, which is contrary to Geber <note>original: "Geberum"; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry," whose Latinized works were foundational to alchemy.</note>, who places the whole art in sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</term> alone; through which the purest part is divided, etc." This does not happen except through a slow fire, which among the philosophers is called the **Heat of the Sun**, because it is as gentle as the sun's own warmth. For the heat of the sun is not violent, but tempered; however, the heat of a furnace fire is stronger than the heat of the sun. Because of this, the philosophers said: **"Cook sweetly and with a slow fire."**

For a strong fire destroys the work and scatters it; but a slow fire leads to wholeness and generates a single substance. And as Geber says: "A slow fire is the preserver of the natural, or radical moisture <note>radical moisture: the fundamental "liquid" essence within a substance that allows it to grow or change; if it is burned away, the matter becomes "dead."</note>, and it grants the ability to melt; whereas a more vehement fire is the consumer of moisture."

Having learned these things, there still remains a doubt as to how much "heat of the sun" is necessary and sufficient for this work: because within "slow" heat, just as within "strong" heat, many degrees can be understood. For there is a heat slower than slow, just as there is a heat stronger than strong. Therefore, the **governance of fire** is the most difficult of all things necessary to the art. For it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: "Know that those who labor in this science are deceived in the governance of fire more than in any other thing, because they do not know the tempering of the fire. Many know the substance, but they are ignorant of its governance." 

Learn, therefore, the governance of the Sun: for therein lies the whole perfection. You can learn this governance from two sources, by recurring to nature and to the writings. First, then, let nature be your guide. For nature performs its own concoction <term>concoction: a ripening process through heat, similar to digestion</term> plainly and continuously through the heat of the sun within the bowels of the earth, until metals are generated from the mineral spirits of vapor. In this same way, you also must rule your work, and you shall find perfect knowledge. Yet we cannot imitate nature in every single respect; nor is it necessary, as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemical author known for the *Precious Pearl*.</note> said, but it suffices to apply a continuous and slow heat, according to the operation required for our work, just as nature does for hers; though perhaps not at the exact same degree of heat.

Secondly, take the sayings of the philosophers and consider what heat they call "slow." Whence Theophilus says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; a famous early alchemical text where ancient philosophers debate the secrets of the art.</note>: "It is necessary to burn with a slow fire, and to use a certain moisture like the nourishing of eggs." And Moysius says: "And it ought to be so burned and whitened as if by the nourisher of eggs—that is, by a light decoction." Just as...

# ON THE STONE

Water overcomes the battle with fire through the length of time taken for corruption, containment, putrefaction, and thickening; specifically, by the heat of the Sun—that is, by a gentle decoction <term>decoction: the process of heating a substance in liquid to mature it or extract its essence</term>—things are congealed. For a bath—that is, intense heat—causes the work to perish. Likewise, Joan. Teb. <note>original: "Ioan. Teb."; likely referring to Johannes Tabaerontus or a similar medieval alchemical authority.</note> says:

->*Cook the egg in heat:*<-
->*cook only in the manner of the sun,*<-
->*with a gentle touch.*<-

Likewise Mireris <note>Mireris: An alchemical authority frequently cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> asks: "Does not the flying rooster arise from the egg through the heat of the brooding hen? Similarly, from our egg, the flying rooster is created by the heat of this putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the chemical breakdown or 'rotting' of a substance, which alchemists viewed as the death of the old form before a new one is born</term>." And for this reason, let it putrefy in the sea of southern Egypt. Indeed, the lands of the Persians stand in need of Egypt's aid <note>This is a metaphorical geographic reference common in alchemy, likely signifying the union of different chemical principles or "salts."</note>. And Rasis <note>original: "Rafis"; likely Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, the Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> says in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a famous early alchemical text.</note>: "Sons of the doctrine, lead the yellow husband with his wife into the bath after their marriage, and do not ignite the powder with fire, lest it be suddenly deprived of work and motion. Restore their sweat to them." And again: "Kindle the fire, and establish rest for them: and take care that you do not drive them away with excessive fire, burning the venerable king." From these things, conclude further that the heat must only be such that you draw out the water by sweating, and that it is in no way hardened or congealed: because through light decoction it sweats, contrary to the nature of other gums, and is coagulated. Others coagulate in cold air, but this coagulates in warm air. 

Therefore it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: "grind and sieve in a philosophical vessel, and cook lightly over the fire, until its color changes to violet." He said this because you must cook with such a fire that the hard part is simultaneously ground down while the moist part drips out. Whence it is said in the *Soliloquy*: "Upon which place a febrile fire <note>original: "ignem febrilem"; a heat equivalent to the temperature of a human fever.</note>," etc. A slow fire is recognized thus, as it is stated in the *Universal Way*. A fire is called "tempered" when you can hold your hand for a long time upon the bottom of the earthen vessel, or dish, without injury. Similarly, in the *Book of Light*, a slow or tempered fire is described as one where you can keep your hand inside the belly of the furnace for a long time. Therefore, the heat of the sun, or the philosophical fire, is called a slow fire—indeed, the slowest. 

But it must also be seen by what fuel that heat is generated. For there is a fourfold fiery heat, caused by art in the manner of the sun, according to the philosophers: first of dung <term>dung: decomposing manure was used to provide a steady, low, and long-lasting warmth</term>, second of the bath <term>bath: likely a 'balneum Mariae' or water bath</term>, third of burial <note>original: "subterrationis"; the practice of burying the vessel in the earth or a pit of warm ashes.</note>, and fourth of coals. Nothing, however, should be said here of the fire of the air, or celestial fire, nor of the fire of flame: because the first is insufficient, as was said above, etc. The second is burning, sharp, and entirely irrelevant: because it was forbidden above that those flames should touch it, lest our most tender infant <note>The "infant" is a common alchemical metaphor for the Stone in its early, fragile stages of development.</note> be harmed. There is, however, a third—

### PHILOSOPHY

there is fire within things, just as there is in oils and sharp substances; and according to this, our stone has its own fire within itself, but it is idle unless it is excited and moved by an external heat. Regarding sharp substances, nothing else should be added to them, because it would immediately corrupt its substance, as has been said before. Therefore, only the heat of our sun is to be applied through the art, so that the fire of the stone may be moved into action, and so forth.

It has therefore seemed to some that the stone ought to be buried under the earth; others say in warm horse manure; others in the Bath of Mary <term>Bath of Mary: known today as a Bain-Marie; a method of heating a vessel by placing it in a container of boiling water to ensure gentle, even heat</term>. This is because the words of the Philosophers seem to command one or the other of these. 

For the *Greater Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius maior"; a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise</note> says: "Cook and distill in the Bath of Mary until you see the whole black substance converted into oil." Alphidius, however, says: "Surround the vessel with moist manure." And Raymond <note>likely Raymond Lull, a prolific but often pseudo-epigraphical alchemical authority</note> commands one to "bury it underground" during the process of composition. 

But if anyone searches well, he will find that the intention of the philosophers is that all things should be done in an Athanor <term>Athanor: a furnace used by alchemists designed to maintain a uniform and constant heat over long periods</term> with a fire of coals. When this fire is slow, it is called the heat of manure, the heat of the bath, and the heat of the sun. For that fire is "moist" because it causes and extracts moisture in the stone. It is also the "heat of manure" because it causes putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the chemical breakdown of a substance, which alchemists viewed as a necessary stage of "death" before transformation</term>. It is also the "heat of the earth," because the Athanor is constructed from earth and manure. 

Such heat can be better continued in a steady equality than the heat of a bath or manure; and it does not only moisten the stone at the beginning, but also dries it at the end. It is permitted for anyone to experiment with individual methods; but reason and authority prevail in showing that this is the intention of the philosophers. For their earlier writings demonstrate this, and their later ones will yet indicate it. 

It is also said in the *Turba* <note>original: "Tur."; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers"</note>: "If you mix the ferment <term>ferment: a substance, like yeast, added to the alchemical matter to trigger a transformation</term> into it, as Hermes says, set it in the sun—that is, in horse manure—for cooking, until these two are reduced into one dry body, etc." And again in the same *Turba* it is said: "Therefore, let a grave be dug, and let the woman be buried with her dead husband in horse manure"—that is, let it be cooked in a light and tempered heat until they are joined of their own accord. 

The "cooking in horse manure" is, among the philosophers, an obscure transfiguration—that is, a conversion into blackness. And it was said above that to make a fire from horse dung or from olive leaves is nothing other than making sure it lasts in an equal and light combustion. And this fire can be nothing else but the fire of a lamp with oil. Whence a certain philosopher says: "Place a well-luted <term>luted: sealed with 'lute,' a tough clay or cement used to make vessels airtight</term> gourd, and bury it in the warm belly of a horse, and make the water fly away <note>meaning: to evaporate or distill</note> continuously with the fire of a lamp, until all has gone out, and the matter at the bottom has become black, etc." And in the *Philosophical Soliloquy*, speaking of febrile fire...

# ON THE STONE

[He] says: It cannot be made except by the wick of a lamp with oil. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: Philosophical fire is not common fire. Many have thought it should be made with coals, with wood, or with olive leaves, or with animal dung, or with oil; and there is good intention there, provided however they know how to make the wick properly. And almost all of these are deceived: because we have but one fire, and this is with the philosophical wick. This wick, however, is never consumed, nor is it diminished. It is made with prepared Talc <term>Talc: in alchemy, this often refers to shimmering, heat-resistant minerals, sometimes including asbestos, believed to be incombustible</term> with cotton threads, or *vibic* threads, that is, made from the swelling of the *vibex* tree <note>original: "tubere vibicis arboris"; likely referring to a fibrous plant growth or perhaps a misunderstood reference to a mineral fiber</note>. Therefore, the operator needs to do nothing except add the oil. With such fire, therefore, our operation is completed, and not otherwise. For I have already taught that excessive fire is the cause of error, but slow fire is the cause of perfection. Therefore, the philosophical fire should come from a wick, and be made of three threads, and the threads should not be thick. And John Teb <note>original: "Ioan. Teb."; likely referring to the mathematician and astronomer Thābit ibn Qurra, often cited in medieval alchemy</note> says,

->*In a white garment it is preserved,*<-
->*it is ignited with three threads,*<-
->*along with a lunar ray.*<-
->*With four threads of the garment it is made,*<-
->*a red light also in the lamps*<-
->*shines from the beginning.*<-

From these things conclude that our philosophical fire is the fire of the sun, of the bath, of dung, and of the lamp. For they are the same thing, so that it may always burn equally, unless perhaps it burns in the final reddening <term>Rubification: also called Rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical Great Work where the matter turns red and reaches perfection</term>, when the sulfur has been made entirely incombustible; then it is increased a little, and as if imperceptibly. For by this method the airy spirit is first extracted with water: then the soul, which is the dissolved sulfur and tincture: which, having been returned to the body, is quickened through that body, and gradually disposed to the endurance of fire, until at last it does not fear the fire. Wherefore the stone finally comes to such perfection that it is melted by fire like oil, but in slightly cold air it is hardened like pitch or wax; yet it is never diminished in the fire, even if it were to stand in the fire for a thousand years. And because it is fire from fire, it must be reduced to fire until it does not fear fire, as Calid says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Calid in Turba"; refers to Khalid ibn Yazid and the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous 12th-century alchemical text</note>. And this is the oil of the philosophers, prepared from the union of soul and body, from which body the soul was first extracted by that subtle substance which is water and airy vapor: which spirit is not joined to the body again except by means of the soul. And therefore it is necessary first [to extract] the soul...

### *The Stone is perfected in a fixed time.*

## CHAPTER XXII.

Next, we must consider the matter of time: namely, how long it takes for the Stone to be perfected. Concerning this, the philosophers have written various things. Some assign a short time, and others a long one, as is evident in *The Lily* <note>original: "Lilio"; refers to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous alchemical treatise often attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note>. From this, it can be determined that the work can be perfected more quickly at one time than at another; similarly, by one operator more quickly than by another. Likewise, it is completed in one place more quickly than in another. For there are two things that accelerate or retard the work, just as they are the same two things that complete or destroy it: namely, the diligence of the operator and the power of the flowing heaven <note>referring to the astrological influences of the stars and planets on earthly matter</note>. 

One master is more ingenious than another, more perceptive in intellect, and more diligent and cautious in practice. Therefore, he who chooses a better root <note>the base material or "prima materia"</note>, prepares more suitable vessels and instruments, applies more moderate governance, looks more deeply into the work by comparing causes to effects and vice versa, selects more noble locations, and serves God and the saints with a more devoted mind, progresses more quickly. 

Therefore, the craftsman is ordered to do two things: first, to worship God, the Best and Greatest, with prayers and a pure heart, so that he may be enlightened in the highest intellect, and all obstacles—which are brought by our adversary the devil and which can occur in countless numbers—may be removed from his work. Second, he should stay often near the vessel and diligently judge and understand the miraculous works of nature and God, with their causes, effects, and signs, from the colors seen and the various forms of nature, so that from these he may know how to direct himself in his governance and take precautions against dangers and inconveniences. 

Whence *The Lily* says: The philosophers set different limits for this combustion or roasting, perhaps because of the difference of locations—between moist and dewy or dry—because this work congeals more quickly in moisture and more slowly in dryness. As Astanus <note>an ancient authority often identified with the legendary Persian magus Ostanes</note> says: "Hold with Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, so that the work may be continued, repeated, and ground in the cooking of dung as many times as necessary, until it becomes plain to the sight, so that the change in the work itself teaches you." Although heaven alone [governs] this work...

# ON THE STONE

...although he does not accomplish the task without the artisan’s skill <note>original: "sine arte"</note>, nature nevertheless cooperates and assists greatly, because it naturally flows into every work of nature. And this work, although it belongs to Art, is also a work of nature because it is perfected by fire. Moreover, it was stated above that celestial power <note>referring to the astrological influence of the stars and planets</note> flows into the creation of things and places primarily through fire, as well as through other mediating elements. This influence is stronger at one time than at another, and similarly more in one place than another, as daily experience makes manifest. For this reason, an acceleration or a delay in the work of the Stone may occur from this influence, just as not all hens hatch their chicks in the same amount of time. Nevertheless, whatever happens, there cannot be a great difference in the total time.

Most authorities commonly assign nine months for the completion of the work; some say more, others less. Whence Plato says that:
> the preparation takes fewer days than the circuit and resolution of the greater luminary <note>original: "luminaris maioris"; a reference to the Sun and its annual cycle through the zodiac</note>.

And Rasis <note>Rhazes, a famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> in the *Book of Three Words* says:
> That spirit is turned into a body, and the body into a spirit, and again the spirit into a body, and so on. Then a friendship is made between the cold and the moist, and between the hot and the dry.

And this is done by the power of God, by the tempering of the fire, and by the moderation of its limits. The limit of this duration is two and seven <note>adding up to the traditional nine months of gestation</note>, etc. Because of this, the artisan must be diligent in the management of the fire. Likewise, in the *Book of Saturn* it is said:
> Place the vessel in our sun while it is in the sign of Aries, and while it is in Leo, remain near the vessel until it comes into Sagittarius, and observe how it turns black, then white, or red, etc. <note>These three signs—Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius—make up the "Fire Trigon" in astrology, considered the most potent times for alchemical heating.</note>

And Rhodianus says:
> In this work is the "leap of the Moon" and the "circle of the Sun." There are three degrees within it: the first is weak, the second firm, and the third perfect.

And there are three milestones: the first when the Sun is in Aries and in its exaltation; the second when it is in Leo; and the third when it is in Sagittarius. Likewise, Water preserves the fetus for three months, Air nourishes it for just as long, and Fire guards and colors it for the final three. And Mireris says:
> the management <term>regimen: the controlled application of heat and timing in alchemy</term> of the stone is threefold: the first is cold and moist, the second is tempered hot and moist, and the third is hot and dry.

Likewise, a certain other philosopher says:
> According to the philosophers, our Stone is not far removed from the generation of a human being; therefore, in forty days it is prepared through its dissolution <term>solutio: the chemical breakdown of a solid into liquid</term> and its putrefaction <term>putrefactio: a stage of decomposition, often marked by the matter turning black</term>. Then, by the fifth month, it is perfected into the "White Medicine," which is White Gold <note>original: "Aurum album"; likely referring to silver or a specific purified state of the matter</note>. For it then becomes like an oil as white as snow, and then it converts Mercury into White Gold—though only in small quantities, unless that composition is afterwards [fed] again with its own milk like an infant...

### CHAPTER XXIII.

Although our stone is made from one thing, and by only one regimen of fire, as was said above: nevertheless, from the beginning: because it is also an imperfect thing, and even an elixir is not made perfect unless it is perfected through art. It is not perfected, therefore, except through various digestions, before one arrives at the perfect digestion. Different digestions also generate different colors, which are nevertheless ordered in relation to each other, as we see with our senses. Moreover, different colors succeeding one another in the same thing show a change of natures and forms: Therefore our Stone, before it is perfected by art,

### ON THE STONE

it passes from nature to nature, and from color to color; corruption occurs often, and generation occurs often; it possesses within itself diverse and contrary effects, and it receives various names. Different operations are performed upon a single thing, which nevertheless, because they tend toward one single goal, are also called a single "work." Therefore, the intention and unity of the work arise from the final goal, while the distinction between operations arises from the diversity of their effects. Thus, the "one work" is sublimation; the "many works" are solution, putrefaction, calcination, fixation, and others like them.

First, then, the one work is sublimation. For Alphidius <note>Alphidius: an Arabic alchemical author frequently cited in medieval Latin texts, often identified with al-Kindi</note> says, and likewise Saturnus, that the whole intention of our work is nothing else but that a stone known to us be taken, which is called *Adrop* in Arabic, but in Latin "lead" <note>original: "plumbum"; in alchemy, "lead" often refers not to the common metal, but to the "Lead of the Philosophers," the raw starting material or "First Matter"</note>. It is the stone of the philosophers, possessing most excellent virtues above all other stones. Let it be placed in a philosophical vessel to be sublimed, and let it be sublimed for as long as it takes to reach the ultimate purity of sublimation.

And this is the first and true operation. Geber <note>Geber: the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy</note> also places the whole of the art in sublimation alone. And he speaks the truth: because this sublimation—the philosophical kind—is not the sublimation of the common people <note>original: "sublimatio vulgi"; refers to simple physical evaporation and re-condensation, as opposed to the complex internal chemical refining of the alchemists</note>. Instead, it indeed comprises all of these seven operations:

The **first** is purification: so that you may receive the purest substance. 

The **second** is solution <term>solution: the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid state</term>: so that you may dissolve the entire matter into waters. 

The **third** is putrefaction: because nothing is born unless it first putrefies. They are putrefied so that, being more "digested," they may be better separated. 

The **fourth** is washing: because a filthy thing must be washed of its corrupting impurity. (In this art, "washing," "inceration" <term>inceration: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy consistency</term>, "cleansing," "mixing," and "complexion" are the same thing). 

The **fifth** is coagulation: because it is necessary that the water be dried gently in the sun along with the earth, and be coagulated, and return to a powder. 

The **sixth** is calcination <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a friable powder or ash</term>: because a calcined thing is more fit for sublimation and is closer to fixation. This is called "fusion" and "the invariable" by many philosophers.

And all these operations exist and occur within sublimation alone. Therefore, he who knows how to sublime perfectly is able to complete the whole work. Sublimation is, then, the separation of the most subtle parts from the coarse, or the separation of the unfixed parts from the fixed. For the unfixed parts are raised by means of dung <note>original: "fimum"; horse dung was used in alchemy as a steady, gentle source of "moist" heat for digestion and slow distillation</note> or by smoke. One must take care that they do not escape, but are "fixed" with the fixed parts. Thus they remain, so that they may provide a faster melting for the coarser parts and defend them from vitrification <term>vitrification: the unintended transformation of the alchemical matter into useless glass due to excessive heat</term>.

Through these seven dispositions which are contained within sublimation, any intelligent person can arrive at the perfection of the work. And all of this is achieved within a single vessel. Therefore...

### PHILOSOPHERS

do not be negligent in the cleansing, which is completed through **sublimation**: for whatever the quality of the cleansing shall be, such will be the perfection that follows through it. From these things, therefore, it is drawn out that sublimation is called the *refining* of the stone, so that, namely, it may become sublime in substance, virtue, and color. Whence Hermes says in the *Turba* <note>original: "in Turb."; the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers" is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic sages</note>: He who knows how to sequester the airy from the watery, and the watery from the earthy dry, and to assist the purer parts—that is, the airy, spiritual, and most subtle parts—and from them to form a medicine, will be an investigator of the most perfect perfection.

And as Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, considered the father of chemistry/alchemy</note> says: In our mastery, we perfect the imperfect by itself, without the mixing of any foreign thing. For our stone is imperfect from the beginning, but we perfect both things that are in it—namely, the body and the spirit—with the most subtle skill, by separating the pure from the impure, the subtle from the gross, the spiritual from the corporeal; and by cleansing the separated parts exceedingly well, and refining them through **digestion** <note>the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat</note> and **decoction** <note>boiling or heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</note>; and by uniting the refined parts, and completing them with the greatest virtues and colors through **fixation** <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, until we produce a medicine most pure and most subtle, penetrating and tinting imperfect bodies into the most noble gold, as Hamis <note>likely a reference to a specific sage quoted within the *Turba*</note> intends in the *Turba* cited above.

And this is the property of sublimation, which does not pass and tend toward this perfection of the stone all at once, but through stages. For this stone must, through the art of sublimation, arrive little by little at the highest degree of completion. Which is also most certainly known by these signs, as John Scotus <note>referring to an author of alchemical "Questions," often associated with the school of Duns Scotus or Erigena in medieval attributions</note> puts forward in his inquiry: namely,
* if it becomes subtler than air and whiter than milk; 
* if it becomes more glowing than wine and redder than blood; 
* if it becomes more liquid than amber <note>original: "electro"; electrum can refer to amber or a natural alloy of gold and silver</note>; 
* if it becomes more bubbly than slender foam; 
* if it becomes more spiritual than a raging wind; 
* if it becomes clearer than living water; 
* if it becomes firmer and stronger against the battle of fire; 
* if it becomes entirely uncoagulable in every cold, however great, and in every heat, however small.

And all these things are signaled through the definition of Alchemy, which the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilium", referring to the *Lilium Alchymiae* (The Lily of Alchemy), a popular 14th-century textbook</note> provides, saying: Alchemy is a corporeal substance composed from one and through one—that is, through one operation making things more precious to one another, through knowledge and effect—and naturally converting the same through natural mixing into a better kind. This medicine, therefore, is the **Mercury**, not of the common people, but of the philosophers, cleansed, refined, tinted, and fixed through sublimation; and it does not tint unless it is tinted, etc. For whatever its disposition and cleansing shall be, such also will be its perfection. For perfection makes things more perfect. From which matter it is weighed, that the virtue of the stone is multipli- <note>catchword for the next page: "multiplicabilis," meaning "able to be multiplied"</note>

# OF THE STONE
<meta>catchword: furthermore</meta>

...[improv]eable into infinity: Because if through proper **sublimation** <note>the process of purifying a substance by heating it to a vapor and then condensing it back into a solid, often viewed as "spiritualizing" the matter</note> it can be perfected to such a degree of virtue and nobility, it will certainly be able to reach a greater degree through even greater sublimation. There is no final state in any one degree, at least not one known to us. Although there is not just one operation in the whole regime which is called sublimation—since one end is intended in all things—there is nonetheless a manifold operation because of the diverse effects, colors, and natures which are clearly made visible at various times during the one work or regime. 

There are indeed two operations, or three, or four—and so on up to ten, or even more. All of these, however, are like parts of a perfect sublimation; in one common sublimation, all particular operations are connected, just like individual parts or singular sublimations. For all have both a particular and a common goal. The common goal is perfect sublimation and coloration, or purification. The particular goal is as follows: Among the other works, there are two principal ones that are, as it were, immediate to the final end: namely, the **white work** <note>original: *opus album*; the stage where the matter turns white, resulting in the ability to create Silver</note> and the **red work** <note>original: *opus rubeum*; the final stage where the matter turns red, resulting in the ability to create Gold</note>. For there is one and the same medicine for the white and for the red, except that they differ by a greater or lesser degree of **digestion** <note>controlled heating over a long period, similar to incubation</note> and perfection, or preparation. 

Whence a certain philosopher says: "Nothing can become Gold unless it was first Silver." Of which more will be said below. Concerning these, Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist, often cited as a teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says in the new translation: "This **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the overall alchemical process or the substance produced by it</note> requires two creations and two preparations, which are so connected to one another that when one of them is perfected, the whole mastery is similarly perfected. And yet its nature consists of one way, and one preparation is such as the other," etc. 

Concerning these, it is said in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, or "The Assembly of the Philosophers", one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "It is from two, and the water is similarly from two natures; the work of the white and the red is one work. The white work is the half and the beginning of the work; the red work is the second half." Therefore, the whole work is one and a primary work which nothing precedes. Another work is the extraction of **tinctures** <note>the soul or coloring essence of a substance, capable of transforming base metals</note>, and according to this, a double regime can also be established. 

Whence Miser. <note>likely an abbreviation for an alchemical authority or the text *Misericordia Dei*</note> says: "Know that the regime of the philosophers is twofold: one is more difficult, in which the moisture must be governed by **roasting** <note>original: *assatione*; a dry heating process</note>. The other form, however, is governed by dryness and moisture." In the same way, three operations could be distinguished, and similarly three regimes for them, and likewise four—and so on for the individual or remaining ones. But now there is no need to prolong this discourse, and so the principal operations must be touched upon briefly, so that...

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the stages of the alchemical "Work." ### PHILOSOPHY
<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

...ordinately the order of natures is maintained, and from these many other things may be understood by the ingenious craftsman: for not everything should be written down, nor indeed can it all be written. But he applies himself to this art in vain who does not know how to devise from within himself more of the things necessary and suitable for the work. It is said, therefore, in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: "lib. Saturni"; likely a reference to a specific alchemical text attributed to the planet/deity Saturn, often associated with lead and the beginning of the process</note>:

> Adjust the fire well in the furnace, and cause all the matter to be dissolved into water: then rule it with a slow fire, until the greater part is turned into a black powder.

Because when our **Stone** <note>the *Lapis*, or Philosophers' Stone in its developmental stages</note> is in our vessel, and our matter feels our **sun** <note>a term for the controlled heat of the furnace</note>, it will immediately be dissolved into water. This water, however, leaps to the head of the vessel through smoke—that is, through the wind, or through the air. And afterward it descends again to the bottom of the vessel, and dissolves the matter and the rest little by little into water. And thus, **sublimation** <note>the process of vaporizing and condensing</note> and **dissolution** <note>melting or breaking down</note> of the Stone happen at the same time, and both—namely the ascent and descent—are called "dissolution." 

Afterward, it begins to thicken and be converted into earth: and little by little the earth, standing above the water, descends to the bottom of the vessel, and is made black and foul-smelling. And then it is called **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactio*; the stage of "death" and decay of the matter, symbolizing the stripping away of old forms</note>. Truly, after a long time, the black earth—by the heat of the sun and the washing of the water—loses its color and its fetid odor. And then it is called **Ablution** <note>washing</note> or **Cleansing**. 

Then indeed the water is diminished, and the earth is dried out by the tempered sun, and then it is called **Ceration** <note>original: *Ceratio*; from the word for "wax," a stage where the substance becomes soft and flowable like wax</note>: because then the whole matter is converted into earth, if you know well how to work. And in this consists the whole power of the regime: namely, that it be converted into earth. When the whole matter is converted into a compressed, standing earth that does not melt away, it is then called **congelation** <note>congealing or freezing</note>. And up to this time, one must act with the greatest caution: because in this consists nearly the whole **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the secret technique or the completed work itself</note>. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says:

> Its power is complete, if it has been turned into earth. <note>original: "Vis eius integra est, si versa fuerit in terram," a famous line from the Emerald Tablet</note>

For the whole mastery is nothing other than making a correct dissolution and a perfect congelation. When the matter is congealed, and perfectly dried out by a greater cooking of the **Sun**, it begins to become white and to melt like white oil: and then it is called **Calcination** <note>reducing a solid to powder through heat</note>, and when it has come to perfect whiteness—so that this whiteness is above all other whiteness—then it is called **Whitening** <note>original: *Dealbatio*; the Albedo stage</note>: and then the Stone is perfect for the "white work." 

Once this is done, the fire must be continued until the Stone no longer varies from color to color, but holds a firm, invariable, and most deep-red color. And then it is called **Fixation** <note>original: *Fixio*; making the substance stable and resistant to fire</note>. And thus our physical Stone is perfected and completed for the "red work."

<summary>This page outlines the specific stages of the alchemical Great Work, moving from the black "putrefaction" through "whitening" to the final "red" fixation. It emphasizes that the process is a cycle of rising and falling vapors that eventually stabilize into a solid "earth."</summary>

# CONCERNING THE STONE

### That the knowledge of colors is necessary for directing our governance. <note>In alchemy, "governance" or *regimen* refers to the controlled management of the furnace fire and the timing of the stages of the Work.</note>

### CHAPTER XXIV.

The diversity of colors shows a diversity of **digestions** <note>Digestion is the alchemical term for the maturation of a substance through steady, gentle heat, much like ripening fruit or digesting food.</note>. In every thing, whether natural or artificial, there are different colors according to the diversity of the digestion, as long as the thing itself is in motion and on the path of generation. However, every thing has its own proper and natural **heat** <note>original: "calor"; while the author focuses on color, alchemical theory holds that internal heat is the agent that produces the observable color.</note> when it is at the completion of its final digestion, as is clear in flowers, fruits, wood, and animals. Since, therefore, the **Philosophers’ Stone** is produced through a long art and passes through many digestions, it is likewise varied by countless colors. 

But because it is a thing of both art and nature, it must determine for itself one single proper color. And because it is made not merely to exist for itself, but is made for the sake of something else, its color must be determined by the end for which it is created. Now, it is made for the sake of **Gold**. Gold is **citrine** <note>original: "citrinum"; a lemon-yellow or golden-orange hue, characteristic of the "Citrinitas" stage of alchemy</note>; therefore, the Stone will necessarily participate in this citrine color. 

And because it is not made so that it simply *becomes* gold, but so that it may *make* gold out of other metals—and since other metals differ greatly from the golden color in their own colors—one colored thing mixed with another varies the color of both. The lesser color hinders the greater, and the intended color is not acquired unless it greatly exceeds the other color and its own proper nature. From this, it is necessarily concluded that, above all, the craftsman must foreknow the proper and natural color which the **Elixir** <note>The potent, finished form of the Stone used for transmutation.</note> ought to have, so that what is to be the last in execution may be first in his knowledge. 

It is not enough, however, for it to be citrine with the citrinity of gold, because in that state it would not "dye" <note>The Stone's ability to "dye" or tincture a metal was seen as proof of its power to change that metal's internal essence.</note> the imperfect metals into the color of gold. Nor is it enough for it to be red with just any redness, because thus it would not dye a great quantity invariably or immutably; for not every red dyes things citrine, but only a red that is exceedingly excellent. Wherefore it is necessary that the craftsman, through suitable digestion, arrives at the color of the Elixir discovered by the art. And that red will be most excellent and immutable according to its kind, and even in lesser amounts—though not in greater, for it must always have the power to be increased. But before this most excellent red color, there are infinite other colors which are imperfect, which neither nature nor art principally considers; nevertheless, they are the path and the **passages** <note>original: "passagia"; transitional stages or signs indicating progress.</note>, or signs and indications of the perfect color. And therefore the art does not consider them much, except insofar as they are indications of reaching the perfect and desired color. And some of these col-

->PHILOSOPHY<-

...colors are the closer and more manifest indicators of a good disposition toward the intended end. Therefore, the art principally intends for a true knowledge of these to be held, and it does not care for others. Thus, this art considers three principal colors: from which it can be conjectured if the work is proceeding well, and if there is hope of achieving the effect. These three are **black**, **white**, and **red**: black at the beginning; white in the middle; and red indeed at the end of the work.

**Black** indicates the **corruption** <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is not a failure, but a necessary stage where the old form of a substance is destroyed so a new one can be born—similar to a seed rotting in the earth before it sprouts.</note> of the matter, and the good mingling or mixing of the moist with the earthy, and it is the beginning of generation. For nothing is generated except from the corruption of another. **Whiteness** indeed is the sign of the ending of superfluous moisture. Hence, heat acting upon the moist generates blackness, and acting upon the dry, by drying up the moisture, it generates whiteness. **Redness** indeed is caused if the heat is continued upon the dry white matter. 

Therefore, all the philosophers commanded that these three colors be diligently considered in the governance of the stone, and in the order in which they have been stated. The *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> said: "Observe diligently, lest your work turn red before it reaches blackness, for then the **tincture** <note>The "tincture" is the soul or the coloring power of the Stone that allows it to transmute metals.</note> will perish by burning. Boil everything together in white water until it has been turned into blackness." For if in the beginning of the mixing you apply a great fire, everything is burned, and corruption follows in the tinctures. 

Hence, Pandulphus in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a debate between Greek sages.</note> says: "Beware that you do not kindle a more intense fire before the proper time: for thus our **copper** <note>original: "aes"; often used by alchemists to refer to the base matter of the work regardless of its actual chemical makeup.</note> becomes red, which is of no use to you, because in the beginning of the governance you desire whiteness; instead, you make it red, etc." And Socrates says: "Cook it until it becomes a thick fat: afterward kindle the fire under it until it becomes a white stone. Afterward cook it again until it is deprived of moisture and becomes a dry powder." 

Likewise, Eximenus in the *Turba* says: "By cooking it, liquefy it until it becomes water, or like **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>: then imbue it with water of nitre, until it becomes like liquefied **minium** <note>Minium is a bright orange-red lead pigment; its appearance here marks a transition toward the final stage.</note>: then cook it until it coagulates and becomes like tin. Then is the greatest secret, namely the stone, which is composed of two things. Govern it by repeated cooking until it becomes like **saffron** <note>original: "crocus"; a deep yellow-orange color representing the "Citrinitas" or the nearing of the final "Rubedo" stage.</note> of most excellent color and perfection, etc."

# CONCERNING THE STONE

...by ingenuity. But this is least of all achieved by a "stiff-necked" <note>A biblical idiom for stubborn or prideful; here referring to a craftsman who relies only on manual labor without philosophical understanding.</note> craftsman. And this is not understood (as the *Rosarius* <note>original: "Rosar."; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers."</note> says) regarding the **sun** and **moon** and **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" represents Gold, the "Moon" represents Silver, and "Mercury" represents Quicksilver.</note> considered in their ordinary metallic nature, but rather concerning our **stone** <term>Stone: The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the work, which is not a literal rock but a perfected substance.</term>, which contains the properties of all three within itself. For it is composed of a **body**—namely, the white and the red—and of a volatile mercurial **spirit** <note>The "spirit" refers to the vaporous, volatile part of a substance that can rise when heated.</note>. 

However, the **Elixir** is not made from these unless those same bodies are reduced to their **first matter**, which is a **viscous water** <note>The "first matter" is the primordial state of all metals; alchemists believed metals must be returned to this liquid, sticky state before they could be transformed.</note>. This reduction is performed most conveniently by nothing else but **Quicksilver** <term>Argentum viuum: Literally "living silver," or Mercury.</term>, which comes from the stone itself: because it has the power to reduce the sun and moon to their first matter. Therefore, you need to labor much in the **dissolution** <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note> of the stone, namely, by separating the subtler parts from the coarser, and the purer from the impure. 

Wherefore the true beginning of the work is the dissolution of the stone. From this it is recognized that the stone is not some mineral thing <note>Meaning it is not a simple mineral found in the earth, but a complex product of the art.</note>, because in those minerals, either **calcination** <note>Reducing a metal to powder through heat.</note> or **sublimation** <note>Turning a solid into vapor.</note> comes first; but through this principle, the bodies are reduced to their first nature because in this way bodies are mixed with the spirit, and become one with it, and are never separated, just as water mixed with water is not, and each acts upon the other, as on a thing close to its own nature. 

And this **solution of the body** happens alongside the **coagulation of the spirit**, and the coagulation of the spirit happens with the solution of the body. And therefore endure patiently, and cook, and reiterate: because the more you grind, the more you soften, and thin out the coarse: for thus the spirit is kneaded <note>original: "impastatur"</note> with the body. Things that are kneaded together are completely resolved, and this kneading happens through **roasting** <note>original: "assatione"</note>. 

From this root it follows: that the body rises and is sublimated with the spirit, and the spirit is fixed with the body; and both receive one and the same nature, the same virtue, and the same color. And although this happens after a long time, the beginning of it is the solution itself: and therefore it is most necessary to the art, and the philosophers agree on this. For **Haly** <note>An Arabic alchemist often cited in Latin texts.</note> says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "Unless you turn every body into water, you will not reach the work." 

And **Pandulph** says: "Know that every body is dissolved, and with the spirit with which it is mixed, it undoubtedly becomes spiritual quickly." 

Similarly **Bonellus** says: "Unless dense bodies are broken down for a long time with a nature lacking a body <note>i.e., a spirit or liquid.</note>, until the bodies become incorporeal and are converted like a thin spirit, you will not be able to extract that most thin **dyeing soul** <note>The "soul" or "tincture" is the essence that has the power to change the color and nature of other metals.</note> which is hidden in the natural womb." 

Likewise **Theophilus** says: "Take **white magnesia** <note>A cryptic term for a primary alchemical ingredient, often associated with the white stage of the work.</note>—that is, living water—mixed with the male..."

### PHILOSOPHY

...and grind it by cooking, not with your hands, until it becomes a thin water. And John the Theban <note>original: "Ioan. Theban."; likely referring to a legendary alchemical figure often quoted in medieval florilegia.</note> says:

> *Let this thing first be rubbed together* <note>original: "Hæc res primo confricetur"</note>
> *and once rubbed, let it be moistened*
> *with invisible water.* <note>original: "aqua inuiſibili." In alchemy, "invisible water" or "water that does not wet the hands" refers to a philosophical solvent, often Mercury.</note>
> *And let no part remain*
> *of the coarse part, but that it be turned to water*
> *[as] an insoluble liquid.* <note>original: "Limpham inſolubilem."</note>

And the author Gallinarius <note>An alchemical authority often cited in the *Theatrum Chemicum*.</note> says: Know that the mastery is not perfected, unless the whole earth is dissolved. These things are said in general concerning the **dissolution** <term>Dissolution: The process of "solving" or melting a solid into a liquid state.</term> of the stone, but it is necessary to discuss it in specific details.

First, the end for which it is done must be considered. It is done for two reasons: first, indeed, so that **bodies** <note>The "bodies" refer to the metallic or solid components of the work.</note> may be reduced to the highest simplicity—that is, so that they are brought back to the simplest state possible, as John Scotus <note>original: "Ioan. Scotus"; likely referring to the philosopher Duns Scotus, whose theories on matter were influential in alchemy.</note> says. Therefore they are first dissolved, so that afterwards, by **subliming** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and then solidifies again; here it implies a spiritual refinement.</term> them little by little, we may be able to reduce them to the greatest subtlety. 

Moreover, the work of dissolution (as the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says) was invented for no other reason except for **subtilizing**. First, therefore, the bodies are dissolved with spirits, so that they become like spirits: and so that after this they may be subtilized more and more, until they are totally reduced to the nature of spirits. Therefore, the more times it is dissolved, [the more] the **medicine** <note>The substance in its state of transformation toward the Elixir.</note> is subtilized and coagulated, the more subtle and powerful it becomes. 

Whence all things that are sublimed are sublimed in two ways: some by themselves, and some with others. **Mercury** <note>The "spirit" or volatile principle.</note>, therefore, since it is a spirit, is sublimed by itself; but our **earth** <note>The solid, fixed residue.</note>, since it is the **ash** <term>Calx: The powdery residue or "lime" left after a metal or mineral has been burned or calcified.</term> of a body, is not sublimed unless it is perfectly incorporated with Mercury. Therefore, grind the ash and saturate it with our Mercury, and cook it until it becomes one body; and do not grow weary of repeating this very thing many times, because the body will not ascend upward unless it is incorporated with Mercury. 

And for this reason it is necessary that you subtilize the body as much as you can, and draw out its **soul** <note>The "soul" is often considered the mediating principle between the solid body and the volatile spirit.</note>, and pound it strongly with Mercury until they become one. Therefore this dissolution is called the **first sublimation** of the stone; and we perform this sublimation so that we may reduce bodies to a subtle nature, so that they become like spirits, and [so that we may] reduce them to their **first matter**, and that they may take on one color; and unless this dissolution precedes, other sublimations are improper sublimations and do not follow fittingly. 

This dissolution is also called a **grinding** <note>original: "contritio"</note> that is not done with hands but by fire, as was said above. This dissolution into water is also not understood to happen as the common <note>The text cuts off mid-word "vul-", likely "vulgaris" (common/ordinary).</note> dissolution...

...common water into the water of the cloud, <note>original: "aquam nubis." Likely referring to distilled water or a vaporous state achieved through heating.</note> but it is a dissolution that is made into an oily or fatty water, as Scotus <note>original: "Scotus." Most likely Michael Scot (c. 1175–c. 1232), a scholar and alchemist who served as the court astrologer to Frederick II.</note> and others say, until the whole is resolved into water, and at last becomes one thing. This dissolution, however, is not properly a dissolution, although it is so called, but rather a **liquefaction** <term>Liquefaction: Here used to describe a solid turning into a liquid like melting wax, rather than dissolving like salt in water.</term> in the manner of wax. From this first dissolution, then, it begins, and thus through many stages the **philosophical stone** is ground down, until at the final stage it remains most perfectly refined, having a completely spiritual power to penetrate all solid and hard things, as Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says.

And in this way it is led out from potentiality into a perfected act. For it was said above that from the beginning the stone is imperfect, and composed of both **body** and **spirit**, <note>In alchemy, the "body" is the solid matter, while the "spirit" is the volatile, vaporous element.</note> having in itself partly a volatile nature (that is, airy) and partly a fixed nature (that is, earthy). For it is of the nature of **Mercury**, <term>Mercury: Not necessarily the common metal, but the "mercurial principle" of fluidity and volatility.</term> and it is still of the nature of the sun and moon. <note>original: "solis & lunę." In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver.</note> Whence the mercurial power flies away, and the power of the body is fixed. However, why one should act upon the other, and both being imperfect, one perfects the other by means of a suitable regimen: therefore both fly like a spirit, and both are fixed like a body, because they are inseparably united. And nonetheless, the natural subtlety and spirituality is increased and completed through frequent iteration of dissolution and **sublimation**, <term>Sublimation: The process where a solid turns directly into gas upon heating, then reverts to solid; used here to purify the substance.</term> as the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosar." Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises of the 16th century.</note> wishes.

Secondly, dissolution is done so that the **soul** <note>The "soul" (anima) was considered the intermediary between the "body" and "spirit," often identified with the color or "tincture" of the metal.</note> may be extracted from the bodies. For in the bodies themselves, having the nature of the fixed, is the soul with the white or red tincture. And this soul is the true **sulphur** of the philosophers and their oil, and the **quintessence** <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance.</term> of bodies, because it has the property of sulphur and the power of coagulating Mercury and of tinging. And therefore it is called by **Maria the Prophetess**, <note>original: "Maria prophetissa." Also known as Mary the Jewess, an early alchemist (c. 1st–3rd century AD) credited with inventing several types of chemical apparatus.</note> the "Coagulating Curd," <note>original: "Coagulū coagulans." A metaphor likening the solidification of the stone to the way rennet curdles milk.</note> and by Hermes it is called the "Ferment." 

This soul, however, cannot have perfect and complete power of coagulating Mercury and tinging metals, unless it is extracted from its "sulphurities" and joined with its body. For in its sulphurs it tinges completely; but united to Mercury it is made more spiritual, and Mercury is the medium for joining tinctures. Neither can this soul be extracted from the bodies unless they are perfectly dissolved, because it is diffused through all their parts. Bodies also are not dissolved except through Mercury; but neither are they dissolved suddenly, but little by little. Wherefore it is necessary to dissolve the stone with the greatest labor and industry, and with time, so that the soul may be extracted and united with Mercury, and refined with the subtle spirit, until it has been made entirely spiritual, and cannot [but] make its body spiritual. And this is what all philosophers want. For Mireris <note>Mireris: An alchemical authority often cited in medieval Latin texts, though his historical identity is obscure.</note> says: Heat...

...the sun, the spirit of the air, and the moisture of the dew extract the soul and cause it to grow. For the fiery nature is separated by the fire of the river <note>original: "ignis fluminis." This may refer to a water bath or a specific temperature range.</note> and the fire of horse dung <note>original: "igni fimi equorum." In pre-modern chemistry, burying a glass vessel in a pile of fermenting horse manure provided a steady, gentle heat ideal for long-term digestion of materials.</note>, and at last it becomes green in color. Therefore it is called the **Bird** and **Sulphur**, and it is like pure and shining pearls, or like fresh white butter. The remaining black dregs are the **body**; but the soul is thin, which is the air, etc. Wherefore **Pandulphus** <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> says in the *Turba*:

> It is necessary first that our copper <term>Copper: original "æs." In this context, it rarely refers to the common metal, but rather to the "bronze" or "base" starting material of the Great Work.</term> be burned with a light fire, just as an egg is nourished by the heat of a hen, so that it is not scorched. And let the vessel be closed on all sides, so that its heat may be increased, its body broken down, and then its tingeing spirit extracted.

Know moreover that every body is dissolved with the spirit to which it is joined, and without doubt it quickly becomes spiritual. Every spirit, however, is altered by bodies: and its color becomes tingeing and stands firm against fire. And if you are patient in the length of the cooking, every spirit will tinge.

Secondly, one must consider by what means this dissolution is achieved. And you should know for certain that it happens only through the **water of Mercury**. For our **Stone** is soft and very tender, and partly cold and moist, as was said above; under a little fire it sweats strongly and generates large drops like the clearest water in our vessel. These descending drops soften the body and pierce it in a wonderful way: and again they frequently ascend and descend, until they thin and dissolve the whole body. When the body of **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: Not the modern element magnesium, but a name for the "crude matter" or "primitive earth" used by alchemists.</term> is melted like water, then all things have become vapor, as it is said in the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilio." Likely referring to the *Lilium inter spinas* (The Lily Among Thorns), a popular alchemical treatise.</note>. Heat, therefore, is the first mover: because it causes the water to exhale; and although flight is essential to it, the water finds no way to escape. If it falls back again into the body, it congeals with it, and its color is changed, etc. As it is said in the same place in the treatise *Miserula*. The first thing in the work is water: because this does not proceed from elsewhere, and through it the **tincture** <term>Tincture: The transformative essence or "dye" that changes the properties of a substance.</term> is extracted for the red and the white work. Now, in the universal way it is said:

> With the vessel placed in a suitable furnace, let the fire be continued. Then the vapor of the matter ascends most subtly upward into the **Alembic** <term>Alembic: The upper part of a still where vapors condense.</term>: and there it is converted into clear, limpid, and bright water, having the form of a tear and the nature of all the species from which it is generated: and it descends again through the **crow's beak**, that is, through the neck of the alembic vessel. And because this water is subtle, it enters the body, and first extracts the soul, then dissolves all the rest and converts it into water.

For it is said in the book of the *Seven Seals*:

> The spirit of Mercury, subtly entering the body itself, and disposing it to a simple nature...

And some say ten days; others around 40 days; and others even add five more to those. 

This water, moreover, is called by many names. For it is called **Sea Water**, because its abundance is greater than that of the earth, and also because it is bitter from the fiery nature which it acquires. Wherefore it is said in the *Turba*:

> Beginners, hearing of "water," think it is common rainwater; but if they had read our books, they would know it is certainly the **permanent water**. 

Which, however, cannot be permanent without its own body, with which it has been dissolved and made one. It is properly called **Permanent Water** <note>original: "Aqua permanens." A central alchemical concept referring to a solvent that does not evaporate easily and has the power to reduce metals to their primary matter.</note>. Wherefore from these it says: 

> Take the stone of Gold, and mix it with its own moisture, which is the permanent water, and place it in its vessel over a light fire until it liquefies. 

It is also called **Sharpest Vinegar**, because it is sharp, penetrating, and dissolving. Wherefore **Eximerus** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name like Anaximander, appearing as a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: 

> Mix our copper with the sharpest vinegar, and cook and manage it until it becomes water. 

Likewise another says: 

> Moreover, it is the sharpest vinegar which makes Gold into a pure spirit; and when it is mixed with the body, it turns it into spirit. 

It is also called **Quicksilver** (Mercury), because it has the color, splendor, power, and property of mineral quicksilver, and also because it is cold and damp. Wherefore the *Lilium* says: 

> For its first moisture is cold. 

And this male <note>original: "mas." In the gendered symbolic language of alchemy, the "spirit" or "mercury" is often labeled as the active, male principle.</note> is called the spirit, or **Quicksilver**; which quicksilver is not obtained except from liquefied bodies, as **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> and many others say, etc. It is also called **White Smoke**, because it ascends in the manner of smoke and tends toward the whiteness of milk. Wherefore the same Morienus says: 

> Three of these species are sufficient for the entire mastery: namely, **White Smoke**, the **Green Lion**, and **Stinking Water**. 

It is also called the **Dragon’s Tail**, because...

Finally, an **airy virtue** remains in it, penetrating and refining bodies. Whence it is read in the *Turba*:
