Finally, it must be considered that the water dissolving the body changes its nature and color. Because the body is dissolved in and with it, it becomes thick like honey, or a fatty broth (as has been said), and is colored with a **white color**. For **citrine** <note>A lemon-yellow color.</note> mixed with white causes a **saffron** or nearly **green** color; because of which the whole liquefied body is called the **Green Bird**, according to the saying of **Mireris** <note>An alchemist cited frequently in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> cited above.

And this first complete **dissolution** is recognized by these signs: namely, when the body and water are poured forth everywhere and in all parts with an equal (or nearly equal) saffron color, sitting between the citrine and white of the component parts. This happens because the white exceeds the citrine in quantity, and only a small or moderate **digestion** <note>The slow heating of the substance.</note> has occurred. Because of this, the color partakes more of whiteness than of citrine. Therefore, after the liquefaction of the stone, the material is more like melted butter than any other oily or fatty substance...

### *That the second [stage] in the regime, the work is putrefaction.*

### CHAPTER XXVI.

Bodies which are not dissolved are not refined: therefore it is necessary that in the dissolution of the stone you endure the labors, refining the thicker parts into more subtle ones, and separating the more subtle from the thicker, until the whole body becomes subtle, spiritual, and volatile. This, however, as was said, is done through **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, which is airy and a dissolver of the body; by extracting the body's soul little by little, the mercury carries it with itself into the heavens <note>Meaning the top of the glass vessel.</note>, and through this its power is continually increased, with the heat of the fire cooperating. Wherefore ultimately it destroys and overcomes the whole body, and carries it with itself into the air. 

But before it reduces the body itself to this perfection, it is necessary that it first dissolves the body into water, and in dissolving it, causes it to putrefy. And therefore the first mode of dissolution is to putrefy the matter. For putrefaction begins at the start together with dissolution, but the putrefaction is not yet complete when the entire matter is dissolved into water; rather, it is completed afterward. And in this putrefaction the stone is again better dissolved than it had been dissolved before: because the more it is increased and the operations are continued, by so much more is the stone refined. The whole mastery <note>The "Magisterium" or the Great Work of alchemy.</note>, therefore, consists in putrefaction: because if it is not putrid, it will come to nothing, as the same author says. Blackness <term>nigredo</term> follows putrefaction, and this happens in the moist state. The moving cause for putrefaction, however, is a temperate heat. Whence **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says: Heat acting upon the moist generates blackness, etc.

<meta>catchword: This (Hæc)</meta>

<summary>This page explains that alchemical dissolution is not merely turning metal to liquid, but a spiritual refinement of matter through "fermentation" and "putrefaction." It identifies temperate heat and mercury as the primary agents that break down the body to reach the "nigredo" or black stage of the work.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from page 324, which concluded the chapter on dissolution and began the discussion of the second stage of the alchemical regime: putrefaction. It explores the philosophical and physical necessity of this "death" of the material.</meta>

<header>PHILOSOPHY</header>

These three things, therefore, follow each other in succession: namely, moisture, putrefaction, and blackness. Whence **Artephius** <note>Artephius was a legendary alchemist, often claimed to have lived for a thousand years by using the "Elixir of Life."</note> says: *Let the glass house stay subtly situated, until the enclosed matter, being moist, gradually becomes putrid and black.*

**First**, therefore, it must be noted that putrefaction is necessary before the stone can be formed: because no generation occurs except after corruption <note>Original: "corruptio." In the Aristotelian physics used by alchemists, for something new to be born, the old form must first be destroyed or "corrupted."</note>, nor is a thing improved unless its form is first entirely destroyed. Since we seek to lead the stone to the perfect form of the **Elixir**, it must first be corrupted. Whence it is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: *And the stone is one, having four colors according to the four elements; if it has not died, it remains alone, but if it has died, it brings forth much fruit.* <note>This is a direct alchemical parallel to the Gospel of John 12:24 regarding a grain of wheat.</note> And in the *Book of the Seven Seals* it is said: *Unless it is putrefied, you will not be able to reach the secret.* And as **Raymond of Terminis** <note>Likely referring to a follower of Raymond Lull, a famous 13th-century polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says: *This putrefaction occurs most conveniently in Aries.* <note>The zodiac sign of the Ram (Aries), which represents the beginning of Spring and the astrological cycle.</note> Whence, in Aries, the whole matter ought to be converted into a **homogeneous substance**. And in this, no one should err, because the whole secret lies in the beginning of the work—that is, in its perfection.

**Secondly**, note that this putrefaction is the perfect and universal mingling of two bodies. Whence it is said in the book *Miserula*: *It is necessary that the Sun <note>Gold</note>, which is of one kind with the Moon <note>Silver</note>, drinks and becomes inebriated, and drinks abundantly of the water of the Moon, and lies with her in a friendly manner, and is joined through the smallest parts.* For nature rejoices in nature because of the conformity of their natures. For then the sperm—that is, the solar fatness—enters into the lunar body and is mixed through the smallest parts, and they are connected to each other by a universal mixture, and through this the Moon becomes pregnant, which happens in forty days. Whence, unless such a mixture were made, no birth would follow, as **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> reports. And unless impregnation occurs, there will be no rising.

**Thirdly**, note that there are three signs of putrefaction: namely, a black color, a foul odor, and the fineness of the powder, such that it is felt without touch <note>Meaning the powder is so fine it feels like a liquid or air rather than grit.</note>. For the fire, combined with the moisture, turns the stone black during the preparation. And this blackening is a sign of perfect mixture and the acceptance of one by the other, as is said in the *Turba*. Just as there is dissolution through **quicksilver** <note>Original: "argentum vivum" (Mercury).</note>, so also is there putrefaction and blackening, because it is moist; and moisture mixed with the other putrefies it, enriches it, and brings about blackness. Whence, as the *Rosary* says: *Although the quicksilver first ascends very white through sublimation, nevertheless, by descending and mixing itself with the body...*

It uses the metaphor of a sexual union between the Sun (Gold) and Moon (Silver) to describe the chemical process of creating a homogeneous mixture.</summary>

By mixing, it passes through dissolution into the form of **Mercury**, which if you later cook in a <term>balneo mariae (a "Mary's bath," or a gentle water bath used for steady heating)</term> until you see the whole converted into a black oil, then it is a sign of true dissolution. And therefore, after the first dissolution, it must be placed into water to be putrefied, cooking it completely with a light fire until another form is introduced into it: black in color, foul in odor, and subtle and discontinuous to the touch. Whence it is said in *The Lily* <note>A reference to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a common alchemical title.</note>: though on that day its blackness lasts, the woman dominates—that is, until the whiteness <note>Original: "albedinem." This refers to the *albedo*, the second major stage of the alchemical process where the matter turns white.</note>—and the humidity of the quicksilver is corrupting, etc. And **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in the new translation: "Our entire mastery is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth and the sending of this back onto the earth until it putrefies. For this water putrefies with the water," etc. And **Raymond of Terminis** asserts: "Until the whole matter is blackened," etc. And **Gallinarius** also: "Until the matter in the bottom has become black," etc. And **Johannes Teb.** <note>Possibly Johannes Tebernerus or a similar author.</note> says:

-> *It offers a sign of corruption,* <-
-> *which is worthy of all praise: a color of blackness.* <-

The odor is also a sign of absolute putrefaction—not just any smell, but a heavy and altogether intolerable one. For dissolution and putrefaction begin with a foul odor and grow continuously until the peak. And for this reason, it is called a "toxic and deadly poison" in the *Book of Saturn* <note>Saturn, associated with the metal lead and the color black, represents the "death" or "melancholy" of the matter.</note> before its perfection, and it kills human bodies; but afterward, it kills metallic bodies. However, this odor of its is perceived more by the intellect than by the sense of smell. Because we have learned by experience what it is like in the work before the work begins. Indeed, in the work itself, one must take the greatest care that its odor is not smelled, because the putrefaction is not completed if the odor can still be detected. This dual property of the stone is expressed through the likeness of a corpse. For in *The Lily* it is said that from the beginning, the stone requires a light fire, and it appears like a dead man for many days, like a man in his tomb. And in the same place **Theophilus** says: "That woman's belly is full of weapons and poison." Whence:

-> *Finally it turns black and pours forth foul odors.* <-

The third sign of completed putrefaction is a powder without touch; which, however, must be proven not by touch but by sight. And this occurs when it all becomes like black oil or deep red blood, so that the whole or the greater part of the matter is uniformly black, and it is not discontinuous, but one part joined to the other. And this is what **Theophilus** says: "Let a grave be dug for that dragon <note>The "dragon" often symbolizes the volatile or crude matter that must be "tamed" or killed.</note>, and let the woman be buried there with him, until they turn into blood."

The fourth note is that this blackness precedes the whiteness.

For it is said in *The Lily* <note>original: "Lilio." This likely refers to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a popular alchemical text.</note>: Where it speaks of whiteness and redness: for neither happens without blackness: because blackness occurs at the first appearance in the work. And we signify this to be the first key of the work. And **Mireris** says: It is necessary that the earth first be buried in a piece of Egyptian cloth, afterwards it is necessary for the composite to be whitened, so that it becomes a staining and permanent sulfur. Then to become red, and so on. And another certain person says:

> *Then you will know the true beginnings of the work*
> *While black magnesia is seen in a dark body.* <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but to a primitive, dark mineral substance considered the "mother" of the Stone.</note>

On account of which **Mundus** <note>The name Mundus (meaning "The World") may refer to a specific author or the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: Place these two wisely into the vessel, and always and humbly pray to God, so that you may see this our stone mixed in the work, then cook it little by little, extracting the <term>soul (the volatile essence or spirit of the matter)</term>, and look to see if it has become a black stone. Because if it is so, you have directed it best: but if not, direct it with white liquor, which is the greatest secret, until it becomes covered in blackness. From these things, therefore, it is clear that blackness is the principal sign of complete putrefaction, solution, mixing, impregnation, and so forth.

->*That the third work in the governance of the stone is whitening.*<-

## CHAPTER XXVII.

Now the body thus blackened is said to be dead. Whence **Gallinarius** <note>A pseudonym, literally "The Poulterer."</note> said: We also call this solution of the black body the "solution of the dead body," and it commonly happens in forty days: wherefore it is necessary to wash it so that it becomes clean, and afterwards to <term>vivify (to "bring back to life" or re-energize the matter)</term> it, so that it may recover life and virtue. Because the *Rosarius* <note>A reference to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers."</note> says: Convert the stone from good to better and not to worse. It is converted to better when the composite Elixir is made. To worse, however, when it is corrupted: because then there is loss and not gain. The stone is therefore "corrupted" not so that it remains dead, but so that it reaches a better nature and greater virtue through digestion. And so it is said in the treatise *Miserula*: In the first work blackness appears, but both bodies are washed by the water ascending above through <term>sublimation (heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again)</term>, and descending again through distillation they are clarified and vivified; afterwards they will be very white in the manner of shining marble and very white salt. And then from all bodies it makes **Moon** <note>original: "lunā." Alchemical shorthand for Silver.</note>: that is, however, when it has wedded, that is, when they have been mixed in their vessel to the smallest parts, and have come together into one nature through the drying of the fire; for then they will generate a son, who [will exceed] all his own parentage...

...will prevail over its own. Because the sun and moon <note>original: "sol & luna". In alchemy, these represent Gold and Silver, or Sulfur and Mercury.</note> do not dye by themselves, but this **son** <note>The "Son" is a common name for the Philosopher's Stone, the child of the Alchemical Marriage.</note> is full of tinctures. And in this is the completion of the first work. This work is "women's work and children's play" <note>original: "mulierum opus & ludus puerorum". This famous alchemical phrase suggests that once the initial difficult preparation is done, the rest of the process is simple and proceeds naturally.</note>, namely, after the preparation: because **Thelon** and **Azoth** <note>Azoth is the "universal solvent" or the essential mercurial spirit of the matter.</note> are sufficient for you. From these things, therefore, the whole process of whitening appears; nevertheless, so that the order and causes with their effects in this operation may be more distinctly clear to the seeker, it must be written about more extensively here.

First, therefore, you should know that it is necessary to wash the "dead body" with fire and water. And concerning this water, **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> testifies: 
> *This earth putrefies with its own water, and is purified with water. All know that their water washes away filth.* 

Of fire, however, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were central to medieval science.</note> says: 
> *Heat acting on the dry causes whiteness: for thus it consumes the corrupting moisture.* 

Therefore, as it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: 
> *Fire whitens the <term>calxes (the powdery remains of a substance after it has been burned or "calcined")</term> of stones.* 

And of both, **Morienus** says: 
> *Azoth and fire wash and purify the **Laton** <note>original: "Latonem". A term for the "impure" metal or material in its dark, unrefined state.</note>, and utterly snatch its darkness away from it.* 

And for this reason, hot water washes more strongly than cold. Just as wax is whitened by dew and heat, while linen is bleached by moisture and the sun. And this is the reason why, after the putrefaction of the stone, it is necessary to continue the fire until it becomes white. For through the continuation of the fire, the earth is calcined and ground down more and more continually, and is gradually dried out, and therefore finally whitened. To which whitening the water contributes, which is continually absorbed with the earth itself and exhales with the heat; or rather, it is incorporated with the earth and dried within. Therefore, the **Anonymous One** <note>original: "Ignotus". Referring to an unidentified author.</note> said: 
> *Grind it often with its water, and calcine it repeatedly, until by the washing of water and fire, the darkness completely recedes.* 

The second method is thus: The putrefied material remains at the bottom of the vessel, although on account of the resolving heat, some subtle and airy spirits always ascend with the watery vapor in the vessel. The matter is like water, or a black oil, still coarse and heavy, and impure, and composed or mixed from body, spirit, and soul. Now Art, desiring to compose the <term>Elixir (the perfected substance of the Stone)</term> from it, seeks to refine it, to dye it with a perfect color, and to fix it. This, however, cannot happen unless one separates the subtle from the coarse, and again refines the coarse by means of the subtle, and joins both together again, and fixes them at the same time. Therefore, with subtle ingenuity, it discovered <term>sublimation (the process of heating a substance into vapor so it rises and purifies before solidifying again)</term>, which happens through a heat that digests, separates, elevates, purifies, strengthens, joins, dries, and fixes. After the matter has been putrefied, therefore, it is necessary to speak of the extraction...

[the separation of] water from the earth: because it is impossible for a union of spirit and body to occur, except [by turning them] into air through sublimation, following, that is, the stage of putrefaction <note>The stage where the matter rots and turns black, seen as a necessary "death" before rebirth.</note>. Therefore, by continuing a gentle fire, the water is separated from the earth through distillation; and simultaneously with the water and through the water, the animal [spirit] <note>original: "animal". In this context, it refers to the "living" or "vital" principle of the matter.</note> is extracted from the body, as the **Rosary** <term>Rosarium Philosophorum</term> <note>A famous 16th-century collection of alchemical treatises.</note> says. And that water is indeed thicker and darker at the beginning, because it rises from the corrupt body; however, in the long run, it is rendered subtle, clear, and white. 

The soul <note>original: "Anima"</note> is indeed extracted with the water and through the water. For the water first rises, and in rising it is refined, and then it descends again and penetrates the body, dissolving it with the help of heat. It separates the body's subtle substance—as if it were a **quintessence** <term>quinta essentia</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, believed to be medicinal and incorruptible.</note>—from the earthly parts, and rising again, it carries that substance with itself into "heaven" <note>In alchemical laboratory work, "heaven" refers to the upper part or "head" of the distillation vessel.</note>. For this reason, the putrefaction of the **stone** <term>lapis</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" in its developing state.</note> occurs so that the soul can be extracted; if it did not putrefy, it could not be extracted. Therefore, let this sublimation be continued until the entire soul is drawn out. 

From this matter, note that the stone is divided into two principal parts: The first is that which rises upward, and this is the water which is moist and clear. And although it rises in the form of a vapor, when it is struck by the colder air [at the top of the vessel], it condenses again like water and descends to moisten the earth. And this is also the soul, which gives life to the whole stone, and it behaves like an oil. By some, it is called **White Smoke** <term>Fumus albus</term>; by others, it is called **sharpest vinegar** <term>acetum acerrimum</term> <note>A metaphor for the powerful, transformative solvent created during the work.</note>, which rises in a snowy color and is very sharp. And this water carries the soul with it—that is, the dissolved **tincture** <term>tinctura</term> <note>The concentrated essence that has the power to "dye" or transform base metals into gold.</note>, purified in the spirit and extracted from the bodies. 

The other part remains fixed below, and this is called the **nurturing earth** <term>terra nutrix</term>, the **dregs** <term>fæx</term>, or **magnesia** <term>magnesia</term> <note>Not the modern mineral, but a traditional alchemical name for the raw, "mother" material of the stone.</note>, though it is better known by other names. It is also called the "body of the dead" in which there is no life, because its soul has been taken away. However, this earth is not to be cast away, because what you seek is found within the dregs. And the first part [the soul/water] must be nourished from this earth. Because of this, many seekers are deceived; they labor for a long time and achieve nothing because they add foreign earths during the sublimation. And they take that which rises above and sublimate it repeatedly, but they throw away the dregs remaining below, being ignorant of what our stone actually is. We, however, do not want the parts that are raised in sublimation to remain separated from those which are below; rather, we want them to come together again into one, etc. Because after the first purification, which is completed through solution, nothing is found to be superfluous nor diminished in our stone. From these things, therefore, it is clear,

[It follows] that in the extraction of the soul from the earth, the soul is further purified, refined, strengthened, and grows in quality, power, and color. For it is finally made as white as snow; while the earth descends below, and continually remains in quantity, but weakens in power. Hence it remains deformed and dead, nor is it brought back to life unless its soul is returned to it. When this happens, the soul flows into the spirit, its body, and takes away all its blackness and impurity. And when it is mixed with its aforementioned body, it becomes one with it, and turns it into spirit, and colors it with an unchanging color. And from this, it takes on the property of oil, just as it previously had that of water. For water washes and cleanses, while oil stains and colors. Just as the water does not rise from the earth suddenly, but gradually, and draws the soul out with it, so also it is returned to the earth not suddenly, but gradually: because it is not all at once coagulated and dried out with its earth, but part by part: so that the quality of the water is diminished more and more over time, until it is completely dried out, so as to be converted into powder. And this happens in the same order with a slow fire, as was said regarding the extraction. And the whole mastery <note>original: "magisterium", referring to the Great Work or the complete alchemical process.</note> consists in this, according to **Morienus** <note>An early alchemist, legendary teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: that water be extracted from the earth, and then let down upon the earth again. Because through this, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says: The Stone receives both the superior and inferior power, and becomes spiritual and corporeal. 

But beware lest you go astray when you hear of the division of the stone into earth and water: For the stone is always one, and in it are spirit, body, and soul. And just as they proceeded together from one womb, and in turn sometimes act and sometimes are acted upon, so also they are of an inseparable society. For in truth, one is never separated from the other, but they only seem to be separated to the sight; indeed, one cannot in any way exist without the other, as the **Lily** <note>original: "Lilium", likely referring to the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae*.</note> says. For their spirits are separated by way of a perfect nature. So that they are not separated from one another, as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in medieval alchemy.</note> says in the **Book of Roots** <term>Liber Radicum</term>. Take from this that the intellect of the craftsman perceives this difference in the parts of the stone more than the eye sees it, even though a diversity may sometimes appear to the senses. For always after the dissolution of the stone, something flies above, and something remains below, so long as the stone is not fixed <note>A "fixed" substance in alchemy is one that has been made stable enough to withstand the heat of a fire without evaporating.</note>. And that which ascends always carries something of the body with it into the air, and that which remains below always drinks in the ascending water. For as much descends as ascends: because in the wheel of its sphere all things are rolled or circulated by the heat from below driving them out, and lifting the vaporous part, and [by the] cold—

...[restrained] by the superior constraining and depressing force. That which descends, however, immediately enters the body and disposes it for flight: because the spirit is subtle and sharpened by fiery virtue. From this it happens that, although from the beginning of the extraction some black earth appears to reside at the bottom of the vessel, yet after a time, at the final softening by water and the grinding of fire, it is all dissipated and refined. At last, the whole ascends into the air; it is caught up with the spirit not all at once, but little by little: and the body and spirit become entirely one. From this, the whole follows, having one color, virtue, and property. Afterward, through continuous precipitation, the entire sublimated <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor, then condensing it back into a solid</term> matter is fixed below, though gradually, until nothing more ascends. 

And then the spirit is converted into a body, and yet the body does not lose the virtue of the spirit. Because the spirits were made most subtle, the body also remains most subtle: because it is a substance existing from the nature of the **quintessence** <term>the "fifth element," a pure, celestial substance superior to the four earthly elements</term>. As the spirits were most clear and most shining, so also is the body. As they were most pure, so the body is most pure. As they were most white, so the body is most white. And so it is with the other properties. 

However, one must not think that as soon as the body rests below, it is sufficiently fixed or sufficiently tinged white, unless perhaps the whole sublimated mass suddenly rests fixed below together, pouring itself out like a most splendid oil. But in whatever way or time this happens, it is certain that the spirit, soul, and body are most perfectly united, and friendship is fully established between the hot and the moist, the cold and the dry <note>The four "qualities" of Aristotelian physics which the alchemist sought to balance.</note>. Regarding this method of governance, **Morienus** <note>An early alchemist, legendary teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> speaks, saying: "And if you have not perfectly cleansed the body, and have not dried it, nor rendered it well whitened, and have not mixed the soul into it, and have not removed all its stench, until after its purification the **tincture** <term>a concentrated alchemical essence capable of transforming and coloring matter</term> falls into it, you have directed nothing at all of this mastery." And know that the soul quickly enters its own body, for it is by no means joined with a foreign body. 

And the **Rosarius** <note>original: "Rosarius Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note> states: "There are two stony elements, namely the dry ones: earth and fire; and two aquatic ones, namely air and water. The calcined <term>calcination: reducing a solid to powder through high heat</term> body, however, is deprived of aquatic moisture. Therefore, since the dry thirsts willingly, it will drink the aquatic." Therefore, bring the water back over the earth by cooking it little by little, until the earth becomes white, etc. Likewise, in the **Book of the Seven Seals**, it is said: "The spirit of **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the volatile, feminine, and transformative principle.</note>, entering the body itself subtly and preparing it for simple matter, extracts from it the soul..."

...carries the **soul** and the dry parts into the air. Afterward, indeed, with the body itself having been prepared and reduced to the nature of the **quintessence** <term>the "fifth element," a pure, celestial substance superior to the four earthly elements</term>—which is simple—it pours the soul back in. The body, embracing her, rejoices. The **spirit**, also entering the body with the soul, perfects it and makes the dead living: and when it rises again, it lives forever. And this soul is the **mediator** <note>original: "mediatrix"</note> between the body and the spirit; she joins them and binds them in an inseparable union. For the spirit cannot be united with the body except through the soul, which is the **tincture** <term>a medicinal or alchemical extract capable of transforming substances</term> of the Sun <note>The Sun is the alchemical symbol for gold</note> and of the philosophers. Therefore, the soul, seeing her body dead and dry, descends in compassion and brings it back to life. And because she has been made sublime, most pure, and most virtuous from her celestial dwelling, she also gifts her body with eternal and immortal life, etc.

And the philosopher **Mireris** <note>A name appearing in various alchemical tracts, often associated with Arabic or legendary Egyptian sources</note> says: The spirit that is extracted is the soul. However, the black dregs <note>original: "Fæx nigra"</note> remaining and left behind are the body, in which there is no life. The soul is thin, which is air; the body is thick, which is earth. It is necessary, however, for each of them to have an ordered regimen, until the thick is thinned and the thin is incorporated. For what you seek is in the dregs. Do not despise the ashes located in the lower part of the vessel <note>original: "testa"</note>: but cook them with the fire of coals for many days, until it becomes coal. Then, with the spirit sequestered from it, grind it and return the moisture to it with which you previously liquefied it, etc. After this, it must become liquefied so that it is altered from its nature, until after dissolution it becomes spiritual and thin. Therefore, with its soul returned to it—which was its essence and life—it becomes thin; for the soul, having been returned to the body, brings the dead to life.

Thirdly, you should know that the craftsman must not only whiten the stone, but also give it a perfect whiteness. Therefore, it is necessary to recognize this beforehand, so that he may know how to reach it through certain stages: because not every whiteness **colors** <note>original: "tingit," referring to the alchemical process of "tinging" or dyeing a base metal into a precious one</note> enough for the **Moon** <note>The Moon is the alchemical symbol for silver</note>; nor is the stone sufficiently fixed as soon as it is white. It is therefore necessary to **sublimate** <term>to heat a substance until it becomes vapor, then solid again, to purify it</term> the stone, and by sublimating to whiten it, until it is most white and fixed against the fight of the fire. Thus, we wait for a long time to go from **blackness** <note>original: "nigredo"</note> to true **whiteness** <note>original: "albedo"</note>, passing through many colors before the proper intended color is generated by the art in the final **digestion** <term>the slow heating of a substance to bring it to maturity or completion</term>. And as Master **Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus (Pietro Buono), a 14th-century physician and alchemist from Ferrara known for the work "The Precious Pearl"</note> says in chapter 6: All the colors preceding the final one, no matter how many there are, result from incomplete digestion. And therefore the craftsman does not stop there, but moves toward the final color as if it were pre-fixed in his mind. Let us see, then, how much it is...

...to be the **whiteness** <term>albedo: the second major stage of the Great Work, representing purification and the transition to silver</term> of the stone. For Ham says in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages</note>: know that when **Mercury** <term>the liquid metal and primary alchemical principle of volatility</term> is whitened, it becomes the incombustible **white sulfur** of the philosophers, containing within itself the poison. It is similar to the splendor of marble, which the envious call **Ethelia** <note>original: "Ethelia"; a cryptic term used to hide the identity of the substance, often referring to a volatile spirit or vapor</note>, and **orpiment** <note>a deep yellow/orange arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, and a **tincture** <term>an alchemical substance capable of infusing its color and properties into another</term>: because only sulfur whitens copper. However, it cannot whiten copper unless it has been whitened in a prior operation; yet this is fugitive <note>volatile; prone to evaporating</note> unless it is held back by the red sulfur, etc.

And the treatise *Miserula* says: They will be most white, in the manner of shining marble and the whitest salt. And then, from all bodies, it makes **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical term for silver</note>. And the Anonymous author <note>original: "Ignotus"</note> says: Strengthen the fire in **calcination** <term>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder</term>, until white earth emerges from the strength of the fire. And for that reason, grind the earth more often with its own water: and calcine it again: until, by the washing of water and fire, the darkness completely recedes. After purification, however, it turns red, and afterward, it turns yellow. 

Indeed, as Gallinarius says, it often turns white, and often turns yellow, and often turns black. And according to another philosopher, it often turns red, and often yellow: and it often melts and often coagulates before the true whiteness appears—indeed, all the colors of the world appear first, and finally, the true whiteness follows. But the Anonymous author added that the whiteness is true when it is as if the eyes of fish shine out in it <note>This likely refers to a specific shimmering or "pearly" luster</note>: and then the congealed stone is in its correct state. 

When you see a whiteness standing out above all else (the same Gallinarius says), though all the colors of the world appeared before, they all end in one color, namely, perfect whiteness, which is like glittering marble. This, moreover, is continued in one vessel and with one fire in warm and moist **horse dung** <note>Alchemists used piles of fermenting horse dung as a natural incubator to provide a steady, gentle, and long-lasting heat</note>, until it dissolves many times, and is again congealed and thickened into a most clear mass of white color, which hardens in the cold like pitch or hard gum. 

And this first cooking is to be continued for as long as it takes for the **Dragon** <term>Draco: a symbol for the raw, volatile matter or "mercury" that must be tamed</term> to be brought to life, and become a crystalline stone—melting, tinting, and congealing Mercury, and changing any metals into true silver. And another philosopher says: The white stone is called **white gold**, and it is like an oil as white as snow, etc. When, therefore, it is thus perfected, so that it flows like wax without smoke or crackling: then it is properly called **virgin's milk** <term>lac virginis: a symbolic name for the purified, liquid mercurial essence</term>, according to Gallinarius. 

And in the *Book of Saturn* it is read: It will be like a waxing milk, melting, penetrating in the manner of "fixed water" against the fight of the fire: and its number falls over a thousand <note>This likely refers to the "projection" ratio, suggesting one part of this substance can transform a thousand parts of base metal</note>. It is also called **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note>, because it illuminates everything filthy, as appears in that same place. It is also called **perennial water** <note>original: "aqua perennis"</note>, and is named by many other names. These things, moreover, according to certain...

# ON THE STONE

...is completed in putrefaction in 36 days, according to others in 70, according to others in approximately 80.

->*That the governance of our stone in the conjunction of spirit and body is divine.*<-

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

This art is called "divine" because the aspect of its governance exists beyond nature and [human] understanding, as all philosophers maintain. That divine governance <term>regimen: the controlled management of the alchemical fire and process</term> occurs at the time of **whitening** <note>original: "dealbationis"; the albedo stage where the matter turns white</note>, namely when the conjunction of the souls, spirits, and whitened bodies takes place; because this conjunction depends upon divine protection. For this happens suddenly—namely, that the medicine coagulates the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the metal mercury</note>—not the common kind, but that of the stone—unless it is suddenly coagulated at its birth with that medicine of which **Geber** <note>original: "Geb."; likely Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the most famous and foundational figure of medieval alchemy</note> speaks. It flies away and flees along with all that medicine. For he does not speak there of common quicksilver, although the words might seem to sound so, but of the quicksilver that has been coagulated and fixed into the **elixir** <term>the perfected alchemical substance capable of transmutation</term>. 

Therefore, it is necessary that from the beginning there is one single matter, in which exists the power of the body, spirit, and soul, similar to a mineral medicine. This matter should not require any external assistance, but should possess within itself everything it needs for its operation in the management of the process—whether for **sublimation** <term>turning a solid into vapor</term>, **fixation** <term>making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, liquefaction, freezing, or any such thing. For the *Lily* <note>original: "Lil."; likely referring to the *Lilium inter Spinas* (The Lily among Thorns), a common alchemical title</note> says: "There is only one single thing, containing within itself body, soul, and spirit, which dye the metal simultaneously; in its operation, no other aiding substance is necessary," etc. 

Each of the aforementioned bodies and spirits, if it has been prepared with perfect preparation, is either the white or the red elixir by itself alone. For there is one **ferment** <term>a substance added to the work to "leaven" the matter and trigger transformation</term> for the white and for the red. Whence **Rhazes** <note>original: "Ras."; Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian polymath and alchemist</note>, speaking of the quicksilver of the philosophers, says: "I do not want you to wonder that I have counted quicksilver among the 'bodies' in this reasoning, and among the 'spirits' in the previous one, for the convertibility of its nature demands this." Therefore, it is associated now with bodies and now with spirits. It is reasonably associated with spirits because of its flightiness from the fire, which it possesses before it is "corrected" <note>purified or stabilized</note>. And because it exalts bodies when it has been corrected, it is also associated by right with bodies: because all bodies can be converted into it, and it can be drawn out from all bodies. Likewise, that beautiful dispute which **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"; a variation of the name Rhazes</note> sets forth between **Mercury** and **Gold**, shows that they [the philosophers] wish the stone to be entirely Mercurial, and to have gold (or sulfur) in its hidden depths. From these things, it is gathered that the philosophers' stone is solely

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the alchemical principles, shifting from the "divine" governance of the whitening process to the specific nature of Mercury (Quicksilver) as both a volatile spirit and a potential solid body. # PHILOSOPHY

This Mercury is so called because it is entirely a **fleeting spirit** <note>original: "spiritus fugiens"; a substance that evaporates or sublimates easily when heated</note>. And therefore, although **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> behaves like a female in the composition of the elixir, its entire first operation is as a male. And this is why it remains volatile for as long as it is not contained by a "body," which is the **sulphur** <term>Sulphur: in alchemy, this is the active, stabilizing principle that "fixes" the volatile Mercury into a solid state</term> that coagulates it.

This body, however, is not added to it from some outside source; rather, Mercury possesses that body potentially within its own nature. It is brought into actuality when, through proper **digestion** <term>digestio: a slow, steady heating process similar to biological digestion</term>, it takes on the property and nature of a body. And then, from itself alone, it is called a "body."

From this, it is also evident that in almost all operations of metals and minerals, the composition is made from spirits alone or from their own vapors, whether they are simple or mixed. These are indeed called "spirits" because of their tendency to flee from heat; yet, at the end of digestion, they are **fixed** <note>original: "figuntur"; the process of making a volatile substance resistant to fire</note> by cold. They are fixed by their own power, along with their hidden bodies that exist within them potentially, without the mixing of any external body. This comes from the earthy nature of spirits: for heavy elements are the cause of fixation—especially **Earth**, which receives an impression with difficulty but afterwards holds it firmly. However, it receives that impression more easily if **Water** is mixed with it.

From this it is clear that even mineral spirits are composed of the four elements; both the heavy and the light elements are made vaporous by the digesting heat. In this way, the light elements lift up (sublimate) the heavier elements mixed with them. Yet the heavier elements do not entirely lose their nature or their specific properties because of this; if they did, they would be unable to return from a bodily state to a spiritual one. Such a claim is entirely false, because **bodies are potentially spirits, and conversely, spirits are potentially bodies.**

The same is true for these spirits from which the **elixir** <term>the perfected alchemical substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> is composed. Since heavy elements are the cause of fixation, when they are ultimately digested and purified, they possess the power of a "body" and of "sulphur." And yet they are never truly separated from the lighter elements, because the lighter elements exist within the heavier ones. It is as if a single thing contains all four elements within itself—both the active and the passive—and everything necessary for the generation of the elixir.

Thus, our Mercury, having been purified by art from its impurities through a suitable fire, is simply a "fleeting spirit" in its current state, but it is a "body" in its most immediate potential. Therefore, it is necessary that we bring it back to being a body in actuality. When this happens, it is also the **solar body** of the philosophers, the **tincture** <term>a concentrated alchemical substance that "stains" or transforms other metals</term>, the "gold of the philosophers," and their "lead" and "bronze." Concerning this, **Miluesindus** <note>An authority often cited in medieval alchemical texts, sometimes identified with Arabic philosophical traditions</note> says: "Our bronze does not become tinging <note>capable of transforming color/nature</note> until it becomes fleeting." And this gold is sulphur...

### CONCERNING THE STONE

...the **sulphur of the philosophers** <term>Sulphur: In alchemy, the active, masculine principle responsible for color and hardness</term>, hidden within their own **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. This is the subject of the dispute. And this gold is the **ferment** <term>Fermentum: Like yeast in bread, a ferment is a small amount of a substance that transforms a larger mass into its own nature</term> of both tinctures—that is, the white and the red. **Quicksilver**, however, is the ferment. Concerning this, the philosophers say: The ferment of gold is gold, just as the ferment of dough is dough <note>original: "Fermentum auri aurum est, sicut fermentum pastæ, pasta est"</note>. Yet they never say the ferment of silver is silver: because every fermentation and every **fixation** <term>fixio: the process of making a substance resistant to fire so it no longer evaporates</term> in the **elixir** <term>Elixir: the perfected medicinal or transmuting agent</term> is accomplished through gold, not through silver.

For this reason, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in Arabic alchemy</note> said: No metal is submerged in Mercury, except for the **sun** <note>original: "sol"; the alchemical name for Gold</note>. And **Alphidius**, in the chapter on the nature of the sun, said: Spirits are mixed together and fixed with salt by the greatest skill, which does not come to an artisan who is "stiff-necked" <note>meaning an artisan who is stubborn or lacks spiritual insight</note>. And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> said: Observe that the true ferment of gold is only from its own nature: and its nature is only from quicksilver perfectly **digested** <term>digestio: a slow, steady heating process</term> by solution.

Of this quicksilver, **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: That the **white smoke** <note>original: "fumus albus"; likely referring to the volatile vapor of mercury</note> is the tincture of the "dead bodies." Because if the white smoke did not exist, the gold of Alchemy could in no way be made. Regarding this quicksilver and the sulphur hidden within it, **Rasis** <note>Al-Razi, a Persian polymath and alchemist</note> says in the *Book of Words*: The dryness of Alchemy tints another thing. For then the moist is coagulated by its own dry part, just as gold or melted wax is coagulated by its own internal dryness. And in this manner, it happens that it is simultaneously a **tincture** <term>tinctura: the power of the stone to change the color and quality of a metal</term> and a mixing of body and spirit. And this is the sulphur that tints but does not burn; and the fire that tints its own earth.

And this is what Hermes intends: "Its power is complete if it has been turned into earth," <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet</note> that is, toward fixation through **coagulation** <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid</note>. In this way, bodies, spirits, and souls are purified together from superfluities and from combustion, and they rise up over their own dregs. And in this **conjunction** <term>coniunctio: the mystical and physical union of opposite principles (like mercury and sulphur)</term> of spirit, soul, and body, divine power alone works within the mind and the guidance of the artisan. 

Regarding this union, Morienus said: At the hour of conjunction, the greatest wonders will appear. And this union is reserved solely for divine power: **GOD** is the creator of natures and works in all natures. Therefore, it is called "miraculous," as it were, because it is beyond human intellect. For man can neither know the time of such a conjunction, nor even fully comprehend the manner of it. This is because at the end of digestion, and near the end of all things, the elements—similarly the bodies, spirits, souls, sulphurs, and all tinctures—are mixed together in one subject. At the end of the digestion of the first purification from all stains, then the soul alone arises and not...

### PHILOSOPHY

...before. And this work happens suddenly: because the soul quickly enters its body (as **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says). For by then they have been converted into **spirits** <term>Spiritus: In alchemy, the volatile substances that can be vaporized by heat</term>, and they ascend together. And again: It is necessary to convert spirits into bodies—that is, to **coagulate** <term>Coagulatio: The process of turning a liquid or vapor into a solid mass</term> them together. And this does not happen unless the purification of the elements is complete: which the artisan must indeed know very well beforehand, along with the determined time for the composition of the elements. For then, suddenly, the **sulphur of the philosophers** <note>original: "sulphur philosophorum"</note> coagulates its own **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, and fixes and perfects it into a **tincture** <term>Tinctura: A substance capable of penetrating and changing the color/nature of other metals</term> and **Elixir**.

And in this lies the root and strength of the whole mastery. Hence all seem to agree that this composition happens suddenly at the moment of completion. Therefore, although that body which is gold—or the sulphur of the philosophers—is **fixed** <term>Fixum: A substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when exposed to fire</term> in itself, nevertheless the quicksilver, which is by its nature **volatile** <term>Volatile: A substance that easily vaporizes or "flies" when heated</term>, tries to drag the gold along with it into flight. And it would indeed fly away together with it, unless the gold suddenly held it fast.

And so there is a great battle between them: because one is a **bird without wings**, while the other is **with wings**. And at this point consists the true perfection of all Alchemy—or its annihilation. And that **sun** <note>original: "sol"; the alchemical principle of Gold</note> which is in the quicksilver of the philosophers first brings forth whiteness because of the nature of the quicksilver, which is the beginning, root, and foundation of the whole work. Therefore it is called **white gold**. Yet there is in it a hidden root of redness, just as **red lead** <note>original: "minium"</note> is hidden in **white lead** <note>original: "cerussa"</note>. And in this way the fixed and the non-fixed ascend together: and the sun rises together with the moon in the **belly of Mercury**.

Therefore, Mercury, fleeing and snatching the other away with him, is himself suddenly caught by it and made to flee in the fire. Wherefore, if the sun had not ascended with Mercury, it would not have been able to fly together with it, nor be mixed with it; nor could Mercury be fixed by the sun. But when they ascend together, and are mixed, and are **sublimated** <term>Sublimatio: The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then collecting the condensed deposit</term> together, one finally cannot be separated from the other. For either the whole recedes, or the whole will remain, and one will not be able to take dominion over the other, nor vice-versa. 

If, therefore, the spirit conquers, the body will fly with it; but if the body conquers, the spirit is fixed with it. The fixed overcoming the volatile perfects the work. The volatile overcoming the fixed, however, annihilates the work. This, then, is the time of perfection and annihilation. And its root and foundation is Mercury, sublimated, purified, and bright. And this spirit, joined with the soul in its **conjunction** <note>original: "contu" [conventu]; meeting or union</note>, is of a most white, wondrous brilliance, like snow in actuality; yet its body is most red, like blood in potentiality, pro—

### ON THE STONE

...nearby. From these things, therefore, it is concluded that this work is deservedly called **divine**, because it is not brought to perfection except by the supreme power of God. For it is not within the power of the artisan, but is bestowed upon whom the most merciful God himself wills. And at this point lies all the danger. However, once this point has passed, there is no longer any danger. Because at this moment alone the spirit is exalted and the bodies melt together. Whence **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of chemistry and alchemy</note> says: The error that happens in the art, and its correction, is in the "point" [the critical moment]: and this is when celestial things are joined with terrestrial things.

There is, therefore, a **threefold danger** in the management of this stone. The **first** is lest the stone be burned, or turned to glass, or corrupted in the **tinctures** <term>Tinctura: A substance capable of penetrating and changing the color and nature of other metals</term>. The **second** is lest the spirits flee, and the body remains dead at the bottom. Both of these certainly depend on the industry of the artisan and the tempering of the fire. The **third** danger—and this is truly the greatest danger—is lest the body fly away together with the spirit and soul. And although this requires moderation in management on the part of the artisan, nevertheless it is not sufficient without divine power. And therefore, as to this, it is said: its management is greater than can be perceived by reason, unless by the highest inspiration of the deity.

Wherefore it was commanded above that the artisan be devoted to God, the Best and Greatest, humble, pious, and of a good mind, as well as diligent and most patient in the operation. Now indeed this must be added: that he also be assiduous and long-suffering, so that he does not hasten, but without any rage of heart, anger, or agitation, quietly and peacefully, he should await the hoped-for fruits after the due time; just as the best farmers do when sowing, as the **Lily** <note>Likely the 'Lilium Alchimiae', a famous medieval alchemical text often attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note> says.

Moreover, the diligent artisan gains a double benefit from these things, and both are of the greatest importance. First, the acquisition of a most great treasure; second, the knowledge and experience of wonderful natural works, all of which are most useful to the body and the soul. And therefore it is called **women's work** <term>Opus mulierum: An alchemical metaphor for the stage of gentle heating (decoction) that requires patience rather than heavy labor</term> and **child's play** <term>Ludus puerorum: A metaphor suggesting that once the difficult initial stages are finished, the process proceeds easily and automatically</term>: because this philosopher has nothing else to do than to cook gently, and to note with skillful care the wonderful works which will indeed come to pass, and to consider them with the greatest delight in the intellect, and to gaze upon them with his eyes, just as children delight in games and are never satisfied. He must, however, always praise God in his works and return due thanks to Him, lest at length laboring with the children, he becomes vain and empty. And because, as was said above, this is called the **Egg** <note>original: "Ouum"</note> by reason of the parts which our stone contains within itself (whence it is likened to an egg), and also by reason of the heat of a brooding hen, so it is called "women's work,"

### *That just as fixation is the fulfillment of the stone, so it is necessary to know the root and order of fixation.*

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

The artisan must always perform each task not by chance, but with the greatest prudence and according to reason, especially regarding the fixation of his medicine. For fixation is that which completes all things and makes them remain in perpetuity, as is evident from the previous discussions in the third chapter: to make the medicine permanent in fire, so that it is neither burned nor destroyed, nor diminished—neither in substance, nor in power, nor in color or tincture—but is rather increased. Hence a certain most skilled philosopher says: Our Stone must be held under the governance of fire for so long until it can no longer be changed from one nature into another. For it is necessary to make the fixed volatile and the volatile fixed so many times, until the whole is fixed and flows, and transforms into the true sun-making and moon-making substance <note>original: "solificum & lunificum" — substances capable of producing gold and silver</note>. For in this way, the war is provoked—that is, it is destroyed into coagulating sulfur and flying <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>—and a friendship is also composed between the elements. Regarding this, **Rhazes** <note>Rafis: Referring to Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian polymath whose alchemical writings were highly influential in the Latin West</note> says: This spirit is converted into body, and body into spirit; and again spirit into body; and then friendship is made between the cold and the hot, and between the hot and the dry. And this occurs only by the power of God and the tempering of fire, and the moderation of its limits, as we have often said before.

But let us see now, I pray, the root and foundation of fixation. The root most proximate to fixation is sulfur, because this alone is what coagulates <term>quicksilver</term>. For the coagulating agent and the fixing agent are the same. Moreover, the medicine must be fixed; therefore, the sulfur that brings the medicine to perfection will necessarily be fixed. Such sulfur is not the sulfur of the common people, because that is combustible <note>original: "adurens" — literally "burning," referring to common sulfur's tendency to consume itself in fire, whereas alchemical sulfur is "non-burning" and stable</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to extract it from bodies in which there is non-combustible sulfur. There are only two such bodies, namely <term>Sol</term> <note>The Sun, the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> and <term>Luna</term> <note>The Moon, the alchemical symbol for Silver</note>. We therefore subtly prepare these two bodies, so that from them we may have sulfur upon the earth, with which we may dye <term>quicksilver</term>. Just as beneath the earth (as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037 AD), a Persian physician and philosopher whose "De Conglutinatione Lapidum" was a core alchemical text</note> maintains), these two bodies are not minerals, but as...

As was said above, these are living things. However, it is necessary to sublime these bodies with Mercury until the whole thing ascends—not with common mercury, but with that specific Mercury which is derived from the bodies themselves. This must be done while the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "cucurbita" — the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distilling apparatus</note> is closed, so that the Mercury cannot escape; for it cannot be sublimed except by the power of air. Therefore, if it finds an open passage, it will fly off into smoke, and thus the <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium" — the alchemical process or "Great Work"</note> will be lost.

That <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum" — mercury</note> will then be coagulated into silver by the power of "white, non-burning sulfur," provided that the quicksilver is pure. This is the finest substance from which Alchemists can produce silver—that is, the <term>Elixir</term>—and reach the White Stage through their mastery.

But if the sulfur used is of the highest quality, bright with redness, and contains within it the power of silver-making and dryness (likewise non-burning), it will be the best substance for making the Elixir of the Sun <note>The "Elixir of the Sun" refers to the medicine for making gold.</note>. And indeed, the white sulfur must come first, and then the red: for nothing can become gold unless it has first been silver. This is the opinion of the Unknown Author, and (as it is believed) of **Alphidius**, and likewise of the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a seminal medieval alchemical text.</note>.

Thus, the immediate cause of fixation is sulfur, but according to the same author, this reaches back to the "first root," which pertains to the elements. For the *Rosarium* says, following the opinion of the same **Alphidius**: Water is the medium joining the tinctures of oil—namely, of air and fire—with the earth. The White Elixir is completed by three elements: earth, water, and air (for fire does not enter into the white). The Red Elixir, however, turns on all four wheels <note>A metaphor for involving all four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>.

Therefore, you must first distill the water, and afterward mix in the oil so that it stands over the water—that is, it is spread through the water. Afterward, the water must be "fixed" with the earth so that it adheres firmly to it; for if you have killed one of the four elements, you have killed them all.

Because the earth is fixed in its own nature, it retains and fixes the other elements within itself—and first among these is water. Because water is cold and moist, the earth connects and binds it. For that which is dry is sparse, and thus it acquires a "continuity of parts" from the moist; conversely, the moist receives a "firm impression" from the dry. Moisture alone receives an impression quickly but loses it just as fast; dryness alone receives an impression only with great difficulty and slowly, but once received, it is hard to let go.

When both are tempered together, they achieve a firm impression and, similarly, a strong resistance against fire. For moisture prevents the dry from being combustible, while the dry prevents the moist from being fluid. Fire has free dominion over either of these elements on their own; but air, because it is hot and moist, [joins] earth and water...

...clarifies and thins <note>original: "clarificat, & rarificat"</note> [the matter], so that it becomes capable of being stretched and melted. **Fire**, however, turns the whole compound red, strengthens it, and matures it; for it causes the **Air** to be mixed through the subtle parts. It also binds and fixes the **Water** with the **Earth**, and consequently grants it a firm <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincturam" — the color or essence that transforms other metals</note>.

Therefore, understand from this that the heavy elements lead more toward <term>fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat without evaporating.</note> and stillness, and they work within the compound more than the light ones. The light elements work more toward the melting of the tinctures. Nevertheless, all elements cooperate with all others for every purpose; but **Fire** cooperates most toward fixation because of its active, penetrating power, which carries others with it and dries them.

Wherefore the primary cause of fixation is **Earth**, because it is more stable than all the elements; then comes **Water**, because it is closer to tempering the dryness of the earth and protects it from burning with its coldness; and finally, **Fire** completes the fixation. The proof of this is that in gold—in which fire dominates more than in silver—there is greater stability, and consequently the **Red Elixir** <note>The medicine for transmuting metals into gold.</note> is also more stable than the **White Elixir** <note>The medicine for transmuting metals into silver.</note>.

And thus understand what was said—that fire does not enter into the **White Elixir**—this refers primarily to its dominance. For all four elements are in that one as well, but its power and effect are not as great there as in the **Red Elixir**, to which is added the fire that is the "red sulfur," joined not from the outside, but extracted from within.

Take this as the foundation of your knowledge: that in the operation of the Elixir, the earthy nature which is called the <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus" — the solid, material part of the alchemical matter</note>, although it is universally mixed with the most subtle <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus" — the volatile or gaseous part</note> and sublimated most finely along with it—and even if it does not seem distinct from the elements themselves—it is nonetheless the immediate cause of <term>coagulation</term> <note>The thickening of a liquid into a solid.</note> and fixation. And from it, together with the watery substance, comes the origin of the **sulfur** and the **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum" — a substance that acts like yeast, "leavening" the base metal into a noble one.</note>.

And this fixed nature is present in all compounds made of the four elements, no matter how much they are refined or led toward a spiritual state: sometimes it is active, and sometimes it is dormant. Therefore, all things have within themselves that by which they may be fixed, unless they fly away as smoke.

To this fixation, the external fire administered by art (as was said above) cooperates most strongly. But if it is untempered, it hinders the fixation, because it preserves the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humiditatem radicalem" — the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all matter.</note> of the stone and does not consume it. For it is primarily from moisture that the stone acquires its ability to melt. From this, learn again which element is present more or less in each stage of the process, because from the beginning the stone is cold and moist, but in the end, it is hot and dry. And this is how it appears to the sight; though to the intellect it is hot...

### CHAPTER 30.

Having spoken before of the whiteness of the stone: now in the final place we must speak of its redness, which is namely the completion of its <term>governance</term> <note>original: "regiminis" — the controlled heating and chemical management of the alchemical process.</note>. For this, you should first know that the same substance serves as the <term>ferment</term> <note>A substance added to the "Stone" to trigger its transformative power, similar to how yeast causes dough to rise.</note> for both the white and the red Elixir: namely, our "egg" <note>original: "ouum nostrum" — a common alchemical metaphor for the sealed vessel or the primary matter containing all necessary elements.</note>. This, however, could not be the case unless its <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter.</note> participated in both natures, or unless there were something in that substance which could reduce the <term>Sun</term> <note>Gold</note> and the <term>Moon</term> <note>Silver</note> back to the common nature and color of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury, the fluid "mother" of all metals.</note>.

Therefore, although in our stone the Sun and Moon are distinct in their location, properties, and color (as is clear from what was said above), yet because they are of a close nature, one is easily converted into the other. For the sake of mutual action and passion, the two "seeds" <note>original: "spermata"</note> are most closely mixed together, which happens most effectively during <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of decomposition or "blackening" where the old forms of the metals are destroyed so they can be reborn.</note>. In this way, they pass into a single nature, power, and color. This is why a single Elixir for both the white and the red can be generated from both by our art—though not at the same time, but one after the other through different modes of <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of slow, constant heating.</note>.

However, because the Sun is worthier than the Moon, more fixed in its nature, and similar to a more stable metal, the leadership of the ferment is attributed to it. Thus, it is said that the Sun is the ferment of both the white and the red Elixir, and that the work is not improved except with it, nor completed with anything else. Therefore, <term>Hermes</term> <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> said: "A true red <term>tincture</term> <note>The essence that changes the color and quality of a metal.</note> is never made without the red stone." For the white alone, without the red stone, would not dye a substance into a perfect red. In the red, there is a greater power of "non-burning sulfur" <note>original: "sulphuris non vrentis" — a specialized sulfur that stabilizes and perfects metals rather than consuming them.</note>. This is because the masculine principle is hotter, purer, oilier, and more "digested" than in the white, where the feminine principle is colder, more impure, and more "fugitive" <note>original: "fugitiua" — meaning volatile or prone to evaporating when heated.</note>. 

But because the Moon holds the first dominion and converts its Sun to itself—giving it its own nature, color, and property—it is not undeservedly called the ferment of the White Elixir, even though it tastes more of the nature of quicksilver than of sulfur because it is volatile. Nevertheless, each ferment is derived from both bodies, though more primarily from the Sun. For both bodies, possessing a proximity of natures and having arisen from one father and one mother, [merge] into one first...

...the nature of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti viui" — Mercury.</note> is transmuted by alteration: so that thereafter from it, that is from its hidden part, two sulfurous ferments can be extracted, the white first, and then the red. For it is not properly called a <term>ferment</term> <note>In alchemy, a ferment is a substance (like yeast in bread) that "infects" the rest of the matter with its own nature, turning it into gold or silver.</note> unless when Mercury is coagulated with it and is tinged into the likeness of silver or gold. From the beginning, however, neither is called a ferment, except because it is the material from which the ferment is extracted. 

Thus, therefore, the <term>Sun</term> <note>Gold.</note> principally gives the perfection and the final completion to the stone; from it comes the soul, the tinging <term>sulfur</term> <note>The active, masculine principle that provides color and "form" to the metal.</note>, and the spirit of Mercury, which is sharpened and impregnated by the <term>Moon</term> <note>Silver.</note>, finally drawing everything to its own nature and color. And this is what is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>: <term>Azoch</term> <note>A name for the "universal mercury" or the essential spirit of the matter.</note> cannot substantially take away the color from <term>Laton</term> <note>An alchemical term for an impure metallic "body"—often brass or copper—that must be purified.</note>, nor change it, except for a time; but Laton substantially takes away the whiteness from Azoch: because there is in it a wonderful strength, which appears above all colors. For once its color is washed away, and its blackness and impurity are removed from it so that it appears white, Laton indeed dominates over Azoch and renders it red. 

And Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist often cited as a teacher to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: There is nothing that can take away from Laton its darkness or its color. But Azoch is like its governance, namely because it is <term>decocted</term> <note>boiled or refined over heat</note>: for it both colors it and makes it white. But again Laton dominates Azoch, that is, it renders the "living animal" red. 

And again it is said in the *Turba*: Although sulfur is male, yet in this place—namely, when the soul which is the spirit of sulfur (also called the "gold of the philosophers") is extracted—nature willing, the male takes on the form of the woman and will <term>suffer</term> <note>original: "patietur" — to be acted upon or to be the passive recipient of an action.</note>. 

And in the *Lillium* <note>The *Lilium Philosophorum* (The Lily of the Philosophers), a medieval alchemical treatise.</note>, Zinon says: This egg, because it has life, extracts the soul and generation from itself, not from another; and from its belly the flowers are extracted, and it makes itself germinate, and that which is inside, it sends out, and that which is outside, it sends inside. Thus the outward improves the inward, and vice versa, until the red—namely, the naturally red which is hidden in the body—is turned into white, specifically in the first part of the work. 

Wherefore Alphidius <note>An Arab alchemist often cited in Latin translations.</note> concludes: The conjunction of those two bodies [Gold and Silver] with Mercury is necessary in this part for the red and white Elixir. Because although gold is the most compact and fixed among all bodies, yet when it is dissolved and separated into the smallest parts, it becomes spiritual and volatile like Mercury, and carries with it the red <term>tincture</term> <note>The concentrated "essence" or "dye" of the stone that transforms other metals.</note>: silver likewise carries the white. Nor was the <term>body</term>... <note>original: "cor[pus]" — likely continuing to "nor was the body able to give this without Mercury."</note>

### ON THE STONE

...some thing more worthy and purer than the Sun, or its shadow, without which no tinging <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum" — Mercury, the essential fluid of the work.</note> is generated.

Secondly, you should know that whiteness necessarily precedes redness. For just as perfect white cannot be made in the stone unless black precedes it, so perfect red cannot be made unless whiteness precedes it. For blackness is the <term>crow’s head</term> <note>original: "caput corui" — a famous alchemical symbol for the first stage of decomposition and purification.</note> and the beginning of the work, as *Ignotus* says; and it appears first in the work, as the *Lilium* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical treatise.</note> remarks. Therefore, no perfect yellow can be made from black unless it was first white (as *Alphidius* reports). And he says "perfect yellow" because the matter often turns yellowish, reddish, or whitish during the process, as was said above; but "perfect yellowness" is not generated in the stone except after an excellent whiteness.

The cause of this is assigned by the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a core 16th-century alchemical text.</note>: Because nothing can become gold unless it was first silver; hence, he who knows how to convert gold into silver also knows how to convert silver into gold. However, gold cannot become silver unless it has first been <term>corrupted</term> <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down or "killing" of a metal's previous form so a new one can emerge.</note>; and when it is corrupted, it becomes black. From black, there is no transition to perfect yellow except through white, just as there is no transition from yellow back to white unless it has first been black.

For <term>citrination</term> <note>original: "citrinatio" — the stage of turning yellow, bridging the white and red works.</note> is nothing other than the washing away of blackness. For heat acting upon moisture causes blackness first; but acting upon dryness—if the heat continues—it causes yellowness. And therefore the *Lilium* says: Unless the bodies are dissected, the colors of the soul do not appear. And later it says: The spirit and the soul are not united with the body in a true way except in the white color; for then all the colors that can be imagined in the world today appear, and then they are fixed into a single color, that is, they meet in whiteness.

For <term>whitening</term> <note>original: "dealbatio"</note> is the beginning and the foundation of the whole work; from there it does not vary into different (that is, true) colors, except into red, in which is the ultimate end. For the yellowness that occurs between redness and whiteness is not considered a distinct color. In the <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of "cooking" or heating the matter over a long period.</note> after whiteness, one arrives at yellowness by increasing the governance of the fire; and after whiteness, you cannot go wrong.

Whence *Miseris* the philosopher says: The earth must first be buried in a piece of <term>Egyptian linen</term> <note>original: "pętia panni Ægyptij" — likely a metaphor for a specific type of pure white filter or the process of "shrouding" the matter in a vessel.</note>; afterwards the compound must be whitened, so that it may finally become a tinging and permanent <term>sulfur</term> <note>The active, "combustible" principle that gives the Stone its power to change other metals.</note>, and then become red. For twice it is blackened, twice it is yellowed, and twice it turns red. The second redness is the tinging one, which does not happen except after the first whitening, if it is performed philosophically.
