...you proceed, that is, if you whiten cautiously <note>original: "caute dealbas"</note>, you will be blessed. But if you see this happen suddenly, a great terror will come upon you. And for this reason, Raymond de Terminis says: After the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of "Nigredo" where the matter decays and turns black.</note>, it is necessary to restore the sulfur; its critical days are ninety at most; after this, no one can go wrong. Wherefore, know thirdly: that after the whiteness is complete, you must proceed to intense redness. For it is necessary for the redness of the medicine to be intense, as <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 13th-century authority on "the heights of perfection" in alchemy.</note> says, which happens thus: after the sulfur of the two aforementioned bodies has been made into a non-burning white, it becomes red through a greater <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctionem" — a process of long-term boiling or heating.</note> of the fire. For in this way, gold is made from silver. And thus white and red sulfur (as the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical florilegium.</note> says) possess their nature from a single matter of metals that has been fully purified, yet digested in different ways.

And **Plato** says: In all silver there is red sulfur, and such sulfur exists in the Sun and the Moon. The *Rosarius* says: For the shining bodies themselves, in which are the <term>tinging rays</term> <note>original: "radij tingentes" — the transformative powers that "dye" or transmute base metal into precious metal.</note>, tinge the other bodies with true whiteness and redness, according to how they themselves were prepared. Since non-burning white sulfur, belonging to silver, can through a greater digestion of fire become red sulfur, belonging to gold. Wherefore it is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, an ancient assembly of alchemical masters.</note>: When you see it entirely black, know that in the belly of that blackness, whiteness is hidden; and then it is necessary that this whiteness be extracted from its blackness. In the second decoction, the whiteness is to be placed in its vessel with its instruments, and they are to be cooked with a slow fire until all things become white.

However, when you see that surpassing whiteness in the vessel, then be certain that redness is hidden within that whiteness. And then it is not necessary to extract it; rather, boil it for so long until the whole becomes red. In this <term>rubification</term> <note>original: "rubificatione" — the final stage of the work, turning the matter red (the stage of Gold).</note>, two things are to be observed diligently and cautiously: first, that the vessel is not removed or touched; second, that a mild and equal heat is continued until the end, just as was demonstrated above. Wherefore **Morienus**, speaking of both, says: After you have directed the unclean body, put into it a fourth part of the <term>ferment</term>, and place it in the sun and boil it, and let its fire be mild; and let the vessel remain inviolably attached to its furnace, until the whole time of the fermentation of <term>Echeb</term> <note>original: "Echeb" — an Arabic-derived term for "Gold."</note>, that is, of the Sun, is completed. And **Alphidius** says: Then it is congealed in its proper state; when you see a whiteness surpassing all things, then be certain that redness lies hidden in the whiteness; and therefore you must not extract it, but boil it well until the whole becomes red...

although it is done, it first becomes ash-colored and lemon-yellow <note>original: "cineritius & citrinus"</note> as the fire is increased.
However, all the philosophers assert that the fire must be kept light until the sulfur becomes non-burning <note>original: "incremabile" — a substance that can no longer be consumed by fire.</note>. From this it is also clear that even in the third <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of intense, long-term heating.</note> the fire must be light: because although the white sulfur is non-burning, it is still in some way combustible, which is shown by the variation of colors before it is fixed in its redness—just as is evident from the things said above, and as is also the case with silver. Fourth and finally, you will know how to recognize when the stone is entirely perfect: first, indeed, when its redness is no longer changed or diminished. And this is when it is most red, like actual blood, as **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century Italian physician and author of the "New Precious Pearl."</note> said. And **Rudianus** says: This is the first of all tests of the oil itself: that it should produce no smoke, nor any noise, but should run through all things, and touch a plate of iron, copper, lead, or silver, and fix itself with them, and not fear the fire, nor be diminished, nor should its <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative color/power of the Stone.</note> be separated from the metals. Wherefore **Gallinarius** concludes: The Stone is reddened and whitened in the same way, and in the same place and vessel and under the same regime: continue the decoction until the whole compound becomes one red stone, <term>tinging</term> <note>To "tinge" is to permanently dye or transmute the nature of a metal.</note> and transforming all things into true Sun <note>original: "verum solem" — here meaning true gold.</note> and according to every judgment and test.

### *That the power of our stone is precious, immense, manifold, and wonderful.*

### CAP. XXXI.

Once the red stone has been made, it then <term>tinges</term> every body to perfection, as **Alphidius** says: Because, as Master Bonus said at the end of the fifth chapter, it not only alters but even transmutes in an instant, and is mixed without violence into the thing to be altered, with the stripping away of all superfluous and combustible parts. And it is like the "form" of gold, having virtually and actively all the distinctions and properties which mineral gold possesses. And therefore it suddenly makes all metals fixed, yellow-gold, shining...

# PHILOSOPHY

...most dense, heavy, of the ultimate weight, mute in resonance <note>meaning it does not ring like a metal when struck</note>, and possessing entirely the same medicinal virtue as true, purest, and most precious gold. And this form, among all forms of the world, is not only a quality, but also a quantity, because it is corporeal. Because of this, it is called the Theriac <note>original: "Theriaca" — a legendary universal antidote or wonder-drug.</note>, the Toxin, and the poison of the philosophers: because it suddenly coagulates and fixes its mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum" — quicksilver</note> as if by killing it, and perfects it into a tincture and the Elixir of other metals. And this is understood regarding the sulfur of Gold, which is not added from the outside, but is extracted ingeniously and almost miraculously through the proper regimen of the art from mercury, with which it is purified together through sublimation: because according to **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar and foundational figure of alchemy.</note>, the tinging sulfur is known only to nature; and yet it is called the "addition of the tinger." Concerning this poison, **Mundus** <note>One of the speakers in the "Turba Philosophorum."</note> says in the *Turba*:

> When this poison penetrates the body, it colors it with an unchangeable color, and the soul never leaves the body: because they cannot be separated further.

Understand then that this stone of the philosophers has the most excellent virtues over all other stones, as **Alphi** <note>Possibly Alphidius, an Arabic alchemical authority.</note> says. Moreover, its immense virtue is specifically threefold. First, indeed, because it converts raw Mercury placed in the fire, and any other metals, suddenly into the truest Sun <note>Gold.</note>, better than any natural gold: as the *Rosary* <note>The "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> and **Morienus** <note>A legendary hermit-philosopher said to have lived in the 7th century.</note> say in the new translation. This is also the secret of this mastery, that one part of this substance converts a thousand parts into the purest *Echeb* <note>original: "Echeb" — a term derived from the Arabic "al-dhahab," meaning gold.</note>. Second, that it preserves men in sweetness and youth, driving away from them all weaknesses. Finally, it dispels leprosy, the falling sickness <note>original: "caducum morbum" — epilepsy.</note>, and soothes as well as removes many other almost incurable infirmities. And it performs all these things more than all the medicines of physicians, or potions, or any confections whatsoever. This medicine also preserves and protects when applied in confections, lest any disease should be able to come to the person in the future, as the *Lily* <note>The "Lilium inter spinas," a common title for alchemical works.</note> says. Thus it becomes an antidote and medicine for all bodies to be cured and purged, metallic as well as human. The *Rosary* also specifies many things, saying:

> It preserves health, and strengthens virtue, repairs youth, purges the spiritual organs <note>The chest and respiratory system.</note>, purges the lungs, expels all poisons, removes diseases, and, when drunk in wine, gradually cures lepers.

Third, because many wonders are done with it in other things.

# ON THE STONE

**Lilius** <note>Likely a reference to the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae*.</note> further reports: It makes glass malleable, and from fused crystal, with the Stone we draw out a carbuncle <note>A legendary deep-red gemstone, often used as a metaphor for the Stone itself.</note>, and from a thousand pearls we compose one very large pearl that appears entirely natural. **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note> says in the book of his *Testament*: that **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> cannot be retained <note>fixed or stabilized so it does not evaporate</note> with any body without the physical stone. Therefore, all other operations are sophisticated <note>deceptive or fraudulent</note> and useless; yet all of them would be led to a good end and achieve their effect if they were completed by means of this stone. From these things, conclude with Lilius: that this medicine must be sought with the greatest diligence above all the riches of the world and lesser treasures, and even more than "potable gold" <note>original: "aurum potabile" — a liquid gold supplement</note> (which ignorant and imprudent empirics name and make from common gold, thinking they understand it), which kings, princes, and magnates use in their preparations to preserve their health. For this medicine of ours is truly divine, more spiritual, and more subtle through its physical solution, and far more effective than all others in price, virtue, and any immortal praise whatsoever.

->*That the medicine can be multiplied infinitely, and concerning its perfection.*<-

### CHAPTER XXXII.

The medicine, if it is perfect, is also judged to be "multiplicable" in a certain way unto infinity. There is, however, a threefold way of multiplying it. The first way is by dissolving it by itself more frequently and congealing it. This solution <note>melting into liquid</note> and congelation <note>solidification</note> is not done except by fire; because after the medicine has learned to endure the struggle against fire, the longer it remains in the heat, the more its goodness is increased. That solution, therefore, is its liquefaction into the form of oil; but it congeals by itself in the open air. This is sufficiently shown from the previous sections. Because the stone reaches its perfection through liquefying and congealing, it follows by the same reason and cause that if it is dissolved and congealed again, it will be even more perfect. And this is what the ***Rosarium*** <note>original: *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: The more often the medicine is dissolved, sublimated, and coagulated, the better <note>original: "melius"</note> and more abundantly it works. Here, however, "solution" is not understood as turning into dew-water, as fools think; rather, it means that you convert the dry into the moist, and the coarse into the simple, and refine it as much as you can. For the work of solution was invented only for the purpose of refining. And this is the intention of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father" of alchemy.</note>, who [associated] the fixed stone with the methods of sublimation...

The second method is by projecting the medicine onto a perfect body <note>original: "corpus perfectum"; in alchemy, this refers to gold or silver, which are "perfectly" refined by nature.</note>, one part onto a hundred parts of the fused perfect body: once the projection <note>The act of "throwing" the alchemical powder into molten metal.</note> is made, cover the vessel and place it in the furnace for several days, and first make a slow fire, afterwards a stronger one: and always increase the fire, yet gradually, and appropriately by its own degrees, and the whole will become medicine.

And this is the intention of **Alphidius** <note>An early Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval European texts.</note>: And this projection can be repeated many times upon a perfect body, or upon raw Mercury: and finally upon an imperfect body <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper.</note>: and then without a doubt it is converted into that metal upon which the medicine was first projected. And this **Raymond** <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully, a philosopher and major figure in alchemical legend.</note> seems to approve in his letter. 

The possibility of this multiplication is argued from these facts: that all the philosophers say the medicine perfectly transforms a thousand parts of raw Mercury or of an imperfect body into the nature, substance, and property of the true Sun, as the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a highly influential alchemical treatise.</note> asserts. Moreover, a perfect body receives the impression of the medicine better because it is purer and more fixed <note>Stable and resistant to evaporation under heat.</note> by its own nature: therefore it will be possible to make [it] from another body through the most perfect medicine. 

And again, it appears from this: because **Hamis** says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages.</note>: If one part of the medicine is projected onto ten parts of an imperfect body, the whole is made into medicine. And if again one part of that is projected onto ten other parts of an imperfect body, again the whole is made into medicine, so that one part of that, projected again onto ten other parts of a body, will transmute it into a perfect body: namely, into true gold or silver, according to the quality of the medicine. And this is said reasonably: because to project one part onto a thousand once, and to project [three times...]

### CONCERNING THE STONE

...[to project] one part over ten parts, it comes to the same thing. But to project <note>The act of "throwing" the alchemical powder or medicine into molten metal to cause transformation.</note> one part over a thousand at once will convert an imperfect body <note>original: "corpus imperfectum"; a base metal such as lead or tin.</note> into a perfect body <note>original: "corpus perfectum"; gold or silver.</note>. Therefore, to project it three times will also convert it. From which another point necessarily follows: that projecting the medicine onto a perfect body renders the second medicine more perfect than if it were projected onto an imperfect body. Thus, its efficacy will be shown to convert itself to a greater quality. 

The foundation of this is as follows: because the medicine is of such virtue and efficacy—owing to its spirituality and subtlety—that it suddenly penetrates bodies through their smallest parts. It separates and joins to itself the pure parts—the watery, airy, spiritual, and subtle—while it either consumes or separates the coarse, corruptible, and combustible parts. But this [impurity] does not exist in a perfect body, and especially not in gold, because it has no impure or combustible parts. 

Therefore, the medicine will unite the whole to itself; and consequently, that "second medicine" will be far greater in quantity than a second medicine made from an imperfect body, even if it is not greater in potency and virtue. Know this, however: that the second medicine cannot reach the level of perfection of the first, nor the third to the level of the second, and so on for the others. For as the same **Hamis** <note>Likely referring to an Arabic alchemical authority, possibly Ibn Umayl (Senior Zadith) or a variant of "Hamet."</note> says: 

> Although the medicine joins to itself the airy, spiritual, and subtle parts, it cannot reduce them to such a high degree of spirituality as the medicine itself possesses; for its virtue is weighty, measured, and determined, just like that of other things: and it is spent through the parts of the body in which it is distributed.

Because of this, projection can be repeated so many times that it would eventually no longer have the power of medicine or of conversion. Similarly, if the medicine were projected onto too large a quantity, it would not convert it into a perfect body. For the medicine always does as much as it can; and therefore, the more it is projected, or the greater the mass it is cast upon, the more its virtue is diminished. 

And thus, from one part of the first-degree medicine, a thousand parts of an imperfect body are perfected into a perfect body; but from one part of the third-degree [medicine], only ten parts are perfected. This is because, just as the medicine is led through many alterations from corporality (or coarseness and imperfection) toward spirituality and a most subtle nature, so also, conversely, through many projections, it is led back from spirituality toward the nature of a coarse body, due to the coarse parts with which it is inseparably incorporated. # PHILOSOPHY

Nevertheless, it must be noted that projection <note>The act of casting the alchemical powder or "Medicine" into molten metal to transform it.</note> is more easily accomplished than the creation of the stone itself. For the creation of the medicine is difficult, because the subtle watery element within the matter of the stone is very strongly united with the dry earthy element, and can hardly—if ever—be separated except by the greatest and most subtle skill of the craftsman, and only over a long period of time. 

And yet, such a separation is required for the creation of the medicine; but after this medicine has been created, such separation becomes easy within metal bodies. This is because the medicine, by its spirituality and subtlety, suddenly penetrates these bodies and, by its own heat, alters, digests, and prepares the matter. It perfectly separates and sets apart the pure from the impure, and the subtle from the coarse; it then assimilates the pure, subtle parts into itself and transforms them into its own substance. 

For although the medicine may be smaller in quantity than the body it is altering, it is nevertheless much greater in virtue <note>original: "virtute"; here meaning power, potency, or inherent strength.</note>. Therefore it overcomes the body, yet it cannot fully assimilate it; for this reason, it cannot strongly separate the coarser and earthy parts from the mixed airy ones, and thus the virtue of the medicine is diminished during the act of projection. 

And yet, here is one of the greatest secrets: the virtue of the medicine can actually be increased even during projection—not only in its physical quantity, but also in the power of its perfection and goodness. This occurs if, for instance, the medicine is projected upon a body in the proper proportion, and the whole is placed in the fire and increased through its proper degrees <note>The "degrees of fire" refer to regulated stages of heat, from gentle to intense.</note>, being frequently dissolved and frequently congealed, until it flows more easily than wax. 

For in this way, with the virtue of the medicine performing the "digestion" and the heat providing the movement, the whole is gradually sublimated and entirely transformed into a spiritual nature. Therefore, if the medicine were so weakened during projection that it no longer possessed "ingress" <note>original: "ingressum"; the technical ability of the alchemical agent to penetrate and permeate the "pores" of a metal.</note>, ingress is restored to it if a portion of the "first medicine" <note>The original, most potent form of the Philosopher's Stone before it was diluted by projection.</note> is joined to it and cooked, by dissolving and congealing it until it flows. 

However, the smaller the virtue of the medicine, the more temperate a fire one must administer from the beginning and through the necessary stages of time. But if nothing of that first and most perfect medicine remained to be added, one would have to proceed differently; the ingenious craftsman, however, must take the greatest care that this does not happen to him. This is because it suffices to have composed the stone only once, and it is not necessary to repeat the primary work again. For the medicine, once brought to its philosophical absolute, is infinitely multipliable.

Furthermore, there is a third method, as the *Rosarius* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a highly influential 16th-century alchemical text.</note> suggests: that a certain part of the medicine, whether white or red, be joined to the stone or...

## *Recapitulation of the whole work, with the conclusion of its sealing.*

# CHAPTER XXXIII and the last.

The sum of the whole work, or our final intention and goal, is nothing else than this: that the stone already known from the previous chapters be taken, and with the persistence of the work, the greatest industry of the first degree of sublimation <note>Sublimation: the process of vaporizing a solid to purify it from "corrupting" heavy elements.</note> be applied to it, so that it may be thoroughly changed from its corrupting impurity. Then, secondly, its addition should be sublimated with the dissolved stone itself—that is, the ferment of white and red sulfur—until it reaches the final mode of sublimation (meaning its most subtle and pure state), and finally becomes volatile, or spiritual. From this point, thirdly, let it be fixed by the method of fixation, until it remains stable even in the harshness of the fire. But the work is not yet complete in the "white" stage, as a certain Poet says:

> *Yet this is not the end; this is not the goal of our labors.* <note>original: "Non tamen hic finis, non est ea meta laborum." A quote from Vergil's Aeneid, often used in alchemical texts to warn that the silver stage is not the final objective.</note>

Although the goal of preparation consists in this one thing (as Geber <note>Geber: the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says), therefore finally and fourthly, let the fixed become volatile, and again the volatile become fixed by the method of sublimation and solution. This solution and coagulation must be reiterated so many times until the substance flows more [easily] than wax, and transforms [metal] into a certain white or red <note>original: "lunificico & solifico"; literally 'Moon-making' (silver) and 'Sun-making' (gold).</note> perfection. This is the final completion of the preparation and of perfection. And this indeed is our Philosophical Stone—a composite both natural and artificial—which performs the most precious secrets of nature in this lower world. These are beyond all price and incomparable to the riches of Kings; they are indeed revealed only to the upright and the faithful, and not to the wicked, the faint-hearted, the idle, or to tyrants, who [act] against the Creator's...

## CONCLUSION.

Many have published books about this **Blessed Stone** <note>original: "lapide Benedicto"</note>, and they have intermingled falsehoods with truths, and sophistry with genuine knowledge. While they strove to hide this most noble art from the wicked—lest they cause harm to themselves or inflict damage upon others—they have simultaneously led the good along with the evil into wandering errors and the countless waste of person, property, and time. This, however, is permitted to no one. But here, the mastery of the stone has been expressed most clearly and openly: no error has been set down, and no falsehood joined to it. Indeed, here all errors and falsehoods are clarified and cast out. 

Truly, one must know that this work is dedicated solely to God, the creator of all, and to Christ, the redeemer of all. Therefore, whoever desires to possess it, to understand its possession, and to fulfill that understanding, let him first study his own salvation, and then the common good and the benefit of God’s most holy Church. If he does not do this, let him know most certainly that he will be most severely punished and condemned, both here and in the world to come, by the Holy Trinity and by Christ, the true and just judge of all the living and the dead. 

Study, therefore, and apply yourself diligently to the best authors, for "day unto day utters speech" <note>A reference to Psalm 19:2, implying that wisdom is revealed continuously over time.</note>, "book opens book," and "night unto night shows knowledge." Try, experiment without weariness, ask, knock, and gradually gird yourself with a great fervor of patience and charity, if you desire to reach the highest investigation of mastery and the longed-for perfection. 

Finally, in your virtue, be such a person as you desire the stone itself to be. You are imperfect; pant after the perfection that is due. You are foul and unclean; purge yourself with tears. **Sublimate** yourself through morals and virtues; adorn and **color** <note>term: Color. In alchemy, "coloring" or "tincturing" refers to the final transformative power of the stone to change the nature of a substance.</note> yourself with sacramental graces. Make your soul sublime and subtle through the contemplation of heavenly things, conforming it to the angelic spirits, so that it may be able to quicken <note>term: Quicken. To bring to life or animate.</note>, whiten <note>term: Whiten. Referring to the "albedo" or whitening stage of the work, representing purity.</note>, and make incorruptible, immortal, and entirely impassible <note>term: Impassible. Incapable of suffering, decay, or being affected by external pain.</note> this rotten body and vile ash, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord. Thus, finally illuminated by the divine vision and bathed in ineffable light, the soul [may make] its own body, though resurrected, eter-

## RIDDLE OF THE PHYSICAL STONE BY
->Lorenzo Ventura, Venetian Doctor<-

*In India, the hottest part of the world,*
*A stone is sometimes born that encloses within itself*
*Infinite virtues, which come from heaven:*
*It is called Pantheora <note>Pantheora: Likely derived from the Greek for "all-divine" or "all-seeing," a poetic name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, though in common sight*
*It is held by many to be worthless and foolish.*
*The Chosen ones, and those who know*
*Nature's high secrets, are accustomed to extract its blood*
*By a craftsmanship second to none.*
*And because within it there is Mercury and sulfur,*
*Gold and Silver—not those of the common crowd <note>original: "del volgo"; alchemists distinguished between "vulgar" metals used for currency and the "philosophical" versions required for the Great Work.</note>,*
*But a celestial humor, hot and oily,*
*With its subtle earthiness, cold and dry,*
*Bound together in a marvelous way.*
*Soul, spirit, and body, four and one:*
*Here, with the gift of God, goodness and patience,*
*Toil, industry, fire, and a long time,*
*The substance rises from the weighted-down,*
*Foul body, and makes it clear and shining;*
*The art darkens and clears those things*
*Many times over, until, well-united,*
*The light and the heavy, the rare and the dense,*
*Stand exposed to the great martyrdom of Vulcan <note>Vulcan: The Roman god of fire; here representing the intense and purifying heat of the alchemical furnace.</note>:*
*This is called Elixir, and a medicine*
*That heals every "leper" <note>leproso: In alchemical literature, "leprosy" is a metaphor for the impurities and corrosion found in base metals like lead or iron.</note>, and transforms imperfect*
*Metal and the human body miraculously.*
*This makes a man rich, makes him happy,*
*Content and joyful in himself, and tranquil,*
*Filled with virtue and kindled charity,*
*Until the very last day of his years.*
*Wherefore we must [give thanks] forever to the great Monarch,*
*First Cause and Mover of nature.*

# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGU-
### RELLO.

<note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524) was a renowned Renaissance humanist. His poem *Chrysopoeia*, dedicated to Pope Leo X, is one of the most famous Latin works blending alchemical theory with classical poetic style.</note>

Come then, mortals, behold this Light brought forth from the shadows, and turn your steps away from blind paths. Forbid such great wickedness, and drive away the deadly poison by which the sluggish crowd <note>original: "vulgus iners"; alchemists often used this term to disparage "puffers" or common laborers who sought wealth without the necessary spiritual and philosophical foundation.</note> thinks it can lay its hands upon the **Divine Art**—an art which is able to look upon the secrets of things and causes so deeply hidden. 

Let the greedy fraudster not touch this with impure hands, nor the bankrupt spendthrift; nor anyone who is skilled only in mechanical craft, nor the soft man whose heart is set on idle ruin; nor the wandering merchant, nor the citizen devoted only to the city; nor he who bends over the earth to till the fields. And especially let him not touch it who threatens many and great things in his mind, or anyone accustomed to seeking such things from the crowd through evil fraud alone, or simply out of the love of possession. 

But let the wise man, who above all worships the powers above, and who finds joy only in knowing causes to their depths, come here; let him follow this art with all his strength. As his companion, there shall cling a serious exploration of things, everywhere observing the innermost footprints of nature. Then delay shall follow, slowing down his anxious paths, and steadfast patience shall one day see the end. 

Soon labor and industry, guiding noble steps, will not be absent; he shall carry a glass vessel—indeed, one single vessel, one single work <note>original: "unum opus"; a core hermetic principle stating that the "Great Work" requires only one vessel and one fundamental substance to reach completion.</note>—and finally he shall bring with him one single thing. Therefore, surrounded by such a company, he will enter upon the long journey, and traversing all things with a slow step, he will continually feed his eyes and mind on wonderful discoveries, and the things he sees will beguile his constant labor, until he reveals the treasures hidden in the secret earth: an unknown weight of silver and gold.

### *Alchemy speaking of herself.*

I am the heavenly radiance of angelic wisdom, the strength of the soldier, the goal of the world’s machine <note>original: "mundialis machinæ"; a common Renaissance term for the universe viewed as a divinely ordered mechanism.</note>, the most excellent work of royal glory, set above all the sciences of this world; I am the secret of God, the breath of life <note>original: "spiraculum"; often implying divine inspiration or the "breath" that gives life to matter.</note>, the sister of philosophy, the favor of Kings, the power of lords, the sweat of the Prophets <note>meaning the fruit of their intense labor and striving.</note>, the envy of philosophers, an incomparable treasure, a mirror of joy, the flight of sadness, the mother of virtues, and the footprint of human nature. Therefore, let those who should be rejected be cast out, and let the righteous be justified unto the better: let my voice, a saving joy, be heard only in the dwellings of the righteous. Therefore, evil sinners, the lewd, the greedy, and the wasteful must be cast out, lest through these secrets of secrets—overflowing with madness—they proceed to commit even worse outrages.

Ruling, I shall rule, and my kingdom shall have no end for all those who come to me and perceive me healthfully, skillfully, and with constancy.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliate scrollwork and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>GOLD, which was once valued so highly, and which we now see valued so highly everywhere, has often come to my mind, my wife, to understand through more exact discussion for what reason it has inserted such an extraordinary estimation of itself into human minds, and having inserted it, has fixed it so tenaciously. For on one hand, I saw it was usually sought with such care and such superfluous effort that it was deservedly said by ancient authors of the Latin language to have drawn its name from "turning away" the minds of men <note>original: "ab auertendis mentibus"; Pico is likely referencing a folk etymology where *aurum* is derived from *a-vertendo* (turning away) and *rum* (corrupted from *mens* or *ratio*). Such moralizing etymologies were common in the Renaissance to suggest that gold distracts the soul from higher things.</note>; and it is sought and guarded with such zeal that it rightly gave the Greeks a reason to suspect its name was derived <term>from "seizing" or "keeping"</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰρεῖν" (apo tou airein). The author suggests a Greek origin for the concept of wealth based on the act of taking or guarding.</note>, because it is guarded above all other things, and from that the word for "treasure" was formed. On the other hand, although gold might perhaps seem useful, it was in no way necessary by its own nature, but only through the conspiracy <note>In this context, "conspiracy" (conspiratio) refers to a "breathing together" or a universal human agreement/social contract, rather than a plot.</note> of mortals did my mind—ever eager for the truth—proceed further. And first of all, I always remembered that gold had not been set over other things—not only metals, but all other external goods—by the consensus of nations. For I was not at all persuaded that either the express or tacit agreement of all ages judged that gold itself should be preferred to other things which are called "external." Indeed, in the earliest times of man’s creation, there is no mention of gold; rather, it is recorded in the most ancient literary monuments that men led their lives for many ages without gold. Nor were there lacking those who wrote that gold was discovered by Aeacus <note>In Greek mythology, Aeacus was a king of Aegina; some traditions credit him with the discovery of gold or the first coining of money.</note> shortly before the times of Troy, and silver...

...by the Indo-Scythian King, and those who have attributed the discovery to Thoas and Eaclus, or to Erichthonius; some to the Sun, others to Vulcan, and even some to Chryso. Hippocrates was of this last opinion, believing that **gold** <note>original: "τὸν χρυσὸν" (ton chryson)</note> was named after its inventor <note>Chryso is a legendary figure whose name is the root for the Greek word for gold, *chrysos*.</note>. I was also aware of the tradition that gold was not used in Europe—and its smelting even less so—before the time of the Phoenician Cadmus <note>Cadmus was the legendary founder of Thebes, credited with bringing the alphabet and mining to Greece.</note>.

What of the fact that even when the power of the Greeks was growing and flourishing, so much gold could not be scraped together from all of Greece (as Athenaeus reports) that the head of the Amyclaean Apollo could be gilded? Such was its rarity, and at the same time its high cost, in the time of King Philip of Macedon, that he considered himself lucky to possess a single golden vial—and a tiny one at that—which he would hide under his pillow. This is if Duris of Samos <note>A Greek historian from the 4th century BCE known for colorful anecdotes.</note> told the truth in his records; I am surprised that Pliny attributed this habit of Philip to extreme extravagance when he was criticizing Philip’s golden cup.

The Greeks were so far from worshipping this metal that they even forbade its use by law. It is clearly known from history that Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note> both stood firm and grew without gold or silver coins, only to falter and collapse when, under the general Lysander, it allowed in the golden spoils from captured Athens.

Plato also agreed, for in his *Laws* he prohibited any private citizen from possessing gold, and he had decreed the same for silver. Perhaps he remembered that the use of silver and gold was once extremely rare in Greece, and was usually seen only in temples. It was found only in the form of tripods and small statues, which were first dedicated by the Kings of Lydia, Gyges and Croesus, and later by the Sicilian Tyrants. It was only later, when the Phocians plundered the temple at Delphi, that this metal began to be spread throughout Greece by any means possible.

Furthermore, to lower the perceived value of gold, I recalled that among the Hebrews, despite the abundance of metals, a type of bronze was found that was more precious than gold—at least if Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> reported the truth in the seventh and eleventh books of his *Antiquities*.

It also came to memory that histories record how, in Italy itself, Spartacus <note>The leader of the famous slave revolt against Rome.</note> forbade anyone in his camp from having gold or silver. Even after the passing of countless centuries, it has persisted among some nations of Asia and Africa that some value gold very little, while others hold it as nothing at all. Even in India, which is thought to be the most fertile land for gold—if we speak of the part conquered by Alexander the Great—we learn from the Greek historians of his deeds that there was no gold there. However, after plundering Persia, the King himself obtained so much gold that to transport it there were hardly enough mule-

### CHAPTER II.

*That gold should not be held in such high esteem based on utility derived from its natural properties.*

I considered of very little weight the argument by which some have tried to persuade common folk: that gold is of the greatest use to mortals. On the contrary, I would put forward iron, without which neither Agriculture—an art no less necessary than common—could exist; and as Xenophon <note>An ancient Greek historian and philosopher who wrote extensively on household management and economy.</note> says, it is the mother and nurse of all arts. Without iron, the Art of Building cannot be properly raised, nor the Art of Navigation clearly maintained—to say nothing of the Military Art, which, although it harms some, does not harm everyone. I was immediately supported by that famous half-line of verse: "Gold is more harmful than iron" <note>original: "ferroque nocentius aurum"; a reference to Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* describing the decay of the world into the Iron Age.</note>, and another similar saying: "In times of war, iron is more welcome than gold."

Related to this was the praise given to the fact that gold has been torn apart with insults by all the best men and was discovered for the ruin of life. Then I also recalled how antiquity both wondered at gold and was indignant toward it at the same time: that it once held it in high regard, while it sought to mock this through the fable of Midas <note>The mythological king who turned everything he touched into gold and nearly starved because he could not eat; a classic allegory for the futility of wealth.</note>, to whom a heaped mass of gold provided no solid help for life at all. Furthermore, its use in the exchange of goods may not have been a strong enough reason to value gold so highly, since the most ancient kings did not mint gold and silver, but clearly bronze <note>original: *æs*</note>. Saturn is said to be the inventor of this practice, from whom the treasury <note>original: *ærarium*, derived from *æs* (bronze/copper).</note> is named; this was the view of Caecilius Cyprianus <note>Saint Cyprian, an early Christian writer and bishop.</note>. However, others write that the first to mint coins was Janus <note>The two-faced Roman god of beginnings and transitions.</note>, a contemporary and host of Saturn, who stamped on the coins the ship in which Saturn had been carried. Among the Romans too, a mark was first stamped on bronze, then on silver, and some years later on gold; since Servius, the first of the seven Roman kings <note>Specifically, Servius Tullius, the sixth king of Rome, credited with many administrative reforms.</note>, stamped a mark on bronze; the consul Fabius was the first to do so for silver; and soon gold was also minted.

### CHAPTER III.

*That the superior estimation of gold does not depend on medicine.*

Now, regarding the medical properties that were being gathered by me—certain common dialectical arguments <note>original: *Epicheremata*</note> against my own position—drawn from afar, both from the joy gold brings and from the help it gives to the bodily temperament...

### IOAN. FR. MIRAND.
360

I also drew arguments from that same faculty: for that joy derived from heaps of gold coins lasts only as long as the mind realizes that other things which please it can be acquired by the spending of those coins. However, this is a property of the imagination, of thought, and of the mind—not of the bodily temperament, which springs from coarse and dreg-filled matter. Added to this is the fact that there are many things said to be more beneficial to the human bodily temperament, and even more highly praised by the ancient physicians for reviving life and providing sufficient strength, which we can obtain much more easily and at less expense. For no metals provide nourishment, *as is accepted among the older Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who believed that only organic substances could be converted into living tissue.</note>. They cannot be digested in such a way *as to be turned into flesh and blood.* This has also been proven by the experiences of those who, struck by the storms of war and the devastation of regions, hiding themselves in underground caves, swallowed gold coins like pills <note>original: "instar Catapotij"; catapotia were medicinal boluses or pills meant to be swallowed.</note> to hide them; soon they found them [excreted] by their own weight and with their color unchanged.

And if by chance any bit was lost or consumed along with its innate color, it was certainly very little. Otherwise, it would have been an excellent remedy for life for the Jews fleeing to Titus Caesar while Jerusalem was under siege, if gold were digested so that it nourished those who swallowed it. For they would not have been cut open by the most greedy Syrians and Arabs <note>Pico refers to the mercenary forces assisting the Romans during the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> to find the gold they had previously sent down into their bellies; the number of these victims was so huge that in one night the intestines of two thousand men were sliced open, an event of which Josephus is the author and Hegesippus the confirmer <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian; "Hegesippus" refers to a 4th-century Latin adaptation of Josephus's works which was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>.

Thus, for those wretched people, gold coins were stored in the stomach as if in a chest; they were not taken to endure hunger, since [if they were food] they would have been diffused through the whole body and transformed like other foodstuffs. Furthermore, gold does not soothe with its scent, nor does its flavor nourish those vapors which rise from human bodies, called "spirits" <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle substances that mediated between the soul and the physical body.</note> by physicians. Indeed, all metals have an unpleasant taste and a sulfurous smell; therefore, they cannot fail to be harmful in some way to those who are lying ill—far from being able to retain the departing soul with their charm. There exists the opinion of Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher famous for his work on minerals and alchemy.</note>, stated generally, that the tastes and smells of all metals are in some way foul, although there is as little stench in gold as there is little odor, because of the bonding of sulfur in its [the metal's] temperament...

...of its own exquisite subtlety. However, there are things that are helpful not only to the sense of smell, but even more to the sense of taste, for the healthy and sick alike, and they are sold at a lower price than gold. Truly, when it came to mind, I recalled that Pliny once wrote that gold is applied to wounds, and to infants to protect against sorcery <note>original: "veneficia," which refers to poisoning, sorcery, or the "evil eye."</note> so they might be less harmed, and that it brings aid to several others. Yet it did not escape my memory that many more condemnations of gold than praises were written by that same Pliny (if his great judgment could carry weight with us). I also remembered he committed to his pages that there is a certain poison <term>virus: a potent or harmful quality</term> in gold; and especially that he published this concluding thought: "for whom is there medicine for the sake of digging?" <note>Pliny’s point is that we mine for profit, not for health; medicine is not the reason we pull metals from the earth.</note> If he does not exclude gold from medicine later, it was certainly done by the authority of others, as is his constant habit.

For he cites Varro, a man of that age; yet Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the standard medical text for 1,500 years.</note>, the preeminent authority on medical materials, brought forward no experiments for any medicine made from gold. <note>The 'p' in 'ptulit' likely stands for 'protulit' [produced/offered].</note> I said that Dioscorides lived in the age of Varro, following the common opinion and the records of Suidas, although I know there are those who prefer to think Dioscorides lived in the age of Pliny because of the mention of Lecanius Bassus. But I wish they had noticed that Dioscorides also lived in the time of Arrius, to whom he dedicated a volume on simple medicine—I mean Arrius the Alexandrian, not the one whom Catullus mocks for his speech <note>The Roman poet Catullus wrote a famous poem mocking a man named Arrius for mispronouncing words by adding "h" sounds where they didn't belong.</note>; nor the one who, as a bitter enemy of our religion, most stubbornly <note>'per' indicated by a stroke through the 'p'</note> hurled blasphemies against Christ the Lord <note>Referring to Arius, the priest whose teachings led to the Arian controversy in the early Church.</note>. Rather, he was the Arrius who was held in great honor by Augustus Caesar after the victory over Antony and Cleopatra. But whether Dioscorides was older than Pliny or his contemporary seems to matter little. Varro was certainly consumed by the triumviral proscription, and Dioscorides himself flourished under Antony the Triumvir, from whom thereafter Greece, Italy, and the foreign lands received their medical knowledge; and we grant this to the former opinion. To the latter opinion, we note that there is mention of a Dioscorides in Pliny, whether an older one, a near contemporary, or, if you prefer, an exact contemporary.

Truly, whatever century this Dioscorides belonged to, he handed down many remedies in their own chapters for mercury, copper, iron, and lead—but not for gold. He hardly even mentions it regarding mercury <term>hydrargyrum: "water-silver," the ancient term for quicksilver or mercury</term>, except for this reason: if it should be swallowed and cause harm, gold shavings may help; and this is mentioned during his treatment of medical materials. Furthermore, while he discusses poisons, he says that pure wine in which glowing gold has been quenched resists aconite <note>A highly toxic flowering plant, also known as monkshood.</note>; but he says this is not unique to gold, but is a common remedy shared with silver, iron, and iron slag, which are just as powerful, as Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> also notes...

# GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
<meta>catchword: Explains</meta>

...[he] receives [it] in his discussion on poisons. Galen, who lived much later than Dioscorides, mentions gold neither in his discussion on the power of simple medicines, nor in his work on their composition, as far as I myself can remember. Nor am I unaware that Nicander of Colophon sang in his *Alexipharmaca* <note>A famous Greek didactic poem about antidotes for poisons.</note> that gold or silver is beneficial. However, whether it was because he was a poet, or because he was not held in such high regard by Dioscorides and Galen that his testimony would be cited as legitimate in this cause, or because he writes that silver is just as effective as gold "in a turbid wine-drink" <note>original Greek: "ἐν οἰνήματι θολερῷ" (en oinēmati tholerō)</note>, his word seems to carry little weight. For he means that the liquid is made cloudy by the metal and then drunk. 

Yet, I would not deny that gold possesses some medicinal power; but what a tiny portion, I ask, will be found if we compare it to the innumerable other things in which there is the power of healing and driving away poisons? Let the judgment regarding silver be the same. 

But if gold brings no help to medical skill, and contributes nothing to pleasure, then whence, I ask, comes that common accumulation of so many vessels, whether of gold or silver, gathered through so much labor? It seems that a table set with at least silver vessels is intended to signify nobility. Yet Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer.</note>, in his eighth book, when discussing waters at the conclusion, showed that there is a defect in lead, and that for this reason waters are tainted by lead pipes; he plainly added that a "silvery taste" <note>likely referring to a metallic tang or the way metal affects flavor</note> is usually avoided. Even those who had tables piled high with silver vessels were nevertheless accustomed to use earthenware <term>fictilia: vessels made of baked clay or pottery</term> for the sake of the integrity of the taste. 

Many princes of our own time certainly agree with this. Setting aside silver cups and dishes for table use, they prefer for the cleanliness of their courses earthenware vessels brought from India, Ethiopia, and Egypt. If these are lacking, they prefer "Prusian" ware brought from Bithynia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey famous for its pottery.</note>, even though these princes were not born of potter parents—as the poet sang of Agathocles <note>The Tyrant of Syracuse (317–289 BC), who was famously the son of a potter and preferred pottery to gold to remember his humble origins.</note>, who for that reason preferred Samian vessels <note>A type of high-quality red Roman pottery.</note> to silver ones. 

Furthermore, the Triumvir [Mark] Antony—who, according to Messalla, used nothing but gold for all his obscene needs—is reported not to have longed for the taste of gold. Poppaea, the wife of Nero, seems to have rejected the common use of it as well, though she did put shoes made of gold on her more noble horses. 

I am not unaware that the Arab physicians recorded that gold, although it does not provide nourishment, nevertheless soothes the eyes. I would add an imaginary power to this, once the reasoning is explained: should gold be valued so highly that it becomes the measure of all things? Shall I believe, by some natural reasoning, that it brings aid to a "trembling of the heart" <note>A historical term for palpitations or anxiety.</note> in any way? For it does not follow, as we were saying before, that those words of Nicander should be seen as entirely in vain.

<summary>Pico argues that gold's medicinal value is negligible compared to other remedies and notes that many ancient authorities and modern princes prefer pottery over silver or gold for dining to preserve the taste of food.</summary>

# ON GOLD. BOOK I.

## CHAPTER IV.

### That the principal nobility of this metal does not depend upon potable gold.

I touch upon these things not by way of decreeing a final judgment, but through the process of discussion, since some are said to use "potable gold" <note>original: "potabili auro"; a legendary medicinal elixir consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid, believed to cure all diseases and grant longevity.</note> to remove all ailments, maintain health, and prolong life as far as the powers of nature allow. Truly, while I would not flatly deny this, I would assert that it can be called into controversy by those who excel in the skill of disputation. They might perhaps say it is well enough established among those who prescribe gold that the metal itself is not strictly "drunk," but rather a subtler and purer portion of it, designated by the name of a "joined essence."

But concerning this <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the "fifth essence" or element, distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, water, air, fire), believed by alchemists to be the life-force of matter.</note> of the celestial bodies, many wars have been fought between the greatest leaders of philosophy, whose soldiers still clash today. As to who claimed the victory, the Platonists and the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> schools certainly do not agree. The Platonists contend that the leader of the Peripatetics [Aristotle] merely wished for that "fifth nature" rather than proved it, and that his arguments have no strength unless five specific suppositions are admitted. Furthermore, if such a nature is not granted to the heavens when they are investigated, shall it be granted to those things beneath the heavens which are formed from the four elements? 

For whether they have gathered "potable gold" from honey, or from sulfur and <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyro"</note>, or from the water of distilled wine <note>Possibly referring to *aqua vitae* or brandy used as a solvent.</note>, or from some secret earth, or if you prefer, from some most noble kind of <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "chalcanthi"; a sulfate mineral often used in alchemical preparations.</note> refined through many stages, they will admit that a subtler power is extracted from it; but they do not agree that a "quintessence" is extracted. If they wish to claim its existence based on its elemental effects—which they will claim cannot be found within it—the answer will be ready: they may contend that these practitioners offer an appearance instead of the reality. They will attribute these effects to various concurring causes that have been brought together and refined, effects which other substances are also able to produce. 

Furthermore, even if they grant this to the Peripatetics for free, how will they avoid contradicting another of their dogmas—namely, that living creatures do not draw life from metals? But just as they leave the dispute to be settled by physicians quarreling among themselves, so they will assert that whatever methods for making potable gold they have considered to this day, these do not actually achieve the drinking of gold "by itself." For it is clear that they usually reduce the gold into ash—or if they prefer to call it <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery substance (oxide) left after a metal has been heated or "calcined."</note>—which is done in many ways, so much so that if you wished to restore it to its original form, you either could not do so at all, or only with great difficulty, since the moisture has departed. If you remove that moisture entirely,

GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...you have taken up gold. It is a decree of Aristotle and Theophrastus that a certain moisture exists in all metals such that their nature is established by it, and they are clearly distinguished from the nature of stones.

Therefore, they themselves will add that gold is not drunk, but rather a portion of that thing which was gold is dissolved in an external liquid. This liquid possesses the power, while softening and thinning the <term>calx</term> <note>original: "calcem"; the powdery substance remaining after a metal has been burned or "calcined," a common step in alchemical preparations.</note> of the gold, to extract something that can be drunk. They make similar promises regarding gemstones, though there is no one who does not know that these cannot properly be drunk. If the defenders of this practice say that gold melts in other ways, the opponents would not deny it, but they would assert that this happens either through "consuming waters" <note>original: "aquis consumptricibus"; likely a reference to strong mineral acids like *aqua regia*.</note> with the addition of various kinds of salt, or through "biting juices," so that force is applied to the gold. In this way, the gold is removed from its natural seat which nature had granted it; therefore, they contend that the gold acquires nothing that would make it more pure for the purpose of nourishing human nature. For if you mention the nature of gold in itself, it will not be suitable for nutrition, as was previously deduced from the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> school. If you speak of its nature when mixed, they will also say that, in their judgment, it will no longer be gold. Indeed, it is well known that the liquid being offered is that which has flowed drop by drop from glass vessels while vapors, carried on high by the heat of fire, are turned into water, and other things are mixed in which are sought from other branches of medical faculty. Indeed, if that is considered "drinking gold" or "drinking gems," why should those people not also be said to "drink excrement" who drink wine produced from soil made fertile for that task by a diverse heap of manure?

I have argued the case for those who would wish to disparage <term>potable gold</term> <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary medicinal elixir.</note>, though I myself would prefer to gather it, and I would wish it could be exceptionally useful for the health of our body and others. This is especially true since it is well established that Antonius, our surgeon, in recent years restored a matron from <term>Forum Cornelii</term> <note>Modern-day Imola, Italy.</note> who was dying of <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "phthisi"; a historical term for pulmonary tuberculosis.</note> to her former health. She was freed from the wasting disease itself in just a few days, using only potable gold, which he had prepared from the teaching of his uncle Nicolaus (who will be mentioned in the third book). I intend to have a more extensive discussion on this matter in those volumes I have titled *On the Remedies for Poisons*, which are still <term>under the anvil</term> <note>original: "sub incude"; a Latin idiom meaning a work is still being refined or is not yet finished.</note>. But even if gold were collected and given as a drink for health, would such great nobility of gold, and such a hunger and madness for seeking it, flow from that? Since one pound of this metal dissolved into liquid could heal not just one King, but an entire region, and among a thousand myriads of mortals, you would hardly find fifteen men who [have] potable gold...

# CHAPTER V.

## *That neither the purity nor the durability of gold is properly the reason why it is held in such high esteem by men.*

Now, if it is believed that purity has won for gold its chief authority, let us consider whether a fallacy underlies this matter; for indeed, gold both gets dirty and stains less strongly than other metals, yet it still stains and soils those who handle it because of the sulfur which is mixed with it—not only in its qualities but in its very substance. This was recorded in the writings of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and Dominican friar who wrote "De Mineralibus," a key text on mineralogy and alchemy.</note> and is proven by experience; hence, perhaps, among the Egyptians, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with the origins of alchemy (Hermeticism).</note> described gold by the name of sulfur. I ask you, is the purity of glass not greater than that of gold? It was for this reason that a certain Roman prince <note>A reference to an anecdote found in Pliny and Petronius: an inventor presented "flexible glass" to the Emperor (usually identified as Tiberius). The Emperor allegedly had the man executed, fearing that if glass could be hammered like metal, it would become more valuable than gold and devalue the imperial treasury.</note> feared that if glass could be made flexible, as it had begun to be, and if it had continued to withstand the hammer, it would have snatched the first rank away from gold and closed off the path for all other metals in commerce.

But its durability is celebrated; yet let it come to mind that stones are more durable and held at a higher price—stones which feel neither the file nor the fire, nor do they contract any dross at all, nor do they stain those who handle them with grime, which cannot be avoided if you rub gold for a long time. But gold is melted, while stones are not; is this not common to all metals? Since metals were accepted for the use of coinage <note>original: "numismatum"</note> so that they might serve as guarantees in the exchange of goods, gold was once placed after copper and silver in this regard. This seems to detract from its charm and its utility. For we know, as we previously hinted and as is recorded in literary monuments, that copper <note>original: "æs"; in early Roman history, this refers to bronze or copper currency.</note> was first stamped at Rome by King Servius, and that the Roman people did not even use stamped silver before the war with Pyrrhus, about six hundred years after the founding of the city. Since a mark was placed on that metal under the consulship of Fabius, and soon after on gold (more than sixty years having elapsed), that same people commanded defeated Carthage and other nations to pay tributes in silver, not in gold. Thus, not only the durability of the metal, but even its use, cannot be the primary cause of its value; for both stamped copper and stamped silver were considered even more enduring among foreign nations. Thus the Transalpine Gauls described stamped money by the common name of "silver"—which was valued less by the prince of philosophers, Plato, who indeed brought a law regarding it, which he insti- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("instituerat"), likely referring to Plato’s "Laws," where he suggests banning gold and silver for common citizens to prevent greed.</note>

<summary>Giovanni Francesco Pico argues that gold's value is not based on inherent physical superiority, noting that glass is purer and stones are more durable. He provides a historical overview of Roman currency to show that copper and silver were historically more significant for commerce than gold.</summary>

### CHAPTER VI.

## *That brightness is not the reason why gold surpasses other things in value, whether because it charms the eyes, or because it is not worn down and is expanded.*

But, one might say, the sweet color of gold delights the eyes. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> denied this and preferred silver to it in luster, as silver is more similar to daylight and to military standards, because its familiar brightness shines from a further distance. Nor did he think gold was preferred to other metals because of its likeness to the stars, since even in gems and other things that color is not the most excellent. He was far from preferring it above all else for the color of the dawn (*aurora*), from which some were pleased to believe the name gold (*aurum*) originated. Why he believed nomenclature was the cause is a mystery, when he could easily have discovered that good authors were not displeased by the idea that the word was transferred from the language of the Sabines <note>An ancient Italic tribe.</note>, who used to say *ausum*, with only one letter being changed. 

Whatever the case may be, silver delighted Pliny's eyes more than gold; if he truly felt what he wrote in this matter, he cannot be faulted. However, he clearly deserves criticism when he reported that gold is surpassed in weight by lead; for the experiments of later generations cry out against this <note>Gold is significantly denser than lead; Pico is noting a scientific error in Pliny’s text.</note>. Furthermore, while he judged that very little gold is lost through use, he could have remembered that by the constant rubbing of fingers, both a gold coin and a ring are worn away; and even what is very small is not nothing. 

There were also those who thought that gold suffers no loss from fire, relying on the authority of Aristotle in the third book of the *Meteorology*. This authority is either not solid or not correctly understood; for it is proved by experiments that gold's weight is diminished by a violent and especially long-lasting fire. It has also been recorded in literature and confirmed in our own age that gold vanishes when placed in a fire with a certain mixed powder, which not only city-dwellers but even peasants and their wives can have in abundance. Likewise, it has been found that through a small thing commonly used by men, the yellow color is stripped from gold, and it can never be restored once it has been taken away; the golden color remains in that powder by whose injection the reddish luster [was drawn] from it.

OF GOLD. BOOK I.

...brightness departed. Truly, that gold can be widely expanded and woven into fabrics is a quality it shares in common with silver. Finally, not to wander too far afield, I have found nothing that rests on such a solid foundation that nations could draw from it strong reasons for their desire in valuing gold so highly and seeking it with such greedy thirst—so much so that some, for its sake, cast themselves into hollowed-out mountains; some lower themselves into the deepest pits, which they call shafts; others busy themselves collecting its scraps from rivers; and others sail to the furthest shores of India, either along the sun-scorched coast of the Ethiopian shore, or from the West <note>original: "Zephyrum," the west wind.</note> toward the dawn <note>original: "auroram," the east.</note> to the antipodes. And they do this not even to acquire refined gold <note>original: "aurum obrizum"; Pico notes he is using the Greek term for gold that has been tested and purified by fire.</note>—to use the Greek term—whether processed in ancient times at Colophon <note>An ancient Greek city in Ionia famous for its wealth and its specialized gold-refining processes.</note> or as is now the custom in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ Pariſiorum."</note>, but rather the raw body of gold and its coarse material. Thus, you will not easily find what might satisfy a man eager to understand the nature of things: why there is such a great desire for possessing it, when its utility is not as great as its price—a price by which most men now measure all human things, and would that they had not enclosed divine things under that same measure.

### CHAPTER VII.

#### *That the primary nobility of gold does not depend on the Holy Scriptures.*

Now, neither the value of its esteem nor its durability will depend on the Holy Scriptures; for even if we read there a divine command that many things ought to be made from pure gold for the worship of the Jewish temple and for solemn ceremonies. Likewise, we know what was sung by the Prophet: "there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia" <note>A reference to Psalm 72:15, traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of the Magi bringing gifts to Christ.</note>. Yet we must remember those things which we noted above from the testimony of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Romano-Jewish historian.</note>: that is, that some bronze is better than gold, from which, having been found among the spoils of David, he wrote that Solomon made a vessel in the temple which was called the "Great Sea" <note>The "Brazen Sea" or "Molten Sea," a massive bronze basin used by priests for ritual washing in Solomon's Temple.</note>. We also remember that Ezra, in the time of Xerxes <note>The Persian king; the author refers to Ezra 8:27, which describes vessels of "fine copper, precious as gold."</note>, restored to the treasurers from the priestly class bronze vessels which weighed twelve talents and were valued as better than gold. We ought also to know that under mystical veils, wisdom is signified by gold in the Holy Scriptures, and eloquence by silver; and that the light of intelligence, compared to gold, is more splendid the less it has admitted of earthly dregs—just like the gold which is recorded in literature to be native to Arabia, pure by its own nature without the use of fire, and for that reason called "fireless" <note>original: "apyron"; a Greek term for gold found in nuggets so pure they required no smelting.</note>.

GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...as has been handed down to memory by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note>. Let these matters be touched upon for now—for should I omit how God, in His goodness, as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father known for his eloquence.</note> testifies, lowered Himself to human infirmity in many things that pertained to the common customs of the nations? What of the fact that from those same scriptures you may find the valuation of gold frequently rejected and condemned? Thus, in the Prophet Hosea, they made idols for themselves from their gold <note>Hosea 8:4</note>; thus, Peter the Apostle called gold and silver "corruptible things" <note>1 Peter 1:18</note>; and thus, James wrote that gold had contracted rust <note>James 5:3</note>. Therefore, it should rightly cause no small wonder in the minds of those who are fair judges of things: from where does such great greed arise? In its own nature, gold’s utility is either nonexistent, or small, or certainly not great, since its qualities are found in common with other substances, and it is vastly surpassed by many of the very things that gold is used to measure.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*That the nobility of gold does not depend on the favor it gains for the wearer.*<-

Indeed, who is so dull as to believe that the seekers of gold sought it so that they might gain favor for themselves by wearing it? For it has been recorded in certain chronicles—though they are empty ones—that an ointment was typically prepared from "unfired" gold <note>original: "auro quod nō esset ignem expertum," gold that has not been refined by heat.</note>, the use of which, by the persuasion of the Magi, would supposedly secure favor for those who were also crowned with the gold-flower herb <note>original: "heliochryso," likely the *Helichrysum* or "everlasting" flower, valued for its golden color.</note>. To me, at least, it seems that favor is usually gained by the *giving* of gold, not by the *wearing* of it; in fact, envy is more often stirred up by the gathered heaps of gold coins, so far is it from love and benevolence being spread by them. 

Besides these points, which mortal man so agrees with these magical vanities that he even knows how to prepare that golden ointment, or possesses the skill of its manufacture? How few, whether in antiquity or in our own age, seek gold for such a reason? Furthermore, if one did seek it, where would you find anyone crowned with the gold-flower and anointed with virgin metal <note><term>apyro metallo</term>: Greek for "without fire," referring to native gold found in a pure state that has never been smelted.</note> begging for favor among the common people or through royal courts? 

From where, then, has such a great greed for gold grown, that men—compelled by no evident cause, other than a certain silent, unnecessary, and (would that it were not) destructive conspiracy agreed upon among them—place gold itself before all other things? They are not even content with the flowing mines of Dalmatia <note>A Roman province on the eastern Adriatic coast, famous for its gold mines.</note> or the caverns of Callaecia <note>A region in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula, modern-day Galicia, known in antiquity for its rich mineral deposits.</note>...

ON GOLD. BOOK I.

...and of the torrents <note>original: "torrentiumque"</note> with their golden sands, nor even with those voyages by which gold was sought from as far back as the time of Solomon, has man been content. Instead, he has seen to it that gold be made through art; at home, so many labors have been undertaken for artificial <term>factitio</term> gold, often no fewer or lighter than the voyages and wars many have endured for natural gold. For we see many not only applying their efforts with their hands, so that they may prepare gold from metallic things with the application of fire, but also seeking out innumerable compositions, or searching out the singular opinions of the Philosophers, so that they might fashion gold-bearing powders or stones—whether these be, as the common folk say, "mineral" (though in Latin they ought to be called "metallic"), or "vegetable" (that is, drawn from herbs and plants), or "animal" (that is, drawn from living creatures), or mixed from two or three of these, or fused from common matter, whether of bronze or earth, from which metals, plants, and animals have drawn their origin. 

For I have heard that there is a man still living among us who boasted that he had read eight hundred volumes on this art; furthermore, that he had examined countless notes, so that the number of recipes reached thirty-seven thousand—certainly not so that he might win favor for himself by wearing gold, but so that by gathering together what pleased him, he might become master of his own desires. Such is the industry for possessing gold among mortals, based on either no cause at all, or a weak one, besides the naked and silent consent of wretched mortals.

->IOAN. FR. MIRAND.<-

...or however these desires might be calmed in general, and indeed universally rather than in small parts or details, a non-negligible utility has invited me to write. For it is in the interest of the people of the Commonwealth <note>original: "R. P.", abbreviation for *Res Publica*</note> that they should not be left in doubt when handling matters that are both common and present before the eyes of everyone. *First, we shall indicate the name, then the origin, and finally the power of the art*, as it has been handled far and wide through various schools of literary study.

The art of making gold was called *Chrysopœia* <term>Chrysopoeia: From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make)</term> by the Greeks, and it is still called by that same name by the Latins. However, the art of changing metals in general was called *Chemia* <note>original: "Chemia"</note> by the Greeks, whom the Arabs followed for the most part, calling it *Alchemia* <note>original: "Alchemia", adding the Arabic definite article 'al'</note>. The Greeks defined Chemistry as the preparation for making gold and silver. For although other metals are produced through it, the art obtained its name from the more noble and principal ones, so that it was later called *argyropœia* <term>Argyropoeia: silver-making</term> as well as *Chrysopœia*. 

Some have thought that Chemistry should be named after "juices" <note>Greek *chymos*; the author is discussing whether the word comes from the word for plant juices or from the word for melting</note>, a view with which *Hermolaus Barbarus* <note>An Italian Renaissance scholar (1454–1493)</note> seems to agree. But it is more truly named from "fusing" or "pouring" <note>Greek *cheein*</note>—that is, from the final operation of the art itself. Indeed, the Greek letter Eta <note>original: "H. litera græca"</note>, which among the Latins is usually turned into a long 'E', seems to provide a point of dispute for legal experts regarding the art of casting. It is well established that it can be called the "metallic art," because those who labor at preparing gold and silver are both called "metallists" and are judged useful to the Commonwealth by civil laws; I shall speak more broadly on this matter as the work proceeds. 

Interpreters of the law have preferred to use the common name of "metal," which encompasses more things; they even saw fit to use the word for "bronze" <note>original: "aeris"</note> to indicate gold coins, just as *Ulpian* <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> wrote. I remain silent on the fact that some think the name should be derived from *Alchimus* <note>A legendary figure sometimes associated with the invention of the art</note>, though I believe there is no reason for it. In this regard, I must wonder at *Erasmus* <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous humanist</note>, a man widely versed in letters, for publishing a dialogue titled *Alcumistica* <note>The Alchemist, one of Erasmus's *Colloquies*</note>. I wonder, I say, that he preferred to follow the common folk and did not recognize the article "al" used everywhere by the Arabs, and that he removed the aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note> which should have been included if the name were derived either from "fusing" or from the power of preparing juices. Nor do I wonder any less—indeed far more—at others who cannot be compared to Erasmus, who have written on this matter yet shunned the name, devising instead some unusual vocabulary.

Others have preferred to name Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure often credited with the invention of alchemy and magic.</note> as the founder of the chemical faculty, which was said to be written on certain stone tablets found near the city of Hebron.
