But for my part, as far as I have been able to gather from Greek and Latin authors, I find the art to be very ancient indeed, but appearing a little before the Trojan War; in those most ancient Greek times, mention of it was indicated under the coverings of fables and the clouds of enigmas. Thus Michael Psellus <note>A Byzantine monk and scholar (c. 1017–1078)</note> interprets the command of Eurystheus, who desired the golden apples; thus Jason’s voyage to Colchis is explained in the *Suda* <note>original: "Suidam"; a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, suggesting that the Argonauts did not go to seek a golden fleece of Phryxus, but rather a parchment made of ram's skin on which the faculty of making gold was described. 

Although it does not escape me that Varro <note>A Roman scholar (116–27 BC)</note> attributed this to the fleeces of cattle, and Strabo <note>A Greek geographer (64 BC–24 AD)</note> to the shaggy skins of sheep used to collect gold shavings from rivers, nevertheless the older Greeks preferred it to have been a parchment and not a fleece, nor the shaggy hides of cattle. <margin>A large hand-drawn brace in the right margin encompasses the following six lines.</margin> Among these are Charax, and Apollonius, and later the interpreters of the Colchian voyage and Eustathius. Concerning these matters I shall say more during the telling of the experiments; for the present, let it suffice to have indicated that many authors believed the description of the art of making gold was signified under the cover of the fabulous golden fleece. 

So too do they interpret the "Lamb of Atreus"—for so the Greek tragedy writers speak of it, as do the Latins (whom Cicero mentions), though Seneca calls it a ram, not a lamb—so, I say, some interpret this Lamb or Ram of Atreus to insinuate to readers the described power of making gold. For Callisthenes of Olynthus, both a disciple and kinsman of Aristotle, left it written that the wealth of Atreus and Pelops came from metals. Some wish these riches to be derived from living livestock, following Varro's example; others from a silver bowl <note>original: "phyala"</note> in which an emblem was fixed, so that it contained a lamb <note>original: "arnon"</note> within itself. 

Furthermore, whether the art of making gold was accepted from Greek authors or flowed from the Persians, Egyptians, and other nations considered closer to the rising sun, I have not sufficiently determined; although even among the Persians, Hostanes...

and in Egypt, it is recorded in memory that both Thamus <note>original: "Tamorum"; likely a reference to the Egyptian King mentioned in Plato's *Phaedrus*</note> and Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> wrote on chemical matters, and that the study of gold-making <note>original: "τῆς χρυσοποίας" (chrysopoeia)</note> persisted in Egypt. Olympiodorus of Alexandria, both a Platonist and an interpreter of Aristotle, also wrote on Chemistry; Heliodorus wrote to the Emperor Theodosius; and Stephanus wrote to Caesar Heraclius. I should also mention Africanus, Synesius <note>original: "Cynesium"; a 4th-century Neoplatonist and bishop</note>, Theophilus, and others, as well as Zosimus himself, the Alexandrian philosopher <note>Zosimus of Panopolis, a foundational alchemical author (c. 300 AD)</note>, who composed twenty-eight volumes on the art. The teachings of all these figures are clearly attributed to Democritus, who was a most skillful investigator of nature and blessed with a very long life. For he lived over a hundred years and discovered many things that remained hidden from the common crowd of the literate. He wrote his instructions somewhat obscurely, not because he did not want to be seen as knowledgeable in Chemistry, but so that those instructions would be known only to his followers and friends, and remain unknown to the common people. For this reason, he changed the names of things <note>A common alchemical practice of using "Decknamen" or cover-names</note> so they would be understood only by those who already grasped the subject. On this point, I cannot help but wonder at Hermolao Barbaro <note>A prominent 15th-century Italian humanist and scholar</note>, a man otherwise well-deserving of literature, for condemning this style of writing only in the Democritean school, attributing it either to malice or arrogance. He might have remembered that since ancient times, starting with Homer, different names were given to the same things, and that it was customary for the gods to use some terms and mortals to use others; likewise, the priests of the nations did not use the same vocabulary as the common people. Nor would it have been difficult for him to recall—since I certainly have no doubt he read it—the most praised...

### ON GOLD. BOOK II. ###

...[the first] and foremost rule in every sect that was considered more excellent than others among the philosophers was to conceal their doctrines. This was especially true among the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their communal secrecy and mathematical mysticism</note> and the followers of Heraclitus. For the former used silence and symbols, while the latter, as Plato writes, used riddles <note>original: "ænigmatibus"</note>; and to those who sought an explanation of these riddles, they responded with yet more riddles. Plato also wrapped his doctrines in many veils, himself imitating the Syrians of Palestine, whose custom—according to Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century Church Father and translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>—was to use parables. I will pass over countless other examples by which even a Barbarian might be refuted, lest a handle for defense be taken from the fact that he did not publish a clarifying appendix if he had noted anything too rashly. So highly did those ancient cultivators of wisdom prize the secrets of their philosophy that **they did not want them to become known to the profane or to the common multitude.**

However, after Greece was depopulated and Italy was left desolate by the frequent devastations of barbarian tribes following the decline of the Roman Empire, literature began to be received and cultivated by the Moors and the Arabian peoples. Many volumes of the chemical art <term>chemical art: at this time, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were the same discipline, focused on the transformation of matter</term> were translated into their language. From these, the Moors themselves—especially those who inhabited Baetica <note>original: "Bethicam"; the Roman name for the region of southern Spain now known as Andalusia</note>—compiled books, sparing neither labor nor expense. From this movement, Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath</note>, Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and chemist</note>, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary father of Arabic alchemy</note>, and finally a numerous crowd of Arabian philosophers published volumes on chemical matters.

Some time later, Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century Dominican encyclopedist</note>, Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus, the influential German philosopher and teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note>, and many others followed them. But the celebrated reputation of this faculty, at least in terms of its writings, had almost ceased until Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist from the borderlands of Spain</note> and later Raymond Lull of the Balearic Islands <note>original: "Raymundus Balearicus"; a Majorcan philosopher and mystic</note> raised up the nearly collapsing discipline. Through their many volumes, new discoveries, and public experiments, they made it more illustrious than it had been for several centuries. 

Because of this, anyone who was even slightly educated and practiced in the debates of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> regarding meteorological matters <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology* included theories on how metals formed underground</note>, or anyone slightly more curious in exploring the nature of things, or a bit too eager to make gold, thought the opportunity was not lacking. They devoted themselves to the transmutation of metals, either to learn it or to teach it. Although you will find few among the modern followers of Aristotle who have disputed this art (except for Timon), you will find a vast multitude—exceeding common numbers—who have attempted to confirm the art through completed experiments. For so great was the gathering and...

...everywhere <note>The text begins mid-word: "-tique", likely "undique" or "ubique", meaning "everywhere"</note> these concepts were being flaunted. Because of this, people began to doubt whether the promise of making gold through art should be considered a true skill or a mere deception, especially since the loss of family inheritances was seen to result from these empty promises. From such financial ruin, it was a very easy slide into the crime of counterfeit money <note>original: "furtiuæ monetæ"</note>. For this reason, Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian scholar and diplomat</note> is our authority for the fact that a decree was once issued in Venice forbidding anyone from attempting to make gold. 

For these same reasons, many disputes arose among those who pass judgment on morals according to the Christian rite and who compile great summaries <note>The "Summists," authors of handbooks for confessors regarding what was sinful or permissible</note> concerning what is permitted and what is forbidden. They debated whether the faculty of alchemy should be banned or allowed. As often happens, when the practitioners of a particular doctrine or those conducting a harmful business—which might otherwise be legal—increase in number, they are suppressed. Thus, in ancient times, the Rhetors <note>Teachers of public speaking</note> were fugitives from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, and not only rhetors but also philosophers and physicians were expelled from Rome. 

However, the doubt was not only whether the study and work of gold-making—or *chrysopoeia* <note>original Greek: χρυσοποίας, meaning the art of making gold</note>—should be counted among permitted activities, but also whether it was even possible. Could art provide a complete assistance to nature in the creation of gold? The first question belongs to the censors and priests; the second belongs to the natural philosophers. Furthermore, physicians investigated whether such artificial gold, if it were actually made, would be useful and compatible with human nature. Both princes and the common folk—the unlearned and the educated alike—inquired whether the matter was merely a thing of belief or something proven by experiments, for which they would have witnesses who were not just "ear-witnesses" <note>Those who have only heard rumors</note> but "eye-witnesses." We shall dispute these matters and many others related to them point by point.

[...the Bishop] of Mende <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a famous canonist</note> and his additions to the work celebrated under the name of the *Mirror of Law* <note>original: *Speculum Iuris*, a foundational medieval legal encyclopedia</note> decrees that the legitimate and true art of making gold is useful to the Common Wealth. This opinion was confirmed by Johannes [Andreae], and Oldradus, and Nicolaus of Palermo <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a prominent canon lawyer</note>, and others. Thus, the legal experts and interpreters of Canon Law were persuaded by those earlier laws of Emperor Valentinian, placed in the Code of Justinian, where the subject of miners <note>original: *metallarijs*</note> is discussed. We shall demonstrate in this very volume, when the subject of experiments arises, that these laws were neither properly understood by the ordinary interpreters nor fully corrected by later ones. Perhaps even Accursius of Florence—who added glosses to the civil laws—was persuaded, if indeed any have read his commentaries on the mastery of the art, which I have examined. For he was not content with merely approving the art carefully, but he even set forth its instructions, always signing his name, no differently than if he were interpreting the *Pandects* <note>The *Digest*, a large part of the Roman law collection</note>.

On the contrary, for many reasons, both Giovanni of Liguria and Sylvester of the Order of Preachers <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian</note>, in their books of *Summae* under the title "A", most clearly resisted the arguments of Angelo of Chivasso while attacking him. Finally, Albert concludes in a sufficiently long discourse that those skilled in the metallic art proceed like physicians, whose path is more probable when it leads to the purging of sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note>, and their mixture is properly prepared. Saint Thomas [Aquinas] <note>The most influential theologian of the Middle Ages (1225–1274)</note> in the second part of the second volume of his *Summa Theologiae*, affirms the truth of alchemy <note>original: *Chemicæ veritatem*</note>, a position he had not asserted in his earlier commentary on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook; Aquinas wrote a commentary on it early in his career</note>. For this reason, he has appeared inconsistent to many in this matter, as will become more clearly manifest in the proper place when we openly interpret his opinion.

As far as the present discussion is concerned, Silvester <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1527), a Dominican theologian</note>, a follower of Thomas, is of the same opinion—that gold can be made through art—an opinion which Giovanni [Pico] did not maintain throughout his life. However, Thomas Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major philosopher and cardinal</note> judges in his *Summula* that the art itself is not to be considered illicit in its own right, provided it is practiced without fraud. Nor should the sale of an object produced by the art be numbered among sins, if the sale is conducted properly for what the item actually is.

Truly, in his commentaries on Saint Thomas’s *Summa Theologiae*, he writes that the art is indeed possible, but that it is either not human, or it belongs only to princes once they have consulted the wise. Regarding the power of the art itself, he does not argue sharply, as he is usually accustomed to doing in other questions. Some wonder at this: if he confirmed the truth of the art through both the authority and the reasoning of Saint Thomas, why did he immediately decree it impossible for a common man? Thomas’s own reasoning is convincing: if he admits the art exists, why is it not "human"? If princes and the wise men they consult are able to practice it, why is it considered "above man"? It is as if princes and the wise were not to be counted among human beings!

These are the very people whom Plato sought by every means for the happiness of Republics—that is, that either princes should devote themselves to philosophy, or philosophers should administer the State. In truth, Cajetan might be defended from criticism by this reasoning: princes who truly understand the workings of nature are rare, and a great many of those who devote themselves to alchemy lack the necessary resources. Therefore, they are unable to perform experiments, which require great expense, unless the wealth of leading men is available to them.

My uncle, Giovanni Pico <note>The famous Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494), known for his Oration on the Dignity of Man</note>, had escaped this criticism before his response was recorded. When his brother Antonio consulted him on whether gold could be made by art, he replied to the inquirer that it could indeed be done, but only with the greatest difficulty. There is no doubt that Saint Thomas, in his *Theologia*—which he was prevented from finishing by death—decreed that the art of making gold should be accepted all the more because greater things than gold can be produced through art (as we shall say as this work proceeds). He decreed the same in his published commentaries on Severinus's <note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a Roman senator and philosopher</note> book *On the Trinity*...

### ON GOLD, BOOK II ###

...that it is a legitimate art and, as the younger [scholars] say, it is "subordinate" <term>subalternatam: a technical Scholastic term for a science that depends on the principles of a higher science, just as music depends on the principles of mathematics</term> to natural philosophy. Beyond this, I have read a book by Saint Thomas [Aquinas] <note>The influential 13th-century theologian</note> on the metallic art itself—if the title does not misidentify the author. The attribution seems legitimate because it mentions Albert [the Great] <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a scientist and Thomas's teacher</note> as his instructor. It was sent to Reginald <note>Reginald of Piperno, Thomas’s longtime secretary and companion</note>, to whom it is well known that Thomas sent other works as well. I have also read commentaries on Thomas’s opinions regarding the production of gold and silver. However, many who are not sufficiently familiar with the name of "chemistry" <note>original: *chemicæ*, used here interchangeably with alchemy</note> have, in my view, sought out something foreign, or rather produced from their own poorly stocked pantry a way to avoid the name of "alchemy." They did this because the word is commonly associated with the low-born rabble, and they did not want the writings on this subject to be tainted by such a shameful association, as we indicated before.

As for what Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536), the famous Dutch humanist</note> wrote—that it is a capital offense if anyone (I am repeating his own words) practices alchemy <note>original: *alcumisticam*</note> without the Prince’s permission—many who are far too addicted to the art do not accept this. Even less do those accept it who have achieved success through long-term experiments. First, they demand of the learned man [Erasmus]: who exactly is this "Prince"? For there are many Princes under a supreme ruler [the Emperor], many under Kings, and many of these have no desire to be subject to the Roman Prince <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note>. Then they ask whether that Prince, whoever he may be, would wish to demolish the laws of previous Caesars—published many centuries ago regarding miners—with his own private edict? Finally, they added that such an edict should have been promulgated through all provinces, and once promulgated, accepted and confirmed by custom; otherwise, it would be counted as antiquated and void. 

They also demand a distinction <note>original: *secretionem*</note> be made for that type of chemistry which fakes true gold and silver, which was mentioned by Pope John, the twenty-second of that name <note>Pope John XXII (r. 1316–1334) issued a famous decree, *Spondent pariter*, against alchemists who promised wealth but produced only fraud</note>. The Tuscan Dante Alighieri <note>original: *Alligerius Ætruscas*; the poet who famously placed alchemists in the Eighth Circle of Hell in his *Inferno*</note> also mentions it. They likewise distinguish it from the art practiced by the unlearned and illiterate who seek the transformation of metals. And finally, they distinguish it from that art which, through either exceptional learning or certain experiments, plainly creates silver and gold either from their own principles or from more imperfect metals. Both doctors of theology and interpreters of canon law have contended that this [latter] art cannot be justly forbidden, based on the definition of a just law. For a law must be considered unjust if it seizes what belongs to another, or if it prohibits and casts aside what is beneficial to many. What excuse, based on either justice or integrity, could be offered for restraining hands that are prepared and equipped for both their own and others' benefit? Power is given over men so that it may profit, help, and bring advantages to them...

One might also have expected him to treat the question in some way to resolve it, at least by the authority of others. For in that book to which Accursius <note>Accursius (c. 1182–1263), a celebrated Italian jurist whose "Great Gloss" became a standard legal reference</note> added his notes, it is written that for the public good, princes should find out who the makers of gold are; yet for private benefit, they may carry out what they know even if the princes resist, provided they pursue the business cautiously. 

Indeed, the edict of John XXII <note>Pope John XXII (r. 1316–1334), famous for the bull *Spondent pariter*, which targeted fraudulent alchemists</note> is of such a kind that, because it was not received among the seven legitimate volumes as a member of the legal body but remained outside, it is called "extravagant" <term>extravagari: a legal term for papal decrees not included in the primary collections of Canon Law</term>. Yet even this decree does not oppose the art itself. For those who want to use it rashly as an argument may be warned at the very threshold—that is, in the heading of the edict—for it is prescribed concerning the "crime of forgery." But we speak *of the true art*, which cannot be condemned under the name of falsehood, let alone dragged before tribunals. This is the decree of Accursius, William <note>Likely William of Duranti, a prominent medieval jurist</note>, and others who followed them correctly, especially in those passages where the crime of forgery is treated. Unless falsehood is detected in either material or form, no penalty can be inflicted; as Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a leading expert on civil and canon law</note> noted in the *Customs of Fiefs* when mention is made of regalia <term>regalibus: the rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</term>.

It is even more clearly seen as we proceed that the Pope’s discourse is directed against lying imposters and false craftsmen. He writes that "poor alchemists promise riches they do not provide," and that they "conceal their falsehood" so that finally they pretend that what does not exist in nature is true gold or silver through "sophistical transmutation" <note>original: *sophistica transmutatione*; refers to chemical processes that only change the surface appearance of a metal rather than its internal essence</note>. Consequently, they are forced to place into the public funds for the use of the poor as much true gold or silver as they have sold or given in payment of the false or counterfeit kind. Those who have produced adulterated coinage from that gold—not true gold, but "sophistical" as it is called—procur-

### CHAPTER IV.

#### *What should be thought concerning the making of gold through art depends upon natural philosophy.*

However, this matter depends not upon the edicts of princes, nor upon the interpreters of laws and canons, nor upon those who have scribbled their pages based on the sayings of others and passed judgment on human conduct. Instead, it depends universally upon the principles of natural philosophy: whether something can be made by art that nature otherwise promises—that is, whether it happens that the same form, substance, and essence can arise and be produced from different starting materials. Likewise, the question of changing forms emerged from the philosophers themselves, who debated extensively whether species could be changed indiscriminately. 

The specific dispute concerning the making of gold <term>chrysopoeia: the alchemical art of making gold</term> arose from Aristotle's volumes on *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, particularly Book IV, was the foundational text for medieval theories on the formation of minerals and metals</note>. These have indeed been handled in various ways, yet they do not offer themselves so clearly to the evaluation of discerning minds that certain and unshakable dogmas can be extracted from them. Therefore, there were those who attacked the art, whom Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Letter on the Soul" famously argued that alchemists could only create clever imitations of metals, not change their underlying species</note> most clearly resists, as does Geber <note>Geber (the Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan), the legendary figure considered the father of Islamic and European alchemy</note> and many others. Although Avicenna denies that a species can be changed entirely, he admits that forms can be introduced into common matter. 

But as for Aristotle, aside from the fact that he made no exact mention of this matter—at least in those volumes considered to be his legitimate works (for some exclude certain texts that favor the art from the Aristotelian corpus)—beyond this, I say, it is certain that he discussed metals only in a general way in his *Meteorology*. He asserted that they arise mostly from moist vapors, just as stones, sulfur, and realgar <note>original: *sandaraca*; a red arsenic sulfide mineral used in ancient and medieval chemistry</note> are generated mostly from dry ones. 

This was done by maintaining a certain proportion to those things that occur not in the caverns of the earth, but in the high region of the air. For this reason, they were called "meteors" by him, using the Greek term <note>original: *meteora*; meaning things "raised up" or "in the air," which for Aristotle included rain, wind, and minerals</note>. For he intended that clouds and rains should condense there from moist breath, while winds, lightning, thunderbolts, and other things of that kind should coalesce from dry breath and fire. Although he placed some distinctions between them, beyond these he certainly gave no clear indication in those books for setting forth any exact discipline, since—

Indeed, among his introductory remarks, Aristotle says he will have some doubts about certain matters, and Alexander, his interpreter <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note>, explains that the things Aristotle treats in that work are difficult to understand. Olympiodorus even calls them by far the most obscure. Thus, from this starting point, you can easily perceive the Aristotelian doctrine in whichever way you wish, and likewise grasp the difficulty of the **chemical art**. For even Aristotle, a man of great learning, confesses his own doubt and treats these matters with a sort of superficiality—matters which, by their very nature, seemed to support the understanding of that art.

But a point can be drawn from Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school</note> that might serve to settle the dispute. For although he writes in his book *On Stones* that he did indeed discuss metals—and that entire work, whatever it may have been, has perished through the greed of time—he nevertheless said that they consist of water, just as stones consist of earth. Hence his words: <note>original Greek: "ὕδατος μὲν τὰ μεταλλευόμενα, καθάπερ ἄργυρον καὶ χρυσὸν"</note> **"metals, such as silver and gold, are made of water."** Shortly thereafter, he sufficiently indicated that gold is customarily made by skilled craftsmen. *For he records for memory that cinnabar was made by Callias the Athenian, while he thought he was making gold.* For unless he had hoped that gold could be drawn from that scarlet sand, there is no reason why he would have labored so hard at the task. It is well known that from the sand called <term>Chryfamos: literally "gold-sand"</term> gold is customarily made in the same way it is usually extracted from mines, which is quite evident in civil laws if they are properly understood. 

On this matter, as we progress in this work, we shall instruct those who are less experienced. For even if **Callias** did not achieve gold, but rather cinnabar,
<margin>Cinnabar</margin>
he nonetheless undoubtedly obtained the beginning of gold. Indeed, it is well known among skilled craftsmen that the principles of both silver and gold lie hidden within cinnabar. We can also infer something from his fellow student **Callisthenes**: that he, Theophrastus, and their teacher Aristotle were of the opinion that metals could be changed into one another. This is because **Callisthenes** himself assigned only one form to them—a view which **Galen** easily admitted, arguing through several reasons that they differ only by "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian terms, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like color or hardness, rather than a change in the fundamental substance</note>, if indeed that book is to be considered a legitimate work of **Galen** and not a forgery.

Truly, I have been able to agree with **Callisthenes** on this reduced reasoning because of my own manifold experience. I have observed gold and silver produced in separate grains by one and the same <term>pharmacum: the alchemical "medicine" or elixir believed to transform base metals</term>. Likewise, I have many times witnessed gold and silver produced at the same time and by the same "medicine." And if ever I found that what remained separated from the gold was acted upon by that liquid which the common people call **aqua fortis** <note>literally "strong water"; nitric acid, used by alchemists to separate silver from gold</note>, it was clearly established by that test that much gold was contained within. But concerning these experiments...

### ON GOLD, BOOK II.

...will be discussed more diligently in its proper place. Vincent of Beauvais <note>Vincentius Burgundus, a 13th-century Dominican friar who compiled the *Speculum Maius*, the most comprehensive encyclopedia of the Middle Ages</note>, who produced the greatest volumes on nearly every branch of literature, when he treats the nature of things, asserts that the true art is known to him—not only the art by which gold is separated, but also that by which he believes it is made. He was moved, perhaps, by the experience of the thing itself, as one who discovered that gold lies hidden within other metals. Others, and indeed very many, contend that gold is not only separated (which cannot be denied) but is also born and made, using arguments clearly drawn from the storehouse of philosophy.

Indeed, I know that among the Greek interpreters of Aristotle was Michael Psellus <note>A prominent 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and official</note>, who, bringing forward many arguments, asserted that gold can be made by art from non-gold, and showed six ways, if I remember correctly, for that matter. Younger scholars felt that gold could indeed be made, but by another method, as we are about to show shortly. Furthermore, many of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> seemed to lean toward the opinion that gold can be made by art, although they cite both difficulty and dangers; among their number is Timon, in the final question on the third book of Aristotle's *Meteorology*.

For some, doubt was increased by the terms **species** <term>species: in this context, the essential category or "kind" to which a substance belongs</term> and **form**, which philosophers are accustomed to use with various meanings. As far as this matter is concerned, they have been accustomed to speak in three ways regarding the changing of a species by art. For there are those who say that the species is not changed, but rather the individual—what others call the unique, singular entity contained under the species. This occurs because certain things are accustomed to originate both from the principles of the species itself and from elsewhere, just like certain living creatures whose origin is not only from male and female, but from elsewhere <note>referring to the theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from non-living matter like rot or heat</note>; yet you cannot distinguish this origin by sight or any other sense.

Therefore, philosophers have often doubted whether those things generated from sexual union and those arising from decaying matter differ in species or not at all. Some of them, while they do not admit remote prior principles, cannot deny the immediate ones—such as I remember reading in Galen <note>The famous Roman physician and philosopher</note> (whether he was the one from Pergamon who commented on Hippocrates or another of the same name). For instance, when a chick is brought forth from an egg, it is not only by a hen’s brooding, but also by the warmth of a woman’s breasts or the heat of a **horse-manure oven** <term>equiclibanus: literally a "horse-oven"; a method of using the steady heat of fermenting horse dung to incubate eggs or provide gentle heat for chemical experiments</term>. 

There are those who wish the question to be understood both through the operation of art alone and also through the mixed operation of nature. By this distinction, they settle the dispute. They themselves then separate the species so that anything can be changed as far as it pertains only to the form while the matter remains; this is certainly achieved by art, albeit with the help of nature, but through itself...

### GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
<page-num>382</page-num>

...anything [of the underlying substance], nor the one performing the work, for whom the art is said to be a servant. However, they consider it by no means absurd if it is argued and defended—as some do—that these words imply that **matter is changed along with form**. This would mean the result is something entirely and fundamentally new, which wise men certainly do not admit can be done by either art or nature. Such a feat is the unique property of **divine power** alone. 

Consequently, when gold is made from silver or any other metal, they say that either an individual thing is made, or, if they prefer to say a "species" <note>original: *speciem*; in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to the "essence" or "kind" of a thing</note> is made, they insist that the **matter remains** while the **form is changed**. After all, that same matter which previously existed under the form of silver is later found under the form of gold. Therefore, only a "part of the species" is said to be transformed—if we accept the view of the **Aristotelian school** <note>original: *schola Peripateticorum*</note> that a species consists of both matter and form. This is especially the view held by **Saint Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian who integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine</note> and those considered the most noble among the modern thinkers. Nevertheless, there have been philosophers who, when they say "species," wish it to be understood as **form alone**. 

It can also be said that nothing is changed in an absolute sense, because as one part departs, another is joined. This occurs when the previous form leaves the matter it occupied. We experience this most frequently when, after food is consumed, its form perishes and its matter is turned through **concoction** <note>The historical term for digestion or the "ripening" of substances through heat</note>. 

Furthermore, I have occasionally read in the works of **legal experts** <note>original: *iureconsultos*</note> that the "species" is understood differently. They write that the species is *not* changed if, for example, gold is made from tin and lead. In this case, they seem to take the "genus" <note>The broader category (e.g., "Metal")</note> for the "species" <note>The specific kind (e.g., "Gold")</note>. Unless, perhaps, only **one single species of metals** is recognized there—such as copper, lead, tin, and silver—all placed under the one "perfect" species of gold, toward whose excellent rank all other metals are able to ascend? Anyone wishing to defend this view could be refuted neither by the Greek etymology of "metal" nor by any valid reason; far from it, such a view would hardly be banished from the schools of philosophy. 

Indeed, this opinion is said to have been accepted by **Callisthenes** <note>A relative and pupil of Aristotle</note>, whom we discussed above. If we accept his view, we must reject those who assign various forms of metals to **various planets**. Among these is **John Versor** <note>Ioannes Versor, a 15th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> and those he followed in explaining Aristotle. In that passage, he displayed that vanity which a thousand eyes have turned away from and two thousand hands have clapped out <note>A rhetorical way of saying the idea was booed off the stage or rejected</note>: namely, the claim that **iron cannot be melted**. In fact, it is established by experience itself that the **"Planetarians"** <note>Astrologers or those who believe the seven metals are strictly governed by the seven planets</note> have already been proven wrong. For at one and the same time, and with one and the same **medicine** <note>original: *pharmaco*; here referring to the alchemical agent or "Philosopher's Stone"</note> as we narrated before, it has happened that gold and silver arise and are created together—sometimes from a single grain, sometimes from several. Thus, they can no longer dream of [planetary influence]...

Astrologers argue in favor of this matter through the conjunction of the **Sun** and **Jupiter**; for this occurs daily through the most diverse alignments of those planets. But since the vanity of astrologers has been refuted once by my uncle **Giovanni Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the author's famous uncle and a renowned Renaissance philosopher who wrote a famous critique of astrology</note> and frequently by myself, I do not wish to rail against it further. 

However, anyone wishing to defend the opinion of **Callisthenes** <note>A Greek historian and student of Aristotle</note> could without difficulty answer **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on minerals and was often skeptical of certain alchemical claims</note>, who proposes a contrary opinion. This is even more true since it is recorded in the memories of **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> that **"glass is turned into metals,"** <note>original: *verti vitrum in metalla*</note> and he says that there was a great deal of that kind of glassy sand in **Ptolemais** <note>An ancient port city in the Levant, modern-day Acre</note>. Nor would **Galen** <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> deny in his work *On the Power of Simple Medicines* that glassy sand and golden sand are found together; and it is clearly established that metallic substances generated in the same or nearby locations are either of the same nature or are very easily turned into one another.

But since this entire question depends upon the ability to distinguish between **"species"** <note>the essential "kind" or identity of a substance</note> and **"form"** <note>the specific qualities that define an object</note>, we must first investigate and decide upon the distinctions between forms and species. No one with even a moderate education is unaware that this is an arduous task, belonging to the deepest levels of philosophy. I remember that I once dealt with this very subject in a long and laborious work, treating it as by far the most difficult of all matters. I did so both in my *Examination of the Vanity of Pagan Doctrine* and in the *Theorems* I wrote concerning human perfection. If I wished to gather all those arguments here, I would wander far from the path and enter, as it were, a **labyrinth of nature**. Not even the famous **Meander** <note>A river in Asia Minor (modern Turkey) famous for its many twists and turns; the origin of the word "meander"</note> sung of by the poets has as many bends as the thousands of disputes that would immediately arise, which would never find an end before human judges.

Therefore, these matters must be set aside and brought back to common sense. Let it suffice to have shown whether or not gold can be made through art. Anyone who desires to know this must take the schools of the Philosophers into counsel. For my part, while my intellectual faculties remain sufficient, I shall first attempt to bring down to a level plane those things which many consider rugged and harsh. Then, I will mark out the **experiments** by which I was taught and which turned me toward writing these things, doing so as much as possible through outlines and shadows, rather than colors and light <note>The author suggests he will provide the "sketch" or essential truth of his experiments rather than a fully "colored" or overly complex narrative</note>, and I will conclude the business with the briefest propositions I can manage. For thus far, we have related what various men have decided regarding the power of art, the **change of species**, and several other matters.

### *That gold can be made through art.*

<margin>{</margin> No person who rightly contemplates the nature of things should doubt that, since the elements that come together in their pure state beneath the moon's sphere <note>The "sublunary" realm, which in ancient science was the only place where change, decay, and transformation could occur</note> are changed by man—and even plants and various animals are renewed through the mixing of those elements—it is possible for metals to be changed by that same man much more easily. We see everywhere that by the benefit of art <term>art: here meaning *ars* or technology, specifically the alchemical craft</term>, fire and water are made from copper <note>original: *ex aere*</note>, and even earth is made from them. We see plants produced by craftsmanship that were never seen before, and their natures mixed and varied. We see even by the mere change of location—that is, the surrounding water and air—a soft herb becomes a stone, which is named coral. Many have seen and recorded in writing that from the descent of mountain water or the spray of lake water, the skins and flesh of animals are changed into stone. I myself have seen both ferns and the leaves of elms converted into tufa <note>A porous rock formed by the precipitation of minerals from water</note>. We read that bees and hornets are created if human industry is applied to the flesh of oxen and horses <note>Refers to the ancient belief in spontaneous generation, specifically *bugonia*, where bees were thought to be born from carcasses</note>. We also read in the Holy Scriptures of the skins of sheep being born marked with various colors <note>A reference to Jacob's breeding of striped and spotted sheep in Genesis 30</note>, and it is clearly known from those same scriptures that after many cycles of years, living animals were fashioned by the Egyptian Magi.

<margin>{</margin> Moreover, I ask, what prevents the same "form" of a thing—which philosophers commonly call the "substantial form" <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is, as opposed to its accidental qualities like color or size</term>—from being introduced into matter from different principles, even those differing in kind? Does not the form of fire provide the most ample proof of this every day? I do not mean heat—lest the rejected and exploded opinion of Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who argued that the "form" was merely a result of the mixture of elements</note> create ambiguity—but the true form, which it obtained from its substance and from its very species. This form of fire is certainly produced in matter by one source or another, or by fire of the same species. And the sun also produces things differing not only in species but in kind, since by the reflection of the solar rays—which are, and are held to be, not merely elemental but celestial—many things on earth burst into flame, burn, and are converted. If this happens on the surface of the earth, why could it not happen in both places—that is, in subterranean caves and in the purer air? You will perhaps say that the form of gold is a "perfection" compared to the form of fire; I will argue against this if I wish, and not without reason: because the element of fire is not so simple that you can prefer gold to it, since gold is a mixture of elements.

For no pure element can be touched, as taught in the schools...

Aristotle’s [teaching] is accepted: if fire were to persist—and it would indeed persist of itself were it not for a lack of fuel—why would it not be more perfect than gold? Is gold more suited to the use of mortals, a point upon which anyone might argue to the contrary? For who, possessing even a little skill, does not know that all nations stand in need of fire? Although fire is a natural and necessary thing, it is produced in many ways: by nature, for instance, from lightning in the air and also by the reflection of the sun’s rays; and by art <term>art: *ars*, referring to human technology or craft</term> through the friction of solid bodies and various kinds of tinder. Among all sublunary forms <note>In the Aristotelian cosmos, the "sublunary" sphere (below the moon) is the realm of change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens</note>, the properties of this fire are considered both wondrous and numerous, as Theophrastus relates in his book *On Fire*. I translated that book from Greek into Latin within the years of my youth, but I did not publish it because the manuscript was defective and half-torn. Regardless, it is certain that all nations conduct their affairs by means of fire itself.

Indeed, it is clearly evident that there were many nations, as we said before, and there are some at present, who do not use gold, just as they use no coinage of either gold or silver. Such were the Spartans once, for they were not permitted to use it in any way by the laws of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, who banned gold and silver currency to prevent greed and corruption</note>, who even forbade the citizens from building walls, objecting, as the poet sang, that he would leave "Sparta naked to wars" <note>original: *nudam Lacedæmona bellis*</note>; yet she was for a time, and was held to be, the leader of Greece. But if you contend that gold is to be preferred to fire, then I shall bring forth forms more perfect than gold, drawn by art from the bosom of nature, such as we read in the Sacred Scriptures were bestowed upon matter by the mystery of the Magi <note>Referring to the biblical Magi or perhaps to the "prisca theologia" where ancient sages understood the hidden powers of nature</note>, to whom nature was evidently a servant: for the sensible soul <note>The "sensible soul" in Aristotelian thought refers to the level of life possessed by animals, which includes perception and movement; it is "higher" than inanimate metal</note> is more excellent than all gold. Furthermore, Augustine accepts that forms which surpass every physical body can be brought forth by the instruments of natural things. Assenting to his authority, [St. Thomas] Aquinas, using the same reasoning in the second volume of the second part of the *Summa Theologica* <note>A reference to Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*, 2a 2ae, Question 77, Article 2</note>, did not deny that *true gold can be made through art, and if it is true gold, it is lawful to sell it.*

### CHAPTER XI.

But it happens in passing that we should declare the opinion of Saint Thomas, which his interpreters have pulled in different directions; for in his second commentary on the *Sentences* of the Fathers, he seemed to reject the art [of alchemy], but in the *Summa Theologica* he seemed to approve of it. Therefore, since he is judged by some to be contrary to himself, I shall reconcile these diverse meanings...

...certain people have exerted themselves, but for most, they did not satisfy the requirements. Whether I myself shall satisfy them, let the readers judge. I certainly do not agree, first of all, with Giovanni Lyguto <note>A lesser-known commentator on alchemy or law; Pico frequently cites obscure legal and theological critics of the art</note> who excluded the "form" of gold from the reach of art for the sake of its nobility, and for that reason, eluded the possibility of the art of making gold. For as we said, Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian. Alchemists often debated his views on whether "artificial" gold was identical to "natural" gold</note> admits a more perfect form, that is, the sensitive soul. Of these things, the Magi <note>In this context, "Magi" refers to natural philosophers or "wise men" who understand the hidden properties of nature</note> showed themselves to be the producers of natural things by using their own instruments.

Nor am I moved by the argument that craftsmen do not know how to find what properly acts and what is properly acted upon. For they are not ignorant that there is a need for heat, moisture, and many vapors, which nature is accustomed to use for transmuting metals. Add to this that *what he [Thomas Aquinas] seemed to deny as a young man, Thomas constantly affirmed a long time later, that is, while he was composing the Summa Theologica, as if it were the final testament of his opinions.* <note>Pico is arguing that the mature Aquinas was more favorable toward the possibility of alchemy than his earlier writings suggested</note> Nor am I moved by that which moved Lygur Silvester <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian and contemporary of Pico</note>, who thought along with Pedro Gomate <note>Likely Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a French theologian and commentator</note> that Saint Thomas, in his second commentary, spoke of "imperfect" craftsmen, and in the *Summa Theologica* spoke of "perfect" ones, granting power to the latter and denying it to the former. For the mention was of the art of making [gold], not of the craftsmen. This art, since it uses the service and instruments of nature, can be brought to perfection by all by whom it can be practiced, whether they be incorporeal spirits or men, whether they are taught naturally or by a power above nature.

For a variety of agents does not remove the art, nor does it diminish an art that relies on the powers of nature; indeed, art sometimes assists nature and sometimes even overcomes it. For although philosophers have often accused nature of "sin" <note>original: "peccatum nature," a metaphor for natural defects or "monsters"</note> because of the stubbornness of fluid matter <term>fluid matter: *materia fluxilis*, a term for the chaotic or resistant state of matter that has not yet taken a stable, "perfect" form</term>—which they nevertheless believed was ruled by an intelligent and separate mind—they much more frequently confessed the errors of art. This happens when not only does the occasion of resistant matter present itself, but when the rules for making things, as prescribed by right reason, are neglected. If a man uses this reason and does not abuse it, he is so far from erring that he may even correct the errors of nature itself, should any occur. Therefore, since nature supplies the materials to art, and art itself relies upon nature, and they assist each other and serve one another in a certain way, it can sometimes happen through the skill of art—with nature helping—that what is produced by nature itself can be achieved, and even sometimes more consistently, in the transformation of sublunary matter. Let us use the example of that very gold about which we are disputing. What prevents men from imparting the "form" of gold into other metals by the benefit of the sun and fire? Which form the sun [only]—

For either Democritus signified quicksilver by that word through an enigma, or he meant a metal dissolved into water which can be called the "first matter" of metals, with the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> also agreeing, whose prince [Aristotle] even declared <note>original Greek: ὕδατος γάρ ἐστι</note> "for it is of water": whether, I say, gold is made from those same things or from other kinds of things which nature has hidden in the innermost recesses of the earth, will men not produce the same thing by using the same materials? Or will they be able to imitate the heat of the sun as far as nature permits? Though I would consider this by no means necessary.

For they are not to be listened to as philosophers who think and repeatedly say that gold is born from the heat of the sun alone—as if the heat of the sun were not the universal cause of things that are generated and corrupted in the sublunary machine <note>The physical world below the moon, subject to change and decay</note>—which heat indeed pours out its gifts in caves and subterranean caverns just as much as on the surface of the earth; as if there were no fire in the hidden passages of the earth by which the vapor of sulfur might be excited—the companion and foster-child of gold—which fire not only Etna of Sicily and the neighboring islands reveal, but is itself visible in many mountains of Europe and in the Apennines. Furthermore, those who honestly hold the art clothe the common matter with the proper forms of metals, having driven out the prior forms; and they accomplish this not only by the power of corrosive waters <note>original: *consumptricium aquarum*, likely referring to strong acids used as solvents</note>, or by the power of various kinds of salt, or by the capacity of oils of various conditions, but sometimes by using gold itself for the propagation of its own kind through the subtlety of the art, to which are sometimes mixed the known first principles of gold itself; and in this way they busy themselves transmuting metals and stones, and they attempt to forge powders by which they may produce much gold from a small thing, the name of which is <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or agent of transmutation</note>, by the phi-

In these ways, therefore, they attempt to draw out the "form" from the very bosom of nature itself—a form which they were certainly able to investigate and inquire about from the <term>Galician miners</term> <note>original: *asturibus Callaicis*, referring to the inhabitants of the gold-rich regions of Roman Spain</note> and other diggers of gold and silver. This was possible insofar as they could make conjectures from afar about the generation of metals while casually attending to other tasks, as they were collecting them. I shall pass over those who are said to search the beds of the <term>Hermus</term>, <term>Tagus</term>, and <term>Pactolus</term> <note>Famous rivers of antiquity legendary for their gold deposits</note>, and other rivers, or those who measure the shores of the Atlantic Ocean to collect grains of gold among multicolored pebbles—not only by dedicated effort, but also while doing other things, unexpectedly and, as most would say, by chance.

Indeed, the wiser among them would assert that many mortals achieve the **transmutation of metals** by divine providence—often hidden, but always just. For I have heard of silver being produced while a medicine for a horse was being sought, in which **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> was mixed with many other substances. I myself have seen *both silver and gold being made when neither was expected.* I have also read that the art of making gold was handed down in ancient times by the revelation of heavenly spirits; and in my own age, I have not merely read but heard that the same has occurred through practice, which I shall indicate more clearly when the experiments are discussed. I suspect it could also sometimes happen through dealings with evil demons, moved by what has been recorded in literature: that demons once revealed medical remedies through sleep in various temples, as I remember discussing more extensively when I refuted superstitious premonitions, especially in the books I titled *On the Foreknowledge of Things* <note>original: *De rerum praenotione* (1506)</note>, and also in my commentaries on my own *Hymns*. Yet antiquity also received many precepts that doctors now use through similar superstition, provided that it committed them to posterity through true literary monuments.

Since it is found to rest upon truth, men can make use of it—not in the sense that a demonic revelation should be embraced, but insofar as the effect itself is a useful thing and true in its own nature. It must be referred back clearly to God as the primary author of all truth and all good; for God, in His great and ineffable kindness, knows how to draw good out of the wicked deeds of men and demons. It is worthwhile to have learned, both by reason and by the authority of the Apostle Paul <note>A reference to Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."</note>, that we must credit Him for the fact that we exist, that we move, and that we live.

But indeed, on the other hand, I do not think the power of making gold was ever revealed by malignant demons. This reason sufficiently persuades me: they would not reveal it except to wicked men, or to those they were convinced were steeped in malice. However, Divine Justice does not permit such men to pour out the poison of their souls, combined with such great power, to the destruction of the human race. This reasoning seems to be supported by practical experience: the demon does not even bestow a few gold coins upon his followers in those obscene games which we discussed in our three-part dialogue titled *The Witch* <note>original: *Strix* (1523), Pico’s influential work on witchcraft and demonology. He argues that "witch-gold" is usually a temporary illusion like dried leaves.</note>. Therefore, let us credit good spirits if anything remarkable has been revealed concerning the truth of this art through some special privilege; yet it is more easily attributed to study and experience.

For as different experts gathered various findings through diverse experiments, they were able to learn much about the art; for nature brings forth gold neither in only one place, nor in only one way. <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on minerals and alchemy.</note>, writing of his own experience, saw pure gold among river sands and heard that impure gold originated mixed with stones, appearing like veins. He adds shortly thereafter that gold born among the sands is of better quality, for which he offers two reasons. One is the greater purity of the sulfur found among hot and dry sands, which is more frequently washed, as is that earthy element <gloss>which</gloss> is present in the <term>living silver</term> <note>original: *viuo argento*; mercury, considered by alchemists to be a primary component of all metals.</note>; the frequent washing of the river both cleaned this substance and rendered it finer and purer. He argued the second cause was the blocking of the passages: when the heat is enclosed at the bottom and in the riverbanks, it is turned back upon itself and is "cooked" <note>In alchemy, "concoction" or cooking refers to the natural maturation of metals within the earth over time.</note> to produce a nobler substance of gold. These were his observations when mentioning the places in which metals are generated.

I, however, can say that the gold collected from the flow of a river, which is kept in my possession, is indeed most brilliant and consists of very small scrapings...

For art not only surpasses more imperfect art, but also—through the help and service of nature, and by emulating nature itself at times—it surpasses it, as we have said before, and as we have found to be certain in the cases of colors, flavors, and many other things. Indeed, it is written in sacred Genesis regarding the land of Havilah <note>Genesis 2:11: "The name of the first is the Pishon; it winds through the entire land of Havilah, where there is gold."</note>; but in the Septuagint <note>The "Seventy" (LXX), the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and the Vulgate edition, it is written as *Euilat*. The ancients report this land to be in India, and say that gold is born there and the gold of that land is the best. If we stand by the Latin translation, the Septuagint interpreters translated the Hebrew context as *beautiful* <note>original: καλὸν (*kalon*)</note>; and even if you prefer to interpret it as "good" or "beautiful," you certainly will not escape the comparison, unless you would rather admit that the gold produced in other provinces is not "good" or "beautiful." For what is the reason that gold should be said to be there by excellence, and called "good gold," unless somewhere else gold was not "good," or was not endowed with that same goodness with which the gold of Havilah flourished? Truly, it cannot be doubted that it is called "optimum" <note>The best.</note> by comparison; likewise, you will not deny that it is called "good" by comparison, provided that in the substance of its own kind it is compared to that which is not endowed with the same goodness. Therefore, *it is necessary for us to gather the distinctions of gold in nature*; a distinction, I say, either in species or in grade. This distinction should certainly not be denied in art itself (if one art is compared to another), nor in art which contends with nature.

This last portion constitutes *electrum* <note>A naturally occurring or man-made alloy of gold and silver, highly prized in antiquity.</note>, which resists poison. This occurs especially in the mountains of the Marsi <note>An ancient Italic people of the central Apennines, historically associated with herbalism and magic.</note>, which are famous for the power of their herbs. The Hebrews have for *obrizon*—where the <term>seventy interpreters</term> <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.</note> have placed it—sometimes a place name, sometimes a word which you could translate into Latin as "purest." Occasionally they did not shrink from using a name that properly corresponds to "most pure," and perhaps it is that very thing which antiquity called <term>apyron</term> <note>Literally "without fire"; gold found in such a pure state it did not require smelting.</note> on the authority of Diodorus. This was dug from the mines of Arabia and was not melted by any fire, having a color so bright that it makes precious stones set in the gold appear even more splendid. From this, I might note in passing that the passage of the Psalm was shown before: *and to him shall be given of the gold of Arabia.* <note>Psalm 72:15. Pico links the physical purity of Arabian gold to biblical prophecy.</note>

For beyond other meanings, it can pertain to the excellence of that metal, so that from it the mind may ascend to the supreme peak of wisdom, which is well known to be indicated by the mystical name of gold. Thus nature produces gold in various ways; likewise art, sometimes the servant of nature and sometimes its rival, and by nature's own help the victor, is also accustomed to produce it in various ways. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the relationship between human skill (Art) and the natural world. Pico is arguing that Art is not merely a passive imitator of Nature, but a rational force that can perfect and even surpass it, specifically in the context of creating gold (alchemy).</meta>

<page-num>393</page-num>

<header>ON GOLD. BOOK II.</header>

...natural faculty, so that they do not think it worthy of the name of "Nature." Yet it is in this very area that Art is most powerful; for it is endowed with a kind of knowledge, being a disposition of a mind flourishing with reason and understanding. Through this office, it governs and arranges Nature—which is otherwise mute and lacking in internal reason—and in the course of governing and moderating, it sometimes imitates Nature, sometimes emulates it, and sometimes surpasses it.

Add to this that among the praises of Nature, it is sometimes noted that she simulates Art. This is clearly seen in the figures delineated by their own nature in marble, in the famous gemstone of Polycrates <note>Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, possessed a legendary emerald ring so perfect it was said to be a sign of his extreme good fortune.</note>, and in many other examples. Even the ingenious Poet <note>The Roman poet Ovid, in his *Metamorphoses*.</note> reported that Nature fashioned a natural arch by imitating Art, through those verses which conclude: "A sylvan cave in a deep recess, worked by no art; nature by her own genius had imitated art. For with living pumice and light tufa she had fashioned a natural arch." <note>original: "Antrumne morale recessu... nulla simulauerat artem ingenio natura suo. Nam pumice viuo, & leuibus tophis natiuum duxerat arcum." This describes the Cave of Diana.</note> But regarding the power of Art, we shall speak a little later; let it only be established here, so that those who persist in denying that Art can aspire to make gold might be restrained. Their contention has no basis in reason; on the contrary, far from being impossible, Art is so capable that, with the help of Nature and diligent application, it can surpass mute Nature.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*On the five general ways gold can be made through art,*<-
->*which in this matter and in many others surpasses nature*<-
->*when nature is deprived of the industry of art.*<-

Art surpasses in the preparation of <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make); the alchemical art of making gold.</note>; it surpasses Nature herself with the help of Nature, when Nature is left without the benefit of Art. This is true not only in splendor, as we have said, but also in the speed of production, which will become manifest as we describe the experiments. It also surpasses Nature in that it achieves its goal through several methods; for there are five general ways gold can be made through Art.

The first is when the metal is extracted from another metal, as when silver is separated from copper, which I remember seeing myself. For metals often lie hidden within one another, especially silver within gold. The reverse also occurs, where gold is found hidden in silver; even lead and copper are sometimes clouded with a portion of a more perfect metal.

Secondly, gold is prepared by the composition of metallic substances...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola’s argument that human Art (alchemy) can perfect and even exceed the works of Nature by utilizing Nature’s own hidden principles. On the previous page, he established that Art is a rational force that governs and moderates natural processes.</meta>

<header>GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

...minerals, for which reason these things were named "minerals" by the common people, following a barbaric <note>The author considers the medieval Latin term *minera* to be "barbaric" compared to classical vocabulary.</note> naming convention. For in these metallic things are the principles of gold, and especially in "living silver" <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> and in sulfur that has not felt the fire—which I do not deny having seen myself.

Thirdly, gold is made from the seed of gold; I call "seed" a prolific force, for a certain power is implanted in every natural thing so that it may propagate itself.

Fourthly, gold is prepared from a substance that is more perfect than gold; yet that substance is not forged without the seed of gold, nor without other principles suitable for generation. In this matter, the genius of the philosophers was supreme, their industry excellent, and their artifice wonderful, since the parts of the matter they choose for making gold or silver, they separate into many natures. These natures correspond in a certain proportion to both the elements and to the heavens—whether they constitute it as a "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the celestial fifth element that is incorruptible and distinct from earth, air, fire, and water</term> in the Peripatetic <note>original: "more Peripatetico," referring to the followers of Aristotle</note> manner, or as a "preponderance of fire" in the ritual of the Platonists. They join the seeds of both gold and quicksilver, so that just as sublunary <note>earthly things "below the moon"</note> things are joined to the heavens and the elements as universal causes, and are propagated by the particular seeds of things, so they themselves use those natures of theirs, and the seeds of metals and metallic things, for the most abundant fertility of gold and silver. *Now, this method is both general and the producer of great things; the three which we described before are called "particular" methods.*

The fifth method is called that which, having cast off the prior and more ignoble form of the metal, induces a later and more powerful form into the metallic matter. *The first is a method of profit; the second of very little; the third and fifth of moderate profit; and the fourth of the greatest.*

Nor should we wonder at what we said before: that Art surpasses Nature by the benefit of Nature. For in other things also which lead to the making of gold, we see that Art excels Nature through the use of Nature's own benefit. Indeed, it is known that in water, in oil, and in salt prepared by Art itself, there are wonderful powers from God, such that it is not possible for the strengths of the water, salt, and oil produced by Nature alone to equal them. Therefore, *those are greatly mistaken who think that Art cannot aspire to where Nature proceeds*, as if that which is native and relying on its own character must always be held more sublime and perfect when compared to that which Art labors to produce.

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical defense of alchemy. <header>ON GOLD. BOOK II.</header>

For we do not wish to compare the powers of nature and the powers of art as if they were separate or standing alone; rather, we say that art, relying on the gifts of nature, can be joined to nature when it is (if I may put it this way) naked and inert. They can be so combined that art sometimes appears to be—and indeed is—the more excellent of the two.

And why should this be a surprise? For art is not cheated of the privilege of nature, since, as we have said, art itself should be classified under the name of "nature." I speak of a nature that is not deaf, but is instead intelligent, organizing, and advancing. We see this in our houses, in our clothing, and in every necessity of life; these things would be utterly raw and unpolished if the art of the human mind—which is a "better nature"—had not intervened as a most noble and living instrument. It is by the industry of this mind that it has come to pass that men, who once hid in the hollows and caves of mountains—in little dwellings eaten away or excavated into vaults—now, after the passage of many centuries, may live not just in huts but in palaces built in a few weeks. Men who were once covered by the leaves of trees or the rough skins of animals are now clothed in woolens and woolen fabrics that could not be produced without art. Those who once fed on raw vegetables, the milk of wild beasts, and bloody meat are now nourished by foods prepared for health and decorous pleasure through the benefit of this same art.

Finally, if you survey the whole universe, you will find that perfected art—that is, the wise nature of man—surpasses the "mute nature" <note>By "mute nature," Pico refers to the instinctive or passive natural world that lacks human reason.</note> which is placed beneath it. From these facts, it is concluded that it is not a cause for amazement that what mute nature struggles to produce in a hundred years, art completes in a few days or even a few hours by using nature’s own service. This is how medicine, painting, and the military arts have been increased and strengthened. This is how philosophy gained its strength and has served theology so greatly: when the contemplation of nature—relying on human genius and confirmed by experiment—tracked down the forces and powers of sublunary <term>sublunary: referring to the Earthly realm "below the moon," which is subject to change and decay</term> things, such as herbs, shrubs, stones, and animals. The knowledge of these things has moved the human race to wonder and led it to consider the secrets of divine providence. Many things are also experienced through art as the centuries progress which could hardly be believed by those of old, simply because they had not perceived the matter with their own eyes. Antiquity once wondered that a stone-making power <note>original: "vim saxificam"; referring to the process of petrification</note> existed in certain springs, when they saw flowing streams of water communicate a stony nature to herbs and turf through continuous irrigation over a long period. I myself wondered at this, having not only read of it often but having even seen it once in...

An example of this can be ready for everyone: Let someone, if the opportunity arises, place ten thousand pounds of both alum and that salt which oozes from baked bricks upon a single silver plate of small weight; even if it were pressed by such great weights for ten years, the silver would never be dissolved into water. # ON GOLD. BOOK II.

<margin>Stygian waters</margin>
It happened to those ancient and learned writers—Pliny, Seneca, and Vitruvius—when they discussed Stygian water <note>original: "Styge aqua"; likely referring to highly corrosive or poisonous mineral waters named after the mythological river of the underworld</note>, which was a work of nature rather than art, that one said the water erodes, another that it freezes, and another that it shatters. These are clearly contradictory and inconsistent effects. Add to this *oil*, by which metals themselves are intimately penetrated, through which they break apart, melt, and dissolve, and by which they are colored both "within and on the skin" <note>An idiom meaning through and through</note>.

Nor should I remain silent about the manifold preparation of salt, which surpasses the sea, mountain, and sand salts known to the ancients. Indeed, any of those salts could (if I may say so) be "salted" by this salt perfected through art. This is produced from things that seem in no way able to burn, and even from things so hot and susceptible to fire as can be; for instance, I do not deny having seen a salt extracted from sulfur that ignores the flame <note>original: "contemptorem flammæ"</note> and is so brilliant and white in its splendor that it cannot be compared even to that salt which the Greek historians of the deeds of Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexandri Macedonis"</note> say the priests of the Oracle of Ammon used to send as a gift from Egypt. Furthermore, just a few days ago (as you know), a salt was prepared at my command from a herb found in my pastures on the borders of the territories of Ferrara and Mantua, which was as beautiful to look at as it was sweet to the taste.

For when foreign shepherds were paying me a tax for that herb—since eating it provided relief to sick cattle—I realized that the salt, which the herb recalled in its taste, was the cause of their health. And so, while the Po <note>original: "Padus"</note> is confined within its usual banks so that it does not flood the neighboring fields, a non-negligible abundance of it presents itself to us. Just as it is more beautiful and sweeter than mountain or sea salt, it is also (unless my conjecture deceives me) more suited to metallic works. I shall pass over its penetrating, drying, and burning power, discovered through art in a short moment of time, <margin>Note</margin> by whose force the prior form of a metal is cast down. Once that form is destroyed, another can easily be introduced and generated through the ministry of the same art and the help of nature. Even if someone were to say that nature, though mute, is guided by an unerring intelligence, one could not argue against the fact that much more help is brought to the completion of the work when the human mind—instructed by art and confirmed by experience—brings its assistance. Certainly, far greater things are seen in person than are read in writings: namely, that metals may be made indiscriminately by human skill in a few days, even though nature does not generate them except after many cycles of years.
