Accordingly, Michael Psellus <note>original: "Michael Psellus"; an 11th-century Byzantine scholar who wrote a famous letter on the art of making gold</note>, in those few pages where he wrote on the art that he had previously undertaken to examine under the balance of philosophy, wonders why people accept the natural power mentioned by Strabo <note>Greek geographer of the 1st century AD</note>—which allegedly transforms the very nature of a spring—yet do not accept the forms of metals being changed into one another by the benefit of art, many examples of which he himself recounts. Otherwise, as he judges, the business is... <note>original: "nisi honesta quadam vi, qui præceperat coegisset"; unless some honorable force, which had commanded it, had compelled him</note>.

### Chapter IX.

### *That it is not necessary for one skilled in the art of making gold to have followed a deep and hidden knowledge of the more subtle philosophy.*

Nor should we listen to those who say it is necessary for us to thoroughly understand the proportion of the elements and the primary qualities springing from them in order to make gold. For those who have fabricated such stories are mistaken; indeed, nothing of what nature <unclear>produces</unclear> would be known to us if it were necessary to have first thoroughly learned their very origins. For neither sense-perception reaches that far, nor does reason penetrate there, except by certain uncertain conjectures that waver greatly in either direction.

But it is also not necessary for the skilled artisan of gold-making to have spent his time investigating hidden causes. It is enough if, by his own natural talent, he presents himself as a servant of nature—which is always generating and bringing forth things according to what has been commanded from above. In this way, a midwife does not investigate the nature of the fetus (of which she is entirely ignorant), but rather she assists the woman who is laboring to bring the fetus forth. In the same way, the farmer—dismissing any need to thoroughly know the qualities of wheat and barley—when he has committed the seeds of those crops to the earth, and when he has harrowed and nurtured them, does not wait in vain for the reward of his labor: namely, a numerous offspring exuberant in every birth. Likewise, when he applies himself to grafting, he does not inquisitively ask what the nature of each tree he joins might be, nor what kind of form the "glue" takes, nor how the inner bark softens against the other bark <note>original: "liber mollescat libro"</note>. Instead, once the wedges are driven in and the "eyes" <note>term: buds used in grafting</note> are inserted, he watches for the budding offspring from which flowers and fruits are produced.

What of the fact that man—who, as Aristotle wrote, "produces man along with the sun" <note>original: "hominem gignere scripsit Aristoteles"; a famous medieval scientific principle stating that human generation depends on both biological parents and the celestial heat of the sun</note>—brings forth offspring from seed? Yet this is not always successful, for out of a hundred, or even a thousand unions, sometimes scarcely one is not in vain. But even when it is successful and results in many children, the man himself is nonetheless ignorant of the nature of his own seed, which...

### ON GOLD BOOK II.

...nor clearly known to philosophers, *nor to physicians who have long since been quarreling* among themselves whether it is that which *is left over from nourishment*, or whether it flows from the brain, or from the whole body, or from elsewhere. Is it cast out from the male alone? Does the woman also pour forth anything in kind? <note>Pico is referring to the historical debate between the "Aristotelian" view (only the male provides the seed) and the "Galenic" view (both sexes provide seed).</note> Since these things are uncertain, and even entirely unknown to the parent, he is not for that reason frustrated of offspring; rather, if his seed be prolific, and the woman (not being sterile) has received it in the proper places, and the remaining duties necessary for the same effect concur—both of the active male and the passive female—the infant is conceived by the very order of nature, and in its own time comes forth into the light.

It must be considered that it happens no differently *in the art of making gold, which is by far the most excellent of all those that operate with instruments*: for it is not necessary that the craftsmen thoroughly know all the genera and species of metallic things, to which the common people have given the name "minerals." Indeed, that parent herself, nature, who is hidden in the caverns of the earth, scarcely knows them thoroughly—so many they are, with such great diversity, and in such an ample and deeply inscrutable number. But it is enough to have thoroughly mastered the relationships and natures known by experiment, and to have thoroughly learned the laws of change. Nevertheless, we do not deny that those craftsmen should be considered wiser who have explored the nature of efficient causes <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of the change or its ending; in alchemy, this is often the agent or the "philosopher's stone."</note>, so that they might master how to instill the proper form of gold into the common matter of the elements; or even after that common matter has been occupied by the form of a more ignoble <note>meaning "base" or "lesser," like lead or copper</note> metal, to favor it, and as if they had learned how to heal, so that they might be able to expel the former form and dislodge it from its seized seat. And, while expelling it, they should master the way by which they might thereafter place the more noble form in that same seat—such as those few earlier ones, *who knew that there are certain hidden seeds in metals for multiplying themselves*. This is also manifest in what Aristotle wrote in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, when he indicates the cause of the prolific seed of natural things and considers it received—not from fire, or such power—but from that heat which is contained in the seed and in the foamy matter, which he expresses by the word *spirit* <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to "pneuma," a vital heat or breath</note>, in which there is a nature corresponding to the proportion of the elements of the stars. It pleased me to subscribe the Greek words of Aristotle, which have been variously translated into Latin:

<note>original Greek: "πάντων μὲν γὰρ ἐν τῷ σπέρματι ἐνυπάρχει, ὅπερ ποιεῖ γόνιμα εἶναι τὰ σπέρματα, τὸ καλούμενον θερμὸν. Τοῦτο δ’ οὐ πῦρ, οὐδὲ τοιαύτη δύναμίς ἐστι, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐμπεριλαμβανόμενον ἐν τῷ σπέρματι, καὶ ἐν ἀφρώδει πνεύμα, καὶ ἡ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι φύσις ἀνάλογος οὖσα τῷ τῶν ἄστρων στοιχείῳ."</note>

"For in the seed of all things there exists that which makes the seeds fertile, namely, what is called heat. This is not fire, nor any such power, but the spirit <note>pneuma</note> enclosed in the seed and in the foam, and the nature in that spirit is analogous to the element of the stars."

For this reason, wise craftsmen have used every effort and care to master this nature extracted from metals. Many of the **followers of Aristotle** <note>original: "Peripateticis"</note> even **gave it the name "quintessence"** <note>original: "quinta fecere nomen essentia"; the "fifth essence" was believed to be a celestial substance beyond the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>, so that they might hold a general cause for their work, just as the heavens are a general cause for all things on earth. They also labored to reduce earthy matter into a powder like burnt lime, and subsequently prepared various kinds of potent salts and oils; they even strove to condense more fluid matter into water, and to refine subtler matter into the thinnest vapors, emulating the power of air and fire. But as we have said, it is not necessary for all craftsmen to have thoroughly mastered these things. Thus, at the beginning of our *Enigmas*—which, if they are enigmas to anyone else, will certainly not be so to you—we wrote the following verses:

->*He who holds the principles, the causes, and the hidden seeds of things,*<-
->*let him indeed be the highest and best among craftsmen;*<-
->*but it is not necessary for you to know so many or such great things,*<-
->*that you must first fly through the heights of heaven*<-
->*and through the high reaches of the air on massive wings.*<-
->*Nor must you then, descending to the great bowels of our mother Earth,*<-
->*crawl to behold the bridal chambers, the offspring, and the grandchildren*<-
->*of **Sulfur** and **Quicksilver** in the blinding darkness.*<-
->*Believe me, it is enough for you to have mastered the nearby powers,*<-
->*so that you may make one thing from the twin birth that depends on them.*<-

And there are other things to be seen there in that poem. But as far as it pertains to the goal of the present dispute, it should be enough for craftsmen not to be ignorant of what we have narrated. It is enough to hold firmly certain secret weights of things unknown to the common people, and to know the varieties of vessels with which the work is prepared. Experience, thoroughly taught by the help of nature, is the master of these tools. **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and saint who wrote "De Mineralibus," a key text on the nature of metals.</note> once discussed these things when he spoke of the places where metals are generated, although the moderns have found and prepared far more vessels, also under the guidance of nature and industry. This industry is strongly supported by experiments; they have also learned the proper degrees of heat and sharp flames, and the suitable time for applying and removing the fire. Likewise, they have learned to prepare suitable containers of either glass or earth for the work, in which they are greatly aided by a new material found in the caverns of the earth which was hidden from the ancients.

### CAP. X.

*Gold can be made more easily in our century than in previous centuries; containing many arguments both against the detractors of the art, and against several even distinguished writers who disagree incorrectly regarding Cinnabar, mercury, and many other things.*

For these reasons, gold can be made more easily in our own time than it was among the ancients: for they performed the work more simply, and the things they used are now used by only a few. Instead, we use other things—and far more of them—even though the ancients did make use of certain metallic substances of which our own craftsmen do not have a sufficiently clear or pure understanding. There is, for example, <term>anthrax</term> <note>original: "ἄνθραξ"; in Greek this means "coal," but in mineralogy it referred to a glowing red stone like a carbuncle or ruby. Here it likely refers to a specific mineral reagent.</note>; for although many think they possess it, they are wandering far from the truth.

<margin>sandarac</margin>
<margin>Cinnabar</margin>
Indeed, I do not doubt that at least three things can be found that might fit that name. Who truly knows <term>Pyrite</term> <note>Fire-stone</note> unless it be that which is commonly called <term>Marcasite</term>? I believe that <term>sandarac</term> <note>A term often confused between a plant resin and the mineral realgar (arsenic sulfide).</note> is not recognized, unless it is that which was brought to me from Venice under the name of "red sulfur." And when you speak of <term>Cinnabar</term>, who does not think you are describing the composition of Bucasis the Arab <note>Referring to Al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis), a famous 10th-century physician and chemist whose works were highly influential in the West.</note>, joined together from quicksilver and sulfur? Yet this is as distant from true Cinnabar as an ape is from a lion: there is some similarity in color, but in nothing else, as will be made clear in its proper place. Who will point out the <term>Chrysocolla</term> <note>Literally "gold-glue"; used in antiquity for soldering gold, often identified with malachite or borax.</note> so celebrated by the ancient craftsmen and masters of gold-making? I mean that native <term>Chrysocolla</term>, not the one Pliny taught (or perhaps only hinted at), nor the one Galen indicated.

For it is within anyone's power to manufacture the common kind: but we nevertheless possess more substances, not only those imported from distant regions, but those discovered in Italy itself. For many metallic things are dug out of the caverns of the earth which the ancients did not possess. I believe that almost every day new and diverse mixtures of metallic things are created—and this is asserted by reliable evidence—which, just as they possess various colors and tastes, also produce various effects, their outward properties revealing their inner substance. These are now available in greater abundance and are sold at a lower price. I would assert this not only because, in ancient times, the Italian mines were spared by a decree of the Romans <note>The Roman Senate occasionally restricted mining in Italy to preserve resources or control the economy.</note>.

For although many things are imported from elsewhere and are supplied everywhere—things which are of the greatest use to our work—most people...

<header>GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

Nevertheless, as I have said, many things are born and even composed today which antiquity did not know. Take <term>Chalcanthum</term> <note>original: "Chalcanthum"; traditionally refers to copper sulfate or "blue vitriol."</note> for example: when the ancients spoke of it, they dealt with the matter in few words. Indeed, they made no mention of the white variety—which reveals a cyan-blue color when rubbed—nor can one find in their writings mention of a Chalcanthum with an ashen paleness, or a green appearance, or a sapphire hue, or other varieties. Just as their colors differ, so too their powers are far diverse. When they spoke of <term>Native Sulfur</term> <note>original: "ἄπυρον" (apyron), meaning "unfired" or "not having experienced fire."</note>, the ancients perhaps did not progress any further.

You may now see this "unfired" sulfur itself in a shining color like <term>electrum</term> <note>An alloy of gold and silver, or amber; here referring to a translucent yellow-gold color.</note>; you may see it as white, ashen, green, yellow, black, and red—so red that it seems to compete with <term>rubrica</term> <note>Red ochre or red chalk.</note> in its flame-like color. I pass over other things which, because they possess neither Greek nor Latin names, I shall by no means review in this place. In the works of Aristotle, you will find—neither by chance nor in serious discussion—hardly anything cited by name other than <term>sandarac</term> <note>original: "σανδαράκην"; here referring to the mineral realgar, an arsenic sulfide.</note>, <term>ochre</term> <note>original: "ὤχραν"</note>, <term>red earth</term> <note>original: "μίλτον" (miltos); a red pigment or bole.</note>, and <term>thyon</term> <note>original: "θύον"; likely referring to a citrus-wood or a specific resinous plant.</note>. A little later, <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "κιννάβαρις" (kinnabaris)</note> is brought forward as if it were a stone. This is not that cinnabar for which <term>Bucasis the Arab</term> <note>Refers to the Andalusian scholar Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Albucasis), though the recipe for synthetic cinnabar—vermilion—is often found in the "Geber" corpus.</note> is considered the inventor of the method for composing it from <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury</note> and sulfur. Nor is it that cinnabar which they claim is produced in India from the battle between dragons and elephants; rather, it is that which was dug out from the caverns of the earth and imported from Africa. In my lifetime, it has been seen in Italy only twice that I know of; and both Dioscorides and Vitruvius—the former writing for medical use, the latter for the painting of houses—left written records that it was rare even in the time of Augustus.

However, those things are called "metallic" which are found in the mines of metals. For according to Theophrastus, it is from these mines that <term>Chrysocolla</term> <note>A green copper mineral, though the name was also used for borax used in soldering gold.</note>, <term>Cyanus</term> <note>A blue stone or pigment, likely azurite.</note>, Ochre, <term>Minium</term> <note>Red lead or vermilion.</note>, and Sandarac are dug out. He recorded that although Chrysocolla and Cyanus are sandy, and Ochre and Minium are earthy, Sandarac and <term>Arrenicon</term> <note>original: "ἀρρενικόν"; the Greek term for arsenic (specifically orpiment).</note> (he cites it by this name, which others call <term>arsenicum</term>) are powdery, and that they do not differ much from one another. From this passage, it should not be overlooked that we can conclude that certain writers—otherwise famous enough—should have their reliability rejected, both in their descriptions of Ochre and in many other matters.

First, Theophrastus teaches that Ochre differs not at all from arsenic. Yet Pliny says something far different; he clearly slips in other matters as well. For when Pliny cited Chrysocolla, sulfur, and Cinnabar, he also wished Minium to be the same thing which the Greeks call *Miltos* and *Cinnabaris*. Yet elsewhere he detests this very idea. Certainly, you will find that *Miltos* is one thing and *Cinnabar* another in the works of Aristotle, Theophrastus, and even Galen...

...who also cites another kind of <term>red earth</term> <note>original: "Milton," Latinized from the Greek "miltos," referring to red ochre or earth colored by iron oxide.</note> from Lemnos, that is, that earth which resists poisons. He says he received twenty thousand little cakes of it, stamped by a priest while he had landed on the island of Lemnos. But besides these, you will certainly find that red earth is different from <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>Mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury, used as a brilliant red pigment.</note> in the works of other excellent writers on nature, some of whom call it not *kinnabari* but *kinnabar*; <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, author of the foundational work "On Stones."</note> indicates two species of it.

One kind is born by its own nature in Iberia and Colchis; the other is made by art—not indeed from quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note> and sulfur, but from a scarlet sand which <term>Callias the Athenian</term> first devised ninety years ago, while he hoped to extract gold from it. In this matter, you may find that <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History."</note> made not just a simple mistake, but a manifold one. For he teaches, on the authority of Theophrastus, that <term>minium</term> <note>Often used for red lead today, but in antiquity, "minium" usually referred to cinnabar/vermilion.</note> was made by Callias instead of Cinnabar; yet Theophrastus most clearly distinguishes one from the other, and speaks separately about minium and separately about Cinnabar.

Furthermore, Pliny himself writes that Cinnabar is sandy, whereas Theophrastus says it is stony, or as he says in his own language, <note>original Greek: "lithōdes"</note> **stony**, which <term>Aristotle</term> had previously stated in these words: <note>original Greek: "to de lithos ek toiautēs geganōs systaseōs hoion kinnabari"</note> **"and the stone produced from such a composition is like cinnabar."**

Moreover, Pliny teaches that minium—which <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica."</note> called <note>original Greek: "ammion"</note> **ammion**—is born in Ephesus, a matter of which there is not a single word in the records of Theophrastus. For Theophrastus writes that Cinnabar is made in Ephesus by art, or as he says, <note>original Greek: "kat’ ergasian"</note> **"by processing."** Just as Cinnabar is born in Colchis and Iberia by the spontaneity of nature, I replace it with his word <note>original Greek: "autophyes"</note> **"naturally occurring."** Thus, he designated the location of artificial Cinnabar in Ephesus, and natural Cinnabar among the Iberians and Colchians. To minium, however—not the kind made today from lead which emulates the color of natural minium, but that which is sought from the deepest hiding places of the earth—he assigned different locations. Nevertheless, he identified two kinds of minium: one born of itself, and the other made by art. From this come his words: <note>original Greek: "esti de hoper kai miltos men automatos, hē de technikē"</note> **"there is that which is like red ochre, the one natural, the other technical [artificial]."** To these points, Theophrastus recorded that Cinnabar is very hard and stony, which I myself can also testify to and place clearly before the eyes of those who disagree.

He teaches that <term>red earth</term> <note>original: "Milton"</note>—that is, minium and <term>Ochre</term>—displays the appearance of a type of earth. In this place, we would also marvel at <term>Hermolaus</term> <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Renaissance scholar known for correcting errors in Pliny's "Natural History."</note> if he had published his *Corollary to Dioscorides* without correcting Pliny’s errors, which he wished to defend in the "Plinian Corrections" he had published. Otherwise, [he notes] only two modes of Cinnabar...

...only <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known as the "father of botany" and author of a major work "On Stones."</note> himself cites it, making no mention of the blood of dragons and elephants, which <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic "Natural History."</note> cites under the name of <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>original: "Cinnabaris." Here referring to the confusion between the mineral mercury sulfide and the plant resin known as dragon's blood.</note>, and which <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica," the primary source for ancient pharmacology.</note> had previously rejected as being different from true Cinnabar. This true version is what (as I believe) <term>Bucasis</term> <note>likely referring to the medieval surgeon Albucasis, or Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi.</note> or some other ancient writer wished to imitate, but was least able to do; he achieved the color in some part but not entirely. For artificial Cinnabar carries its redness on the surface, while the natural kind possesses a much more splendid color in its depths, and represents blood more closely. This is the source of the opinion that it is the blood squeezed out from the battle of <term>dragons and elephants</term> <note>A popular ancient myth claiming that cinnabar was formed when dragons and elephants crushed each other in combat, mixing their blood.</note>, whether a true History was the origin of this matter, or a fable.

Add to this that when natural Cinnabar is burned, its flame is more brilliant and pure, while that of the artificial is cloudier, leaving nothing behind after it is consumed. From that which nature brought forth, there remains a residue in which you may see crumbs of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "vivi argenti," literally "living silver," our modern mercury.</note> sparkling; in the artificial kind, there are instead certain dense lines of <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>From the Greek "hydrargyros," meaning "water-silver."</note>. For I would not separate quicksilver from hydrargyrum in the manner of Pliny, who thought the latter was artificial and the former native, contrary to Dioscorides who cites them by the same name. It is just as much an artificial product made from <term>minium</term> <note>In this context, minium refers to cinnabar ore or red lead.</note> as it is a natural one produced in two ways: either when it hangs from the arches of silver-bearing caves where it has hardened into drops, or when it is collected by itself from the mines.

Furthermore, a great error (as it seems to me) is detected here in Pliny, which has also been criticized by others at times; for he distinguishes them into two types, thinking that only one kind flows from the stone. He calls its <term>pustule</term> <note>original: "vomica," used by Pliny to describe a pocket or "boil" of liquid mercury found within a rock.</note> an "eternal liquid" which is a poison to all things, yet he thought this came from elsewhere. Therefore, in the works of Dioscorides and other writers of good reputation, *hydrargyros* is the same as quicksilver; in Pliny, it is not the same. Indeed, the Greeks called it "silvery water" because of its color and its fluid liquid state, while the Latins called it "living" because of its very motion.

Pliny also seems to be inconsistent with himself in this matter when, using the name *hydrargyrium*, he says that silver alone is gilded with it; for he has sufficiently betrayed that it does not differ from the quicksilver which craftsmen use alone when they produce gilded vessels from pure silver ones. Without doubt, those of whom <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>A Roman architect and engineer whose work "De Architectura" includes descriptions of chemical processes.</note> mentions in his seventh book used the very same substance. He writes that quicksilver is made from marble fragments when craftsmen collect it after the smoke of the fire has settled, having been stirred up by the vapor. And who doubts that they use it in the same way? For they extract it not only from minium and marble, but from all metals. In this matter, he is even surpassed by later...

### ON GOLD, BOOK II.

...antiquity; for now, <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum." Also called hydrargyron or mercury.</note> is extracted—not even with great difficulty—from every metal, and not only from metals, but from many metallic substances. This provides an occasion for wonder that so great a man as <term>Galen</term> <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, so well-versed in letters and experiments, estimated that mercury was not born naturally, but made. For when he spoke on the power of simple medicines, these are his words: "It is not among the drugs that grow spontaneously, but among those that are prepared." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔστι τῶν ἀυτοφυῶν Φαρμάκων, ἀλλὰ τῶν σκευαζομένων."</note>

Furthermore, one cannot read such a numerous heap of things as is now used by those who fashion gold and silver in the works of <term>Vincent</term> <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century Dominican friar and author of the massive encyclopedia "Speculum Maius."</note> or <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist who wrote extensively on minerals and alchemy.</note>, who were the first among the learned after the Greeks and Arabs to mention these matters.

For if I have counted correctly, Albert recorded eight kinds of substances after the nature of metals: salt, <term>atramentum</term> <note>original: "Atramentum." Literally "blacking," usually referring to metallic sulfates like vitriol used for ink or dyes.</note>, alum, and arsenic—in which he included <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, which indeed ought most of all to be called by that name. For <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>The 1st-century BC Roman architect and engineer.</note> writes that orpiment, which is called *arsenikon* in Greek, is mined in Pontus. <term>Dioscorides</term>, a man of that same age, did not want that kind to be of the best quality, but rather the paler kind; he held the golden-colored kind from Mysia near the Hellespont to be of the first quality. However, he used the terms orpiment and arsenic interchangeably, a practice followed after Vitruvius by <term>Celsus</term> and <term>Pliny</term>. A third kind, which is white, was recorded by the Arabs, the Latin physicians, and Albert, though some have said it is not white but of a middle color.

If these authors wished to be understood as Albert recorded, they are rejected by the senses, let alone by authority. To these, Albert cites nitre and <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "tuchia," an impure zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note>, although in his view the latter is not a work of nature, but of art.

As for <term>marcasite</term> <note>original: "Marcafita." In the Middle Ages, this term was used for various shiny metallic sulfides, especially iron pyrites.</note>, it was known to the ancients (as has been said) but is not found today unless it is that which Dioscorides and Galen called <term>pyrite</term> <note>original: "Pyrité." Literally "fire-stone," known for sparking when struck.</note>. Following <term>Democritus</term> <note>The ancient Greek "laughing philosopher," often associated with early chemical and atomic theories.</note>, it is said these are found in golden, silver, copper, and I add, tin and lead colors—even though those authors seem to designate copper pyrite specifically for medicinal uses. There are some who wish to substitute tutty for <term>cadmia</term> <note>a zinc-rich ore or furnace deposit.</note>. In the last place, Albert cited <term>electrum</term> <note>a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver.</note>; however, if nature brought it forth, it should be placed among the metals, but if art produced it, it is not to be numbered among those things dug out from the deepest caves.

But the things that miners now bring to light for the preparation of gold are so numerous that you could hardly review them in a short space of time. For besides that white <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenicum." Arsenic trioxide, often called "white arsenic" in early chemistry.</note>—which they named after crystal—and <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "tuciam." Zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note>, which, although cited by some Greeks by this name, was called <term>cadmia</term> <note>original: "Cadmia." A term used in antiquity for various zinc ores or furnace deposits.</note> in ancient times, there are many kinds of <term>marcasite</term> <note>original: "marchesitæ." In early mineralogy, this term was used broadly for various iron and copper sulfides, like pyrite.</note> of which they [the ancients] perhaps made no mention. There are also many kinds of <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "Chalcanthi." Metallic sulfates, used in making inks, dyes, and acids.</note> unknown to the ancients, as previously mentioned, and many types of sulfur. 

Add also many kinds of <term>talc</term> <note>original: "Talchi." A soft mineral, often used in cosmetics and alchemical preparations for its "silvery" sheen.</note> and many types of <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "Antimonij." Stibnite, used to purify gold and in medicinal preparations.</note> never cited among the ancients, even if some have dared to classify it under <term>stibium</term> <note>original: "stibio." The Greek and Roman name for antimony sulfide, used as eyeliner.</note>—though with neither distinguished authority nor valid reason, in my opinion. To these, add many kinds of <term>alum</term> <note>original: "aluminū." Chemical compounds used as fixatives for dyes and in tanning leather.</note> which antiquity mentions neither by name nor by effect, though they provide wonderful assistance in making gold.

I shall now commit to writing what I learned through experience a few days ago: a rusty-colored <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "Cinnabarim." Mercury sulfide, the most common ore of mercury, usually bright red.</note> was shown to me. Since there is no mention of it among the ancients, I would believe it was never even used. I state clearly that I did not find it, nor did I seek it; for who finds what they do not seek? And who would seek what they have never heard exists in the nature of things? I certainly discovered through many conjectures that it should be classified under cinnabar (if such a thing exists) or among metallic matters. It has a heavy weight; at first glance, its color is blackish and ashen, which remains if it is ground; but if it is roasted, it displays a redness. 

Furthermore, the sulfurous part within it, which is blue, departs first with a flame; then the part which is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "viui argenti." Liquid mercury.</note> vanishes entirely. The remaining part of the sulfur is stubborn and defies the flame. But if it is immersed in the liquid vapors of "consuming waters" <note>original: "consumtricium aquarum." Likely a reference to mineral acids like aqua fortis (nitric acid).</note>, the opposite happens. For the sulfurous portion is dissolved into the water with great force—far from resisting the fiery liquid—while the portion of quicksilver resists, remaining white and unconsumed at the bottom of the vessel. 

I have related a wondrous thing which, I conjecture, was unknown to antiquity; for although they also labored to produce gold, as was said before, they nevertheless used fewer substances. Furthermore, by means of <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts or cause oxidation.</note> (to use the words of <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century scholar.</note>), <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back to a solid, used to purify substances like sulfur or mercury.</note>, <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of purifying a liquid by heating it to vapor and then condensing it back into liquid.</note>, and other actions of which there was either no knowledge at all or no clear explanation among the ancient makers of gold, the craftsmen of our time perform many works. For to them is given—by the same author—the <term>elixir</term> <note>original: "elixirū." From the Arabic "al-iksīr," referring to a substance capable of transforming base metals into noble ones.</note>, a name borrowed from Arabic writers, which the Latins express as "medicine." It is established that it so penetrates the prior species of metals that it can corrupt them in such a way that, with only the "common matter" <note>The underlying prime matter of all metals, stripped of its specific characteristics.</note> remaining rather than their own specific nature, a different species of metal results through the effort of the art.

### ON GOLD. BOOK II. ###

CCc 4

The same [author], discussing the vessels of craftsmen, teaches that any metal you wish can be tinged with the color of gold, and (to quote his own words) perhaps even more beautiful, if there is a noble <term>elixir</term> <note>original: "elixir." In alchemical theory, this refers to a transformative substance or "ferment" capable of changing base metals into gold.</note> in which the craftsman has made no error. From this position, those who would defend the idea that there is only one form in metals could more easily protect the art; nor would he who wishes to defend several forms remain entirely without protection, not being content with those which Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote *De Mineralibus*, a key medieval text on mineralogy and alchemy.</note> admitted. For he would respond to the arguments thought up against him, asserting that those things which Albertus admitted into the primary matter of things capable of being generated and corrupted are not indeed perfected, but in a certain way inchoate.

But these matters are, and are held to be, too subtle to seem appropriate for treatment in this place; they are brought here only so that those bound by common opinions may realize not only that various ways of defending the art are not lacking, but also that more ways are present than those used by the ancient craftsmen. Furthermore, those who strive to drive the gold-making art from its seat without valid reason can be much more easily restrained—a seat which it has possessed for a long time by both legitimate title and long prescription of time. For they can learn from what we have said that gold can be made in many ways, not just one, and much more conveniently than was practiced in earlier centuries. For they are able to master those things which were known before, and the industry of the art has grown through long use; and subsequently, through brilliant minds turning over the same matter, ingenuity has come forth. Wherefore the detractors of the <term>chemical faculty</term> <note>original: "Chemicæ facultatis." Here referring to the discipline of alchemy/chemistry.</note> ought by right to cease from their more troublesome slanders. These detractors, although they are not among the number of those who grasp the subtler causes of nature, nor are they capable of those reasons which philosophers have investigated most sharply, nevertheless cannot deny that a trace of divine goodness—which pours out its gifts—is not lacking in each thing according to its own measure, and that these gifts can be strengthened by art so that they produce similar things.

Likewise, they cannot deny experiments that are not dissimilar, such as a small scent blowing across very long distances; or a small amount of <term>leaven</term> <note>original: "fermenti." Often used as a metaphor for the alchemical agent that "raises" or transforms the "dough" of base metals.</note> lifting a massive lump of dough; or a <term>magnet</term> <note>original: "Magnetis." The lodestone, whose invisible pull was a favorite example of "occult" or hidden natural forces.</note> joining iron to itself from a distance; or the <term>echeneis</term> <note>original: "echeneidos." The remora or "suckerfish," which ancient lore claimed could stop a massive ship in its tracks despite its small size.</note> creature bringing delay to vast ships; or a small infected vapor, by which many thousands of men are afflicted by the <term>pestilential</term> <note>original: "pestilentia." Referring to the plague or infectious miasmas that spread disease through invisible particles.</note> wasting. For why, if the things we have narrated [work] by contact itself and (so to speak) a certain

...as if by the sight of nature's virtue and power, they change, lead, and lead back things which, had they not been perceived by the senses themselves, no mortal would have previously believed. Why then should they deny that metals can be changed, when the senses support it and reason does not protest? Let them consider, I ask, whether any man by his own study and labor has ever been able to learn in detail why the great mass of a ship's hull is held motionless by a small fish? <note>Pico refers to the *echeneis* or remora, a fish which ancient writers like Pliny the Elder claimed could stop a galley in full sail by merely clinging to its hull.</note> Why a huge pile of flour is raised by a modest amount of leaven? Why the entire house is filled with scent from the smallest burning of a fragrant substance, and clothes shine? Why a thin and invisible vapor has the power to infect whole regions and their inhabitants, bringing destruction? For although many things have been disputed concerning primary qualities, intermediate ones, specific ones, supreme ones, lowest ones, and unknown ones—so that philosophers might arrive at a knowledge of these kinds of hidden things—it has reached the point where we read almost as many dissenting opinions as there are heads. Nothing else has been found to this day by which the mind can find rest, except that the thing to which this is attributed is what is called the mutual friendship or enmity of things—or as it was called by the Greeks, <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "sympathia." The idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected by invisible bonds of attraction and repulsion.</note>—which is ultimately a certain hidden and unperceived nature of things. *The same must be said when, by the modest juice of one or several herbs, mobile and fluid silver <note>Pico uses "argentum" here to refer to mercury, often called "quicksilver."</note> is fixed and hardens; or likewise when <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "hydrargyros."</note>, which otherwise vanishes entirely at the power of fire, is turned into either silver or gold; or when this is done with the thinnest grains of salt and alum, or various kinds of oil or waters, or other things not commonly known, since the art in all such matters is of such wide and far-reaching consideration that it overlooks nothing elementary, nor anything composed of the elements. It likewise composes, separates, joins, tears away, and turns upside down whatever it takes up to be handled, so that it may vary, move, and perfect what it finds either in subterranean caves or on the surface of the earth for the purpose of completing the task it has set for itself.*

There was a question among the disputing theologians: Could the Creator himself communicate to a created thing the power of "Creating"?—that is, the power of making something out of nothing, which is proper only to God and assigned to Divine Omnipotence? Opinions were voiced long ago in favor of either side, but however one decides concerning <term>creation</term> <note>original: "creatione." In theology, "creatio ex nihilo" is strictly the act of making something from nothing, distinct from "generatio" or "transmutatio" (transforming existing matter).</note>, there is no doubt that it has not been communicated either to nature or to

...to the art belongs a greater power, by which anything loses its prior form and receives a later one: for that which is said to be made by nature in a hundred years, is made by art in half an hour, and often in a hundredth part of an hour.

I myself have seen, shown by a friend more than once, in less than a tenth part of an hour, a metal split apart in such a way that the <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphur." In alchemical theory, sulfur was the active, masculine principle responsible for a metal's color and combustibility.</note> sought the heights, and the <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyros." Literally "water-silver," this was considered the passive, feminine principle of all metals.</note> the depths: I saw the form of the previous metal utterly abolished, and suddenly a new form—that is, a golden one—imposed by the skill of the art. Nature alone, which is to say, when destitute of the benefit of art, does not act thus; nor did antiquity act thus, as is clearly seen from ancient books, but there was a need for a longer bench <note>original: "longiore subsellio." Likely a legal or academic metaphor suggesting the ancients required a more protracted process or longer period of "sitting" with the work.</note>. Later practitioners have imitated and clearly rivaled nature, since it becomes clear every day how quickly [nourishment] is converted into blood, flesh, and food, whether through <term>coction</term> <note>original: "coctionem." The process of "ripening" or "digestion" through heat, a concept shared by medicine and alchemy.</note> or in any other way: for since antiquity, various opinions have been voiced concerning nutrition. We have touched upon only this one excellent way of changing metals in this place; we indicated others in the previous discussions, which, since we treated them above, it is by no means fitting to repeat at length.

# GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO OF MIRANDOLA, LORD AND COUNT OF CONCORDIA, ON GOLD.

## CHAPTER I.

### CONCERNING ANCIENT EXPERIMENTS IN MAKING GOLD *through the Chemical art.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' decorated with foliate patterns.</image-desc>

We dealt in the first book with the valuation of gold, showing that no cause can be found that is effective in persuading us that so much gold ought to be made that it measures all things; in the second, having brought forward various opinions from authors of different faculties, we then proved from the principles of philosophy—with theologians also in agreement—that gold can be made by art. In the third [book], which we have in hand, by examining both ancient and more recent experiments, we will demonstrate that gold has both been made and is made repeatedly; we will also subjoin most wholesome warnings concerning its use, lest in ab... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates it continues with "use."</note>

...so that it might be a slippery fall into misuse and disgrace. Furthermore, it is most certain and steadfast, and established by public consensus, that gold was once produced by the art and industry of men. To trace this back to the most ancient times, Vincent of Beauvais <note>Vincentius Belluacensis (c. 1184–1264), a Dominican friar and author of the *Speculum Maius*, one of the most significant medieval encyclopedias.</note> established the first man [Adam] as the master of the art, as we mentioned at the beginning. This knowledge reached through those closest to him, and through Moses, even to the apostolic Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221), founder of the Dominican Order. Pico suggests a lineage of secret knowledge passed through religious figures.</note> and his own times. It is related by the Greeks—which we have also indicated elsewhere—that the Argonauts did not sail to the region of Colchis for any other reason, nor, as it is told poetically, did Jason carry the golden fleece of Phryxus from the house of King Aeetes to Greece, but rather a book made from a ram’s skin, in which was known the methods by which gold could be made through the alchemical art <term>artem chemicam</term>. Therefore, it was not without injury to the truth that those ancients called it the "Phryxean fleece," for it was called a "golden fleece" because of its power to produce gold.

This can easily be seen in both common and hidden books. In the records of Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia. Pico refers to the entry under "deras" (fleece).</note>, this is widely commended to posterity under the letter [Epsilon]; moreover, it is mentioned briefly and somewhat obscurely by Apollonius in the second book of the *Argonautica*, where he sings that the golden Phryxean fleece was placed there by Mercury. In that passage, the Greek commentator <note>A scholiast or ancient annotator of the text.</note> writes that by the contact of Mercury, the skin of the ram was made into gold; what could more clearly favor the alchemical art? For these are his words: <note>original: "τῇ ἐπαφῇ τοῦ ἑρμου τὸ δέρμα τοῦ κριοῦ γένεσθαι χρυσόν"</note> "by the touch of Hermes, the skin of the ram became gold." 

Most clearly indeed, Charax <note>Charax of Pergamon, a Roman-era historian whose work survives only in fragments cited by others.</note>, noble not so much for history as for philosophy, has recorded that the skin for which the Argonauts sailed was not to be considered that of a living ram, but was a method for the making of gold—a "parchment" <note>original: "μεμβράνην"</note> as he says, "encompassing" <note>original: "περιειλημένην"</note>, that is, a method contained within a parchment. Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Thessalonica (c. 1115–1195), a Byzantine scholar and archbishop.</note> cites this same thing in his work on the geography of Dionysius the Libyan. What more? The "golden fleece" had even passed into a proverb among the Greeks when someone made precious things out of cheap materials. Under the veils of fables, the ancient writers did not only hide the written dogma of the making of gold as being contained in a ram's parchment kept in the house of King Aeetes, but they also intended to indicate the manner and the method signaled under the names of the Dragon and Mercury. Indeed, it is very well known among professors of the alchemical art that <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "vivum argentum," or liquid mercury.</note> is signified by both the name of Mercury and by the word "Dragon." Consequently, they claim that gold is said to be "made by the contact of Mercury," and that a "watchful Dragon" was placed to guard the golden fleece. We also read it written in the Orphic verses concerning the theft of the golden fleece, that it was under a tree which supported the Phryxean skin...

Not only shrubs and vegetables, but *chalcantum*—that is, vitriol <note>original: *atramentum*. While this usually means ink, in a metallurgical context it refers to metallic sulfates or vitriols.</note>—not *calachanton* nor *psalachantan*, so that it might be distinguished from the names of plants by its metallurgical term. Nor is it far from the likeness of truth that among the ancients, the written recipes for *Chrysopoeia* <term>Chrysopoeia: The alchemical art of "making gold" (from the Greek chrysos, "gold," and poiein, "to make").</term>—that is, the making of gold—were noted by the name of the golden skin, and the golden lamb or ram. From this, it is likely that the name "golden tree" used by the poet Ovid arose, since fruits are brought forth from a tree just as effects, which are wished for, are prepared from a written composition; and that verse also seems to point here: "that he might carry off the gold of the stolen skin."

  Nor were there lacking those who attributed the riches of Tantalus <note>A figure in Greek mythology known for his great wealth and his eternal punishment in the underworld.</note> to a chemical composition written on lambskins. From this comes the kingdom of his son Pelops and the descendants of Pelops, spread far and wide. Thus, it did not seem out of place that Thyestes, the younger son of Pelops, sought the lamb—that is, the composition for making gold inscribed on a lamb’s skin, which the elder son Atreus kept among his secrets—and that Thyestes extorted it from his brother’s wife through adultery, which led to hatred and the tragedies of blood-stained banquets. Ancient poets mention this matter, though under an obscure veil, as do Cicero, Seneca, and Papirius. Above, it was also related by us on the authority of Callisthenes that the riches of the Pelopidae arose not from sheep fleeces or taxes, but from metals—though these accounts are faded by their great antiquity.

  Let us not linger; from the Phrygians and Greeks the art spread to other nations, which the Egyptians, most devoted to the study of wisdom, practiced above all. Among them, in the time of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 AD) who famously ordered the burning of Egyptian alchemical texts to prevent them from funding rebellions.</note>, the ability to make gold was as public as the cultivation of the fields. It is reported that this art was carried forward with its own authority to the times of Constantine, so that at that time the philosopher Michael Psellus <note>A 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar. Pico notes his work on alchemy as a bridge to later Greek knowledge.</note> composed an elegant little book in the Greek language about making gold.

  Perhaps someone will say: why does the art itself not exist today, which is said to have once existed publicly? I will say (to omit many things that could be answered): why does the art of dyeing garments purple no longer exist? It was once celebrated not only in Tyre and Sidon, but sung of throughout the whole world. Today it is nowhere, and neither is that shellfish from whose blood the color was prepared among

...recognized by artificers: the material for making gold is ready at hand, and the ability is present in many places, even if it had utterly perished in Egypt. Furthermore, a way of producing gold was not lacking to Latium <note>The region of Italy including Rome.</note> in earlier times; for there exists the testimony of Pliny in the thirty-third book of his *Natural History*, who taught that there was one method of making gold from orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*. Orpiment is a bright yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and long associated with alchemical gold-making due to its color.</note>, which was mined in Syria for painters from the very surface of the earth, having the color of gold.

"He ordered," [Pliny] says, "a great weight [of orpiment] to be smelted, and he clearly produced excellent gold, but of such small weight that he felt a loss." Pliny puts forth this well-known matter regarding orpiment alone, and says that gold was produced through art, of which thing perhaps he could have been an eyewitness.

For he had lived in the age of the earlier Caesars, and not only reached the reign of Caius <note>Caius Julius Caesar Germanicus, better known as Caligula.</note>, but lived through the reign of Claudius (who ruled after Caius) and even to that of Vespasian. For he served as a soldier with Germanicus Caesar and committed his deeds to memory; he also says he saw Claudius's son—the one who succeeded as princeps to his nephew through his brother Germanicus—and saw Messalina sitting beside him while he held public spectacles. Pliny the Younger affirmed that his uncle also wrote under Nero, and the title of the *Natural History* indicated he dedicated it to Vespasian.

But Caius felt a loss <note>i.e., the process cost more to perform than the value of the gold it produced.</note>; perhaps the cause was a smaller supply than was necessary, and the greater expense of sailing and transporting orpiment to Rome. He might perhaps have felt a profit if such a mass had been available to him as Onesicritus <note>A Greek historical writer and officer under Alexander the Great.</note> wrote was found in Carmania; he would have felt it if he had thoroughly understood the Egyptian methods, which were a source of fear to Diocletian (whom we mentioned above). It is written in the records of the Greeks that when the Emperor Diocletian had afflicted the Egyptians with inhumane cruelty, fearing lest by the art of making gold—in which they were powerful—they might take up the daring to rebel with restored riches, he ordered all the books of the chemical art <note>original: *Chemicæ facultatis*.</note> to be searched for and burned. This can be seen in the *Suda* <note>original: *Suidam*. A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> under the tenth collection of elements. After Diocletian, there was such a power of making gold—not from orpiment but from golden sand—that it was done publicly by those who held the art, provided that they paid certain golden *scruples* <note>A *scrupulus* was a small unit of weight or a coin value.</note> to the Emperor. For this reason, those first two laws were placed in the *Code of Justinian* under the title *On Mine-workers*. This sand, called *Chrysamos* <term>Chrysamos: From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *ammos* (sand).</term> by the Greeks, was called *Balux* by both Spaniards and Latins; this is clear enough in the civil laws and in Pliny, to say nothing of the ridiculous explanations <note>original: *glossematibus*.</note> of these words, *balaca* and *Chrysamos*, by Accursius <note>A 13th-century Italian jurist famous for his "Great Gloss" on the Roman Law.</note>.

A certain man of our time, otherwise diligent and learned, thinks that one should read "Chrysamon" rather than "Chrysamos," and interprets this as the vessel in which gold is poured. But "Chrysale" is the name of that vessel, even in the works of Plautus, and it is now commonly pronounced with three letters inverted. "Chrysamos," however, ought beyond any doubt to be read, meaning **golden sand**, which was not dug out of the earth but collected from the seashore, and from which gold was prepared by certain mixtures.

The first two laws [of the Roman code] decree concerning this [sand], while the remaining laws are to be understood as concerning mines, which can easily be discerned from the sequence of the words and from the difference in the tax—or as the Law says, the *Canon* <note>original: *canonis*. Here referring to a fixed tax or tribute paid to the state.</note>. For the "Chemists" <note>original: *Chemici*. This refers to alchemists or those practicing the chemical arts.</note> owed only a few <term>scruples</term> <note>A very small unit of weight, here used to denote a minor tax or fee.</note>, whereas the miners owed a tenth part to the Imperial Treasury. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar known for his works on philosophy and the occult.</note> was the first of seven to reveal this kind of gold-making through chemistry, teaching that there is a certain maritime or coastal sand which is called "golden" because of its color, and is called **golden sand** by some. His words are: "There is a certain coastal sand called gold-bearing <note>original: *chrysitis*</note> because of its color, and some call this very thing *chrysammos* <note>original: ἄμμος τίς ἐστι παραλία χρυσῖτις καλουμένη ἀπὸ τοῦ χρώματος, οἱ δὲ τοῦτο αὐτὸ χρύσαμμον ὀνομάζουσιν.</note>." Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> also, while discussing the power of simple medicines, began a discourse on the earth and made mention of gold-bearing and silver-bearing earths; soon after, he speaks of golden sand, and mentions how they estimated the profit from its quantity by sight. Thus, a certain distinction can be found in reality between *baluca* <note>A term used by Pliny for small grains of natural gold.</note> and *chrysamos*, since according to Pliny, *baluca* refers to the smallest filings of that [natural] gold.

*Chrysamos*, however, although it consists of the most minute grains, those grains are not themselves gold, but rather the color of gold; gold is prepared from it by much "cooking" <note>original: *coctura*. In alchemy, this refers to the prolonged heating or digestion of a substance.</note> and various mixtures. Otherwise, it would not have been so inexpensive for the metal-workers to be counted among the Emperor’s [subjects]. Psellus himself taught how to extract gold from this, and recorded five or six other preparations in writing. Yet, he professed this with much protestation, as if he were doing so compelled by a certain honorable force; hence his words: "my master, my ruler, the tyrant of my soul <note>original: ὁ δεσπότης ὁ ἐμὸς δυνάστης, ἡ τῆς ἐμῆς ψυχῆς τυραννίς.</note>."

In addition to these, there exists the testimony of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on the natural sciences and alchemy.</note>, based on experiments he had read, that gold can be made through art; for he assented to that common and legitimate proverb (as was fitting): "everyone is to be believed who is an expert in his own art." What of the fact that he brought forward not only the experiments of others, but his own? For when discussing **quicksilver** <note>original: *viuo argento*. Mercury.</note>, he said that it is the material substance of all metals, in which...

Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath known for his works on natural philosophy.</note> did not see this in the caves of the earth or the hidden retreats of nature; for he does not report that he ever penetrated such places with a crowd of miners. In alchemical theory, metals were thought to be composed of these two "principles."</note>, which perhaps is celebrated only once every hundred years, just to learn how they are made in those foul chambers. 

Indeed, there exists the testimony and experiment of Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, a noble philosopher and physician, recorded in writing among the legal monuments and the additions of William—who obtained the surname "the Speculator" <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), author of the *Speculum Iudiciale*, a foundational legal text.</note>. For he writes that Arnaldus himself, who is extolled there with wondrous praise, submitted rods of gold which he had fashioned in Rome to every test. This is recorded in the title concerning the **crime of forgery** <note>original: *de crimine falsi*. This refers to legal cases determining if alchemical gold was "counterfeit" or true gold.</note>. It is unlikely that they omitted the use of the **water** <note>original: *aquam*. Likely "aqua fortis" (nitric acid), used to separate gold from silver.</note> which separates gold from silver—the most certain and effective proof of gold in all respects—if indeed its use was known at that time. Certainly, however, the test of fire was not lacking, in which fictitious gold vanishes if it is burned seven times, as was handed down by Albertus, who was quite a bit earlier than Arnaldus. But—to remain silent about the Balearic Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>, noble for his many works, before I come to the men of our own time—I shall relate the testimony of Albert of Cologne, of the **Order of Friars Minor** <note>original: *ex ordine minorum*. This is a curious attribution, as the famous Albertus Magnus was a Dominican (Order of Preachers), not a Franciscan (Minor). Pico may be referring to a different "Albert" or a pseudo-Albertine text.</note>, concerning himself.

For when he had written a volume on the **fifth essence** <term>Quinta Essentia</term> <note>The "quintessence" or purest part of a substance, believed in alchemy to be the key to transmutation.</note> of sublunary species, and in how many ways it could be extracted from almost every single thing, he added that he could have shown, had he wished, how a reader might finally arrive at the point where, in the blink of an eye, imperfect metals could be changed into silver and gold. He asserts that the principle of this matter was revealed to him in an intellectual manner while he was held in an old prison. Or perhaps he held it to be so, having attested to it from the decrees of his own mouth (as he says) to the **Evangelical men**—the name he gave to the men of the order subject to the institutes of Saint Francis—lest, at the instigation of a malignant demon, they should fall into alchemical operations, since none of the philosophers has ever revealed the truth in his books...

## CHAPTER II.

### *Concerning the experiments of our own time in the making of gold, including many remarks on the excellence of the chemical faculty.*

It is most certain—proven not only by hearing but by sight, and by the testimony of many living people as well as my own—that in my age, silver and gold have very often been produced through the art of metallic conversion <note>transmutation</note>. This has been achieved not by one single method of composition, but by many. I am not moved to believe this merely by the volumes I read a short time ago, which were dedicated to Leo, the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521), a great patron of the arts and sciences</note>, and which seem to point toward the true art. Indeed, the experiments are so undeniable that one of the authors who wrote a book in verse began it this way:

> *The gold-bearing art, sought by us with the modest*
> *powers of our mind, and brought forth over a long time.*
> <note>original: *Auriferam paruis animi pro viribus artem, Quæsitam nobis & longo tempore partam.*</note>

And he had closed another *Chrysopoeia* <term>Chrysopoeia: From the Greek, meaning "the making of gold."</term> singing of himself:

---

> *Thus like a second Jason,*
> *he carried off the Golden Fleece from the fortunate Colchis.*
> <note>original: *Sic alter Iason, Aurea felici deuexit vellera Colcho.* A mythological reference comparing the alchemist's success to Jason obtaining the Golden Fleece.</note>

For poets easily write what is plausible in place of what is true—all the more so because that author revealed enough that he was writing in the manner of poets at the end of his previous volume, when he mentioned the gates of horn and ivory <note>A classical literary trope: true dreams pass through the gate of horn, while false or deceptive dreams pass through the gate of ivory.</note>. Many historians, too, are not to be counted as eyewitnesses in this matter, such as the one who left a record in a massive volume of three or four recipes for "fixing" mobile silver <note>original: *argenti mobilis*, a term for mercury or quicksilver</note> and making gold; let us dismiss such accounts.

I shall instead report first what I have heard, and then what I have found most certain by my own eyes. There died a few years ago Nicolaus of Mirandola, a priest of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>. He was an old man known to us, of upright life and pure from any crime, and moreover a man of great abstinence and solitude. Both in life and after death, he was held by his brothers to be of great sanctity and a participant in divine revelations. You can easily remember, my spouse, some of these revelations being sent to me in Germany by you—including the prediction of the war brought upon the Venetians under Pope Julius <note>Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513), known as the "Warrior Pope," who formed the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508.</note>...

<header>GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

<margin>+</margin>
By this art, he produced silver at Bologna and gold at Carpi, according to the testimony of many. He also did so in Jerusalem, where he stayed for many years for the sake of his religion as a superior of his order. There, too, he made gold, and he reported this to me with his own lips; he is still alive to testify to it. Recently, Antonio, a surgeon from Mirandola and the man's nephew by his brother, also told me that his uncle freely and frankly confessed to him that he was thoroughly skilled in the art of making gold <note>original: *auri faciendi artem*</note>. He showed me a book written in his uncle's own hand concerning various matters. In that book, through both the reasoning provided, the testimony of a companion, and even two successful experiments, I discovered that the art of making gold was indeed recorded there for his own use. However, to others, he clearly disguised the art by interposing many irrelevant things and using indirect speech.

<margin>+</margin>
Furthermore, there was among mortals in our own age a man named Apollinaris, a priest of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note> of good reputation, who did not hesitate to affirm to his friends that he consistently held more than twenty methods by which he could produce true gold. After completing their religious duties, he and his companions had no other pursuit in which they more willingly occupied their minds than in new discoveries of metallic conversions <note>transmutations</note>. They believed, and not without reason, that such things were more beneficial for the common good than spending every day in literary battles and philosophical arguing. For they saw that such practical application perhaps belonged to the very heart of philosophy and medicine, in which they had previously been professors. They had read in Aristotle that "the generation of one thing is the corruption of another" <note>original: *unius rei generationem alterius esse corruptionem*; a fundamental principle of Aristotelian physics suggesting that when one substance is formed, another is destroyed</note>, and that this occurs not universally, but in particular instances. They had also read that elements are mixed, and that the things that coalesce from those elements can be transformed.

<margin>A note on things made by nature and by art</margin>
They knew that God and nature have made nothing in vain. They held it as a certainty that man was established as the master of the lower world of nature, *and by his wit, things could be brought about through nature which nature would never achieve of its own accord if it were left without man’s ingenuity.* This is clearly seen in the grafting of trees, in painting, in medicine, and in almost every duty of life. If this is so conspicuous elsewhere, why should it be obscure in the case of metals? For metals are bound together in such close society that one often lies hidden within another. They knew that the diligence of talented minds ought to look toward this: that they should not be content merely to have known the things of nature in a general or common way, but should aspire of their own accord to that knowledge which is introduced piece by piece and submitted to the senses. They knew that "cyclic disputes" <note>original: *disputationes Cyclicas*; likely referring to repetitive, circular scholastic debates that do not lead to new discovery</note> wander in uncertainty, and that those who give themselves too much to such things usually worship their own imaginings instead of the truth; but that truth lies open to the senses and is confirmed by the public agreement of men—

<margin>Note this Testimony</margin>
I come now to those things which have been revealed before my own eyes without any veil: there lives to this day a man known to me and a friend, who in my presence has produced gold and silver with his own hands from metallic substances more than sixty times, and he achieved this not by one way only, but by many. I also saw, during the preparation of a "metallic water" <note>likely a corrosive acid or solvent used in metallurgy</note> in which neither silver, nor gold, nor even sulfur or mercury—the principles of gold—were placed, that silver and gold were unexpectedly generated. However, this was not in such a quantity that it could be practiced regularly, for the profit was less than the expense. 

<margin>+</margin>
I also saw, as I disclosed at the beginning of the work, that silver and gold were frequently brought forth beforehand, with grains of them poured out separately, and no small amount of gold hidden within the silver. I saw a tiny amount of silver extracted from bronze by the power of waters <note>chemical solutions or acids</note>. And this is one method of making gold and silver, as we said before, but it is not to be highly valued, since it merely draws out that which is perfect from within more imperfect metals. However, when gold is made not from metals but from metallic things <note>mineral ores or non-metallic salts</note>, a greater utility is sometimes obtained; but this matter, though true, is often so varied...

He was drawn to this more by the benefit of art and nature than by poverty, since he possesses quite ample wealth and even more ample skill in the art. At this very moment, unless he passed away a short time ago, there lives a man who does not lack the means to maintain the status of a semi-noble person; by his hands, I saw copper turned into silver and gold by a certain juice, whether of a herb or a shrub, with a powerful fire driving its force into that metal.

I will not cease to recount what a certain poor man told me he achieved through a dream, and soon proved by the work itself. While he was anxious in spirit, not knowing where to turn to endure hunger—for he was oppressed by the great scarcity of grain, oppressed by debt, and oppressed by a huge number of children—he gave himself over to sleep and saw a certain heavenly being listed in the catalog of saints, who taught the art of making gold through riddles <note>original: *per ænigmata*</note>. Then he indicated a "water" that he should use to produce the gold. Using that, he made gold, first from his own resources <note>original: *ex sese*</note>, though not of great weight, but enough then that he provided food for his family. He also made gold from iron twice, and from orpiment three or four times; and by experiment, he made it manifest to me that the gold-bearing art is not empty, but true. For that reason, a little later for my own amusement, I composed those riddles in hexameter verses, some of which I cited above, and I added a prologue and epilogue where I discussed in those same poems who is truly wealthy.

Finally, in recent days, I both drank in with my eyes and handled with my hands gold that was made in my presence from silver in the space of about three hours, without any prior conversion of the silver into either quicksilver or into "water"—that is, into the first...

### CHAPTER III.

->*A warning to those who imprudently reproach those skilled in making gold, to whom the title of "philosophers" belongs more than to other investigators of nature.*<-

I have thought that these examples, fortified by many reasons and various authorities, would serve to exercise both myself and others, and would satisfy you in part. I wished to reveal what I know to be most certain in order to remove the fog from many minds; for I could not restrain myself from writing these things both for your sake and as a warning to those who imprudently pass judgment on things they do not understand. Therefore, I shall consider my effort worthwhile <note>original: *precium operæ*</note> if they are thus warned by me to learn not to argue; and henceforth to stop asserting that what they themselves do not know cannot be known by others. Even worse and more detestable is when they either treat men as criminals or hiss them off the stage <note>original: *exsibilare*; a theatrical term for rejection</note> as if they were suspected of madness—men who either rightly possess the art of making gold or practice it skillfully. *And what is no less worthy of pity than laughter: they ascribe to a malignant demon what should be ascribed to God (the author of all truth), to good spirits, to nature, to art, and to human industry.*

For why should it be doubted—if the power and cunning of the demon is brought into the discussion—whether someone not unlearned in higher things, nor ignorant of letters, could so silence such detractors through the experiments of the chemical faculty <term>Chemiæ facultatis; the art and study of chemical transformations</term> that even the birth from their own mother, from whom they themselves were born, might be placed in doubt? Since a wicked demon could have changed into the form, not of Amphitryon <note>In Greek myth, Zeus disguised himself as Amphitryon to seduce Alcmene; Pico uses this to argue that if we blame demons for everything we don't understand, we could even doubt our own parentage</note>, but of a husband or any other, and embraced a mother who believed her husband was the one laboring to produce children.

Well known is the story concerning the conception of both Alexander the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great</note> and King Seleucus, and a long time later, of Merlin. The various accounts recorded in the writings of our theologians, both ancient and modern, regarding the wickedness and deceit of succubus and incubus demons <note>Demons believed to have sexual relations with humans</note> in these matters are extensive. Shall the health derived from the medical art also suffer slander, simply because a demon is able to involve himself and bring invisible [remedies] to diseases or wounds...

<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s argument that alchemical knowledge, like medical knowledge, is a gift from God. He is addressing critics who believe alchemy is either impossible or the work of demons, arguing instead that a true "philosopher" must understand the physical world through experience and experiment.</meta>

<page-num>420</page-num>
<header>GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

remedies, and to do many other things, which others have remembered, and we ourselves have also addressed in those dialogues titled *Strix, or on the Delusion of Demons* <note>original: *Strix siue de ludificatione dæmonum*; Pico's famous 1523 work on witchcraft</note>. I will omit the decrees of Hippocrates, the prince of physicians, for whom the false god of the nations, Apollo, was held to be the author—Apollo, who in antiquity deluded people in many ways with demonic oracles. We have already mentioned above that it is recorded in memory that these decrees of Hippocrates came from the burned temple of Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius was the Greek god of medicine; his temples served as early hospitals</note>; yet among our people, the use of those decrees remains insofar as they are held to be true.

Since the greatest and best God is the primary author of all truth, let the detractors learn that they are rebuked by Aristotle, who says that those who pass judgment after inspecting only a few things are at fault. Let them learn that they are disapproved of by legal experts as "uncivil" <note>original: *inciuiles*; a legal term for acting against the spirit of the law</note> when they judge without perceiving the entire law. Let them learn that they are vehemently condemned by Annaeus <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher</note> and that Claudius Caesar is mocked for settling disputes after hearing only one side, and often neither. Let them then learn that gold can indeed be made through experience without a knowledge of the more subtle letters <note>meaning formal academic study or literature</note>; but a professor of the chemical art cannot be perfect in all his parts <note>original: *numeris omnibus*; an idiom for being complete or perfect</note> if he has not thoroughly mastered natural philosophy and applied to the experiments of the senses those things whose wandering consideration tortures so many—things, I say, that are often discussed but never confirmed, yet are frequently discovered through the benefit of experiments.

Why should I grant the name of "philosopher" to one who has seen certain books of *Philosophical Physics* <note>original: *philosophicæ auscultationis*; a reference to Aristotle’s *Physics*</note> but remains utterly ignorant of herbs, shrubs, metals, stones, and their powers, mixtures, and transformations? Is not the title of philosopher more justly suited to him who first knows the things of nature in general, and then thoroughly masters the powers of the sublunary and subterranean seeds through their specific parts? From this, he may perceive with his mind the harmony and strife <note>original: *concordiam & litem*; a reference to the classical theory that the universe is governed by the forces of attraction and repulsion</note> of lower things, and consequently their generation and destruction. May he then rise to the admiration of the divine majesty, which has granted man not only the ability to recognize hidden things enclosed in the bowels of the earth, but also the power to produce them himself by God's own gift and the assistance of nature. Thus, in many ways, he can easily help mortals, both in the health of the body and in external matters.

Will not he who holds these truths stand as far above babbling disputants as a body stands above the shadow of a body? Or as much as truth stands above fickle and jumping operations? For if in words...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that true philosophy requires practical, experimental knowledge of nature (alchemy) rather than just book learning. He defends alchemy as a divine gift and rebukes critics who judge the art without understanding its physical and philosophical foundations.</summary>
