--- Page 432 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of alchemy. Having previously argued that truth can be found through experience, he now contrasts the practical demonstrations of the alchemist with the abstract, often uncertain theories of traditional "sophists."</meta>

<page-num>421</page-num>
<header>ON GOLD. BOOK III.</header>

If deeds excel words, and if it is better to perform great things than to speak of them, then the name of "philosopher" <note>literally "lover of wisdom"</note> will more truly and excellently suit a man of action. Would a fair judge of matters prefer one who demonstrates a thing and places it before one’s very eyes, or one who—relying only on his own imaginings, whether through the common rules of dialectic <note>the art of logical debate</note> or through metaphysical concepts—believes himself to know something, yet is never certain, always wavering, and always occupied with borrowed arguments? To the latter, antiquity would surely have given the name of "sophist," while to the former, it would have granted the name of "wise man." Not even the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy emphasized physical observation</note> would object to this, for their own doctrines rely on the senses, from which they strive to draw their proofs. It is by these same senses that those skilled in the Chemical faculty <note>the practitioners of alchemy</note>—scorning the same abstract arguments—bring forth evidence against a resisting adversary and secure victory over him. Thus, you will find it was neither rashly nor without reason that the Greeks called such men "wise" and gave that name to their decrees.

Among the Arabs, indeed, their very instruments, and even the clay which the professors of Chemistry are accustomed to use, are honored with the title of "wisdom" <note>original: *lutum sapientiae* or "clay of wisdom," a specialized paste used to seal alchemical vessels airtight</note>. Both the unrefined and the skilled craftsmen, taught by those we have named, know that they stand above all those who practice the organic or instrumental arts <note>mechanical crafts that require tools and physical apparatus</note>. For it is well known (since who is there who does not know it?) that among the people with whom we have lived for many centuries, it has been agreed that gold should be the measure of all external things—those things which the Peripatetics called "goods" and the Stoics <note>a school of philosophy that taught virtue as the only good, viewing wealth as a secondary "advantage"</note> called "advantages" <note>original: *commoda*</note>. What is even more surprising is that a great many mortals expose their own bodies to the risk of death for the sake of obtaining gold—to say nothing of those impious men, completely forgetful of themselves, who even value gold above their own souls. This gold the wicked certainly abuse, while the upright and well-mannered use it rightly. If this rarest gift has been sent to them from heaven, it is fitting that they both feel and, as far as possible, return the greatest thanks to God; as such, they should not envy any mortal, no matter how wealthy or powerful.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*If the title of "wealthy" truly belongs to anyone because of external things, it rightly belongs to those skilled in making gold through the chemical art.*<-

**C**ertainly, among the ancients, there was no small question among philosophers and orators as to who was truly rich and how such a person should be described...

->### GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

This theme has not been left untouched by the poets, as when one said of Crassus <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus (c. 115–53 BCE), a Roman general and politician famously considered the wealthiest man in Roman history</note>, "Are you alone rich?" From this, another arose who measured the rich man by philosophy alone. Yet there were those who did not lack the opinion that a man is rich who has land, or money put out at interest, or even one rich in embroidered garments and gold. *But the one who would truly call that man rich who is first imbued with the religion of Christ, then flourishes with a sincere health of mind and body, and finally is endowed with the power of making silver and gold, would by no means seem to be deserving of disapproval.*

For he who entirely lacks the primary goods of the soul is the poorest of all, being so far from being rich that he does not even deserve the common name of "man." The same applies to one who suffers from physical misery, forever and repeatedly lacking his desired health; or one who will never be secure from war and will always hang upon the whim of princes; or one who lacks foreign trade and will always dread either bandits or the angry sea; or one who relies on the wealth of the countryside and will frequently fear weather that is harmful to the crops. As for those who occupy themselves with dishonest gains and devote themselves to the deceits of usury <note>the practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates</note>, besides the fact that they have a bad reputation among well-educated men, they are also tortured by the internal bite of a wicked conscience. How could such people ever be numbered among the blessed by any right? Even wealth prepared by one's ancestors can be snatched away most easily; everyone knows that kingdoms and princedoms often change—even he who knows of the man who begged for bread after Carthage was conquered <note>a reference to the dramatic reversals of fortune seen in the Punic Wars, where even the powerful were reduced to nothing</note>. But who shall take away that art which resides in the mind of a healthy man, as long as he shall live? Who shall stop him, wherever in the world he may be, provided that fire is present and certain liquids or powders are not lacking, from making gold for himself?

Certainly, what the German and Pannonian <note>Pannonia was a province of the Roman Empire, roughly corresponding to modern-day Hungary and parts of its neighbors</note> princes dig out from the deepest caverns of the mountains over many months, and what the Kings of Spain prepare for themselves with a great fleet over three years—when, setting sail from the ports of Baetica <note>Southern Spain/Andalusia</note> and Portugal, they measure the Atlantic and Indian waves to visit unknown regions fertile in gold—that, the master of the **golden art** <term>Alchemy; the "art" of transforming base metals into gold</term> prepares with less expense, with greater profit, and in a few days, either at home or trusting in a small inn, and even more often with a small household of servants. It was my pleasure to signify this matter, which is hidden in those "golden and silver enigmas" we cited before, through verse:

> *The man rich in land, rich in embroidered clothing, and in a*
> *Lofty hall, or a kingdom, is never rich in my judgment;*
> *Never is he truly rich, even if relying on a Spanish ship*
> *Across the Atlantic sea, a despiser of the North and South winds...*

...with that gold, which is either drawn out from the caverns of the earth, or gathered from the sands of rivers, and that it [alchemical gold] possesses the same properties for common use as the gold dug out from metallic mines. For the opinion of those has been rejected who tried to reconcile differing views by conceding that one could be made by art, but denying the other.

For never is corporeal nature found without its qualities or properties, or if you prefer, its gifts; nor can we ever arrive at the knowledge of any essence, if we follow nature, once those gifts have been abolished. Therefore, Aristotle judged that these very conditions—which, although many and varied, he called by the single term <term>symbebekota</term> <note>original: συμβεβηκότα</note>, that is, "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that a thing possesses (like color or weight) which are not part of its essential definition but help us identify it.</note>—help us to know that which is, namely the nature of a thing. If indeed gold produced by art possesses the same essence, it follows that it will possess the same qualities as the gold nature has brought forth, and thus it will be of exactly the same price, and it will be permitted to be valued and sold for as much. We have said "all accidents" which can indeed be recognized by those skilled in handling gold, not just some of them, or even most; for if even one were missing from the whole, it could be held suspect under the name of falsehood. And although those who debate on ethics wish that counterfeit gold or silver—which is usually called "sophistic"—be allowed to be sold as counterfeit, so that it may be sold for as much as it is worth if properly valued; nevertheless, because it presents one thing at first sight while carrying another hidden in its inner depths, the matter is full of danger. For this reason, I would never support their opinion with "hands and feet" <note>A Latin idiom, *pedibus manibusque*, meaning to support something with all one's might or completely.</note>, since the less prudent—who make up a great part of those living among mortals—could be openly deluded.

Added to this is the fact that a certain path seems to be laid out for fraudulent men toward false and stealthy coinage through the manufacture of counterfeit gold and silver, which is called "sophistic." For although the duties of making metal and minting it are different, and the arts that prepare either one are and are held to be different (since one precedes and the other follows), nonetheless, imposters seem to have found an easier way for malicious trickery when they already possess false metal than those who try to pervert legitimate metal by mixing in something worse. Indeed, the opportunity for committing a crime should never be increased for evil men. For this reason, perhaps, Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a famous scholar and theologian who was rumored to have discovered the philosopher's stone.</note>, while [considering] the art by which metals are changed as...

...just as he would have left the true kind, he rejected it as false, by which many craftsmen merely counterfeit the colors of either gold or silver. When these craftsmen believe they have successfully imparted the yellow paleness of gold or the silvery whiteness to lesser metals, they exult as if they have become masters of the art, yet they are plainly deceiving their buyers.

It can also be established by prudent men that if it is true gold—even if man-made <term>factitium</term> <note>Latin: "factitium," meaning produced by human skill or alchemy rather than mined.</note> rather than natural—provided it is not fake, false, or sophisticated, it can be presented and mixed with medicinal foods <note>original: "alexipharmacis," referring to alexipharmics, which were ancient remedies used as antidotes to poison.</note> or boiled in waters. This is no different from the gold said to be dug out from the hidden chambers of the earth. Indeed, it is even much more useful than that which is stamped with the mark of a Prince or the Republic. Since this fact remains hidden from many, I will attempt to explain the matter more extensively. For I have known those who, although they knew how to make gold, refused to teach the art of making it to their friends and kin, fearing they might abuse it; that is, they feared lest the man-made gold might still retain the nature of mercury <note>original: "viui argenti," literally "living silver," the common name for quicksilver or mercury.</note> or of some other thing thought to be harmful if consumed. For they had perhaps heard that verse: *he mixed lethal weights of quicksilver, so that the doubled force might compel a swift death;* and they had easily read the books of certain authors who affirm that the properties of natural gold—especially its power to bring joy and to resist leprosy <note>In medieval and Renaissance medicine, gold was frequently used in "cordials" to treat melancholy (to "bring joy") and for skin diseases like leprosy.</note>—are not found in man-made gold. Timon rightly opposed these people during his disputes on meteorological matters, though he wrongly allowed for the use of astrological images <note>Talismans or symbols engraved under specific planetary alignments, which Pico generally opposed as superstitious.</note> to be summoned for the making of gold.

I would free those who labor under this suspicion from all fear: for if it is true gold produced by art, it possesses the true essence of gold, and consequently all the accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are the physical properties that follow the internal essence of a thing.</note> that flow from it according to nature, as we have shown before. Therefore, it will also bring joy, provided those are the properties of gold, and it will oppose leprosy, if that power belongs to gold.

But you might say perhaps that mercury and other poisonous substances enter into the gold that art strives to produce. To this I would affirm that gold is procreated from those very same things in the deepest seats of the earth. Furthermore, I would suggest that gold can be made by art in many different ways, not just one. I would also add this: if any poisonous agents are perhaps used to complete the art, they do not reach the essence of the final product, but are instead used as the instruments of transmutation. To this I will also bring another point: that once quicksilver has been reduced into either solid silver or gold, just as it has ceased to be quicksilver, so too has it lost its lethal property—whether that property flowed from some occult quality, or as it pleased Albert <note>A reference to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on alchemy and minerals.</note>...

...[Al]bertus <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, a prominent medieval philosopher and theologian who wrote 'De Mineralibus' (On Minerals).</note> regarding its evident sharpness, which formed from cold and moisture. For even if he did not wish it to exceed the second degree of cold and moisture, he nevertheless concluded it harms the nerves for that reason; though there are those who prefer that quicksilver <term>viuum argentum</term> <note>Latin: "vivum argentum," literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note> is not cold, but hot by nature, and they contend that this is easily defended by its own agreement and by several other qualities.

Nor should I omit that through many transformations, all things called poisonous are purified by the benefit of fire, *and take on another form, another nature*, which certainly also happens in subterranean caverns, where sulfur, copper, and quicksilver come together to produce the substance of gold. Although this gold is considered most healthy even among those who think otherwise, nevertheless the things from which it was made—before they matured and obtained a different nature—were counted among harmful things even by those same people.

If you should say that the nature of things has certain ready-made alexipharmics <term>alexipharmaca</term> <note>From the Greek 'alexipharmakon,' a remedy or antidote against poison or venom.</note> which human art lacks: I will ask, who is it that consulted Nature herself when she brought forth gold? Who will be able to question the midwives of nature so that he might know by prescription which things are rejected, which are repelled, which are free from all suspicion, which are those that lose their venom before they combine in that work, and which are those that are stripped of it while being prepared or after they have completed it? These things could be confirmed by the examples of animals that eat healthily of those things by whose consumption others would be killed; the cause is the various power of cooking and transforming, remaining from the different nature of the living being.

And again, we could use examples of poisonous things which, through certain mixtures and "concoctions" <note>In alchemy and ancient medicine, "concoction" refers to a process akin to digestion or ripening through heat.</note>, turn out to be healthy, as is clearly found in theriac <term>theriacis</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made from dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> and many other antidotes. The opposite also happens: that from healthy things they become destructive, with no harmful quality added from the outside. Take for example a chicken egg: if it is raw, it excites nausea in almost everyone; if it is lightly cooked so that it is fit for sipping, it is remarkably healthy; if it has been thoroughly hardened by too much fire, it is numbered especially among harmful foods. For various natures do not only burst forth from the various mixtures of things, and various properties flow out, but also from cooking that is either too much or too little. To this we add that since man-made <term>factitium</term> gold is not distinguished from natural gold by human knowledge—otherwise it could neither be, nor be called, of the same species if it were separated by different "accidents" <note>A philosophical term referring to observable qualities (color, weight, etc.) that are not part of the essential essence.</note> which lead to the knowledge of the substance of a thing—since in—

# ON GOLD. BOOK III.

...since it cannot be distinguished, there is now no danger, no cause for peril. For the gold which you place in the pot to be cooked, which you scrape, which you strike, which you cut into the finest filings, which you submerge in boiling hot water—you simply do not know whether it was dug from the bowels of the earth or fashioned by the art of man. Add to this that gold was produced in antiquity; otherwise, this art would not have persisted among so many people, but would have been exploded and hissed off the stage in every place by the consensus of all nations. Nor would a living man be found who could boast of having read eight hundred legitimate volumes of that art, and thirty-seven thousand precepts besides—since, as I say, it was produced in antiquity, which we have already proven by experiments.

What reason or argument do you have to separate the manufactured gold from the natural? Is it a sign or a branded mark? For antiquity, like our own age, used to mark gold with the insignia of leading men and carry it to public workshops to be set apart. It is not the color; for the touchstone <term>Index lapis</term> <note>Also known as the Lydian stone, used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave when rubbed against it.</note>, like an honorary arbiter between equal colors, gives a verdict for neither side. It is not the weight, since the balance scale does not tip from the center. It is not the tenderness or softness, since neither resists the one bending or handling it. It is not the effect; for if gold is eaten or drunk, you cannot rightfully attribute an effect to it that another person might attribute to a different substance with no less reason. For when many things are taken together rather than separately to achieve some result, if different effects are produced, you cannot be certain to which nature of a thing you should attribute that diversity—unless you have thoroughly mastered the individual natures of those things that came together. For an opportunity will never be lacking to attribute to one thing what is attributed to another, and this opportunity will appear all the greater the larger the mixture or the more numerous the heap of ingredients.

Therefore, if you do not know how to distinguish true gold obtained through the birth of nature from that which the industry of art has brought forth for you, you will never properly prescribe gold as a drink. For either everything must be considered harmful, if any part is said to be unhealthy (since we lack, as we have seen, a legitimate means of discernment); or everything is healthy, if gold, insofar as it is gold, is said to suit the nature of humans; or everything is doubtful, if you do not separate one from the other—either by the touchstone <term>lapis Lydius</term> <note>The Lydian stone or touchstone.</note>, or by the scales, or finally by the water that has been given its name from "partitioning" <term>aqua partitionis</term> <note>Commonly known as nitric acid, used in the process of "parting" or separating gold from silver.</note>, because it divides gold from silver—and thus you do not exclude danger from either one.

What of this? Even if some gold is wholesome, that which bears the mark of princes and states and is used by buyers and sellers must be considered unwholesome. For copper is mixed in, as the colored Heraclian stone <note>original: *lapis Heraclius*; another name for the touchstone or Lydian stone used to test metal purity</note> has revealed. Several other things are also mixed in, including a very sharp artificial salt, which is falsely called *ammoniacon* <note>original: *ammoniacon*; here referring to sal ammoniac, though the author notes the name implies it is "sandy" or from the desert</note>. Sometimes saltpeter <term>nitrum</term> and that harmful quicksilver <note>mercury</note> are added—the latter named for the way it is raised on high <note>a reference to the process of sublimation, where mercury vaporizes and rises when heated</note>. Through the smelting of all these, a poison is contracted: for who is ignorant of how much the rust or dross of copper harms the stomach? There are also the other pernicious things we mentioned, which are used by silversmiths and goldsmiths to give a brilliance to gold coins; for they color the gold, which is naturally rather pale, so that it might shine and glitter more. But enough has been said regarding health; now let us mark the limits of the art and refute the false opinion of the common people.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*A manifold warning to those who devote their labor to making gold through Chemistry <note>original: *Chemiam*; in this context, alchemy</note>, and at the same time a resolution to that common question of why so many who pursue the gold-bearing art are destitute.*<-

Now, I would wish those who seek gold through art to be warned not to surrender themselves to experiments beyond their resources, nor to abandon more certain studies because of it, nor to promise themselves great riches, nor to affect high offices and kingdoms, deceived by vain hope. For just as God does not permit all men of humbler fortune (as is commonly said)—whether they strive for glory or practice trade—to obtain a kingdom or princedom, or to overflow with immense riches; and just as He did not wish all those who apply themselves to the study of letters to equal or surpass the glory of the ancients; so it must be thought in this matter. Such great things are very difficult and rare, since God distributes His gifts according to His own will, not ours.

For if those who prepare gold and seek to change metals harbor vain and harmful thoughts, if they promise themselves too much and build "castles in the air" (as the proverb says), they should recognize that they are easily deceived and mocked: both by themselves, and by the fraudulent wickedness of both evil spirits and men. I remember a certain man was once taught by a friend, to whom a heavenly oracle was said to have been given, that he would not obtain the faculty of making gold which he sought if he intended to abuse it for pride or for doing harm—

# ON GOLD, BOOK III.

...he might use it for himself, it should be granted if his success turned out for the good of his soul and body. I knew another man who asserted to me that he once made stable and true silver from the mobile silver called "living" <note>original: *argento quod viuum dicitur*; quicksilver or mercury</note> using the juices and leaves of herbs. He sold it to those skilled in testing metallic truth, but soon after he used those same leaves in vain; what he had once accomplished, he could never do again, though he tried often.

I know another, still among the living, for whom silver and gold were produced through the art about fifteen times. He then lost that art and received word through an oracle from a companion during sleep <note>this refers to a dream-vision or a spiritual visitation</note> that this happened because of the vice of an ungrateful mind. From this we may learn the truth of the Apostolic saying: *neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God gives the increase* <note>original: *neque qui plantat, neque qui rigat est aliquid, sed incrementum dat Deus*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:7</note>. Someone else reported to me that he once made gold from silver in great quantity; the second time, using the same materials, he indeed made some, but always in such a tiny amount that he calculated the loss to be greater than the profit. It occurred to him that he might escape this loss if he tried to achieve his goal not from silver but from copper <note>original: *aere*; often used for bronze or copper in early mineralogy</note>, a metal of a better condition. Relying on strong conjectures, he attempted it; yet when he was on the verge of obtaining what he hoped for, it happened in strange ways <note>original: *mitis modis*, likely a typo for *miris modis*</note> that he achieved nothing at all. Sometimes it vanished, sometimes various accidents intervened, yet of such a nature that he clearly recognized the obstacles proceeded from somewhere other than human power.

The same man affirmed he had heard from a friend who had experienced this very thing: having made excellent silver from cinnabar <note>original: *cinnabari*; mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral central to alchemical theory</note>, he afterwards applied himself to the work many times with greater diligence, only to be always frustrated in the outcome. You, however, should confirm these outcomes with reason. For among those things dug out from the caverns of the earth, you will see things most necessary to you, but also monsters and, occasionally, abortive births <note>the author views failed or corrupted minerals as "monsters" of nature, similar to biological defects</note>. Lucius Annaeus Seneca points out in his *Natural Questions* <note>original: *naturalibus quaestionibus*; Seneca’s work on meteorology and natural philosophy</note> that just as in our bodies, so too in those [minerals] the humors often contract defects when a blow, or a shaking of the place, or old age, or cold, or heat have corrupted nature—not to mention the excess or lack of fire, or the lack of skill or diligence of the artisan. I shall remain silent on the manifold deceptions of the malignant demon. But even if everything you desire flows according to your wish, if the gift of God is not present, you will lose your labor; and in time, you will suffer the loss of your expenses. We remember singing of these things in our riddles <note>original: *aenigmatibus*; Pico likely refers to his own cryptic or allegorical philosophical writings</note>, yet without the confusion of riddles.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola recounts anecdotes of alchemists who achieved success only once or twice before failing, arguing that the "art" is subject to divine favor and natural corruption. He concludes that without God's blessing and a pure mind, alchemy results only in financial and spiritual loss.</summary>

### IOAN. FR. MIRAND. <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533)</note>

*As long as nature preserves its perpetual course,*
*As long as the craftsman’s hand and mind do not waver,*
*For Nature is accustomed to produce many monsters,* <note>In this context, "monsters" refers to biological or physical abnormalities—results that deviate from the intended "perfect" form.</note>

*Sometimes failing through lack of it; just as a cold*
*Aged Mother is wont to carry her offspring in her womb,*
*And the artist’s mind, too often exhausted and intent*
*Upon harsh labor, is prone to wander through various pathless ways.*
*Thus the weary hand deflects from the right path.*
*Yet you would seek all these things in vain*
*Unless the Almighty wills it, by whose fixed decree all the strivings*
*Of nature and art are always rendered void; nor can either*
*Life or strength persist in those things without Him.*
*And sometimes an evil Demon thrusts himself in*
*And throws everything into confusion, unless he be restrained by Heaven.*

*I wondered at it, and at the same time I searched Heaven for the cause,*
*When a light shone upon my mind, driving away the darkness.*
*For the sign of the cross drove away the mockeries of black*
*Dis,* <note>original: *Ditis*; Dis was the Roman god of the underworld, here used to represent the Devil or a demonic entity.</note> *and the matter was restored to its former vigor.*

*Or what the Asturian dug out in Callaecian caves;* <note>Refers to the gold mines of northwestern Spain (Asturias and Galicia), which were the most productive in the Roman Empire.</note>

Therefore, I shall repeat what I said before, not without purpose; for the ignorant cannot be taught enough, nor the stubborn reminded too much. I shall repeat it, I say, not without purpose: the detractors of this art cannot fashion a slander from these failures. For just as a prudent person would not speak against agriculture or medicine because a field’s harvest was lost or because the sick die—since such things clearly depend upon Nature and Divine decree as the primary causes, rather than the art alone—so you should not shrink from the making of gold and silver because the effects are sometimes...

# ON GOLD, BOOK III

...sometimes failed, or less fruitful. For the rules of Art are not eternal, nor are they established in every single detail. Why then do you not criticize the necessary and ancient art of farming when the harvest is sometimes empty? Nor do you reject the art of healing human bodies—which is no less useful than it is old—when it does not succeed? Surely it is because you know that the promised effects of those arts can frequently be frustrated by various causes, as learned perhaps from Cornelius <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – c. 50 AD), a Roman encyclopedist whose work *De Medicina* was a primary source for medical knowledge in the Renaissance.</note>, the writer on these very arts.

For as he says, agriculture promises nourishment to healthy bodies, just as medicine promises health to the sick. He says nourishment and health are not *guaranteed*, but *promised*: this is a most prudent observation, given that results are sometimes failed. In no different a way does the professor of the Chemical art promise gold and silver. Would he himself be more confident in making gold than Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> was in restoring good health? It was his opinion that "experimentation is full of danger." <note>This refers to the first of Hippocrates' *Aphorisms*: "Life is short, and Art long; the crisis fleeting; experience perilous, and decision difficult."</note> Since neither the <term>malagmata: emollient poultices or medicinal plasters applied to the skin</term> always help, even though the ancients wrote that they would, nor do simple medicines always provide what they promise; nor can even colleges of physicians ensure that a patient does not die—even when they are always present—though they have often pledged health.

Add to this that it belongs to only a few to reach that sublime peak of making great weights of gold with small expense. For by a peculiar gift of God, this is granted to the very few, so that there is a great difference between doing much with profit [and doing little]. For what does it matter to have made only a little? That pertains only to speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" means theoretical proof or intellectual observation rather than financial gambling.</note>, so that it may be recognized as true that metals are transformed into one another. It contributes nothing to wealth or the achievement of great things, even if you could prepare gold in six hundred ways. For there are those who can hardly bear the expenses, those who have suffered losses, and those who do not have a steady state or fixed order, but a varying one. From this, you can easily resolve the question of the common people who repeatedly ask: "Why are those who do not deny they can make gold so often in need?" The solution is at hand.

For either they produce too little gold, or if they produce much, it is with the greatest expenses; or they vary their experiments so that what happens once does not follow in a perpetual course. Either the fear of cruel and most greedy Princes <note>Alchemists often feared being kidnapped or imprisoned by rulers who wanted to monopolize gold production.</note> disturbs them, or a suitable location is lacking, or a partnership and staff are not present. Not to mention the light and foolish credulity of many, combined with ignorance, and the [frauds] of the deceitful...

But why is it a wonder? From small furnaces sometimes no profit comes, but often losses; this frequently happens in the mines in our own time, and likewise in antiquity. Hence that false reproach of Demetrius of Phalerum <note>Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BC) was an Athenian statesman and philosopher. The "reproach" refers to his criticism of those who waste real wealth searching for uncertain gold underground.</note> against those seeking gold through the caverns of the earth: that they squander manifest things for the sake of uncertain ones, and not becoming masters of the things they search for, they lost what they already possessed. But even if everything is present—which you have prepared with great zeal and great expense, and which you have desired with all your prayers—*if the divine decree is not present, you will have labored in vain.*

One may see this very thing in the works of nature, since in the conception and origin of mortals there are various conditions of female sterility and useless male seed. There can also be very many causes by which an abortion occurs; and beyond those, the purpose of the divine will is necessary so that the infant, who was hidden in the womb, may come forth into the light. How much more will that same thing be observed in the effects of art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to human technology and alchemy, as opposed to "Nature."</note>. In short, there is no art resting upon conjectures that is always fixed and immovable, nor is any so certain or unshaken that it is not for the most part liable to the changeability of matter, and entirely subject to the divine will. If that will favors you in the making of gold, beware of all pride of mind and greed. Never stop fearing: *was this granted to you as a benefit, or as a punishment?* and often reflect on that saying of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian.</note>. It is an elegant eulogy and no less true: *God mercifully denies many things which he grants in anger.* <note>original: "Quod multa Deus negat propitius, quæ concedit iratus."</note> Therefore, first give immortal thanks to God, and return them as much as possible; then, with all modesty, receive that heavenly gift, and use it both holily and piously, for the honor and glory of the most Holy Trinity, which is one God, and for

# THE LITTLE BOOK 
# OF ROGER BACON 
# ON ALCHEMY, TO WHICH 
# HE GAVE THE TITLE, 
# The Mirror of Alchemy.

### PREFACE.

In various ways and in many fashions, the Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi"—in this context, the term refers specifically to the ancient and medieval alchemists and natural philosophers like Aristotle or Geber.</note> of old used to speak through their writings, as if in riddles; and with a sort of clouded voice, they left to us a certain science, noble above all others, yet thoroughly obscured from us, and hidden under a veil of despair as if altogether denied—and this was not without cause. Therefore I instruct that, above all the writings of others, you firmly ground your mind upon these seven chapters, which contain within them the transformation of metals. Revolve their beginning, middle, and end frequently in your heart, and you shall find in them such subtlety that your soul will be fulfilled.

### ON THE DEFINITIONS OF ALCHEMY. CHAPTER I.

In many of the books of the ancients, several definitions of this art are found, the intentions of which we ought to consider in this chapter. For Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy ("the Hermetic art").</note> says of this science: "Alchemy is a corporeal science composed from one thing and through one thing, simply put, joining more precious things to each other through knowledge and effect, and by that same natural mixing, converting them into a better kind." Another says: "Alchemy is the science teaching how to transform every kind of metal into another; and this is done through its own proper medicine, as is evident in many books of the Philosophers." Therefore, Alchemy is a science teaching how to make and generate a certain medicine, which is called the Elixir <term>Elixir: Derived from the Arabic *al-iksīr*, this refers to the "Philosopher's Stone" in liquid or powder form, capable of curing disease and transmuting metals.</term>, which, when it is cast upon metals or imperfect bodies, completely perfects them at the very moment of projection <term>projection: the final act of the alchemical process, where a small amount of the Elixir is "thrown" onto a molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</term>.

### On the natural principles and the procreations of minerals. CHAPTER II.

Secondly, I will perfectly declare the natural principles and the procreations of minerals. From this it must first be noted that the mineral principles in mines are **Quicksilver** <term>original: "Argentum vivum"—mercury, considered by alchemists to be the feminine, fluid, and "metallic" principle of all matter.</term> and **Sulfur** <term>considered the masculine, active, and "combustible" principle of matter.</term>. From these are procreated all metals and all minerals, of which there are many and diverse species. But I say that nature always proposed and strove toward the perfection of gold. However, various intervening accidents <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "accidents" are external circumstances or qualities (like heat, cold, or impurities) that affect a substance without changing its underlying essence.</note> transform the metals, as is openly found in many of the books of the Philosophers. For according to the purity and impurity of the two aforementioned substances—namely, Quicksilver and Sulfur—pure and impure metals are generated, namely: Gold, silver, tin, lead, copper, and iron. Concerning their nature—specifically their purity and impurity, or their unclean excess and deficiency—receive these truths:

**On the nature of Gold.** Gold is indeed a perfect body, generated from pure, fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance's ability to withstand the heat of fire without evaporating or being destroyed.</note>, clear, and red quicksilver, and from clean, fixed, red, and non-burning sulfur; it possesses no defect.

**On the nature of Silver.** Silver is a clean, pure, and nearly perfect body, procreated from pure, nearly fixed, clear, and white quicksilver and from such sulfur; it lacks only a little fixation, and color along with weight.

**On the nature of Tin.** Tin is a clean but imperfect body, procreated from pure quicksilver—partially fixed and partially not—that is clear and white in its outward appearance <note>original: "manifesto"—the visible, physical qualities of a substance.</note> but red in its hidden nature <note>original: "occulto"—the internal or essential qualities that are not immediately apparent.</note>, and from such sulfur; it lacks only decoction or digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" or "decoction" refers to the process of maturing or "ripening" a metal through steady heat, similar to how fruit ripens on a tree.</note>.

**On the nature of Lead.** Lead is an unclean and imperfect body, procreated from impure, unfixed, earthy, and dreg-filled quicksilver—somewhat white in its outward appearance and red in its hidden nature—and from a sulfur that is combustible in some part; it lacks purity, fixation, color, and resistance to fire.

**On the nature of Copper.** Copper is an unclean and imperfect body, generated from impure, unfixed, earthy, burning, and non-clear red quicksilver, and from such sulfur; it lacks fixation and purity of weight, and it possesses too much impure color and non-burning earthiness.

**On the nature of Iron.** Iron is an unclean and imperfect body, generated from impure, overly fixed, earthy and burning quicksilver—white and red but not clear—and from such sulfur; it lacks fusion <note>The ability to melt easily when heated.</note>, purity, and weight, and it has too much fixed, un-

### *From which things the material of the Elixir is more closely to be drawn.*

## CHAPTER III.

In the things already said, the procreation of both perfect and imperfect metals has been sufficiently determined. Now let us return to the choosing and perfecting of the imperfect material. Since it is sufficiently known from the preceding chapters that all metals are procreated from **quicksilver** and **sulfur**, and how their impurity and uncleanness corrupts them, and since no thing ought to be applied to metals which is not composed of or risen from them, it is left quite clearly to us that no foreign thing, which did not take its origin from these two, is powerful and sufficient to perfect them, or to make a new transmutation of them. Wherefore it is to be wondered at that any prudent man should base his intention upon animals or vegetables, which are very far removed <note>In alchemical theory, substances were "remote" or "near" based on how many steps of refinement were needed to turn them into the desired metallic essence.</note>, since minerals are found to be close enough. Nor is it to be believed at all that any of the Philosophers placed the art in the aforementioned remote things, except by way of metaphor <note>original: "similitudinarie"—speaking figuratively or using analogies to hide the true chemical components from the uninitiated.</note>. But from the two aforementioned substances all metals are made, and nothing adheres to them, nor is joined to them, nor transmutes them, except that which is from them. And so by right we must take **Quicksilver** and **Sulfur** <term>as</term> <note>original: "pro"</note> the material of our stone. Neither quicksilver by itself, nor sulfur by itself, generates any metal, but from the mixture of both, diverse metals and many minerals are procreated in various ways. Therefore, it is certain that our material must be chosen from the mixture of both. But our final secret is most excellent and deeply hidden: From which mineral thing [the Elixir] ought to be most closely and nearly made; and we are bound to choose this very thing with care. I suppose, therefore, <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> our material might be chosen first from vegetables, such as herbs, trees, or everything that comes forth from the earth. In that case, quicksilver and sulfur would first have to be made from them <term>through</term> <note>original: "per"</note> a long decoction <note>A process of heating or boiling a substance in liquid to extract its essential components or "ripen" it.</note>, from which tasks and from whose operation we are excused, since nature proposes Quicksilver and Sulfur to us directly. And if we were to choose from animals, such as human blood, hair, urine, excrement, hens' eggs, and all things that proceed from animals, it would also be necessary to make quicksilver and sulfur from them by decocting, from which we are excused, as before.

And since nature has handed down to us only the imperfect along with the perfect, it is necessary for us to "more than perfect" <note>original: "plusquam perficere"—to bring a substance to a state of transformative power beyond even that of pure gold.</note> the matter noted in our chapters through our own work and artificial labor. Do we not see that in the mines, through continuous heat which exists in the mineral mountains, the thickness of water is so far cooked and thickened that, over time, it becomes <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury, often called "argentum vivum" (living silver) in Latin.</note>? And from the fatness of the earth, through that same cooking and heat, is <term>sulfur</term> generated? And do we not see that by that heat, persevering continuously upon them, all metals are generated from the aforementioned substances according to their purity or impurity? And that nature perfects all things, both perfect and imperfect, through cooking alone—or rather, makes the metals so? <margin>|||</margin> O, what great madness! What, I ask, compels you to wish to perfect the aforementioned things through strange, melancholic, and fantastical regimes? As a certain man says: "Woe to you who wish to overcome nature and 'more than perfect' the metals through a new regime or work born of your own senseless headstrongness." For the God of nature gave a linear path, namely continuous cooking <note>original: "decoctionem"—the alchemical process of heating a substance in a sealed vessel to mature it.</note>, and you fools either despise or are ignorant of how to imitate her. Likewise: "Fire and <term>azoth</term> <note>Azoth was considered the universal solvent or the essential transformative agent, often associated with the "mercury of the philosophers."</note> are sufficient for you." And elsewhere: "Heat perfects all things." And elsewhere: "Cook, cook, cook, and do not let it weary you." And elsewhere: "Let your fire be gentle and mild, which through each passing day may endure by burning always equally, nor should it increase; if otherwise, the greatest damage will follow." And elsewhere: "Patiently and continuously." And elsewhere: "Grind it seven times." And elsewhere: "Know that the whole mastery is finished with one thing—namely the stone; one way—namely cooking; and one vessel." And elsewhere: "It is ground by fire." And elsewhere: "This work is much like the creation of a human being." For just as an infant in the beginning is nourished with lighter foods, but once the bones are strengthened, with always stronger ones: so also this mastery first requires a slow fire, which must always be used in every essence of the cooking. And although we always speak of a slow fire, in truth we mean that

# ROGER BACON.

## *On the quality of the vessel and the furnace.*
### CHAPTER V.

We have already determined the limit and the method of acting; now we may hear about the vessel and the furnace, how and from what materials they should be made. Since nature, with natural fire, cooks <note>original: "decoquat"—referring to 'decoction,' the process of heating a substance to extract its essence or thicken it.</note> metals in the mines, she denies that cooking without a vessel suited for the purpose. And if we propose to follow nature in cooking, why should her "vessel" be rejected? Let us see first, therefore, what kind of place the generation of metals is.

It is clearly perceived in mineral regions that at the base of a mountain there is a heat, enduring evenly, whose nature is always to ascend. In ascending, it always dries everywhere and coagulates the thicker or coarser water—hidden in the "belly" or veins of the earth or mountain—into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "arg. viuum" (argentum vivum), the liquid metal Mercury.</note>. And if the mineral fatness <note>The alchemical "fatness of the earth" refers to the oily, combustible principle that forms sulfur.</note> of that place was gathered from the earth heated in this way into the veins of the earth, it flows through the mountain and is <term>sulfur</term>. And as can be seen in the aforementioned veins of that place, that sulfur—generated from the fatness of the earth, as was mentioned—also meets the quicksilver in the veins of the earth and procreates the mineral thickness <note>The "thickness" or body of the metal itself.</note>. There, by the heat enduring evenly within the mountain, different metals are generated over a long time, according to the diversity of the location. In mineral regions, indeed, one finds a heat that is always lasting.

Because of these things, it stands as a point of law for us to note that the external mineral mountain is everywhere closed in on itself and stony; for if the heat were able to escape, metals would by no means be procreated. If, therefore, we intend to imitate nature, we must provide a furnace in a similar way, after the likeness of mountains—not in size, but in continuous heat—so that the fire placed within, when it ascends, finds no exit, and the heat may reverberate against the vessel containing the matter of the stone, which is itself firmly closed. This vessel should be round with a small neck, made of glass or of some clay representing the nature or density of glass. Its mouth should be marked or sealed with a suitable cover and <term>bitumen</term> <note>A sealant or "lute" used to make the vessel airtight, often called the Lute of Hermes.</note>. And just as in the mines the heat does not immediately touch the substance of the sulfur and quicksilver, because the earth of the mountain is everywhere in between, so the fire should not immediately touch the vessel containing the aforementioned matter. Instead, that vessel is to be placed inside another vessel that is similarly closed, so that a tempered heat may reach the matter from above, from below, and everywhere in the best and most suitable way. Hence Aristotle says in the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumine luminū"—a medieval alchemical treatise traditionally but falsely attributed to Aristotle.</note>, that Mercury...

## *On the accidental and essential colors appearing in the work.*

### CHAPTER VI.

Having chosen the refined material of the <term>stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the Great Work, capable of transmuting metals and prolonging life.</note>, you will recognize a certain way of acting; by this method, through a specific regimen, the stone is frequently transformed into various colors during the process of cooking. Whence a certain man says: "As many colors, so many names." According to the different colors appearing in the work, its names have been varied by the Philosophers.

Hence, in the first operation of our stone, the process is called <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The "nigredo" or blackening stage, symbolizing the death of the old form before a new one can be born.</note>, and our stone becomes black. For this reason, someone has said: "When you find it black, know that in that blackness, whiteness is hidden, and then it is necessary to extract it from that most subtle blackness of its own."

But after the putrefaction, it turns red—not with the true redness—of which a certain man says: "It frequently turns red and frequently turns lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrineſcit"—referring to 'citrinitas,' a transitional stage between whiteness and redness.</note>, and often it melts, and often it coagulates before the true whiteness." And it even dissolves itself, coagulates itself, putrefies itself, colors itself, kills itself, brings itself to life, blackens itself, whitens itself, and adorns itself with redness along with whiteness.

It also becomes green, whence another says: "Cook it until the 'born-green' appears to you, and that is its soul." And another: "Know that in that greenness, that soul is dominant."

There also appears before the whiteness the <term>peacock's color</term> <note>original: "color pauonis"—the 'cauda pavonis' or peacock's tail, a stage of iridescent, shifting colors.</note>, of which a certain man says: "Know that all the colors that exist in the world, or can be imagined, appear before the whiteness." After that, the true whiteness follows, of which a certain man says: "When it is cooked pure until it shines like the eyes of fish, its usefulness is to be expected, and then the stone is frozen <note>original: "congelatus"—meaning solidified or coagulated into a stable state.</note> into a roundness."

Another says: "When you find a preeminent whiteness in the vessel, be certain that in that whiteness, redness is hidden, and then you must extract it: nevertheless, cook it until the whole becomes red." For there is between the true whiteness and the true redness a certain ash-gray color, of which it is said: "After the whiteness, you cannot go wrong, for by increasing the fire you will arrive at the ash-gray." Of this, another says: "Do not despise the ash,"

## Preface. How art imitates nature.

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing floral scrolls and foliage patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

SINCE every improvement of things increases the nature of that thing to which it belongs: Therefore, in many of the teachings of the Philosophers, nature is improved through art, beyond its own movement which it had in its first form. And yet no thing can work except by the mediation of nature, since nature itself works secretly and intrinsically within art through the administration of art. By this it follows that the improvement of nature is the increase of power, and the labor of art is the improvement of that thing. Since nature completes its own degree, which it can naturally complete, and it cannot pass beyond that, unless nature itself is assisted <note>The OCR reads *impedita* (hindered), but context and other manuscripts suggest *adiuta* (helped/assisted) or *iuvata*; the sense is that art removes the "hindrances" of nature to allow it to reach perfection.</note> by the administration of art. nature through simple labor, yet Art transcends Nature regarding that nature which it can specifically refine. And so it is said: **Art imitates nature** <note>original: "Ars imitatur naturam"—a foundational Aristotelian principle in alchemy: human skill cannot create matter from nothing, but it can accelerate or guide natural processes toward perfection.</note>, not that it builds something new, but that it refines the power of that nature. At this point Art begins to progress where Nature fails: uncovering the subtle nature enclosed within a thing and manifesting it. While Nature generates metals, it cannot generate tinctures <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a concentrated substance—often the Elixir—capable of "staining" or transforming the quality of a base metal into gold or silver.</note>, even though it secretly contains the fullness of that tincture within itself. Wherefore the philosopher says:

> Nature contains within itself those things which it lacks, and it is not perfected unless it is moved by art and operation.

Therefore, in our work, Art is nothing other than a helper to Nature, which is evident in many crafts of the laypeople: where Nature first produces wood. Secondly, the burning of fire produces ash from the wood. Thirdly, Art produces glass from the ash. And this must be understood completely: if that first matter <term>materia prima</term> <note>The primal, formless substance from which all things are made; alchemists believed that by reducing a substance to its "first matter," it could then be "re-formed" into a more perfect state.</note> of glass had not been hidden in the ashes, Art could never have produced or perfected glass from them without the pre-existing Nature. 

And so you should consider that nothing can be drawn out of any thing that does not already exist within it. Therefore, every species within its own species, and every genus within its own genus, and every nature within its own nature, naturally seeks the increase of its virtue and brings forth fruit according to its own nature, and not in another nature contrary to it—since every seed corresponds to its own sowing. We say this regarding generation: nothing is generated by a human except a human, nor from any such thing except its like. 

And as for imitating Nature through Art, no thing does this simply by laboring through the ministry of Nature, except through the constitution <term>complexion</term> <note>Latin: *complexio*. The specific mixture of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that determines a substance's character and health.</note> of that nature. For if a worse, foreign nature is introduced, Art immediately fails to imitate Nature; instead, those worse foreign natures infect that nature, and immediately what was expected to be made does not happen. For every worse thing working within a thing strives to destroy the better, and every better thing working within a thing strives to perfect the worse. And therefore, it is necessary for every artisan to imitate Nature and to know the nature of the thing whose nature his art imitates:

### *That the study of philosophy is necessary for this art.*
## CHAPTER II

Study, according to the Doctors <note>original: "Doctores"—referring to the established Scholastic authorities and academic teachers of the time</note>, removes ignorance and leads the human intellect back to true science and the knowledge of any given thing. Therefore, it is first necessary to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work, and to sharpen one's wit through philosophical sayings, since the way of truth is known within them. If, therefore, those who labor do not despise the effort, they shall sweetly taste the fruit arising from it. Indeed, those who shrink from study should weigh carefully in their thoughts, while laboring, whether their art is an imitation of nature—especially of that thing whose nature their art ought to refine. For without the imitation of nature, it is impossible for them to bring the secrets of the philosophers to a perfect end, just as the philosopher speaks of such people. These men proceed to practice like a donkey to hay, not knowing toward what it stretches its muzzle, except insofar as the exterior senses, without intellect, lead it to its fodder through sight and taste.

Thus these "donkeys," without true principles and fruitful studies, and without a knowledge of natures, seek to perfect the works of nature and the most secret of secrets <note>original: "secretum secretissimum"—this may be a reference to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a famous medieval book of wisdom attributed to Aristotle</note> of all natural philosophy <term>naturalis Philosophia</term> <note>In the Middle Ages, this term referred to the study of the physical world and the laws of nature, the precursor to modern science.</note>. They seek that best work which adorns a person with morals, enriches them with benefits, assists the poor, and preserves the human body unharmed, providing it with health.

And afterward, it is added concerning the medicine of that hidden nature: And therefore all who love the benefit of this art are bound to apply themselves to studies, and to draw the truth out of books and not from fabricated fables or lying works. For this art is by no means truly found (even though many sophistries <note>Deceptive or fake alchemical processes that look real but lack the true essence.</note> may appear to men) except after the limit of study and the knowledge of philosophical sayings, or through the faithful information of a scholar when it is taught. For he who is lazy in reading books will not be able to be prompt in preparing things; and further, he whose mind refuses to sweat in studies cannot easily become accustomed to practice.

### *Concerning natural principles.*
## CHAPTER III.

One must not doubt that this art has true natural principles, since nature herself forms metallic bodies in the mine <note>original: "minera"—referring to the ore or the subterranean "womb" where metals were thought to grow.</note>, which is clear through Aristotle in the fourth book of *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica* was the standard text for understanding the formation of minerals and weather phenomena in the Middle Ages.</note>, where he distin—

...distinguishes mineral bodies into four species: into stones, into liquefiable substances, into sulfurs, and into salts. ### *How many parts of minerals there are.* CHAPTER IV.

Mineral bodies are specifically divided into two parts: namely, the metallic part—that is, the metals—which derive their origin from Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"—referring to the philosophical principle of fluidity and metallic luster, rather than just the raw element</note>, such as gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron; these are called the "greater minerals." Then there is the mineral part which does not derive its origin from Mercury, such as salts, inks <note>original: "atramenta"—a term for black vitriolic substances used in making ink or dyes</note>, alums, vitriol, arsenic, orpiment, sulfur, and similar things; these are called "lesser minerals." They are, however, non-metallic bodies, although it is manifest that the greater minerals—that is, the metallic bodies—have their origin from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver." In alchemy, this is the purified, "living" essence of mercury that serves as the maternal principle of all metals</note>, according to whether they are more or less purified. I shall now set down the difference of their generation and state from where they have their origin, though this is sufficiently clear in many books of the philosophers.

### *Concerning metals which derive their origin from Mercury in general.*
### CHAPTER V.

All liquefiable metals that derive their origin from Mercury are ductile: for their matter is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in a strong union, and one cannot be separated from the other. Therefore, the watery substance is congealed by great cold after the action of heat, and for this reason they are ductile and workable. But water alone does not congeal, except through a dryness that has altered the wateriness and the earthiness, since the moisture in them is not excessively oily. Their solidification comes from earthly dryness; therefore, they do not easily melt except by the action of vehement heat upon them, depending on how strongly they are mixed.

### *How metals are made from Mercury in particular.*
### CHAPTER VI.

<header>THE CORRECTORIUM</header>

The nature of all liquefiable things was naturally produced from **Mercury**, or **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver." In alchemy, this refers to the fluid, feminine principle of all metals.</note>, and the substance of its own **sulfur**. This occurs because it is the property of quicksilver to be coagulated by a vapor, such as by the heat of **white or red sulfur** that is "non-burning" <note>original: "non vrentis"—referring to philosophical sulfur which provides stability and color without the destructive, combustible qualities of common brimstone</note>. Regarding this, **Aristotle** says in the 4th book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "4 Met."—While the text says "Metaphysics," these theories of mineralogy actually originate in Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*.</note>: If the sulfur be white and non-burning, it congeals Mercury into **good silver**. If the sulfur be pure, clear, and red, and contains the power of "fireness" that is simply non-burning, it congeals Mercury into the **purest gold**. This is because every dry thing naturally "drinks up" its own moisture, so that the moisture is consumed into its own parts. Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that coagulates the quicksilver from its own substance is earthy, subtle, airy, cooked, and digested from its first mixture—united to it by the cooking of heat. Afterward, it is elevated, cooked, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of coagulating Mercury into metallic bodies, depending on whether the sulfur was simple or "burning" <note>combustible or impure</note>, which causes the perfection or imperfection in metals, as will appear later.

An example of this—that their **prime matter** <note>the fundamental "first stuff" from which things are made</note> is quicksilver—is seen when they are liquefied by heat, for they are converted into it. It is certainly established that they were quicksilver before, because every thing consists of that into which it can be resolved; for since **ice** is converted into water by means of heat, it is necessary that the ice was previously water.

### CAP. VII.

It must be noted here that **sulfur** comes from the "fatness of the earth" <note>a traditional alchemical term for the oily, combustible element of the soil</note>, thickened in the mine by a temperate cooking until it becomes hardened and dry. And when it has been hardened, it is called Sulfur. **Quicksilver**, however, in its first root, is composed of a white, subtle, and highly sulfurous earth, strongly mixed with clear water; it is united in such a way—part by tiny part—until the moisture is tempered by the dryness, and the dryness by the moisture equally, until it becomes a single substance. It does not rest on a flat surface, nor does it stick to what touches it, because the dryness has altered the wateriness within it. It is, moreover, **homogeneous** in its nature, because either the whole of it remains in the fire and is fixed, or the whole of it flies away in smoke.

...since it is incombustible and airy <term>aereum</term>, and this is a sign of perfection. For this reason, when it later flows down from the sulfurous earth, it ascends upward once heated. Thus, it is in its very nature to be **sublimated** <term>sublimetur</term> <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor through heat, then back into a solid; in alchemy, this is seen as a way to purify a substance by "elevating" its spirit.</note> by heat. However, through continuous sublimation—by being sublimated excessively—it is purified, decocted <note>boiled down or "cooked" by natural heat</note>, and thickened. It is then gradually congealed by **white and red sulfur**. This sulfur is dissolved many times and afterwards congeals the **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term>. Through its sublimation, the substance is "waxed" <term>inceratur</term> <note>original: "inceratur" — a technical term for bringing a substance to a soft, waxy state so it can be easily melted or combined</note> by the action of heat, until, over the course of perhaps thousands of years and by the successive operation of nature, it is congealed into a perfect metal.

And so it is that nature itself works upon metals in mineral "vessels" <note>natural cavities or veins in the earth's crust</note> by the mediation of heat. Therefore, in these works, whoever wishes to perfect the **medicine** <note>The "Medicine" or "Elixir" is another name for the Philosopher's Stone, which was believed to "heal" base metals into gold.</note> for the perfection of the imperfect must imitate nature. This is true even though these metallic bodies differ in their composition from the quicksilver from which they are generated; they vary according to whether the quicksilver was pure or impure, and whether the sulfur was clean or unclean and foreign to it, as has been said.

*   If the **quicksilver** is coagulated by **white sulfur** that is non-burning <note>original: "non vrente" — meaning sulfur that does not contain the corrosive, combustible qualities of common brimstone</note>, it will become **silver**.
*   If it is coagulated from **pure sulfur** which contains the power of "fireness" (and is likewise non-burning), it will become **gold**.
*   If, however, the **sulfur** is bad and weak, but the **Mercury** is of good substance, it converts it into **copper** <term>aes</term>.
*   If the **quicksilver** is porous, earthy, and unclean, and the **sulfur** is also unclean, stinking, earthy, and of a fixed substance, **iron** <term>ferrum</term> is made from it, which afterwards cannot be melted.
*   **Tin** <term>stannum</term> appears to have good quicksilver, but bad sulfur that is not well mixed and, as it were, not well congealed.
*   **Lead** <term>plumbum</term>, however, has bad and gross quicksilver—foul-tasting, stinking, and of weak virtue—which is why it is continually corrupted by the violence of fire.

Thus do metallic bodies differ from quicksilver, according to whether there is foreign sulfur within them, or burning sulfur, or simple sulfur. In this way, one considers what virtue lies within them. For while a great quantity of sulfur results in infection <note>impurity or corruption</note>, a great quantity of quicksilver is recognized as perfection, since it is incombustible and airy; for sulfur burns and is burned, and always hinders perfection. These words are taken word-for-word from the sayings of the Philosophers regarding **Aristotle** in the 4th book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "4. Meteor."</note>. It must be believed that the truth of these Philosophers has never been found in any lie. Thus, the Art in doing this follows the way of nature, from whi—

### *On the formation of minerals which do not take their origin from Mercury. CHAPTER VIII.*

There are, however, intermediate minerals <term>media mineralia</term> <note>A category of substances like salts and vitriols that alchemists believed were "halfway" between common stones and true metals.</note> as has been said, which do not take their origin from Mercury—that is, from proximate Mercury <note>The immediate, raw material used by nature.</note>—and are of a weak substance. Some of these are **salts**, which liquefy easily in moisture, such as alum <term>alumen</term>, blue vitriol <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>original: "chalcanthum" — likely copper sulfate, used for dyes and in chemical processes.</note>, simple salt, sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniacus</term>, saltpeter <term>sal petrę</term>, and all types of salts. And some are **unctuous** <note>Oily or greasy in texture; alchemists associated this with the "sulfur" principle.</note>, nor do they liquefy easily by moisture alone, such as orpiment <term>auripigmentum</term> <note>A yellow mineral (arsenic trisulfide) often used to give a gold-like color to other substances.</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and other sulfurous things. For the wateriness of sulfurous things is mixed with viscous earth through a strong mixing with the boiling of heat, until they become unctuous; and afterwards they are congealed by cold.

**Inks** <term>atramenta</term> <note>original: "atramenta" — a general term for vitriols or dark mineral substances used to make ink or pigments.</note> are truly composed of salt, sulfur, and stones. It is believed that there is a mineral power of some liquefiable things within them which are made from them, such as blue vitriol and colcothar <term>colcotar</term> <note>Red iron oxide left over after the distillation of sulfuric acid.</note>, which is generated from the larger grains of "ink." They do not dissolve unless the saltiness <note>original: "falsedo" — referring to the saline or "salt-like" quality of the substance.</note> within them is dissolved, which is in the sulfur itself, and afterward it is congealed in the cold. This substance already takes its mineral power from certain bodies naturally in the earth; that which takes an **iron-like** power will be red, or earthy, and is colcothar. That which takes a **copper-like** power <note>original: "æream" — related to "aes," meaning copper or bronze.</note> will be verdigris <term>viride æris</term> or blue vitriol. Hence it is possible for these two—namely colcothar and blue vitriol—to be generated from it.

Although all the aforementioned things share a mineral power with metals, nevertheless metallic bodies cannot be made from them artificially, since they are of a different nature and did not take their origin from the same **proximate matter** <note>Alchemists believed you could only make a metal if you started with the "proximate" or direct ingredients of metals (Mercury and Sulfur).</note>. I do not deny, however, that metals can be purified or dissolved with them, and a **sophistic** <note>Deceptive or "fake."</note> form can be introduced through them so that men may be led into error. The blackness or impurity of lead can also be wiped away; nevertheless, lead always remains lead, even if it looks like silver, and they introduce into it other new qualities so that it appears to be silver. Thus craftsmen can also create "congealments" through them—that is, extract the moisture from Mercury with dry things—so that the Mercury appears congealed, but

### On the generation of common and simple sulfur, and of Mercury.

### CHAPTER IX.

Since it has already been said that sulfur is an impediment in metals, I now set down the difference in the generation of Mercury and of sulfur. Although they both cause a metal to form—namely, Mercury as the essential part, and sulfur as the accidental part—nevertheless that sulfur is itself of two kinds: **living** <term>vivum</term> and **burning** <term>adurens</term>. 

Living sulfur causes metals to form (though one metal differs from another according to how much it exists as earth-stained viscosity); yet simple living sulfur, which produces gold and silver, is nothing but a hot and dry vapor, generated from the purest terrestrial dryness, in which fire predominates in every way. This is called the "elemental sulfur" along with the Mercury of metals. 

But the generation of **common sulfur** <term>sulphur vulgi</term> differs from the generation of Mercury, as it has been said: the wateriness of common sulfur is mixed with a most viscous earthiness through a boiling heat, and they have become oily <term>unctuosa</term>. Thus, the generation of Mercury differs in this second part from the generation of that sulfur, since Mercury is generated from a most subtle, white, and sulfurous earth, combined with the clearest water. The earth produces this through a most powerful mixing, so that one cannot be separated from the other, until it no longer rests upon a flat surface, nor does it stick to what it touches because of the dryness of the earth, which alters the wateriness by reason of the strength of the mixture, and there—

### *That it is impossible for intermediate minerals to be artificially*
### *made into metals.*

## CHAPTER X.

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that lesser minerals cannot be artificially made into metals: therefore, for the sake of greater truth, it remains to prove this more strongly. First, in this way: Because lesser minerals are not generated from the primary matter <term>prima materia</term> of metals, which is Mercury. Since, however, their generation differs from the generation of Mercury in its beginning, in form, and matter, and composition: therefore they also cannot become metals. This is because for one species there is one primary matter, and one seed <term>sperm</term> <note>original: "sperma" — Alchemists used biological metaphors, believing metals grew in the earth from a "seed" or "sperm" just like animals or plants.</note> from which it is generated. But the first part of this premise is clear, because lesser minerals are not generated from Mercury, as is clear through **Aristotle** and **Avicenna** <note>original: "Aristotelem & Auicennam" — These were the two most cited authorities in medieval science. Aristotle represents the Greek tradition, and Avicenna the Islamic tradition of mineralogy.</note>. Therefore, if they were to become metals, it would be necessary that they first pass into the primary matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, metals will not be produced at all. Thus the second part of the premise is sufficiently clear, as was declared in the preceding chapter. 

Second, regarding the same point: Because lesser minerals cannot artificially become the "beginning of the art," which is Mercury, they therefore do not reach the "middle" or the "end," which are metal and the tincture <term>tinctura</term> <note>The alchemical "tincture" is the perfected substance or Elixir capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold.</note>. The logic holds: because nourishment in a man through generation cannot become a man, unless it is first converted into seed, and thus with its like added, a new man is generated. But because lesser minerals are of a foreign nature from metals, although they participate in some mineral power, yet they are of a weaker

For example: If water and earth were mixed, they would then separate from one another, because the earth seeks the bottom—since it is heavy and dry—while water seeks the surface. Therefore, if he sows dung, he will find dung. It is no wonder, then, that no one achieves perfection in such filth, as they and all who follow them are utterly deluded. 

Sow, therefore, gold and silver, so that they may bring forth fruit through your labor with nature as the mediator; for nature possesses this, and it is the very thing you seek, and no other thing in the world. All other things are foul-smelling, and they yield to nature through the persistence and the trial of the fire. 

There are also some Alchemists laboring in the lesser minerals, namely in the **four spirits**: common sulfur, arsenic, orpiment <note>A deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment.</note>, and sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride; used as a flux in soldering and as a reagent.</note>, wishing to create tinctures from these. This must happen so that the nature of the tinting agent and the thing tinted are in harmony. For example: if you have tinted lead or tin, or some such thing, with gold or silver...
