### *Regarding the difference between common sulfur and the simple, non-burning sulfur of the Philosophers.*
### CHAPTER XI.

Now we must ask about the difference between the simple, non-burning sulfur of the Philosophers and common sulfur. Since the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle, or perhaps Geber in this context.</note> states generally: "sulfur coagulates Mercury." Does every sulfur coagulate Mercury? It must be said: No. Because all common sulfur, according to the Philosopher, is contrary to metals. Likewise, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says: "It does not enter into our mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>The *Magisterium* refers to the specialized process or 'Great Work' of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, because it did not originate from it, since it always stains, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it may be prepared by artifice." For it is itself an "infected fire." 

Therefore, if it is fixed <term>figitur</term> <note>In alchemy, "fixing" a substance means making it stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note>, it prevents melting, nor is it possible for it to be joined to a body. An example of this is seen in iron, which is known to have fixed, coarse, and unclean sulfur within itself. If, indeed, it is calcined <note>Reduced to a powder through high heat.</note>, it returns to an earthy substance, like dead dust. And how could it breathe life into other metals? For it has a double superfluity: a flammable substance...

...substance, and earthy dregs. Therefore, consider by this the sulfur of the common people, and not that of the Philosophers <note>Alchemists often distinguished between "common" substances bought from an apothecary and the "philosophical" versions of those same substances, which were purified or symbolic principles.</note>, since it is a simple fire, living, giving life to other dead bodies, and maturing them; it does this in such a way that it supplies the defects of nature, as it is by itself of a superfluous maturity, being perfect in its own nature and increasingly purified through the craft. The Philosophers have subtly imagined how those sulfurs could be drawn out from these more perfect bodies, and how their qualities might be better purified by art, so that through art—with nature as the mediator—that which did not appear in them before might be realized, even though they possessed it fully in a hidden state. And they concede that this can by no means happen without the dissolution of the body and its reduction into the "first matter," which is quicksilver <note>Latin: *argentum viuum*, literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>, from which they were made from the beginning. This must be done without any mixing of foreign things, since foreign natures do not improve our Stone; for nothing suits a thing except what is most closely related to it, since it is a medicine of a simple and mineral nature, produced from Mercurial water, in which gold and silver were previously dissolved. 

For example: if a power has created ice <gloss>*</gloss> from snow in simple frozen water, it is dissolved by heat and returns into the primary watery substance; thus the water is "tinged" <note>To "tinge" means to fundamentally change the color and nature of a substance, the goal of the alchemical transformation.</note> by the power that was hidden in the ice. If, however, the ice is not resolved into water by heat, it does not join with the water in which it lies, nor does it tinge that water with its power, which was previously coagulated within it from its constituent parts. In the same way, if you do not resolve the body into Mercury by means of Mercury, you cannot have the hidden power from it—namely, the sulfur that has been digested and "cooked" by the work of nature in the mine.

It represents the union of opposites, such as male and female or spirit and body.</term>, that is, from a "double thing"—namely, from the body and a white or red spirit. ...tincture and medicine for purging all bodies, which to many fools seems impossible. Therefore, the medicine is perfected from one single thing, which is the water of the body and the spirit. Whence the verses:

And many verses follow according to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath often cited as a premier authority on alchemy.</note>, to which I refer the studious. The verse:

> *Four are made from one, and the four become one,*
> *These are the secrets; thus you shall rejoice without end.*

And if, according to the Philosophers, we have the nature of sulfur and Mercury upon the earth, from which gold and silver are made beneath the earth, it is seen from these sayings how art imitates nature, and by no other way.

...white in the Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note> through a lesser degree of digestion. Whence the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, the authorities cited by alchemists</note> says: Citrination <term>The "yellowing" stage of the alchemical process, indicating the transition from the white "Silver" stage to the red "Gold" stage.</term> is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon a moist substance first generates blackness; acting upon a dry substance, it generates whiteness. When the fire transcends this whiteness, acting upon it further, it causes the purest yellow color. All of these stages can be observed in the calcination <note>reducing a metal to a fine powder through heat</note> of lead.

The Philosopher also says: that each of the perfected bodies now actually contains its own "good sulfur" together with its Mercury—namely, golden sulfur in gold, and silvery sulfur in silver. Therefore, white sulfur becomes golden through citrination because "red sulfur" (which is the very substance of fire) is present there, which has digested this white substance further. Thus, both white and red sulfur exist on both sides within the Sun <note>original: "Sole," the alchemical name for Gold</note>. For this reason, fire is its highest perfection, as gold is generated in fire. And so, its fiery nature joyfully joins with its own nature in a friendly way.

Whence it is asked: Can any external things cause this in these bodies? Since Art <note>the alchemical craft</note> is nothing else, by the mediation of Nature, but the "cooking" and digestion of that nature through simple labor. For example: When I rise in the morning and see that my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; therefore, I go back to sleep, and having received sleep, the urine becomes yellow <note>original: "citrina"</note>. This happens in no other way except through the digestion of the natural heat existing within me. 

In the same way, follow Nature through Art by similarly decocting, digesting, maturing, and refining. For Nature already actually contains within itself the natural fire by which it is matured; other things do not have this fire, and they cannot give it. In the Moon <note>Silver</note>, however, there is only simple white sulfur, which is not as digested as the red, since it has not been deprived of its blackness by the action of the heat which it naturally contains within itself. However, the "species of fire" is covered and hidden, acting both in Art and in Nature, and vice versa. 

And therefore, it is not impossible for Art, through the mediation of Nature, to digest and perfect this further, since Nature naturally desires to be perfected; but it cannot do so by itself unless it is aided by Art and operation. However, these labors, I believe, do not reach the "stiff-necked" man <note>a biblical reference to the stubborn or prideful</note>, because good workers are rarely found. And so, true silver and gold are not made unless they are so digested and cooked—either as the metals themselves or as the Medicine <note>the Elixir or Stone</note> with which the "worse" is tinged and improved into the "better." For the intention of all Philosophers is to perfect the worse with the better. Fools understand this in the opposite way: for they strive to perfect the better with the worse, and that is what they seek

### CHAPTER XIII.

It may indeed be asked, and not without reason, whether this sulfur—namely the white and the red—can be drawn out from other "sick" <note>Alchemists referred to base metals like lead or iron as "sick" or "imperfect," while gold was "healthy" or "perfect."</note> bodies to dye Mercury? I say it cannot. For it was stated before that in them there is no matter of greater temperance <note>original: "temperantiæ," referring to a balanced mixture of elements</note> or less dross than in these two bodies [gold and silver], in which the "tingeing rays" are present, which you can use for dyeing. But you will not dye with others, since it was previously said that they contain within themselves a foul and combustible sulfur, and not one of a powerful nature like that in gold and silver; for all Art has no power unless it follows a nature that is already present. 

You might be able to purge imperfect metals with lesser minerals, but even when they were purged, they would not have a golden or silvery nature in them, because the golden "decoction" or "digestion" <term>digestion: The process of maturing a substance through gentle, sustained heat, similar to how the earth "ripens" metals over centuries.</term> was not in them as it is in these two bodies, nor is their sulfur so mature. Therefore, these immature substances must be assisted by that which is mature, so that they may be ripened. Thus, they do not dye, but are dyed, because the tincture <term>tincture: In alchemy, a concentrated essence or "medicine" capable of staining or transforming the entire substance of a metal into gold or silver.</term> of gold or silver has a proportional nature within them, as they all share a common origin from Mercury. 

From these things it is clearly evident that lesser minerals cannot dye. For if imperfect metallic bodies—which share a common ground with gold and silver in their Mercury—cannot dye or infuse a golden or silvery nature, how then could those things which share no nature with them do so? Therefore, one should not attempt to dye except with those things in which the power of dyeing resides. Dye, therefore, with gold and silver, because gold gives a golden color and nature, and silver gives a silvery one. For this reason, you should despise all other things, as there is no fruit in them, but only the loss of resources, as well as of time and labor.

->*That gold cures infirmities, both in human and metallic bodies.*<-

### CHAPTER XV.

First, I declare universally to all observers into whose hands these presents shall come, that in the entire sequence of this art, there are only two "particulars" <term>particularia: specific alchemical procedures or substances that produce a limited result (like making a small amount of gold), as opposed to the "Universal" Elixir which transforms everything.</term> which are perfected according to the Philosophers and nature. This is true even though deceivers create infinite deceptions, whitenings, and reddenings <note>original: "dealbationes, & rubificationes." These refer to the two main stages of the alchemical work, but here they imply surface-level treatments meant to fool the eye.</note> by which the faithful are deluded. The first particular, both in the white and in the red work, exists in Mercury without the administration of the "perfect medicine," although the "body" with which it is perfected contains the tincture <term>tincturam: the coloring or transforming power of the alchemical substance.</term> within itself specifically, provided it is moved by art and operation as nature requires. The first thing that is perfected specifically in nature from both species is this: since Mercury is the **primary matter** <note>original: "materia prima." The fundamental substance from which all metals were thought to originate.</note> of all metals, composed of a very sulfurous white earth and clear water, the whiteness of the earth shines through the clarity of the water, and its color is the whitest, as experience teaches. And since this substance is "immature," it is possible for **the Sun and the Moon** <note>In alchemical texts, "Sol" (the Sun) always refers to Gold, and "Luna" (the Moon) refers to Silver.</note> to be made from it. Hence the Philosopher says: *Let it be mixed with other metallic bodies, because they are of its own matter, and they themselves were generated*

And thus, it becomes like the metals it embraces, without any foreign admixture, since nature simply rejoices in its own nature, and not through another foreign medium—namely, Gold with Gold <note>original: "cum Sole Sol"</note>, Silver with Silver <note>original: "cum Luna Luna"</note>, Copper with Copper <note>original: "cum Venere Venus"</note>, and so on for the others. Therefore, other metals thus coagulated and colored by sulfur in a particular way <note>The "particular way" refers to specific, limited transmutations rather than the universal "Great Work."</note> cannot become like Gold and Silver themselves. The first reason is this: if imperfect metallic bodies were transformed and mixed with Gold and Silver, then their Mercury would contain that pre-existing "bad sulfur." Even if they were purified, they could not be purified to such an extent that they would be reduced back to Mercury as it was before such excess, nor could a perfect body be dissolved in it.

And since it could not be dissolved in it—the natures on both sides being locked <note>original: "seratis." Alchemists believed metals were "closed" or "locked" in their solid state and had to be "opened" or dissolved to be transformed.</note>—each would be separated from the other during the testing <note>original: "examinatione," referring to the fire-test or cupellation used to check purity.</note>. This is because it would not possess a hidden perfect nature within itself through which their own solutions could be completed by means of the art, so that other perfect bodies might assist with their own nature, which is naturally perfect.

The second reason: if they were joined to perfect bodies while undissolved, they could even less become gold and silver, since by natural congelation the natures of both sides are locked. Since there is no medium to open those natures, nor can one power be joined to another by natural conjunction, nor transmitted so that they return to Mercury (from which both sides drew their origin), they are separated from each other by the harshness of the fire—namely, by the burning away of the imperfect nature and the resistance of the perfect nature, as is clearly seen.

But when you wish to join them, you must create a medium through Mercury, which dissolves and opens the natures so that one can simply pass into the other, and transmit perfect power into the imperfect, so that it may be perfected with it. And these are the labors of the particular way by which gold and silver can be made, but not universally.

### RICHARD THE ENGLISHMAN

<meta>The catchword "sicut" from the previous page begins the first sentence: "sicut de cæteris" (as with the others).</meta>

...and so with the others. For this reason, another "Mercury of bodies" <note>original: "Mercurius corporum." This refers to mercury extracted from already solidified metals, rather than raw quicksilver.</note> cannot act in this way, because through coagulation <note>original: "congelationem"</note> that crude sulfur, which was previously in it, has been altered in its nature. Therefore, it does not corrode as the first kind does, nor does it open what is locked <note>original: "seratum aperit." Alchemists viewed solid metals as "locked" or "closed" spirits; to transform them, they had to be "opened" or liquefied.</note>. Thus, one power is not sent into the other, but each remains by itself, even if they are joined together in a state of conflict; secondly, they are naturally locked on both sides. Consequently, during the testing <note>original: "examinatione," usually referring to the trial by fire or cupellation.</note> and through the harshness of the fire, the imperfect part is consumed, since one nature cannot come to the aid of the other.

But since crude quicksilver <note>original: "arg. viu. crudū" (argentum vivum). This is the common liquid mercury found in nature.</note> can do this—namely, open the locked natures so that each thing may be a help to its neighboring nature—it follows that if it dissolves silver, it will find a silver nature; if gold, it will find a golden nature; if lead, a leaden nature; and so on for the others. Their sulfur is coagulated by it, as the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle, though here likely meaning an alchemical authority like Geber or Avicenna.</note> says, and a similar thing happens to them. If indeed these bodies which share its nature—namely the imperfect ones—cannot perfect it, then certainly those things which are not of its nature, nor share in its mineral origin, cannot do so either—such as those things you seek in various dungs <note>original: "stercoribus." A critique of alchemists who tried to produce the Stone from organic waste rather than minerals.</note>. And therefore, it is "particularly" possible for gold and silver to be made from it, and not in other bodies, as you have heard.

**Note:** There is a twofold dissolution <note>original: "solutio"</note> of bodies into Mercury: namely, through Mercury into Mercury, and into Mercurial water. The first dissolution is required for "particular" works, the second for "universal" works <note>The "Universal" work refers to the creation of the Philosopher's Stone, while "particulars" are specific, limited transmutations.</note>. The first dissolution of bodies into Mercury is nothing other than the resolution of what is coagulated; that is, through dissolution alone, the "locked" is opened because of the entry of one nature into another, and this resolution belongs to particular works. 

The second dissolution is into Mercurial water, and this belongs to the universal works. This is not achieved solely by the dissolution of immature sulfur into Mercury, but through the putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactionem." In alchemy, putrefaction is the stage where the matter turns black and "dies" before being reborn.</note> of the body and the spirit in heat and moisture. Since the putrefaction of all things bound together by nature is a dissolution and separation, the parts previously bound are thus separated from one another, so that each part is distinguished from the other. # THE CORRECTORIUM

...just as the water of a cloud, and similar things; but water is moist, earth is cold, air is hot, and fire is dry. And thus they exist in the natures of composed things <note>Literally "elementated things," referring to physical matter made of the four elements.</note>, since art <note>The "Art" always refers to the practice of Alchemy.</note> cannot naturally separate the parts in such a way that they are simply changed back into the elements as they were, because nature first changed one quality into another. In such a way, art can indeed separate them, so that the moist is separated from the dry and the cold from the hot. 

But nonetheless, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part due to the natural mixing; through this, they can be reunited by art in reverse, just as they were divided. For if one quality did not participate in the nature of another—namely, water in the nature of earth through coldness, and air in that of water through moisture, and so on with the rest—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed, since the elements would be simple <note>Pure elements, unmixed and therefore unusable in physical form.</note>, just as they were before the generation of Mercury. Art would have destroyed nature starting from the head—that is, from gold and silver—down to the first, which is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>; and beyond these principles to the simple elements as they were before the generation of Mercury; yet this is so remote as to be impossible in the art. 

And if it were possible, then it would follow that art would compose elements anew outside of the first matter—namely, the Mercury of metals—and conversely would generate Mercury just as it had destroyed it, which is impossible to be done artificially. But art indeed destroys from the head down to the feet—that is, building from the feet up to the head <note>The "feet" represent the base starting matter (Mercury), while the "head" represents the perfected state (Gold).</note>—in a more subtle form of natural substance than it was before. Thus the species of things are divided when they are transmuted into another form than they were before, which Aristotle says: *Let the masters of alchemy know that the species of things cannot be transmuted* <note>original: "Sciant artifices Alchemiae..." This is a famous, often debated quote from Pseudo-Aristotle’s "De Mineralibus" which alchemists spent centuries trying to contextualize or bypass.</note>, which is true, as he himself confirms, *unless they are converted into the first matter*—that is, into quicksilver—and beyond this I do not advise going, since it is impossible to happen.

### *On Particular Counterfeits*
#### CHAPTER XVII.

Aristotle says:
> Let the craftsmen of Alchemy know that the species of things 
> cannot be changed, but they can make things similar to them, 
> and dye a red thing with yellow so that it looks like gold, 
> and dye a white thing until it is very similar to gold or silver.

They can also wipe away the impurities of lead, or of another body, so that it appears to be gold or silver; nevertheless, lead always remains lead, since it does not have gold and silver within itself, as was said before. This is like those who take **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metal surfaces and in various chemical reactions</term> or other lesser minerals to deceive people with them; they only make "sophistical" <note>deceptive or counterfeit</note> gold and silver. 

For **tin** and **copper** are joined with **Mercury** so that it appears to men to be silver, and is in some way workable and testable in fire according to those who have experience with fire; yet they are deluded in this and in the examination of its nature. The combustible and foul substance, according to its essence, does not have the true nature of silver within it, as appears somewhat in its color and during the fire-test. The first reason is: Copper contains within itself a Mercury that is clean to some extent, except for the defect that exists in its sulfur. Because it possesses a foul and combustible sulfur, it burns. It possesses its redness not by reason of "digestion" <note>proper alchemical ripening</note>, but by reason of red and impure sulfur. However, Mercury has more substance than the sulfur, and therefore it [resists] slowly...

# THE AMENDMENT
## PAGE 464

...Mercury perishes in the fire <note>original: "Mercurius in igne deficit"</note> more slowly than lead or tin: because Mercury resists the fire, except insofar as it suffers violence from the sulfur mixed into it. And the fact that it is burned away more quickly by lead is due to the nature of the imperfect Mercury found within lead. Because infected Mercury, when paired with infected sulfur—as is the case in lead—seeks out something close to its own imperfection.

When silver and copper are mixed together, the lead finds no "infected" substance in the silver; however, it does find it in the copper. In the copper, it first encounters **burning sulfur**, with which it mixes more quickly. In this universal mixture, the Mercury of the copper becomes more "infected," since lead is corrupted in both its parts—that is, in both its Mercury and its sulfur. Indeed, "evil" <note>here meaning impurity or corruption</note> adheres more quickly to evil than it does to good.

To the extent that a greater evil clings to another evil, the resulting substance will be that much weaker and worse. Therefore, the lead clings more quickly to the copper than to the silver, infecting and burning it away. Since the natures of copper and silver—as you have heard—are "locked" <note>original: "seratæ," meaning their internal structures are tightly bound</note> on both sides, they cannot assist the inferior metal. Thus, the copper is burned away from the silver with which it had been fluidly joined. 

Naturally, their internal compositions are "locked." Thus, lead successfully burns the copper away from the silver—a separation that would happen much more slowly without the lead. This is because the more a substance is burned, the weaker and more combustible it becomes.

However, in the joining of tin with copper and Mercury, the Mercury "opens" the locked natures in some way and joins these two: namely, tin and copper. Since both metals possess a somewhat clean Mercury but also contain a "bad" sulfur that is only weakly mixed in, the Mercury of one joins to the Mercury of the other. 

Because this mixture possesses the power of sulfur, it alters the color of the copper (which resides in the sulfur) so that a **new form** appears. At this stage, the sulfur cannot be burned away as quickly as it could before the Mercury was added. The crude Mercury is "coagulated" <term>coagulation: the process where a liquid or volatile substance is turned into a solid or fixed state</term> through them and is altered alongside them in its nature. 

In this way, it may appear to be silver, though it is not **true silver**, as it has not undergone the necessary digestion <term>digestion: a process of prolonged heating to "ripen" a substance toward perfection</term> and decoction <term>decoction: the process of refining a substance through boiling or intense heat</term>. Its sulfur is not of such a simple and powerful nature as that of true quicksilver. In contrast, the Mercury and sulfur of real gold and silver have been sufficiently "digested" and have reached a state of good maturity and perfect refinement.

Thus you have **sophistic silver** <term>sophistic silver: an imitation or counterfeit metal that looks like silver but lacks its weight and stability in fire</term> produced from tin, copper, and Mercury. If one were then to mix in certain powders of "lesser minerals," they would further weaken the sulfur, and thus it would not be impossible for Mercury to act upon the power of nature...

### CHAPTER XVIII.

Having concluded the Prologue of this art and its particular operations, we shall now speak of the **Universal Way**, in which art imitates nature. As you heard above, the Universal Way is possible within the natures of metals: to plant branches upon which grow flowers of wonderful fragrance, and little roses both white and red <note>These colors refer to the "Albedo" (whiteness) and "Rubedo" (redness), the final stages of the Great Work</note>.

The first step is to dissolve the stone into its **first matter** <term>Prima Materia: the primitive, formless base of all substance</term>, which is the conjunction of body and spirit so that they become one **Mercurial water**. Thus says **Avicenna**: "The first step is to dissolve the stone into its Mercury." Thus says **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"</note> the Philosopher: "Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain"—namely, silver and Mercury for the white elixir, and gold and Mercury for the red elixir. This is done in a **dewy bath** <note>original: "balneo rorido," a gentle water bath or bain-marie</note> for the purpose of putrefaction, so that the bodies may be dissolved by the viscosity of the Mercurial water.

Thus says **Parmenides**: "When the permanent water—which was there from the beginning—is joined into one, then follows the division of the elements and their purification." Thus says **Albertus Magnus**: "Four are made from one, and the four become one" <note>original: "Quatuor ex vno fiunt, & quatuor vnum"</note>; that is, from the Mercurial water.

The third step is the purification of the earth, of which the philosopher **Morienus** says: "This water putrefies with its earth; through this, the entire mastery is directed." Thus says **Rhazes** the philosopher: "Join the dry to the moist"; the moist is the water, while the dry is the earth. Afterward follows the **sublimation** of the earth, of which the philosopher **Parmenides** says: "Sublime that which has been whitened with a swift fire, so that the spirit you found within it may depart, and the earth remains calcined." Regarding this earth, the philosophers **Parmenides** and **Morienus** say: "Do not despise the ash that remains at the bottom, for it is the crown <note>original: "diadema"</note> of your body and the ash of permanent things." The Author of the book called the *Rosary* says: I descended into my garden to see the plants of various things growing, and among the other flowers of my Rosary <note>A "Rosarium" or Rosary refers to a rose garden, but in alchemy, it symbolizes a collection of "blooming" truths or the stages of the Great Work</note>, I found a snow-white (or white) rose, and likewise a blood-red (or decorated with redness) rose. ...their deceptions and sophistry, and they write the names of good **Philosophers** <note>In alchemy, "Philosophers" refers to the legendary masters of the craft, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber, rather than academic philosophers.</note> upon their chapters so they might seem to possess a good art and a perfect **elixir** <term>Elixir: the transformative substance or "medicine" of the metals, often synonymous with the Philosopher’s Stone.</term>. ### *Concerning the same: that fixed Mercury brings completion; and the division of operations, and the division of the booklet into two parts.*

#### CHAPTER III.

I have already clearly proven, according to the right truth, that the defect in metals is a lack of fixed and pure **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: also known as Mercury or "argentum vivum."</term>, and whatever is chosen in this art for the sake of completion is the cause of it. Therefore, perfection lies in it alone, and not in anything else. Know this, and do not let it be forgotten: wherever you find it, hold it as the **greater stone** <note>original: "lapide maiori"</note>, for nothing else exists like it, nor can anything do what it does. If it is corrected, it corrects; if fixed, it fixes; if liquid, it dissolves; if thick, it coagulates; if tinted, it tints. For it surpasses all bodies in purity. And one who could endure the punishment of fire could make from it—together with its own congealed **sulfur**—a most excellent **elixir** <term>Elixir: the transformative medicine used to transmute metals.</term>. It is taken both living and dead, but that which is living and pure is always to be chosen. Many operations are performed from it, which are divided into two parts. The first is done with assistance; the second by itself, but nature proceeds with its own sulfur. In two chapters, I shall perfectly complete these two operations. And I shall write whatever I have proven, or done, or seen. Of the sayings of the **Philosophers** <note>referring to the ancient masters of alchemy</note>, I hold nothing at present except that which confirms my own words, because I shall tell the truth, and I have been made free from **envy** <note>In alchemical literature, "envy" refers to the practice of intentionally obscuring the truth to keep the secret from the unworthy. To be "free from envy" means the author claims to be writing clearly and honestly.</note>. Let him, therefore, who wishes to understand my words.

<meta>This page continues the practical instructions for the "calcination"—the process of reducing metals to a fine powder—begun on the previous page. It concludes the instructions for Tin and Lead and moves into Chapter III, which focuses on Copper and Iron.</meta>

->ROSARY<-

White vinegar is effective, as are common salt water, alum, and many other acidic substances. After soaking, they are dried by fire or the Sun until they have reached the state of a white or red **calx** <term>Calx: the powdery oxide produced after a metal has been burned or "calcined."</term>. Likewise, they are calcined with the help of salts, and another good method of calcination is through the help of vitriol and other sharp substances. They are also calcined with the help of sulfur or **orpiment** <term>Orpiment: a yellow arsenic mineral used as a reagent.</term>, and that way is better. 

But they are calcined best of all with **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> in this manner: first they are **amalgamated** <term>Amalgamated: blended into an alloy with mercury.</term>, ground, and washed with sharp acids until they are perfectly purified. Then, they should be mixed with sharp salts by grinding, and with alums and other acidic things, then dried and eroded, and finally the saltiness should be removed by washing. However, before it is dried, let the Mercury be extracted with salt through **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again.</term>, and in this way there remains a white calx, than which nothing can be better. And I give you a general rule: in whatever way **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter: the alchemical name for the metal Tin.</term> is calcined with fire, it produces a white calx; **Saturn** <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for the metal Lead.</term> always produces a red one, unless it has been whitened with sharp acids.

### *Concerning the Calcination of Venus and Mars.* **CHAPTER III.**

**Venus** <term>Venus: the alchemical name for the metal Copper.</term> and **Mars** <term>Mars: the alchemical name for the metal Iron.</term> are calcined with the help of fire, first in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>Reverberatory furnace: a furnace that reflects heat back onto the material rather than applying flame directly.</term> if their filings are placed inside. By the reflection of the flame, the metal is calcined, and from Mars is made **saffron of iron** <note>original: "crocus ferri," a reddish iron oxide</note>, which is called the "cement of iron." From Venus is made simple **burnt copper** <note>original Latin: "aes ustum"</note>, or **burnt copper** <note>original Greek: χαλκὸς κεκαυμένος (chalkos kekaumenos)</note>. 

They are also calcined by heating them to a glow and quenching them in sharp acids until they are totally converted into scales, just as Jupiter and Saturn are calcined by the removal of their dross; then the calx is soaked with sharp and salty liquids until it becomes red and pure. The calx of Venus and Mars can also be whitened. They may also be calcined with sulfur and orpiment mixed with plates or with their filings, or even with salts, alums, and other corrosive substances. The calx is then prepared by washing and drying until it is as desired. 

They are also calcined very well by heating to a glow and quenching in Mercury; whatever can be scraped off during each quenching is scraped off with a knife, and the work is repeated until it is as desired. It is then prepared by washing and drying with salts and by drawing off the Mercury; thus, an excellent calx will be made. And you should know that the calx of a metal "body" is not **fixed** <term>Fixed: rendered stable and resistant to fire.</term> unless it is calcined with fire. I say this because all bodies can be calcined over the vapors of sharp acids or with the acids themselves. But the better calcination of metal bodies is done with Mercury.

->MINOR.<-

## On the calcination of the Sun and Moon.
### CHAPTER IV.

**Sol** <note>original: "Sol" — Gold</note> and **Luna** <note>original: "Luna" — Silver</note> are calcined in the same manner as Copper and Iron, but it is even better and most effective when done through **amalgamation** <term>Amalgamation: the process of alloying a metal with mercury to break down its structure.</term> with Mercury, followed by washing and drying, or by the removal of the Mercury through **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind.</term>, as has been described before. However, the **spirits** <term>Spirits: volatile substances such as mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that "fly" from the fire.</term> cannot be calcined unless they have first been **fixed** <term>Fixed: rendered stable and non-volatile so they do not evaporate when heated.</term>.

## On the calcination of other things and mixtures.
### CHAPTER V.

Many other things are also calcined in order to extract the **tincture** <term>Tincture: the essential "soul" or coloring principle of a substance used in transmutation.</term> from them, and so that their parts may be refined and purified. And you should know that while any body can be calcined by itself, if certain things are joined and calcined together, a **calx** <term>Calx: the fine powder remaining after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burned.</term> of miraculous effect is produced. Do not forget this; experiment, and keep that which is best. This is sufficient regarding these matters.

## On the sublimation of spirits.
### CHAPTER VI.

Both spirits and mineral intermediates are sublimated with assistance. Spirits are sublimated either by salts, or by **vitriols** <note>original: "atramentis" — literally "inks," referring to the dark, metallic sulfates used as reagents.</note>, or by alums, or by the metallic bodies, or by mixtures of these. Note that sublimation is performed for the sake of purifying the tincture. If spirits are sublimated with impure things, they become fouled; if they are sublimated with substances they can cling to, they remain more fixed with the tincture below, which is what we seek. Therefore, it is necessary that they be cleaned first by **sharp substances** <note>original: "acuta" — acidic or caustic reagents like strong vinegar or mineral acids.</note> and by washing, or by a single separation of the impure from the pure. Think diligently on this, for that method is a secret. Sublimate the purified spirits with the pure calxes of the metallic bodies until they are fixed, and you will see that I have spoken the truth.

## On the sublimation of imperfect bodies.
### CHAPTER VII.

**Bodies** <note>In this context, "bodies" refers to solid metals.</note> are sublimated with the help of fire, and specifically by the force of the fire. This is done to obtain a matter that is purely **temperate** <note>Balanced in its elemental qualities.</note>. For that which is too volatile, and the impure earthiness, are separated through sublimation, and there remains the temperate substance we seek. They are also sublimated with "elevating" things such as sulfur, **orpiment** <term>Orpiment: a yellow arsenic mineral.</term>, Mercury, and other spirits. I say this regarding "unfixed" bodies, such as **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iupiter" — Tin</note> and **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus" — Lead</note>, which can be sublimated without dregs or any other thing, or with any of the aforementioned substances; and also **Venus** <note>original: "Venus" — Copper</note> and **Mars** <note>original: "Mars" — Iron</note>, which are sublimated with the same aids.

### On the sublimation of perfect bodies.
#### CHAPTER VIII.

But it must be noted especially that fixed bodies can also be **sublimated** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance to a vapor and then condensing it into a solid, used here for purification.</term>, namely **Sol** <note>original: "Sol" — Gold</note> and **Luna** <note>original: "Luna" — Silver</note>. However, the reason for this elevation is so that we may purify them, either with **sulfur**, **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmento" — arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</note>, or **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo" — Mercury</note>, which causes them to ascend more quickly through repetition, and they are then fixed more rapidly. And this is the innermost secret, which I tell for certain, and which almost everyone else conceals. I say, nonetheless: Bodies must become incorporeal in ascending, and incorporeal things must become corporeal in descending. The greatest industry consists of making a spirit from a body, and vice versa. But it is true that if the total amount of the volatile exceeds the total of the fixed, it will finally return into a spiritual body, either white or red. Truly, I am not envious <note>The author uses "envious" here in the sense of "begrudging" or "secretive," a common trope in alchemical literature where masters claim to withhold nothing from the worthy student.</note>, for I have laid it entirely bare.

### On fixation.
#### CHAPTER IX.

Furthermore, every volatile thing is **fixed** <term>Fixation: rendering a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when exposed to fire.</term> when it is cleansed through assistance or through the help of some fixed thing—that is, through **imbibition** <term>Imbibition: the repeated process of adding liquid to a dry substance and allowing it to be absorbed or "drunk" by the material.</term> and the repetition of the aforementioned things, as I have described openly in the section on sublimation. And this is one of my great secrets. Bodies are also fixed, as I have prefigured, by **calcining** <note>original: "calcinando" — reducing to a powder through heat</note> or by cooking with fire alone.

### On distillation.
#### CHAPTER X.

Many things are also **distilled** to aid in this work. Water is distilled from green or **Roman vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolo Romano" — likely copper sulfate or iron sulfate</note>, from **saltpeter** <note>original: "sale petræ" — potassium nitrate</note>, and from **plumose alum** <note>original: "alumine plumoso" — a feather-like form of aluminum sulfate</note>, which is of the greatest value for the assistance of this work. For with this water, all raw and calcined bodies, as well as calcined or fixed spirits, are dissolved in a wonderful and beautiful solution. Many other waters and oils are also distilled from salts, inks <note>original: "atramentis" — a category of metallic salts and corrosive liquids used for pigments</note>, alums, and many other things—mineral, vegetable, and animal—just as is found in the books of the Philosophers who treat this art.

### On solution.
#### CHAPTER XI.

All bodies and spirits are **dissolved** with the help of the aforementioned corrosive water, or with other corrosive waters which are made in many ways. Because such things are found in many of the Philosophers' books quite truthfully and openly, we are excused from treating them here in our Rosary. But hold this, my friend: that a better solution is made in fire through the **heat of dung** <term>Heat of dung: a gentle, steady heat provided by a pile of decomposing manure, used for long-term digestion of substances.</term>, and with **quicksilver** <note>original: "Mercurio vivo"</note> and **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ" — concentrated alcohol</note> while it is washed; but in the first stage, it is called a "venom" or a "mortifying thing."

### *On ceration.* <term>Ceration: derived from the Latin "cera" (wax), this is the process of softening a hard or brittle substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency, allowing it to merge with other materials.</term> CHAPTER XII.

Calcinated bodies are cerated with resolved bodies <note>original: "corporibus resolutis" — substances that have been dissolved or melted</note>, and this is done through both imbibing <term>Imbibition: the repeated addition of liquid to a solid until it is saturated.</term> and cerating. Although there are many ways to imbibe bodies, the best is done with Mercury, specifically when it is purified "living water" <note>original: "aqua viva depurata"</note>. The best ceration is achieved with living azoth <term>Azoth: the "universal medicine" or essential spirit of Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the soul of all matter.</term> and a drop of soap <note>original: "gutta saponis" — likely referring to an alkaline cleansing agent or a surfactant to help materials blend.</note>. For the "water" of the body, once the body has been reduced into Mercury, is called "blood." Whatever way something is softened with oils, it is worth nothing unless the oil has first been fixed and made incombustible. This oil is obtained only from fixed metals. Know this to be a most excellent secret, and one found to be quite precious among the Philosophers.

### *On coagulation.* CHAPTER XIII.

All resolved things are **coagulated** <term>Coagulation: the process of turning a liquid or dissolved substance back into a solid form.</term> with the help of fire, and this must be done in firmly closed vessels. But keep this secret from me: a thing is perfectly coagulated when it flows <note>i.e., melts or moves like wax</note> under appropriate heat and can withstand the test of fire. If it does not, repeat the work, and through repetition you will reach your goal, the Lord permitting.

### *On Particulars for the white work in general.* CHAPTER XIV.

First, then, how bodies are augmented, and afterwards regarding the shortening of time and labor, and the elixir. And because the "True Red" <note>The Gold-making stage</note> can in no way be achieved unless the "White" <note>The Silver-making stage</note> precedes it, I give you these instructions for augmenting the "white roses" so that perfect Luna <note>original: "Luna" — Silver</note> may be made.

First, the body of Luna must be dried out, and this is done through the calcination I have described. The reason for this is so that the moisture of the substance with which we propose to augment the Luna may adhere to it more radically and firmly without separating. Next, the other non-fixed body you intend to work with must be calcinated, so that it may be fixed by the first. For the volatile part in them flies away through the calcination of the fire, and there remains a pure and unleavened earth <note>original: "terra azyma" — earth that is "unfermented" or free of impurities, like unleavened bread.</note>. By this same calcination, the greasy oiliness and impurity are deleted from the body, and it is reduced to its original state; it remains a clean earth, neither burning nor blackening the bodies. Then, resolve the lime <note>original: "calcẽ" (calcem) — the powdered residue left after calcination.</note>...

Another good [water] is made in this way: Take one pound of egg yolks, one pound of fresh human blood, and two pounds of well-cleaned human hair; mix these in a round glazed vessel. Then take two pounds of well-ground sal ammoniac <term>salis ammoniaci: ammonium chloride, used in alchemy as a powerful solvent and flux</term>, and mix all together. Place those glazed vessels in sifted ashes and light a gentle fire beneath them. When the whole has been resolved into water, then throw yellow sulfur <term>sulphure citrino: common sulfur or brimstone</term> upon it, in an amount equal to half of all the medicines. Quickly remove the vessel from the fire, stirring everything together, then pour the whole into a cucurbit <term>cucurbitam: a gourd-shaped distillation flask</term> to be distilled. Distill it over its dregs as many times as needed, mixing it with the water that distills from them, until everything remains dry at the bottom. This mixture, when ground with dissolved limes and congealed, tints particularly well; and this is a vegetable or animal tincture.

### Apostrophe to the Reader, and a prayer to 
### God.

## C A P. XVIII.

Behold, my beloved friend, behold how many good things I have now narrated from those contained in my Rosary <note>original: "Rosario" — referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a seminal alchemical text attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note>. Yet you are not yet able to gather any roses from it through the aforementioned things. For my Rosary is so strongly fortified by the deepest ditches, the strongest walls, and many ramparts, that no one is able to enter by any ingenuity, except through seven very firm metallic gates, closed in a wonderful way by many keys. 

> O most clement and merciful God, if I have now sinned in any way, look upon me with the eyes of your kindness, for you alone know the hearts of men, and [know] that I have spoken this only from the fountain of mercy. And I pray you humbly and devotedly, Heavenly Father, that it may not enter the hearts of the wicked; let the sons of wisdom and understanding know, however, that my Gardener <term>Hortulanus meus: "My Gardener," a traditional alchemical authority or allegorical figure representing the guide to the philosophical garden</term>, infused and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit the Comforter, has shown me the single key through which all the gates are opened wonderfully, and almost miraculously, in the blink of an eye, in the first chapter of my Rosary. And the grace which my Gardener granted me by his kindness, I shall piously and amiably write for all the learned and intelligent.

### *The Composition of Strong Water, which is the key of the Rosary.*
<note>original: "Compositio Aquæ fortis, quæ est clavis Rosarij"</note>
->CHAPTER XIX.<-

For the Gardener <note>original: "Hortulanus" — a common persona in alchemical allegories representing the practitioner who "tends" the metallic seeds</note> took three herbs which he found growing in the place of the Rosary, from the same earth out of which the Rosary itself emerged: these were Celandine, Sea Purslane, and Mercury-herb <term>Mercurialis: likely refers to the plant *Mercurialis annua*, but in alchemy often alludes to the element Mercury</term>. From these three he composed the aforementioned key, the method of which I shall most perfectly explain to you. Take <note>original: "R." — recipe</note> two pounds of green vitriol <term>vitrioli viridis: ferrous sulfate, used to produce sulfuric and nitric acids</term>, two pounds of saltpeter <term>salis petræ: potassium nitrate</term>, and one pound of "feathery" alum <term>aluminis plumosi: a fibrous form of alum or possibly asbestos, used for its heat resistance</term>, grinding each one by itself. Then combine them. Afterward, have a glass aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot used in sublimation and distillation</term> well-coated on the outside and all around with the "lute of wisdom" <term>luto sapientiæ: a specialized sealant made of clay, dung, and hair designed to withstand high heat</term>, and place the powder of the aforementioned ingredients into it. Place a glass alembic <term>alembicum: the "cap" or still-head of a distilling apparatus</term> on top, and seal the joints firmly with good lute so that it cannot breathe <note>meaning: to ensure the vessel is completely airtight to prevent the escape of vapors</note>. Place it upon the distillation furnace, giving it a gentle fire.

First, the "first water" is distilled, which you should receive in a glass vial with a long neck; let the vial be sealed to the alembic with the aforementioned lute. Continue the gentle fire until the inside of the alembic is colored with a lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrino"</note> hue; this is the sign of the "second water." Then remove the first water with its vial and seal it with wax, and put on a new vial, which you will seal firmly while increasing the fire until the alembic turns red inside, which is the sign of the "third water," the strongest of all. Remove the vial with the second water and seal it, then put on a new, thick vial with a very long neck, sealing it very firmly with the best lute. Always increase the fire until all the water has come out. Remove this, seal the opening firmly with potter's clay <note>original: "luto figulorum"</note>, and reserve it for use.

Undoubtedly, whoever has this key with them will find that everything existing within the Rosary becomes known to them. ### *On the Difference of Mercuries. CHAPTER II.*

But I say this to you: that quicksilver made from Gold is of incomparably greater virtue, and grants a faster fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term> than that which was not yet a body <note>referring to crude mineral mercury that has not yet been matured into a metal</note>. Nevertheless, it is always quicksilver derived from quicksilver, and it is hot, moist, and masculine. 

Indeed, quicksilver made from the Moon <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term> grants a fast fixation, but it is cold, dry, and feminine. Truly, the quicksilver that was not a body—from which bodies are nevertheless generated—does not differ from the other quicksilver except in its digestion <term>digestion: the process of maturation through gentle, consistent heat</term> alone; and through it alone, and in no other way, are all bodies returned into quicksilver.

### *A Likeness Suggesting the Universal Way.*
### CHAPTER III.

Do not all growing things or plants that come out of the earth always return to the earth? And after these have been in that same earth, having rotted over time, then the whole becomes earth again. But it is not the same kind of power that the [original] earth possessed. For we see that grain is born from the earth, having stalks and many seeds; and if then the stalks are artificially put back into the earth, once they have become dung <note>original: "fimus" — manure or compost</note>, we see that all the dung returns to the earth through putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the chemical and spiritual process of rotting or decay, seen by alchemists as the necessary first step to rebirth and multiplication</term>. But the reserved seeds, if they are placed again in that same earth made of their aforementioned stalks, they increase much more, as is well known to experienced farmers. Thus bodies submerged in Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> return to the quicksilver they were previously through appropriate putrefaction, and afterward the metallic seeds <note>original: "grana metallica"</note> cast into that same rotted earth are multiplied and grow beyond number.

### *The Practice Veiled in Darkness.* CHAPTER IV.
<note>original: "Practica caligine obducta" — this title warns the reader that the following instructions are written in the "twilight" language of alchemy, meant to be obscure to the uninitiated.</note>

Now the way of acting is modeled after the way of nature. Our quicksilver—congealed or thickened by the power of unleavened <note>original: "azymi" — pure or unfermented</note> or red non-burning sulfur—must first be cleansed of all filth and superfluity which can be removed by skill. That skill is sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, used here for purification</term>, which is done thus: Let the stone be placed in an open vessel over a moderate fire, stirring the Mercury itself so that all the superfluous moisture flies away—which is accidental to it and by which the work would be corrupted—and do not omit this. Then there will remain (after all the watery and undigested part, which was too volatile, has been deposited, provided the fire does not overcome its radical fixation) a substance tempered between the fixed and the non-fixed, suitable for completing this work. 

And let there be seed or ferment <term>fermentum: a substance, like yeast in bread, that transforms and "leavens" the base material into a higher state</term> most cleanly purified, one part of which is enough for twelve parts of the purified stone. Let a skillful amalgamation <term>amalgamation: the physical blending of mercury with another metal, usually gold or silver</term> of both be made. Then let the whole amalgam be placed in a very strong glass vessel with a narrow neck, or in an earthen one that maintains the density or compactness of glass, which is better; and let the mouth be firmly sealed. Then let a large and thick philosophical furnace <term>furnus philosophicus: a specialized alchemical oven designed for maintaining long, steady, and controlled heat</term> be made, in the middle of which is placed a very strong, large earthen vessel, capable of [withstanding] fire...

Thus, the truest tincture of whiteness is sulfur extracted from the true Moon [silver], most white; and the most perfect tincture of redness is sulfur from the true Sun [gold], most red. Therefore, one is as possible as the other. This the prudent and discerning craftsman knows.

### *Epilogue or recapitulation of all things said.*

## CHAPTER VI.

If by the help of raw, cold, and moist quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>, and through its benefit, the hot, dry, and clean sulfurous nature is extracted—which burns all things because of its scorching power—there remains in the bodies pure quicksilver, cooked and congealed by the power of sulfur. So, by the help of some quicksilver, the purest sulfur is extracted from the Moon [silver] or the Sun [gold], and there remains pure or red sulfur, which tints blackness and is fixed <term>fixed: rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by fire</term>. One part of this tints two, or three, or four, or six parts into silver, with the help of the first part. One part of the red sulfur tints two, three, four, or six parts of the quicksilver "cooked" in the first chapter, according to the purity of that quicksilver, just as with the white. In the second and final chapter, however, one part of the sulfur of the Moon or Sun tints a thousand parts of the body—that is, of cooked quicksilver. Among these, the most precious and best found among us are always eggs, hair, and the blood of a young male, from which the four elements are extracted. After these elements have been rectified <note>purified</note>, they supply the defect of the elixir prepared from metals. Neither the metals alone, nor the "stones" alone, are brought to perfection. Instead, the elements extracted from these four <note>eggs, hair, blood, and metals</note> are used as the "oil" or as the "tinted soul" within the stone. But the lime <note>original: "calx" — the powdery residue left after heating a metal</note> of the metallic bodies is prepared for the pure <note>original: "azimo" — literally 'unleavened,' meaning uncontaminated</note> or red body. Truly, the white or red spirit is extracted from the bodies, or is fixed and prepared by those same spirits. If the stone is washed and cleansed by other stones, it is fixed, tinted, and rectified with haste in the work. Truly, from the proportioned mixing of the aforementioned prepared substances, a new form results; and thus the elixir is made, insofar as the matter is more digested and tinted than natural Gold <note>symbol: Sol</note>.

# ON ALCHEMY.

Therefore, at the beginning of my discourse, I invoke the help of Him who is the fountain and origin of all good things, that He, through His goodness and piety, may deign to fill the smallness of my knowledge by the grace of His Holy Spirit. May I be able, through my teaching, to manifest the light that lies hidden in darkness and to lead those who wander back to the path of truth. May He deign to grant this, He who sits on high. Amen.

Since I have traveled through many regions and many provinces, as well as cities and castles, for the sake of the science called <term>Alchemy: the medieval forerunner of chemistry, concerned with the transformation of matter and the creation of the "philosopher's stone."</term>, with the greatest labor; and since I have diligently inquired about this art from learned and wise men so that I might investigate it more fully; and since I have transcribed all their writings and have very often toiled over their works, I did not, however, find the truth in those things which their books affirmed. Therefore, I looked into the books of those who contradicted and those who affirmed it, and I found them to be void of any progress and alienated from all good. For I found many very wealthy learned men—Abbots, Priors, Canons, Physicians, and unlearned men—who undertook great expenses and labors for this same art, and at last they failed because they were not able to investigate the art successfully. But I did not despair; I did not cease from infinite labor and expense, staying watchful and moving from place to place at all times, and meditating, just as <term>Avicenna: the Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational in the Middle Ages.</term> says:

> If this thing exists, how does it exist? And if it does not exist, how does it not exist?

At last, I persevered by studying, meditating, and working in the operations of this same art, until I found what I was seeking—not by my own knowledge, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when I understood and perceived that it surpassed nature, I began to watch more diligently over the decoctions and sublimations, the solutions and distillations, the <term>cerations: the process of softening a hard substance to a wax-like consistency.</term>, and <term>calcinations: reducing a substance to a powder by heating it to high temperatures.</term>, as well as the <term>coagulations: the process of turning a liquid or fluid substance into a solid state.</term> of Alchemy, and in many other labors, until I found that the <term>transmutation: the supposed conversion of one element into another, specifically base metals into gold or silver.</term> into the sun and the moon <note>original: "solem & lunam" — in alchemical shorthand, the sun refers to gold and the moon refers to silver.</note> is possible. This result is much better than any natural metal in every test and hammering. I, however, the least of the philosophers, intend to write the true art for my associates and friends, easy and infallible; yet in such a way that "seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand." <note>A common biblical allusion used by alchemists to indicate that their texts are encoded with symbols to prevent the unworthy from misusing the knowledge.</note> Therefore, I ask and adjure you by the Creator of the world that you hide this book from all the foolish. For to you, I shall reveal the secret, but from others I withhold the **Secret of Secrets**, on account of the envy surrounding this noble science. For fools [despise] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "despise" (despiciunt), which would continue on the next page.</note> it—

### *On various errors.*

Now, however, I will briefly and simply inform you in this little work of mine how you ought to approach the labor of such a great work. I will show you first, however, all the deviations and errors, and the stumbling blocks of this art, in which many and nearly all err. For I have seen some who made certain <term>sublimations: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term> with great diligence, and were not able to proceed further because they had no foundation. I have seen others having a good beginning, but because of excessive drinking and other vanities, they were not able to perform the work. I have seen others who made good <term>decoction: boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence</term>, <term>distillation: purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into liquid</term>, and sublimation: but because of the excessive prolongation of the work, they left the work unfinished. I have seen others who had the true art, and diligently presided over the works, but in the sublimations they lost the <term>spirits: the volatile, gaseous parts of a substance</term> because of porous vessels, whence they also doubted, and cared no further for the art. I have seen others who, desiring to investigate the art and not being able to wait for the appointed time, performed sublimations, distillations, and <term>solutions: the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</term> too quickly; and therefore they found the spirits infected and rusted, and the dissolved and distilled waters turbulent; whence they also doubted. I have seen very many who insisted upon the work with diligence, and at last failed because they did not have the things for their support; whence the verse:

Alchemy is an art discovered by Alchimus, and is named from *archymos* in Greek, which is "mass" in Latin <note>meaning a lump or body of material</note>. Now we must see how the work should be done, and at what time, and in what place. And first, we must begin to establish the precepts.

The first precept, therefore, is that the practitioner <note>original: *artifex*; the craftsman or alchemist</note> of this art should be silent and secretive, and reveal his secret to no one; he must not manifest it further for any reason, knowing for certain that if many people knew of it, it would surely be spread abroad. And once it has been spread abroad, he will be considered a counterfeiter <note>original: *falsario*; alchemists often faced legal execution if accused of minting fake coins</note>; and thus he will be in ruin, and the work will remain unfinished.

The second precept is that the practitioner should have a special place and a house removed from the sight of men, in which there are two or three chambers where the operations for subliming <note>heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>, dissolving, and performing distillations may be done, as I shall teach hereafter.

The third is that he observe the time in which the work must be done, and the specific hours for sublimations, solutions, and distillations; for sublimations would not be effective in winter, though solutions and calcinations <note>reducing a metal to powder through heat</note> can be done at any time; I will clearly teach all these things in the descriptions of the works.

The fourth is that the practitioner of this art be diligent and frequent in his operations, and not be easily bored, but persevere until the end. For if he begins and does not persevere, he will lose both his property and his time.

The fifth is that he work according to the instructions of the art: first in grinding <note>original: *contritionibus*</note>, second in sublimations, third in fixations <note>original: *fixionibus*; making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, fourth in calcinations, fifth in solutions, sixth in distillations, and seventh in coagulations—and so in that order. And if you do not lead the work to a good end, you will acquire perpetual indignation from them. If, however, you do reach a good end, they will plot to keep you forever and will not permit you to leave; and so you will be ensnared by the words of your own mouth, and entangled by your own speeches. **The eighth precept** is that no one should involve themselves in these operations who does not have at least full funds to cover expenses, and so that he can purchase everything that is necessary, as well as useful, for the art; for if he involves himself and the funds fail, then he will lose the materials and everything else.

### *That furnaces are necessary, and of what kind, and how many.*

Now we must see how the small furnaces <note>original: *furnelli*</note> are made, and which and how many are necessary. Regarding this, it is to be known that the furnaces ought to be made according to the scale of the work. For if your materials are sufficient and you wish to begin a large work, then larger ones must be built. If, however, your supply is meager, you shall build the small furnaces according to the quantity of the powders and medicines. Nevertheless, I wish to set down the doctrine of furnaces and their size according to what is suitable for both the rich and the poor. First, therefore, we must speak of the **philosophical furnace**. Let the furnace be placed near a wall where the wind can reach it; but let the furnace be a distance of an arm's length from the wall in this manner. Let a pit be made in the earth to the depth of an ell <note>a historical unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm</note>, and a width of two spans <note>the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger</note> or a little

moreover, let it be smeared with the clay of the mastery <note>a specialized mixture used by alchemists for sealing and insulation</note>, upon which a wall shall be built all around from that same clay.

### *Of the quality or size of the furnace.*

**T**ake simple clay and add to every four parts a fifth part of potters' clay <note>original: *argillae figulorum*</note>, and grind it very well; then add a little sand, and grind it again (some intentionally add horse dung <note>original: *fimum equinum*; used as a binding fiber to prevent the clay from cracking</note>, or at least water in which that dung has been dissolved). Having done this, build a wall, as I said, over a pit to the height of two feet, or a little less, and to the thickness of one span <note>a historical unit of length based on the distance between the thumb and little finger; about 9 inches</note>, and allow it to dry. Then, you must have a grate <note>original: *rotam*; literally "wheel"</note> made of potters' clay which can withstand a strong fire; it should be perforated all over, having 50 or 60 holes depending on the size of the grate, narrow at the top like a finger, but wide at the bottom so that the ash may fall more freely. Beneath this, a passage <note>original: *meatus*</note> should be made through the ground and the wall before the grate is placed on top; this should be narrow near the pit, but wide outside the wall—about one span—so that the wind can enter. This passage must be lined with clay. Once this is done, the grate should be placed on top so that the wider side of the holes is facing down. Then, build the wall further upon the first wall and the grate to the thickness of a span. This wall should be one cubit <note>original: *brachij*; literally "an arm's length," about 18 inches</note> in height above the grate. The furnace should have a hole in the middle above the grate where the coals are placed. At the top, it should have a hole where the calcination vessels <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to effect chemical change or pulverization</term> are placed; this hole should later be covered with a lid fitted to it. The furnace should also have four or five small holes underneath (or elsewhere, above) about three fingers wide. And this is the form of the furnace.

Furthermore, it should be known that you must place a tripod made of clay upon the grate, on which the calcination vessels are placed, so that coals can be put underneath them.

### *What and of what kind the sublimation furnaces are, and where they are placed.*

**N**ow we must consider the small sublimation furnaces <note>furnaces specifically designed for sublimation, the process of turning a solid directly into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note>, of which there should be at least two or four. They are made in every way like the philosophical furnace <note>original: *furnus philosophicus*; the primary, versatile furnace used by alchemists</note>—with a grate, an air passage, and holes—except that they should not be of such great capacity. These should stand together so that one can attend to all of them at once.

### *What distillation furnaces should be like.*

**D**istillation furnaces <note>original: *furnelli destillatorij*</note> are to be made in this way: let them be made of clay as described above. Build a round wall from the ground to a thickness of four fingers <note>approximately 3 inches</note>, and a width of three palms <note>approximately 9 to 12 inches</note>. Let the furnace have a hole around its circumference three fingers wide. The furnace should be wider at the top than at the bottom, in the manner shown in its illustration. Only two of these furnaces are needed, which are sufficient for distillation. The vessels <note>original: *vasa*; the flasks or containers</note> should be fitted to the furnaces—some for distillation, some for calcination <term>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to remove volatile components or reduce it to ash</term>, and some for coagulation <term>the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid into a mass</term>. You will find their forms at the end of the book. You may also find these in the *Heaven of the Philosophers* by Ulstadius <note>Philipp Ulstadt, a 16th-century physician and alchemist famous for his work on the "quintessence" and distillation</note>, etc.

### *Of the Glassmakers’ furnace.*

**T**he glassmakers' furnace, which is quite necessary for glazing, should be made with the others at the end.

### *How clay vessels are glazed.*

**T**ake whatever vessel you wish to glaze <note>original: *deuitreare*; here referring to the application of a glass-like finish</note>—specifically a well-fired clay vessel—and smear it well with red lead <note>original: *minio*; lead tetroxide, used here as a primary ingredient for ceramic glaze</note> prepared in this way: take water and add beer or wine yeast <note>original: *fermento ceruisiæ vel vini*</note> to the amount of one-tenth part of the water; mix them together, and afterward add as much red lead as you wish and mix well. From this, coat the vessel with a small brush or with your hand, and allow it to dry. Once dried, place it in the furnace, turning the hollow side downward so that it rests upon two strong iron tools <note>likely iron bars or supports across the fire pit</note> placed in the middle of the furnace. If you wish to put in several vessels, it is better to close the mouth of the furnace with stone and clay. Use a slow fire at first for the space of one hour; afterward, strengthen the fire until you see the red lead flow like wax. Then stop and allow it to cool; then open it, and you will find your vessels excellently glazed. Note this, however: that red lead made from white lead <note>original: *cerussa*; basic lead carbonate</note> is ten times more effective than red lead made from lead ash. Having given the instruction on the furnaces, we must now speak of the spirits and medicines.

### *That there are four spirits of metals that tint.*

**I**t should be known, therefore, that there are four spirits of metals, namely Mercury, sulfur, orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide; original: *auripigmentum*</note> or arsenic, and sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>. These four spirits tint metals into white and red—that is, into Silver <note>original: *Lunam*, the Moon</note> and Gold <note>original: *Solem*, the Sun</note>. However, they do not do this by themselves unless they are first prepared for this purpose with various medicines and do not flee from the fire. When they remain stable in the fire, they perform wondrous works: for they make Silver out of Mars <note>Iron</note> or Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and Gold out of Venus <note>Copper</note> or Saturn <note>Lead</note>. And to speak briefly, all metals are transubstantiated <term>the fundamental change of one substance into another</term> into Gold and Silver, which are equal to any natural metal in all operations, except that alchemical iron is not attracted by a magnet <note>original: *adamante*</note>, and alchemical gold does not gladden the human heart, nor does it cure leprosy; furthermore, a wound made by it swells up, which does not happen with natural gold. In all other operations, however—namely hammering, testing <note>original: *examinatione*; likely cupellation or assaying</note>, and color—it lasts forever. From these four spirits the tincture is made, which is called *Elixir* in Arabic and *fermentum* <note>ferment</note> in Latin.

### *What the Elixir is, and how the masses of metals are transformed by these four spirits.*

**E**lixir is an Arabic name, while in Latin it signifies "ferment." Just as bread is fermented and raised by a good leaven, so the masses of metals are transubstantiated by these four spirits into white and red—and most especially by Mercury, because it is the source and origin of all metals.

### *On the types of medicines and their names.*

**C**oncerning the other spirits and medicines—what they are and how they are named—it is to be understood thus: namely common salt, alkali salt, salt of nitre <note>potassium nitrate</note>, salt of borax, sugar alum <note>original: *alumen zucharinum*</note>, Yemeni alum, tartar <note>potassium bitartrate from wine casks</note>, atramentum <note>vitriol or ferrous sulfate</note>, verdigris <note>original: *viride æris*; copper acetate</note>, calamine stone <note>zinc ore</note>, copperas, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>, minium <note>red lead</note>, ceruse <note>white lead</note>, hen’s eggs, eggshells, vinegar, urine, cadmia <note>an oxide of zinc or other furnace byproduct</note>, marcasite <note>iron pyrite</note>, magnesia <note>not modern magnesium, but likely manganese dioxide or another dark ore</note>, and many other things which we have no need of in this book. These things do not tint by themselves, but are aids to the spirits so that they may be prepared and dissolved more quickly; and with the waters of these substances, the calxes <term>powdery oxides produced by heating</term> of metals are ground, acquiring a moisture that rectifies the bodies themselves. How these are prepared, and where they are found, and how they are calcined, dissolved, and distilled, we shall show in order in the following pages.
