### *What Mercury is, and where it is born.*

**M**ercury is a viscous water in the bowels of the earth, a subtle substance of white earth united by a very temperate heat in a balanced union. For this reason, it flees easily on a flat surface, and because of its wateriness it does not stick, even though it possesses a viscous substance; this is due to its dryness, which regulates it and prevents it from adhering. It is also the material of metals when combined with sulfur—namely, the red stone from which quicksilver <note>original: *arg.viuum*</note> is extracted. It is found in mountains, and especially in great quantities in old sewers <note>likely referring to old mine shafts or drainage cavities where minerals accumulate</note>. Its nature is cold and moist, and it is the source of all metals; from it, all things are procreated, as was said above. It is created alongside all metals and is mixed with iron; without it, no metal can be gilded. 

<insert>Quicksilver <note>original: *Arg. viu.*</note> sublimated with sulfur and sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> is converted into a shining red powder; and when burnt again in the fire, it returns to a moist and flowing substance.</insert>

### *What sulfur is, what it does, and where it is found.*

**S**ulfur is truly the "fatness" of the earth, thickened in the mineral veins of the earth by a temperate boiling <term>decoction; the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract or concentrate its essence</term> until it hardens and becomes thick. When it has been hardened, it is called sulfur. Sulfur has a very powerful effect and is of a uniform substance throughout its parts. Because of this, its oil is not removed by distillation as it is from other oil-bearing things, but rather by boiling the sulfur in sharp waters <note>corrosive liquids like vinegar or mineral acids</note>. It is found in the earth, sometimes in mountains and sometimes in marshes. It is also found in many varieties: namely white, red, green, yellow, black, and also a certain "dead" kind. "Living" sulfur <note>native sulfur</note> is that which is extracted from the earth as a clean melt, and it is useful against the itch <note>scabies</note>. "Dead" sulfur is that which has been cast into sticks <note>original: *cannis*; literally "reeds" or "tubes"</note> and is found in apothecary shops. 

<insert>Sulfur has a fiery nature; it melts like gum and is entirely consumed as smoke.</insert>

### *What orpiment is, and where it is born.*

**O**rpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide; original: *auripigmentum*</note> is a mineral stone, and it is formed thus: Earthly dung in the caverns of the earth, through a long boiling, passes into the substance of orpiment. There is a twofold viscosity in it: one is subtle and the other is coarse. One is removed by washing...

### *What Arsenic is.*

**A**rsenic is made of a subtle matter, having a sulfurous color, and it is a red stone: its nature is like that of orpiment: its "flower" <note>the fine powder or essence produced during sublimation</note> will be white and red: it is easily sublimated. For it is whitened in two ways, namely through decoction and sublimation.

### *That Sal Ammoniac is of two kinds.*

**S**al ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, used in alchemy as a flux and cleaning agent</note> is of two kinds: namely, natural and artificial. Natural is that which is found in the earth in two forms, namely white and red: yet both are extracted from a hard and clear mineral, having a powerfully salty taste; its nature is hot and dry. It is also cleansing, purifying, and thinning. Artificial is better than natural for our work: and it is more noble than all salts, and it converts Mercury into water when it is roasted and ground with it, and placed in some damp place to dissolve: and with it iron and lead are dissolved. It is also an "oil" which the dryness of fire has congealed. Its nature is hot and moist, and it is a subtle spirit for the elixir: for without it, substances are neither dissolved nor can they enter <note>referring to the "penetration" of the elixir into the base metal</note>. And it must be known that bodies are not whitened by it, nor reddened, nor transubstantiated like they are by other spirits: but it gives the others entry, and it purges and cleanses bodies from blackness: then it leaves the spirits mixed there with the bodies, and assists them, and afterward departs. <insert>Addition. Water of sal ammoniac, whether sublimated or not, but strained through a filter, or several times through a fine and thick cloth, provides entry into another fusible body for any calcined body <note>a substance reduced to powder through heat</note>, if that calcined substance is often soaked in it, and afterward congealed, and finally pulverized and dissolved. Wherefore the "saffron of iron" <note>original: *crocus ferri*; iron oxide or rust used as a coloring agent</note> prepared in this way provides a tint of the finest gold to silver.</note>

### *The value of common salt, and how it is prepared.*

**C**ommon salt <note>original: *sal commune*; sodium chloride</note> is the key-bearer of this art, because it closes and opens all things, and without it no work of Alchemy can be completed. It is prepared in this way: Take as much of it as you wish and dissolve it in a small mortar with warm water by stirring until it is dissolved; then strain it through a thick cloth into a linen vessel. That which remains at the bottom, dissolve again with warm water as before until the whole is dissolved. Then boil that water in a glass, lead, or copper vessel until the water vanishes and the salt returns to its former state. Then take that salt and place it in a new pot in the calcination furnace <term>a high-heat oven used to oxidize or dry substances</term> (the pot must be closed), dry it thoroughly, and keep it until I teach you how you ought to dissolve and distill it. <insert>Addition. This should not be done in metal, because it is not good, as I have experienced, but in a glazed <note>original: *plumbato*; literally "leaded," referring to a lead glaze</note> earthenware vessel, as Geber <note>Abu Musa Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century Persian alchemist</note> says in the first part of the book *The Investigation of Perfection*. Dissolve the salt in warm water, distill the dissolved liquid through a filter, and congeal <note>to turn back into a solid through evaporation or cooling</note> the distillate in a suitable vessel with a slow fire.</insert> Others afterwards place it in a calcination or bread oven, dry it thoroughly, and store it.

---

### *Salt-water from any salt.*

**F**usible salt <note>original: *sal fundens*; salt treated to melt or act as a flux more easily</note> is made thus: Take salt of Poitiers <note>original: *sal de Pictauia*; salt from the Poitou region of France, highly valued in the Middle Ages</note> and grind it finely in a copper mortar. Afterward, fill four sheep bladders and tie them with a cord by the neck so they do not breathe <note>i.e., so they are airtight</note>. Then have a cauldron full of rainwater and place a stick across the cauldron, from which you will suspend your bladders and submerge them in the water up to the neck. Leave them there for a natural day <note>a full 24-hour period</note>, then extract them and strain the water you find inside. That which is not dissolved, place back in the cauldron for another day as before; do this as many times as necessary until all the salt is resolved into water. Afterward, distill and congeal it. Then place the congealed salt in an earthenware pot over a charcoal fire lit on all sides—having first sealed it well with clay <note>original: *lurato*, likely a corruption of *lutato*</note>—and then leave it in the fire or furnace until the fire is extinguished. After it has cooled, open your salt, which will be like metal; let this be done seven times and no less.

---

### *The value of alkali salt, and how it is prepared.*

**A**lkali salt <note>original: *sal alkali*; typically potassium carbonate derived from plant ashes</note> is that which pertains to this art; when it is well prepared, it dissolves all calces <note>original: *calces*; the powdery metallic oxides remaining after a metal has been burned or "calcined"</note> of bodies into a solid mass. Its nature is hot and moist. It is made thus: Take ashes of rotted oak in great quantity, or lees-ashes <note>original: *cineres clauellati*; potash</note>...

...potash <note>original: *cinis clavellatus*; literally "clubbed ashes," a high-quality wood ash used as a cleaning agent and chemical reagent</note> specifically, which is used for washing clothes, and grind it very finely. Next, take this salt and put it into a pot until it is half full, and place it uncovered in the furnace. Give it a slow fire at first, until it stops spitting <note>original: *insaniat (sive saliat)*; literally "acting insane" or "leaping," referring to the crackling of salt when heated</note> while boiling. Afterward, give it a stronger fire until the whole thing glows red and melts like wax. Then pour it with tongs into another pot immediately, because if you delay at all, you will not be able to pour it, as it hardens quickly. Then you will have white alkali salt, which you should place in a glass vessel in a warm and dry place, because if you were to put it in a damp place, it would dissolve <note>original: *solueretur*; referring to deliquescence, where the salt absorbs moisture from the air and turns into liquid</note>.

Then let it be placed in a clean and dry place.</insert> 

*Alumen faseolum* <note>a variety of alum, possibly named for its bean-like crystalline shape</note> is called alkali alum, *alofor*, and potash, or is made from it. Take Yemen alum <note>original: *Alumen iameni*; a high-quality alum sourced from the East, prized for its purity</note>, grind it, and dissolve it in three pounds of distilled urine. Then distill it through a new filter, and then solidify the white part. Afterward, grind it upon a marble slab. Then rub another marble with distilled vinegar and place that ground alum on top, tilting the marble to one side so that the clear water falls into a glass vessel, while the earthiness remains upon the marble like white earth. This should be done in a cold and dewy place, and then placed in a glass vessel that is well-sealed. You can solidify this water over a very light "moist" fire. Spirits are fixed <term>the process of making a volatile substance, like mercury or sulfur, stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term> with this alum, and calcined bodies <note>metals or minerals that have been reduced to a powder through high heat</note> are washed with this water.

### *The value of common salt, and how it is prepared.*

Take as much alum <note>original: *alumen*; a mineral salt used as a mordant and in chemical processing</note> as you wish, and place it into a pot until it is half full or less. Close the vessel and place it in the furnace. First, apply a slow fire, and afterwards a strong one, and allow it to dry for an entire day in such a fire. Afterwards, remove it once it has cooled, and you will find the alum to be whiter than snow. Keep this, because from it a "water for whitening" <note>original: *aqua ad album*; a solution used to treat metals to give them a silver-like appearance</note> is made upon a marble stone in a cold and damp place. **Addition.** In the manner described, any alum can be resolved into water, either by grinding it with a little sublimated sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniaci*; ammonium chloride</note>, or by placing it to dissolve upon marble, or in dung, or in the vapor of hot water, or by other means.

### *How vitriol is turned red, and dissolved into water.*

Vitriol <note>original: *atramentum*; literally "ink," but in an alchemical context it refers to metallic sulfates like green vitriol or copperas</note> is a black earth, having a sulfurous odor when it is burned in the fire. Its black color is changed into red through calcination <note>original: *calcinatio*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or cause oxidation</note>, a color which it never loses thereafter. Take as much ground vitriol as you wish and put it into a pot until it is half full or up to the top. Close it with a lid and seal it with clay. Once dried, place it in the calcining furnace. Apply a slow fire at first for three hours, then a stronger fire for three hours, until the whole pot glows red. Allow it to stand in such heat for a day and a night, taking care that it does not melt. Afterwards, allow it to cool and remove it; you will then have red vitriol, which is called the "flower of vitriol" <note>original: *flos atramenti*; likely red iron oxide, used as a pigment and reagent</note>. Save this, for when it is dissolved in water, both spirits and metallic bodies are reddened with that red color, which they will never lose. 

**Addition to the chapter above on Alum.** Lead alum <note>original: *alumen plumbae*; likely a specific crystalline form of alum or a lead-based salt</note> is prepared thus: Grind it finely and boil it in purified urine. Add enough urine so that it stands two fingers' depth above the alum, and boil until the alum is dissolved in the liquid. Afterwards, distill it through a filter, then congeal and dry it between two earthen plates over a slow fire. In this way, you ought to dry things that you cannot dry in the sun, unless they are "spirits" <note>volatile substances</note>, because their drying process is different, and is done thus: Place the substance in a vessel closed on all sides except for the top, where a small hole the size of a pea is made. Place the vessel with the material in the oven to dry after the bread has been removed, or when it has become slightly warmer. Leave it there the whole night, and in the morning you will find it dry. This preparation is called **Exsiccation** <note>the thorough drying of a substance</note>. Seek more on this in Aristotle's *On the Perfect Mastery* <note>original: *Aristotele de Perfecto magisterio*; a famous alchemical treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages</note>.

## How tartar is prepared, and how oil is made from it, by which calxes are dissolved.

Tartar <note>original: *tartarum*; the potassium bitartrate crust that forms in wine barrels</note> is a substance of great value for this art. It is prepared in this way: Take thick tartar from either red or white wine, fill a pot with it, and seal it. Then, place it in a furnace and apply a slow fire at first, and later a stronger one. Do this for three days and nights, until the pot glows red. Afterward, remove it and set it aside; I will teach you how to make an oil from it with which you can dissolve all the calxes <note>original: *calces*; the powdered oxides or residues left after a metal is burned</note> of "bodies" <note>metals</note> and "spirits" <note>volatile substances like mercury or sulfur</note> in water. This oil is one of the "retainers" <note>original: *retinaculis*; substances used to "fix" or hold volatile spirits so they do not evaporate under heat</note>. **Addition.** It is not good to fill the pot when using a strong fire; I have experienced this many times.

## How verdigris is made, and how it is turned red, and it is valuable above all else for this art.

Make verdigris <note>original: *viride æris*; literally "green of copper," a green pigment or crust</note> in this way: First, smear plates of copper with sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride</note> and honey that have been dissolved together. Suspend these over the vapors of strong vinegar in a sturdy pot. Seal it very well so that it cannot breathe in any way, and place it in a warm spot so the vinegar evaporates. Let it stand for three or four weeks. Then open it, and you will find verdigris clinging to the plates. Scrape this off and save it, then suspend the plates over vinegar again as before, until they are totally converted into verdigris. Afterward, place it in the fire and calcine <note>heat to a high temperature</note> it thoroughly, just as I taught you regarding vitriol <note>original: *atramentum*</note>. It will become a red color that will never be destroyed. When this is dissolved in water, the bodies and spirits can be reddened with it with a perpetual color. This is also one of the retainers of spirits, and there are many secrets in that water.

**Addition.** Alternatively, verdigris is made this way: Take one pound of copper filings <note>original: *limaturæ Veneris*; "filings of Venus," the alchemical name for copper</note>, half a pound of vitriol, and half a pound of sal ammoniac. Make a paste of all these with strong vinegar. Place it in a glass vessel in horse dung; there it will putrefy <note>the alchemical stage of breaking down through gentle, moist heat</note>, and a noble verdigris will be produced.

**The Flower.** <note>original: *Flos*; referring to the "flower" or purest essence of the substance</note> Take a very clean pan made of copper and suspend it over the sharpest vinegar. Place it in the Sun without moving it. After fourteen days, open it and take the pan; collect the "flower," and you will make it most pure.

**Note** that Geber <note>a famous 8th-century alchemist, though these texts are often attributed to a "Pseudo-Geber"</note> says in the *Book of Furnaces*, in the chapter on the Moon <note>Silver</note>, that Venus <note>Copper</note> must be purified and dissolved, and from it is extracted a most pure sulfur, which is both coloring and fixed.

### *How cinnabar is made, and from what.*

Cinnabar <note>original: *Cinnabrium*; red mercuric sulfide, highly valued as a red pigment and a source of mercury</note> is a noble substance that belongs to this art, and it is called Uzifur <note>original: *Vfifur*; a term derived from Arabic alchemical vocabulary for cinnabar</note>. It is made from quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur in this way: Take two parts Mercury and a third part sulfur, and grind them together in the manner of vermilion <note>a bright red pigment</note>. Place this in a glass vessel with a narrow neck, and coat the vessel everywhere with clay to the thickness of one finger. Once dried, place it upon a tripod and block the mouth of the vessel well. Apply a slow fire for nearly half a day; afterward, strengthen the fire further and roast it for an entire day until you see red smoke coming out from the top. Then allow it to cool, remove it, and break the vessel; you will find good, fixed cinnabar. Therefore, practice this and you will find the truth.

And note that when it appears to you that the vessel containing the cinnabar begins to "sweat" at the top, open it very cautiously, and you will see saffron-colored smoke exhaling, which after a short hour will be transformed into a red color, or that of cinnabar. Afterward, take a wooden stick and put it into the flask and draw it out, and you will see: if it is sufficient, then allow it to cool.

**Addition.** But first let the Mercury be washed with ashes and salt, and passed through a thin cloth. Similarly, let the sulfur be boiled in urine and vinegar, removing the "cloud" <note>scum or impurities</note> floating on top, and afterward let it be dried—specifically, for one day in vinegar, and a second time let it be boiled in urine. But I have seen this written: Take two parts Mercury, three parts sulfur, and four parts sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, often used as a flux in alchemy</note>. These are the words of Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>.

### *How and from what Azure is made.*

Even if Azure <note>original: *Azurium*; likely a synthetic blue pigment similar to blue frit or a copper-based compound</note> is not necessary for our art, I will nonetheless provide the teaching for it: Take two parts Mercury, a third part sulfur, and a fourth part sal ammoniac. Grind these together just as I taught you regarding cinnabar, and place them in a glass vessel. Roast it in every way like the cinnabar; and when you see a blue <note>original: *blaueum*; a Latinization of a Germanic word for blue</note> smoke through the glass, then it is enough. When it has cooled, break the vessel and you will find a noble azure. Then grind it upon a stone without water, and you will make back your expenses from it <note>implying the pigment is valuable enough to sell for a profit</note>.

**Addition.** Some say that the glass vessel ought to remain open until the moisture of the material has evaporated over the fire. I saw in a certain treatise regarding the weight of azure: 22 weights of Mercury, 8 of sulfur, and 4 of sal ammoniac. Likewise, I saw in another treatise that one should use one weight of sal ammoniac, double that of native sulfur, and triple that of Mercury.

Then allow it to cool, and you will find the white lead has become somewhat red. Do this again as before, grinding for half a day; then take it out, and you will find good red lead.

### What sublimation is and in how many ways it can 
### be done.

Sublimation is the elevation of a dry substance by fire so that it adheres to its vessel <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again on the cooler upper parts of the apparatus</note>. Sublimation is varied according to the diversity of the spirits to be sublimated. Some occur with intense heat <note>original: *ignitione*; literally "firing" or "kindling"</note>, such as marcasite <note>iron pyrite or similar metallic sulfides</note>, magnesia <note>likely manganese ore or a form of talc</note>, and tutia <note>zinc oxide residue collected from the flues of brass-making furnaces</note>. Some occur with moderate heat, such as Mercury and arsenic; some with a mild fire, such as sulfur. 

One form of sublimation is for Mercury, so that its earthiness is stripped away and its wateriness is changed. The technique involves separating the superfluous earth that is often mixed with things for which it has no affinity; thus, its sublimation is repeated frequently. Among the substances used for this purpose are the lime <note>original: *calx*; the powdery residue left after a substance is "burnt" or calcined</note> of eggshells, white marble, very finely ground glass, and every kind of prepared salt. By these substances, it is cleansed; by others, however, it is not—unless those bodies are already in a state of perfection. Rather, they corrupt it, because all such things contain a "sulfurousness" <note>the alchemical principle of combustibility and impurity</note> which, ascending with the mercury during sublimation, corrupts the work. For this reason, if you sublimate from tin <note>original: *stanno*</note> or lead <note>original: *plumbo*</note>, after sublimation you will see it stained with blackness. Therefore, sublimation is better performed with those things with which it does not naturally combine; yet it would be better with those things with which it does combine, provided they do not possess that sulfurous quality. ### *What calcination is, and in how many ways it is performed.*

Calcination is the reduction of any substance into powder by means of fire through the removal of the moisture that holds its parts together. Bodies that have been diminished from their perfection are calcinated. Furthermore, there are various types of calcination. Bodies are calcinated so that the defiling and corrupting sulfurousness <note>original: *sulphureitas*; in alchemy, the "sulfur" principle was associated with flammability and impurities that caused metals to tarnish or decay</note> may be destroyed; for every sulfurousness from any combustible thing is burned away, which could not be removed without calcination. A specific purpose for soft bodies is to harden them through this process, but it is imprinted more clearly and they harden more quickly. The reason for the calcination of spirits <note>volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic</note> is so that they may be better "fixed" <note>rendered solid and non-volatile</note> and more quickly dissolved into water: because every type of calcinated material is more fixed and easier to sublimate than those which are not calcinated. Therefore, soft bodies can easily be calcinated by fire; but hard bodies require a vehement fire, as I shall teach at the end. **Addition.** Silver <note>original: *Luna*; alchemists referred to silver as "Luna" (the Moon) due to its white, reflective luster</note> is calcinated thus: Take one ounce of the purest silver, or more as you wish, and from it make thin sheets like the fingernails of a hand. Take a third part of common salt, prepared and calcinated in the usual way, and a fourth part of sublimated mercury <note>mercury that has been vaporized and re-solidified to purify it</note>. Make a powder of the said mercury and salt ground together. Afterward, cement the said sheets in a sublimation vessel <note>original: *sublimatorio*</note>, placing first a layer of the said powder, then a layer of the said sheets, and so on layer by layer. Then perform the sublimation with a slow fire until all the moisture of the mixed substances vanishes. Then close the opening well, and increase the fire for a natural day <note>a period of 24 hours</note>. Take care not to remove the vessel from the fire immediately, but allow it to cool for three hours; do not open the vessel until it is cold, because the spirits would exhale. When the vessel is cold, remove it and extract the sublimated mercury, which will be clear as crystal, and set it aside. Afterward, extract your silver, which remains semi-calcinated with the common salt, and grind the salt and the semi-calcinated silver together upon a platter <note>original: *paropside*; a side-dish or shallow bowl</note> if possible. If it cannot be done there, place it in a glass pan, and with boiling water separate all the salt until you feel no saltiness on the tongue. Then dry the calx <note>the resulting powder</note> left at the bottom of the platter, and...

### *What coagulation is, and for what purpose it is done.*

Coagulation is the reduction of a liquid substance into a solid mass through the removal of moisture. The reason for its discovery is the hardening of Mercury, and the washing away of the "wateriness" mixed into dissolved medicines. Mercury is coagulated through its frequent precipitation with force against the harshness of fire. The harshness of that fire removes its wateriness, and this is performed in a long and narrow vessel.

### *What fixation is, and in how many ways bodies may be fixed.*

Fixation is the proper adaptation of a substance that "flees" from fire <note>referring to volatility—the tendency of substances like mercury or sulfur to evaporate when heated</note>. The reason for its discovery is so that every tincture <note>the color or transformative essence imparted to a metal</note> and every alteration may be made permanent in another substance and not be changed. Bodies that have been diminished from their perfection are fixed through calcination, once they are released from their volatile and corrupting sulfurousness. Sulfur and arsenic are fixed in two ways: in one way, by repeating the sublimation over them in other substances, or until they remain stable. <margin>L</margin> Spirits <note>volatile alchemical substances</note> are also fixed in another way, namely with the "waters" of metals, or with oil of tartar <note>a solution of potassium carbonate</note>, as I shall describe below. *Addition.* Take mercury sublimate and sal ammoniac in equal parts, sublimate seven times, or until it melts; then a stone will remain at the bottom. Grind that and dissolve it in a damp place so that it becomes "water" <note>liquid</note>. With this water, soak metallic arsenic, then dissolve it with distilled vinegar, and distill seven times, or congeal and dissolve it. It will become a stone.

Arsenic is made metallic by melting it with two parts of white soap and one part of arsenic. It is done differently in the *Book of Furnaces* by Geber <note>an influential 8th-century alchemist, known in Arabic as Jabir ibn Hayyan</note>; look there if you wish. Sublimate Mercury, or sulfur, or prepared arsenic—or several of them together—with salt of tartar, or saltpeter <note>original: *sale pettae*, likely *petrae*</note>, or sal ammoniac, and let this be done as many times as necessary until they remain fixed; then extract the salt with hot water.

->What distillation is, and how, and<-
->why.<-

Distillation is the rising of watery vapors within their vessel. It varies, for some is done without fire, and some with fire. That which is done with fire is found to be of two types: one is by elevation, like that performed with an alembic <note>a chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>; the other is by descent, like that performed through a pipe with fire placed above the vessels, and so on.

The general reason for any distillation is the purification of liquids from their dregs <note>original: *faece*; the sediment or waste left at the bottom</note>. For we see that a distilled thing is made purer. The specific reason for [producing] pure water is the soaking <term>imbibition: the process of a solid absorbing a liquid until it is saturated</term> of spirits and clean medicines. Thus, if we ever need to perform a soaking, we may have pure water that does not contain or leave behind dregs after its resolution, which could infect our medicines and cleansed spirits. 

The reason for the invention of distillation by descent through a pipe is the extraction of pure oil in its own nature, when oil that is naturally combustible could not otherwise be obtained by the senses, as is evident in petroleum <note>literally "rock oil," used here to describe naturally occurring mineral oils or bitumens</note>. The reason for the invention of distillation performed by a filter <note>original: *per filtrum*; referring to "wick distillation" where liquid travels along a fabric strip into a new container</note> is solely for the clarity of the water.

**Addition.** Mercury is sublimated <note>the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind</note> as follows. Take: one ounce of dried vitriol <note>a sulfate mineral</note> and one ounce of previously calcinated common salt. Let them be powdered and mixed. Add, bit by bit, one ounce of Mercury. Grind them together while sprinkling a little distilled vinegar so that it is better strengthened; or, what is even better, a little *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," a historical name for nitric acid</term>, as it will be better strengthened. Afterward, place it in the sublimatory vessel. 

And if the sublimatory vessel is made of glass, let it be heated by means of ashes <note>an ash bath used to distribute heat evenly and prevent the glass from cracking</note>, and let the luting <note>original: *lutum*; a paste used to seal joints in chemical apparatus</note> be made of powdered chalk mixed with flour and tempered with egg whites. And if the sublimatory vessel is made of earthenware, let it be placed over coals, and let the luting be made of clay and quicklime with horse dung, along with salt water and thoroughly soaked paper.

Ceration is the softening of a dry substance that cannot be melted. From this, it is clear that the reason for its invention is so that what [is hard may be made soft]...

...had no entry <note>original: *ingressionem*; the ability of a substance to penetrate or combine with another</note> because it lacked the ability to melt into the body for alteration; thus it must be softened (or "waxed") until it flows and gains entry. Some have thought that ceration <term>ceration: from the Latin *cera* (wax); the process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax, allowing it to melt without evaporating</term> ought to be performed with liquid oils and waters, but this is an error: for in no substances is the total humidity found better than in sulfur and arsenic. Now, the method of ceration by these means is to repeat their sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again</note> over the material to be softened as many times as necessary, until, finding humidity in it, they provide a good melting. However, this will not happen before they are perfectly cleansed of every corrupting thing. But it seems better to me that their "oils" should first be fixed <note>made stable under heat</note> by oil of tartar <term>oil of tartar: a thick, saturated solution of potassium carbonate, often used as a powerful alkaline agent</term>, and with those oils, every suitable ceration may be performed: and let these words suffice concerning these things.

<margin>Addition</margin>
**Addition.** Ceration is indeed necessary in all Elixirs, whether of spirits, stones, or bodies: in this all Philosophers agree. The method of ceration is as follows: Let the body be "waxed" until it appears like soft wax and water floats upon it. Dissolve it in a phial placed under dung <note>decomposing horse dung was used as a source of gentle, steady heat in alchemical laboratories</note>, then distill it once, and remove the dregs <note>original: *faecem*; the sediment</note> because they are somewhat black. Then, let it congeal in a small furnace. The signs of transmutation <note>the successful change of the substance</note> are these: if a little of that Elixir is taken after congealing and placed in a crucible over the fire, and it melts, it is good; if not, return to the regimen <note>the systematic procedure or "recipe" being followed</note>.

->*How you shall prepare Mercury, and whiten it like snow.*<-

<margin>Mercury</margin>
Take one pound of Mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*; quicksilver</note>, and grind it upon a stone like this: Take lime of eggshells <note>original: *calcem corticis ouorum*; eggshells burned into a white powder</note>, or white marble lime, or verdigris <term>verdigris: a green pigment or crust formed on copper, used here as a reactive agent</term>, and place some of it upon the stone, and pour strong vinegar over it, and grind it into a paste. Afterward, add a little of the Mercury, and grind until none of it appears [to the eye], and again add a little Mercury and grind it together as before, and add a little sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metals and promote chemical reactions</term>. Or, grind everything together until the Mercury is no longer visible. Then make small pieces from this in the manner of pastilles <note>small cakes or tablets</note>, and place them in a vessel until nothing [of the liquid] remains. Then make the pastilles from it, and place them in a vessel made in the fashion of a bowl, and set it to dry in a moderately heated furnace, lest the Mercury evaporate through too much heat. Let there be 1 pound of Mercury, 1 pound of Lime; and the measure of Sal Ammoniac should be such that you always take as much as you did of the lime and the Mercury. It must be ground until no Mercury is visible. When it has been well dried, grind it again as before with vinegar, until it does not appear, and place...

# [WORKS OF] ALBERTUS MAGNUS

...to be dried. This, moreover, is the sign of perfect grinding <note>original: *contritionis*; the process of pulverizing a substance into the finest possible powder</note>: when a small amount of it is moistened with saliva and smeared upon a silver coin, the Mercury does not stick to it. If it does stick, it has not been well ground. When it has been sufficiently prepared, grind it most finely without fail, and having placed it in the vessel for sublimation <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in the upper part of a vessel</note>, place the cover on top. This, however, must not be overlooked: when you have put in the "medicine" <note>original: *medicinam*; here referring to the chemical substance being treated</note>, you should level its surface by combing it with a feather. Then, most carefully seal the vessel where the parts join with clay so that it does not "breathe" <note>leak vapor</note>. Once placed upon the sublimation furnace, apply a slow heat for half a day until that humidity evaporates. You can test this by holding a metal plate over it until it comes out dry. When it is dried, seal it well with clay and apply a stronger fire, and at the very end apply the strongest fire of all. When night comes, allow it to cool. In the morning, open it, and whatever remains "living" <note>original: *viuum*; mercury still in its liquid, metallic state</note> will appear in the upper part of the aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot, often one in a series, used as a receiver in the sublimation process</term>. The other part will lie upon the dregs like snow, able to be powdered, around the walls of the lower vessel (and sometimes in the upper vessel); collect this and save it. Grind the "living" part with the dregs as before and sublimate it until you have it entirely "dead" <note>original: *mortuum*; stabilized or oxidized into a powder</note> and able to be powdered; and so grind and sublimate as many times as necessary until you have it all "dead" and powderable. Then, do not add any more liquid to it, because it would immediately regain its "liveliness," and your labor would be in vain. Take then some of the salt prepared as I have taught, well-purified and dried—take one part of this and add half a part of the sublimated Mercury. Mix them together by hand and place them in the sublimation vessel; level the top, seal it, and sublimate as before. In the morning, take it out, and collect and test what has been sublimated. If anything remains in the dregs, note this: take a little of the dreg (that is, the salt) and place it upon hot coals. If it smokes, then on the second day sublimate that same material again for a day, and afterward very diligently collect all those sublimates. On the third day, place it with new salt for sublimation. Do as before, and you will find it whitened like snow. Then test if anything still remains in the dregs; if anything remains, sublimate until you have it all. Then take new salt again and do as before four times or more until it reaches fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates</term>, and keep it.

**Addition.** It is also very well calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note> by Talc. Master Jean de Meung <note>original: *Ici de Meun*; a famous 13th-century French author and alchemist</note> in his "Great Work" also adds verdigris <term>verdigris: the green pigment or crust (copper acetate) that forms on copper or brass</term>, which is, however, contrary to the teachings of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy</note> in his chapter on sublimation.

## ON ALCHEMY

...of Mercury: because it is said that it must be sublimated with those substances that do not possess "sulfurousness" <note>original: *sulphureitatem*; in alchemical theory, sulfur was the principle of combustion and impurity that needed to be removed from metals</note>, etc. The best method of all for sublimating Mercury: Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist highly cited in the Middle Ages</note> says in the *Book of Divination*, which is the 23rd of the 70: Take one part rock salt <term>sal gemmae: a pure, crystalline form of common salt</term> and another part of Egyptian ink <note>original: *atramenti Ægyptij*; a term often used in medieval chemistry for vitriol or copperas (metal sulfates)</note>, which you should grind well. Then, throw upon these as much quicksilver as there is of them, and let the whole be ground well together. Next, let it be placed in the bottom of a parchment aludel <note>original: *alludel pergameni*; likely referring to a vessel lined with or shaped like a parchment roll</note>, and upon it place roasted rock salt. Upon this, the "medicine" <note>the prepared chemical mixture</note> should be placed after it has been dried, so that no moisture is left in it. A small fire should be kindled under it first, then increased until the quicksilver is sublimated. Afterward, take it and grind it most thoroughly, and sublimate it again. Let the head of the aludel be wide at the start, then successively narrower and more constricted until it returns to the size of the palm of a hand. For it will be sublimated like a crystal in the parts of the aludel beneath the shield <note>a protective plate or lid within the apparatus</note>. As for that which is above the shield, it does not become a stone, but will be a white powder; and this process should be done seven times. If it is then fixed <note>made stable and non-volatile</note> over the fire and a glowing plate, it will be well; if not, repeat the sublimation with the "ink" and salt, so that the head of the vessel is narrowed. For it will flow (or stick) and create a white plate and pure silver.

If you sublimate Mercury frequently, you must decrease the amount of the dregs <note>original: *fęcum*; the solid residue left after heating</note> by a fifth part each time. If you sublimate with vitriol and salt as described above, they must be roasted beforehand.

The lute <term>lute: a sealing clay used to make joints in chemical apparatus airtight</term> with which the joints are closed is made from ash, clay, and common salt dissolved in urine. Some people make it with egg white and quicklime.

### *How sulfur is dissolved, whitened, and fixed.*

First, let the sulfur be boiled in strong vinegar for an entire day; let it first be well ground so as to remove the film <note>original: *nebulam*; literally "cloud" or "mist"</note> that floats on the surface. Afterward, allow it to dry and grind it. Add as much prepared alum as I have taught you, and throw it into a vessel for sublimating just like Mercury. Be aware that a fire as great as that used for Mercury is not to be made; instead, sublimate it with a mild and slow fire for a whole day. In the morning, take it out and you will find the sublimated material is black. Sublimate it a second time and it will be white. Sublimate it a third time and add salt, and it will be very white. Repeat its sublimation a third and fourth time, even until "fixation" <note>the process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable under heat</note>, and keep it. Addition: It is sublimated like arsenic, but it requires a greater and longer boiling.

# THE WORKS OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

### *How orpiment is whitened.*

You must grind **orpiment** <note>original: *auripigmentum*; literally "gold pigment," this is yellow arsenic trisulfide, a mineral used by alchemists to simulate the color of gold or as a base for whitening</note> and boil it for one day in vinegar, and on another day in urine. Afterward, add to it an equal amount of **iron soot** <term>iron soot: likely the scale or oxide (rust) produced when iron is heated, used here to help strip sulfur from the mineral</term> and mix them well together. Then, sublimate it, following every step I taught regarding sulfur, and it will become white.
**Addition:** <term>Orpiment</term> is also called **yellow arsenic**. Orpiment prepared with vinegar and salt until it is clear is highly exalted; for as far as purity is concerned, none is better. **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and foundational figure in alchemical literature</note> says the same elsewhere: Salt prepares it above all other things.

### *How arsenic is whitened.*

**Arsenic** <note>here referring to white arsenic or arsenic trioxide</note> is truly of the same nature as orpiment, but it is not necessary to boil it. Therefore, grind it well and soak it with strong vinegar (**Roger Bacon** <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1219–1292), the influential English Franciscan philosopher and alchemist</note> says distilled vinegar; see where he speaks of the **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or "calx"</term> of bodies) two, three, or four times, drying it just as many times. It can then be kept as a powder which will be fit for calcining the "bodies" <note>the seven metals, such as lead or copper</note>. If, however, you wish to sublimate it, grind it well by itself and add to it an equal amount of **iron soot**, and sublimate it seven times or more in every way as I taught concerning **Mercury**, and it will be whiter than snow.

### *How sal ammoniac is prepared.*

Sublimate **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, a salt crucial to alchemy for its ability to help dissolve metals</note> in this way: grind it well with an equal amount of well-prepared **common salt** without any liquid, and set it to sublimate with a slow fire for three hours, and afterward with a strong fire for a day. In the morning, take it out and save what has been sublimated, and do in all things as I taught concerning Mercury. Sublimate it two or three times with the same (or elsewhere, with new) dregs, and keep it aside.
**Addition:** Concerning prepared common salt dissolved into a "wax" <term>inceration: the alchemical process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it becomes soft and waxy</term> with **sal ammoniac**; after the waxing, dry it. Do this waxing and drying as many times as necessary until the **sal ammoniac** has absorbed its own weight of the salt water; then use it. For sal ammoniac dissolved in vinegar, filtered, and dried in the Sun, add an equal amount of salt burned in a cloth and hot ashes, and let them be ground together; let it be sublimated without any other soaking, and it will be sufficiently prepared for every use. This is proven if it melts without smoke upon a glowing hot metal plate. These are the words of **Roger Bacon**. Others sublimate it with **rock salt** <term>sal gemma: pure, crystalline rock salt</term>, but that salt must be very well dried before the fire and ground most finely with the **sal ammoniac**. Others sublimate it with common salt and prepared **talc** <note>likely mica or a similar flaky mineral</note> ground together, layered with prepared common salt, and placed around the **sublimatory** <note>the vessel used for the sublimation process</note>, and it is well sublimated four times.

# ON ALCHEMY

or five times. *The preparation of sal ammoniac according to **Rhazes**:* <note>original: *Rasim*; referring to the Persian alchemist Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> Take crystalline **sal ammoniac**, grind it with an equal amount of **sea foam** <note>original: *spumae maris*; likely referring to cuttlebone or a specific porous mineral</note> and **saltpeter**, and sublimate it (place a piece of parchment at the bottom of the **aludel** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped sublimation vessel, often stacked in series</term>, above a layer of roasted salt). Take the sublimated material and boil it, placed in tubes, in water, and it will dissolve. Distill it, or dissolve it in a **bladder** <note>original: *vesica*; a common alchemical flask shaped like a bladder</note> or in **kistifeli** <note>original: *kistifeliis*; a specialized alchemical vessel or basket-like container of Arabic origin</note> over water and distill it; then work with it.

It is difficult to dissolve **fixed** <term>fixed: a substance that has been treated so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire</term> sal ammoniac. Therefore, soak it in vinegar and bury it in **dung** <note>original: *fimo*; horse manure was used as a source of gentle, steady "moist" heat for digestion</note>, and it will dissolve; then distill it. Take care that you do not take all the water, but only as much as the amount of the "spirit" you wished to dissolve, etc.

### *From what substance the fire should be made.*

Having obtained the doctrine concerning the **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process where a solid turns into a gas when heated and then reverts to a solid on a cooler surface</term> of spirits, it remains to see to the substance of the fire. I say, therefore, that the fire ought to be made from **charcoal** for two reasons: first, because there is less labor in managing charcoal than wood; second, because wood gives off much smoke. Because of the smoke, one cannot observe the process well, and the vessels might crack from the heat of the fire, as often happens when the clay is not of good quality or when the vessels have not been well-fired. When they crack, white smoke will immediately appear, which is easily seen over a fire made of charcoal. When the vessels smoke, they must be removed from the fire immediately, otherwise the sublimation will be lost. Thus, care must be taken that this does not happen. Note that the upper vessel—namely, the **aludel**—ought to be glazed, but it is not necessary for the lower one. Sometimes the medicine also hardens in the small dish and cannot be sublimated; in such a case, there should be no doubt, but it must be ground a second time, a little more of the **dregs** <note>original: *faecibus*; the residue or "lees" left over from a previous process</note> should be added, and it should be subtly sublimated, and it will be well sublimated.

### *On the fixation of spirits, an added chapter.*

**Fixation of sulfur:** Pulverize it and tie it in a linen cloth. Boil it in water with **quicklime** <note>original: *calce viva*; calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance</note>, first placing the lime up to the middle of the vessel and filling the rest with common water. Ensure that the bag does not touch the bottom of the vessel but stays in the middle; tie it well at the top and bottom, adding a small stone so that it sinks. Let it boil this way for 24 hours or thereabouts, always adding new hot water as the water diminishes. Then extract your sulfur and boil it in **sweet water** <note>original: *aqua dulci*; fresh, non-saline water</note> so that it is purged of the lime, and it is finished.

*A very strong water for fixing every spirit.* First, rectify the **water of the white secret stone** <note>original: *aquam lapidis occulti albi*; likely a reference to a specific mineral distillate or a proprietary alchemical name</note>, specifically four pounds with one pound of **lime made from eggshells** <note>original: *calcis corticū ouorum*</note>, by burying it in dung and distilling it, and do this several times. Then, into that water—specifically into one and a half pounds—add two ounces of **common salt** prepared to the second degree, two ounces of the best prepared **alkali salt**, one ounce of **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux and for its ability to sublimate</term> sublimated four times, and one ounce of **plumose alum** <note>original: *albuminis plumae*; likely *alumen plumosum*, a feathery form of alum or asbestos</note> coagulated after its preparation. All these salts should be dissolved in that water, and with this, fix all **spirits** <term>spirits: volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that evaporate easily when heated</term> in **double cucurbits** <term>cucurbit: the bottom part of a distilling apparatus, shaped like a gourd</term>, sealing the vessels well with **lute** <term>lute: a fireproof clay or paste used to seal alchemical joints</term>. 

Thus says **Arnold**. <note>referring to Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note> However, with these salts, many distillations are performed, along with the sublimation of the salts, reduction with the dregs, and resolution into the water distilled from them. This is done with the spirit and without those double vessels. Sometimes, in the seventh sublimation, the spirit will be **fixed** <term>fixed: rendered stable so that it remains a solid even when exposed to intense heat</term> with the water by the power of the salts at the bottom of the cucurbit, like a metal plate withstanding fire; and sometimes in the fourth sublimation, the water was fixed for a fourth part of itself, and it was necessary to add more for the completion of the fixation of the spirit.

Some say that by placing **sublimated mercury** on a tin or iron plate in a **cellar** <note>the cool, damp air of a cellar was used to make salts "deliquesce," or turn into liquid by absorbing moisture</note>, it will immediately turn into water, which is more easily fixed by the King through dissolutions and congealings. Water drawn from egg whites, and then rectified with lime from shells, with one ounce each of **alumen iameni** <note>a specific type of alum, possibly from Yemen</note> and sal ammoniac, is highly effective for fixing spirits above all other waters, as follows below. 

Likewise, **mercury** shall be fixed in this way: Grind sublimated mercury in a mortar with raw **tartar** <note>potassium bitartrate, a sediment from wine making</note> and common salt, and then sublimate it. Grind and sublimate again, and continue up to ten times or more, renewing the salt and tartar at each grinding; and from this, the mercury will be fixed. Mercury is also fixed in double cucurbits in a single day by pouring **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated liquid form of potassium carbonate</term> over it, using a slow fire for the first two hours, then continuously strengthening the fire throughout the day until no liquid rises. This is tested by uncovering the cucurbit or opening the vent, or by inserting a **hazel rod** <note>original: *virgulam corili*</note> to check if there is still liquid at the bottom. If it is hard, then it is fixed; if not, strengthen the fire for three hours, then allow it to cool, extract it, grind it, soak it, and cook it seven times.

I have already taught you how to collect various flowers full of good scents, in which health and beauty redound with the glory of this world. I will teach you how to fix sublimated powders so that they may remain in the fire and be united and mixed with bodies, and this in two ways.

# OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

->*Here he teaches how to fix powders, and how they*<-
->*should be mixed with the bodies.*<-

Take then whichever of these you wish, one or two pounds without any other substance, and place it in the vessel of fixation <term>vessel of fixation: a specialized container designed to withstand high heat while preventing volatile substances from escaping</term>, which should be formed over the openings using good glassmaker’s clay to the thickness of a finger. It should not be glazed. Close the cracks with good clay, namely the **lute of wisdom** <term>lute of wisdom: "luto sapientiae," a sealing paste made of clay, dung, and other fibers used to make alchemical vessels airtight</term>. Once this is done, place it over the sublimation furnace and apply fire for an entire day. If it is summer, the quantity of fire should be like that used for **sublimated mercury** <term>sublimated mercury: mercury that has been vaporized and re-solidified to purify it</term> in the afternoon. When morning comes, turn what is on top to the bottom. Do this at least twice. Then open it and see if the powder is fixed <term>fixed: "fix," meaning the substance has become stable and no longer evaporates or vanishes when heated</term>. Test it this way: place a little of it upon coals; if it gives off smoke, it is not yet fixed; but if it does not smoke, then it is fixed. This is the sign for every **spirit** <term>spirit: in alchemy, volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that "fly" or evaporate when heated</term>. If it is not fixed, return it to the furnace, closing the vessel as before, and apply fire for 5 days, or until you hear a sound in the vessel like falling pebbles—which often happens when it is over-burned. (Elsewhere it is said that it should be tested on an ignited metal plate to see if it melts and flows, or if it does not give off smoke.) 

The second method is by soaking it with **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated, caustic solution of potassium carbonate, often used as a solvent</term>. It is done like this: take **sublimated arsenic**, or **sulfur**, or **orpiment** <term>orpiment: "auripigmentum," a bright yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, and grind it upon a stone with the oil of tartar until it becomes entirely liquid. Afterward, place it in a glass vial and put that into ashes that have been well-sifted through a sieve. Place the vessel with the ashes upon the distillation furnace and apply a very slow fire at first, as if "devouring" <note>original: *vorando*, implying a slow, steady consumption of heat to prevent thermal shock</note>, so the vessel does not break. Later, when the glass is heated, make a larger fire, and thus dry out the **medicine** <term>medicine: "medicina," a term alchemists used for the transformed substances or elixirs they were creating</term> in an open vessel if you wish—though it is better in a closed one, where you place an **alembic** <term>alembic: the "head" or cap of a still used to collect and condense vapors</term> over it to receive the water distilled from it, as this is useful for many things. Once the medicine is dried, break the vessel, because you cannot get it out any other way. You will find the powders hardened like a stone. Grind this well as before, distilling more oil over it; again, break the glass and remove it. Grind it well and place it in another flask, and place it in warm horse manure <note>Horse manure was used as a natural, low-heat incubator for "digesting" or slowly reacting chemical mixtures</note> for seven days, and then it will be dissolved into water. Then place the vessel in warm ashes and coagulate it with a slow fire until it hardens, and you will have **fixed spirits**, and it will be a firm and permanent **tincture** <term>tincture: a substance capable of "staining" or transforming the color and properties of a metal</term>. Therefore, cast one part of this powder upon fifty parts of **calcined Mars** <term>calcined Mars: powdered iron oxide; "Mars" is the alchemical name for iron</term>, or **Venus** <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper</term>, and it will be good in every hammering and examination <note>This indicates the resulting metal will be durable and pass the tests of a goldsmith or assayer</note>.

<summary>This page describes two practical methods for "fixing" volatile substances like arsenic and sulfur so they remain stable under heat. The resulting "fixed spirits" are then used to create a permanent "tincture" to transform iron or copper.</summary>

# OF ALCHEMY

### *How and in what way spirits are dissolved into water.*

**Spirits** <term>spirits: volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that evaporate when heated</term> are also dissolved in two ways. I have taught one way using **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a liquid solution of potassium carbonate, often used as a strong alkaline agent in alchemical recipes</term>; but after the seventh congealing, it ought to be placed upon a marble stone in a very humid cellar. The stone should be tilted so that whatever dissolves may immediately flow down into a glass vessel placed beneath it.

Spirits are dissolved into water in another way, namely through the **water of sal ammoniac** <term>water of sal ammoniac: a solution of ammonium chloride, a salt used to help dissolve metals and other minerals</term>, which is made thus: Place this salt, or any other prepared salt, upon a stone in a **pit of resolution** <term>pit of resolution: a cool, damp place, often a hole dug in a cellar floor, used to encourage substances to absorb moisture from the air and liquefy</term>, or in a glass-lined cellar, and it is immediately resolved into water. With this water, grind the **sublimated powders** <term>sublimated powders: substances that have been purified by heating them into a vapor and letting them solidify again</term> that are to be dissolved. Note this: after **Mercury** <term>mercury: also called quicksilver, the primary metal of alchemical study</term> has been sublimated, it must never be mixed with any liquid except with the water of common salt, or sal ammoniac, or oil of tartar. Therefore, grind the powder with this water seven times, and dry it as many times. Afterward, place the ground powder upon the stone, and without a doubt, it will quickly be dissolved into water; reserve this for distilling. **Calcinated bodies** <term>calcinated bodies: metals or minerals reduced to a fine powder through intense dry heat</term> are dissolved in the same way as spirits—namely, **flower of copper** <term>flower of copper: "flos aeris," the greenish oxidation or chemical byproduct of copper</term> and **flower of ink** <term>flower of ink: "flos atramenti," a term for vitriol or metallic sulfates used in making pigments</term>—concerning which one must do in all things as with the spirits, and each must be distilled by itself.

**Additions.** Again (refer this to the beginning of the chapter), for every solution, salt will be necessary.

**Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis." Refers to Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential figures in the history of alchemy and medicine</note>. **Oil of the eagle** <term>oil of the eagle: a poetic alchemical name for a specialized solution, usually involving sal ammoniac</term> is made thus: Take one pound of sal ammoniac and grind it upon a stone with enough urine to make a paste. Then make a layer first of common lime, second of sal ammoniac, and third of lime. Upon the salt, place a small quantity of **lime of eggs** <term>lime of eggs: powdered eggshells that have been burned until they become a white, caustic powder</term>. Place it in the fire to melt, and when it has melted, take it from the fire and place it upon a stone; let it dissolve into oil within four days, then place it in a glass vessel and keep it. Some people make a paste of sal ammoniac, egg white, and lime, form it into a ball, seal it with clay, dry it, and fix it in the fire.

**Quicksilver**, however, is never dissolved until a good, dried, or ground salt or **alkali** <term>alkali: a basic, caustic substance, often derived from wood ashes</term> is introduced upon it. Extinguish it seven times, and afterward revivify <note>original: "viuifica." To "revivify" usually meant to restore a substance to its original or a more active state, in this case likely referring to washing or purifying the mercury</note> it with hot water, and then dissolve it; and unless you do it this way, it will not be dissolved.

**Rhazes**: Let the water of sal ammoniac be taken, which has been sublimated three or four times, and let the sublimated Mercury be soaked in this water little by little. After each soaking, dry it in the Sun or over a weak fire. Afterward, close the mouth of the vessel firmly and place it in **dung** <term>dung: "fimus," animal manure used as a natural, low-temperature heating source for long-term chemical digestion</term>, and let it stay there for seven days. If it is not dissolved, renew [the dung]...

Take one part each of **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to dissolve metals and encourage chemical reactions</term> and common salt, and two parts of **quicklime** <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic substance produced by heating limestone</term> that has not been extinguished, with a little pig fat. Place these in a glass vessel and distill over a slow fire. When the distillation is complete, put it back to be distilled again, and do this three times. This is the **white oil for waxing the elixir** <term>elixir: here, the transformative substance used to change base metals into silver</term>, and for sweetening or softening the **calxes of metals** <term>calx: the powdery residue or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or burnt</term>, and all things which serve the "White Work" <note>The 'White Work' or Albedo is the second major stage of alchemy, aimed at the creation of silver</note>; however, this ought not to be here.

**Water of Mercury** is made with one ounce of **Mercury** <term>mercury: also known as quicksilver, the primary liquid metal of alchemical study</term> and two ounces of **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid</term>, made from two parts of **Yemen alum** <term>Yemen alum: a specific high-quality mineral salt used as an astringent and in chemical preparations</term> and another part of saltpeter. It is made another way like this: Coagulate **sublimated Mercury** <term>sublimated mercury: mercury that has been purified by being turned into vapor and then back into solid form</term> by pouring boiling **tin** <term>tin: a base metal often associated with the planet Jupiter</term> over it seven or eight times. Each time, cover the crucible so that no smoke escapes, and it will be made black or the color of oil. Then grind it very well upon a marble stone with a little water of sal ammoniac and place it in **dung** <term>dung: a warm pile of manure, used by alchemists as a natural, steady source of low heat for fermentation or digestion</term>. When it has been dissolved, distill it either through a filter or in a distilling vessel. With this water, the elixir is made with the **calx of the Moon** <term>calx of the Moon: powdered silver, as the Moon was the alchemical symbol for silver</term>, and **sublimated arsenic** <term>sublimated arsenic: arsenic purified through heating and cooling, used to whiten metals</term>, and the **White Oil of the Philosophers**.

***Dissolution of Sulfur:*** Take one pound of cleansed white **amizadir** <term>amizadir: an Arabic name for sal ammoniac</term> (sublimated) and an equal amount of distilled white vinegar, which should be equal to five parts of sulfur. Let it be placed in the **refuse** <note>original: "cœno," referring to a warm, decomposing mass like a compost heap</note>, stirring it every third day. **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a famous Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: You have this at length in **Aristotle** <note>referring to 'De Perfectione', a work traditionally but likely falsely attributed to Aristotle</note> concerning perfection, in the chapter on the **Separation of Sulfur**. Take one part amizadir, three parts **sea foam** <term>sea foam: possibly meerschaum or a specific porous mineral</term>, two parts salt, and one part urine. Grind, sift, and put it back in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</term>, adding enough **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: another name for mercury</term>. Then apply a light and spacious fire. When white water flows out, save it, as it is necessary for the work. Burial in the earth <note>inhumatio: the practice of burying a vessel in warm soil or dung to provide gentle heat</note> is always necessary. The refuse must also be moved for four days until you see with your own eyes what you seek. But I think Rhazes said this concerning the dissolution of the body to be made for the **Greater Work** <term>Greater Work: the Magnum Opus, the ultimate goal of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>; therefore, take note. Mercury, distilled a second or third time from Yemen or rock alum, is dissolved by itself upon a marble stone in a dewy or humid place; and I believe it would be better if it were placed with the raw material.

### How water is distilled in two ways.

Distillation is performed thus: place the water you wish to distill in a distilling vessel, and place the vessel in ashes, as described above, and distill; and this is achieved by heat and dryness. If, however, you wish to distill using heat and moisture <note>This refers to a water bath or "bain-marie," providing a gentler, more even heat than direct ashes.</note>, place water in the vessel where the ashes were previously, or into a cauldron over the distillation furnace. Into this water, place hay <note>The hay acts as a cushion and insulator to prevent the glass from touching the metal cauldron and cracking.</note>, and place the glass vessel upon it. Secure it so it does not lean to any side but stands perfectly upright. And take the greatest care that you never place cold glass into hot water, or vice versa; otherwise, it would shatter, and you would lose your labor. And note that when you wish to remove the vessel, you must allow it to cool with the water once the distillation is complete. Furthermore, take care during distillation that the water does not boil. And by this method of distillation, preserve all waters; keep all this as the following instruction and form demonstrates. *Addition. Water of bodies:* Take **calx of the Sun** <term>calx of the Sun: gold that has been roasted into a fine, powdery oxide</term> or **of the Moon** <term>calx of the Moon: silver roasted into powder</term> and **sublimated sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to dissolve metals</term> in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note>, and grind them together upon a stone. Then, let the sal ammoniac be **sublimated** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then reverts to a solid, used here to separate it from the metal</term> from the calx of the metals, and repeat this seven times by grinding and sublimating. Then place it upon a stone to dissolve. Some, however, before they sublimate, soak the material and grind it with water of dissolved **borax** <term>borax: a mineral salt used as a flux to help materials melt or dissolve</term>; and they do this seven times. To dissolve metallic bodies into water: Grind **calcined bodies** <term>calcined bodies: metals reduced to powder through heat</term> with equal parts of sal ammoniac and **calx of eggshells** <note>Powdered eggshells provided calcium carbonate, used here as a chemical base.</note>. Then place this in a glass vial over a slow fire until the whole becomes a single mass. Let it cool and break the vial; then pulverize the mass and place the powder in a place of dissolution. In this same way, **sublimated spirits** <term>spirits: volatile substances such as mercury or sulfur</term> can be resolved into water upon marble, or in horse dung <note>original: "fimo"; decaying dung provided a steady, low heat for long-term chemical reactions.</note> that is frequently renewed. If you truly wish to reduce them back into their metallic bodies, congeal them over a slow fire and melt them with **attincar** <term>attincar: an Arabic term for borax, used as a flux in the melting of metals</term>. Gold calcined with salt is dissolved into a red water by the sharpest vinegar.

In alchemy, this refers to ensuring the seal is airtight to prevent the loss of spirit or vapor.</note>, and allow it to dry. Then block the vessel from below with earth. Afterward, maintain a slow fire above it for one hour, then a stronger fire, increasing the heat hour by hour until you have completed half a day. ### The coagulation of all waters is done thus.

The coagulation of all waters is achieved through heat and dryness. Therefore, place the water you wish to dry out into a glass vessel with a narrow neck, and place it in ashes over a slow fire. Within six hours, it will be coagulated into a white or red plate <note>A "plate" or "lamina" refers to the solid residue or crust left behind after the liquid has evaporated or solidified.</note>.

### How the Sun and Moon are calcined.

We must now consider the calcinations of all metals. First, the calcination of the Sun <term>the Sun: alchemical code for Gold</term> and the Moon <term>the Moon: alchemical code for Silver</term>. Take the filings of whichever metal you wish and, having placed them in vinegar for nine days, remove them and grind the dried material into a powder. Afterward, pour on ammoniac water <term>aqua armoniaca: a solution of sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride), used as a powerful solvent or flux</term>, grinding and drying it six times. Then place it upon a stone, as I taught for the process of dissolving, and distill it, and save the result. Add some of this water to the powders. Note this, however: you must add the waters of the Sun to the red water, and the waters of the Moon to the white water.

### Concerning the cucurbit.

The cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the lower part of a still.</note> is a vessel that must stand in water, fixed up to the joint in a cauldron so that it does not move. The cucurbit must not touch the bottom of the cauldron, otherwise it would break. When the water level decreases, pour in more water—specifically hot water and not cold—because the temperature shock would shatter the vessel.

### How other metals are calcined.

Take plates of metal and heat them; then smear them with salt water, because salt corrodes all the "corrupt humidity" <note>In the Aristotelian physics of the time, metals were thought to contain a moist, "corrupt" element that had to be removed to reach their pure essence.</note> found within the metallic bodies. Place them in a clay vessel shaped for this purpose, fill it with the plates, and place it in the calcining furnace upon a tripod. Put coals beneath and create a strong fire, keeping the furnace closed. When the plates glow red, let the fire be extinguished, though take care that the metal does not actually melt. Allow them to stand in that heat until they are destroyed by the fire. In the morning, take them out; scrape off what has been calcined and save it. For whatever remains, smear it again with salt water, repeating the process until it is entirely calcined.

Another method for the calcination of the Sun <term>the Sun: alchemical code for gold</term> and the Moon <term>the Moon: alchemical code for silver</term> and other metals is found in Aristotle’s *On the Perfection of the Magistery* <note>A famous medieval alchemical text falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Aristotle.</note>. Likewise, a double calcination of the Sun and Moon is found in the book of Brother Roger Bacon titled *On the Manner of Composing Medicine by the Balancing of the Elements*, in the chapter on the Calcination of Metals, where he also describes the calcination of other substances.

*Calcination of gold*: Melt it and make thin plates from it. Fill an iron crucible, cover it, and let it melt with common salt or a little prepared sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metal surfaces and act as a flux</term> and pomegranate vinegar; because of the sharpness of the salts and vinegar, it is ground into a powder. Then place it in a bread oven for a day and a night, and extract a red-yellow powder beyond compare.

*Calcination of silver*: Melt it and make plates from it. Fill an iron crucible, then place a little crushed, prepared common salt into the crucible until it is full. Cover and melt it, for it melts quickly with the help of the salt. Afterward, grind it—as it also grinds well because of the salt—and place it in a bread oven for one day and night, then extract the powder of the Moon <note>i.e., silver powder</note>, which is beyond compare.

*Calcination of lead*: Melt the lead and quench it in salt water and very sharp white vinegar, so that the salt is somewhat prepared and dissolved. Afterward, quench the molten lead in this water forty times. Then place the ground material in a sealed, raw clay pot. Dry it in a bread oven for a day and a night. In the morning, extract a heavy, snow-colored powder like salt.

*Calcination of tin*: Melt and quench it ten times in common salt water dissolved in very sharp white vinegar, mixed with two ounces of bee's honey. Then grind and place in a pot in the bread oven for a day and a night. Extract the powder of the Moon <note>In this context, it refers to a white, silver-like powder made from tin.</note>.

*Calcination of iron*: Grind and soak it with common salt water and vinegar of sorb apples and pomegranates in which the salt is dissolved. Dry it ten times in ashes. Afterward, let water float above it to a depth of five fingers while grinding strongly; place it under dung <note>fimo: decomposing dung was used by alchemists as a source of gentle, constant heat.</note> for ten days, and it will be dissolved. Then congeal the water for one day, and it will be tinted. Next, grind and place it in the bread oven for one day and night, and you will have a red powder like blood. This is the powder of the Sun <note>Though usually meaning gold, here "powder of the Sun" likely refers to the iron powder's solar-red color or its high medicinal status.</note>, which is called the Saffron of Iron <term>Crocus ferri: "Saffron of Iron," a term for iron oxide (rust) used both as a pigment and in early medicine.</term>.

*Calcination of copper*: Make copper plates and hang them in strong vinegar with tongs in a pot placed in dung for ten days. Remove and scrape them...

->*How you shall calcinate plates of Venus <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper</term>.*<-

Cut plates of Venus to the width of coins <note>original: "denariorum" — denarii, common small silver coins used here as a measurement of size.</note>, and coat them with salt water, and place one layer at the bottom of the crucible, but first wrap and re-wrap them on both sides with arsenic prepared with vinegar, and so place layer upon layer until the vessel is filled, and seal it with clay so it does not breathe <note>i.e., making it airtight/hermetically sealed</note>, and allow it to dry; and then place it in the calcination furnace, and let it stay there for a good four hours, so that the entire small vessel becomes glowing red: take care, however, lest the Venus should melt and liquefy through too much heat, which happens quite often. The reduction of the calx of bodies <note>original: "calcis corporum" — the powders created by the "burning" or oxidation of metals.</note> into a solid mass is done thus: Take the calx of whichever metal you wish, and grind it very well upon a stone, afterward wash it with hot water two or three times, and throw away the cloudy water: when the water comes off clear, then it is enough: then grind the well-dried material, and apply Yemen alum water <term>alum iameni: a specific type of alum, likely named for Yemen, prized for its purity in chemical reactions</term> mixed with common salt water, and grind vigorously, and soak it with that water, soaking and drying it so many times until it becomes a living and white calx: (and this is for the "white work" <note>original: "ad album" — the stage of alchemy aimed at creating silver.</note>) and in this way all sulfurous accidents <note>impurities or "accidental" qualities associated with sulfur in alchemical theory that prevent a metal from being pure or "noble."</note> are removed from it, which it contracted in the earth: afterward grind it once with alkali water <term>aqua alkali: a solution of alkaline salts, such as potash or soda</term>, and when it is dried, place it in a vessel, namely a crucible, and seal it well with c-
