The calx of <term>Venus</term>, however, is made by "cementing" it with common salt until it can be ground and washed.

->*Here the primary work begins.*<-

Take therefore, in the name of the pious God, one part of white <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>, and a second part of sulfur, and a third part of arsenic: mix all these together, and add half a part of silver water <note>original: "aquæ argenti" — likely a mercurial solution or "water of mercury."</note>, and place it in a glass vessel, and heat it from above with a white-hot iron until the glass melts and is sealed: then place it in the ashes over the fire, and let it congeal: when it has been congealed, it will be a "fixed tincture," which enters through a mixed coagulation; it is conjunctive, unitive, and preservative. Place therefore one part of this tincture upon a hundred parts of purified iron or copper, and it will always be good without doubt, in every hammering and examination, and it will last forever. **Addition.** Note this: that the tincture ought to be dissolved and mixed into a body that has been calcined and turned into a liquid state: and while water is mixed with water, they are never separated from one another, just as a small amount of red wine tints a large amount of water. I have seen other treatises where this chapter was not present, but only the following one.

# How from all the aforementioned is perfected
->**Sun & Moon** <note>original: "Sol & Luna" — Alchemical code for Gold and Silver.</note><-

Take one part of **Mercury**, sublimated <term>sublimated: purified by heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again</term> and fixed, and another of **fixed arsenic**, and a third part of **calx of the Moon** <note>silver powder</note>, which you must grind well upon a stone; soak it [imbibe] with water of sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis armoniaci" — ammonium chloride, often used as a solvent</note>, and do this three or four times by grinding, soaking, and roasting, as described above. Place it similarly to dissolve, and reserve that which is dissolved; and when it is not dissolved, grind it better and add a little sal ammoniac, and thus the whole will be dissolved. When the whole has been dissolved, set it to distill, and the whole will distill, as I have taught, into warm water.

Be careful, however, not to place it in ashes <note>referring to an ash-bath or sand-bath used to regulate heat</note> for distillation, because it would harden for the most part, and you would need to dissolve it again as before. When all has been distilled, place it in a glass gourd [cucurbit] and coagulate it; it will become a white substance, hard and clear in the manner of a crystal, melting over fire like wax, penetrating and permanent. Therefore, place one part of this substance upon a hundred parts of any purified and calcined metal, and it will be good for all time. I advise, however, that you do not dye [tinge] any unpurified metal with it, because the tincture would vanish after two or three examinations <note>tests of purity, such as cupellation or acid tests</note>.

**Additions.** In the book of Aristotle <note>This refers to *De Perfecto Magisterio*, an alchemical text falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages.</note> *On the Perfect Mastery*, it is said: Of sublimated and calcined **Mercury**—which I think is the same as "fixed": because it cannot be calcined unless it is first fixed; and unless it were calcined, it could not be dissolved. Near the end, some say a certain "white oil of the Philosophers" ought to be added to wax <note>original: "incerandam" — to bring a substance to a waxy, meltable consistency</note> that medicine. 

If a **fixed spirit** <term>spirit: a volatile substance, usually mercury, sulfur, or arsenic, that can "fly" from the fire</term> cannot penetrate [the metal], add some of its non-fixed likeness, and dissolve and congeal it, and it will enter, etc. So also, if the calcined body [metal] cannot be reduced back into a solid body, add some of its likeness when melting it, and thus it will be reduced. Divide the **Philosophers' Egg** <note>A term for the hermetically sealed glass vessel, or the "First Matter" containing all four elements.</note> into four parts, each of which has one nature [elemental property]; then combine it equally and proportionally, so that there is no division or conflict within it, and you will achieve your purpose, the Lord granting. This method is universal: but I will divide it for you into special operations. It is thus divided into four: and it is done well and without corruption in two ways. When, therefore, you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you shall have it. Therefore, arrange the airy substance by discernment, and arrange the earthy substance by moisture and heat.

## THE WRITING OF ALBERT UPON
### the Tree of Aristotle.

This is the figure of heaven, which is called the sphere of heaven, which indeed contains within itself eight most noble figures: namely, the first figure, which is called the first circle, and is the circle of the deity, because it contains within itself the words of divinity. The second figure contains within itself the sevenfold number of the planets. The third figure, the corruptible and generable things, contains within itself the four elements. The fourth figure contains a most savage Dragon <note>The "Dragon" in alchemy often represents the volatile "First Matter" or crude Mercury that must be tamed.</note> emanating from the aforementioned sevenfold number of the planets. The fifth figure clearly contains the head and the death of that same Dragon. The sixth figure, which touches the tree, contains six faces and two animals, namely storks. The seventh figure, which touches the tree with the planets, where there are white letters, is named the sixth circle. The eighth figure, in the manner of the Sun’s brightness, contains within itself a radiant golden tree with its roots. 

The exposition of the first of these figures, namely the circle of divinity, is this: that we call it by such a name because the names of divinity—that is, the institutions of the sacred page <note>Holy Scripture</note> and the legal and natural laws, which are believed to have emanated infallibly from God—are circumscribed there. The explanation of the second figure, namely of Saturn and the other planets, is this: For Saturn, by its coldness and dryness, forms the Dragon. Jupiter indeed provides the Dragon with its heat by digesting it into a certain appearing muddy substance, which is full of heat and fire: and for that reason, it does not stick to what touches it. Mars, indeed, by its heat and dryness, divides the Dragon himself and makes him run through heaven. The Sun, however, gathers him and makes him live for a little while, because he himself is the father of creatures; and the aforementioned Dragon loves him because of his heat, his tincture <term>tincture: the soul or essence of a substance that can transform the color and nature of metals</term>, and the most sweet odor which is fragrant in him. Venus, indeed, with her heat and dryness gathered together, disjoins from here and there...

...the limbs of the Dragon <note>In alchemy, the "Dragon" usually represents the *materia prima*—the raw, volatile starting material that must be "tamed" or "killed" to be transformed.</note> by passing through many piercings, stinging him through all his joints, and leaving the Dragon itself as if dead. However, Mercury and the Moon, pouring their moisture over him, bring him back to life; for they make him live, run, walk, and change his color into the appearance of blood. And in the beginning he appears **black**, and in the middle declining toward **whiteness**, and in the end there is a **redness** declining into the color of his own head. <note>These colors—black, white, and red—refer to the three primary stages of the Alchemical Great Work: *Nigredo*, *Albedo*, and *Rubedo*.</note>

The explanation of the third figure of the four corruptible and generable elements is this: they are called "corruptible and generable" because they are always being destroyed and reborn, and because they alternate with one another on account of heat and dryness, cold and moisture. And for this reason, the <term>Art and the Artisan</term> <note>The "Art" is Alchemy, and the "Artisan" (*artifex*) is the Alchemist.</note> arrange the matter of these elements; by dividing them and joining them to one another, the Artisan removes them from their deadly nature. Then their quality is changed: for the "hot and moist" becomes nourishing, because of the heat and moisture within it. The "cold and dry" which were in it [are removed], and the "cold and moist" becomes a refreshment for the thirsty and a cure for the sick: for it opens the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf, cleanses the lepers, extends the nerves, opens the veins, and makes the dead rise again. <note>The alchemist here claims that the perfected "Stone" or Elixir has Christ-like healing powers, acting as a "Universal Medicine" for both metals and the human body.</note>

The fourth figure is of the Dragon emanating from the aforementioned seven planets, because he proceeds through the most subtle influences flowing down into the elements. Then, with his matter scattered in the heavens, he has his <term>work-prison</term> <note>original: "ergastulum" — a Roman term for a private prison for slaves; here it suggests a place of confinement or intense labor within the clouds.</note> in the clouds; then, with the rainwater and hail, he descends again into the earth, bonds himself with it, and makes for himself a new skin. And so he begins to crawl in the caverns of the earth, and always tends toward the depths unless something hinders him, and he goes even to the waters of the sea. From there he goes out, if no hindrance is met, until he sees the second pole; and from there he is moved and returns to the first. Thus he never stops walking, because he hates the light and always seeks to hide himself from the rays of the Sun; therefore he is poisonous, and a man cannot kill him without a greater poison.

We name the fifth figure from his head, and from the death of that same Dragon. His head lives forever, and therefore the head is called "Glorious Life," and angels serve it. And God placed this image in the paradise of delights, and in it He placed His own image and likeness; and there the Dragon fought with the image of God, until he caused it to fall into mor-

In it is the <term>transmutation</term> of all corruptible and generable things and of all precious stones. And therefore the Kings of the earth wear it on their heads; wise women hide it; foolish virgins wear it publicly because they desire to be plundered. High priests and religious priests and nuns tear it, because it was so commanded to them by divine law. The merchants of the earth and the farmers have become rich by it, and sailors carry it from the East to the West; and it thrives most in the Islands that are in the South.

The eighth figure, which we named above, contains the <term>golden tree</term> <note>original: "arborem auream"</note> with seven branches and visible roots: which tree we call the <term>figure of the sun</term> <note>original: "figuram solis"</note>, because Kings...

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'Q' containing a circular diagram with a central point and radiating lines, surrounded by decorative scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>
*Although we should have passed over our unrefined investigation in silence rather than speaking any word of such and so admirable a metallic mixture—as the ancient fathers warn:* <note>original: "Nolite arcana propalare mortalibus."</note> *Do not reveal the secrets to mortals. Nevertheless, with the First Cause* <note>In alchemical and philosophical contexts, the "First Cause" refers to God as the ultimate source of all creation and motion.</note> *assenting: having weighed the immense supernatural matter, hidden from almost all, and not without the best instructions received long ago from the inspiration of the First Cause—to whom we confess we owe everything. We have considered it worthwhile to show the truth in brief under the shadow of the Solar reflection* <note>A term likely referring to the reflected light of the sun or a specific alchemical process involving "solar" (gold-related) influence.</note> *and to illuminate this most serious province of transmuting metals thoroughly for the chosen. But because its virtue will perhaps seem to hide under the cloak of a riddle (as is fitting), we wish it to be known that the* <term>Schema</term> <note>Refers to the diagrams and symbolic figures throughout the text designed to organize alchemical knowledge.</note> *was applied for no other reason than on account of the Ungrateful, the Unworthy, the Guilty, Foreigners, the Profane, Flatterers, Apostates, the Accursed, the Slanderous, Infidels, and gloomy Hypocrites. Now everything shall be said correctly, briefly, and openly. Since it is narrated more copiously in the section on Division and in the* <term>Mirror of the Insight of our Mind</term> <note>This likely refers to Pantheo's previous work, the "Ars et Theoria Transmutationis Metallicae," or a specific chapter within this volume.</note>. *So that the coming light may clarify the Luminous in the light, and those Wandering may be corrected by this approaching light, and those possessing grace may enjoy unity by its gift.*

### *The movements & alterations of the Metallic Art.*

<margin>Matter <note>original Greek: $\delta \lambda \eta$ (hyle), transcribed here as $\delta \lambda \alpha$.</note></margin>

It is read in the "Secret of Secrets" that what has been received should not be betrayed; nevertheless, we say that the letters, or elements, **A, V,** and **E** are the equal mixtures of Matter, Form, and the disposing Medium. **C**, however, signifies the First Movement: that is, Killing, Corruption, <term>Calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often to reduce it to a powder.</note>, or <term>Putrefaction</term> <note>In alchemy, the stage of decay or "blackness" (nigredo) necessary for rebirth and purification.</note>. **G** is the second movement, which is Generation. **H** is the third movement, namely Augmentation. **D** is called Disjunction, Diminution, or Separation, and it is the fourth movement. **F** and **B** are the altering elements, which are called <term>Fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable or resistant to heat.</note>, Beatification, and Life.

### THEORY AND PRACTICE.

The termination <note>The final state or defining boundary of a substance.</note> of the recipients is the change of the received natures through the ineffable mixing of the Hot—that is, Fire <gloss>spirit <note>original: "pn," likely for the Greek "pneuma," meaning spirit or breath.</note></gloss>—with the Cold; and of the Moist—that is, Water—with the Dry, by a perpetual disposition <gloss>sealed <note>original Hebrew: "בלום" (balum), meaning shut, blocked, or sealed.</note></gloss>. This perpetual disposition is the "white smoke": and it is the Water whitening the Indian stone, as Maria <note>Referring to Maria the Prophetess, an early alchemist often called "Mary the Jewess," credited with inventing the bain-marie.</note> says. This thing is the water whitening the *indrademus* stone <note>original: "indrademum," likely a corruption of a Greek lapidary term or "adamantine."</note>, that is, the Indian stone. And that water is the "living water," which is called a dry <gloss>distribution <note>original Greek: "ἀνάδοσις" (anadosis), referring to the rising of vapors or the spreading of nutrients.</note></gloss>, as all the masters assert. And it is the Quicksilver <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>Also known as "Argentum Vivum" or Mercury; in alchemy, this is not just the common metal but the "Mercury of the Sages," a transformative fluid principle.</note> of the Sages, of which Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure and reputed author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> said: "Guard this coagulated Quicksilver, which is in the innermost chambers, in which..."

For Quick-silver itself is from the **HEART OF SATURN**, and is the secret of the School <note>Likely referring to the particular lineage or tradition of alchemical practitioners.</note>, and is called the residual Earth. Therefore, let him who hears these words investigate for himself. He who wishes to profit in this wisdom must compose this admirable mixture, or greatest secret, and afterwards change it from nature to nature, as Lucas <note>A figure cited in the Turba Philosophorum, often associated with ancient Greek philosophy.</note> says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a famous 12th-century Latin translation of an earlier Arabic alchemical text.</note>: "You have no need of many things, but only one. And this one thing, in each degree of our works, is turned into another nature." For as Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note> testifies, such Art does not consist in a plurality of things, when he says: "For there is **one Stone**, **one Medicine**, in which our mastery consists, to which we add no foreign thing nor take anything away, except what we remove as superfluous during its preparation."

In one thing, therefore, consists this whole mastery: namely, in Quick-silver. And this is what Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemist frequently cited in medieval European texts.</note> says expressly to his son: "Know, my son, that this stone, which is the root of which all the Sages have treated, is Quick-silver." And it is a certain Quick-silver of white color, and shining more than a mirror. Likewise, it is said in the *Turba*: "The beginning of the whole work is whiteness, that is, Quick-silver. And redness follows."

...we omit the names of others to avoid being overly wordy <note>original: "prolixitatis vitandæ gratia"</note>. In the composition of this wonderful mixture, or greatest secret, we must follow nature. For (as Geber <note>The Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar often called the father of chemistry.</note> says) nature acts by itself. We, however, must know three things: namely, what nature is, how many natures there are, and how nature operates.

According to Aristotle in the second book of his *Physics* <note>original: "secundo physicæ auscultationis"</note>, Nature is defined thus: Nature is a Principle and a Cause of motion and of rest in that in which it is primarily and by its own essence, and not by accident. Likewise, according to the Author of the *Perfect Mastery* <note>Likely referring to the *Summa Perfectionis*, a foundational alchemical text.</note>: the Natures and complexions of the primary qualities are four: namely, Heat and Dryness, as in Fire; Heat and Moisture, as in Air; Moisture and Coldness, as in Water; and Coldness and Dryness, as in Earth. All these complexions are unequal, nor is any one of them that which we seek. For we seek the *equal* <note>referring to a perfectly balanced state of matter</note>, about which Joannicius <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous 9th-century translator and physician.</note> says that an equal mixture is one where the body is said to be unharmed with moderation. <margin>Note well.</margin> Note therefore that he says "with moderation"—that is, of the aforementioned natures: heat, moisture, coldness, and dryness. For when none of these natures exceeds another, then the body is called "equal," because there is as much of one as there is of another. Also note that "unharmed" means healthy, or clean from every cause of corruption. <margin>Note well.</margin> And according to Geber: Tin <note>original: "Stagnum"</note> is the purest lead, and in it there is an equality of fixation or thickness <note>original: "spissitudinis"</note> of the two components, namely Quick-silver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur; however, it is not the same equality as found in the mixture of Quick-silver itself.

Likewise, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many alchemical works are attributed.</note> says: The sons of the philosophers have seven bodies <note>The seven metals of antiquity: Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead, and Mercury.</note>, of which the first is the Sun <note>Gold</note>, their best king and head, which neither the earth corrupts, nor burning fire consumes, nor water alters, because its complexion is temperate and its nature is direct in Heat, Moisture, Coldness, and Dryness. Nor is there anything superfluous or lacking in it. And therefore the Philosophers preferred it and magnified it, and they said that the Sun stands among the bodies just as the Sun stands among the Stars. For by its light and splendor, it makes all changeable things sprout and perfects all fruits by the will of God.

Why say more, if we can reach this point? We have almost the whole thing in proportion, according to Socrates <note>The Greek philosopher, who often appears in alchemical dialogues as a teacher of secrets.</note> who says: Already...

# ART IS THEORY

Therefore, I have demonstrated to you the arrangement of the **White Lead** <note>original: "Albi plumbi"; in alchemy, this usually refers to tin or a specific purified state of matter rather than common lead.</note>, which, once produced, is nothing other than "women's work and children's play" <note>A famous alchemical saying suggesting that once the "Stone" is prepared, the remaining process is easy and follows natural laws without constant intervention.</note>. Likewise, you should note that **Ingression, Submersion, Conjunction, Connection, Complexion, Composition**, and **Mixture** all mean the same thing in this art. <margin>Note well.</margin> For nothing enters, is submerged, is joined, is connected, is embraced, or is composed, except when it is mixed. Therefore, let us see what a **Mixture** is, because once this is understood through its definition, all other things will be known.

According to the **Philosopher** <note>The standard medieval title for Aristotle.</note> in the first book of *On Generation*: A Mixture is the union of altered mixables joined at their smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; this refers to the theory of "minima naturalia," the smallest units of a substance that still retain its specific properties, similar to an early concept of molecules.</note>. <margin>Note well. Union.</margin> Note "of mixables," that is, of the **elements**. For these are the first principles of every mixture, and we cannot know the manifest or hidden nature of the mixture itself unless we know how to mingle or compose the elements themselves. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the origins of alchemy were attributed.</note> says: *Understand, my son, the science of the four elements, which are placed by their own principles in their hidden appearance.* For their hidden appearance is by no means revealed unless they are composed, because they are not perfected until their colors are fully realized. <margin>Note well.</margin> Note also "at their smallest parts," that is, through indivisible parts. For if anything could be divided, it would not be the minimum, since every part is smaller than its whole. It appears, therefore, that the mixture of the **Elements** occurs through these smallest, indivisible parts. And that an Element is the smallest of apparent bodies is evident from its definition: for an **Element** is the smallest particle of a body.

Thirdly, let us see how **Nature** operates. And certainly, she does so in four ways: namely, according to four movements, which are **Corruption, Generation, Increase,** and **Decrease**. For **Alteration** is a change according to quality. Nature therefore acts by corrupting. But because there are many species of Corruption, let us deal only with the one that concerns our purpose. And certainly, that one is **Putrefaction** <note>The first major stage of the alchemical "Great Work," characterized by the substance turning black (the nigredo).</note>. Whence Hermes says in his allegory: *Know that the origin of the art is the **Raven’s Head** <note>original: "caput Corui"; a symbolic term for the black stage of the matter.</note>, which flies without wings in the blackness of night and the clarity of day; and from our bitterness, as it leaves in its blood, coloration is received, and from its back, pure water is received.* The Raven's Head is nothing other than the blackness of night. For just as these things are black and dark in respect to the day, so is the putrefied body in respect to the pure body <note>original: "corporis mundi"; can be read as "clean body" or "world body."</note> which arises from putrefaction or is extracted through our artifice.

# ON METALLIC TRANSMUTATION

But what color ought that purified body to be? Certainly, of a white color. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: "Know, you seekers of rumors and sons of Wisdom, that the **Vulture** <note>In alchemy, the vulture often symbolizes the volatile principle or the process of sublimation—rising above the "mountain" of the material body.</note> stretched out upon the mountain peak cries out with a great voice, saying: 'I am the **White** of the black, and the **yellow** of the white, and the **Red** of the yellow; I am certainly truthful, and I do not lie.'" Note, therefore, "the white of the black." For we extract the white itself from the black.

<margin>Note well</margin> Likewise **Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemical author frequently cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> says: The **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> which is extracted from that—namely, from the black body—is moist, white, and cleansed of its husks <note>impurities or outer layers</note>, lest the work perish. Having seen, therefore, that the first movement of nature is to **putrefy** <note>to decompose or break down matter into its primal state</note>, it must be seen how this is done. And so that we may know how to perform this perfectly, it is necessary for us to have knowledge of both natural and artificial principles. For those who are ignorant of the principles will not find the end.

The first natural principle, therefore, is matter—the material cause of earth, water, fire, and air—under the **Will of God** <note>original Latin: "nutu Dei"</note>, or *Marthek*, which in Greek is called **the will of God** <note>original: "neusi theu"; a transliteration of the Greek "νεύσει Θεοῦ"</note>, and in Hebrew **the Will of God** <note>original: "Recon heloim"; likely a phonetic rendering of the Hebrew "Ratzon Elohim"</note>, expressed in letters and numbers. This was seen as proof of a divine mathematical harmony in the universe.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of alchemical transformation. <page-num>537</page-num>
<header>METALLIC TRANSMUTATION</header>

The second requirement is Heat, that is, an external Fire, which is the instrument that moves the material itself toward putrefaction, and there is no other active agent in the world.

Whence Alphidius <note>An early alchemical authority, often cited in medieval Latin texts, likely of Arabic origin.</note> says: "Know, my son, that the active substance in this whole world is one: namely, Heat. For if heat is removed, there is no motion at all." Motion is an act, and therefore heat is the root of the disposition and of the work. But since there are many degrees of heat, or of Fire, let us see what this particular one is, and in what degree it exists.

And certainly this Fire, or Heat, is a most intense Fire or Heat, as Maria <note>Maria the Jewess, a foundational figure in alchemy credited with inventing various laboratory apparatus.</note> testifies: "Let the measure of your fire be like that of the Sun in the days of June and July." And it is called "Horse dung" <note>original: "Fimus equinus." A common alchemical term for a source of gentle, steady, moist heat, often achieved by burying a vessel in fermenting manure.</note>, as Alphidius says: "It is cooked by fire: which I will show you." And it is hot and dry in the fourth degree, the property of which is to increase dryness by condensing humidity. For just as the Fire of Dung increases the cold and the moist because of its own coldness and moistness (which is restrained), so the strength of a hot and dry Fire disposes dryness, by terminating the moist nature into a dry nature (as you know). Nothing else in the world is likened to this except Natural heat, which is the Fire of the Sun in the bowels of the earth. Having thus seen the natural principles, let us look at the Artificial ones.

The Artificial Principles are the instruments in which this putrefaction is perfected. And the first is the **CARAHA** <term>likely a cucurbit or gourd-shaped glass vessel</term>; the second is the **ALUDEL**, that is, the "Horse’s Belly" <note>original: "Venter equi."</note>: in which the material must be placed. Regarding this, Vincent <note>Likely Vincent of Beauvais, a medieval encyclopedist.</note> says: "The dissolutions of bodies and spirits involve many instruments; yet one is called the Horse’s Belly." And it is made of two vessels: one of which is the Aludel <term>a pear-shaped pot or condenser used in sublimation</term>, and the material is placed within it. It stands in the Furnace, and the Fire is nourished underneath so that it may boil. Avicenna says that these dispositions cannot be made except in a recognized double vessel, which is the Horse’s Belly named above. Likewise, since a definition signifies the very essence of a thing, let us see what the putrefaction of a thing is, so that we may better understand it.

According to Joannicius <note>The Latinized name of Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous scholar and physician.</note>: "Putrefaction is the corruption of a thing's substance resulting from the retention of vapors." For if they are dispersed through the air, the thing does not putrefy. Therefore, the aludel must be so adjusted that it cannot breathe. Or it can be otherwise defined thus: "Putrefaction is the corruption of substantial moisture resulting from a lack of natural heat, while an external artificial heat overabounds from the outside..."

...acting. You should note that this is caused by an overabundance of external heat <note>original: "calore alieno." In alchemy, this refers to heat applied from outside, such as a furnace or bath, as opposed to the internal heat of the substance.</note>. For external heat itself is the active instrument, or that which completes the putrefaction through moist corruption.

But in what way does heat produce this corruption? We answer: Heat warms the thing placed upon it, and by warming, it causes the humidity to evaporate—the humidity by which all the dry, earthy parts were held together, making one continuous body and one thing. Thus heat corrupts and putrefies the thing itself, just as is seen in wood placed in a fire. For the strength of the fire's heat causes the Water and Oil to evaporate from the wood—substances through which the wood was first a continuous body—but after the separation of the Water and Oil, there remain ashes and dry parts, entirely disconnected and pulverized. And because of this similarity, putrefaction was called "ash" by the Philosophers. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical works are attributed.</note> rightly says: 
> Do not leave the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> to neglect; it whitens the black ash, and the work is accomplished through the fire of the wise. 

Therefore it was also called calcination—that is, Putrefaction—because of the same similarity. For just as the strength of fire deprives a stone of its humidity and makes lime from it, so does putrefaction. Whence Parmenides says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "in turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>: 
> Unless you turn nature around, and know its compositions and temperaments, and well join like to like <note>original: "consanguineum consanguineis," literally "blood-relation to blood-relation."</note>, and the first to the first, you act improperly and achieve nothing; for natures follow their like natures and rejoice in them. 

For they putrefy, or are pulled apart, because nature rules nature, which destroys it and turns it into dust, and leads it into dust. It appears, therefore, that through putrefaction a thing is destroyed and reduced to nothing, just as a stone is through calcination. Having seen what putrefaction is and how it happens, let us see the signs by which we can know when it will be perfect and when not.

There are indeed two principal qualities <note>original: "accidentia," an Aristotelian term for outward properties or characteristics.</note> by which we can know if it has been completed or not: namely, Color and Touch. The Color is Black; the Touch is Heavy. Whence the author of the *Perfect Mastery* <note>Likely referring to the "Summa Perfectionis," a highly influential medieval work attributed to "Geber."</note> says: Lead in its height is lead and silver; it is cold, dry, earthy, melancholic <note>A reference to the four humors; the melancholic humor was associated with the element of earth, the planet Saturn, and the color black.</note>, black, withered, foul-smelling, heavy, and feminine.

# METALLIC TRANSMUTATION.

From these things, therefore, it appears that putrefaction is perfect when it is black and heavy. Also note that our silver <note>original: "argentum nostrum." In alchemy, this refers to "philosophical mercury," the refined base material of the work, rather than common metallic silver.</note>, Calcination, Incineration, Melancholy, Blackness, Night, Putrefaction, Pregnancy, and Spittle all signify the same thing <note>Alchemy often used a wide variety of metaphorical names to describe the same stage of the process—here, the "nigredo" or blackening stage.</note>. But what remains corrupted after Putrefaction? We answer:
The substance of the form, which before putrefaction was in the potentiality of the thing, introduced by the proportion of the Elements from which it was composed. Because matter is not corrupted in such a way as to be utterly annihilated or reduced to nothing—since it is not possible for the elements to be destroyed by us—but the Essence and Form, which they had received from the mixture, are indeed utterly annihilated. For the integral whole (for example, a house) consists of its integral parts. But once one part is destroyed, or separated from its place—the place it previously held in the whole—the form or Essence of the entire house is destroyed, and yet there remain the Stones, Wood, and Foundations of which the house consisted. So it is also in our proposal. For when the moisture is separated from its place, which it held in the elementary mixture as an integral part of the whole—and this occurs through heat raising it up and separating it from the other parts—the form and essence of the mixture itself are utterly annihilated. Nevertheless, the substance of the moisture is not annihilated, nor can it be annihilated.

But on the contrary: If we place a pot full of water on the fire, will it not be consumed by the power of the heat, so that nothing remains? Certainly so. Therefore, its substance is utterly annihilated. We answer: That Water has a very subtle and rare substance. Also, it has qualities entirely contrary to the qualities of fire. For the Heat of fire is opposed to the coldness of water, and dryness to moisture. Therefore, when the heat of fire meets the coldness of water, they fight against each other; and if the heat overcomes the coldness of the water's moisture, it thins and rarefies the substance of the water to such an extent that it transmutes it into the substance of Air. For Air is generated from the Heat of fire and the Moisture of water. And Earth from the Dryness of fire and the Coldness of water. Whence Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary early medieval alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says:

> There are four Elements, of which two are principal and most greatly contrary, namely Fire and Water. The other two are generated from these, namely Air and Earth.

Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous scholar and theologian often cited as an authority on the transformation of matter.</note> also explains this excellently in the book *On Generation* <note>original: "Peri geneseos," a Latinized Greek title for the Aristotelian work "De Generatione et Corruptione," on which Albert wrote a commentary.</note>. Likewise, we see a rain cloud ascend upward by the power of heat and be raised against its own nature. For Water, by its nature, always [seeks] downward... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "tit," likely for "petit" (seeks/aims).</note>

<summary>This page defines the "blackness" (nigredo) stage of alchemy and explains that while the form of a substance may be destroyed during putrefaction, the underlying matter is merely transmuted into other elements rather than being annihilated.</summary>

# ART AND THEORY
<meta>catchword: vapor</meta>

...[the vapor] as a heavy thing, and when it reaches the place of perpetual cold, in which coldness overcomes heat, then the cloud is converted into Water by the power of its thickening coldness, which condenses and turns the substance of the cloud into water, and thus rain is generated. And also when the northern wind, whose nature is cold and dry, meets the southern wind, then if the northern cold overcomes the southern heat, the cloud is condensed and congealed; this is sometimes converted into Water, sometimes into hail, and sometimes into snow. From this it appears that the substance of the Elements cannot be annihilated, but rather undergoes transmutation when the nature of one element overcomes the nature of another.

The second motion of nature is Generation. For the Corruption of one thing is the Generation of another, as the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> testifies in the first book of *On Generation* <note>original: "de generatione"</note>. And it is impossible for matter to exist without being under some Form, according to the first book of the *Physics*. For when the agent has destroyed the first mixture, or the proportion of the elements that caused the thing to exist under its first form, it immediately introduces another. And what form is that? Truly, it is that of the "corrupted body," which is called by the Sages of this art Saturn, or lead, or copper, because of its blackness and impurity. It is from this blackness and impurity that a cleansing must be performed. Wherefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: "Know this, my son: unless one knows how to guide the pregnancy, to bring about generation, to mortify, and to vivify the species, to induce light, and to cleanse them until they are purged by fire, colored, and purified from the final stains—such as from blackness and darkness—nothing is accomplished." But if anyone performs this, he shall be the possessor of a greater dignity, such that kings may honor him.

Likewise, alteration is a change in quality produced by a certain local rearrangement of matter. This motion indeed contains within itself the principal operations of this mastery, about which Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century chemist whose works formed the basis of medieval European alchemy.</note> speaks: "Therefore, the principles of this art are the modes of its operations by which the Artist applies himself to this mastery, which are indeed diverse from one another." For one mode is sublimation, and another is descension (that is, the second). And one is distillation (that is, the third). And one of the modes is calcination (that is, the fourth). And another is solution (the fifth); the sixth is coagulation; the seventh indeed is Fixation. Finally, the eighth is ceration <term>Ceration (cæratio)</term><note>The process of softening a hard or brittle substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency, making it easier to melt or mix.</note>.

The first mode, therefore, was sublimation. And the cause of its invention was because neither the ancient Philosophers, nor we, nor those who will come after us, knew of anything that would unite the bodies...

Note therefore what we say: "without their cleansing." Therefore, a cleansing must occur; that is, the cleansing of this matter from blackness and darkness. And so Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> feels. But what is it that produces that blackness? Certainly, a watery and combustible moisture <note>original: "humiditas adustiua"; refers to sulfurous impurities that cause the matter to char or "burn" during heating.</note>. Item, regarding this same thing: "Note that you have asked about the white smoke; it is fitting for you to know: The **white smoke** is the soul and spirit of those bodies whose souls we have already extracted and have again joined to their bodies." Therefore, that Soul, having entered its body, whitens it and cleanses it from all blackness. Whence Parmenides in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "Know that if the surfaces are whitened, their interiors are whitened; and if one has whitened the surface of the copper, its interiors will be whitened." Also Lucas: "When quicksilver <note>mercury</note> is governed, every body is whitened, and nature converts nature."

Therefore, take the dry and the moist, and extract the **white smoke** from them, and guard it lest it perish. But how is that white smoke generated? Certainly, through putrefaction and purification. First, the matter is corrupted, and through the heat of fire a separation occurs of one combustible smoke (which dyes the matter into Blackness) from that **White Smoke**, which was previously mixed with it in the primary matter, yet under one form; and so it receives one cleansing by fire. For it receives another afterwards through our artifice—namely, through **Sublimation** and **Distillation**, as described below. And this is what Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician; alchemists often adapted his medical observations to describe chemical processes.</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: "In disturbance and vomiting that occur spontaneously, if such things as ought to be purged are purged, it will be well. But if not, the opposite." Which we explain thus: "In the disturbance of the belly"—that is, the **Putrefactions** that occur in the **Aludel** <note>term: Aludel; a pear-shaped pot or condenser used specifically for sublimation.</note>. "And in vomitings that occur spontaneously"—that is, the **Sublimations** and **Distillations** that occur in the **Carana** <note>term: Carana; likely referring to the cucurbit or the head of the distilling apparatus.</note> by ascending upward just as vomit does. If such things as ought to be purged are purged, it is well. If not, poorly. From these things, therefore, it appears...

...it would follow that if we know well how to perform **Putrefaction** <note>In alchemy, putrefaction is the "death" or breakdown of the initial material, allowing its elements to be rearranged.</note>, which is the disturbance of the Elements, or the Unbinding, or the Cleansing; and if we know well how to separate this from that through **Sublimation** and **Distillation**—that is, the pure from the impure—it will go well for us; and if not, it will go poorly. <margin>Note well.</margin>
And when that Smoke has been made clean and white, then it will be fit for joining with its body, as we said above; otherwise it is not, as you know. Whence Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit often cited as a teacher of alchemical wisdom.</note> says:
> If anyone has extracted the soul, and made it ascend upwards, and has washed away all blackness and stench from it, and afterwards joined it with its body, and finally mortified <note>In this context, "mortified" means to fix or stabilize the volatile spirit back into a solid form.</note> it, he will see the greatest wonders in the world.

The generation of that white Smoke having therefore been seen—which is produced by the separation of the burning Smoke <note>original: "Fumi adustiui"</note> from it during putrefaction and cleansing—let us now look at that generation which occurs through sublimation and distillation. And first, let us see what sublimation is, and why it was invented.

**Sublimation** is the elevation of a dry thing by fire, with it adhering to its vessel. The reason for its invention was the cleansing of spirits; otherwise, this is impossible, as has already been said above.

**Distillation**, however, is the separation of a putrefied liquid thing from the dregs of its turbulence, and this was a general method. A special goal, however, was the search for pure water, so that the dissolved body, after the resolution of its water, cannot be infected or corrupted.

We establish Distillation in several ways: namely, by the **sleeve-furnace** <note>original: "manica"; literally a sleeve, referring here to a specific conical or sleeved distillation apparatus.</note> and the **ash-bed** <note>original: "cineritium"; a method of heating a vessel by burying it in hot ashes to ensure even, gentle temperature.</note>. By the sleeve-furnace, it is done thus: Let a distillation furnace be made, in which charcoal is first placed and well-fitted to it, and afterwards, upon the lit coals, place the substance to be distilled to the thickness of one finger, and above that also place coals even to the top of the furnace, and let it be allowed to work until the whole is distilled. The other way, by the ash-bed, is done thus: Let the substance be placed in the pit of the ash-bed, and lit wood placed above it, and let it be allowed to work until the whole comes out clean. The first distillation is greater than the second, because the sleeve-furnace applies a more piercing heat than the ash-bed. It is also done by a **sand bath** <note>original: "balneum arenæ"; a vessel filled with sand that is heated, providing a very steady and controlled heat to the alchemical flask inside.</note>. And the cause of the invention of such a bath was the extraction of the pure substance into its own nature. Since through...

# THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

...the first and second distillation of the substance was only the clarity of the **Bath of Saturn** <note>original: "balnei Saturni"; likely a lead-based solvent or a low-temperature heating method associated with the planet/metal lead.</note>. Having seen the ways of distilling and what distillation is, let us come to the dregs <note>original: "fęces"; the solid sediment left after distillation.</note>. Truly, according to Hermes: In every corruptible thing, three things are to be considered. First, that which is useful, the **water**; second, the **oil**; third, the **dregs**. However, none of these has its own existence in this corrupted body, but they are confused and undivided. This body is called <term>hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for "matter" or the primordial substance without form.</note> by some, whence it is said: "God first created the heavens and the earth," where we call the "heavens" **sublimation** and the "earth" the **black body**.

And out of the mud of this earth, God molded Adam, and out of Adam the **woman** <note>original: "viraginem"; here meaning Eve, often used in alchemy to represent the volatile or "mercurial" principle taken from the "solid" body.</note>, which is our body, in which there are some essences of corruption that are forbidden. Whence Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemist often quoted in Latin medieval texts.</note> says:

> Know, my son, that in the book occurs the perfection of books, and the work is most certain to those who reason. I have already commanded you that which you propose, namely **Adam**, and I have forbidden those things which corrupt the work—that is, the **Woman**. By physicians, however, this corrupted body is called the **ptisana mass** <note>original: "massa ptyssanaria"; likely referring to a thick, pulpy medicinal paste or sediment, used here as a metaphor for the raw material.</note>, from which **chyle** <note>The milky fluid produced during digestion.</note> is generated in the stomach, and from this chyle four humors are generated in the liver: namely, **Blood, Choler, Phlegm, and Melancholy**; and from these, the body is sustained, nourished, and ruled.

They say the same thing in other words. For nature proceeds first in the stomach by **whitening**, second in the liver by **reddening**, and lastly in the limbs by **refining**.

Let us therefore take the **red earth**, and join it equally with its purified water in an <term>aludel</term> <note>A pear-shaped ceramic pot used for sublimation, often stacked in series to capture rising vapors.</note>, through the mediation of fire and air, so that one living body—or **dry water**, or **white smoke**—may be made by way of **putrefaction**. This water, or putrefaction, was called the "beginning of works" and the "key of works" by Alphidius, who says:

> Know, my son, that the treasures are not hidden inside, but are kept in it before your eyes when you enter the house. I wish, however, to grant you one key, which I call their signs; if you have reason, you will know the remaining three keys and extract them from it by your knowledge.

Furthermore, this one key is the **dry water**, which is made by the vessel of the wise and the method of **putrefaction**. Through this key, the work begins, and afterwards the extraction of the remaining three keys is performed and they become known. Therefore, remember all the necessary things until the whole is perfected.

The third mode of nature is **increase**, which occurs in the manner of the **waxing of the moon**. For just as the moon begins to be illuminated by the sight of the sun, and afterward its light increases every day until it is fully illuminated, so also <term>magnesia</term> <note>In this context, magnesia refers to the crude "living" matter of the alchemical work, not the modern chemical element.</note> begins to be reddened by the "dung" <note>referring to "fimus," a low, steady heat like that of decomposing organic matter</note> until it has been entirely reddened. And this is what **Hermes** says in his secret, namely the *vine of the wise*: "The juice is extracted in 42 days, its wine is completed at the end of 30; for the rest, it diminishes it, but the grinding increases it, because the moon diminishes after 15 and increases in 30." This **conjunction** also happens in the manner of the **body and the soul**. For just as the soul enters the body and contains it, so the **white smoke** <note>The volatile or spiritual principle.</note> enters its own body. Whence **Alphidius** says: "By pursuing the fugitive, the flight is taken away from them by the one meeting them, and the truth follows, and nature has seized its partner like an enemy, and they have contained and do contain one another, because the soul has entered the body." This point is the second point of **Mars** according to Hermes. But according to the order, it is of **Jupiter**, in whose house we have placed Mars. And why it was placed there, let the portion of our division be seen, under the title of the *cineritium* <note>original: "cineritij"; a technical term for cupellation or the refining of metals using ashes.</note>, chapter: *The thing cleaned from the stone*. **Rodianus** says the same when he leads back with the **embryo**. 

<margin>Note well.</margin>Observe the <term>embryon</term> <note>original: "embryon"; the primal, unformed mass of the alchemical work.</note>.

*For the embryo is a piece of flesh, or a mass, from which nature forms the fetus in the womb and arranges all its members.* Thus, this point is the **mass**—or the stone—from which the whole mastery is perfected. Likewise, this point is also the **matter** from which all metals derive their origin. Whence **Alphidius** says:

*So that you may more clearly understand me speaking, I want you to know from what matter metals derive their origin. Attend, therefore. Heavy and viscous **water** in the bowels of the earth, having no exit outward, if its **Sulfur** is near, is converted into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> by the baked heat.* And thus note that **viscous water** and **sulfur** are the matter of all metals and of quicksilver. 

<margin>Note well.</margin> **Geber** says this same thing when he defines quicksilver, saying: *Quicksilver is viscous water in the bowels of the earth, of a subtle substance, united to white earth by a most tempered heat in a total union through the smallest parts, until the moisture is tempered by the dry—*

Also note <margin>Note.</margin> the manner of perfecting when he says: "until the moist is tempered with the dry." Also note that: copper; the tree, silver, Clay, <term>Argyrion</term> <note>original: "Argyrion"; Greek for silver.</note>, <term>caspa</term>, <term>chesseph</term> <note>original: "caspa, chesseph"; transliterations of the Hebrew *kesef*, meaning silver.</note>, the Blood-related body, the improper body, the black body, Eve, the fate, the woman, the hen, <term>Giummis</term> <note>original: "Giummis" or "Gumma"; likely referring to an alchemical gum or resinous stage of the matter.</note>, white Gum, white <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; here meaning a sediment or underlying substance.</note>, Wood, the Line, the Moon, white **Magnesia**, Matter, the Mother, the <term>Prussian mass</term> <note>original: "Massa pryssanaria"; a specific alchemical preparation of the base matter.</note>, the Mid-heaven, Midday, blackness, black ash; the Sheep, Blood, the Second, the sister; the subtle substance; spring, the <term>virago</term> <note>A heroic or masculine woman; here a symbol of the dual nature of the material.</note>, virility, the Union of spirits; the sour grape, and darkness—all these are the same thing.

<margin>Note.</margin> Having observed the mixing, putrefaction, generation, and increasing of **quicksilver**; let us now look at its **fixation**. This fixation occurs through "diminution," which is the fourth movement of nature. This diminution is achieved through **decoction** <note>The process of heating a substance in a liquid, or long-sustained heat to thicken a substance.</note>, as was related above in the previously cited secret of **Hermes**, namely: *The Venom of the Wise*, etc. For just as the **Moon**, after it is full, begins to diminish from day to day until nothing of it appears, so the whiteness and illumination of this "body" begins to diminish through decoction until all the whiteness is diminished; then, **redness** appears through the stages of blackness and yellowness. This redness will appear fully if none of that watery moisture remains which produces the whiteness. If, however, any of that watery moisture remains which produce whiteness, then **desiccation** <note>Drying out.</note> has not been achieved. Therefore, let it be dried until it reaches that state, and then it will be well. And this is what **Hippocrates** says in his *Aphorisms*: "Evacuation, if it is done as it ought to be done, brings benefit and it will be well. If truly not, then the opposite." <gloss>Note: Evacuation, that is, Desiccation.</gloss>

Likewise, **Hermes** says: "Place its moisture to the fire, and in the moisture make the fire dwell; this fire increases the color of this kind of moisture by dryness and burning, until it is led to the end, that is, made perfect." Likewise, **Alphidius** says: "Look, my son: for I am about to write you a book, and if you understand its words, you will find this art—if you are among those destined to find it. But if you do not understand these words, do not approach the work, unless you begin by experimenting and cooking the 'waters.' These waters are thickened by putrefying through the moisture of the putrefaction and the power of dryness. Nor does it belong to him whose nature is two stones of the genus of stones, for it is extracted from the stones <margin>Note.</margin> which are generated in every season of the year." ## ART AND THEORY

...that through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of breaking down or "killing" the base matter so it can be reborn.</note> there occurs a thickening of the waters—that is, of the Cold and the Moist—and conversely a shift toward the nature of dryness. This becomes apparent, as was said above, through <term>putrefaction</term> and generation in the secret process. Let us therefore take the red earth, and so on. For when the cold and the moist begin to be altered, they are made black, like charcoal. Regarding this, Hermes says in his Allegory: "Our sought-after Stone lacks an equal; it is yellow-green and golden, both on the outside and the inside. However, when its body is altered, it becomes black and dark, like coals. But the Spirit taken from it is Red in color. When the spirit and soul are restored to it, it lives and rejoices, and you see it laughing and cheerful, and free from death. Blessed, therefore, be He whose disposition is this, who kills and brings to life, and is almighty." Likewise, Hermes says in the same place: "I am the white of the black, and the black of the white." And so it appears that the alteration moves from <term>whiteness</term> into <term>blackness</term>, and from <term>blackness</term> into <term>whiteness</term>. And further, this desiccation—or disposition—continually causes its conversion into the nature of heat, which is the <term>redness</term>, which nevertheless arises from a scarcity of the blackening agent. Rosinus says this same thing when he states that the art of <term>Marthek</term> <note>original: "Marthek"; an alchemical term often referring to litharge or lead dross used in the refining process.</note> is not made except from Tin. From these things it can be understood that there is one disposer of the white, the black, the yellow, and the red. And this is what Alphidius says: "Know, my son, that in the depths of this sea, pearls of various colors are born, in which the hyacinth <note>A precious stone, likely zircon or sapphire in this context.</note> of various colors also rises, and even the <term>Marthek</term> itself colors bodies through its own color." For when it is hot, it will be red; but when it is cold, it will be white. Similarly, it shares the color and brightness of the Sun and the Moon; the red is heat, and <term>whiteness</term> is coldness—understand, therefore, and observe.

<margin>Note.</margin> Also, let it be noted that <term>redness</term> is a sign of heat, and <term>whiteness</term> is a sign of coldness. And this is the Third Point of the art according to Hermes, when he says: "In the third month, Mars, acting upon the matter through his <margin>Note.</margin> heat and dryness, divides and sequesters the mass itself, and arranges the limbs." Note the "limbs." For just as in the womb <note>original: "matrice"; the matrix or uterus.</note> nature arranges the limbs of the fetus itself, as integral parts of the fetus, so too this red body is an integral part of the <term>elixir</term> <note>The "philosopher's stone" in liquid or powdered form, capable of transmuting metals.</note> or <term>medicine</term>. For in every composition that is made after this body has been created, it always falls in as an integral part of the composition, as will be declared below. Also, <margin>Note.</margin> note that this body has many names. For it is called Adam, Summer, <term>almagra</term> <note>original: "almagra"; red ochre or earth.</note>, the High, the Soul, Aries, Gold, Cancer, Camereth, <term>ash of tartar</term> <note>original: "cinis tartari"; a chemical salt used as a flux.</note>, Choler, the Proper Body, the Red Body...

Thus also, this body, through the loss of the moisture that first made it <term>Volatile</term>, must now remain fixed. 

For all bodies that are not fixed become fixed through such a deprivation of moisture, which has been called <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of reducing a metal or mineral to powder by roasting or burning.</note> by many Philosophers. Regarding this, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> says: "Calcination is the purification of a thing by fire, or its reduction to powder through the deprivation of the moisture that consolidates the parts and makes them flow." And the reason for the invention of the calcination of spirits is so that they may be better fixed therein. Thus, by the deprivation of moisture, the volatile becomes fixed and hard in its mass. # ART AND THEORY

Philosophers, as it is written in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>. Likewise, there is a change of temperaments <note>original: "complexionum," referring to the four medical humors and their qualities.</note>, such as from a cold and moist temperament into a hot and dry one, or from a phlegmatic temperament into a choleric one, according to the physicians. Likewise, the spiritual becomes corporeal, according to the author of the *Perfect Mastery*. Likewise, the manifest becomes hidden <note>original: "occultum."</note>, according to Rodianus in the *Book of Three Words*. <margin>A point to be noted.</margin> Likewise, you should note that in every single body there are three dimensions, namely: Height, Width, and Depth, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> testifies in the first book of *On the Heavens*.

**Height** is that which appears manifest in a body and is the first thing subjected to our sight. For example: our Stone, in its first creation, is white, and so it appears at first glance because we call it cold and moist (as it is), with Rodianus asserting it thus: "Our stone is aquatic, because it is cold and moist; water is cold and moist, and moist water flows." Therefore, I swear by my very self that this is true; and such a disposition is called the **height** of the body.

**Width**, however, is the arrangement of that medicine through which one travels to the **depth**. This is our "medicine" <note>In alchemy, the 'medicine' or 'elixir' is the substance that heals base metals into gold.</note>, and it is the life of both height and depth, acting as a medium between two extremes or contraries. Through this medium, the extreme is reached, because it is impossible to pass from one extreme to another without a middle state. For it has often been said that our stone is of a moist and cold temperament. Now, if we wish to make it pass into the "disposing medicine," it is necessary that one quality be destroyed within it. It is destroyed, however, through **putrefaction** <note>The stage of the work where the substance breaks down and turns black.</note>. For the cold and moist are thickened through putrefaction, and its moisture is turned into dryness; thus the transition is made to the disposing medicine, which is heat and dryness, and this is called **width**.

Yet Nature receives coldness from the cold and moist, and dryness from the hot and dry, and thus it becomes Earth. Afterward, indeed, through heat exceeding the heat that remained in the body, a transition is made to the contrary by destroying coldness and introducing heat. This disposition is called the **depth**, or the hidden part of the body; and this is best seen in the *Book of Perfect Mastery* in that specific section: "Iron in its **height** is cold, moist, hot, dry, choleric, red, sharp, fragrant, male," and so forth.

Having seen finally how quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum," literally 'living silver' or mercury.</note> is transubstantiated from nature to nature—that is, from coldness and moisture into hea-

...humidity, and dryness. And because at this point, the majority of the Philosophers begin to speak. As Alphidius said regarding the mineral: he called it "Red Sulphur." # METALLIC TRANSMUTATION

## PRINCIPAL AND NECESSARY MATTERS,
*noted below.*

Even though in our small book we have openly, clearly, and abundantly demonstrated the matter of the Philosophers' Stone (as is well known) to all, and have even led its regimen <note>The "regimen" refers to the specific sequence of operations or "rules" of heat and timing required to complete the alchemical work.</note> to completion; nevertheless, so that we may open the whole secret and divine gift more clearly and briefly to the sons of doctrine <note>A traditional term for initiates or students of alchemy.</note>, we say there are three stones of the Philosophers: the Animal, the Vegetable, and the Mineral. 

Therefore, whoever wishes to perfect the animal stone, let him take his beginning from animals, and let him understand that without them and the proper timing, a living image cannot be brought forth. If, however, he should perhaps greatly desire to obtain the vegetable stone, let him know that "unless a seed falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it will bring forth much fruit." <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24, used here to describe the stage of "putrefaction" where the substance must "die" to be transformed.</note> 

But if he prefers to choose the mineral stone, he will not obtain the desired result without 472, 304, 272, and 224. <note>These numbers are a coded reference to the four elements, decoded in the table below.</note> Therefore, he who has ears to hear, let him hear. For we have judged it right that the greatest secret itself be made known to all who are well-deserving. For whatever the ancient Philosophers handed down shrouded in shadows and the gloom of night, we have now openly revealed. 

If anyone, therefore, attains the perfection of the discovery of such an admirable treasure—the greatest of all—we beseech him by that greatest name of God, ineffable to mortals, and we adjure and bind him to keep it inviolably with the integrity of a sincere mind, lest he throw the bread of the wise sons to the dogs. <note>A warning against sharing secret knowledge with the uninitiated or "unworthy," echoing Matthew 7:6.</note>

## TO WILLIAM HYEROSKIPOLONOS, A MAN
### Noble and endowed with all virtues, John Augustine Pantheus, Venetian priest, [wishes] eternal

->happiness.<-

How much we value you—whom we might call our second self—is for you to judge from this: you can now easily gather that for your sake alone we have undertaken this labor of Commentary. From our own Treasures, we have forged <note>original: "excudimus," literally "to hammer out," fitting for a work on metals.</note> this new Work for you, and we dedicate it to you alone. In this work, we have clearly and lucidly preserved and interpreted all the difficult passages that required an Interpreter—specifically those which seemed more obscure in those teachings of ours on metallic transmutations <term>metallic transmutations</term> <note>The alchemical process of changing "base" metals like lead into "noble" metals like gold.</note> which we published in previous years. 

We were advised by friends common to both of us, and informed by letters, that you are diligently occupied with those writings; that you turn over our manuscripts with a "nightly hand and a daily hand" <note>A scholarly idiom meaning to study a text incessantly, borrowed from the Roman poet Horace.</note> (as they say), but that you were tormented because you could not achieve your heart's desire due to certain difficulties in them which seemed unintelligible to you. 

We certainly composed those original Teachings—insofar as the subject matter demands, the faculty permits, and the profession allows—using proper, specific, and common terms <term>terms</term> <note>Technical vocabulary unique to a specific trade or science.</note> used among the professors of this art. For every Art has its own peculiar terms and modes of speaking. However, while we strove for brevity, we perhaps became a bit too obscure for beginners. Nor should those be listened to who think, regarding our teachings, that they can be called "partly published and partly unpublished," or that they will only be knowable to those for whom they have been personally interpreted by us. Such a thing is a trait unique only to the cabalistic art <term>cabalistic art</term> <note>Pantheus refers here to the "Kabbalah," a tradition of mystical interpretation which he integrates into his alchemical theory.</note>, about which more will be said elsewhere. ## OF JOHN AUGUSTINE PANTHEUS OF VENICE
### *priest, on the published theory of metallic transmutation*
### *A commentary.*

Let no wonder seize you, William—a man most learned in every science—if in our commentaries we have not used Latin words in a way that perhaps your most learned ears expected to hear. For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in this period.</note> says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*: It is not the part of every knowledgeable person to ask every question, nor to answer every question asked about everything, but only those which pertain to a specific Science. <note>original: "Scientiam determinatam." Pantheus is arguing that alchemy has its own technical vocabulary that does not need to conform to the literary standards of classical Latin.</note> For if one disputes with a Geometrician <term>Geometrician</term> <note>A practitioner of geometry; here used as an example of a specialist in a technical field.</note>, insofar as he is a geometrician, it is clear that it is done well if something is demonstrated from these...

...demonstrates. If not, then not at all well. It is clear, however, that one does not argue against the geometer except by accident. For this reason, if we wish to discuss with you **alchemy** <note>original: "archemia"; a common medieval spelling. The author is defending the use of "jargon" or technical terms that might seem obscure to outsiders.</note>, the investigator of the marvelous mysteries of nature, it is necessary for us to use such words as are suitable for a science of this kind (as has been said by the **Philosopher** <note>This title almost always refers to Aristotle in Renaissance texts.</note>), and such as the matter itself seems to require. But when we speak with you concerning the duty of an orator or a poet, we shall then imitate the charms of Cicero or Virgil.

<margin>YHWH</margin> <note>The Hebrew Tetragrammaton (יהוה), the sacred four-letter name of God.</note>
Receive, therefore, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The text provides the phonetic names of the Hebrew letters: "Iud he voph he" (Yod, He, Vav, He).</note> in the name of God, just as was commanded by **Plato** in the *Timaeus*: that in all things, whether the greatest or the smallest, divine help must be implored. And in a glazed earthenware vessel, with a fire of the first degree <note>Alchemists categorized fire into four degrees; the first degree is the gentlest heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen.</note> (†) for twenty-four hours, extract the whitest soul, and carefully wash it all through **ascent** <note>A term for sublimation or distillation, where the substance rises as vapor to the top of the vessel.</note>.

Afterward, join it with the spirit and body of GOD in such a way that, according to the balance of this secret, through the **putrefaction** of such a body, a **chyle** <note>original: "chylus"; a biological term for digestive fluid, here used metaphorically for the refined essence of the metal.</note> is generated along with the spirit and soul, by the proportion of the joining and mixing—namely, four parts, or weights of five and nine—preserved upon porphyry stone, and then by grinding it thoroughly without the washing of any water. And do this until you reach a weight of twenty-five and a half pounds, so that they may suffice for you for seven multiplications at one time.

Then, hide it away in an unglazed **aludel** <note>A pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process.</note> (which is made of earth) and under horse manure (which acts as a coal fire) in the place of Putrefaction, Generation, Alteration, and **Fixation**. This fire is called the "exterior" fire, acting upon the Coldness itself—that is, stripping away the **Nigredo** <note>The "Blackness," the first major stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing the death of the old form.</note>. And such a fire should not be permitted to exceed the limit of twenty-four hours in total. However, let that number of hours be distributed into two equal parts, each comprising twelve hours, as is marked with the character **M**.

After these things, strive to induce "eternal death," which is the **rubification** <note>The "Reddening," the final stage of the process where the substance reaches its highest perfection.</note> of the chyle, now brought to its end through putrefaction, generation, alteration, and fixation. Specifically, grind it four times during its putrefaction, three times in generation, twice in alteration, and only once in fixation; yet always with the addition of its own spirit existing in the **vessel** <note>original: "charaha"; likely a carafe or glass jar.</note>.

## ON THE QUANTITY OF CHARCOAL FOR THE COMPLETION OF THE WORK.

Lest we should seem to omit anything—since, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*: "A small error in the beginning becomes the greatest error in the end"—we have therefore decided to discuss the quantity of charcoal, without which the craftsman cannot rightly perform any part of the work.

The sum of all the charcoal, calculated at three days per basket <note>term: corba; a traditional Venetian basket used as a unit of dry measure for coal or grain.</note> (which is the measure in use in Venice), will be 84 baskets. The medicine itself will weigh 64 pounds. And the ratio of its projection <note>The act of "throwing" a small amount of the alchemical elixir onto a base metal to transform it.</note> will be one part over one hundred.

## ON THE REITERATION OF THE MEDICINE.

By the reiterations of the medicine, however, one part shall fall upon <note>In this context, "fall upon" means to transform or transmute.</note> 1,000; then 10,000; 100,000; 1,000,000; 10,000,000; 100,000,000; and finally, one part shall fall upon an incomprehensible number. For this, let the Triune and One ineffable God be praised through all ages, who has so freely granted such great grace to us and to you by His mercy.

## ON THE PROPORTION OF SILVER AS WELL AS GOLD.

Since, as Pliny says in the first chapter of his thirty-fourth book <note>original: "Plinius... xxxiiii. Lib. Cap. primo"; Pliny the Elder's *Natural History*, though the sentiment regarding greed is more famously found in Book 33.</note>, all things began to be practiced for the sake of profit which men previously used to embrace for the sake of glory. Hence we—who hold the profane and ignorant crowd in hatred, and are not moved by their idea of glory—rather sing with our Poet: *Far be the glory of the common people.* 

If we have decided to commit this material to writing, it is so that "the refined may be extracted from the refined" (as they say), and especially for you, William <note>The identity of "Gulielme" (William) is likely the author's patron, a man of learning.</note>, a most learned man in every branch of science. You do not worship gold like that greedy Midas, nor do you seem to thirst for it like that "thirsty" Crassus <note>original: "Dipsas ille crassus"; a play on Marcus Licinius Crassus, a Roman known for extreme wealth, and "Dipsas," a snake whose bite causes unquenchable thirst.</note>. Instead, for the delight of the good arts and for the sake of study, you spare no effort. With all your strength, by day and night, with continuous late-night toils, sweat, and great expense (just as the nobles of nations seeking brilliance used to do in olden times), you pursue this work. But coming now to the matter itself, we say that if you wish to gather the Apples of the Hesperides <note>A mythological reference to the Golden Apples of the sun; here, a metaphor for the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note> without the danger of the Dragon, you should proceed along this path with me as your guide.

<header>ON METALLIC TRANSMUTATION</header>

Take therefore one part of white earth <note>Likely a reference to a purified base material, such as calcined bone or a specific white clay used in the "Great Work."</note>. Two parts of white copper <note>Often referring to an alloy of copper and arsenic or nickel that appears silvery.</note>. And three parts of 224 <note>This number refers to a specific weight or substance defined in the author's numerical system on previous pages.</note>.

With an iron pestle and in a bronze mortar, you shall reduce the earth and the white copper into a very fine powder.

Afterwards, you shall place this, sprinkled with human washings <note>original: "hominis lotione"; a common alchemical euphemism for urine, used for its ammonia content.</note> along with the 224 and reduced into thin plates <note>term: bracteis; extremely thin sheets of metal, similar to gold leaf.</note>, buried in a well-glazed earthenware vessel.

Afterwards, you shall close this with its own lid—a small hole having been made in the top of it—very well with common, simple clay, and you shall cook it among lit coals and the flame of wood for one hour.

Then, once cooled, having placed it again in a new earthenware vessel among lit coals, you shall melt the material. By extracting the dross with water using a hazel rod <note>Hazel was often attributed with special divinatory or purifying properties in folklore and alchemy.</note> until it becomes clear, you shall pour it from the vessel into an iron goldsmith’s tool <note>Likely a casting mold or an ingot tray.</note>, and keep it once cooled.

When, however, you wish to begin the work:
CERVCRA <note>Possibly a variant of *cerussa* (white lead), or a specialized alchemical term.</note>: 1 ounce.
2 grains.
1 grain. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 10 Karats of the mixture you shall take.

You shall melt one after another in a new earthenware vessel over lit coals, and you will have a real silver mixture.
