### CONCERNING GOLD.

Most learned William, the same things that we have stated above regarding silver are to be done in such a way for gold, if you seek its mixture.

For let one part of "Sea water" <note>original: "Aquæ marinæ"; an alchemical metaphor, possibly referring to a salted solution or a specific acidic solvent like aqua regia.</note> be taken. Two parts of "Etnean fire" <note>original: "Ignis æthnæ"; a poetic name for intense heat or a corrosive substance like sulfuric acid, named after the volcano Mount Etna.</note>. And of the 224 <note>See the previous page regarding this specific numerical substance.</note>.

In the rest, moreover, let one proceed as has been said above, with only two things excepted. First, <gloss>that</gloss> whereas in silver the material is cooked for one hour: in gold it is cooked for four hours. The second is that once the vessel has been cooled, such a mixture does not at all require being melted, nor should it be reduced into a "body" <note>original: "in corpus"; to bring the material back into a solid, metallic mass.</note>.

Therefore, when you wish to undertake the work of bound gold:
->**ERVARGA.** <note>This term may be a cipher or an acronym for a specific alchemical compound.</note> 1 ounce.<-
->2 quarters.<-
->1 quarter, 16 carats are to be taken.<-

Let them be melted together one after the other; and in the iron tool of the goldsmiths, let the whole be cast out of the vessel and, once cooled, be preserved.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS ANDREA GRITTI,
## PRINCE OF THE VENETIANS, John
## Augustine Pantheus, a Venetian priest, [wishes]
-> A happy and long-lasting reign. <-

<margin>Bernardo Giustiniani, *On the origin of the city of the Venetians*, at the beginning. Chapter: "The high bank [Rialto] was situated." <note>Bernardo Giustiniani (1408–1489) was a prominent Venetian diplomat and historian; his work was the standard history of Venice's founding at the time.</note></margin>
THAT HIGHEST Maker of things <note>original: "Summus ille opifex rerum"; a common Renaissance way of referring to God as the Divine Architect.</note>, whose wisdom has no end, by His omnipotence, reconciles man to man for the fellowship of life. Moreover, this society and gathering is called a City, and a Republic. Every city, although it is forged and preserved by the natural and common consent of the whole people and by the strength of Justice: nevertheless, the HOLY CITY of the Venetians, by a certain special providence of the divine will, was established and gathered from the nobility of many cities all around, fleeing the cruelty and savagery of Attila then devastating all of Italy (as once a few were saved from the flood by Noah's ark) first in this place, as follows below (In the year of Jesus Christ four hundred and twenty-one, on the twenty-fifth of March <note>original: "octauo Calendas Aprilis"; the traditional, symbolic founding date of Venice, coinciding with the Feast of the Annunciation.</note>: in the hour and the angle of the south). 

Then, although it has been frequently tossed and troubled by various whirlwinds of wars: yet, always aided by divine help, it grew so much that it stands in need of absolutely none of all other Republics (whatever might be celebrated by fame). For it cannot be said by how many upright counsels of the wisest Princes, how many brave deeds, and how many holy institutions of the Fathers it was founded, and daily propagated more effectively and happily. Since therefore the eternal, universal, heavenly Lord, through whom Kings reign and Princes command: has deservedly placed You, most Serene and Most Invincible Prince—after many embassies and distinguished magistracies wisely completed; after the illustrious and at the same time successful command and governance of the Venetian army; and finally after various labors of sea and land, both willingly undertaken and gloriously overcome—as the Prince, Moderator, and Father of the Fatherland <note>original: "patriæque Parentem"; a prestigious title of Roman origin bestowed upon leaders who had saved or significantly improved the state.</note> for this best of Republics: so that you might be the one who—in such a great tumult of wars, and such great misery of famine and plague—might support with your prudence and greatness of soul the Venetian people and the subject cities, which are somewhat faltering; just as Hercules [supported] the heavens...

# DEDICATION.

<page-num>565</page-num>
<sig>NNn 3</sig>

not only would you receive and console [the city], but indeed, you would protect and preserve it. Who, then, would be so out of his mind <note>original: "impos mentis"; a legal and philosophical term for being mentally incapacitated or "not master of one's mind."</note> as to not rightly proclaim You a true Father and Defender to all? Or not venerate You as if you were a high Divinity? Especially since You are one who helps all, benefits all, and looks out for the convenience and safety of all. For who does not know that a good Prince is born not just for himself, but for his Republic, for his Citizens, and finally for his People? While he suppresses the seditious and the discordant, he punishes the proud and the rebellious, and he raises and exalts the humble and the studious. 

For indeed, the bond of human society would be dissolved unless some Presiding Ruler were present; by whose effort, zeal, and authority, the audacity of the wicked might be repressed, the innocence of the good might be preserved, the talents of the studious might be attracted and nurtured with rewards fitting for their virtue, and the safeguards of life and honor might be provided. For it is a beautiful thing for a man to excel others, and to lead the well-born and the illustrious; but who would not judge it more beautiful and praiseworthy to be able to make many people happy? This power (certainly) must be extolled with the highest praise, since, Most Serene Prince, it was acquired for you not by fortune, but by virtue. 

To you, Pantheus <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo (c. 1475–1535), the author of this work and a Venetian priest who sought to distinguish his "true" alchemy from the fraudulent practices of others.</note>, most devoted to your greatness, flees for refuge; as a suppliant, he invokes and implores your Divine Spirit that you might receive and protect both himself and this little work of his—concerning the <term>transmutation</term>, <term>purification</term>, <term>multiplication</term>, and proportion of Silver and likewise of Gold, titled <term>Voarchadumia</term> <note>A term coined by Pantheus, likely from a pseudo-Chaldean or Hebrew root meaning "Gold of two testimonies" or "Two-fold refined gold"; he used it to distance his work from common, often illegal "alchemy."</note> against Alchemy—with your cheerful and serene countenance; and that you might follow it with your protection (as you are accustomed to do for the monuments of each of your humble clients). Farewell.

# TO THE MOST REVEREND IN CHRIST
## FATHER AND LORD, LORD ALTOBELLO AVEROL-
->do, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See, Bishop of Po-<-
->la, Referendary <note>A high-ranking official in the papal court who processed petitions.</note> of our Most Holy Lord the Pope, and throughout the whole<-
->Venetian territory, with the power of a Cardinal Legate<-
->from the side <note>original: "Legati de latere"; a papal legate of the highest class, representing the Pope as if he were "at his side."</note>, a most worthy Legate. Giovanni Agos-<-
->tino Pantheus, Venetian priest,<-
->wishes eternal happiness.<-

For a long time now, the offspring of our *Voarchadumia* <note>A term coined by the author, likely from Chaldean or Hebrew roots, referring to a "true" alchemy or gold-making process that he distinguishes from common alchemy. He defines it as a "way and reason" distinct from ordinary alchemy and wisdom.</note> would have emerged into the light (Most Reverend Prelate), had not a certain Spirit <note>original: "Genius"; a personal guardian spirit or inner voice.</note>, constantly scolding me with such words, deterred me from the undertaking: "Pantheus? What madness drives you? With what audacity do you claim so much for yourself? That you would drive a still-featherless little bird from its nest? One that is so far from having the strength to fly that it cannot even walk safely on its feet? Who would suspect this of you, Pantheus? That the more obstacles present themselves, the more greedily you hasten to release this offspring of yours? And what is more absurd: you wish it to travel not only through Italy, but the entire world? And furthermore (which is contrary to your own judgment), do you dare incautiously to interrupt **ANDREA GRITTI**, the most radiant star of the Venetian Republic, upon whose most auspicious nod or refusal the entire state of the empire depends? See (I pray) what you are doing. He is entangled in greater business than to have time for anyone's words. And unless you bring things worthy of a reader, it will undoubtedly happen that where you hope for favor, you will instead bring back contempt and hatred. Therefore, my advice (if not my command) is this: either this still-powerless offspring must be nurtured for a while longer until it can go forth stronger and far more pleasing; or, if you think it must be published at all, strive to adorn it so that it does not, at the very least, appear shameful." 

Being very often corrected by these warnings, I'll admit I hesitated for some time, lest the excessive love of a most indulgent father <note>The author refers to himself as the "father" of the book.</note> should deceive my correct judgment. Therefore, I consulted two Censors, who would turn over the whole work again, three and four times from beginning to end, to explore and diligently weigh it. Having discussed each individual point, nothing was found in the whole work which...

# DEDICATION.

...it seemed that nothing ought to be added, taken away, or changed. For they asserted that the work was perfect in its proportions: that all the parts harmonized, excelled in distinguished form, and were a vigorous body, full of sap <note>original: "succiplenum"; a metaphor for vitality and richness of content</note>, and strengthened by steady and long-lasting labor. Thus, it need not fear the judgment of any critic. Only one thing was excepted: namely, a charming elegance of expression. Yet we, knowingly and willingly, have left that to the masters of oratory, being content with a simplicity of words. We did this so that the words might serve the ideas, rather than the ideas ambitiously serving the words. In this (unless my judgment fails me), the most humble style of the Sacred Scriptures, in which we have long been occupied, encourages and protects this negligence of our speech. It uses common and familiar words rather than elegant and exquisite ones, because nothing is considered more inept than to be anxious about the decoration of words when the question is one of perceiving the truth. The credibility of an author is not usually suspected without cause when unusual enticements of language are affected. Those who value the flowers more than the fruits are not undeservedly rejected as empty by more serious men. We by no means seek the applause of the people; we have enough and more if a few silent observers look within and marvel at something—as if stunned—dug out from either the innermost shrines of nature or the most remote sanctuaries of heaven. But the rest we value little, as being unworthy and ignorant of our concepts, whether we are judged as unrefined for our simple talent or our humble speech. Indeed, we consider this especially glorious for us: if these things (whatever they may be) should displease the unskilled multitude. For it is not for the sake of speaking alone, or for wit, that a man is made wise. Furthermore, we even do this by deliberate effort: so that with the truth hidden under a more bitter bark <note>A common metaphor in alchemical and theological texts where the "bark" or "shell" is the difficult language and the "fruit" or "pith" is the secret knowledge.</note> of speech, the ignorant crowd might be deterred from reading such great matters. This is just as the Voarchadumians <note>Followers of the author's specific "Voarchadumia" art, a term he coined for a sacred alchemy.</note> and Archicanopians <note>Another technical term used by Pantheus for practitioners of his higher art.</note> are accustomed to do, who hide Silver <note>original: "Argentum"</note> and Gold <note>original: "Aurum"</note> in oils or waters, so that "seeing they may not see, and understanding they may not perceive." <note>A biblical reference to Isaiah 6:9 and Matthew 13:13, frequently used by esoteric writers to justify concealing secrets from the uninitiated.</note> Shrewd merchants do not look for the surface, but for the enclosed substance within the bundles <note>original: "Fionis"; likely a reference to Phoenician bundles or general merchant bales.</note>. Here, too, the prize is sought not for a flowery circuit of words, but for serious matters—a prize all the more perennial because those things are being pressed which are to be forged not in Gems, or in the air, but in Gold <note>original: "Auro"</note>, or rather in eternal minds. For these things, when known and kept, make a man truly blessed, if he gives his effort diligently to the things that must be done—not if he has merely been steeped in the charm of every language. Indeed, I do not think in this matter...

# DEDICATION.

...we can boast that we shall see the pure (though unadorned) truth be more pleasing to the Cabalistic nature of metals <note>original: "Cabalisticis metallorum"; Pantheus is referring to "Archymia," his system of spiritual alchemy that applies Cabalistic principles to the transmutation of metals</note> than if that same truth had come into public view through the fictions of eloquence and a vain veil of rhetorical coloring. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, a common justification for looking past the literal surface of a text to its hidden "mystical" meaning.</note> But if these criticisms were true, something might perhaps be justly said against us; therefore, we must implore the help of an Advocate and a Leader, under whose patronage a free entrance may lie open to whichever path one chooses to enter.

And so, let us delay no longer: behold Altobello Averoldo <note>Altobello Averoldo (c. 1468–1531) was a powerful diplomat and Bishop of Pola; he served as the Papal Legate to Venice.</note>, a nobleman of Brescia, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See, the Bishop of Pola and an excellent pro-pontiff. Behold, he is a patron who offers himself freely to all candidates of mystical philosophy. Under his guidance and authority, if this little book is published, it will be able to fly like a victor—without any fear of reproach—not only among all other Lords of these lands, but especially before the most serene Duke <note>The Doge of Venice.</note> and the most pious Senate of the Venetians.

This Most Reverend Prelate—to pass over the ancient nobility of the Averoldo family and the imposing dignity of his person, which so stands out that he presents the air of a terrestrial deity <note>original: "terrenum Numen"; high-flown Renaissance flattery suggesting the Bishop possesses a god-like presence on earth</note> rather than a man even to those looking from afar—is of a divine genius, always prepared to earn new favor. He possesses an incredible sweetness of manners, combined with an approachable and ready courtesy for everyone; thus it happens that wherever he turns, all things immediately brighten.

Because of this, we have a more certain hope and greater confidence in obtaining what we pray for. We pray, Most Reverend Father, that as far as your sacred authority extends far and wide, you take this work of ours (now to be published) into your protection. Fortified by your defense, it may come more safely into the hands of the most learned men. For it has long been proven to us that if it is approved by your vote, your favor, and your divine-like authority, it will be placed beyond all risk <note>original: "extra omnem aleam"; literally "outside the throw of the dice"</note> and will fly through the entire world secure from all envy. If this should happen through your kindness, Pantheus, most observant of your Greatness, promises that he will be most devoted to you with all the strength of his mind and body for as long as he lives. Farewell.

He emphasizes that the "pure truth" of his alchemical-cabalistic secrets is more valuable than flowery language.</summary>

# VOARCHADUMIA:
## AN ART DISTINCT FROM ALCHEMY,
## ARCHIMIA, AND SOPHIA; WITH
## THE ADDITIONS, PROPORTIONS OF NUMBERS,
## and appropriate Figures, by Giovanni Agostino
## Pantheo, a Venetian priest.

### *THE AUTHOR'S INTENTION CONCERNING THE VOARCHA-*
### *dumic profession, as an art distinct from Alchemy,*
### *Archimia, and Sophia.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial F featuring two figures, possibly putti or classical figures, within an ornate frame of foliage and architectural motifs.</image-desc>WE BELIEVE that many will easily wonder, most kind reader, as they read through this work called *Voarchadumia* <note>original: "Voarchadumia"; a word coined by Pantheus, likely from Chaldean and Hebrew roots, meaning "Gold of two earths," representing his unique system of metallic transmutation.</note>, published against Alchemy and separated by no small margin from *Archimia* and *Sophia* <note>Pantheus distinguishes his work from three other fields: "Alchemia" (which he considers a fraudulent or "sophistical" practice), "Archimia" (legitimate chemical transmutation), and "Sophia" (philosophical or spiritual wisdom).</note>. Indeed, when they have calmly reflected upon each thing contained within it, we think they will by no means turn their minds away from the reading of this work. For this reason, we have deemed it not at all outside the bounds of reason to make known to studious readers at the beginning of this volume why this has occurred to us. We do so especially for the reason that we observe not only countless peoples (so to speak) who are largely unskilled in philosophy, but even men of the highest honor and dignity, who greatly desire to search into the inner chambers of nature. Regarding the primary transmutations, purifications, multiplications, and proportions of Silver and Gold, these men spare no expense and devote their efforts day and night with no lack of labor and sleepless nights. They seem to occupy themselves with this matter either led by the desire for profit, or rather enticed by the opportunity of gaining knowledge, and thus they search into the more secret mysteries of nature. Concerning what we think should be more truly asserted in this matter, we shall—by the path of the more experienced and with the favor of the eternal, almighty Lord—briefly reveal it.

<margin>
The fourfold
transmutation
of metals.
</margin>
For we say that all practitioners of metallic transmutations can be occupied and labor in a fourfold manner.

<margin>
The first
way: Sophis-
tication.
</margin>
In the first way (certainly), by feigning the "luminaries" <note>original: "luminaria"; an alchemical term referring to the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note>—that is, Silver and Gold—namely, by coloring the more imperfect metals through many kinds of tinctures and types of sophistications <note>original: "sophisticationum"; here meaning deceptive imitations or chemical "tricks" that change the appearance but not the substance.</note>, and by altering them, while their own proper essence and substance nonetheless remain.

He identifies the first of four ways people approach metalworking: "sophistication," or the mere coloring of metals to look like gold or silver.</summary>

<margin>What Archimia is. From Heber, not however from Abraham.</margin>
...[remaining]. This profession we call Alchemy by the common consensus of all (named after *Alchemus*: which is indeed interpreted from a Hebrew word as the "leaven of vain counsel" <note>original: "fermentum vani consilij"; Pantheus uses a pseudo-etymology to dismiss common alchemy as a deceptive "leaven" or fermentation of bad advice.</note>). Since it has no true existence of Silver or Gold, but only a completely empty and false appearance: it is deservedly (as we will show below by both reasons and authorities) condemned, and to be condemned, and utterly removed from our midst.

<margin>The second mode. Transmutation. What Archimia is.</margin>
In the second mode, many good men and even high-ranking leaders labor everywhere, hoping they can fashion certain Elixirs from various materials (as they believe): and lead those to such a peak of vigor and subtlety that, once a "projection" <note>The act of casting a small amount of the philosopher's stone or elixir onto a base metal to transform it.</note> of that Medicine is made upon any metal, it is immediately transmuted into pure silver or glowing Gold: and this almost infinitely. This metallic profession (even if I do not call it vainly hoped for, but rather to be attained by divine grace) they call **Archimia** <term>Archimia: a term used to distinguish legitimate, though difficult, metallic transmutation from fraudulent "Alchemy."</term>: as if it were the "Prince of unity and of the one true counsel." Concerning this truly admirable transmutation, many volumes of both ancients and moderns are circulated everywhere: namely the *Tubalchiam* of *Hermes*, *Geber*, *Alphidius*, *Avicenna*, the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>, *Hortulanus*, *Rosinus*, *Albert*, *Arnald*, *Raymond*, *Mary the Prophetess*, *Morienus*, *Christopher of Paris*; and many other Arabs, Chaldeans, Greeks, Hebrews, Indians, and Latins. 

From their readings, additions, contradictions, figures, lines, letters, metaphors, notes, prophecies, points, similarities, syncopes, synonyms, and enigmatic books: has this possible transmutation been found up to now, or does the hope of finding it increase daily, in a matter we know easily enough? Rather, that adage of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> comes to mind, asserting in the *Categories*: "If the squaring of the circle is knowable, it has not yet been known." <note>original: "Si circuli quadratura est scibilis, nondum tamen est scita." A famous philosophical comparison for problems that are theoretically possible but practically unsolved.</note> Nevertheless, since they attempt to reach the true form of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refers to the Sun (gold) and the Moon (silver).</note> by casting aside sophistic methods, we think they are by no means to be blamed with a mark of ignorance, but rather raised up with praise as investigators of nature’s secrets. Even if most of them could not achieve such a great work, they nevertheless invented (as experience witnesses) admirable operations and arts: as can be seen in Crystal made from glass, "purpurina" from colors, brass <term>Auricalcum: Orichalcum, a gold-colored alloy of copper and zinc (brass).</term> from metals, and things of this sort, as [discussed] below: as well as in volumes both our own and those of others concerning Minerals, Colors, Stones, Glass, Gems, and metals...

...has been treated. This is certainly worthy of knowledge and marvelous to see, although no ability for profit <note>The author suggests that while you can change the form, you do not necessarily gain more total gold than you started with unless you reach the "First Matter."</note> emerges for the worker without its own Body (that is, without reduction to the **First Matter** of the art). Instead, the power and abundance of Silver and Gold resulting from the **projection** <note>The act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a metal to transform it.</note> of that Fifth Essence is (scarcely) as much as the Silver and Gold that was first uncovered. 

Truly indeed, most people have been so excited by admiration of this kind of transmutation that they more easily believed that, through further refinement of that Fifth Essence and added perfection and virtue, that vigorous **Elixir** must be made to carry out transmutation (though erroneously) unto infinity. But let us let these things go for now, since they seem to require a longer discourse, which indeed we shall treat elsewhere, the eternal and almighty Lord favoring us.

What Voarchadumia is.

In this, they operate in three particular ways, which offer the greatest benefit to Lords and Merchants.

<margin>

Multiplication.
What Sophia is.

Which, even if it is difficult (though possible) or of a mediocre nature...

->OF THE AUTHOR<-

...of profit, though many experience this daily, there are nevertheless those who hope and promise to make it very great.

We have judged that this secret profession of the purification of gold should rightly be called **Voarchadumia** <term>Voarchadumia; a term coined by the author, Pantheus, likely derived from Hebrew and Chaldean roots to mean "Gold of two purifications."</term>, which is entirely contrary to the faculty of **Alchemy**. For whereas there is no actual existence of Silver or Gold in Alchemy <note>The author argues that common alchemy deals with the *process* of making these metals from base substances, whereas his art begins with the metals themselves.</note>, in this art the **Luminaries** <note>original: "luminaria"; the alchemical Sun (gold) and Moon (silver).</note> exist in their most perfect state. We have separated this from **Archimia** and **Sophia** <note>original: "Sophia"; meaning "Wisdom," often used here to refer to the philosophical or theoretical side of the craft.</note> for good reason, because the operation of Voarchadumia and the **Wisdom of Gold** is brought to effect more truly and easily; whereas in **Archimia**, the promise is greater than the execution of the work.

From these things, anyone may easily guess why we have produced this work on Voarchadumia in opposition to **Alchemy**, and why we have distinguished it from **Archimia** and **Sophia**. No one should be angry that we have now explained the intention of the work briefly, nor should they be in the least terrified by the reading of this work; rather, with the help of this undertaking, one will be able to search out the more secret mysteries of Nature more easily and effectively, and guard against the hidden traps of the **Sophists** <note>original: "sophismata"; here referring to fraudulent alchemists who use trickery.</note> and forgers. We believe it will bring no small amount of grief and loss to them that our little work has come to light, since through it the frauds, deceptions, and veils of such detestable forgers are uncovered. Men of sound mind must abstain from them in the future, following the warning of this our work.

# PART ONE.

## *By what better and more suitable name the faculty of gold purification should be called. Chapter One.*

Since the tradition of every doctrine and discipline—following the path of the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripateticorum"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who prioritized defining names and terms before examining the things themselves.</note>—must take its start from the question of the *name* <note>original: "quid nominis"</note> before that of the *essence* <note>original: "quid rei"</note>, like a preliminary arrangement of things to be known by the intellect so that the summit of that profession may be reached more easily; we do not at all think it foreign to reason, most kind reader, to show first by what better or more suitable name the secret faculty of **Gold Purification** may be called, and whether that word **Alchemy**, or rather **Voarchadumia**, should be thought more fitting for it. Truly, we do not think that the word **Voarchadumia** is so hidden from you that it [signifies] nothing...

### INTENTION.

...than you might think. Since in this our own time, through the diligence of scholars, the Chaldean profession has come to light and into public knowledge—which in our days has easily revealed what was previously hidden to most concerning the art, namely the purification of Gold by two 
<margin>Inquirers of Voarchadumia.</margin>
perfect **cementations** <term>cementation; a high-temperature process used to decopper or purify gold using chemical salts</term>. The inquirers [of this art] claim that after **Tubal-cain** <note>A biblical figure (Genesis 4:22) considered the first blacksmith and instructor of every artificer in brass and iron</note> himself, the first authors of it were the Chaldeans or rather the Indians. They elsewhere called this the "Celestial Discipline," as witnessed by **Solinus**, **Strabo**, and **Pliny**, as well as **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**. Nor should anyone doubt why the authors of so noble a profession of metals gave it such an abstruse name, that is, **Voarchadumia** <term>Voarchadumia; the author's coined term for his "true" alchemy, distinguishing it from common practice</term>, which is a most fitting word and worthy of all praise. It is not, however, **Alchemy**, as [discussed] below; for that art is imperfect, illiberal, endowed with no virtue, and no sharer in secret wisdom. Rather, it is greedy, unnecessary, utterly false, illicit, vain, and by no means to be learned or sought after. Indeed, it is an adulterous operation, a sophisticated mixture and tincture—appearing to be something, but in truth being nothing—infamous, execrable, exploded, and deservedly condemned. We also entirely blame and curse it, along with the **Extravagant** <note>referring to the "Extravagantes" or decretals of the Canon Law</note> of **John XXII**, which begins: *They promise riches which they do not provide, these poor Alchemists* <note>original: "Spondent, quas non exhibent diuitias, pauperes Alchemistæ"; a famous 1317 papal bull against alchemists who counterfeit money</note>. Likewise, we stand with the constitution of the divine Emperor **Constantine**, ever August, which begins: *Since some coiners practice adulterated coinage through clandestine crimes...* under the Title of the Code, *concerning false money*. By this constitution, such adulterators are punished with capital punishment. And we pursue [this condemnation] along with the decree of the **Council of Ten of Venice**, December 17, 1488, with the addition beginning: *They are to be removed from our midst* <note>original: "Tollenda sunt de medio"</note>. Nor do we affirm that the name is derived from the Greek particles *Archos* and *Mia*, as some think, which would signify "Prince of one," or more truly, "of the unity of true counsel." But now 
<margin>Derivation of Voarchadumia, and of the name.</margin>
coming to the word **Voarchadumia** itself, we say it is derived and named from "Gold of two reds," which in the Chaldean idiom is composed of *Voarth*, meaning Gold (an original Indian particle), and *Mea à adumot* in Hebrew, meaning "from two reds." In Latin, this signifies **Gold of two reds**, that is, 
<margin>of the two.</margin>
of two perfect cementations. These parts joined together form this expression: *Voarch mea à adumot*, which expresses the greatest property and efficacy of this art. Truly, we do not think that the term "Alchemy" would be at all consistent with this 
<margin>Objection.</margin>
admirable profession. But

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his specific terminology, specifically distinguishing his "Voarchadumia" from "Voarchaumena" and common alchemy. He concludes the introductory "Intention" and moves into the second chapter.</meta>

AUTHOR

<margin>Reply.</margin> Perhaps someone will object to us that it matters little from where this word **Voarchadumia** is derived. To such a person we say that it matters a great deal—indeed, everything—as will soon be apparent even at a glance. But if a persistent critic stands in our way, saying: "Even if that is so, what of it? Since it is clear that the art of **Voarchaumena** <term>Voarchaumena; a term the author uses to describe common, fraudulent alchemy, as opposed to his 'true' Voarchadumia</term> is illiberal, greedy, base in its pursuit of profit, and not at all necessary, impossible, and not to be sought after, as you said above." Indeed, we judge such a deceptive objector to be greatly mistaken. We utterly deny that our profession of purification—of the Gold of the two reds <note>original: "Auri duarum rubearum"; likely referring to the two stages of perfecting gold through high-heat purification</note>—is **Voarchaumena**, and we believe that **Voarchaumena** and **Voarchadumia** are far apart from one another. Therefore, the critic is greatly deceived by the ambiguity of the words. Recalling this to memory, we can easily recount the poetic line: *May you not be a hindrance to us, by God, guests* <note>original: "Ne nobis impedimento sitis per Deum hospites"</note>, since it has been sufficiently shown above that **Voarchadumia** is praiseworthy, while **Voarchaumena** is certainly not. Let all abuse of vocabulary be absent from this secret profession, just as many people are daily accustomed to being entangled and deceived, thinking that the same thing can be signified by various words. For that reason, we believe this wonderful faculty can be called by many names according to its various and entirely different effects: such as **Alchemy**, **Chemia**, **Calcimia**, **Calcecumia**, **Voarchaumena**, and **Voarchadumia**. Since we accept and approve the last of all these with a favorable mind, we do so because it deservedly signifies a liberal art, endowed with virtue, consistent with Nature, belonging to secret wisdom, not greedy, not vain, possible, most true, and necessary—to be learned and sought after with all the powers of one's mind. The rest, however, we detest as signifying an entirely illicit and false art, especially by that most just argument: the decree of the most illustrious **Council of Ten** <note>The "Decemviri," a powerful governing body in Venice, where this book was published, which regulated the practice of alchemy to prevent fraud</note>, the constitution of the Emperor **Constantine**, ever August, and the *Extravagant* decree of **John XXII** <note>Referring to the papal bull "Spondent quas non exhibent" issued around 1317, which banned alchemists for making false promises of wealth</note>, as is prohibited above. *If anyone shall have labored at Alchemy, let him be restrained by incurring the penalties of the Council of Ten.* From what has been said, therefore, it can be clear by which superior word anyone should deservedly call this secret faculty of purification, the Gold of two perfect **cementations** <term>cementation; a chemical process for refining gold by heating it with salts to remove impurities</term>.

# INTENTION.

<margin>Voarchadumia and what it is.</margin>
...[let] me [explain] what it is itself, since **Voarchadumia** is defined as a liberal art, endowed with the virtue of hidden wisdom; it is not greedy, not vain, but possible, most true, necessary, and consequently to be sought after. It is called the <term>Cabala</term> <note>Derived from the Hebrew word for "tradition," the author uses this to mean a secret, mystical system of knowledge applied here to metallurgy.</note> of metals, as well as <term>Prophecy</term> and <term>Notation</term>. For this reason, it is said not to be suitable for everyone in general, but specifically only for the anointed, the masters of things, the wise, and men who are worthy, liberal, and well-mannered, by reason of their liberty.

<margin>To whom Voarchadumia belongs.</margin>
<margin>Second definition of Voarchadumia, and what it is.</margin>
**S**econdly, it is like a certain hidden and secret governance, which is handed down only through the hands of the "sons of the wise" <note>A traditional alchemical term for initiates or students of the hermetic arts.</note> under the light (though commonly enveloped in darkness). It demonstrates the disposition, illumination, conversion, constriction, retention, metallification, purification, multiplication, and proportion of the natural bonds of the hidden and the hider, of soul and body, of the dense and the rare, of the divine and the human, of form and matter, of the fixed and the volatile, of the interior and the exterior, of metal and stone, of the soft and the hard, of the hidden and the manifest, of the pure and the mixed. This is achieved through a certain craftsmanship instituted by the eternal, almighty Lord, under Fire, Air, Water, and Earth, or the great secret <note>original: "arcano"</note> of these four letters: <term>Lamed</term>, <term>Kuph</term>, <term>Cadic</term>, and <term>Samech</term>.

In **Voarchadumia**, these letters signify the same thing as <term>Zain</term>, <term>Nun</term>, <term>Mem</term>, and <term>Iod</term>, the characters of which are held in fourfold difference among the Hebrews. However, the newest and most common ones are those (concerning which the <term>Diagrams</term> <note>original: "Schemata"; refers to the symbolic illustrations or tables common in occult texts.</note> will be revealed a little below) which in **Voarchadumia** signify the same as Gold created from elementary Nature—that is, in the bowels of the earth—and purified because of the craftsmanship of Division and Cementation <note>Cementation was a historical metallurgical process used to refine gold by heating it with salts to remove impurities.</note>, and so named in Hebrew: <term>Zahay niura mi Teuahiesodij</term> <note>A Latinized transliteration of Hebrew, likely intended to mean "Gold purified from the elemental nature."</note>:

<margin>
Properties of the form of Gold.
</margin>
**T**hirdly, it is the art that supplies the substance for the vein of Gold, containing within itself the extractive metallic power. It explains how its intrinsic form—fixed, non-diminishing, non-consuming, and naturally tinted a saffron yellow—is (lest it be obvious) hindered by a certain elementary mixture unrelated to the metal of Gold. Through the mediation of artifice, this art leads the metal to perfection from the manifest, extrinsic material which is volatile, combustible, and deficient, yet universally united and adhering to the Gold itself.

# PORTIO
<meta>catchword: ras</meta>

<margin>What Voarchadumia achieves</margin>
...brought to its perfected state. This art relaxes the mixture (by the power of fire and cement) through its uniform potency. It leads the Gold itself—divided for its determined purification—into <term>Adunota</term> <note>original: "Adunota," a term likely derived from the Greek "adunatos" (impossible/mighty) or a corruption used as a technical jargon by Pantheus</note>, which is <term>Berthadumor</term> <note>original: "Berthadumor," an invented pseudo-Hebrew term probably meaning "House of Red Gold"</note>. These are the "two reds," namely, two perfected cementations <note>Cementation is a dry refining process where gold is heated with additives like salt or brick dust to remove impurities</note> resulting in a softness and a brilliance of quality, as it is said, reaching the twenty-fourth degree <note>referring to 24-carat purity</note>.

<margin>Upon what Alchemy relies</margin>
<margin>Petrarch, Dialogue 3</margin>
However, that infamous alchemical art does not achieve this with its "waters of vinegar," nor (as it is said) with quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, nitre, wine, or urine, nor any other such solvents of similar dregs. Nor does it succeed with the spirits of strong waters <note>acids like nitric acid</note>, nor the manifold smoke of calces <note>metal oxides</note> and metals, nor with antimonies, arsenics, vitriols, saffron-pigments <note>iron oxides</note>, Spanish hematite, "flower of copper" <note>verdigris</note>, gums, litharges <note>lead monoxide</note>, marcasites, magnets, metallic earths, talcs, or calamine. Nor does it work with oils of brick, linseed, nitre, sublimate, sulfur, cinnabar, or even skulls; nor with dyed earths, realgars, or the juices of celandine, moonwort, silverweed, or cloves, and other herbs, nor with tutty <note>zinc oxide</note> or dire poisons. They labor in vain and with a totally empty result in I-know-not-what fragile and fantastical glass vessels, using the falsest instruments for the task. They follow a procedure that is varied, uncertain, and confused, projecting various materials upon "pure silver"—as they call their "fixed" metal—sophisticating and burdening the matter of every metal with a greater, volatile, black, and burnt imperfection.

For these reasons, the logic and definition are now clear from all that has been said: why **Voarchadumia** is a liberal art by the aforementioned power, an occult wisdom, not greedy, not vain, but necessary, possible, most true, and skilled—an art to be learned and sought after with the highest study.

### How Voarchadumia itself is made. Chapter III.

<margin>The composition of Voarchadumia.</margin>
Take one measure of proportioned Gold leaf (as described below) and an equal amount of crushed salt. Take two measures of burnt and finely ground clay.

Let the salt and clay be sifted through a sieve. Once mixed layer upon layer in unglazed pots and a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material from the roof</note>, let them be cemented.

<margin>Note.</margin>
It must be noted, however, that every cementation (that is, "The Red," or in Hebrew <term>Aduma</term> <note>original: "Aduma," Hebrew for "red" or "earthy"</note>) requires certain hours for each turn...

## FIRST PART
[Ooo 3]
<meta>catchword: Mixture</meta>

...twenty-four hours of fire. Specifically, nine for augmentation <note>Increasing the intensity or potency of the substance</note>, nine for fixation <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat without evaporating</note>, and finally six for alteration.

<margin>Note</margin>
Furthermore, every <term>cementation</term> <note>A dry refining process where gold is heated with additives like salt or brick dust to remove impurities</note> must begin from a divided proportion of twenty-three <term>carats</term> <note>A unit of purity; 24 carats being pure</note> and three grains, with two fourths of a grain of yellow gold. And for each stage, the cementation itself withdraws from that proportioned division only half a grain of that proportion, and no more. Nor can it be said that it withdraws this from the gold in any way (regardless of what others may say), since gold itself is <term>indestructible</term> <note>original: "inannihilabile"</note>, lacking all superfluity. It is the most perfect and most stable of all the <term>combustible metals</term> <note>original: "metallorum adustibilium"; metals like iron or copper that oxidize or "burn" when heated</note>. It is a "jubilant" substance that persists in the fire; it is neither corrupted by the cement, nor burned by any combustible thing, nor killed or devoured by "coloring," "green," or "dividing" waters <note>Refers to corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid, often called "aqua fortis"</note>.

<margin>Question</margin>
For what is superfluous or lacking in yellow gold?
<margin>Solution</margin>
Certainly nothing. If there were in it a loss of substance or a superfluity (which is immediately denied)—as is found in iron and other combustible metals, whose natural mixtures retain a great deal of combustible waste—a great absurdity would follow, stripping away every veil: namely, that gold could be entirely stripped away and annihilated over time. This is an absurd thing to say and truly false in practice. Because yellow gold must not vanish, just as it cannot; unlike what happens to other combustible metals. Indeed, let this delusion be far from the minds of those practicing philosophy: that yellow gold could in any way be destroyed.

<margin>Note</margin>
It should also be known that every cementation significantly increases the weight of the gold itself because of the salt entering it through the melting of the fire. This salt is hot and dry (as is well known) and enters through the pores of the gold, which are opened by the heat and dryness of the fire itself. The salt is never removed from the gold by the opposite—that is, by the humidity and coldness of elemental water—because water does not open the pores that have already been "intoxicated" <note>saturated or filled</note> by the salt, even with the washing and boiling of the water (which, though unnecessary, is nonetheless permitted).

<margin>Note</margin>
It must be noted, therefore, that such gold is not accepted as a sufficient result unless, after the cementation itself (for which the furnace is described immediately hereafter), careful attention is given to a proper melting. This ensures that the salt, along with the dross <note>original: "scobibus lopæ"; the scale or impurities</note> floating on top during the melting, is entirely removed from the gold.

<meta>This page continues the description of the "First Matter" of Voarchadumia, which the previous page identified as being white and dense. It now specifies its composition from three types of salts and provides its various names across different languages and traditions.</meta>

# FIRST [MATTER].

It consists of three very white salts: namely, animal, mineral, and vegetable. These are extracted from specific solid materials—that is, those composed of fire, air, water, and earth—existing within the four natural elements of all formed things <note>original: "elementatorum"; things composed of the four elements</note> which are found in earthly mixtures <note>original: "sublunaribus mistis"; substances found in the realm below the moon</note>: excepting only quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and any metal.

<margin>Epithet.</margin>
And although it is named differently by different people (as Eleazar says in the primary and true language, which is described as the one, perfect, and immediate medicine of metals: the "Help of God," or more truly the "Assembly of God Raised Up"), the Fathers of hidden wisdom agree with us: among the Chaldeans and Arabs, however, it is called in Arabic *Alicali*, or *Calopali*. This word is composed from *ali* (which is "highest") and *calop* (which signifies "good"), so that in Latin it is called the "Highest Good."

<margin>Action.</margin>
This first matter of the art naturally prepares, converts, constrains, binds, and proportions every <term>calx</term> <note>a powder produced by roasting an ore or metal</note>, ore, and metallic body, or volatile spirit. It is supplied and prepared in the following manner.

<margin>Preparation</margin>
The formative, constraining, continuous, and oily or viscous virtue is extracted from a drop of five hundred and four pounds of white living and fresh fire, with seventy-two pounds of celestial water. Once purified by the evaporation of sufficient fire in a solid earthen pot, these salts are converted into the likeness of liquefied oil.

Then, by the fire of continuous <term>reverberation</term> <note>a furnace where the flame is "thrown back" or reflected onto the material</note> in the furnace, this gathered substance is kept for a night and a day in the best pot made of Valencia earth. ### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Measurement of the balance.</margin> We say that a balance scale <note>original: *Aequilancem* or *Bilancem*; terms for a two-pan scale based on the concept of "equal sides"</note> is composed of a perfect square and a half. The length of its beam <note>original: *Fusti*; the horizontal bar of the scale</note> measures exactly as much as one side of that same square. The thickness of the middle and the ends has a "sesquialter" <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2</term> proportion, specifically three to two. The needle of the scale—also called the "invisible"—rises from the base above the axis, positioned exactly in the middle between the ends; it stands upright at the top like a pyramid. It tapers from three units down to one minute <note>a "minute" here refers to a small unit of geometric measurement</note> and extends to the size of half a square (namely, thirty-three minutes). The yoke, which grips the scale on both sides of the axis, should have the same width as the "invisible" needle itself, and the bracket <note>original: *Bracha*</note> located at the lower part of the yoke should be one-eighth the length of the scale itself. Finally, the strings hanging from the ends of the beam to the pans <note>original: *Conchas*; literally "shells," referring to the weighing cups</note> are, together with the pans themselves, of the same dimension as the side of the square. ## *Description of various specific operations for the further elucidation of this art.*
# CHAPTER IX.

### Burned copper with an image of its furnace.

<margin>G.</margin>
Take one part of copper <note>original: *Cupri*</note>, two parts of alum or tartar, and three parts of arsenic. Let the latter two be joined together and reduced to powder with an iron pestle in a bronze mortar. Then, having been sprinkled with water, let them be placed in a jar layered with "Venus" <note>original: *Venere*; the alchemical name for copper</note> that has been drawn out into thin sheets <note>original: *bracteas*</note>. This jar, with its lid perforated at the top to the thickness of a fine reed, should then be very well sealed with common and simple clay. Let the mixture be cooked for an hour in the fire, or a sublimation furnace. Then, once it is extracted and cooled, place the mixture again in a clay melting pot—the image of which, along with the furnace, is expressed here immediately following—and let it be melted among the coals. Let the dross be cleaned away with an iron rod until it shines. Finally, let it be poured from the melting pot into an iron instrument called a channel, or a *rielum* <note>original: *Rielum*; a casting mold or ingot groove</note>, and be kept once cooled.

### Roasted copper.

What we previously said should be done regarding "burned" copper, we judge should also be done to obtain "roasted" copper <note>original: *Aes vstum*</note>, providing the mixture for it in this sequence:

Take one part of copper, two parts of Roman vitriol <note>original: *Calcantis Romani*; likely copper sulfate</note> (or salt), and three parts of sulfur. Let all the rest be heated <margin>G.</margin> as in the previous instructions.

### White and black niello.

Finally, once this whole mass is cooled and thoroughly purified of dross through melting, let it be kept in the form of small rods.

### Water for separating silver from gold.

Take equal parts of refined saltpeter <note>original: *Nitro refecto*</note> and alum.

Once joined in equal measure and pulverized together in a mortar, let them be distilled through a well-sealed retort <note>original: *Tortam*</note> over an open fire until the total exhalation of the spirits, keeping a vent-hole in the seal for the appropriate moment.

Let this "water of separation" <note>this refers to nitric acid, or *aqua fortis*, which dissolves silver but leaves gold intact</note> be "discalcined" by fire, also using six carats of pure silver for every pound of the aforementioned water, and let it be kept for use.

H.

### Calx of silver and gold.

Take three parts and three-quarters by weight of copper <note>original: *Æris*</note>. Then take one part and one-quarter of calamine <term>Zelamina: a zinc ore used in making brass</term> found in the Syrian valley in a village called Oneda. This calamine is otherwise called white tutty <note>original: *Tuthia alba*; a crude zinc oxide collected from furnace flues</note>, and it is a mineral from Bergamo. Let these be spread in layers in a crucible and melted with glass by a continuous twelve-hour fire. Let the mixture be kept for use, having first been cast into sheets and thoroughly cleaned of all dross.

<meta>catchword: Calx</meta>

Take silver <note>original: *Arg.* / *Argentum*</note> beaten into thin sheets, and in an unglazed earthen pot, let it burn in a furnace for 18 days with one part of crushed sulfur. Every three days, add fresh sulfur. Afterward, let it be macerated by long grinding in a stone mortar <note>original: *Potsido*; likely a phonetic variation of the Italian *pozzetto* or a specific type of grinding vessel</note> with six parts of mercury <note>original: *Argenti viui*</note> that has been slightly warmed. Let it be washed with water and, when well dried, kept in a very clean glass or glazed vessel.

### Macerated Gold.

Let sheets of yellow gold drawn out to great thinness and heated to glowing be macerated together with six parts of mercury. Finally, wash the macerated mass with water, and once well dried, let it be kept for use, just as was said above regarding the silver.

### Boiling solution for Silver.

Take 10 pounds of "heavenly water" <note>original: *Aqua cælesti*; typically refers to distilled rainwater, valued for its purity in chemical processes</note> and 1 pound 3 ounces of crushed white tartar <term>Tartar: a salty crust found in wine barrels, used here as an acidic cleaning agent</term>.

Place the silver works themselves—which have been blackened by the fire—into a bronze vessel. Let everything boil together until the pieces become as white as snow. Then, once extracted, let them be plunged <note>original: *brustientur*; likely related to quenching or vigorous rinsing</note> into clear, cold water. Finally, let them be polished and maintained with ivory Tripoli <note>original: *Tripoli eburnita*; a fine powdered earth used for polishing</note>.

### Boiling solution for Gold.

Take 10 pounds of human urine <note>original: *Lotio hominis*; widely used in pre-modern metallurgy for its ammonia content, which helps clean and color metals</note>:
Five ounces of sulfur,
10 ounces of tartar.

Let all these be mixed and crushed in a bronze vessel. Place the gold works into this, having first heated them in the fire, and let them boil until they are rendered as golden-yellow as orpiment <term>Auripigmentum: a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment</term>. Let all the remaining steps be followed properly according to the previous order described for silver.

<margin>Note.</margin> It should be noted, however, that one part of verdigris <note>original: *Floris æris*; literally "flower of copper"</note> with an equal part of Roman vitriol <note>original: *Calcantis romani*; blue copper sulfate</note>, and two parts of saltpeter with an equal part of sal ammoniac <term>Sal armoniaci: ammonium chloride, used to deepen the color of gold</term>, all boiled together with the aforementioned urine as described, gives gold a most vivid color, exceeding 18 carats.

<margin>Note.</margin> The same result is achieved by reducing the aforementioned simple ingredients into a paste <note>original: *bitumē*</note> with very sharp vinegar—namely the verdigris, Roman vitriol, saltpeter, and sal ammoniac—by way of a "re-cooking" process.

<summary>This page details the chemical preparation of silver and gold powders using mercury and sulfur, as well as "boiling" recipes (blanching baths) to clean and enhance the color of finished precious metal objects. The use of substances like tartar, urine, and vitriol highlights the transition from traditional craft to early chemical science.</summary>
<keywords>metallurgy, alchemy, silver calx, gold maceration, blanching gold, verdigris, saltpeter, vitriol, orpiment, workshop recipes</keywords>

->FIRST<-

### Silver Calx.
Proceed as was described above. Take silver <note>original: *Arg.* / *Argentum*</note> beaten into thin sheets, and so forth.

### Calx of Iron, and of all other hard metals.
With sheets or plates of any hard metal <note>original: *metalli duri*</note> burning in a cementation furnace for twenty-two days, combined with two parts of Roman Vitriol <term>Roman Vitriol: a sulfate of copper or iron, used here as a reactive agent</term> and three parts of crushed sulfur—or even without any other mixture—an impalpable metallic powder <term>Calx: a fine, crumbly powder produced by heating a metal or mineral to its breaking point</term> is created.

### White Lead, Red Lead, and Yellow Pigment.
Let sheets of soft black lead <note>original: *Plumbi nigri*</note> be suspended in an earthen vessel, the bottom of which is glazed only up to four fingers deep and filled with very sharp vinegar. They should be hung so that they are continuously touched by the vapor of the vinegar for twenty-two days. Once the essence of the black lead is corrupted and reduced to a white powder, it is called Ceruse <term>Ceruse: white lead, a common white pigment in the Renaissance, though highly toxic</term>.

This Ceruse—the residue of burnt black lead as described above—should be ground very finely with water and placed in long earthen trays <note>original: *Capellis*; small shallow vessels or cupels</note> measuring about a cubit in length. These are not sealed with clay but are kept covered in a furnace, positioned so that the fire only strikes their bottom but does not swirl back over them <note>original: *reuerberationē*; the reflection or "reverberation" of heat</note>. Let it burn for 48 hours. During this time, the residue should be frequently stirred with an iron tool until it turns a red color; at that point, the name is changed, and it is no longer called Ceruse, but Minium <term>Minium: red lead, used as a vibrant red pigment</term>. If this is ground again with white vinegar and dried in the shade, it turns into a lemon-yellow color, which is *Zololino* <note>original: *Zalolinum*; a yellow lead-based pigment, often known in art history as Giallorino</note>.

### The Construction of Cinnabar.
One part Quicksilver <note>original: *Argenti viui*</note>.
One and a half parts Sulfur, melted over a slow charcoal fire.

Let them be mixed in an open bronze vessel using an iron tool, never a wooden one. Once this mixture has hardened in the cold and been crushed, let it be placed in a suitable glass vessel that is well-sealed with protective clay <term>Lutatum: sealed with "lute," a paste used to make laboratory vessels airtight and heat-resistant</term>. Place it in a sublimation furnace with the bottom exposed and the area open to the air for 14 hours over a low fire, cleaning away any oiliness with an iron rod until it passes through the neck of the vessel. Then, for an equal amount of time, let it be fixed with an intense fire, with the vessel covered by iron plates. Finally, once the vessel has cooled, let it be broken to retrieve the Cinnabar <term>Cinnabar: a bright red mercury sulfide used as a pigment (vermilion) and in alchemy</term>.

### Stabilizer for the Cupel.
Take one measured part of burnt clay, finely crushed. Add two parts of ashes that have been drained in lye, neutralized <note>original: *mortificati*; "killed" or rendered chemically inactive</note>, and dried. Then, after sifting both together, let them be heated together.

## The Cupel, and its Furnace.

Take one part by measure of raw clay powder. Take four and a half parts of finely crushed *spodium* <term>Spodium: a powder produced by burning bone or the horns of castrated animals (ash), essential for absorbing impurities in metal refining</term> made from burnt bones or horns.
Let these be carefully sifted and kept; then, after being moistened with water, let the whole mixture be pressed together into a metal mold.

<margin>Note.</margin>
It must be noted, however, that whoever fashions a Cupel <term>Cupel: a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals like gold and silver from base metals like lead</term> from *spodium* alone does not have the best judgment for the merchant regarding the extraction of silver and gold. Therefore, for a greater and safer yield of metal, and to ensure the least amount of loss, let the Refiners of metals, Goldsmiths, and Mint-Masters <note>original: *Cudimiæ Mercatores*</note> pay heed to this secret. For their knowledge, we also provide here the Furnace for cupellation.

## Flower of Copper.

Let 640 lbs. of green earth be incorporated with 240 lbs. of very sharp vinegar, along with 26 lbs. and 8 oz. of Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux and in the preparation of pigments</term>, and 160 lbs. of copper dissolved in 320 lbs. of parting water <term>Parting water: usually nitric acid, used to separate (or "part") silver from gold</term>.
When all these things are thoroughly mixed, let them be placed in large, unglazed, scattered pots and pressed down by adding more on top. Then, let them be kept in very thick leather bags.

## Metalline.

Take equal weights of the powders of the simple ingredients listed below, namely: Realgar <term>Realgar: a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, or Orpiment <term>Orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> (otherwise known as Arsenic), fresh white quicklime, and white tartar. Add a half part or more of chicken egg whites, with which the powders themselves—having first been thoroughly mixed through a well-covered sieve—are to be incorporated.
<margin>Lute of wool.</margin>
Then, this kind of bitumen <note>original: *bitumē*; here meaning a thick paste or bonding agent</note> is placed in a suitable glass vessel <note>original: *Botia*</note> and sublimated <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form on a cooler surface</term> for 12 hours over a rising fire. The bottom of the vessel, however, should be smeared up to the middle with a "lute" <note>original: *luto*; a protective sealing paste</note> made of wool or shearings and clay—specifically two parts clay and one part wool—and the mouth of the vessel likewise stopped with cotton or oakum. At last, you will find the "Metalline" adhering to the neck of the vessel, possessing a silver color.

## Oil of all metals.

See (as above, under H) the section on Parting Water, near the end.

## Silver and Gold Purpurine.

A mixture of mercury <note>original: *Arg. viui* / *Argentum vivum*</note>, marcasite or tin, arsenic, and sal ammoniac in equal parts, if placed in a glass vessel and cooked for 32 hours over a fire, will be colored with a silver hue. But if, in place of arsenic, yellow sulfur in a clean cake <note>original: *in pane nitido*</note> is used, it will be tinged with a golden color, and then it shall be called "Golden Purpurine" <term>Purpurina: a metallic pigment or "bronze powder" used to imitate gold or silver finishes</term>.

### Refining of Chrysocolla.

In 270 lbs of refiltered rainwater <term>Aquæ cæleſtis: literally "celestial water," referring to collected rainwater, prized for its purity</term>, take 90 lbs of the paste or stone of Chrysocolla <term>Chryſocolla: historically a term for various green copper minerals used as pigments or as "gold-glue" for soldering</term>, along with 10 lbs of Alum and 8 lbs 4 oz of the dregs of Alum of the same weight. Let these be liquefied in a bronze vessel by the steady, continuous evaporation of fire until they are as thin as water. Then, cover the vessel perfectly with woolen cloths so that it cannot breathe or vent in any way; let the vessel be placed in a steady location for three days to cool. The Borax <note>The author here identifies the refined chrysocolla as a form of "Borax," which in this period often referred to any flux used in soldering</note> that has attached itself to the sides of the vessel should then be pulled away (once the water has been carefully poured off by tilting). After being washed in cold water and thoroughly dried in the sun until shining and oily with raw linseed oil, it should be weighed and kept in a clean vessel.

### Third Solder for Silver & Gold.

Take three parts of Silver for Silver, or Gold for Gold. And take one part of burnt copper <term>Æris arſi: copper that has been roasted or oxidized</term> for Silver, or one part of Silver for Gold. Once an excellent mixture has first been made in the melting furnace, let the resulting plates be kept.

<margin>1.</margin>
### Fragile Metallic Mirrors.

After remelting three parts of copper and one part of tin, let the plates be cast onto a flat surface and a small bridge in dove-colored stone <note>original: *petra columbina*, likely a type of fine-grained gray marble or slate</note>, one overhanging the other. This mixture must first be melted in a blast furnace <note>original: *ignem venti*, literally "fire of the wind"</note>. Then, the plates should be leveled to measure and trimmed of excess with a blade. They are to be smoothed with medium and fine emery <term>Smerillo: a dense mineral substance used as an abrasive for grinding and polishing</term>, polished dry along the length and across. This is done first on wooden blocks where the mirrors are glued with raw gypsum and water. Afterward, let them be polished with a coarse linen cloth or the inner side of leather, using bone ash <note>Spodium</note>, Tripoli <term>Tripoli: a fine-grained weathered limestone used as a polishing powder</term>, and white lead or "tin-ash" <note>tin oxide</note>, though they must first be sprinkled with oil. Finally, they should be wiped with the dry palms of the hands, polished until bright, and stored in cases.

### Unbreakable Mirrors.

Unbreakable mirrors of any dimension are made by hammering the remaining material (following the process described just above in Note 1), except for the underlying substance, which consists solely of cupelled silver <term>Arg. cupellato: silver refined in a cupel to be extremely pure and malleable</term>.

### Bone Ash (Spodium).

Shinbones of oxen, burned in a continuous fire in a cementing furnace for two hours, are called *Spodium* of bones.

### ->*Earth for silvering and gilding metal.*<-

**S**ilver dissolved by fire from the cupel <note>A shallow, porous cup used in refining to separate precious metals from lead</note>. Take one ounce of this into one ounce of <term>aquæ diuisionis: "Water of separation," usually referring to nitric acid, used to separate silver from gold</term>, and let it be joined with six ounces each of powdered salt and <term>Tartari albi: White tartar, the acidic sediment found in wine casks</term>.

And so, let this "earth" <note>Here, "earth" refers to a prepared paste or powder</note>, thickened by heat, be kept mixed in a glazed vessel with a wooden spatula (but not a metallic one).

<margin>Note well.</margin>
It should also be noted that this same order must be strictly followed in preparing the "earth" for gilding: which, having been set apart from the water of separation and the silver, should be moistened with <term>oleo auri: "Oil of gold," likely gold chloride or a similar chemical solution of gold</term>, specifically one ounce for every pound of the aforementioned powders.

### ->*The construction of Tutty.*<-
<note>Tutty was a substance, often zinc oxide, collected from the flues of smelting furnaces and used in both metallurgy and medicine.</note>

Take 48 lbs. of <term>Calce silicis: Lime of flint, produced by heating flint until it can be powdered</term>. 24 lbs. of <term>alumine catino: Potash or soda ash, a salt derived from plant ashes</term>. 1 lb. and 4 oz. of burnt copper. Of lead and tin calcinated together, 8 lbs.: specifically, for every one part of lead, use two parts of tin.

Let all these be incorporated together with water and ground in a potter’s mortar. Then, the mixture taken from here—having been dried like a cake on a flat surface strewn with bran—should be cooked in a charcoal fire for one hour; afterwards, let it be crushed, ground, and sifted. From the finer powder, let a "bitumen" <note>A thick, sticky paste or cement</note> be made with egg whites, and let the same be wrapped around iron rods, sprinkled with the coarser powder of the same, and thus, having been dried in the shade, let it be baked again for an hour by a <term>ignem reuerberationis: A reverberatory fire, where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material being heated</term>.

<margin>Note well.</margin>
Whenever it becomes too black: let the rods coated with the paste as described above be quenched while glowing hot in lime water of lead and tin, as was said above. K.

->Why the preceding special preparations were included.<-

## CHAPTER TEN

Let no one think that these specific items—namely, the <term>water of parting: nitric acid used to separate gold from silver, known as aqua diuisionis</term>, the refining of <term>chrysocolla: borax or a similar flux used in soldering gold</term>, <term>burnt copper: copper oxide used in metallic recipes, known as aes arsum</term>, calcined materials, and the other specifics mentioned above—were placed here at random, as if they were foreign to the main business or entirely superfluous. For they were not included in vain; indeed, they are necessary steps, as if by certain degrees, toward the perfection of this mastery of the <term>purification of Gold: the process of refining gold to its highest purity</term> (as is obvious to anyone with an eye for such things). For just as a tree indicates a fertile and abundant harvest of fruit by its flowers, and wherever smoke exhales there must be a fire, so too are these exercises both signs and certainties of the efficacy and truth of what has come before. Furthermore, they serve as a target upon which the false professors of this art (commonly called Alchemists) strike and are immediately broken and revealed in confusion. Thus, with their fraud and falsehood exposed and removed, the simple may be made safe and more cautious.

## CHAPTER ONE

<image-desc>A faint, large schematic engraving of an armillary sphere or celestial globe is visible in the background of the lower half of the page. It depicts several circular bands representing meridians and the ecliptic, overlaid with a grid of coordinates.</image-desc>

O most kind reader, it might have been better for us to skip over this crude and unpolished investigation of ours, rather than allow such a sublime art—the remarkable rival of Mother Nature herself—to be disclosed to mortals even in a faint whisper (especially contrary to the decrees of the authors of this science, who prohibit publication, where it is said to be a sin <note>original: "nefas," a divine or moral prohibition</note> to reveal secrets to the unworthy). 

<margin>Raymundus [Lullus] in the *Apertorium*, chapter 2: "Art therefore..."</margin>
Yet, since we have convinced ourselves that we have come to know the power of almighty nature, inspired by the supreme divine will of the Son of Wisdom (even though it remains hidden from most mortals), we deemed it a sin and entirely contrary to human duty to keep it forever locked in darkness as a gift from God. This is especially true since nothing more excellent or more useful in human affairs can be found or even imagined, provided it is revealed to the <term>Sages: the "Sophis" or wise philosophers of the art</term> who are elevated far above these falling and fleeting things. Furthermore, the more obscure and difficult to know this matter has been considered until now, the more lucid and plain we shall make it for everyone. For the reason that the <term>Schema: the plan or diagram of the work</term> was set forth as an enigma was so that the detractor Alchemists—the unworthy and the ungrateful—might not think they have an easy path to these mysteries. However, to the initiated, the whole logic of this art in a compendium will...

### Explanation of the Voarchadumic Diagram.
## CHAPTER TWO

<margin>Ramon [Lull] in the Codex, chapter 4: "Since therefore..."</margin>
It is read in the *Secret of Secrets* <note>original: "arcanis arcanorum"</note> that a vision received from the eternal, omnipotent Lord should not be made public to the unworthy, because the Lord is entirely to be feared. Nevertheless, we say that the letters **A**, **V**, and **E** (as mentioned in the preceding sections) represent a mixture of an equal weight of "oil of glass" <note>original: "olei vitri"; likely a highly refined flux or acidic distillate</note>, the primary matter of the art, air, and fire, the greater and lesser light, along with quicksilver <term>quicksilver: Latin "argentum vivum," the metal mercury</term> purified seven times through sublimation with white sand, and at the same time turned red <note>original: "rubificatam"; a reference to the "rubedo" or reddening stage, the final goal of the alchemical Great Work</term>.

<margin>Synonyms.</margin>
**C**, however, represents the first motion—that is, killing, corruption, calcination, or putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the decomposition of a substance, seen as the necessary "death" before spiritual rebirth</term>.

<margin>Synonyms.</margin>
**G** is the second motion, which is generation. **H** is the third motion, namely augmentation. **D** is called fixation, diminution, disjunction, or separation, and it is the fourth motion. **F** and **B** are the elements that cause alteration through a change of place, which are called the transformation of fire: the "work of the floor," and the completion of the reddening; this is the fifth motion.

---

### *The theory and practice of the Voarchadumic art, etc.*
### *The use of the diagram in the multiplication of the tincture.*
## CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>Gold [Metube lim].</margin>
The completion of the recipients is the transformation of the natures of the things received through an ineffable mixture of the hot (that is, of fire, *lim* <note>a term for gold or light in this specific alchemical dialect</note>, which is tawny gold) with the cold (that is, non-vulgar quicksilver, which is quicksilver purified seven times by fire and white sand, as was said regarding quicksilver). This is combined with the moist (that is, Air: which is pure silver, along with tawny gold and quicksilver as described above, simultaneously reddened) and with the dry (that is, oil of glass) in a perpetual disposition. This perpetual disposition is the matter of metals and the primary matter of the art (that is, glass that cannot be annihilated, which is the aforementioned oil: a medium that retains quicksilver and whitens gold) as Matia says. And this is the "heavy water" <note>original: "aqua grauis"</note> which is called "mercurial," as everyone asserts.

And it is the quicksilver of the wise (that is, quicksilver, as mentioned, purified from common quicksilver), of which Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "Guard this coagulated (that is, purified) quicksilver, which is in the innermost chambers where it was coagulated." For it is itself *Azoch* <term>Azoch: an alchemical name for the universal spirit or the mercury of the philosophers</term>; it is the "secret of Scotland" <note>original: "secretum Scotiæ"; possibly referring to the alchemical secrets of Michael Scot</note>, and it is called the "residual earth." Therefore, let him who hears these words investigate them himself. But we testify by Him who justifies the evildoer and [condemns] no one acting rightly...

<margin>The Selection,</margin>
...condemns: we have now revealed whatever we previously concealed in this wisdom: we have opened both the greatest secret of the sciences and the intellect to those who possess it. Therefore, whoever wishes to progress in this wisdom must compose this miraculous **Selection** (the cleansing, mixing, grinding, and calcining of Silver, Gold, Quicksilver, and "oil of glass" <note>original: "olei vitri"; likely a highly refined flux or acidic distillate</note>) or "greatest secret" <note>original: "arcanum maximum"</note>, and afterward change it from nature to nature: as Lucas says in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, "you do not need many things, but only one thing." And that one thing, in each single grade of our works, is converted into another nature. Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note> testifies to the same when he says:
<margin>Note, however, that there is another primary matter of the art.</margin>
Such an Art does not consist in a plurality of things. For there is one matter (that is, of metals) in which our mastery consists: to which we add no foreign thing, nor do we take anything away, except that in its preparation we remove what is superfluous.
<margin>Note.</margin>
The whole of this mastery consists, therefore, in one thing—as we rightly judge—namely in "oil of glass" and pure, animated, and reddened Quicksilver <note>original: "Arg. [Argento] vivo mundo, animato, rubificatoque"; "animated" usually implies the mercury has been "awakened" or prepared to receive a new form</note>. And Alphidius <note>an Arab alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note> says this expressly to his son: "Know, son, that there is a matter (and the primary matter of the art) which is the root, about which all the wise have treated; it is (oil of glass, and) Quicksilver." And there is a certain Quicksilver of a white color, more shining than a mirror. The same is reported in the *Assembly*: "The beginning of the whole operation is the Whiteness <note>original: "Albedo"; the second major stage of the alchemical process, representing purification</note>, that is, pure animated Quicksilver, which is succeeded by redness."

<margin>Note. †</margin>
You will note, therefore, that: Vinegar <note>original: "Acetum"</note>, Balanced <note>original: "Aequatum"</note>, Whiteness, White lead, Holy water (metallic, dry, of talc, living, viscous of life, urine of boys), animated Quicksilver, coagulated [Quicksilver], Living silver <note>original: "Argyrion zoticon"; from the Greek "argyrion zōtikon"</note>, arsenic, orpiment, *azoch* <note>a term for Mercury</note>, *cambar*, *caspa chaia*, Living silver <note>original: "ches seph chai"; Hebrew "kesef chai"</note>, *compar*, Heart of Saturn, December, **E**, Euphrates, the west wind, phlegm, White gum, the enemy, the tasteless, the slippery, the one matter of metals, the one medicine, the menstruum, Mercury, the west, the egg, the false boy, *sedena*, old age, *serinech*, Seth, the left hand, the companion, the sperm of metals, the sublimated, the juice, *teuōs*, the wind, the evening, twenty-one, the anointed, the vulture, *zibách*, and *ziuá*—all signify the same thing. And there are many of that kind, which we omit here for the sake of avoiding prolixity.

<image-desc>A small woodcut illustration consisting of a double-lined square frame containing the alchemical symbol for Antimony or Earth: a circle topped with a cross.</image-desc>

In the composition of this admirable mixture, or greatest secret, it is necessary for us to follow nature: For (as Geber says) Nature acts by itself. We, therefore, must know three things: namely, what nature is, how many natures there are, and in what manner nature works in the produced metals.
