<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of alchemical materials, transitioning from the general definitions of the "Great Work" to specific Aristotelian and Hermetic definitions of nature and the elements. It follows the previous page's list of synonyms for the primary matter by narrowing down the specific qualities—heat, moisture, cold, and dryness—required for the perfect metallic "balance" found in Gold.</meta>

<page-num>601</page-num>
<header>SECOND PART</header>

<margin>What nature is.</margin>
According to Aristotle (in the second book of his *Physics* <note>original: "Physicę auscultationis," referring to Aristotle's lectures on nature</note>), nature is defined thus: Nature is a principle and a cause of motion and of rest in that in which it exists primarily and by itself, and not by accident.

<margin>How it is divided.</margin>
The author of the perfect mastery <note>magistery: the successful completion of an alchemical process</note> says: the natures (or if you prefer to call them qualities) are four: namely Heat and Dryness, as in fire; Heat and Moisture, as in air; Moisture and Coldness, as in water; and Coldness and Dryness, as in earth. However, all these temperaments <note>complexions or mixtures of qualities</note> are unequal, and none of these is what we seek. For we seek the equal one, of which Johannicius <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a 9th-century physician and translator influential in medieval science</note> says: that an equal mixture is one where, through moderation, the body is said to be unharmed <note>original: "incolume"</note>.

<margin>Moderation.</margin>
You will note, therefore, that he says "with moderation"—namely, of the aforementioned natures or qualities: heat, moisture, cold, and dryness. For when none of these natures exceeds another, then the body is said to be temperate and equal, because there is as much of one as there is of another, according to the proper proportion of qualities required for the existence of a metal.

<margin>Synonyms. The first key. Cleansing.</margin>
Likewise, you will note that "unharmed" is also called healthy, distant, calcined, separated, purified, prepared, dry, or clean from every cause of corruption. And (according to Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy</note>) the **Key** is tin or the purest white lead <note>alchemical term for tin</note>. In it, there is an equality of fixation or thickness of the two components: Quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and (metallic) sulfur; however, this is not an equality in terms of the mixture (that is, the quantity) of the Quicksilver.

Likewise, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says: "Sons of the wise, there are six metals" (for Quicksilver is not a metal, but the matter of metals, as you will note under the section for "Embryo" and elsewhere). Of these metals, the first is Gold <note>original: "Sol" (The Sun)</note>, their best king and head. Neither the earth corrupts it, nor does a burning thing consume it, nor does water (whether coloring, green, or dividing <note>referring to corrosive acids like *aqua fortis*</note>) mortify or devour it. This is because its substance is perfectly bounded and its nature is balanced in heat, moisture, cold, and dryness. 

There is nothing superfluous in it, nor is anything lacking. For this reason, the wise have preferred it and magnified it, saying that Gold is among the metals as the Sun is among the stars. For by its light and splendor all plants sprout, and all fruits are perfected by the will of God. What more is there to say if we can attain this? We have the proportion of nearly the whole thing, according to Socrates, who said: "Now therefore, the arrangement of white lead..."

<meta>This page continues the transition from defining Nature to explaining its mechanics. While the previous page established the four qualities (heat, cold, etc.) that constitute the elements, this page introduces "Mixture" as the Second Key of the alchemical art, relying heavily on Aristotle’s physics and the legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</meta>

<page-num>602</page-num>
<header>PORTION</header>

...I have shown to you, which once produced is nothing other than **women’s work and children’s play** <note>original: "opus mulierum, & ludus puerorum." A common alchemical aphorism meaning that once the "First Matter" is found, the rest of the process is easy or requires only gentle, steady heat.</note>.

Therefore, having recognized what nature is through the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, and its fourfold character through the author of the perfect mastery <note>the *Magisterium*</note> and the opinions of other wise men, it remains to see how nature operates.

<margin>
How nature operates. Synonyms.
</margin>
Nature operates in many ways: but most especially through **mixture**, which the wise have called by various names: namely, Ingress, submersion, conjunction, connection, complexion, composition, and mixture—all signifying the same thing. For nothing "enters," is "submerged," "joined," "connected," "embraced," or "composed," unless it is **mixed**.

<margin>
The Second Key.
</margin>
Let us see, therefore, what mixture is (for it is the **Second Key**), because once mixture is understood through its definition, all other things may be known.

<margin>
Mixture, and what it is.
</margin>
According to the Philosopher (in the first book of *On Generation* <note>Aristotle's "De Generatione et Corruptione"</note>), mixture is the union of altered mixable things joined at their **smallest parts** <note>original: "per minima." This refers to the theory of *minima naturalia*, the smallest possible particles of a substance that still maintain its essence, similar to the concept of atoms.</note>.

<margin>
Mixables.
</margin>
You will note "Mixables," that is, the **elements**. For these are the first principles of every mixture. But we cannot know the manifest or hidden nature of the mixture itself unless we know how to mingle or compose the elements themselves. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founding figure of alchemy</note> says:
> Understand, my son, the science of the four elements, which are placed by their own reasons in their hidden appearance. For their hidden appearance is by no means revealed unless they are composed, because they are not perfected until they are colored with their own colors.

<margin>
The Minimum.
</margin>
You will also note "at their smallest parts," that is, through **indivisible parts**. For if a thing could be divided, it would no longer be the "minimum" <note>the smallest</note>, since from that division even smaller parts would come forth, as every part is smaller than its whole. It appears, therefore, that the mixture of elements occurs through these smallest parts, that is, through indivisibles. And that the element is the "minimum" of the 
<margin>
Definition of an element.
</margin>
component metals is clear through its definition: for an **Element** is the smallest particle of a metal.

<margin>
The First Motion: The Third Key and the first point. Corruption.
</margin>
For this purpose, however—so that the mixable things may be mixed—a prior arrangement is required, which does not happen except through **motion**, which is necessary in every action, not least in mixture. Now, motion (or change) is said to be sixfold (according to Aristotle in the *Categories*): namely, **corruption**, **generation**, **increase**, **decrease** (which we call **fixation**), **alteration**, and **change of place**. But omitting the others for the present, let us choose only **Corruption**: and yet not even all parts of it. For it has many species under it.

<summary>This page defines the "Second Key" of alchemy as Mixture, using Aristotelian physics to explain that substances combine at the level of their smallest indivisible parts (minima). It introduces the role of the four elements and identifies "Corruption" as the first necessary motion to begin the transformation of metals.</summary>

<header>-> THE SECOND <-</header>

...[Nature] possesses. But out of these, we shall discuss the one which is called **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactio"</note>, as it serves our purpose.

For Nature, which never ceases to arise, uses every kind of motion in its work: and first of all, **corruption**. Here, "corruption" and "putrefaction" are equal in meaning. Concerning this, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says in his allegory: "Know that the origin of the artifice is the **Raven's Head** <note>original: "caput Corvi"; the stage of *Nigredo* or blackening</note>: which flies without wings in the blackness of night and the brightness of day. From our bitterness exiting in its blood, coloration is received, and pure water from its back." Therefore, the Raven's Head is nothing other than the blackness of night; for just as these things are black and dark in respect to the day, so is this putrefied spirit in respect to the **pure spirit** <note>original: "spiritus mundus"; here "mundus" functions as an adjective meaning clean or purified</note>, which arises from putrefaction and is extracted through our art.

<margin>
Question. Solution.
</margin>
But of what color should this pure spirit be? Truly, white. Whence Hermes says: "Know, seekers of reports and sons of wisdom, that the **Vulture** <note>original: "Vultur"</note> stretched upon the mountain peak cries out in a loud voice, saying: I am the White of the black, the Yellow of the white, and the Red of the yellow; I am certainly truthful and do not lie."

Note, therefore, "the white of the black." For we extract the white itself from the black. Likewise Alphidius <note>A famous, though semi-legendary, Arabic alchemist</note>: "The **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, which is extracted from that black bark, is a white moisture cleaned of its husks, lest the work perish."

<margin>
The White of the black.
Two principles.
</margin>
Having seen, therefore, that the first movement of nature is to corrupt, we must see how it is done. To know how to do this perfectly, we must have knowledge of the principles, both natural and artificial. For those who are ignorant of the principles do not find the end.

<margin>
The First.
</margin>
We call the first natural principle, as stated before, **Quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, which has been purified seven times from the quicksilver with white sand through fire, and coagulated. It contains the materials of fire and air under the names **Antybar**, **Marthek**, **Tin**, or **Risoo**—which is called **Will** in Greek <note>original: "Thelima" / "θέλημα"</note> and **Desire** in Hebrew <note>original: "Reçon" / "רָצוֹן"</note>. It is placed in marked letters and numbers (as seen here below and above), beginning from the second-to-last through a perpendicular line, ascending upward, and ending at the last.

E. 5. Greater Light <note>original: "Lux maior"</note>.
H. 8. Coagulum <note>A thickening agent or curdling</note>.
T. 19. Fire, that is, Greater Light.
R. 17. Air, that is, Lesser Light <note>original: "Lux minor"</note>.

<margin>The second.</margin>
The second principle is **Heat**, that is, **External Fire** <note>original: "Ignis alienus"; literally "foreign fire," referring to heat applied from outside the vessel, such as a furnace or bath</note>, which is the instrument that moves the mixed Matter itself toward putrefaction—and there is no other such agent in the world. Regarding this, Alphidius <note>a legendary Arab alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts</note> says: "Know, my son, that the substance acting in this entire world is one, namely heat. For if heat is taken away, there is no motion at all." Now, motion is an act. Therefore, heat—the fire—is the craftsman of the arrangement and of the entire work.

But since there are many degrees of heats, or of fire, let us see what this is and in what degree it resides.

<margin>External fire.</margin>
And certainly this fire, or heat, is a most intense fire, as Maria <note>Maria Prophetissima, or Mary the Jewess, an early alchemical authority credited with inventing the bain-marie</note> testifies: "The measure of your fire (that is, the external fire) should be like that of the Sun in the days of *Tamuz* <note>original: "tamūq" / "Tammuz"; the height of summer</note>, from the **Head of the Zenith** <note>original: "Noch ach ros" (likely a transliteration of the Hebrew 'Naso ha-Rosh'), glossed as "caput zenit"</note>." And it is called **horse dung** <note>original: "fimus equinus"; a common alchemical term for a gentle, steady heat produced by fermenting manure</note>, though it is not literally so (that is, by way of contrast), as Alphidius says: "By fire (that is, external fire) is cooked that which I shall show you." And it is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>in the medieval system of four "qualities," the fourth degree was the most intense level</note>, the property of which is to increase dryness by condensing moisture. For just as the heat of manure increases heat and moisture because of its own inherent heat and moisture, so does the strength of a hot and dry fire increase dryness. It disposes the moist nature toward a dry state by bringing it to a limit. No other fire in the world is comparable to this, except for the natural fire, which is the fire of the sun in the bowels of the earth.

<meta>This page follows a discussion on natural principles of alchemy, specifically the "Second Principle" of Heat from the previous page. <page-num>605</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>THE SECOND.</header>

Having therefore seen the natural principles, let us look at the artificial ones.

<margin>Artificial principles.</margin>
The Artificial Principles are two main instruments in which this putrefaction <note>The alchemical stage of "death" or decomposition, where the matter turns black; often called the "Raven's Head."</note> is completed. The first is the stone *Caraha* <note>original: "Caraha"; likely a corruption of the Arabic word for a glass flask or cucurbit</note>, and the second is the stone *aludel* (that is, the "horse’s belly") in which the mixed matter must be placed. Concerning this, Vincentius <note>referring to the medieval encyclopedist Vincent of Beauvais</note> says: The instruments for the solutions of bodies and spirits are many; however, one is called the "Horse’s Belly" <note>original: "Venter equi"; typically refers to a warm dung bath used for gentle, steady heat, though here it is identified with the vessel itself</note>. It is made of two vessels: one of which is the stone *aludel*, and the mixed matter is placed within it; it stands in the furnace, and the fire is nourished underneath so that it may boil. Avicenna <note>a famous Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were foundational in Europe</note> says that these arrangements cannot be made except in a recognized double-vessel, which is the "horse’s belly" vessel named above.

Likewise, since a definition signifies entirely what the essence of a thing is, let us see what the "putrefaction" of the mixed matter itself is, so that we may better understand it.

<margin>What is putrefaction? The second definition of putrefaction.</margin>
According to Johannitius <note>original: "Ioannicium"; likely Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous translator and physician</note>, putrefaction is the corruption of the substance of the mixed matter resulting from the retention of vapors. In our own work, if the vapors are dispersed through the air itself, the mixed substance of the matter neither putrefies nor is it corrupted. For this reason, the *aludel* must be so fitted with a stopper <note>original: "obice"; a barrier or seal</note> that it cannot "breathe." Or, it can be defined another way: Putrefaction is the corruption of substantial moisture, resulting from a lack of natural heat while an "external" <term>alien heat (ignis alienus)</term> <note>heat applied from the outside, such as from a furnace, as opposed to the internal heat of a living thing</note> acts upon it from the outside in superabundance.

<margin>By external heat. Question, Solution.</margin>
Note well: "by external heat in superabundance." For this external heat is the acting instrument that brings about the moist corruption.

But if it is asked: in what way does heat cause this corruption? We answer: the heat warms the mixture applied to it, and by warming, it causes the moisture to evaporate. It is by this moisture that all the dry parts were held together and made into one continuous mixture and one single thing. And so heat corrupts and putrefies the thing itself; because the mixture which was previously continuous by reason of the moisture is made discontinuous by reason of that same moisture being breathed out. It no longer persists in the substance of the mixture, just as is seen in wood placed in a fire. For the strength of the heat of that fire causes the water and oil to evaporate from the wood; it was by means of these that the wood was first a composed and continuous mixture. Now, after the evaporation of the water and oil, only ashes and dry parts remain, which are entirely disconnected and turned to powder.

<margin>Putrefaction, otherwise called ash: or calcination.</margin>
And because of this similarity, Putrefaction was called "ash" by the wise. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> rightly says: "Do not leave the quicksilver <note>original: "arg. viuum" (argentum vivum); mercury</note> to negligence; for it whitens the black ash, and the work is accomplished through the fire of the wise." Therefore

<summary>This page describes the "artificial" tools of alchemy, specifically the Caraha and Aludel (Horse’s Belly), and explains the scientific theory of putrefaction as the process of driving out moisture to reduce matter to ash.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the definition of "putrefaction" (alchemical decay) from page 605, comparing it to the process of calcination (reduction by fire) and providing signs for identifying when the process is complete.</meta>

<page-num>506</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>PORTION</header>

It was also called calcination, due to the same similarity. For just as the intensity of fire deprives a stone of its humidity and makes lime from it, so does putrefaction. Hence Parmenides in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: "Unless you transform nature, and know its compositions and complexions, and well-fit kin to kin and the first to the first, you act improperly and accomplish nothing, because natures will follow their like-natured companions and rejoice in them. For they will putrefy or be separated, because nature rules nature, which destroys it, turns it into powder, and leads it away." It appears, therefore, that through putrefaction, our matter is destroyed and led into another state of being, just as a stone is through calcination.

Now that we have seen what putrefaction is and how it happens, let us look at the signs by which we can recognize when it is perfect or not.

<margin>
Signs of putrefaction.
Qualities of mixed Mercury.
</margin>
There are indeed two principal accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are outward characteristics (like color or weight) that do not change the core essence of a thing.</note> by which we can recognize whether it is perfect or not: the color, namely black; and the touch, which is heavy. Hence the Author of the *Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "Auctor perfecti magisterii"; likely referring to the influential 13th-century chemist Pseudo-Geber</note> says: Lead—that is, mixed Mercury <note>original: "Arg. vivum" (Argentum vivum)</note>—in its depth is lead and Mercury: cold, dry, earthy, melancholic, black, withered, stinking, heavy, and feminine. From these things, therefore, it appears that putrefaction is perfect when it is black and heavy.

<margin>
Synonyms.
</margin>
You shall also note that "our Mercury," calcination, incineration, melancholy <note>In the medieval theory of humors, melancholy was associated with the element of earth, the color black, and a cold, dry temperament.</note>, and blackness mean the same thing.

<margin>
Question.
Solution.
</margin>
But you will say: what remains calcined after incineration? We respond: the essence of the mixed metallic matter, which before calcination was introduced into its potentiality by the proportion of the elements from which it was composed. For such an essence is not corrupted so as to be annihilated in any way or reduced to nothing, since it is not possible for us to destroy the underlying essence or Nature; rather, it is the quantity and the virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or specific properties that make a substance what it is.</note> that gave "being" to such a mixture that is now destroyed and calcined through the process of calcination and an external influence. This virtue and quantity, which it had received from the mixing, is indeed completely annihilated. For just as an integrated whole (for instance, a house) consists of its integrated parts joined together, and if one part is displaced from its position which it previously held in the whole, the "being" of the whole house is destroyed, yet the stones, wood, and mortar from which the house was made remain. Thus it also happens in our proposal. For when the "moist" is separated from the elementary mixture in which it inhered...

It identifies the "Black Stage" (nigredo) through signs of black color and heavy weight, citing the Turba Philosophorum and Geber.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of putrefaction and calcination, specifically addressing the "annihilation" of substances. The previous page ended while discussing the nature of mixed Mercury/Lead.</meta>

<page-num>607</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>SECOND [PART]</header>

...remained as an integral part of the whole; and through the heat that lifts it up and separates it from the other parts, the quantity of the mixture's moisture is annihilated. However, the underlying essence of that moisture is not annihilated, nor can it be annihilated.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But, you will say, experience shows the opposite. For if a pot full of water is placed on a fire, as the heat of the fire grows stronger, the water will gradually diminish by evaporating until absolutely no water remains in the pot. Therefore, has its essence not been annihilated? 

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this objection, we respond that it in no way works against our position, because we are speaking here about the nature of a metallic mixture. Even if such a mixture is calcined <note>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile components or reduce it to a powder.</note> in terms of its state as a whole composition, it is nonetheless not utterly destroyed, as we explained above using the example of a house. Furthermore, if the pot is covered so that the vapors cannot escape, the water itself does not seem to be annihilated. Thus, this clever argument is not directed against our intention; even according to the intention of the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>original: "peripateticorum princeps"; referring to Aristotle, whose followers were called "Peripatetics" because he famously taught while walking about.</note> (in the first volume of his works on nature), a simple escape from the doubt raised would be possible: the matter of the water itself is not annihilated in that opposing action of the fire, but rather remains. For it does not follow that because nothing remains in the pot, the underlying water is annihilated. It is said then that water has a subtle and rare matter, and consequently, it is very easily acted upon.

Likewise, it possesses qualities entirely opposite to those of fire. For the heat of fire is opposed to the coldness of water, and dryness to moisture. Therefore, when the heat of fire encounters the coldness of water, they fight each other. If the heat overcomes the coldness, it thins and refines the water so much that it transforms it into air; thus, the matter of the water will not be corrupted in any way, even though it takes on the form of air. For air is generated from the heat of fire and the moisture of water, and earth from the dryness of fire and the coldness of water. Hence Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist said to have taught the first Arab alchemists.</note> says: "There are four elements, of which two are primary and supremely opposite, namely fire and water. The other two are generated from these, namely air and earth." This same point is very well explained by **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prolific medieval scholar and saint known for his works on natural science.</note> in his book *On Generation* <note>original: "Peri geneseos"; likely referring to Albertus's commentary on Aristotle’s *De Generatione et Corruptione*.</note>. 

<margin>On those things generated in the air.</margin>
Likewise, we see watery vapors ascend upward by the power of heat, being lifted against their own nature. For water, by its own nature as a heavy substance, always seeks its place below. When these vapors reach the place of extreme cold, where the coldness overcomes the heat, they are then turned back into water by the power of that coldness thickening them into clouds; thus they naturally descend, and rain is generated. And also when the North wind (whose nature is cold...

<header>PORTION</header>

(cold and dry) meets the southern wind; then, if the northern coldness overcomes the southern heat, it is condensed and frozen into clouds, and these are sometimes converted into frost, sometimes into hail, sometimes into snow, and sometimes into ice. From this it appears that the matter of things cannot be annihilated, but rather undergoes conversion, as the nature of one element overcomes the nature of another within a mixture.

<margin>Second movement. Key 4 and the second point: Generation.</margin>
The second movement of nature is generation. And since the corruption of one thing is the generation of another (as the Philosopher <note>original: "philosopho"; referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts</note> testifies in the first book of *On Generation*), it is impossible for matter to exist without being under some "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or identity of a thing, while "matter" is the raw substance.</note>, according to the first book of the *Physics*. Therefore, when the agent has destroyed the first mixture or the proportion of elements that caused the thing to exist under its first form, it immediately introduces another form; it is through the introduction of this new form that the movement of generation occurs.

<margin>Question. Solution. Synonyms.</margin>
And what form is that in our current proposal? It is certainly that of "corrupted" mixed Gold, which is called by the wise Chyle <note>original: "Chylus"; usually referring to a milky fluid, here used metaphorically for the initial stage of the alchemical matter</note>, or the Lamb, Jupiter and tin, or Saturn and lead, because of its blackness and impurity. It is from this blackness and impurity that it must be cleansed. Wherefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note> says: "Know this, my son, that unless one knows how to lead forth the pregnancy, to mortify, to generate, and to vivify the species, to introduce light, and to cleanse them until they are purged by fire, colored, and cleansed from their final stains—such as blackness and darkness—he accomplishes nothing. If, however, anyone among mortals shall do this, he will be a man truly worth beholding."

Let it suffice us to have touched briefly upon these matters of selection, cleansing, mixture, corruption, and generation; in the following pages we shall speak more extensively of what remains. Now, however, we believe we must speak of alteration, along with its subordinate and concurrent parts.

<margin>Fifth movement, Key 7 and the third point: Alteration, with change of place.</margin>
<margin>Modes of operations. .D.</margin>
Alteration is a change in quality performed by us through a certain local permutation <note>meaning a change in the physical arrangement or position of the parts</note>. This movement contains within itself the principal actions of this mastery, of which Geber <note>Geber: the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and foundational figure in chemistry and alchemy</note> says: "The principles of this art are the modes of its operations, by which the craftsman applies himself to this mastery, and these are indeed diverse from one another." For the first mode is Sublimation, the second is Descent, the third Distillation, the fourth Calcination, the fifth Solution, the sixth Coagulation, the seventh Fixation, and the last is Ceration <note>Ceration: the process of softening a hard substance until it has a wax-like (cerea) consistency.</note>.

<margin>Why Sublimation was invented.</margin>
The first mode, therefore, is Sublimation. It was invented for this reason: because the ancient sages did not know (since it is utterly impossible), nor do we, nor those who will follow us, any other means by which...

...souls would not be joined, unless they were spirits alone, or because the substance contained the nature of spirit and soul within itself, like a curd <note>original: "coagulum"</note>. This curd, when cast upon Quicksilver <note>original: "Arg. viuum" or "Argentum vivum"; the metal Mercury</note> or Metal without its proper cleansing and thickening, was seen to yield imperfect colors; instead, it would entirely corrupt, blacken, burn, and foul the work.

<margin>.A.</margin>
You will note, therefore, what we say regarding its "cleansing." Thus, the cleansing of the body, as well as of the soul and spirit, must be carried out to remove this blackness and darkness. Such is the opinion of the Sages.

<margin>Question. Solution.</margin>
But what is it that gives birth to this blackness? It is a watery and burning humidity. Hence the *Author of the Three Words* <note>An anonymous alchemical authority often cited in medieval texts</note> says that burning humidity is a watery smoke. Of this it is said: "Watery and burning humidity corrupts the work and dyes it into blackness." Furthermore, that humidity which produces blackness hinders the "white smoke"; if this smoke is lacking, the Gold of Archemy <note>original: "Aurum Archemiæ"; Archemy was a term used by some authors to describe a higher or "true" alchemy</note>—that is, the Gold of two perfect cementations—cannot be made. *Morienus* <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> testifies to this: "Unless the white smoke had been, the Gold of Archemy—that is, the *Voarchadumic work*—would not have been." Likewise, concerning this same point: "As for what you asked regarding the white smoke, it is proper for you to know that the white smoke is the spirit of Quicksilver of those bodies—that is the truth—from which we have already extracted the souls (namely the metals or elements), and to which we have rejoined them." <margin>Synonyms.</margin> Therefore, this soul, having entered into that spirit of Quicksilver, is whitened and cleansed of all blackness, and a brilliance of this kind overflows within it. Whence *Parmenides* says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Know that if the surface is whitened, its interior parts will be whitened. And vice versa." Likewise, *Lucas* says: "The soul, having entered the Quicksilver, is whitened, and nature converts nature."

Therefore, take white sand and Quicksilver: and through the fire of sublimation, draw out from the stone *Aludel* <note>A pear-shaped glass vessel used in sublimation</note> into the stone *Caraha* <note>A receiving vessel</note> a white smoke from them, and preserve it with the greatest diligence so that it does not perish.

<margin>Question. Solution.</margin>
But how is this white smoke generated? Without a doubt, it is through conjunction and refinement. First, the Quicksilver is joined with the white sand; afterwards, through the heat of the fire of refinement, a separation occurs. One part is a burning smoke which dyes things black, and it is separated from this white smoke, which was previously joined to it in the matter of the Quicksilver within a single mass. In this way, it receives one cleansing by fire. For it receives a second cleansing afterward through our artistry—namely, through grinding, corruption, generation, augmentation, fixation, and alteration—along with a change of place, as mentioned above and below. We could quite aptly and elegantly adapt Hippocrates in his *Aphorisms* <note>original: "Aphoriſmis"; refers to the famous medical maxims of the Greek physician Hippocrates</note> to our intention here: "In the case of spontaneous disturbance and vomiting, if those things which ought to be purged are purged, it will be well; but if not, the opposite." We explain this by translating it as follows: In the disturbance of the belly—that is, the putrefactions that occur in the stone **Aludel** <note>A modular alchemical pot used for sublimation</note>—and in the vomitings that occur spontaneously—that is, the sublimations that occur in the stone **Caraha** <note>A gourd-shaped vessel or cucurbit</note> by ascending upward, just like a vomit—if those things which ought to be purged are purged, it is well; if not, it is ill. ...so that it may remain incorruptible after the dissolution of the water itself.

<margin>Triple filtration.</margin>
Indeed, we posit that **filtration** <note>original: "Colamentum"; refers to a process of straining or refining metals and chemicals</note> is performed in three ways: namely, by the **sleeve**, by the **ash-cupel**, and by the **sand bath**.

By the **sleeve** <note>original: "manicam"; likely a conical filter bag or a specific furnace pipe arrangement</note> it is done thus: Let a filtration furnace be made, in which charcoal is first placed and well fitted; afterward, upon the burning coals, let the **ore** <note>original: "vena"; literally "vein," meaning raw metal-bearing ore</note>—crushed and mixed with eight parts more of **black lead** <note>original: "plumbi nigri"; usually refers to galena or lead ore used as a flux</note>—be placed to be filtered to the thickness of one finger. And above this, let more charcoal be placed up to the top of the furnace. Then, with the wind-bellows, let the gold be forced to flow out from the **Lopa** <note>A technical term for a tap-hole or a specific part of the hearth</note>. The other method, by the **ash-cupel**, is done as follows.

<margin>Ash-cupellation.</margin>
Let the substance mentioned above, mixed with black lead, be placed in the hollow of the **ash-cupel** <note>original: "Cinericij"; a porous vessel made of bone-ash used in cupellation to separate precious metals from lead</note>, and let wood be kindled above it. Let it be forced to be filtered as above until the imperfect parts flow out through the **Geta** <note>A channel or drain for dross</note>, and the golden form remains entirely clean. However, the first filtration is greater than the second, because the "sleeve" method brings a sharper heat than the ash-cupel.

<margin>Sand bath</margin>
It is also done by the **sand bath**, as shown below in the section on the Furnace, the figure of which is found under the title of the master furnace module, just as described above in the purification of the **Voarchadumic spirit** <note>original: "spiritus Voarchadumici"; "Voarchadumic" is a term coined by the author, Pantheus, referring to a specific "gold-of-two-justifications" or a highly refined alchemical state</note>. And the reason for our first invention of such a sand bath was the cleansing of the pure essence of **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Arg. vivi" (Argenti vivi); Mercury</note> (as has been said) performed through **elevation** <note>sublimation</note>. For through the first and second filtrations, only the clarification of the substance and the essence of the elements results.

Having seen the modes of filtration and what filtration is, let us proceed to the remaining matters.

Since (according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>) in every corruptible thing three things must be considered: first, that which is useful, which is the **water**; second, the **oil**; and third, the **dross** <note>original: "fex"; the sediment or waste</note>. Yet none of these has a distinct existence in that corrupt mixture, but they are confused and undivided. This mixture is called by some **First Matter of the Arts** <note>original: "Chomerriſſon mea à melachot"; a Latinization of the Hebrew "Homer Rishon mi-Melachot," meaning "The First Matter from the Works"</note>, which is "un-annihilable glass." From this it is said: God—that is, the Artificer—created—that is, mixed—first the **heavens**—that is, the rare—and the **earth**—that is, the dense. Transferring these "heavens" to our purpose, we call them **sublimation**, while the "earth" we call the black mixture. And with the red of that earth He fashioned—that is, multiplied—**Adam**—that is, gold—and with Adam, the **woman** <note>original: "viraginem"; referring to Eve, here symbolizing the "tincture" or the complementary part of the alchemical marriage</note>—that is, the tincture—our mixture, in which there are some corruptions that are purged away by fire. Whence **Alphidius** <note>An Arab alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts</note> says: "Know, my son, that in the book is the perfection of books."

-> # PORTION # <-

<margin>
The fourth
motion,
Key 6,
and the second
point.
Fixation through
diminution.
</margin>
Having dealt with generation, alteration, change of place, sublimation, and the augmentation of form, let us now see its **fixation** <note>The process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable and resistant to fire</note>, which is achieved through **diminution** <note>original: "diminutionem"; here meaning a reduction of volume or a "waning" of specific qualities</note>. This is the fourth motion of nature, called diminution, and it is performed through **decoction** <note>Long-term heating or boiling in a sealed vessel</note>, as was related above in the previously cited secret of Hermes, namely, the **vine of the wise** <note>original: "vitis sapientum"; a metaphor for the starting material or the mercurial water</note>, and so forth. For just as the Moon, after it is full, begins to diminish from day to day until nothing of it appears, so the whiteness (*albedo*) and illumination of this balanced substance begins to diminish through decoction, until all the whiteness is diminished and redness (*rubedo*) appears by way of blackness and yellowness. This redness will appear inwardly if none of that watery moisture remains which sends forth the whiteness. But if any remains, then desiccation (drying) has not been achieved. Therefore, let it be dried until it reaches this state, and then it will be well. To this matter we also apply that saying of **Hippocrates** in the *Aphorisms*: "If **inanition** <note>original: "inanitio"; a medical term for emptying or voiding the body</note>, such as ought to be made, is made, it is beneficial and will be well. But if not, the opposite." <gloss>Inanition, that is, desiccation.</gloss> Likewise **Hermes** says: "Expose its moisture to the fire, and make the fire dwell in the moisture; which fire, by its heat, increases the color of such manifest moisture and the combustion of the hidden dryness, until it is made perfect." Likewise **Alphidius** says: "Look, my son, for I am about to write a book for you, whose words if you understand, you will find this art—if you are among those who, by the grace of God, are to find it. But if you do not understand these words, do not approach the work unless you have begun to experiment and to cook the waters, which are thickened by **putrefaction** <note>The stage of breaking down or "rotting" the matter to its primal state</note> through the manifest moisture of that putrefaction and the power of the hidden dryness of the body itself, the kind of which is a certain **salt** from the genus 
<margin>Salty things.</margin>
of salts. For it is extracted from **salty things** <note>original: "Salsosis"</note>, which at any time of the year are generated in the **shores of the seas** <note>original: "gingiuis marium"; literally "the gums of the seas," referring to the salt-crusted edges of the tide</note>."

<margin>Thickening.</margin>
You will note, therefore, that through putrefaction comes **thickening** <note>original: "inspissatio"</note> from the conversion of the cold and moist into heat and dryness, which appears above. "Take, therefore, in the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity," and so forth. For gold mixed with **quicksilver** <note>original: "Arg. viuo" (Argentum vivo)</note>, when it begins to be altered, is made black as coal. Whence Hermes says in his allegory: "Our **Marthek** <note>A term often referring to litharge or the "metallic body" of the stone</note>, when sought, lacks an equal, and is a golden yellow both without and within. But when its mixture is altered, it becomes black and dark as coal. Yet when the spirit is taken from it, the color is red; and when the spirit and soul are returned to it, it lives and rejoices, and you see it laughing and cheerful, and lacking death." Blessed, therefore, be he who knows this disposition, who kills and brings to life, and is almighty. Likewise Hermes in the same place: "I am the white of the black, and the black of the white."

<summary>This page describes the stage of 'Fixation through Diminution,' where the alchemical matter is dried and heated until it transitions from white to red. It emphasizes the necessity of 'putrefaction' and 'thickening,' comparing the chemical changes to the waning of the moon and the cycle of death and resurrection.</summary>

white. And so it appears that the alteration is from whiteness (*albedo*) into blackness (*nigredo*), and from blackness into whiteness. And furthermore, this desiccation <note>The process of drying out the substance to remove "superfluous" moisture</note>, or disposition, continually brings about a conversion into the nature of heat—that is, into redness (*rubedo*)—which nevertheless comes from a small degree of whitening. **Rosinus** <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note> says the same thing when he asserts that the "Art of Marthek" <note>Marthek or Litharge; often refers to lead oxide or a specific metallic state in the work</note> is not made except from **Risoo** <note>Possibly a corruption of a Greek or Arabic term for a starting material</note>, tin, and so forth. From which it should be understood that one thing is the disposer of the Black, the White, the Yellow, and the Red. And this is what **Alphidius** <note>An influential, though semi-legendary, Arab alchemist</note> says: "Know, my son, that in the depths of this sea, pearls of diverse colors are born, in which also the hyacinth <note>A reddish-orange gemstone, often used to describe the color of the Stone</note> of diverse color ascends; and also Marthek itself colors bodies by its own color." For when it is hot, it will be red; but when it is cold, it will be white; similarly, it will possess the heat and brightness of the Sun and the Moon. And Redness is heat, and Whiteness is coldness; 

<margin>Signs of the qualities.</margin>understand, therefore, and observe. Likewise, you shall note that Redness is the sign of heat, and Whiteness of coldness. And this is the third point of the art, and in the **House of Mars** <note>A reference to the astrological timing or the specific stage of "warring" elements characterized by heat and iron</note>, which is the stage of alteration. As **Hermes** asserts: in the third month, Mars operates, acting upon the matter, who by his heat and dryness divides the Mass itself and disposes the members.

<margin>Note.</margin>You shall note the "members" [the parts]. For just as in the womb nature disposes the members as integral parts of the fetus itself, so also is this **red body** disposed as an integral part of the whole composition of the medicine. For in every composition made after this body is finished, it always falls in as an integral part of the composition, as will be declared below.

<margin>Note. Synonyms.</margin>Likewise, you shall note that this body has many names. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the transition of the alchemical substance from the white stage to the red stage. It expands on the nomenclature of the "Red Body" and begins a philosophical explanation of the physical dimensions (length, width, and depth) as they apply to the "Medicine."</meta>

-># P O R T I O N<-

<margin>Red color.</margin>
Those who have named it Aduma <note>A term derived from the Hebrew for "red" or "earth," often linked to Adam</note>, red gum, red oil, redness, ruby, Sericon <note>A term for red lead or a specific red alchemical tincture</note>, red substance, red sulfur, yolk <note>original: "vitellum"</note>, or red vitriol, have said this because of its **red color**. <margin>Inability to melt.</margin> Those, however, who named it iron or oil of Mars <note>Mars is the traditional alchemical association for the metal iron</note>, said this because of its **inability to melt**—that is, its hardness. For when this body is deprived of superfluous humidity through decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance to concentrate it</note>—which previously caused it to flow—and it becomes necessary for a dry body not to flow, they therefore called it "iron," because iron is said to be the most fixed <note>stable and resistant to change by fire</note> among the other metals. In this same way, this body, through the removal of the superfluous humidity which first made it fluid, must now remain fixed. For all bodies that are not fixed are made fixed through such a removal of humidity, which many wise men have called **calcination**. <margin>What calcination is.</margin> Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry/alchemy</note> says: "Calcination is the purification of a thing by fire, or its reduction to powder through the removal of the humidity that holds the parts together and makes them flow." <margin>Why it was discovered.</margin> And the reason for the discovery of the calcination of the "lights" <note>referring to the Sun (gold) and the Moon (silver)</note> and the quicksilvers together is so that the "earth"—the remaining earth converted in the lights—may be more greatly and better densified. Thus, through the removal of humidity, that which was volatile becomes **fixed**, and that which was soft becomes **hard**. Likewise, a change occurs from one nature into another: from water into fire, according to the natural philosophers, as is read in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or Assembly of the Philosophers, an ancient alchemical text</note>. Likewise, there is a change of temperaments <note>original: "complexionum"</note>, such as from a cold and moist temperament into a hot and dry one, or from the phlegmatic into the choleric, according to the physicians. Likewise, that which was spiritual becomes corporeal, according to the author of the *Perfect Mastery*. Likewise, that which was manifest becomes hidden, according to Rhodianus in the *Book of Three Words*.

It must also be known that in every body there are three dimensions—namely, length, width, and depth—as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies in the first book of *On the Heavens*.

Length and width are those parts of the body which are clearly visible and are the first to meet our sight. <margin>Triple dimension.</margin> For example, the "body of our art" in its first disposition is **white**, and it appears so at first glance because we call it cold and moist, as it is. Rhodianus asserts this, saying our body is aquatic, because it is cold and moist, and water is cold and moist. Moreover, that which is moist flows. Both of these are true, and such a disposition is called the "length and width" of the body.

**Height** (or depth) is the disposition of that medicine through which one reaches the "profound" <note>the inner core or hidden essence</note>, which is our medicine; it is the life of the height and depth, acting as a middle ground between two extremes, or contra-

<meta>catchword: tra-</meta>

<summary>This page explains the nomenclature of the red stage of the alchemical Great Work, attributing its various names to its color and its "fixed" (non-melting) state achieved through calcination. It also introduces a philosophical framework using Aristotelian dimensions to distinguish between the outward appearance (length and width) and the inner essence (depth) of the alchemical substance.</summary>

-># S E C O N D [PART]<-

...contraries, through which the extreme is reached, because it is impossible to pass from one extreme to another without a middle state—as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, the foundational authority for medieval science</note> testifies in the sixth book of *Physics*. For it has often been said that the first matter of the art <note>the raw material used in alchemy</note> is of a moist and cold complexion. If we wish to make it pass into the "dispositive medicine" <note>the stage where the substance is prepared for transformation</note>, it is necessary that one quality in it be destroyed. It is destroyed through **putrefaction** <note>the process of decomposition or "blackness" intended to break down the material</note>. For the cold and the moist are thickened through putrefaction, and their humidity is turned into dryness; thus the transition is made to the dispositive medicine, which is heat and dryness, and this becomes **Height** <note>original: "Altitudo," referring to one of the philosophical dimensions of the alchemical body</note>. Yet Nature receives coldness from the cold and moist, and dryness from the hot and dry, and thus a body is formed. Later, through excessive heat, if any humidity remains in the body, the transition to the opposite is made by destroying the coldness and introducing heat; this disposition is called the **depth** <note>original: "profundum"</note> or the **hidden** part of the body.

<margin>Qualities of Red Sulfur.</margin>
And this is clear in the *Book of the Perfect Mastery* in that section: iron—that is, **Red Sulfur**—in its "height" is cold, moist, hot, dry, choleric, red, sharp, fragrant, masculine, and so on.

Thus far, it has been seen how the matter—that is, the **Sperm of the metals**, or well-disposed passive Mercury <note>original: "Arg. vivi passivi"</note>—is converted from one nature into another: namely, from coldness and humidity into the heat and dryness of the form of **active Gold**, the perfect tincture. And because at this point the majority of the wise men begin to speak—such as Alpidius regarding the mineral, who mentions "red sulfur," or Lucas, who calls it "masculine" when he says: "Take **Marthek** <note>likely litharge or a lead-based substance used in the process</note> and whiten it," etc. We could bring forward many other wise men to the same opinion, whom we omit at present for the sake of brevity. However, the reason why almost everyone has taken their beginning from this red form is this: because this red form is the principle of the entire Tincture <note>the substance capable of transforming other metals</note>, and no true Tincture is made without it. Whence Rosinus <note>Zosimos of Panopolis, a major Greco-Egyptian alchemist</note> says:
> Know that there was no one in this art who spoke a word stripped of every veil, except **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>.
For he says:
> Know that there is never a tincture except from the red stone: that is, yellow Gold with reddened Mercury.
Likewise, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note> asserts regarding the Essence (that is, the substance) of the Sun <note>Gold</note> that the Sun was created from the most subtle substance of Mercury and from a moderate substance of clean metallic Sulfur—of pure redness, fixed, clear, and purified by its own nature—which tints that substance. Likewise, Geber says of the Sun:
<margin>The form of metals.</margin>
> **Gold** is the most precious form of metals and the tincture of redness: for it tints, transforms, and illuminates every body, since it is light, the true tincture, and the perfection of the entire divine work, which God grants to His chosen ones; to whom be praise, honor, and glory forever.

It cites legendary authorities like Hermes, Geber, and Rosinus to establish that true transformation only occurs through "Red Sulfur" and "Reddened Mercury."</summary>

### CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>Columns;</margin> Among other things required for the Voarchadumic art, a furnace furnished with its own equipment is proposed, without which the craftsman can perform nothing at all. We have stated that this is to be constructed from clay stones, or cut Tufa <note>a porous volcanic rock</note>, and hair-tempered clay <note>original: "luto tomenti"; clay mixed with wool or hair to act as a binder and prevent cracking under high heat</note>: according to the model placed here below. Therefore, let four columns resting on their bases be erected separately from one another at the four corners; three and a half feet in height, 
<margin>Three layers.</margin> three and a half feet in length, and two feet in width. These columns contain three layers or floors among themselves, separated by two intervals. The middle floor specifically is suspended in arches from the lowest one by 
<margin>Middle floor. House of fire.</margin> half-feet, and separated from the top by a double half-measure <note>one foot</note>. This middle floor, I say (where the fire lies), shall be paved and enclosed on this side and that by earthenware supports <note>original: "spondilibus"; likely cylindrical spacers or architectural supports</note> half a foot in thickness. In the middle of this, a hearth, or "house of fire," of quadrangular shape shall be placed, whose sides across measure two and a half feet, while the other two measure a space of one and a half feet, 
<margin>Earthven grate. ...billows through the flues into the ovens <note>original: "furnos"; these are the internal heating chambers</note>) of three inches <note>original: "dimidiati semipedis"; half of a half-foot. A Roman foot is approximately 11.6 inches, making this about 2.9 inches</note>, while the outer

<margin>Register.</margin>

Underneath the grate, however, where the burning ashes fall (to avoid the danger of fire), let there be 
<margin>Dimension of the ash-pit.</margin>

<margin>Uppermost floor.</margin>

<margin>Pipe.</margin>

In many ways in the preceding portions it was taught what the Voarchadumic art was, what it treated, and what it contained within itself; as well as the nature of the fire, air, and water <note>original: "metallicas"; referring to the "metallic" versions of these elements used in the laboratory</note>...

# THIRD [PART]

...metallic: together turned red <note>original: "rubificata"; the 'Red Work' or Rubedo is the final stage of alchemy</note>, and potential earth, and others diffusely narrated above. Now it remains to complete what is left of the art and commit it to writing. Therefore, most diligent reader, through the "first substance" <note>original: "Chomer rison", Hebrew-derived 'Chomer rishon'</note> from the "works" <note>original: "melachot", Hebrew for crafts or tasks</note>, you will note the first matter of the art of the nature of glass.

<margin>Note.</margin>
By *Muchabelim* [the receivers], and *Mecubalim* [the things received]. <note>These terms likely refer to the relationship between the alchemical vessel and the substances placed within it, using Kabbalistic terminology.</note>
By *Cheffeph chai* <note>original: "Cheffeph chai", Hebrew for 'Living Silver'</note>, [he means] Quicksilver, [obtained] from Quicksilver purified seven times with white sand through fire.
By *Gophrit* <note>original: "Gophrit", Hebrew for Sulfur</note>, [he means] red sulfur, which is *Marthek* <note>litharge or lead oxide</note> multiplied seven times.
*Ithochodut horucot*, *Iachid baruchot* <note>original: "Ithochodut horucot", likely Hebrew 'Ichud haruchot', the union of spirits</note>, the Union of spirits; that is, fire and air, called the "white of hen’s eggs."
And by *Douor*, *Dauar echad* <note>original: "Dauar echad", Hebrew for 'one thing'</note>, [he means] one single thing, namely simple raw clay, the oil of glass, Gold, Silver, and Quicksilver—disposing, converting, constraining, binding, and also providing the proportion.

For we judge it superfluous, even absurd, to discuss specifically which, how many, and of what kind the metallic and natural elements are that enter into the Kabbalistic mastery of metals in Voarchadumia <note>The author's specific alchemical system for purifying gold</note> in any other way. What the "form" is, what the "first matter" of the art is, what the "matter of metals" is—likewise what the "disposing medium" is—again, what the "oil of glass" is, what Gold is, what Silver is—then what the "Quicksilver from the heart of Saturn" (that is, from the bowels of the earth) is, and finally what "simple raw clay" is—it was decreed to pass over these in silence. For we consider that these things, as primary elements without which greater things cannot be known, should be noted by anyone even moderately learned.
<margin>Note.</margin>

Let this secret mystery be completed by means of horse manure <note>original: "fimi equini"; in alchemy, the heat of fermenting dung was used for gentle, long-term digestion of a substance</note>, that is, by fire, by the means (as we have already said) under the Divine Will <note>original: "Nutu", meaning a nod or command, often used for God’s will; also used as an acrostic for the timing table below</note>, and in a determined space of time, with that three-fold Degree of heat as we have elucidated above; and there will be further discourse in what follows.

# PORTION

For all the aforementioned movements must be finished at that triple-cross degree <note>original: "tricruci illo Gradu"; likely referring to a specific temperature or stage in the furnace marked by a triple cross symbol</note>.
The total number of days, including the hours, is 36 days.
The siftings <note>original: "cribrationes"; the process of refining or cycling the material</note>—that is, the repetitions—are completed by the number seven. Therefore, the total days for all these gathered together are 52.

->*The quantity of charcoal for the completion of Voarchadumia.*<-

### CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>Quantity of charcoal.</margin> An error which is not met immediately upon its emergence later grows to such an extent that it cannot easily be corrected. Lest anything required for perfection be lacking in a work of this kind through our negligence, we also add the quantity of charcoal. For without this, the craftsman will never succeed in his desire.
The total of this is 84 *corbe* <note>original: "Corbarum"; a *corba* was a traditional Venetian basket used as a dry measure for charcoal</note> by the measure we use in Venice: namely, one for every three days, with the *Aduma* <note>a term in this system for the "Red" substance or the work itself</note> weighing 473 pounds, 0 ounces, which is 15 carats and 3 grains. These are 23 *poste*, 1 *rubus*, 6 *marche*, and so on. One part projected upon ten parts of black lead <note>original: "plumbi nigri"; likely galena or lead ore</note>.

->*The alternative repetitions of the Voarchadumic medicine.*<-

### CHAPTER FOUR.

In the repetitions of the Voarchadumic medicine <note>the "medicine" or "elixir" is the substance used to transform base metals</note>, one [part] falls upon 100 parts, then upon 500 parts, and so on for the rest. Therefore, let the one and triune ineffable Creator <note>original: "Opifex"; the divine Craftsman or Architect of the universe</note> be praised through all ages, who by His immense goodness has bestowed so much grace and gift upon the Kabbalistic aspects of metals—that is, to those who perceive with their sight.

->*Diagram of the proportion of silver.*<-

The triple Lopa <note>original: "Lopa sapientum triplex"</note> of the wise.

The <term>Metamorphosis</term><note>Transformation</note> of animated <term>Quicksilver</term><note>original: "Arg. viui" (Argentum vivum), referring to mercury</note> has indeed been published by us openly, abundantly, and clearly in the present volume, most skilled reader (as is clear to your wisdom), by its very inspection. ...know that he can achieve this. But seeking the vegetable <note>The "vegetable" work in alchemy refers to processes using organic matter or referring to the "growth" and "life" of the metals.</note> path similarly, let him not be ignorant that **unless a grain falling into the earth dies, it will remain alone and unfruitful. But having died, it becomes fertile.** <note>A reference to John 12:24, used here to explain the alchemical necessity of "mortification" or the breakdown of matter before it can be transformed.</note> Finally, if he seeks the mineral path, let him recognize that he will by no means obtain his wish without the proper process and intelligence. 448. 400. 344. & 512. Therefore, let everyone prick up their ears to hear. We have already revealed openly above, and shall below, whatever the wise have hitherto written shrouded in their enigmas and coverings. 

Therefore, whoever obtains knowledge of so great and so wonderful a mystery, denoted under that name of the "element," we warn and adjure him by the holy name of God to keep it cautiously and treat it in such a way that we do not freely bestow the **bread of the children** <note>A biblical metaphor (Matthew 15:26) suggesting that sacred knowledge should not be given to the "dogs" or the unworthy.</note> upon alchemists or those unworthy of so great a gift.

### Epilogue of the aforementioned. Chapter eight.

Now, therefore, we have set forth for your contemplation, most kind reader, the matters pertaining to the **Goldsmith's art**, <term>Cudimia</term>, <note>The art of minting or coining.</note> the **minting office**, and the **cabala of metals**, which are secrets belonging to the perfection of metals. This includes the first matter of the art, as well as the theory, practice, and required proportions for the silver ore and the two red golds. Finally, we have presented the mystery of the <term>Voarchadumic</term> art itself—directed entirely against **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchemiam"</note> and distinguished not a little from **Archemia** <note>The author uses this term for "false" or "common" alchemy.</note> and **Sophia** <note>Wisdom.</note>. 

Following this, in our "Mirror," <note>Referring to the author's other work, the *Speculum*.</note> with the eternal and almighty Lord breathing life into our efforts (if we find these things have not displeased you), we shall certainly reveal higher things out of our singular benevolence toward seekers of virtue and those eager for the truth, and out of gratitude and sincerity of spirit.

### *The author’s excuse for the manifold use of terms in the <term>Voarchadumic</term> <note>Pantheus's unique name for his alchemical art, which he translates elsewhere as "Gold of two rubies," signifying a higher, more spiritual form of metallurgy.</note> art. Chapter nine, and the Last.*

We judge it to be truly fair, most skillful reader, since we have thus far explained the Voarchadumic art with words consistent with it, that learned Grammarians grant us pardon—as they are accustomed to doing for professors of other disciplines—if anything written in this volume of ours is said with obsolete words (as they say), or in a way that goes beyond or against the decrees of our ancestors. For they should not think this was done rashly, or out of negligence or ignorance. Rather, it has happened by right, because the profession itself demands it. Or perhaps some word was used for the sake of removing ambiguity <note>original: "æquivocationis"</note> from the term itself, or more often to indicate a truer property of a thing. This was done so that something consistent with the art might be more readily explained—even if it falls outside common usage—provided it still presents the true concepts as it should. Since this right is denied to none of the authors (not only in our judgment, but by the common consent of all) in whatever branch of writing they may be: that they are allowed to use certain terms as if they were their own, and to keep their own style, lest they seem to exceed or depart from the proper limits of that art (which would be altogether profane). Indeed, this truth is most clearly supported by the doctrine of the leader of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" refers to Aristotle and his followers. Pantheus is citing Aristotle’s *Categories* or *Metaphysics* to justify the invention of new technical language.</note> who teaches (in the category of relation) that it is sometimes necessary to invent names for explaining the properties of things. Therefore, let no one be angry that we also have kept this manner of writing, as the Voarchadumic art itself demanded it.

->*Conclusion of the Edition.*<-

Voarchadumia, edited by Giovanni Agostino Pantheo, a Venetian priest, concludes with happy auspices. Published during the reign of the most Just Andrea Gritti. <note>Andrea Gritti was the Doge of Venice from 1523 to 1538.</note>
